additional_notes: Used to express relief that something good happened or a bad outcome was avoided. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence as an aside (“Dieu merci, …”), but it can also come at the end (“…, Dieu merci.”). It’s common in everyday speech; it mentions God but is often used non-religiously.
target_language_example: Dieu merci, personne n’a été blessé.
native_language_example: Thank God, nobody was hurt.

meaning: 'God knows' (said to stress that something is unknown or uncertain).
additional_notes: Used either literally (“God knows…”) or as a set expression meaning “who knows / goodness knows,” often to emphasize uncertainty, doubt, or that there are many unknown details. Common patterns: “Dieu sait + question word” (Dieu sait où/qui/ce que…), “Dieu sait si…” (“who knows whether…”), and “Dieu sait.” alone (“God knows.”).
target_language_example: Dieu sait quand il va rentrer.
native_language_example: God knows when he’ll be back.

meaning: “Thank God!” / “Praise God!” (said in relief or gratitude).
additional_notes: A set, somewhat old-fashioned and religious-sounding expression used when something good happens or after a scare (someone is safe, healthy, alive, etc.). Often used like an exclamation: “Dieu soit loué !” You may also see “Que Dieu soit loué.”
target_language_example: Dieu soit loué, on est enfin arrivés sains et saufs.
native_language_example: Thank God, we finally arrived safe and sound.

additional_notes: A very formal title used when addressing a prince, princess, or other high-ranking royal. It’s typically used as a direct form of address, often set off by commas (e.g., « Merci, Votre Altesse. »).
target_language_example: Par ici, Votre Altesse, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: This way, Your Highness, please.

meaning: "Your Majesty." (a very formal way to address a king or queen)
additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to a monarch, often set off by commas (e.g., « Je suis venu(e) vous voir, Votre Majesté. »). « Votre » is the formal "your". Usually capitalized in writing as a title of address.
target_language_example: Pardonnez-moi, Votre Majesté, je ne savais pas.
native_language_example: Forgive me, Your Majesty, I didn’t know.

meaning: "has she been" / "was she" (in a question; often passive).
additional_notes: This is the verb phrase in an inverted question with “elle” (she/it): a (avoir, present) + -t- (for pronunciation) + elle + été (been). Very common in the passive voice: a-t-elle été + past participle = “was/has it been + done?” e.g., « a-t-elle été tuée ? » = “was she killed?”; « a-t-elle été envoyée ? » = “was it sent?”
target_language_example: La facture a-t-elle été payée ?
native_language_example: Has the bill been paid?

additional_notes: Used in questions with subject–verb inversion: **a** (avoir, present) + **dit** (past participle of *dire*) + **il** (“he”). The **-t-** is inserted for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel (a) and the pronoun starts with a vowel (il): *a-t-il…?* Common in formal/neutral speech and writing. In everyday spoken French, you may also hear *Il a dit… ?* or *Est-ce qu’il a dit… ?*
target_language_example: Qu’a-t-il dit exactement ?
native_language_example: What exactly did he say?

meaning: "did he do?" / "has he done?" (formal question form).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of *faire* (a fait) used with subject–verb inversion in questions: *a-t-il…?* = “did he…?” / “has he…?”. The **-t-** is added only for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel (*a*) and the subject pronoun starts with a vowel (*il*). Common special use: *Quel temps a-t-il fait ?* means “What was the weather like?” (with *faire* used for weather).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'il a-t-il fait exactement ?
native_language_example: What exactly did he do?

meaning: “has it been / was he (it) … ?” (question form, past tense).
additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of the passé composé: "a" (has) + "-t-" (a linking sound) + "il" (he/it) + "été" (been). It’s very common in passive questions with "été" + past participle: "Quand a-t-il été décidé ?" = “When was it decided?” (literally “When has it been decided?”). "Il" can refer to “he” (a person like Tom) or “it” (something like a book or a decision).
target_language_example: Où cela a-t-il été trouvé ?
native_language_example: Where was it found?

meaning: "has one / did someone" in a question (with on).
additional_notes: Used in formal/inverted questions: avoir (a) + -t- + on. The -t- is added only for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel (a) and the next word starts with a vowel sound (on). Often corresponds to English passive/impersonal phrasing like “Has it been…?”, “Did they…?”, or “Have people…?” depending on context.
target_language_example: A-t-on déjà appelé un médecin ?
native_language_example: Has a doctor been called already?

additional_notes: This is the *passé composé*: **a** (present of *avoir*) + **accepté** (past participle). It changes with the subject: *j’ai accepté, tu as accepté, il/elle a accepté, nous avons accepté, vous avez accepté, ils/elles ont accepté*. Often used for accepting an offer, proposal, gift, invitation, or job.
target_language_example: Elle a accepté l'invitation.
native_language_example: She accepted the invitation.

additional_notes: Passé composé of acheter (“to buy”) with avoir. Used with il/elle/on or a singular noun as the subject. In English, it often translates simply as “bought.”
target_language_example: Paul a acheté du pain ce matin.
native_language_example: Paul bought some bread this morning.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of « acheter » with « avoir »: « il/elle a acheté … » = “he/she bought/has bought …”. « un » changes to « une » before a feminine noun (e.g., « elle a acheté une robe »). With « avoir », « acheté » usually doesn’t change here because the direct object comes after it.
target_language_example: Il a acheté un cadeau pour son frère.
native_language_example: He bought a gift for his brother.

additional_notes: "a acheté" is the passé composé of "acheter" (to buy) with "avoir": it means "bought/has bought" (3rd person singular: he/she/it bought). "un cadeau" means "a gift/present". Often used with an indirect object pronoun for the recipient: "Elle lui a acheté un cadeau" (She bought him/her a gift) or "Paul leur a acheté un cadeau" (He bought them a gift). You can also add "pour + person" to specify who it’s for: "… un cadeau pour Rima". "de Noël" specifies the occasion: a Christmas present.
target_language_example: Elle lui a acheté un cadeau de Noël.
native_language_example: She bought him/her a Christmas present.

additional_notes: "a acheté" is the passé composé of acheter (to buy) for il/elle/on: it means "bought/has bought." Add details after it: what kind of car (une voiture neuve/rouge) or for whom with "à" (a bought a car for someone): "Marco a acheté une voiture à son fils."
target_language_example: Elle a acheté une voiture d’occasion.
native_language_example: She bought a used car.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « aider » (to help): « il/elle/on a aidé » = “he/she/one helped / has helped.” Often followed by « à » + infinitive to say what someone helped with: « a aidé à marcher » (helped [someone] to walk), « a aidé à déménager » (helped [someone] move).
target_language_example: Elle a aidé sa sœur à faire ses devoirs.
native_language_example: She helped her sister do her homework.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "appeler" with "avoir": "il/elle/on a appelé" = "he/she/one called" or "has called". Used for making a phone call or calling someone (e.g., calling a friend, calling for someone). Doesn’t mean "appealed" in the English sense.
target_language_example: Il a appelé son ami ce matin.
native_language_example: He called his friend this morning.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone learned how to do something: « Il/Elle a appris à + infinitive ». This is the passé composé of « apprendre à » (to learn to). It can also mean 'was taught to' depending on context: « Qui vous a appris à danser ? » (= Who taught you to dance?). Related pattern: « apprendre quelque chose à quelqu’un » (to teach someone something): « Il a appris le français à son ami » (= He taught his friend French).
target_language_example: Tom a appris à conduire quand il avait treize ans.
native_language_example: Tom learned to drive when he was thirteen.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of **arrêter de fumer** (“to stop/quit smoking”). Use **a arrêté** with singular subjects (il/elle/on; a name). With plural subjects, it becomes **ont arrêté de fumer** (“stopped smoking”).
target_language_example: Elle a arrêté de fumer l’année dernière.
native_language_example: She quit smoking last year.

additional_notes: Formed with the auxiliary avoir (a) + past participle attrapé. Used for things you can literally or figuratively "catch": a fish (attraper un poisson) or cold/chill (attraper froid / attraper un rhume). Subject changes the auxiliary (il/elle/on a attrapé; j'ai attrapé; nous avons attrapé, etc.).
target_language_example: Elle a attrapé froid en rentrant de l'école.
native_language_example: She caught a chill on the way home from school.

additional_notes: This is the *passé composé* of **boire**: **avoir (a)** + past participle **bu**. It’s used for a completed action in the past. It’s commonly followed by **de/du/de la/des** (“some/any”) or a quantity: *a bu du lait*, *a bu une bière*.
target_language_example: Elle a bu de l’eau après le sport.
native_language_example: She drank some water after ورزش / working out.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « changer » with « avoir » (3rd-person singular: he/she/it changed). Often used with « tout a changé » = “everything changed.” Common pattern: « changer de + noun » = “to change (jobs/direction/etc.)”, e.g., « Il a changé de poste » (He changed jobs/positions).
target_language_example: Après son déménagement, tout a changé.
native_language_example: After his move, everything changed.

additional_notes: This is the passé composé form (3rd person singular) used in the pattern **changer de + noun** (“to change/switch to a different …”). In French, the noun that follows **de** often appears **without an article**: *changer de poste* (change jobs/position), *changer de direction* (change direction), *changer de vitesse* (change gear). You can change the tense/person as needed: *je change de…*, *il va changer de…*, *on a changé de…*.
target_language_example: Il a changé de poste.
native_language_example: He changed jobs/positions.

additional_notes: Past tense of "commencer" with "avoir" (il/elle/on a commencé à...). It is followed by an infinitive verb to say someone started doing something: "a commencé à + infinitive". For other subjects, change "a" (e.g., "j'ai commencé à", "ils ont commencé à").
target_language_example: Il a commencé à pleuvoir.
native_language_example: It started to rain.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "continuer à". Use it with an infinitive verb to say someone kept doing an action: "Il/elle a continué à + infinitive". In speech, "à" often sounds like a short "a".
target_language_example: Elle a continué à travailler malgré la fatigue.
native_language_example: She kept working despite the tiredness.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the verb « couler ». Most commonly used for a boat/ship that sinks: « Le bateau a coulé » = “The boat sank.” It can also be used for liquids (blood, water) that flowed: « Le sang a coulé » = “Blood was shed/flowed.” In a more poetic sense it can describe the sun setting: « Le soleil a coulé derrière… » = “The sun set behind…”.
target_language_example: Pendant la nuit, le petit bateau a coulé près du port.
native_language_example: During the night, the small boat sank near the harbor.

additional_notes: Passé composé of **courir** with **avoir**: **il/elle/on a couru**. It can mean a completed past action (“ran”) or, depending on context, “has run.” With **avoir**, the past participle **couru** usually doesn’t change spelling (no extra -e/-s). Often used with **après** (“after”) to mean “to run after/chase.”
target_language_example: Elle a couru jusqu'à la gare.
native_language_example: She ran to the train station.

additional_notes: Passé composé (3rd person singular) of **demander à** = “to ask (someone)”. It’s followed by the person being asked: **il/elle a demandé à Marie...**. You can then add either (1) an indirect question: **a demandé à Marie où/pourquoi/comment...**, or (2) a request with **de + infinitive**: **a demandé à Marie de venir / de faire...**. Note: French **demander** can look like English “demand,” but **demander à quelqu’un de + infinitif** usually means a polite “ask someone to…,” not a forceful demand.
target_language_example: Tom a demandé à Marie où elle était.
native_language_example: Tom asked Marie where she was.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « disparaître » (auxiliary « avoir » + past participle « disparu »). Used for someone/something that is no longer there; for a person it can mean they went missing or vanished (and in some contexts can imply they died, especially in news-style language).
target_language_example: Mon passeport a disparu hier soir.
native_language_example: My passport disappeared last night.

additional_notes: Passé composé of dire with il/elle/on or a singular noun as the subject. It often translates as simple past in English: Tom a dit = Tom said. With an indirect object, it can also mean "told": Tom a dit à Marie la vérité = Tom told Marie the truth.
target_language_example: Paul a dit qu'il viendrait demain.
native_language_example: Paul said that he would come tomorrow.

additional_notes: “a dit” is the passé composé of *dire* (“to say/tell”), used with *avoir*. The full phrase is usually *[person] a dit la vérité (à [someone])* = “[someone] told the truth (to [someone]).” It agrees with the subject only through context (no extra ending on *dit*).
target_language_example: Il a dit la vérité à ses parents.
native_language_example: He told the truth to his parents.

additional_notes: Third-person singular passé composé of dire + que. It is used to report what a person or thing said: after a noun, or after il/elle/on. In natural French, que often shortens to qu' before a vowel.
target_language_example: Paul a dit que tout allait bien.
native_language_example: Paul said that everything was fine.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of « dire »: « (il/elle/on) a dit… ». Used when someone said something (at some point in the past) or has said something (recently). You can add details after it, e.g. « a dit quelque chose en français » (“said something in French”).
target_language_example: J'ai entendu un bruit, mais personne n'a dit quelque chose.
native_language_example: I heard a noise, but nobody said anything.

meaning: "said that" / "said this" (past tense; literally “has said that/this”).
additional_notes: Passé composé of **dire**: **a dit** = “(he/she) said / has said.” **ça** = “that/this” (very common in speech). Used when the subject is **il/elle/on** (3rd person singular). With other subjects it changes: **j’ai dit ça**, **tu as dit ça**, **ils ont dit ça**, etc.
target_language_example: Quand est-ce qu’il a dit ça ?
native_language_example: When did he say that?

additional_notes: Passé composé of donner. It is used for both concrete and abstract meanings: giving something, giving an order, giving permission, or giving agreement. In English, it is often translated as simple past ('gave') rather than present perfect ('has given').
target_language_example: Elle m'a donné un livre hier.
native_language_example: She gave me a book yesterday.

meaning: 'gave to' / 'has given to' (passé composé of « donner à »).
additional_notes: Used to say someone gave something to someone. Structure: subject + « a donné » + (direct object) + « à » + person (recipient), e.g., « Il a donné un cadeau à Marie. » The person after « à » is the indirect object (recipient). In spoken French you may hear « On a donné à Steve » when what was given is understood from context. With pronouns, « à + person » often becomes « lui/leur »: « Il lui a donné un cadeau. »
target_language_example: Le professeur a donné à John une récompense.
native_language_example: The teacher gave John a reward.

meaning: “lasted” / “has lasted” (talking about how long something continued).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of durer. Used for completed events or periods of time, often with a duration: deux heures (two hours), quatre jours (four days), toute la nuit (all night). Common in questions like « Combien de temps a duré… ? » (“How long did … last?”).
target_language_example: Le trajet a duré trente minutes.
native_language_example: The trip lasted thirty minutes.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone made a decision to do something: « il/elle/on + a décidé de + infinitive ». This is the passé composé of « décider » and is common for talking about a decision that has been made (often recently). Note: « a décidé de » is 3rd-person singular (he/she/one has decided to).
target_language_example: Tom a décidé de vendre sa maison.
native_language_example: Tom decided to sell his house.

additional_notes: Common in the passé composé: a is the 3rd-person singular form of avoir used with a past participle (for il, elle, on, or a singular noun), and déjà means "already." For other subjects, the auxiliary changes: j'ai déjà, tu as déjà, ils ont déjà, etc.
target_language_example: Elle a déjà vu ce film.
native_language_example: She has already seen this movie.

additional_notes: Passé composé of commencer: avoir (a) + past participle (commencé). Déjà usually goes between the helper verb and the past participle: « a déjà commencé ». Often used with a subject like « ça » (= it/that): « Ça a déjà commencé. »
target_language_example: Le film a déjà commencé, dépêche-toi !
native_language_example: The movie has already started—hurry up!

meaning: has already been (has already happened / has already been done).
additional_notes: Uses the past perfect tense with passive voice: "a été" = "has been" (passé composé of être), and "déjà" = "already". Common in passive sentences with a past participle after it: "a déjà été fait/dépassé/amené" = "has already been done/exceeded/brought". Without a following past participle, it can mean "has already been" in the sense of having been something before: "Il a déjà été traducteur" = "He has been a translator before."
target_language_example: Le message a déjà été envoyé.
native_language_example: The message has already been sent.

additional_notes: Passé composé of devoir for il/elle/on or a singular noun. It is usually followed by an infinitive. It can express past necessity ("had to") or a strong guess about the past ("must have"), depending on context.
target_language_example: Il a dû attendre longtemps.
native_language_example: He had to wait a long time.

additional_notes: Passé composé of entendre with il/elle/on. It is used for completed actions in the past, often translated as either "heard" or "has heard" depending on context. It can be followed by a thing heard, or by an infinitive: "a entendu le chien aboyer" = "heard the dog bark." In "en a entendu parler," it means "heard about it."
target_language_example: Marie a entendu un bruit étrange dans la cuisine.
native_language_example: Marie heard a strange noise in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of « envoyer » with « avoir »: « il/elle/on a envoyé » = “he/she/one sent/has sent.” Often followed by a direct object (« a envoyé une lettre »). You can also use « envoyer + someone + infinitive » to mean “to send someone to do something”: « Elle a envoyé son fils chercher un médecin » = “She sent her son to look for a doctor.”
target_language_example: Il m'a envoyé un message hier soir.
native_language_example: He sent me a message last night.

additional_notes: Passé composé of envoyer (to send): avoir + envoyé. The direct object is une lettre (“a letter”). Often used with an indirect-object pronoun: lui/leur (to him/her/them), nous (to us), vous (to you), e.g., « Il leur a envoyé une lettre » = “He sent them a letter.”
target_language_example: On vous a envoyé une lettre hier.
native_language_example: A letter was sent to you yesterday.

additional_notes: “a essayé de” is the passé composé of “essayer de” and means someone tried (in the past) to do something. It is followed by an infinitive verb: “a essayé de + verb” (e.g., “a essayé de cacher…” = “tried to hide…”). With a pronoun, the pronoun goes before the infinitive: “a essayé de le faire” = “tried to do it.”
target_language_example: Elle a essayé de m’appeler, mais je n’ai pas répondu.
native_language_example: She tried to call me, but I didn’t answer.

additional_notes: Passé composé of avoir with a singular subject (il/elle/on or a singular noun). In natural English it is often translated as simple past 'had', though literally it is 'has had'. Depending on context, it can also mean 'got' or appear in common expressions like a eu raison ('was right').
target_language_example: Tom a eu une bonne idée.
native_language_example: Tom had a good idea.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of « avoir lieu » = “to take place.” Used mainly for events (a meeting, a wedding, an accident, an earthquake). Often appears with time or place details: « a eu lieu hier », « a eu lieu en Inde ». The subject is usually the event itself (not a person).
target_language_example: Le concert a eu lieu malgré la pluie.
native_language_example: The concert took place despite the rain.

additional_notes: Past form of avoir with a masculine singular noun after it. It often means 'had', but depending on context it can also mean 'got', 'received', or 'experienced'. Common related forms are a eu une (feminine) and a eu des (plural).
target_language_example: Il a eu un problème ce matin.
native_language_example: He had a problem this morning.

additional_notes: Passé composé of "avoir": "il/elle/on a eu" + a feminine noun with "une". Used to talk about having/experiencing something in the past (an illness, a meeting, an accident, an adventure, a good year, etc.). "Eu" doesn’t change with gender; "une" agrees with the noun (for a masculine noun: "a eu un").
target_language_example: Elle a eu une très bonne idée.
native_language_example: She had a really good idea.

additional_notes: Passé composé of the verb « faillir ». It’s usually followed by an infinitive: « a failli + infinitif » = someone almost did something (often something bad or something that was very close to happening): « Il a failli mourir » (He almost died). Not the same as English “failed” — « faillir » means “to almost,” not “to fail.”
target_language_example: Elle a failli se noyer.
native_language_example: She almost drowned.

additional_notes: Passé composé of faire with a singular subject (il/elle/on or a singular noun). It often means "did" or "made," but the exact English translation depends on the expression: for example, faire une erreur = "make a mistake," and faire partie de = "be part of."
target_language_example: Paul a fait un gâteau pour sa sœur.
native_language_example: Paul made a cake for his sister.

meaning: did his best (tried as hard as he could).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of « faire de son mieux » = “to do one’s best.” « son » changes with the subject: « j’ai fait de mon mieux » (I did my best), « elle a fait de son mieux » (she did her best), « nous avons fait de notre mieux » (we did our best). Often followed by « pour + infinitive » to specify what someone tried hard to do.
target_language_example: Tom a fait de son mieux pour ignorer Marie.
native_language_example: Tom did his best to ignore Marie.

additional_notes: Part of the passé composé of faire with a singular subject: "X a fait un...". It is followed by a masculine singular noun. The exact English verb often depends on the noun that follows: faire un câlin = give a hug, faire un cauchemar = have a nightmare. With a feminine noun, it becomes "a fait une".
target_language_example: Paul a fait un dessin pour sa mère.
native_language_example: Paul made a drawing for his mother.

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of faire (il/elle a fait) + une + a feminine singular noun (e.g., une présentation, une vidéo). In English you often translate it as “gave” with presentations/performances: Il a fait une présentation = “He gave a presentation.”
target_language_example: Elle a fait une vidéo pour expliquer le projet.
native_language_example: She made a video to explain the project.

additional_notes: "a fait" is the passé composé of "faire" (to do / to make): "il/elle a fait" = "he/she did" (literally "has done"). "ça" means "that/it" and refers to a specific action or thing mentioned or understood from context. You can change the subject: "j’ai fait ça" (I did that), "tu as fait ça" (you did that), etc.
target_language_example: Pourquoi est-ce qu’il a fait ça ?
native_language_example: Why did he do that?

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of « fermer »: « il/elle a fermé » = “he/she closed.” « la porte » = “the door.” Often used with extra details like « derrière lui/elle » (“behind him/her”) or « la porte de… » (“the door of…”).
target_language_example: Elle a fermé la porte parce qu'il faisait froid.
native_language_example: She closed the door because it was cold.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « finir » (to finish), 3rd person singular with « avoir »: « il/elle/on a fini ». Use « a fini » + direct object (e.g., « a fini le travail », « a fini ses études ») or « a fini de » + infinitive to mean “finished doing” something (e.g., « a fini de parler »). It can also stand alone to mean “is/was done” when the context is clear (e.g., « Rima a fini. »).
target_language_example: Quand il a fini de parler, il y a eu un silence.
native_language_example: When he finished speaking, there was a silence.

meaning: "ended up" / "eventually" (after a process or series of events).
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened in the end, often after hesitation, difficulty, or time passing. It’s the past tense of "finir par" and is followed by an infinitive: "a fini par + infinitif" (e.g., "a fini par partir"). You can also use other tenses: "je finis par…", "il finira par…", "on a fini par…".
target_language_example: Après des heures de discussion, on a fini par trouver une solution.
native_language_example: After hours of discussion, we ended up finding a solution.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *gagner* with *avoir*: **il/elle/on a gagné** = “he/she/one won”. Often used for winning a game/competition (**gagner un match, un prix**). Note: although *gagner* can sometimes mean “earn” (money), **a gagné** is very often “won” in everyday contexts.
target_language_example: Elle a gagné le match hier soir.
native_language_example: She won the match last night.

additional_notes: This is the *passé composé* of *grandir* (auxiliary *avoir* + past participle *grandi*). It’s used both for (1) growing up in a place/family (*a grandi à/dans…*) and (2) becoming taller/older (“He’s grown!”). In English, when talking about childhood/background, it usually translates as “grew up.”
target_language_example: Il a grandi dans une petite ville.
native_language_example: He grew up in a small town.

additional_notes: This is the *passé composé* of *jouer* (auxiliary **avoir** + past participle **joué**). It can mean playing a game/sport (**jouer à**: *a joué au tennis*), playing an instrument or music (often **jouer** + instrument/song: *a joué au piano*, *a joué une chanson*), or acting/portraying a role (**jouer un rôle**: *a joué le rôle de…*). In English it’s often translated as simple past (“played”).
target_language_example: Hier soir, elle a joué aux cartes avec ses amis.
native_language_example: Last night, she played cards with her friends.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « laisser » (avoir + laissé). Often means “left” (forgot/abandoned: « Elle a laissé son téléphone »), “left behind” as a result/trace (« La blessure a laissé une cicatrice »; « Son discours a laissé une marque »), “let/allowed” (« Qui vous a laissé entrer ? »), or “left (to someone) / bequeathed” in a will (« Il lui a laissé la maison »).
target_language_example: Il a laissé ses clés sur la table.
native_language_example: He left his keys on the table.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "manger" (to eat): "[he/she/it] a mangé". It’s formed with the present of "avoir" (a) + past participle (mangé). Used for a completed action in the past; in English it can be "ate" or "has eaten" depending on context.
target_language_example: Il a mangé trop vite.
native_language_example: He ate too fast.

additional_notes: “A marché” is the passé composé of *marcher*. It can mean physically “walked” (often followed by a place or direction: *jusque chez lui*, *devant*) or that something “worked / functioned / went well” (common in *Ça a marché ?* = “Did it work?”). Don’t confuse *marché* here with the noun *le marché* (“the market”).
target_language_example: J’ai essayé ton idée et ça a marché.
native_language_example: I tried your idea and it worked.

additional_notes: Passé composé of **mentir** (to lie): **avoir + menti**. Used for a completed action in the past (often translated as “lied” or “has lied”). You can say **mentir à quelqu’un** (“to lie to someone”): *Il a menti à ses parents.* The past participle **menti** doesn’t change (no agreement) because it’s formed with **avoir**.
target_language_example: Je suis sûr qu’il a menti à la police.
native_language_example: I’m sure he lied to the police.

additional_notes: Passé composé of mettre with il/elle/on. It often translates as simple past English: 'he/she/it put.' Used for placing something somewhere, and in some contexts for 'put on' clothes or 'set' something like a table or password.
target_language_example: Elle a mis son téléphone dans son sac.
native_language_example: She put her phone in her bag.

additional_notes: Used with *avoir* to form the passé composé of *montrer* (to show). It agrees with the subject (e.g., *il a montré*, *elle a montré*). Common patterns: *montrer quelque chose à quelqu’un* (show someone something), and *montrer comment + verb* (show how to do something).
target_language_example: Il m’a montré son passeport.
native_language_example: He showed me his passport.

meaning: "forgot to" / "has forgotten to" (didn’t remember to do something).
additional_notes: Uses the past tense (passé composé) of *oublier* + *de* + infinitive: *[someone] a oublié de + verb*. It expresses that the person failed to do an action because they didn’t remember (e.g., *a oublié de fermer* = forgot to close).
target_language_example: Tom a oublié de déclarer ses impôts.
native_language_example: Tom forgot to file his taxes.

meaning: 'opened' / 'has opened' (passé composé of ouvrir: il/elle/on a ouvert).
additional_notes: Formed with the auxiliary verb avoir + past participle ouvert. Used for a completed action in the past. English translation depends on context: “opened” (simple past) or “has opened” (present perfect). Often followed by a direct object (la porte, la fenêtre, la lettre, etc.).
target_language_example: Il a ouvert la fenêtre, puis il est sorti.
native_language_example: He opened the window, then he went out.

additional_notes: Passé composé: avoir (a) + past participle (payé). Used for a completed action in the past. Often followed by what was paid (a payé l’inscription) or for whom (nous a payé quelques verres = “bought us a few drinks”). With avoir, the past participle usually doesn’t change, except it can agree if a direct object comes before: « Les verres qu’il a payés ».
target_language_example: Elle a payé le repas pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: She paid for the meal for everyone.

meaning: "painted" / "has painted" (3rd person singular *passé composé* of *peindre*: "he/she painted").
additional_notes: This is the *passé composé*: **avoir (a)** + past participle **peint**. It expresses a completed past action: *Il a peint la maison* = "He painted the house." Often used with **en + couleur** to say what color something was painted: *Elle a peint le mur en rouge.* With *avoir*, **peint** usually doesn’t agree, but it can agree when the direct object precedes it: *la porte qu’elle a peinte* (feminine singular), *les murs qu’il a peints* (masculine plural). Also possible figuratively: *Tout ce qu’il a peint s’est réalisé.*
target_language_example: Il a peint la porte en blanc.
native_language_example: He painted the door white.

additional_notes: Passé composé of perdre ('to lose'). Used for misplacing something, losing sight of someone, or saying something has diminished, as in a perdu de son éclat ('has lost some of its shine').
target_language_example: Il a perdu son portefeuille dans le train.
native_language_example: He lost his wallet on the train.

meaning: "lost his" / "has lost his" (for a masculine noun, or a vowel-starting feminine noun).
additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of *perdre* (to lose): *[subject] a perdu* + *son* + noun. *Son* agrees with the thing that’s lost (masculine singular), not with the owner. Common with objects (*son passeport*, *son porte-monnaie*) and also with abstract nouns like *son intérêt* (his interest).
target_language_example: Il a perdu son téléphone dans le métro.
native_language_example: He lost his phone on the subway.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *plaire* in the passé composé: *X a plu à Y* = “Y liked X” (literally “X pleased Y”). The person who likes something is introduced with an indirect object (*lui*, *vous*, *à Marie*, etc.). Example pattern: *Ça t’a plu ?* = “Did you like it?” Not to confuse with *il a plu* (from *pleuvoir*) = “it rained.”
target_language_example: Le film t’a plu ?
native_language_example: Did you like the movie?

additional_notes: *A posé* is the **passé composé** (completed past) of *poser* with **avoir** (il/elle/on **a posé**). It commonly means **poser une question** = “to ask a question” or **poser [objet] sur [surface]** = “to put/place [object] on [surface]”. The intended meaning is determined by what follows (a question vs. a physical object).
target_language_example: Elle lui a posé des questions, mais il a refusé de répondre.
native_language_example: She asked him questions, but he refused to answer.

additional_notes: Passé composé of prendre with a singular subject (il/elle/on). It often translates as either simple past or present perfect in English, depending on context. It also appears in common expressions like a pris soin de ('took care of') and a pris le temps de ('took the time to').
target_language_example: Elle a pris le bus ce matin.
native_language_example: She took the bus this morning.

additional_notes: "a pu" is the passé composé of *pouvoir* for **il/elle/on** (e.g., *il a pu*, *on a pu*). It can express (1) **ability/opportunity in the past**: *On a pu parler…* = “We were able to talk…”, and (2) **a guess about what happened**: *Où il a pu aller ?* = “Where might he have gone?” (often with a question or context of uncertainty).
target_language_example: On a pu le voir hier soir, mais on ne sait pas où il a pu aller ensuite.
native_language_example: We were able to see him last night, but we don’t know where he might have gone afterward.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the verb « quitter » = to leave (a place/someone). It’s used with a direct object: « quitter la table / la ville / Boston / les lieux » (no preposition like “from”). Beware: « quitter » is a false friend of English “to quit” (it usually means “to leave,” not “to stop doing”).
target_language_example: Il a quitté la maison très tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: He left the house very early this morning.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "refuser de" + infinitive: "il/elle a refusé de + verb". Often implies a firm decision or unwillingness (e.g., refusing to answer, eat, reveal, file a complaint). Use "refuser de" (not *refuser à* + verb).
target_language_example: Il a refusé de venir avec nous.
native_language_example: He refused to come with us.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *regarder* with *avoir*: *[subject] + a + regardé* = “(he/she) watched/looked.” Often followed by a direct object (*a regardé la télévision*, *a regardé le sol*) and can also be used with adverbs (*a regardé nerveusement*, *a regardé à nouveau*). Note: *regardé* looks like English “regarded,” but usually means “looked (at)” or “watched” in everyday French.
target_language_example: Il a regardé le film hier soir.
native_language_example: He watched the movie last night.

additional_notes: Passé composé of "recevoir" (to receive): subject + "a" + "reçu" + object. Used for something someone received in the past (orders, calls, praise, gifts, a letter, etc.). In formal writing you may see "a reçu" translated as "has received" (present perfect) or "received" (simple past), depending on context.
target_language_example: Elle a reçu un message important hier.
native_language_example: She received an important message yesterday.

additional_notes: Usually used with the negation "ne … rien": "(ne) … a rien dit" = "didn’t say anything". It’s the passé composé of "dire" (to say): "a dit" (said) → with "rien" it becomes "a rien dit" (said nothing). You can add objects/pronouns: "Elle ne m’a rien dit" (She didn’t tell me anything), "Elle ne m’en a rien dit" (She didn’t tell me anything about it).
target_language_example: Je suis inquiet : il ne m’a rien dit.
native_language_example: I’m worried: he didn’t tell me anything.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « répondre » (a + répondu). Often used with « à »: « répondre à une question / à quelqu’un ». You can also add how someone replied (« brièvement », « avec précaution ») or use « répondre que… » to report what they said.
target_language_example: Elle a répondu à ma question tout de suite.
native_language_example: She answered my question right away.

additional_notes: Passé composé of "réussir à" + infinitive. Used to say someone managed to do something (often with effort, difficulty, or overcoming an obstacle). Common pattern: "[subject] a réussi à + infinitive" (e.g., "a réussi à trouver", "a réussi à traverser").
target_language_example: Comment est-ce que le chat a réussi à grimper sur le toit ?
native_language_example: How did the cat manage to climb onto the roof?

additional_notes: Passé composé of the verb « sauter » with « avoir »: « il/elle a sauté » = “he/she jumped.” Often used with a direction: « sauter dans… » (jump into), « sauter par-dessus… » (jump over), « sauter par… » (jump through/by). Don’t confuse « sauté » here with the English cooking word “sauté.”
target_language_example: Il a sauté du bus en marche.
native_language_example: He jumped off the moving bus.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « sauver la vie (à [quelqu’un]) » = to save someone’s life. Often used with an indirect object introduced by « à » (or with an indirect object pronoun): « Il m’a sauvé la vie » / « Il a sauvé la vie à Tom ». The phrase is literal and commonly used in both everyday and dramatic contexts.
target_language_example: Il vous a sauvé la vie.
native_language_example: He saved your life.

meaning: “rang / has rung” (past tense of *sonner*: to ring).
additional_notes: Used for a sound like a bell, doorbell, alarm, or phone: *Le téléphone a sonné* (“The phone rang”). It can also be figurative with *l’heure a sonné* to mean “the time has come” (often in a serious or fateful sense).
target_language_example: Le téléphone a sonné pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: The phone rang during the meeting.

meaning: “shot at / shot” (fired a weapon at someone/something).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of tirer sur. Used when someone fires a gun, crossbow, etc. at a target; it can imply hitting them or simply firing in their direction (context clarifies). Pattern: [subject] a tiré sur + person/thing.
target_language_example: Il a tiré sur la cible, mais il l’a ratée.
native_language_example: He shot at the target, but he missed it.

additional_notes: Used with a singular subject to say something has been true continuously up to now (present perfect): *[subject] a toujours été + adjective/noun phrase*. For plural subjects, use **ont toujours été**. Often followed by an adjective (*bon*, *mauvais*) or a description (*un problème*, *utile*, etc.).
target_language_example: Il a toujours été très gentil avec moi.
native_language_example: He has always been very kind to me.

additional_notes: "a travaillé" is the passé composé: avoir (a) + past participle (travaillé). It describes a completed action in the past ("he worked") or past experience up to now ("he has worked"), depending on context/time words like "hier" or "dans le passé".
target_language_example: Elle a travaillé toute la journée.
native_language_example: She worked all day.

additional_notes: Passé composé of trouver with il/elle/on or a singular noun subject. In everyday English, it is often translated simply as "found" rather than "has found."
target_language_example: Elle a trouvé ses clés sous le canapé.
native_language_example: She found her keys under the sofa.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of **tuer**: **avoir (conjugated) + tué**. Often translates as simple past in English (“killed”), even though it’s literally “has killed.” With **avoir**, **tué** usually doesn’t change form; it only agrees if a direct object comes before the verb (e.g., *La souris qu’il a tuée*).
target_language_example: Il a tué le moteur avant de descendre de la voiture.
native_language_example: He turned off the engine before getting out of the car.

additional_notes: "A volé" is the passé composé (past tense) of *voler* meaning "to steal." It’s used with the auxiliary *avoir* (il/elle/on **a** volé; j’**ai** volé; ils/elles **ont** volé). Note: *voler* can also mean "to fly," but with objects like *portefeuille* (wallet), *montre* (watch), etc., it clearly means "to steal."
target_language_example: Quelqu’un a volé mon téléphone dans le métro.
native_language_example: Someone stole my phone on the subway.

additional_notes: *A vu* is the passé composé of *voir*: **il/elle/on a vu** = “he/she/one has seen / saw,” depending on context. With negation: **n’a pas vu** = “didn’t see / hasn’t seen.” You’ll also often see **n’a vu que…** = “only saw…”.
target_language_example: Tom a ouvert les yeux et a vu Mary.
native_language_example: Tom opened his eyes and saw Mary.

additional_notes: Third-person singular passé composé of *vivre* with the auxiliary *avoir*: *il/elle/on a vécu*. Commonly used to say someone lived somewhere for a period of time, or to point out a place where someone lived. In English, it’s often translated as simple past (“lived”) in these contexts, though it can also correspond to “has lived” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ma famille a vécu ici pendant trente ans.
native_language_example: My family lived here for thirty years.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « écrire » (to write): « il/elle/on a écrit ». Used for a completed action in the past (often like simple past “wrote” in English, or “has written” depending on context). Can also refer to what is written somewhere: « Qu'est-ce qu'il y a écrit ? » = “What does it say (what’s written there)?”
target_language_example: Elle a écrit un email à son professeur.
native_language_example: She wrote an email to her teacher.

additional_notes: Form of être used with a singular subject. It often appears in the passive voice with another past participle: a été + past participle = 'was/has been ...'. Depending on context, English often uses simple past ('was') rather than the literal 'has been'.
target_language_example: La porte a été fermée trop tôt.
native_language_example: The door was closed too early.

additional_notes: Passive past form of annuler (“to cancel”). Used to say an event, trip, flight, etc. was canceled. It agrees with the thing that was canceled: masculine singular a été annulé; feminine singular a été annulée; plural ont été annulés / annulées.
target_language_example: La réunion a été annulée au dernier moment.
native_language_example: The meeting was canceled at the last minute.

additional_notes: Passive past tense (passé composé) of arrêter: "[someone] was arrested" (usually by the police). Often followed by pour + reason (e.g., pour excès de vitesse) or by + agent with par (e.g., arrêté par la police). Can also be used for being stopped/detained, depending on context.
target_language_example: Il a été arrêté par la police après la bagarre.
native_language_example: He was arrested by the police after the fight.

additional_notes: Passé composé in the passive voice: "a été" (was/has been) + past participle. Used for someone being deliberately killed (often an important person, but it can be used more generally). The past participle agrees with the person: "a été assassiné" (male) / "a été assassinée" (female). You can add the agent with "par" (e.g., "par un tueur").
target_language_example: Le journaliste a été assassiné devant chez lui.
native_language_example: The journalist was assassinated in front of his home.

additional_notes: This is the passive form in the past: **a été + past participle**. It’s used when you focus on the thing that was built, not the builder. You can add the builder with **par**: *a été construit par...* In sentences, it often answers **Quand ?** (when) or **Par qui ?** (by whom). Agreement: **construit** changes with the subject—*a été construite* (feminine), *ont été construits/construites* (plural).
target_language_example: Cette école a été construite en 1998.
native_language_example: This school was built in 1998.

additional_notes: This is the passive form of *prendre* in the past (*a été* + past participle). It means something "was taken" or, with *décision*, "a decision was made." The past participle agrees with the feminine subject (*prise* for *la décision* / *la photo*; masculine would be *pris*). Common in formal/neutral statements: *La décision a été prise.* / *Où a été prise cette photo ?*
target_language_example: La décision a été prise hier soir.
native_language_example: The decision was made last night.

additional_notes: Passive form in the past: **être** (present) + **tué** (past participle). Used to say someone died because another person/thing caused it. The cause/agent is often introduced with **par** (e.g., *a été tué par une explosion*). If the agent is unknown or unimportant, it can be omitted (*Il a été tué.*).
target_language_example: Le journaliste a été tué pendant le conflit.
native_language_example: The journalist was killed during the conflict.

additional_notes: Passive voice: **a été + past participle** (“was/has been + -ed”). Here **volée** agrees with the stolen thing because it’s feminine singular (e.g., **ma valise**, **ma montre**, **la poubelle**). For a masculine thing: **a été volé** (e.g., *mon sac a été volé*). Plural: **ont été volés/volées**.
target_language_example: Ma carte bancaire a été volée dans le métro.
native_language_example: My bank card was stolen on the subway.

meaning: “was / has been” (past tense of être); also “has been to / went to”.
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of être: avoir (a) + past participle été. Common in questions about how something went: « Ça a été ? » / « Comment ça a été ? » = “Was it okay?” / “How did it go?”. With a place (au/à la/aux/à + place), « Il a été… » often means “He went to…” or “He has been to…”.
target_language_example: Ça a été difficile, mais ça a été.
native_language_example: It was difficult, but it was okay.

meaning: "has she?" / "does she have?" (question form of "elle a").
additional_notes: Used in formal or written questions with inversion: verb (a) + -t- + subject pronoun (elle). The -t- is added only for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel (a) and the pronoun starts with a vowel (elle). Equivalent to the more common spoken form: « Est-ce qu’elle a… ? » or « Elle a… ? »
target_language_example: A-t-elle besoin d’aide ?
native_language_example: Does she need help?

additional_notes: This is the inverted (more formal) way to ask a yes/no question with "elle" (she) using the verb "avoir" (to have): "A-t-elle… ?" The "-t-" is added only for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel (a) and the subject starts with a vowel (elle). It’s commonly used in writing and formal speech; in everyday speech you often hear "Est-ce qu’elle a… ?" or "Elle a… ?".
target_language_example: A-t-elle un billet pour le train ?
native_language_example: Does she have a train ticket?

additional_notes: Used when the subject is singular and the verb is avoir in the form a: il/elle/on a, or a singular noun like Marie or ce magasin. It is followed by a noun to say someone or something has a large quantity of something. With other subjects, a changes: j'ai beaucoup de, tu as beaucoup de, nous avons beaucoup de, etc.
target_language_example: Elle a beaucoup de travail aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: She has a lot of work today.

additional_notes: From **avoir besoin de** (“to need”) + **toi** (“you,” informal singular). Used to say someone/something depends on you or requires your help/presence. The subject can vary: *il/elle a besoin de toi* (he/she needs you), *Tom a besoin de toi* (Tom needs you), *le monde a besoin de toi* (the world needs you). More formal: **a besoin de vous**.
target_language_example: Tom a besoin de toi ici.
native_language_example: Tom needs you here.

meaning: tastes good; has a good flavor.
additional_notes: Used with the verb « avoir » to talk about taste/flavor: « X a bon goût » = “X tastes good.” Common in questions like « Est-ce que ça a bon goût ? » (“Does it taste good?”). In other contexts, « avoir bon goût » can also mean “to have good taste” (e.g., in clothing/decor), but in these examples it’s about food and drink.
target_language_example: Ce fromage a bon goût.
native_language_example: This cheese tastes good.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir (to have): « il/elle a de la chance » = “he/she is lucky.” You can also say « Tu as de la chance ! » to tell someone “You’re lucky!”
target_language_example: Tom a de la chance.
native_language_example: Tom is lucky.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **avoir** (here: **a** = "has") to say someone/something possesses a lot of something. It’s followed by a **plural noun**: **a de nombreux + nom pluriel** (e.g., *a de nombreux amis*). **Nombreux** agrees with the noun (masc. plur. **nombreux**, fem. plur. **nombreuses**).
target_language_example: Cette ville a de nombreux musées.
native_language_example: This city has many museums.

additional_notes: "a" is the 3rd-person singular of "avoir" (to have): il/elle/on a = he/she/one has. "des" is an indefinite article used before a plural noun, often translated as "some" or left untranslated in English (e.g., "a des droits" = "has rights"). Used to say someone/something possesses or has certain features: "il a des cheveux blancs" (he has white hair).
target_language_example: Elle a des questions pour le professeur.
native_language_example: She has some questions for the teacher.

meaning: has trouble / has a hard time (doing something).
additional_notes: Structure: subject + « avoir du mal à » + infinitive. « a du mal à » is the 3rd person singular present form (il/elle/on). The expression means someone finds it difficult to do something (because of ability, confidence, resources, circumstances, etc.). Other forms: « j’ai du mal à », « tu as du mal à », « nous avons du mal à », « ils/elles ont du mal à »; also other tenses like « avait du mal à », « aura du mal à ».
target_language_example: Tom a du mal à dormir.
native_language_example: Tom has a hard time sleeping.

additional_notes: Used with an (optional) subject to say someone is afraid. Common patterns: "avoir peur de + noun" (a peur de tous les docteurs = is afraid of all doctors) and "avoir peur de + infinitive" (a peur de tomber / de le faire = is afraid to fall / to do it). "a" is the present tense for il/elle/on (he/she/one) in "avoir"; other forms: "j'ai peur de", "tu as peur de", "nous avons peur de", "vous avez peur de", "ils/elles ont peur de".
target_language_example: Il a peur de parler en public.
native_language_example: He is afraid to speak in public.

meaning: "has more (of)" / "has more than"; also "is over" (an amount/age).
additional_notes: From the verb "avoir" (to have) + "plus de" (more of/than). Used to compare quantities ("a plus de X que...") or to say something exceeds a number ("a plus de 100 ans" = over 100 years old). Be careful: "n'a plus de" means "doesn't have any ... anymore" (no longer has).
target_language_example: Cette ville a plus de deux millions d'habitants.
native_language_example: This city has over two million inhabitants.

additional_notes: "a" is the present tense of "avoir" (to have): il/elle/on a = he/she/one has. "Plusieurs" means "several" and is followed by a plural noun (plusieurs amis, plusieurs sens).
target_language_example: Ce musée a plusieurs salles.
native_language_example: This museum has several rooms.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avoir" to state that someone/something has four items/parts (wheels, rooms, sides, etc.). It can be followed by a noun ("a quatre roues") or stand alone when the noun is understood from context ("Elle en a quatre" = she has four of them).
target_language_example: Mon vélo a quatre vitesses.
native_language_example: My bike has four gears.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *avoir*: *il/elle a raison* = “he/she is right.” It expresses that someone’s opinion or statement is correct. The opposite is *avoir tort* (“to be wrong”). Even though *raison* looks like “reason,” *avoir raison* usually means “to be right,” not “to have a reason.”
target_language_example: Cet homme a raison.
native_language_example: That man is right.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: « avoir + un beau + nom » (e.g., « un beau sourire »). For a feminine noun, use « a une belle … » (e.g., « une belle voix »). Often translated as “has a nice …” in natural English.
target_language_example: Il a un beau jardin.
native_language_example: He has a beautiful garden.

meaning: “has a taste/flavor” (often followed by an adjective or de + noun).
additional_notes: Used to describe what something tastes like: **avoir un goût + adjective** (amer, étrange, sucré) or **avoir un goût de + noun** (“a taste of …”, like citron, carton). With food it’s literal; it can also be used figuratively for a “feel/air” (e.g., *Ça a un goût de déjà-vu*).
target_language_example: Cette sauce a un goût trop salé.
native_language_example: This sauce tastes too salty.

additional_notes: Used with a person or thing as the subject: "X a un problème". It can mean a practical difficulty (a problem to solve) or something wrong (e.g., a medical/genetic/behavioral issue). In spoken French you’ll often hear it as "On a un problème" (“We’ve got a problem”).
target_language_example: Il a un problème avec sa voiture, alors il va être en retard.
native_language_example: He has a problem with his car, so he’s going to be late.

additional_notes: "a" is the present tense (3rd person singular) of "avoir" (to have). "une" is used before a feminine singular noun (une amie, une vitesse, une carrière). In negatives, it becomes "n’a pas une..." or more commonly "n’a pas de..." (e.g., "Il n’a pas d’amie ici.").
target_language_example: Elle a une voiture rouge.
native_language_example: She has a red car.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir (“to have”) + the feminine singular indefinite article une (“a”) + grande (feminine singular of grand). It must be followed by a feminine noun: une grande maison, une grande télévision. For a masculine noun, use un grand (un grand jardin). Note: French grand/grande often means “big/large/tall,” not “grand” in the English sense.
target_language_example: Elle a une grande voiture.
native_language_example: She has a big car.

additional_notes: Used with avoir ("to have") + une (feminine "a") + grosse (feminine form of "big/large"). It must be followed by a noun: e.g., "une grosse voiture". Commonly, "gros/grosse" just means "big/large," but with some body-related nouns like "bite" or "queue," it can be a vulgar sexual meaning ("penis").
target_language_example: Elle a une grosse valise.
native_language_example: She has a big suitcase.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to describe what something smells like. Often followed by an adjective (ex. une odeur délicieuse / désagréable) or by “de + noun” to name the smell (ex. une odeur de fumée = a smell of smoke). The verb is “avoir” (to have): il/elle a une odeur = it has a smell.
target_language_example: Cette pièce a une odeur de peinture.
native_language_example: This room smells like paint.

additional_notes: A formal, common term used in news, reports, and everyday speech for an accident involving vehicles on the road. You may also hear: « accident de voiture » (car accident) or « accident de circulation » (traffic accident).
target_language_example: Il y a eu un accident de la route sur l'autoroute ce matin.
native_language_example: There was a road accident on the highway this morning.

meaning: Hang on! / Hold on tight! (also: Brace yourself!)
additional_notes: Informal/colloquial imperative with tu. Often used literally (hold on physically), especially with à: « Accroche-toi à la barre. » It can also be figurative to warn someone something intense is coming: « Accroche-toi, ça va secouer ! »
target_language_example: Accroche-toi, ça va aller très vite.
native_language_example: Hang on, it’s going to go very fast.

meaning: to buy a new one (or: to buy a new …).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun introduced by un: acheter un nouveau tapis / jouet. The adjective nouveau agrees with the noun (feminine: acheter une nouvelle voiture). You can also use it without repeating the noun when it’s clear from context: en acheter un nouveau = “buy a new one.”
target_language_example: Mon téléphone est cassé, je vais en acheter un nouveau.
native_language_example: My phone is broken; I’m going to buy a new one.

additional_notes: Used to talk about purchasing a (different) car that is new. "Acheter" is the verb "to buy"; "une nouvelle voiture" means "a new car" (nouvelle agrees with the feminine noun "voiture"). You can change the article and adjective to fit your meaning: "acheter une voiture neuve" (buy a brand-new car), "acheter une autre voiture" (buy another car).
target_language_example: On va acheter une nouvelle voiture le mois prochain.
native_language_example: We’re going to buy a new car next month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the act of purchasing a car. In the present (j’achète), future (je vais acheter / j’achèterai), or with vouloir/vouloir (je veux/je voudrais acheter…). In questions, it often appears as: « Veux-tu acheter une voiture ? » (informal) / « Voulez-vous acheter une voiture ? » (formal).
target_language_example: On économise depuis un an pour acheter une voiture.
native_language_example: We’ve been saving for a year to buy a car.

additional_notes: Used with the passé composé of acheter: « (j'/tu/il/elle/nous/vous/ils/elles) ai/as/a/avons/avez/ont acheté du pain ». « du » is the partitive article meaning “some” (an unspecified amount) with an uncountable noun like bread. Note: « pain » looks like English “pain” but it means “bread”.
target_language_example: J'ai acheté du pain pour le petit-déjeuner.
native_language_example: I bought some bread for breakfast.

meaning: an act of faith; a leap of faith.
additional_notes: Used for something you do without proof or certainty, relying on trust or belief. It can also have a religious sense (“act/statement of faith”). Common phrasing: « faire acte de foi » = “to make an act of faith / to take a leap of faith.”
target_language_example: Accepter ce travail sans garantie, c'était un acte de foi.
native_language_example: Accepting that job without any guarantee was a leap of faith.

additional_notes: Used for someone who likes/adores you but keeps their identity hidden. Often appears with the verb « avoir »: « Tu as un admirateur secret. » You can also say « une admiratrice secrète » for a female admirer.
target_language_example: Depuis quelques jours, elle reçoit des fleurs de son admirateur secret.
native_language_example: For a few days, she has been getting flowers from her secret admirer.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "adorer" + "les" (= "the" for plural nouns). In everyday French, "adorer" often means "to really love" (not necessarily romantic). The noun after "les" is plural (e.g., les gâteaux = cakes).
target_language_example: J'adore les films d'aventure.
native_language_example: I love adventure movies.

additional_notes: Used in formal or neutral contexts (forms, customer service, sign-ups). You’ll also hear "adresse e-mail" or just "e-mail". Often appears with verbs like "donner" (to give), "saisir" (to enter), or "avoir besoin de" (to need).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me donner votre adresse électronique, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you give me your email address, please?

additional_notes: A fixed, somewhat literary expression used to show determination or acceptance of uncertainty: you’ll do what you can and accept the outcome. Often used alone as a full sentence. The verb form "advienne" comes from "advenir" (to happen) and is in the subjunctive.
target_language_example: On va tenter notre chance, advienne que pourra.
native_language_example: We’re going to try our luck, come what may.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to explain the goal/purpose of an action. It’s slightly more formal than "pour"; in everyday speech, "pour" often works the same way. Often followed by "ne pas" + infinitive for a negative purpose: "afin de ne pas rater…"
target_language_example: J’éteins mon téléphone afin de me concentrer.
native_language_example: I turn off my phone in order to focus.

additional_notes: Introduces a purpose (goal) clause and is followed by the subjunctive: « afin que + [subjunctive] ». Often interchangeable with « pour que » (also “so that”). Example pattern: « Je le fais afin que tu comprennes » = “I’m doing it so that you understand.”
target_language_example: Je parle plus lentement afin que tu puisses comprendre.
native_language_example: I speak more slowly so that you can understand.

additional_notes: Job title for someone who protects people or property (in a store, building, event, etc.). Often used without an article when stating your profession: « Je suis agent de sécurité. » You can also use it with an article when talking about a specific person: « Trouve un agent de sécurité. »
target_language_example: Il y a un agent de sécurité à l'entrée du magasin.
native_language_example: There is a security guard at the entrance of the store.

additional_notes: Job title for someone who helps buy, sell, or rent property (houses/apartments). Often used with un/une: « un agent immobilier ». You can say « Elle est agent immobilier » (no article, focusing on the profession) or « Elle est un agent immobilier » (identifying the person as one). Feminine form also common: « une agente immobilière ».
target_language_example: On cherche un agent immobilier pour louer un appartement.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a real estate agent to rent an apartment.

meaning: "Oh really?" / "Oh, I see." (reaction showing surprise or interest).
additional_notes: Used very often in conversation as a short reaction to what someone just said. Depending on tone and context, it can express genuine surprise, mild skepticism, or simply that you’re acknowledging new information. It’s also common before a follow-up question: « Ah bon, pourquoi ? » / « Ah bon ? »
target_language_example: — Je déménage à Lyon. — Ah bon ? Quand ça ?
native_language_example: — I'm moving to Lyon. — Oh really? When?

meaning: “oh yes / oh right” (showing realization, agreement, or mild surprise).
additional_notes: Used as a reaction to what someone just said: to acknowledge/agree (“Ah oui, bien sûr.”), to realize/remember something (“Ah oui, j’ai un truc à faire demain.”), or to express surprise/irony (“Ah oui, vous êtes en retard !”). With a question intonation (“Ah oui ?”), it means “Oh really?”
target_language_example: — Il faut partir maintenant. — Ah oui, j'avais oublié.
native_language_example: — We have to leave now. — Oh right, I forgot.

additional_notes: Inverted form of "j’ai" used to ask a question (verb before subject): "Ai-je… ?" = "Have I…?" / often "Did I…?" in English depending on context. It’s most common in formal speech and writing; in everyday conversation people often use "est-ce que j’ai… ?" or intonation: "J’ai… ?".
target_language_example: Ai-je bien compris ?
native_language_example: Did I understand correctly?

meaning: "did I say" / "have I said" (question form of "I said").
additional_notes: Used to ask a question in the past about what you said. It’s the passé composé of *dire* (j’ai dit) with **inversion** for questions: *Ai-je dit… ?* It often appears with question words (*Qu’ai-je dit ?* = “What did I say?”) or with an object pronoun: *L’ai-je dit ?* = “Did I say it?” This inverted form is quite formal; in everyday speech you’ll often hear *Est-ce que j’ai dit… ?*
target_language_example: Ai-je dit quelque chose de mal ?
native_language_example: Did I say something wrong?

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of faire (“j’ai fait” = “I did / I have done”) with subject–verb inversion (“ai-je…?”) to form a question. It’s common in more formal or written French, often with a question word: “Qu’ai-je fait ?” (What have I done?), “Pourquoi ai-je fait ça ?” (Why did I do that?). You can also use it with an object pronoun: “Vous ai-je fait attendre ?” (Have I made you wait?).
target_language_example: Qu’ai-je fait de mal ?
native_language_example: What did I do wrong?

additional_notes: Inversion of the verb "avoir" ("j’ai" → "ai-je") used to ask a question in a more formal/literary style. Often followed by a noun (Ai-je le droit… ?) or used with pronouns: "en ai-je" = "do I have any (of it/them)?" and can also mean "do I need any?" depending on the verb phrase (e.g., "besoin" → "en ai-je besoin ?").
target_language_example: Ai-je oublié mon passeport ?
native_language_example: Have I forgotten my passport?

meaning: I have something to… / I’ve got a thing to…
additional_notes: Used (usually with "j’") to introduce an action you need/want to do: « J’ai un truc à faire/te dire/te demander ». « Truc » is very common and informal, meaning “thing/stuff” when you don’t want to be specific or can’t find the exact word. In careful French, you can replace it with « quelque chose à » (“something to”).
target_language_example: J’ai un truc à te dire.
native_language_example: I’ve got something to tell you.

additional_notes: Imperative of aider (to help) + moi (me) + à + an infinitive verb. Used to ask someone to help you do an action or accomplish a task. In everyday English you often drop “to”: “Help me choose.” You can add an object after the infinitive: « Aide-moi à le soulever » (help me lift it).
target_language_example: Aide-moi à remplir ce formulaire, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Help me fill out this form, please.

additional_notes: "Aidez" is the formal or plural command form of "aider" (to help). "moi" is the object pronoun (me), and "à" is followed by an infinitive verb to say what you need help doing (e.g., "aidez-moi à apprendre"). In informal singular you’ll also hear "aide-moi à".
target_language_example: Aidez-moi à remplir ce formulaire, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Help me fill out this form, please.

additional_notes: "Aimer" means "to like/love" and "beaucoup" means "a lot." With objects/things (music, school), it’s usually "really like." With people (Je t'aime beaucoup / Je les aime beaucoup), it means strong affection ("I like you a lot"), and is generally less intense than "Je t’aime" ("I love you"). Word order: subject + aimer (conjugated) + beaucoup + object (or object pronoun before the verb: "Je t’aime beaucoup").
target_language_example: J'aime beaucoup cette chanson.
native_language_example: I really like this song.

meaning: likes (quite) a lot; is fond of.
additional_notes: "Aimer" alone can mean "to love" (people) or "to like" (things). Adding "bien" often softens it and clearly means "to like" / "to be fond of" someone or something (not romantic love). It can also suggest "rather/quite a lot" depending on context.
target_language_example: Je t'aime bien, mais je ne suis pas amoureux.
native_language_example: I like you, but I’m not in love.

additional_notes: "aime" is the 3rd-person singular of "aimer" (to like/love). Used with a subject (il/elle/on or a name): "Cathy aime la musique." For "I like music," say "J’aime la musique." You can add a style or adjective after "musique" (e.g., "musique acoustique", "musique country", "musique lente").
target_language_example: Mon frère aime la musique classique.
native_language_example: My brother likes classical music.

additional_notes: Used to express liking (a moderate, friendly positive feeling) without the stronger sense of “aimer” alone (which can mean “to love”). Common patterns: “J’aime bien + noun” (I quite like + noun) or “J’aime bien + infinitive” (I like to + verb). Can also soften opinions: “J’aime bien, mais…” (I like it, but…).
target_language_example: J'aime bien ce film, mais je ne l'adore pas.
native_language_example: I like this movie, but I don’t love it.

additional_notes: This is the conditional form of aimer (“to like/love”) with inversion (-tu), used to ask a polite question: “Would you like…?” It can be followed by a noun (Aimerais-tu un café ?), an infinitive (Aimerais-tu venir ?), or a question word like où (Où aimerais-tu aller ?). More formal than Tu veux… ?
target_language_example: Aimerais-tu venir dîner ce soir ?
native_language_example: Would you like to come for dinner tonight?

additional_notes: Conditional form of « aimer » used to make polite offers or questions. It’s the formal/plural « vous » form, common with strangers, in customer service, or when speaking to more than one person. Often followed by an infinitive (aimeriez-vous discuter ?) or by « que » + subjunctive (aimeriez-vous que Marie fasse… ?).
target_language_example: Aimeriez-vous prendre un café ?
native_language_example: Would you like to have a coffee?

additional_notes: Inversion form of the question "tu aimes…?" (verb + subject). It’s the present tense of "aimer" with "tu": "aimes" + "-tu". Common in writing and more formal speech; in everyday conversation you’ll often hear "Tu aimes… ?" or "Est-ce que tu aimes… ?". Use "aimer" for liking things (food, hobbies) and also for loving people; context makes it clear.
target_language_example: Aimes-tu la musique classique ?
native_language_example: Do you like classical music?

additional_notes: Formal or polite question form using inversion: « aimez-vous + noun/infinitive ? ». Often translated as “Do you like…?” (and sometimes “Do you love…?” depending on context). In everyday casual speech, people often use « vous aimez… ? » or « est-ce que vous aimez… ? » instead. Can also be used alone after a choice: « Lequel aimez-vous ? » = “Which one do you like?”
target_language_example: Aimez-vous ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: Do you like this restaurant?

meaning: "Do you like the..." (asking if someone likes a type of thing).
additional_notes: "Aimez-vous" is the formal/inverted way to ask "Do you like...?". "Les" is used for plural nouns or general categories (e.g., movies, strawberries). In casual speech, you’ll often hear: "Vous aimez les… ?" or "Tu aimes les… ?".
target_language_example: Aimez-vous les desserts au chocolat ?
native_language_example: Do you like chocolate desserts?

additional_notes: Often links two items or people to add information: X ainsi que Y = “X as well as Y” (similar to “et aussi”). It can also introduce a comparison, especially with a pronoun or clause: ainsi que vous le savez = “as you already know” / “just as you know.”
target_language_example: J’ai invité Marie ainsi que Paul.
native_language_example: I invited Marie as well as Paul.

additional_notes: Commonly used after a noun to describe a place that has air conditioning: une chambre avec air conditionné (a room with air conditioning), un bureau à air conditionné (an air-conditioned office). Also used with appareil to mean an air-conditioning unit (appareil de climatisation is another common way to say this).
target_language_example: Est-ce que l'hôtel a l'air conditionné ?
native_language_example: Does the hotel have air conditioning?

additional_notes: Used for travel (train/plane/bus): « Aller-retour ou aller simple ? » = “Round trip or one-way?” It can mean the ticket itself (« un aller-retour ») or the act of going somewhere and coming back (« faire un aller-retour »). Often used with destination: « un aller-retour à Paris » / « un aller-retour chez toi ».
target_language_example: Je voudrais un aller-retour pour Lyon, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a round-trip ticket to Lyon, please.

additional_notes: Used in travel/transport when buying tickets. Often said as "un aller simple" or with "billet" ("un billet aller simple"). Contrasts with "aller-retour" (round trip/return ticket).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un billet aller simple pour Marseille, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a one-way ticket to Marseille, please.

meaning: to go to the movies; to go to the cinema.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re going to watch a movie at a movie theater. Conjugate "aller" to match the subject (je vais, tu vas, il/elle va, nous allons, vous allez, ils/elles vont). Often paired with a time: "On va au cinéma ce soir."
target_language_example: On va aller au cinéma samedi soir.
native_language_example: We’re going to go to the movies on Saturday night.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re going to bed (usually to sleep). Common with devoir (“Tu dois aller au lit”) and in questions (“Tu es prêt à aller au lit ?”).
target_language_example: Je vais aller au lit tôt ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to go to bed early tonight.

meaning: to go to the bathroom (to use the toilet).
additional_notes: Common, polite way to say you need to use the toilet. Used with devoir/je dois (I have to) or as a request: « Je peux / Puis-je aller aux toilettes ? » (Can/May I go to the bathroom?). Literally “to go to the toilets,” and it’s typically plural in French: « les toilettes ». In casual speech you may also hear « aller aux WC ».
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je dois aller aux toilettes.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have to go to the bathroom.

meaning: to go with; to match; to be compatible with
additional_notes: Used to say that two things match well or are compatible (clothes, colors, accessories, styles, etc.). It can also mean that something ‘goes with’ something else in a more general sense (fits, suits). In the negative ("ne pas aller avec"), it means something doesn’t match or doesn’t work well together.
target_language_example: Il choisit une paire de chaussettes pour aller avec son costume.
native_language_example: He chooses a pair of socks to go with his suit.

additional_notes: Used when you leave to fetch someone or something and bring them/it back (or at least retrieve them/it). Common with objects (mon portefeuille, une glace) and people (Maria, grand-mère). Literally it’s “to go + look for,” but in everyday French it often means “go get/pick up.”
target_language_example: Je vais aller chercher les enfants à l’école.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up the kids from school.

meaning: to fit perfectly; to suit someone perfectly (“fit like a glove”).
additional_notes: Used primarily for clothing/accessories that fit extremely well (size and shape), and by extension for something that suits someone very well (a role, a style, etc.). Commonly used with a clothing item as the subject: « Cette veste va comme un gant. »
target_language_example: Cette veste va comme un gant.
native_language_example: This jacket fits like a glove.

meaning: to move forward; to move on (make progress).
additional_notes: Used when you want to continue, make progress, or stop dwelling on the past and take the next step. Very common with expressions like "Il est temps de..." (It’s time to...) and "Il faut..." / "On doit..." (We have to...). Often about life decisions or a situation, not just physical movement.
target_language_example: Après cette erreur, on doit aller de l'avant.
native_language_example: After that mistake, we have to move on.

meaning: to be obvious; to go without saying.
additional_notes: Used to say something is self-evident or taken for granted. Commonly appears in impersonal constructions such as « Il va de soi que… » or as a standalone reassurance « Ça va de soi. ». The base expression is « aller de soi » (infinitive).
target_language_example: Pour elle, aider ses amis, c’est aller de soi.
native_language_example: For her, helping her friends is a given / goes without saying.

meaning: “come on!” / “go on!” (urging someone to do something).
additional_notes: Often used as an imperative; in real speech you more commonly see it conjugated (« Va donc ! », « Allez donc ! »). Using the infinitive « aller donc » can sound like a brusque instruction (e.g., on a sign or in clipped speech). « donc » adds insistence or impatience, similar to “just” or “come on.” Tone depends on context: it can be encouraging or annoyed.
target_language_example: Aller donc, dis-moi la vérité !
native_language_example: Come on, tell me the truth!

meaning: to go to; to go on
additional_notes: Used with en before many places, especially feminine countries, regions, and continents (for example en France, en Europe). It also appears in some set expressions like aller en promenade, where it means going on an activity or outing.
target_language_example: Pourquoi veux-tu aller en Europe ?
native_language_example: Why do you want to go to Europe?

meaning: to go to prison; to be sent to jail.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the possibility or consequence of being imprisoned (often after breaking the law). Common with pouvoir (could/might) or devoir (must/have to).
target_language_example: Si tu fais ça, tu risques d'aller en prison.
native_language_example: If you do that, you risk going to prison.

meaning: to come and go; to go back and forth (often freely).
additional_notes: Used to talk about moving in and out of a place or moving around without restrictions: “Tu peux aller et venir…” = “You can come and go…”. It can be literal (physical movement) or more abstract (people/characters coming and going in a story).
target_language_example: Ici, les visiteurs peuvent aller et venir librement.
native_language_example: Here, visitors can come and go freely.

meaning: to go far; (figuratively) to go too far; to have a lot of potential/success.
