additional_notes: Literal use: physical distance (“go far”). Figurative use: to exceed acceptable limits (“to go too far”), or to indicate future success (“He’ll go far”). Note: "loin" means "far" and is a false friend with English "loin" (meat).
target_language_example: Avec ce talent, il peut aller loin.
native_language_example: With that talent, he can go far.

additional_notes: “Aller” means “to go.” “Là-bas” means “over there / to that place” (often a place not right here, sometimes a bit far away). You can change the verb to match the subject: je vais là-bas, tu vas là-bas, il/elle va là-bas, etc. You can also use “y aller” to mean “to go there” when the place is already known from context.
target_language_example: On peut aller là-bas demain ?
native_language_example: Can we go there tomorrow?

meaning: to go faster; to speed up.
additional_notes: Used to compare speed (plus vite = faster). Often with a subject (Je/Nous) to mean “go faster,” or with faire + infinitive (faire aller) to mean “make something/someone go faster” (e.g., a car, machine, or person).
target_language_example: On peut aller plus vite si on prend l'autoroute.
native_language_example: We can go faster if we take the highway.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re going to an unspecified place. Often followed by another action: « aller quelque part et + verb » (“go somewhere and …”). In questions/invitations, it can suggest going to a quieter or more private place to talk.
target_language_example: On peut aller quelque part de plus calme pour discuter ?
native_language_example: Can we go somewhere quieter to talk?

meaning: to go without saying; to be obvious.
additional_notes: Used to say something is self-evident and doesn’t need to be stated. Common patterns: « Ça va sans dire. » (“That goes without saying.”) and « Il va sans dire que… » (“It goes without saying that…”). Note: the infinitive form « aller sans dire » is less common in full sentences than the conjugated forms « ça va sans dire » / « il va sans dire ».
target_language_example: Ça devrait aller sans dire : je serai là à l’heure.
native_language_example: It should go without saying: I’ll be there on time.

meaning: to go and get (something) done; to go get yourself + [verb].
additional_notes:
Usually used as a pattern: **aller se faire + infinitive** (often with a verb like *couper, soigner, masser*), meaning you go somewhere to have something done for you: *aller se faire couper les cheveux* = “to go get your hair cut.”

It can also introduce rude expressions like **aller se faire voir** (“go away / get lost”) or the very vulgar **aller se faire foutre**.
target_language_example: Je vais aller se faire couper les cheveux.
native_language_example: I'm going to go get my hair cut.

meaning: to go alone / by oneself (all alone).
additional_notes: Used to say someone goes without help or without company. Very common when talking about children doing something independently. You’ll often hear it with pronouns: « y aller tout seul » (to go there alone) or « Je vais y aller tout seul ». You can also agree with the subject: « toute seule » (feminine), « tout seuls / toutes seules » (plural).
target_language_example: Il veut aller tout seul à l’école.
native_language_example: He wants to go to school by himself.

meaning: to go too far (to overdo it; to cross a line).
additional_notes: Used literally for distance or figuratively for behavior, words, jokes, or actions that are excessive or unacceptable. Often said as a warning or criticism: « Tu vas trop loin » (You’re going too far).
target_language_example: Je plaisantais, mais là, tu vas aller trop loin.
native_language_example: I was joking, but now you’re going to go too far.

additional_notes: A common, compositional phrase meaning to go and see someone or something. With a person, it often means "go see" or "go visit"; with a film or show, it means "go watch"; and without a direct object, it can mean "go check" or "go see for oneself."
target_language_example: Je vais aller voir le médecin demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to go see the doctor tomorrow.

meaning: to look elsewhere; to go somewhere else (instead).
additional_notes: Used when you should search for something in another place or choose another option. In the imperative it can sound dismissive: « Va voir ailleurs ! » = “Go away / Look somewhere else!”
target_language_example: Si ce magasin n’a plus ta taille, on peut aller voir ailleurs.
native_language_example: If this store doesn’t have your size anymore, we can look elsewhere.

additional_notes: In standard French, the usual form is « y aller », not « aller y ». The sequence « aller y » is generally not used in normal sentence word order, so this entry is best understood as a reference to the components of the expression rather than a standard standalone phrase. In commands, related forms like « vas-y » or « allez-y » can mean « go ahead ».
target_language_example: On dit « y aller », pas « aller y » en français standard.
native_language_example: People say "y aller," not "aller y" in standard French.

additional_notes: Used for going to a place or destination. Often contracts with articles: à + le = au, à + les = aux (for example, aller au cinéma, aller aux États-Unis).
target_language_example: Peux-tu aller à la mer demain ?
native_language_example: Can you go to the seaside tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used with "aller" (to go) + "à" to express going to a place. "à l'hôpital" means going to the hospital (for treatment, a visit, or work depending on context). Common with "devoir" (must/need to) or "il faut" (it’s necessary to).
target_language_example: Je dois aller à l'hôpital.
native_language_example: I have to go to the hospital.

meaning: to go to the train station.
additional_notes: Used when talking about getting to the train station (la gare). Often appears in questions asking for directions: « Comment aller à la gare ? » or « Des indications pour aller à la gare ». To express the means of transport, you can add « en bus » (by bus) or « en métro » (by metro). You may also hear « à la gare » alone after a verb like « aller » or « être ».
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, comment puis-je aller à la gare ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how can I get to the train station?

meaning: "Come on, let's…" (to urge or encourage action).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French to get things moving or motivate someone. "Allez" literally means "go" (imperative of aller), but here it functions like "come on". Often followed by "on y va" (let’s go) or a verb phrase: "Allez, on le fait" (come on, let’s do it).
target_language_example: Allez, on commence !
native_language_example: Come on, let’s start!

additional_notes: Common spoken prompt used to encourage or urge someone to come (often to start doing something): “Allez” works like “come on” (not literally “go”), and “viens” is the command “come” (to one person). You’ll often hear it alone (“Allez, viens !”) or with a destination/activity (e.g., “Allez, viens ici / au lit / manger / voir…”). For more than one person, you’d say: “Allez, venez.”
target_language_example: Allez, viens, on y va !
native_language_example: Come on, come on, let’s go!

additional_notes: This is the verb "aller" (to go) in the present tense + "vous" (you) with inversion to form a formal/plural question. It can be literal about going somewhere ("Allez-vous à Paris ?"), and it also appears in the common expression "Comment allez-vous ?" meaning "How are you?" (literally "How are you going?").
target_language_example: Allez-vous au travail en métro ?
native_language_example: Do you go to work by subway?

additional_notes: Imperative of "aller" + the pronoun "y" ("there"). Often used to encourage or invite someone to do something: "Allez-y !" = "Go ahead!" You can repeat it for emphasis ("Allez-y, allez-y"). Used with both singular and plural "you" (same spelling for "tu" and "vous" forms here); context tells which one.
target_language_example: Allez-y, je vous écoute.
native_language_example: Go ahead, I’m listening.

meaning: "who knows?" / "go figure." (used to say it’s impossible to know or explain).
additional_notes: Often used as a rhetorical comment when the reason/explanation is unknown or hard to understand. It can stand alone ("Allez savoir.") or be followed by a question word: "Allez savoir pourquoi...", "Allez savoir ce que...", "Allez savoir ce qui...". Common in spoken, conversational French.
target_language_example: Il n’est pas venu, allez savoir pourquoi.
native_language_example: He didn’t come—who knows why.

additional_notes: Informal spoken expression (often written “allez, va”). Used to (1) give in or agree after hesitation (“Okay then, fine.”) or (2) encourage someone to continue or do something (“Go on then.”). Built from imperatives of *aller* (“allez” + “va”), but the overall meaning is idiomatic.
target_language_example: Allez va, je t'accompagne jusqu'à la gare.
native_language_example: All right then, I'll walk you to the station.

additional_notes: Extremely offensive insult. Uses the imperative with « vous » (addressing one person formally or several people). A common variant with « tu » is « Va te faire foutre ». Avoid in polite conversation; it can easily start or escalate conflict.
target_language_example: Je suis furieux : allez vous faire foutre.
native_language_example: I’m furious: go fuck yourself.

meaning: 'are we going…?' / 'are we going to…?' (question form).
additional_notes: This is the verb *aller* (nous form: *allons*) followed by *nous* in an inverted order to form a question (more formal/written style): *Allons-nous + infinitive ?* or used with question words: *Où allons-nous… ? Quand allons-nous… ?* In everyday speech, people often say *On va… ?* or *Est-ce que nous allons… ?* instead.
target_language_example: Allons-nous prendre le bus ou marcher ?
native_language_example: Are we going to take the bus or walk?

additional_notes: This is the 1st-person plural present of aller (“to go”) with inversion (verb + nous) to form a question: Allons-nous au cinéma ? (“Are we going to the movies?”). It can also mean “How are we?” in Comment allons-nous ? You may see it with pronouns like y or en: Y allons-nous ? (“Are we going there?”) and Allons-nous-en ! (“Let’s go / Let’s leave!”). In everyday speech, people often prefer Est-ce que nous allons… ? or On va… ? instead of inversion.
target_language_example: Allons-nous au restaurant ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we going to the restaurant tonight?

additional_notes: Common encouragement to start or move on. Literally “let’s go there” (aller + y), but it’s used like “come on, let’s go” or “go ahead.” Often said on its own, or followed by a short instruction: « Allons-y, … ». Can also mean “let’s get started” in a non-literal sense.
target_language_example: Bon, allons-y : on commence maintenant.
native_language_example: Alright, let’s go: we’re starting now.

meaning: “went to” / “has gone to” (used with **en** for feminine countries, countries starting with a vowel, or continents).
additional_notes: Past tense of **aller** formed with **être**: **être allé(e)(s) + en + place**. Use **en** with feminine countries (e.g., *en France*), countries starting with a vowel (e.g., *en Italie*), and continents (e.g., *en Europe*). With masculine countries, you usually use **au** (*au Canada*), and with plural places **aux** (*aux États-Unis*). The past participle **allé** agrees with the subject: *il est allé*, *elle est allée*, *ils sont allés*, *elles sont allées*.
target_language_example: Il est allé en France.
native_language_example: He went to France.

meaning: "So, it's..." / "Well then, it's..." (to introduce a conclusion, decision, or next step).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to move things along: to sum up, confirm a decision (Alors, c'est décidé.), check an answer (Alors, c'est oui ?), react to a situation (Alors, c'est parfait.), or ask what comes next (Alors, c'est quoi la suite ?). Often sounds like "OK, so..." in conversation.
target_language_example: Alors, c'est bon, on y va ?
native_language_example: So, it’s settled—are we going?

meaning: “So, I…” / “Then, I…” (used to introduce what you did or will do).
additional_notes: “Alors” is a very common connector at the start (or in the middle) of a sentence to show a consequence, next step, or conclusion. With “je”, it often continues a story or explains what happens next: “Alors, je suis venu.” It can also be used in questions: “Alors, je viens ?” = “So, should I come?” In faster speech you may hear it without a clear pause/comma.
target_language_example: Alors, je vais essayer une autre solution.
native_language_example: So, I’m going to try another solution.

meaning: "So, shall we…?" / "So, we…" (to start or move things along).
additional_notes: Common conversational opener used to transition, prompt action, or tease/comment on a situation. It’s often followed by a verb with "on" meaning "we" (e.g., "Alors, on commence ?" = "So, shall we start?"). The tone depends on context: it can sound friendly, impatient, or joking.
target_language_example: Alors, on y va ?
native_language_example: So, are we going?

additional_notes: Used in conversation to start a question, often as a follow-up or to prompt someone to explain. "Alors" means "so/then" and adds a conversational tone (like “So,”). It’s followed by "qu’est-ce que" + subject + verb: « Alors, qu’est-ce que tu veux ? »
target_language_example: Alors, qu'est-ce que tu veux faire ce soir ?
native_language_example: So, what do you want to do tonight?

additional_notes: Used as a conversational opener before a question, often to move things along, ask for an update, or prompt someone to respond. In writing you’ll often see a comma after alors: « Alors, que… ? ». It can sound a bit insistent depending on tone (like “So…?”).
target_language_example: Alors, que faisons-nous maintenant ?
native_language_example: So, what are we doing now?

meaning: "So, you…" / "Well, are you…?" (used to start a question or prompt).
additional_notes: Very common conversational opener. It uses "alors" to introduce what comes next (often a question, conclusion, or decision) and addresses someone directly with "tu" (informal "you"). Often implies “so, what now?” or “so, do you see?”.
target_language_example: Alors, tu viens avec nous ?
native_language_example: So, are you coming with us?

meaning: “So…?” / “So, how is it?” (to ask for a reaction or result).
additional_notes: Common spoken lead-in before a question, often about how something went or what someone thinks of something: “Alors, ça donne quoi ?” (So, what’s the result?), “Alors, ça fait quoi ?” (So, what does it do / how does it feel?), “Alors, ça te plaît ?” (So, do you like it?). You can also use it on its own to prompt someone to answer: “Alors, ça ?” ≈ “Well?”
target_language_example: Alors, ça s’est bien passé ?
native_language_example: So, did it go well?

additional_notes: Commonly introduces a contrast between two facts (often translated as “whereas” or “even though”): « Mes chaussures sont vieilles, alors que les siennes sont neuves. » It can also mean “when/while” to situate one action during another: « Il est parti alors que je dormais. » With the imperfect, it often describes an ongoing background situation.
target_language_example: Elle est sortie alors que je préparais le dîner.
native_language_example: She went out while I was making dinner.

meaning: (for a woman speaking) in love with him.
additional_notes: Used with the verb être: « Je suis amoureuse de lui. » It describes a woman/girl who is in love; masculine form is « amoureux de lui ». You also commonly see « tomber amoureuse de lui » = “to fall in love with him.”
target_language_example: Je crois que je suis amoureuse de lui, mais je n'ose pas lui dire.
native_language_example: I think I'm in love with him, but I don't dare tell him.

additional_notes: Used to talk about romantic love toward a person: « être amoureux/amoureuse de + someone ». The adjective agrees with the subject: amoureux (male), amoureuse (female). Often used with intensifiers like « follement » (madly).
target_language_example: Je suis amoureux de toi depuis longtemps.
native_language_example: I’ve been in love with you for a long time.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is in love with you: « Il/Je suis amoureux de toi ». Adjective agreement: a man says « amoureux », a woman says « amoureuse ». With formal/polite “you,” use « amoureux/amoureuse de vous ». In the negative you may see « ne … pas » and « plus »: « Je ne suis plus amoureux de toi » = “I’m not in love with you anymore.”
target_language_example: Je suis amoureux de toi depuis longtemps.
native_language_example: I’ve been in love with you for a long time.

meaning: Have fun! (to one person you address as “tu”).
additional_notes: Imperative form of “s’amuser” (to have fun). You say it to wish someone a good time: before a party, a trip, an outing, etc. For more than one person or a formal “you,” use: “Amusez-vous bien.”
target_language_example: Amuse-toi bien pendant ton voyage !
native_language_example: Have fun on your trip!

additional_notes: Imperative with "vous" (polite to one person or to a group). Often used as a friendly send-off: "Allez, amusez-vous bien !" You can also ask "Vous amusez-vous bien ?" = "Are you having fun?"
target_language_example: Merci, amusez-vous bien ce soir !
native_language_example: Thanks, have fun tonight!

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to say “pet.” Often used with the verb avoir: « J’ai un animal de compagnie » (I have a pet). You can specify the type with « comme animal de compagnie » (as a pet): « un lapin comme animal de compagnie ».
target_language_example: On a un chat comme animal de compagnie.
native_language_example: We have a cat as a pet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about animals kept by people, usually at home (e.g., a cat or dog). In everyday conversation, you may also hear just "un animal" when the context is clearly pets. Agreement: masculine singular "un animal domestique", feminine singular "une chèvre domestique", plural "des animaux domestiques".
target_language_example: Le chat est un animal domestique.
native_language_example: A cat is a domestic animal (a pet).

additional_notes: A common way to say “camera” in French, especially for still photos. Often used with possessives: mon/ton/son appareil photo (“my/your/his/her camera”). In casual speech you may also hear “un appareil” when the context is clear, but “appareil photo” is the safe, clear term.
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon appareil photo à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot my camera at home.

additional_notes: Used when you want to contact the police (usually by phone) to report something, ask for help, or to say you will report someone. Common with "je vais" / "on va" (I’m going to / we’re going to).
target_language_example: Si tu vois quelque chose de suspect, on va appeler la police.
native_language_example: If you see something suspicious, we’re going to call the police.

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) form of appeler addressed to vous (one person formally, or more than one person). Often used to ask someone to phone you later: Appelez-moi ce soir / demain / après… You can also use it to mean “call me [a name]”: Appelez-moi Marie.
target_language_example: Si vous avez des questions, appelez-moi demain matin.
native_language_example: If you have questions, call me tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) form of appeler + the object pronoun moi (“me”). Used to ask someone to phone you, often with a time or condition: appelle-moi quand… (call me when…), appelle-moi si… (call me if…), appelle-moi à… (call me at…). Commonly paired with s’il te plaît to be more polite.
target_language_example: Appelle-moi quand tu arrives.
native_language_example: Call me when you arrive.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to phone you later, when a certain condition is met (e.g., quand tu as fini / as le temps / es prêt / seras à Paris). “Appelle-moi” is the informal (tu) command form; with someone you address as vous, say “Appelez-moi quand vous…”.
target_language_example: Appelle-moi quand tu arrives à la maison.
native_language_example: Call me when you get home.

additional_notes: This is the past form (passé composé) of the verb phrase « appeler la police » (“to call the police”): « (subject) + avoir + appelé ». Example: « J’ai appelé la police. » In questions you may see « As-tu… ? / Avez-vous… ? » (tu vs vous), or the informal spoken form « T’as… ? ». « On a appelé la police » often means “someone/we called the police.”
target_language_example: Il a appelé la police tout de suite.
native_language_example: He called the police right away.

additional_notes: Imperative of the verb *apporter* (“to bring”) + the indirect object pronoun *moi* (“to me”). Used to ask/order someone to bring something to you. Often followed by a noun: *Apporte-moi mes lunettes.* You can swap the pronoun: *apporte-lui* (bring him/her), *apporte-nous* (bring us).
target_language_example: Apporte-moi un verre d’eau, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Bring me a glass of water, please.

additional_notes: Uses the verb apprendre (“to learn”) with a language. You can swap in other languages: apprendre l’anglais, apprendre l’espagnol, etc. If you want to say you’re currently doing it, French commonly uses the present tense: J’apprends le français (“I’m learning French”).
target_language_example: Je devrais apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I should learn French.

additional_notes: A common phrase for studying a language that isn’t your native language. "Apprendre" means “to learn,” and "une langue étrangère" means “a foreign language.” You can add which language with "apprendre le français / l’espagnol", or say "apprendre une langue" (learn a language).
target_language_example: J’essaie d’apprendre une langue étrangère pour voyager.
native_language_example: I’m trying to learn a foreign language to travel.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb (apprendre à + infinitive) to mean “learn to do something.” It can also mean “teach someone to do something,” often with an indirect object (e.g., Je peux t’apprendre à… / Je peux vous apprendre à…).
target_language_example: Je veux apprendre à nager.
native_language_example: I want to learn to swim.

additional_notes: Used with apprendre + à + infinitive to talk about learning how to do something. You’ll most often see it in the past with avoir (passé composé): j’ai appris à…, il/elle a appris à…. Agreement can change with gender/number in some contexts (e.g., elle a appris à…, elles ont appris à…; also apprise/appris in certain constructions). Common in questions like « Quand avez-vous appris à… ? ».
target_language_example: J’ai appris à conduire l’année dernière.
native_language_example: I learned to drive last year.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening two days from now. It can be placed at the beginning or end of the sentence (e.g., « Après-demain, je pars » / « Je pars après-demain »).
target_language_example: On se voit après-demain à 10 heures.
native_language_example: See you the day after tomorrow at 10 o’clock.

additional_notes: Means the part of the day after noon. Common in time expressions: « trois heures de l’après-midi » (3 p.m.). You can also say « dimanche après-midi » (Sunday afternoon). Usually masculine (« un/cet après-midi »), but « une/cette après-midi » is also heard/written, especially in some regions.
target_language_example: On se voit cet après-midi vers 15 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we see each other this afternoon around 3 p.m.?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an earlier action (avoir + past participle) that happens before the main action in the sentence. Common pattern: après avoir + past participle (parlé, étudié, vu, etc.). It refers to the subject of the main clause (e.g., Je vais me coucher après avoir étudié = I studied, then I go to bed).
target_language_example: Après avoir fini le travail, on est rentrés à la maison.
native_language_example: After finishing work, we went home.

additional_notes: Used to say something is realized, felt, or judged only later (often with regret or hindsight). With events, it can mean something happened too late or arrived after everything was already over.
target_language_example: Après coup, j’ai compris que c’était une mauvaise idée.
native_language_example: Afterwards, I realized it was a bad idea.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than lunchtime. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence to set the time (“Après le déjeuner, …”) or after the verb (“… après le déjeuner”). You can also say “juste après le déjeuner” = “right after lunch.”
target_language_example: On se voit après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: See you after lunch.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens after the evening meal. Often appears with timing words like "juste" (right) or "tout de suite" (immediately): "juste après le dîner" = right after dinner; "tout de suite après le dîner" = immediately after dinner.
target_language_example: On fera une promenade après le dîner.
native_language_example: We'll go for a walk after dinner.

meaning: after work (after finishing your job for the day).
additional_notes: Used to say what happens once the workday is over. Often comes at the beginning or end of a sentence as a time expression (e.g., « après le travail, je… » / « je… après le travail »).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au café après le travail.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the café after work.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause: « après que + subject + verb ». In careful/standard French, « après que » is followed by the indicative (often a past tense in narratives). In everyday speech you may also hear the subjunctive after « après que », but many speakers consider it nonstandard.
target_language_example: Nous sommes rentrés à la maison après que le film a commencé.
native_language_example: We went home after the movie started.

meaning: "after you" (polite: "you first"), or "after you" (later than you).
additional_notes: Used literally for time/sequence: "Elle est sortie après toi" = she left after you. Also used as a polite way to let someone go first: "Après toi." Common related expressions: "d’après toi" = "according to you / in your opinion"; "en avoir après toi" = "to have it in for you" (to be angry at you / hold a grudge).
target_language_example: Vas-y, après toi !
native_language_example: Go ahead, after you!

additional_notes: Used to introduce a final thought, justification, or change of mind after considering the situation. It can appear at the start of a sentence (Après tout, …) or at the end (…, après tout) and often supports an argument: “he has the right…, after all.”
target_language_example: Après tout, on peut toujours essayer.
native_language_example: After all, we can always try.

additional_notes: Often said as a polite way to let someone go ahead of you (e.g., holding a door): « Après vous. » Literally means 'after you.' Don’t confuse it with « d’après vous », which means 'according to you / in your opinion.'
target_language_example: Après vous, madame.
native_language_example: After you, ma’am.

additional_notes: Refers to the decorated tree used for Christmas. You can say "décorer l’arbre de Noël" (to decorate the Christmas tree) and "sous l’arbre de Noël" (under the Christmas tree), where gifts are often placed.
target_language_example: On met les cadeaux sous l’arbre de Noël.
native_language_example: We put the gifts under the Christmas tree.

additional_notes: A common noun; usually masculine: (un) arc-en-ciel. Often used with weather contexts, especially after rain: « après la pluie ». It can be used literally (a rainbow in the sky) and in expressions like « au bout de l’arc-en-ciel » (“at the end of the rainbow”). Plural: des arcs-en-ciel.
target_language_example: Après l’orage, on a vu un arc-en-ciel au-dessus de la ville.
native_language_example: After the storm, we saw a rainbow above the city.

additional_notes: Used for weapons that fire bullets using an explosive charge (e.g., a pistol, rifle). More formal/technical than "pistolet" (handgun) or the broad word "arme" (weapon). Often used in questions about owning or carrying a gun: "posséder/avoir une arme à feu", "porter une arme à feu".
target_language_example: Il est interdit de porter une arme à feu ici.
native_language_example: It’s forbidden to carry a firearm here.

meaning: “does it happen?” / “what happens?” or “does he arrive?” (in a question).
additional_notes: This is the verb *arriver* in an inverted question with *il* (“he/it”): *arrive-t-il ?* The extra *-t-* is added only for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel (like *arrive*) and the subject pronoun starts with a vowel (*il/elle/on*): *arrive-t-il*, *arrive-t-elle*, *arrive-t-on*. Depending on context, *arriver* can mean “to arrive” (reach a place) or “to happen/occur” (especially in questions like *Qu’arrive-t-il ?* = “What’s happening?”). This inversion style is fairly formal; in everyday speech you often hear *Il arrive à quelle heure ?* / *Qu’est-ce qui arrive ?*
target_language_example: Pourquoi arrive-t-il toujours en retard ?
native_language_example: Why does he always arrive late?

additional_notes: With a place or abstract noun, arriver à often means "arrive at" or "reach" (for example, arriver à la station, arriver à une conclusion). With an infinitive, it often means "manage to" or "succeed in" doing something: je n'arrive pas à comprendre = "I can't manage to understand."
target_language_example: Combien de temps cela prend-il pour arriver à la station ?
native_language_example: How long does it take to arrive at the station?

meaning: can you (manage to) / are you able to.
additional_notes: From the verb "arriver à" + infinitive, meaning "to manage to do" or "to succeed in doing". Often implies difficulty or effort. In questions, inversion gives "Arrives-tu à…?"; you can also say "Tu arrives à…?" (more common in speech).
target_language_example: Arrives-tu à comprendre cette phrase sans aide ?
native_language_example: Can you manage to understand this sentence without help?

additional_notes:
Used with an infinitive: « Arrivez-vous à + infinitive ? » asks whether someone succeeds in doing something (often like “can you manage to…?”). Example: « Arrivez-vous à lire ça ? » = “Can you read that?”

Note: if it’s followed by a place (no infinitive), « arrivez-vous à + place ? » can mean “are you arriving in/to…?” (e.g., « Quand arrivez-vous à Paris ? » = “When do you arrive in Paris?”).
target_language_example: Arrivez-vous à comprendre cette phrase sans traduction ?
native_language_example: Can you manage to understand this sentence without a translation?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the place where buses stop to pick up and drop off passengers. Very common with location phrases like « où est… ? » (where is…?), « il y a… » (there is…), and « à l’arrêt de bus » (at the bus stop).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à l’arrêt de bus à 8 heures.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the bus stop at 8 o’clock.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to tell one person to stop doing something. arrête is the tu-form imperative; with vous, use arrêtez de.
target_language_example: Arrête de te plaindre.
native_language_example: Stop complaining.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone ("tu") to stop an action that’s affecting you. It’s followed by an infinitive: "Arrête de me + infinitive" (e.g., "arrête de me regarder"). "me" is the object pronoun meaning "me" placed before the infinitive. Note: "arrêter" can mean "to stop" (not "to arrest" in these contexts).
target_language_example: Arrête de me déranger, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Stop bothering me, please.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop speaking. Can be a firm command; adding "s’il te plaît" makes it more polite. Pattern: "Arrête de" + infinitive (e.g., "Arrête de crier" = Stop shouting).
target_language_example: Arrête de parler et écoute-moi deux minutes, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Stop talking and listen to me for two minutes, please.

meaning: "Stop (yourself) ..." (telling one person informally to stop doing something).
additional_notes: Used in the tu imperative: arrête + de + reflexive infinitive (te + verb), especially with reflexive verbs like se disputer (argue), se débattre (struggle), se quereller (quarrel). It’s a common way to tell someone to stop an action. Note: arrêter usually means “to stop,” not “to arrest.”
target_language_example: Arrête de te plaindre !
native_language_example: Stop complaining!

additional_notes: Used with the verb arrêter de + infinitive (“to stop doing something”). Here, fumer = “to smoke.” Often used with advice/obligation expressions like devoir (“must”), il faut (“it’s necessary”), and (tu/vous) devrais/devriez (“should”).
target_language_example: J’essaie d’arrêter de fumer depuis le mois dernier.
native_language_example: I’ve been trying to stop smoking since last month.

meaning: "Stop" + verb (telling people to stop doing something).
additional_notes: This is the command form (imperative) of "arrêter" addressed to "vous" (you plural or polite you). It’s followed by an infinitive: "Arrêtez de crier" = “Stop shouting.” Can sound firm or annoyed depending on tone; for a more polite request you can add "s’il vous plaît".
target_language_example: Arrêtez de courir dans le couloir !
native_language_example: Stop running in the hallway!

additional_notes: Used to tell one person formally (vous) or several people to stop doing something that affects you. It’s typically followed by an infinitive: « Arrêtez de me + infinitif » (e.g., regarder, fixer, tirer). Note: « arrêter » often means “to stop,” and is not the same as English “to arrest” in this context.
target_language_example: Arrêtez de me parler comme ça !
native_language_example: Stop talking to me like that!

additional_notes: Used as an imperative with *vous* (talking to more than one person, or to one person politely). It’s followed by an infinitive reflexive verb: *Arrêtez de vous disputer* (“Stop arguing”), *Arrêtez de vous moquer de moi* (“Stop making fun of me”). Literally “stop yourselves from …”. Note: *arrêter* looks like English “arrest,” but here it means “to stop.”
target_language_example: Arrêtez de vous inquiéter, tout ira bien.
native_language_example: Stop worrying; everything will be fine.

additional_notes: Used for a fighting discipline or combat sport (often taught in a school/dojo), e.g., kung-fu, judo, karate. Usually masculine: un art martial; plural: des arts martiaux.
target_language_example: Elle pratique un art martial depuis trois ans.
native_language_example: She has been practicing a martial art for three years.

additional_notes: Question form of tu as, made with inversion. It is common in more formal or written yes/no questions. When followed by a past participle, English often translates it as 'did you ... ?' rather than 'have you ... ?'.
target_language_example: As-tu fini tes devoirs ?
native_language_example: Did you finish your homework?

meaning: 'did you buy' / 'have you bought' (informal question form).
additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of "tu as acheté" (you bought / you have bought). It uses inversion: verb + "-tu" + past participle. Often used in writing or more formal speech; in everyday conversation you may hear "Tu as acheté… ?" or "Est-ce que tu as acheté… ?".
target_language_example: As-tu acheté du pain en rentrant ?
native_language_example: Did you buy bread on your way back?

meaning: "have you brought" (asking if someone brought something).
additional_notes: This is a question using inversion: "tu as apporté" (you brought / you have brought) becomes "as-tu apporté… ?" In the passé composé, "apporter" uses "avoir" + past participle "apporté". With "Qu'…" it becomes "Qu'as-tu apporté ?" (= "What did you bring?").
target_language_example: As-tu apporté ton passeport ?
native_language_example: Did you bring your passport?

additional_notes: Used to ask a yes/no question in the past about something that has happened (or been done) at least once. Literally it’s the inversion question form of "tu as" (= "have you") + "déjà" (= "already"). In questions, "déjà" often translates as "ever" (experience up to now): "As-tu déjà… ?" = "Have you ever… ?" It can also be "already" when asking if something is done yet: "As-tu déjà pris ton médicament ?" = "Have you taken your medicine already?"
target_language_example: As-tu déjà visité Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever visited Paris?

meaning: "have you ever seen a" (asking someone if they have seen something before).
additional_notes: A common question pattern: « As-tu déjà vu un/une … ? » = “Have you ever seen a …?” Use « un » with masculine nouns and « une » with feminine nouns. « As-tu » is informal/singular “you” (tu); in more formal situations use « Avez-vous déjà vu … ? ».
target_language_example: As-tu déjà vu une girafe ?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a giraffe?

meaning: "have you ever been…?" (asking about past experience).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has ever had an experience up to now. Built from inversion for questions (as-tu = "have you") + déjà ("ever/already") + été (past participle of être, "been"). Often followed by an adjective (malade), or by a past participle in the passive voice (été trahi/embrassé/traité) meaning "been betrayed/kissed/treated". Agreement: été is followed by forms that may change for gender/number (blessé/blessée, trahi/trahie, traité/traitée).
target_language_example: As-tu déjà été à Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Paris?

additional_notes: Inverted question form of "tu as entendu" (from entendre = to hear). Used to ask if someone heard a sound, a question, news, a story, or something about a topic. Often followed by a noun or clause: "As-tu entendu ce bruit ?", "As-tu entendu parler de… ?" (have you heard about…?).
target_language_example: As-tu entendu parler du nouveau restaurant ?
native_language_example: Have you heard about the new restaurant?

meaning: “did you have…?” / “have you had…?” (past of avoir, in a question).
additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of **tu as eu** (passé composé of *avoir*). It’s used to ask whether someone **had/experienced** something: *As-tu eu des ennuis ?* (“Did you get in trouble?”), *As-tu eu du café ?* (“Did you have/Did you get some coffee?”). The **-tu** inversion is common in more formal or neutral questions; in everyday speech you’ll also hear **Est-ce que tu as eu…** or **Tu as eu… ?**
target_language_example: As-tu eu le temps de déjeuner ?
native_language_example: Did you have time to eat lunch?

meaning: "have you done" / "did you do" (passé composé question).
additional_notes: This is an inversion question form: **as** (from *avoir*) + **tu** + **fait** (past participle of *faire*). It asks about something completed in the past, often translated as either **“Did you do...?”** or **“Have you done...?”** depending on context. *Faire* is very broad in French and can mean **do**, **make**, or **get (something) done** (e.g., *faire la vaisselle* “do the dishes”, *faire les achats* “do the shopping”).
target_language_example: As-tu fait tes devoirs ?
native_language_example: Did you do your homework?

additional_notes: Uses inversion for a yes/no question: "as" (tu as) + "-tu" + past participle, often with "jamais" meaning "ever" in questions. More neutral/standard than "tu as déjà... ?"; in casual speech you’ll also hear "T’as jamais... ?".
target_language_example: As-tu jamais voyagé seul(e) à l’étranger ?
native_language_example: Have you ever traveled abroad alone?

additional_notes: This is the inversion form used to ask a question in the passé composé: as (have) + tu (you) + lu (read). It’s addressed to one person you’re on “tu” terms with (friend, child, etc.). Often followed by a direct object: As-tu lu ce livre ?
target_language_example: As-tu lu cet e-mail ?
native_language_example: Have you read this email?

additional_notes: A yes/no question using inversion (verb + -tu). It’s the passé composé of manger: "tu as mangé" (you ate / you have eaten). In everyday speech, you’ll also hear: "Tu as mangé ?" or "T’as mangé ?"
target_language_example: As-tu mangé avant de venir ?
native_language_example: Have you eaten before coming?

additional_notes: Question form of the verb *perdre* (to lose) in the *passé composé*: **as** (you have) + **perdu** (lost). Used with a direct object (keys, ticket, money, weight) or in expressions like **As-tu perdu la tête ?** (“Are you crazy?/Have you lost your mind?”). With **Combien…?**, it often means “How much did you lose?” (money, weight).
target_language_example: As-tu perdu ton téléphone ?
native_language_example: Did you lose your phone?

meaning: "did you take" / "have you taken" (formal/inverted question form).
additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of the passé composé of **prendre**: **tu as pris** (you took/you have taken) → **as-tu pris… ?** (did you take…?). It’s used in more formal written/spoken French than **Tu as pris… ?** or **Est-ce que tu as pris… ?**. The exact meaning depends on context: taking something (photos), having something (breakfast), taking a side (**prendre parti**), taking a measurement (**prendre sa température**).
target_language_example: As-tu pris tes médicaments aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: Did you take your medicine today?

meaning: "have you noticed" (asking someone if they observed something).
additional_notes: This is a question using inversion: "as-tu" = "have you" + past participle "remarqué". It’s used to check whether someone has observed a change, detail, or sign. Often followed by a noun or clause: "As-tu remarqué un changement ?" / "As-tu remarqué que… ?".
target_language_example: As-tu remarqué que la porte est ouverte ?
native_language_example: Have you noticed that the door is open?

additional_notes: Inversion question with "tu" (to one person you address as tu). Used with "recevoir" to ask if someone got/received something (a note/grade, letter, message, reply). The past participle is "reçu"; you can also ask "As-tu reçu… ?" + object.
target_language_example: As-tu reçu le mail que je t’ai envoyé hier ?
native_language_example: Did you get the email I sent you yesterday?

additional_notes: Question form with inversion: **as** (from *avoir*) + **tu** + **trouvé** (past participle of *trouver*). Used to ask if someone found a person/thing, or found an answer/solution. In casual speech, you’ll often hear **Tu as trouvé… ?** instead. With inversion, a **-t-** can be added for pronunciation with *il/elle/on* (e.g., *A-t-il trouvé… ?*), but not with *tu*.
target_language_example: As-tu trouvé une solution ?
native_language_example: Did you find a solution?

additional_notes: Inversion question form of "tu as vu" (you have seen). Used to ask whether someone saw a person/thing, often with a time expression: « As-tu vu ça ? » / « Quand as-tu vu … pour la dernière fois ? ». In casual speech, you’ll also hear « T’as vu… ? ».
target_language_example: As-tu vu mes clés ?
native_language_example: Have you seen my keys?

additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of "tu as été" (passé composé of "être" with "avoir"). It’s used to ask if someone has been in a state (sage, seul/seule, amoureux) or has experienced something (invité, maltraité, piqué, vacciné). Often corresponds to English "Have you been…?" or, depending on context, "Were you…?".
target_language_example: As-tu été fatigué hier ?
native_language_example: Were you tired yesterday?

additional_notes: Question form of tu as (“you have”), used when speaking to one person informally. This inverted form with a hyphen is common in writing and more formal speech; in everyday conversation, tu as ... ? is often more common.
target_language_example: As-tu les clés ?
native_language_example: Do you have the keys?

additional_notes: Question form of **avoir besoin de** (“to need”). Used with **de + noun/infinitive**: *As-tu besoin de ce livre ?* (“Do you need this book?”), *As-tu besoin de boire ?* (“Do you need to drink?”). This is the **tu** form (informal singular). More formal: **Avez-vous besoin de… ?**
target_language_example: As-tu besoin de mon aide ?
native_language_example: Do you need my help?

additional_notes: "As-tu" is the inverted question form of "tu as" (you have). Use "des" before a plural noun (often meaning "some" or just indicating an unspecified amount/number): "As-tu des frères ?" = "Do you have (any) brothers?" In very formal speech, prefer "Avez-vous des... ?".
target_language_example: As-tu des questions ?
native_language_example: Do you have any questions?

meaning: "do you have a" (asking if someone has something; masculine singular).
additional_notes: This is the verb "avoir" (to have) in the "tu" form (as) with inversion to make a question: "As-tu… ?" It’s used before a masculine singular noun: "As-tu un sac ?" For feminine singular, use "as-tu une… ?"; for plural, "as-tu des… ?".
target_language_example: As-tu un stylo pour écrire ?
native_language_example: Do you have a pen to write?

meaning: “do you have a…?” (addressing one person; before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Question formed with inversion: "as" (you have) + "tu" (you) + a noun phrase. Used with "une" because the following noun is feminine (e.g., une opinion, une suggestion). For masculine nouns, use "as-tu un…?".
target_language_example: As-tu une question ?
native_language_example: Do you have a question?

additional_notes: This is the 2nd-person singular form of the expression **avoir l’air** (tu **as l’air**…). It’s often used with an indirect object pronoun: **Tu m’as l’air…** = “You seem/you look… (to me).” It can be followed by an adjective (**Tu m’as l’air fatigué**), by **de + noun** (**Tu m’as l’air d’un étudiant**), or by **de + infinitive** (**Tu m’as l’air de comprendre**). Note: in normal French spelling, **l’air** takes an apostrophe (l’).
target_language_example: Tu m'as l'air en pleine forme.
native_language_example: You look in great shape (to me).

additional_notes: Imperative form of « s’asseoir » used when speaking to one person politely (vous) or to more than one person. Often used on its own, or after another instruction: « Venez… et asseyez-vous. »
target_language_example: Asseyez-vous, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please sit down.

additional_notes: Used to say there is sufficient time to do something. Very common with "pour" + infinitive ("assez de temps pour + verb"). You can also use it in questions like "Assez de temps ?" / "Avons-nous assez de temps ?".
target_language_example: On a assez de temps pour manger avant le film.
native_language_example: We have enough time to eat before the movie.

additional_notes: Imperative form of **s’asseoir** (“to sit down”), used when speaking to someone you address as **tu** (a friend, child, etc.). For a more polite or plural version, use **asseyez-vous** (“sit down”). Often followed by details like **avec moi** (with me) or **plus près** (closer).
target_language_example: Assieds-toi ici, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Sit here, please.

additional_notes: Means not deciding or acting yet, and seeing what happens first. In modern usage, « attendre et voir » is more common, but « attendre voir » can be encountered, especially in more informal or elliptical speech.
target_language_example: On va attendre voir ce qui se passe.
native_language_example: We'll wait and see what happens.

additional_notes: Used at the beginning of clauses in legal or official documents (contracts, court decisions) to introduce background facts or reasons before a conclusion. It’s very formal and mostly written; in everyday French you’d usually say “comme”, “puisque”, or “étant donné que”.
target_language_example: Attendu que le locataire n’a pas payé le loyer, le contrat peut être résilié.
native_language_example: Whereas the tenant has not paid the rent, the contract may be terminated.

additional_notes: Used as a warning about something potentially dangerous or something you might bump into. "Aux" = "à + les", so it’s followed by a plural noun (e.g., aux marches, aux portes). For a singular noun you’ll often see "attention au" (masc.) or "attention à la" (fem.).
target_language_example: Attention aux vélos !
native_language_example: Watch out for bikes!

additional_notes: Most often used after verbs like « faire attention à » (to pay attention to / to be careful about) and « porter une grande attention à » (to pay close attention to). With a person, it often means “to pay attention to them” (or in the negative, “don’t pay them any attention”).
target_language_example: Fais attention à la marche !
native_language_example: Watch out for the step!

meaning: to catch a cold; to get chilled.
additional_notes: Literally “to catch cold.” Commonly used as a warning (often in the near future): « Tu vas attraper froid ! » It can mean either getting sick (a cold) or simply getting too cold from exposure, depending on context. Often used with « ne pas »: « Pour ne pas attraper froid ».
target_language_example: Mets ton manteau, tu vas attraper froid.
native_language_example: Put your coat on, you’re going to catch a cold.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going past a limit in space ("au-delà du fleuve" = on the other side of the river) or in a more abstract sense (looking beyond appearances, beyond distance, etc.). Often followed by "de" + noun: "au-delà de ...".
target_language_example: Il faut penser au-delà des apparences.
native_language_example: You have to think beyond appearances.

additional_notes: Used to express going past a limit (physical, numerical, or figurative). It can mean a place “past” something (Au-delà de la gare), a quantity/age “over” something (au-delà de cent ans), or an idea “beyond” a certain point (au-delà de…). Often contrasts with “en-deçà de” (below/under).
target_language_example: Au-delà de 50 euros, la livraison est gratuite.
native_language_example: Over 50 euros, delivery is free.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a lower position (on a page, in a building, etc.): « au-dessous » = “below/underneath.” Often followed by « de » to compare levels/standards: « au-dessous de… » (below…). In the fixed expression « au-dessous de tout », it means “beneath everything / beyond unacceptable” (very bad, disgraceful).
target_language_example: Le garage est au-dessous de l'appartement.
native_language_example: The garage is below the apartment.

additional_notes: Often used with **de** to say what something is above: **au-dessus de + noun/pronoun** (e.g., *au-dessus de moi* = above me). It can also be used alone to mean “up above/overhead.” Contrast with *sur* (“on top of,” in contact).
target_language_example: Il y a un pont au-dessus de la rivière.
native_language_example: There is a bridge above the river.

additional_notes: Used for physical position ("above/over" something): « au-dessus de la rivière », « juste au-dessus de zéro ». Figuratively, it can mean being "beyond" something (not affected by it) or thinking you are "above" rules/criticism: « Je suis au-dessus de tout ça », « se croire au-dessus de tout ». Note the opposite: « au-dessous de » = below/under.
target_language_example: L’appartement est au-dessus de la boulangerie.
native_language_example: The apartment is above the bakery.

additional_notes: Used to describe something located or happening higher than where you are (in the sky, on a higher floor, etc.). Often answers “Where?” (Où ?) and can be used with movement verbs like voler (“to fly”).
target_language_example: Un avion passe au-dessus de nous.
native_language_example: A plane is flying over us.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something is higher than or positioned over something else. Often expresses physical location (au-dessus du lit) but can also be figurative, meaning 'beyond' or 'not subject to' (au-dessus du soupçon = above suspicion). Contraction: au-dessus du = au-dessus de + le; also au-dessus de la, au-dessus des.
target_language_example: Le tableau est accroché au-dessus du canapé.
native_language_example: The painting is hanging above the couch.

additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le" and is used with many sports/activities after "jouer". So "jouer au baseball" = "to play baseball". With preferences/comparisons: "préférer X au baseball" = "prefer X to baseball".
target_language_example: Le week-end, on joue souvent au baseball au parc.
native_language_example: On weekends, we often play baseball at the park.

meaning: right in the middle of; smack in the middle of.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens at the exact middle of a time period or place, often suggesting it’s surprising or inconvenient (e.g., in the middle of the night / day). Often followed by a noun: au beau milieu de la nuit, au beau milieu de la journée, au beau milieu de la rue.
target_language_example: Il m’a appelé au beau milieu de la réunion.
native_language_example: He called me right in the middle of the meeting.

additional_notes: Often used as an adverbial phrase meaning “if needed” (Je suis là, au besoin. = “I’m here if you need me.”). It can also appear with a noun to mean “to meet (someone’s) needs”: répondre au besoin du client = “to meet the customer’s needs.”
target_language_example: Tu peux m’appeler au besoin.
native_language_example: You can call me if necessary / if you need to.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens at an appropriate or convenient time. Common in set phrases like « au bon endroit, au bon moment » (“in the right place at the right time”) and « Tu arrives au bon moment » (“You’re arriving just in time / at the perfect moment”).
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé au bon moment pour t’aider.
native_language_example: I arrived at the right time to help you.

meaning: at the edge of; on the verge of.
additional_notes: Used for a physical location near the edge of something (au bord de la rivière = by the riverbank) and also figuratively for being very close to a situation happening (au bord de la guerre = on the brink of war). Often followed by a noun with a definite article (de la, du, des) or a place name (au bord de Paris).
target_language_example: Le village est au bord de la mer.
native_language_example: The village is on the edge of the sea (by the seaside).

meaning: by the sea; at the seaside.
additional_notes: Literally “at the edge of the sea.” Used to talk about being near the sea (a seaside town, the coast, the beach area). Common after verbs like aller (to go), vivre/grandir (to live/grow up), or être (to be).
target_language_example: On a loué une maison au bord de la mer pour le week-end.
native_language_example: We rented a house by the sea for the weekend.

additional_notes: "Boulot" is an informal word for "work/job." "Au boulot !" is a common way to say “Back to work!” or “Let’s get to work!” With verbs of movement like "aller", it means going to work ("aller au boulot"), and with "être" it means being at work ("être au boulot").
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas répondre : je suis au boulot.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't reply: I'm at work.

meaning: after (a period of time); at the end of (a place/thing).
additional_notes: With time expressions, it means “after”: « au bout de trois jours » = “after three days.” With locations/objects, it means “at the end of”: « tout au bout de la rue » = “at the very end of the street,” « au bout de la table » = “at the end of the table.” It’s often followed by a duration (quelques jours/semaines, trois jours, combien de temps) or a noun (la rue, la table).
target_language_example: Au bout de dix minutes, le bus est enfin arrivé.
native_language_example: After ten minutes, the bus finally arrived.

additional_notes: Used to sum up the final outcome after considering everything (similar to “when all is said and done”). Often appears at the start or end of a sentence as a conclusion.
target_language_example: Au bout du compte, on a décidé de rester à la maison.
native_language_example: In the end, we decided to stay at home.

meaning: at the end of the hallway/corridor.
additional_notes: Used to give directions indoors (hotels, apartments, offices). Often followed by "à droite" (on the right) or "à gauche" (on the left): "Au bout du couloir, à droite." It can describe where a room or door is: "La salle de bains est au bout du couloir."
target_language_example: Les toilettes sont au bout du couloir, à gauche.
native_language_example: The restrooms are at the end of the hallway, on the left.

meaning: completely exhausted; at the end of your rope.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to say someone is mentally or physically worn out, sometimes because of stress or difficult circumstances. Often used with "être" (Je suis / Il est / Vous êtes au bout du rouleau) or after "avoir l’air" (Elle a l’air au bout du rouleau).
target_language_example: Après trois nuits sans dormir, je suis au bout du rouleau.
native_language_example: After three nights without sleeping, I'm at the end of my rope.

meaning: at the office; to the office.
additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le". With verbs of being/location (être, rester, arriver), it often means "at the office" (arriver au bureau = arrive at the office). With verbs of movement (aller, se rendre), it means "to the office".
target_language_example: Je suis au bureau aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I'm at the office today.

additional_notes: Used to express a precaution or possibility: you do something now because something might happen later. Often followed by a clause with the conditional (e.g., « au cas où vous voudriez… »), or used alone (« au cas où ») meaning “just in case.”
target_language_example: Prends un parapluie, au cas où il pleuvrait.
native_language_example: Take an umbrella, in case it rains.

additional_notes: Used to locate something in the middle of a place or object: au centre du parc/de la ville/de la cible. Can also refer to a “center” as a place people go (e.g., au centre-ville = downtown, au centre commercial = the shopping mall).
target_language_example: Le restaurant est au centre de la ville.
native_language_example: The restaurant is in the center of the city.

meaning: in/to downtown; in/to the city center.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a location in the central part of a town/city, or movement there. Often follows verbs like être/se situer/se trouver (to be/located) and aller (to go). With motion, English may use “to” (aller au centre-ville).
target_language_example: On va au centre-ville ce soir.
native_language_example: We’re going downtown tonight.

meaning: (to be/keep) warm; in a warm place.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like être/rester (to be/stay), garder (to keep), or mettre (to put) to talk about staying warm or keeping someone/something warm (often indoors, out of the cold). Common in instructions: « Restez au chaud » = “Stay warm / Stay inside where it’s warm.” « Bien au chaud » emphasizes extra warmth/coziness.
target_language_example: Il fait froid dehors, alors on reste bien au chaud à la maison.
native_language_example: It’s cold outside, so we’re staying nice and warm at home.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "être" to say someone doesn't currently have a job: "être au chômage". It can refer to being unemployed in general, and sometimes implies being registered for unemployment benefits.
target_language_example: Depuis janvier, elle est au chômage et cherche un poste.
native_language_example: Since January, she’s been unemployed and is looking for a position.

additional_notes: Means going to (or being at) a movie theater. Used with verbs like aller/venir (go/come): « On va au cinéma. ». It can also be used figuratively in expressions like « comme au cinéma » (“like in a movie”) or « Tu te crois au cinéma ? » to say someone is acting as if real life were a movie.
target_language_example: On va au cinéma ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we going to the movies tonight?

meaning: clear; clarified (used in expressions meaning “to clear things up”).
additional_notes: Mostly used with verbs like **mettre au clair** or **tirer au clair**: **mettre/tirer quelque chose au clair** = “to clarify/clear up/sort out something,” often after confusion or a misunderstanding. Commonly appears with **les choses** (“things”): **mettre les choses au clair** = “to set things straight.”
target_language_example: Avant de partir, j’aimerais mettre un point au clair.
native_language_example: Before leaving, I’d like to clear one thing up.

meaning: at/on the corner (of a street, building, etc.).
additional_notes: Used for a physical corner or nearby spot: *au coin* = “at the corner”; *juste au coin* = “right around the corner”; *au coin suivant* = “at the next corner”. Often followed by **de** to name what the corner belongs to (*au coin de la rue*, *au coin de Michigan Avenue*, *au coin du bois*). With verbs like **tourner**, it means turning at the corner (*Il a tourné au coin*).
target_language_example: Le café est juste au coin de la rue.
native_language_example: The café is right around the corner.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located right at the corner where streets meet. Very common for giving directions or describing where a place is (shops, cafés, where you live). Often follows verbs like être (to be), habiter (to live), se situer (to be located).
target_language_example: Le café est au coin de la rue, juste à côté de la boulangerie.
native_language_example: The café is on the street corner, right next to the bakery.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like se préparer ("to get ready") to mean "get ready for battle". It can also appear after expressions like mettre fin ("to put an end") to mean "put an end to the fighting". Literally "au" = "à + le" ("to the/at the") + "combat".
target_language_example: Les soldats se préparent au combat.
native_language_example: The soldiers are preparing for battle.

additional_notes: Used to say that everyone who is expected is there (a group is complete), or that a place/organization is fully staffed/occupied. Common in announcements or roll-call contexts: « Au complet ! » = “Everyone’s here / All present.”
target_language_example: Pour la réunion, nous sommes au complet.
native_language_example: For the meeting, everyone is here.

meaning: to the account of; in the name of (an account).
additional_notes: Mostly used in banking/accounting contexts to say money is credited/transferred to someone’s account (often followed by a name or account number). Related expression: « mettre quelque chose au compte de + noun » = “to attribute something to …” (e.g., fatigue, chance).
target_language_example: Veuillez verser la somme au compte de Marie Dupont.
native_language_example: Please transfer the amount to Marie Dupont’s account.

meaning: On the contrary; quite the opposite.
additional_notes: Used to contradict or correct what was just said or implied. Often comes at the start of a sentence ("Au contraire, ...") or as a short reply ("Au contraire !", "Non, au contraire."). You can strengthen it with "bien": "Bien au contraire" = "Quite the contrary".
target_language_example: Tu penses que je suis fâché ? Au contraire, je suis très content.
native_language_example: You think I’m angry? On the contrary, I’m very happy.

meaning: aware; in the know; up to date.
additional_notes: Usually used with être: « Je suis au courant » = “I know/I’m aware.” Often followed by de + noun/verb: « être au courant de quelque chose » = “to be aware of something.” Not a literal translation of “current.”
target_language_example: Je suis au courant de la réunion de demain.
native_language_example: I’m aware of tomorrow’s meeting.

additional_notes:
Used mainly with verbs like:
- « être au courant de … » = to be aware of / to know about something: « Je ne suis pas au courant de ce rendez-vous. »
- « tenir quelqu’un au courant » = to keep someone informed / updated: « Je vous tiendrai au courant. »
You can also use it without « de … » when the context is clear: « On te tient au courant. »
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas au courant des changements, tu peux me résumer ?
native_language_example: I’m not aware of the changes—can you sum them up for me?

additional_notes: Used to situate something within a period of time or during an event (a conversation, a discussion, a century, a year, etc.). Often followed by a noun phrase: au cours de la journée / au cours de la réunion. Common in more formal or written French; in everyday speech you can often use "pendant" instead.
target_language_example: Au cours de la soirée, j’ai rencontré ses parents.
native_language_example: During the evening, I met his parents.

additional_notes: An exclamation used to reject, dismiss, or curse someone/something: "Au diable + noun" = "To hell with + noun" (Au diable Noël !). Said to a person, it’s an insult roughly like "Go to hell." Can also be used alone (Au diable !) to show anger or frustration. Strong/impolite; often sounds a bit old-fashioned.
target_language_example: Au diable les excuses, on y va !
native_language_example: To hell with excuses, let’s go!

additional_notes: Used to talk about the start of a time period, story, process, or relationship. Often sets the scene at the start of a narration (Au début, …). It can also refer back to someone’s initial opinion or feeling (Je pensais ça au début = “I thought so at first”), and in expressions like Reprenons au début (“Let’s go back to the beginning”) or Pas au début (“Not at first”).
target_language_example: Au début, je ne comprenais rien, mais maintenant ça va mieux.
native_language_example: At first, I didn’t understand anything, but now it’s better.

meaning: at first; initially; at the start (of something).
additional_notes: Often used to contrast an initial situation/feeling/idea with what happens later: « Au départ…, mais ensuite… ». It can also mean returning to the starting line/position, especially in contexts like sports, races, or games (« On se remet au départ »).
target_language_example: Au départ, je pensais que ce serait compliqué, mais finalement c’était simple.
native_language_example: At first, I thought it would be complicated, but in the end it was simple.

additional_notes: Used as a conversation transition to introduce a new question or bring up something you just remembered (similar to “by the way…”). It can also mean “actually” in the sense of “speaking of the facts / in reality,” but very often it’s just a topic-changer. Often placed at the start of a sentence and followed by a comma: “Au fait, …”.
target_language_example: Au fait, tu as des nouvelles de Marie ?
native_language_example: By the way, have you heard from Marie?

meaning: “to/at the fire”; also “at the traffic light.”
additional_notes: “Au” = “à + le” (“to the / at the”). With real fire, context decides the best English translation: **mettre/jeter X au feu** = “to throw/put X into the fire,” while **(se détendre) face au feu** is “(relax) by/in front of the fire.” In directions, **au feu** refers to a traffic light: **Tourne à droite au feu** = “Turn right at the light.”
target_language_example: On se retrouve au feu, puis on tourne à gauche.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the traffic light, then we’ll turn left.

meaning: over the course of; as time goes by; gradually over time.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that unfolds or changes gradually during a period of time. It is followed by a noun introduced by de (which often contracts: de + le → du; de + les → des), e.g., au fil de la journée (over the course of the day), au fil des années (over the years).
target_language_example: Au fil de la journée, j’ai commencé à mieux comprendre le français.
native_language_example: Over the course of the day, I started to understand French better.

additional_notes: Used to sum up or give the final outcome after considering everything. Often placed at the start of a sentence as a discourse marker ("Au final, ..."), but it can also appear at the end ("... au final") or even stand alone as a short conclusion ("Au final, oui.").
target_language_example: Au final, on a décidé de rester à la maison.
native_language_example: In the end, we decided to stay home.

meaning: at the back; deep down (at heart).
additional_notes: Used for physical location to mean “at the back”/“in the far end” of a place: Au fond à gauche ! (“At the back on the left!”), Restez au fond (“Stay in the back”). With de + noun (au fond de…), it means “at the back/bottom of”: au fond de la classe (“at the back of the classroom”). Figuratively, it means “deep down/at heart”: bon au fond de leur cœur (“good at heart”).
target_language_example: La salle de bain est au fond du couloir.
native_language_example: The bathroom is at the end of the hallway.

meaning: at the back/bottom of; deep inside.
additional_notes: Used for both literal place (“at the back of the room,” “at the bottom of the bottle”) and figurative meaning (“deep down inside me”). Often followed by a noun or pronoun: au fond de la bouteille, au fond de la mosquée, au fond de moi.
target_language_example: Au fond de mon sac, j'ai retrouvé mes clés.
native_language_example: At the bottom of my bag, I found my keys again.

additional_notes: Used to give directions inside a building. Often followed by extra details like "à gauche" (on the left) or "à droite" (on the right).
target_language_example: La salle de réunion est au fond du couloir, à droite.
native_language_example: The meeting room is at the end of the hallway, on the right.

additional_notes: Short for « au football ». Used after verbs like « jouer » (jouer au foot = to play soccer) and with « être bon au foot » = to be good at soccer. In France, « foot » normally means soccer (not American football).
target_language_example: On joue au foot après l'école.
native_language_example: We play soccer after school.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like jouer (à) to talk about playing the sport: jouer au football. It can also describe someone’s ability at the sport, often with être bon/nul au football (“to be good/terrible at soccer”). In France, football usually means “soccer” (not American football).
target_language_example: Mon frère joue au football le samedi.
native_language_example: My brother plays soccer on Saturdays.

meaning: in the oven; into the oven.
additional_notes: Used with cooking verbs like mettre/enfourner (to put in the oven) and cuire (to bake/roast): « mettre au four » = put into the oven; « être au four » = be in the oven (currently baking). It can also be used jokingly/threateningly in a literal sense (“I’ll put you in the oven”).
target_language_example: Mets le gâteau au four pendant 30 minutes.
native_language_example: Put the cake in the oven for 30 minutes.

additional_notes: Literally describes a horse (or rider) moving at a gallop: « Le cheval va au galop. » By extension it can be used figuratively for doing something quickly or rushing: « Il est parti au galop. » Can also be used as a command: « Au galop ! » (= “Gallop!” / “Hurry up!”).
target_language_example: On est rentrés au galop avant la pluie.
native_language_example: We got back quickly before the rain.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like jouer (à) to say someone plays golf: jouer au golf. In a question like « Au golf ? », it can mean “To the golf course?” or “Golf?” depending on context. « au » is a contraction of « à + le ».
target_language_example: On va au golf cet après-midi.
native_language_example: We’re going to the golf course this afternoon.

meaning: in broad daylight; out in the open (publicly).
additional_notes: Often used literally for something happening in daylight, but very commonly used figuratively to mean something is revealed publicly or done openly (not hidden): « dévoiler/mettre au grand jour », « la vérité éclate au grand jour ».
target_language_example: Ils ont enfin mis la fraude au grand jour.
native_language_example: They finally brought the fraud out into the open.

meaning: according to; at the mercy of (depending on).
additional_notes: Used to say something changes or happens depending on someone’s wishes (“as X pleases”) or depending on circumstances like the weather or events (“as things go”). Often followed by a noun: au gré du vent (with the wind), au gré des envies (as one feels like), au gré des saisons (according to the seasons).
target_language_example: Nous changerons de programme au gré de la météo.
native_language_example: We’ll change the plan depending on the weather.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done without a plan, selection, or specific target. Common with verbs like choisir/tirer (to choose/draw), poser (des questions) (to ask), and can also describe moving or wandering with no direction (errer au hasard).
target_language_example: J’ai choisi un livre au hasard dans la bibliothèque.
native_language_example: I picked a book at random from the library.

meaning: day by day; from one day to the next.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that changes daily (prices, schedules, weather) or a way of living without planning ahead—just getting through each day. Often used with vivre: « vivre au jour le jour » = to live day to day.
target_language_example: Avec ce travail instable, je vis au jour le jour.
native_language_example: With this unstable job, I live day to day.

additional_notes: Used mostly in questions to press for precise information or to clarify what someone really means. It can sound a bit insistent depending on tone. Often placed after the word or clause it clarifies: « Qui, au juste ? », « Où, au juste ? ».
target_language_example: Tu veux dire quoi, au juste ?
native_language_example: What exactly do you mean?

meaning: offshore; out at sea (away from the coast).
additional_notes: Used with places to mean “off (the coast) of …”: au large du Chili = offshore of Chile. Can describe something located or happening at sea, away from land. As an exclamation (“Au large !”), it can mean “Set sail!/Head out to sea!” or “Off you go!” depending on context.
target_language_example: On peut apercevoir des dauphins au large de la côte.
native_language_example: You can spot dolphins offshore (off the coast).

meaning: off (the coast of); out at sea near.
additional_notes: Used mainly with places (often coastal) to indicate something is offshore, away from the coast: « au large de Marseille » = off the coast of Marseille. Common with verbs like « naviguer », « se trouver », « être », and in news/weather reports. Not used for general distance on land (use « loin de » for “far from”).
target_language_example: Un voilier se trouve au large de la Bretagne.
native_language_example: A sailboat is off the coast of Brittany.

additional_notes: Used to replace one option/action with another. Often followed by a noun or an infinitive: «au lieu de + nom» (au lieu de ça/cela) or «au lieu de + verbe» (au lieu de travailler). You can also use it at the start of a sentence: «Au lieu de ça/cela, ...».
target_language_example: Au lieu de prendre la voiture, on va marcher.
native_language_example: Instead of taking the car, we're going to walk.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like être/rester (au lit = in bed) and aller (aller au lit = go to bed). Also used in expressions like faire pipi au lit (“wet the bed”).
target_language_example: Je suis malade, alors je reste au lit aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I'm sick, so I'm staying in bed today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happening far from where you are. Often comes after the verb (voir, entendre, apercevoir, distinguer): « Je vois une ville au loin. »
target_language_example: On entendait de la musique au loin.
native_language_example: We could hear music in the distance.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something stretches alongside a place (often written/said as **le long de** in modern French: *le long de la rivière* = along the river). With **tout au long de + time period**, it means “throughout/over the whole course of”: *tout au long de l’année*, *tout au long de nos études*.
target_language_example: Je l’ai soutenu tout au long de son traitement.
native_language_example: I supported him throughout his treatment.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of location or movement. "au" is the contraction of "à + le" and is used because "lycée" is masculine (le lycée). Refers to the French high school level (roughly ages 15–18).
target_language_example: Je suis au lycée, mais je veux aller à l’université l’an prochain.
native_language_example: I’m in high school, but I want to go to university next year.

meaning: to the store; at the store.
additional_notes: "Au" is the contraction of "à + le" and is used with masculine singular places like "le magasin". With verbs of movement, it often means "to the store" (Je vais au magasin). With other verbs, it can mean "at the store" (Je suis au magasin / J’étais au magasin).
target_language_example: Je vais au magasin acheter du lait.
native_language_example: I'm going to the store to buy milk.

additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le" (to/at + the). Used with "aller", "venir", "se rendre" to say you’re going to the (open-air) market; it can also mean being there depending on context.
target_language_example: On se retrouve au marché samedi matin.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the market Saturday morning.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened at an unlucky or inconvenient time. Often paired with "au mauvais endroit" (“in the wrong place”), as in "au mauvais endroit au mauvais moment".
target_language_example: Désolé, je t'appelle peut-être au mauvais moment.
native_language_example: Sorry, I might be calling you at a bad time.

meaning: to the maximum; as much as possible.
additional_notes: Used to mean doing something to the fullest extent. With verbs like « utiliser / informer », it means “as much as possible.” With states like « Je suis au maximum », it can mean “I’m at my limit / maxed out.” It can also describe an action pushed to the furthest point (e.g., sliding as far as you can).
target_language_example: Profite au maximum de tes vacances !
native_language_example: Make the most of your vacation!

meaning: as best as possible; at one’s best.
additional_notes: Used to say you did what you could in the circumstances: « J’ai fait au mieux » (I did my best). It can also mean “at best” when talking about the best-case outcome. In the expression « être au mieux de sa forme », it means “to be at one’s best / in top form.”
target_language_example: Je ferai au mieux avec le temps qu’on a.
native_language_example: I’ll do my best with the time we have.

additional_notes: Used to locate something/someone in the center of a place or situation (au milieu de la route, au milieu de la fête). With groups, it often means “among/in the midst of” (au milieu de la foule). Can also sound like “right in the middle of” when expressing surprise (Qu’est-ce que tu fais au milieu de… ?).
target_language_example: Je l’ai rencontré au milieu de la foule.
native_language_example: I met him in the middle of the crowd.
