additional_notes: Used to say a place is very remote/isolated, far from towns or anything familiar. Often expresses inconvenience or surprise (e.g., being stuck or wondering why someone is there).
target_language_example: On a pris la mauvaise route et on s'est retrouvés au milieu de nulle part.
native_language_example: We took the wrong road and ended up in the middle of nowhere.

meaning: in the middle of; halfway through.
additional_notes: Used to place something in the center of a location ("au milieu du parc") or to say something happens halfway through a period or event ("au milieu du mois", "au milieu du film/concert/cours"). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun (du = de + le). For feminine, use "au milieu de la"; for plural, "au milieu des"; before a vowel, "au milieu de l’".
target_language_example: On s’est rencontrés au milieu du voyage.
native_language_example: We met halfway through the trip.

additional_notes: Used to state a minimum amount/number or lower limit. Often placed after the quantity it refers to ("sept heures, au minimum") or before it ("au minimum sept heures"). Can also be used alone as a short answer meaning “at least/minimum.”
target_language_example: Il faut économiser 50 € par mois, au minimum.
native_language_example: You need to save €50 a month, at least.

additional_notes: Used to give a minimum amount, time, or degree. It can also add emphasis in questions or suggestions, like 'at least' in English: Est-ce que tu m'écoutes au moins ? = 'Are you at least listening to me?'
target_language_example: On peut au moins essayer.
native_language_example: We can at least try.

additional_notes: Introduces a time clause to say something happens exactly as/when something else happens. Often used with the imperfect to describe an action in progress that another action happens during (e.g., « au moment où je sortais… »). You’ll also see it with emphasis like « juste au moment où » (“just as / right when”).
target_language_example: Au moment où je m’endormais, le téléphone a sonné.
native_language_example: Just as I was falling asleep, the phone rang.

additional_notes: Often used after a superlative: « le/la plus … au monde » = “the most … in the world.” Also appears in the expression « mettre au monde » = “to give birth (to),” literally “to bring into the world” (e.g., « Elle a mis au monde un garçon. »).
target_language_example: C'est le meilleur restaurant au monde.
native_language_example: It’s the best restaurant in the world.

additional_notes: Used to express the method, instrument, or means by which something is done. It’s a fairly formal way to say "using" (often close to "à l’aide de" in many contexts). Pattern: au moyen de + noun/noun phrase. Note the spelling is fixed: "au moyen de" (no apostrophe).
target_language_example: Les oiseaux volent au moyen de leurs ailes.
native_language_example: Birds fly by means of their wings.

meaning: on the wall; against the wall.
additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le". With "au mur", French often uses "à" where English uses "on" (e.g., "accrocher au mur" = "hang on the wall"). It can also mean facing/with your front toward the wall: "Face au mur" = "Facing the wall."
target_language_example: Il y a une photo au mur, juste au-dessus du canapé.
native_language_example: There’s a photo on the wall, just above the couch.

meaning: in the same place; in the same spot.
additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone stays in one location or that two things happen at one identical location. Often used with verbs like habiter (to live), travailler (to work), rester (to stay), and with toujours (still/always): « Tu habites toujours au même endroit ? ».
target_language_example: On se retrouve au même endroit demain à midi.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in the same place tomorrow at noon.

meaning: "in the name of" / "on behalf of"; also "in (someone's) name" (registered under).
additional_notes: Common uses: (1) to speak or act for someone/a group: « Au nom de tous, merci… » = “On behalf of everyone…”. (2) to say something is officially registered under a person’s name: « un compte au nom de Marie » = “an account in Marie’s name.” With « répondre au nom de », it means “to go by the name of.”
target_language_example: Je signe ce document au nom de mon entreprise.
native_language_example: I’m signing this document on behalf of my company.

meaning: 'in the name of' (invoking an authority, principle, or group; sometimes used as an emphatic exclamation like 'for heaven’s sake').
additional_notes: Used to invoke an authority, principle, person, or group as justification: *Au nom du peuple* (“in the name of the people”). Common in religious formulas: *Au nom du Père, du Fils et du Saint-Esprit…* Also used as an exclamation to express surprise/indignation: *Au nom du Ciel !* ≈ “For heaven’s sake!” Note the form varies with gender/number of the following noun (*au nom du* + masculine singular; *au nom de la* + feminine singular; *au nom des* + plural; *au nom de l’* before a vowel).
target_language_example: Au nom du peuple, je vous demande de vous taire.
native_language_example: In the name of the people, I ask you to be quiet.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a total count (often with a number): « Ils étaient au nombre de dix » = “There were ten of them.” Also used with « compter (qqn) au nombre de… » to mean “to count (someone) among…” (a group, friends, participants, etc.). In negative form: « Il ne compte pas au nombre de… » = “He doesn’t count as one of… / He isn’t among…”.
target_language_example: Nous étions au nombre de cinq à la réunion.
native_language_example: There were five of us at the meeting.

meaning: to the north; in the north.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a northern direction or location. Common patterns: « au nord de + place » = “north of (a place)”; « plus au nord » = “further north.”
target_language_example: Le village est au nord de la rivière.
native_language_example: The village is north of the river.

meaning: to the park / at the park.
additional_notes: "Au" = "à" + "le" (used before masculine singular nouns like "le parc"). With movement verbs (aller, se rendre, conduire), it usually means "to the park"; with context about location, it can mean "at the park."
target_language_example: On se retrouve au parc à 15 h.
native_language_example: Let's meet at the park at 3 p.m.

meaning: at a walking pace; (in “attention au pas”) watch your step.
additional_notes: Literally “at the step.” Common in instructions and signs: “rouler au pas” = drive very slowly (walking speed), especially in parking lots or near pedestrians. In the expression “mettre (quelqu’un) au pas,” it means “to bring (someone) into line / make them obey.” In “attention au pas,” “pas” means a step/ledge (e.g., when getting off a train).
target_language_example: Dans cette zone piétonne, il faut rouler au pas.
native_language_example: In this pedestrian area, you have to drive at walking pace.

meaning: “heel!” (to a dog) / “at the foot (of), at the base (of)”.
additional_notes: As a command to a dog, « Au pied ! » tells it to come next to you and walk close by your leg (like “heel!”). In location phrases, it’s usually « au pied de + noun »: « au pied du lit » (at the foot of the bed), « au pied de la pente » (at the bottom of the slope), « au pied du mont… » (at the base of the mountain).
target_language_example: Le chien est resté au pied pendant toute la promenade.
native_language_example: The dog stayed at heel for the whole walk.

meaning: for the worst; in the worst case.
additional_notes: Most often used with verbs like se préparer à / être prêt(e) à to mean “prepare for the worst.” You can also use it to introduce a fallback scenario: Au pire, on prendra un taxi (“Worst case, we’ll take a taxi”).
target_language_example: Au pire, on restera à la maison.
native_language_example: Worst case, we'll stay at home.

meaning: “Looking forward to it/seeing you again.” (as a goodbye)
additional_notes: Used as a polite closing, often after “au revoir” or with an infinitive: “Au plaisir de vous revoir.” It can also appear in the literal sense “to the pleasure” after verbs like “ajouter” (“ajoute au plaisir” = “adds to the pleasure”).
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide — au plaisir de vous revoir.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help — I look forward to seeing you again.

meaning: at most; to the most (in set phrases like “au plus offrant/bas/haut”).
additional_notes: Commonly used after a number to mean “at most” (maximum): « Deux, au plus » = “Two at most.” It also appears in fixed expressions with an adjective/noun, e.g. « au plus offrant » (to the highest bidder), « au plus bas/haut » (at its lowest/highest point).
target_language_example: On en aura trois, au plus.
native_language_example: We’ll have three at most.

meaning: no later than; at the latest.
additional_notes: Used to set the latest acceptable time for something to happen (a deadline). It often follows the time/date: « à 18 h au plus tard ». Also common with « au plus tard à + time » or « au plus tard le + date ». Similar in meaning to « au maximum » when talking about time.
target_language_example: Envoie-moi le document demain au plus tard.
native_language_example: Send me the document by tomorrow at the latest.

meaning: as early/soon as possible; at the earliest.
additional_notes: Used to express the earliest possible time something can happen. Often placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence. Can also follow a time phrase: « la semaine prochaine au plus tôt » = “next week at the earliest” (not before next week). Common in scheduling and planning questions: « Quand pouvez-vous… au plus tôt ? »
target_language_example: Je peux vous rappeler demain au plus tôt.
native_language_example: I can call you back tomorrow at the earliest.

meaning: as quickly as possible; as soon as possible.
additional_notes: Used to express urgency. Often said alone as an instruction (“Au plus vite !”), or after a verb: “faire au plus vite” = to do it as fast as possible. Can also follow an infinitive: “à faire/à écraser au plus vite” = to do/crush as soon as possible.
target_language_example: Envoyez-moi le document au plus vite, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Send me the document as quickly as possible, please.

additional_notes: Very common informal expression to say that something is exactly right or works perfectly (often as a quick reaction: « Au poil ! »). Used for things, situations, or results: « tout est au poil » = “everything is great / all set.”
target_language_example: Ton idée est au poil, on fait comme ça.
native_language_example: Your idea is spot on; let's do it that way.

meaning: 'at this point/stage'; also 'ready/accurate' (depending on the expression).
additional_notes: Often used in set phrases: **au point où j'en suis / on en est** = “at this stage (given where I/we are)”; **mettre (qqch) au point** = “to finalize, work out, clarify/straighten out (a plan, details, a misunderstanding)”; **être au point** (or **une réponse est au point**) = “to be ready, correct, well-prepared/accurate.”
target_language_example: Au point où on en est, autant finir aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: At this point, we might as well finish today.

meaning: to the point of (doing something); so much that…
additional_notes: Used to show degree/intensity that leads to a result, often with an infinitive: « au point de + infinitif » (e.g., « fatigué au point de s’endormir »). Can also be followed by « que »: « au point que + phrase » (e.g., « au point que je ne pouvais plus parler »).
target_language_example: Il était épuisé au point de s’endormir dans le train.
native_language_example: He was exhausted to the point of falling asleep on the train.

additional_notes: Used after verbs/adjectives that take « à » (e.g., « jouer à » = to play, « être bon/mauvais à » = to be good/bad). « Au » is the contraction of « à + le »: « jouer au poker », « être bon au poker ».
target_language_example: Il joue souvent au poker avec ses amis.
native_language_example: He often plays poker with his friends.

additional_notes: Used about people or groups who currently control the government or have authority. Common patterns: « le parti au pouvoir » (the ruling party), « être au pouvoir » (to be in power), « arriver/venir au pouvoir » (to come to power), « revenir au pouvoir » (to return to power), « porter quelqu’un au pouvoir » (to bring someone to power).
target_language_example: Le nouveau président est au pouvoir depuis 2024.
native_language_example: The new president has been in power since 2024.

meaning: on the first floor (France: the level above the ground floor).
additional_notes: Used to say where something/someone is located or where to carry/take something. In France and many French-speaking places, "le rez-de-chaussée" is the ground floor, so "le premier étage" is one floor up (what Americans often call the second floor). Often used with verbs like "monter" (go up), "descendre" (go down), "porter" (carry), and "se situer" (to be located).
target_language_example: La salle de réunion est au premier étage, juste à gauche de l’ascenseur.
native_language_example: The meeting room is on the first floor, just to the left of the elevator.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens in spring in general (a recurring season). You can use it at the start of a sentence to set the time: « Au printemps, … ». Similar patterns: « en été » (in summer), « en automne » (in autumn), « en hiver » (in winter).
target_language_example: Au printemps, il commence souvent à faire plus chaud.
native_language_example: In spring, it often starts to get warmer.

meaning: at the cost of; at the expense of.
additional_notes: Introduces a sacrifice or negative consequence that is the “price” paid to achieve something (health, time, lives, privacy, etc.). Often used with nouns like sa santé, sa vie, de gros efforts, leur vie privée. Can also appear with même au prix de… (“even at the cost of…”).
target_language_example: Elle a obtenu ce poste au prix de nombreuses heures de travail.
native_language_example: She got that job at the cost of many hours of work.

additional_notes: Used to say something should happen earlier, before another action or event. Common with verbs like demander (to ask), prévenir (to warn), téléphoner (to call), or discuter/parler de (to discuss). It’s a fairly formal way to say "avant" / "d’abord".
target_language_example: Merci de me prévenir au préalable si vous êtes en retard.
native_language_example: Please let me know beforehand if you’re going to be late.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens regularly in your daily routine (habits, work, life). Often follows verbs like vivre, faire, utiliser, aider, or donner la force: « vivre au quotidien », « au quotidien, je… ». It’s close to « tous les jours », but emphasizes the day-to-day reality rather than a specific calendar day.
target_language_example: Au quotidien, je prends le métro pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: Day to day, I take the subway to go to work.

meaning: in slow motion; at a slow pace.
additional_notes: Used with videos/images/scenes to mean “in slow motion” (e.g., passer/repasser une scène au ralenti). Also used more generally for things running sluggishly or operating below normal speed (e.g., le travail marche au ralenti, mon cœur bat au ralenti, une ville fonctionne au ralenti).
target_language_example: Depuis la panne, l’usine tourne au ralenti.
native_language_example: Since the breakdown, the factory has been running at a slow pace.

meaning: at the restaurant; to the restaurant.
additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le". With a verb of location (être, manger, travailler), it often means "at the restaurant"; with a verb of movement (aller), it can mean "to the restaurant". Used for a general place rather than a specific named restaurant (otherwise you might use "dans ce restaurant" or name it).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au restaurant à 19 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the restaurant at 7 p.m.

additional_notes: A common time + place phrase. **Au** = **à + le** (“at the”). Often used with **aller** (“to go”): *aller au restaurant* = “to go to a restaurant / go out to eat.” In questions with **aller** in the past, you may see agreement in **allé/allée/allés/allées** depending on who went (male/female, singular/plural), e.g. *Êtes-vous allée… ?* (to one woman), *Êtes-vous allées… ?* (to several women).
target_language_example: On est allés au restaurant hier soir.
native_language_example: We went to a restaurant last night.

additional_notes: A standard, polite way to say goodbye when leaving or ending a conversation. It is more neutral/formal than salut.
target_language_example: Je dois partir maintenant, au revoir !
native_language_example: I have to leave now, goodbye!

meaning: “Goodbye, my …” (said to a male person, often affectionately).
additional_notes: Used when saying goodbye while adding a term of address after mon (my): mon ange (my angel), mon petit (my little one), mon vieil ami / mon vieux (my old friend / my buddy). Because mon agrees with a masculine noun, you’ll often hear it with male people or with masculine nicknames; with a feminine noun you’d use ma (e.g., Au revoir, ma chérie).
target_language_example: Au revoir, mon ami, à bientôt !
native_language_example: Goodbye, my friend—see you soon!

additional_notes: Used to say something is located on the building’s street-level floor (the level you enter from outside). In French, the ground floor is the "rez-de-chaussée" (the next level up is the "premier étage"), which can differ from US English where the "first floor" is usually street level.
target_language_example: Les toilettes sont au rez-de-chaussée, juste à gauche de l’entrée.
native_language_example: The bathrooms are on the ground floor, just to the left of the entrance.

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to call for help in an emergency or urgent situation. It can be said alone ("Au secours !") or used with verbs like "crier" ("Il/Elle a crié au secours"). Stronger/more dramatic than "à l’aide" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Au secours ! Je n’arrive pas à sortir d’ici !
native_language_example: Help! I can’t get out of here!

meaning: within; in the heart of (a group/organization/family).
additional_notes: Used to locate something inside a group, institution, or community (often in a formal tone): au sein de l’entreprise, au sein du gouvernement, au sein de la famille. It emphasizes being part of the group rather than just physically inside a place. Common pattern: jouer un rôle au sein de + group.
target_language_example: Au sein de l’équipe, chacun a une tâche différente.
native_language_example: Within the team, everyone has a different task.

meaning: on the ground; on the floor.
additional_notes: Literally “to the ground” (à + le = au, sol = ground). Common with verbs like tomber (to fall) or être (to be): tomber au sol = “fall to the ground.” In some contexts (e.g., aviation/military), it means “ground” as opposed to “in the air”: unité au sol = “ground unit,” remettre au sol = “bring/put back on the ground” (e.g., land). Often similar to par terre in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Après l’explosion, tout le monde s’est retrouvé au sol.
native_language_example: After the explosion, everyone ended up on the ground.

meaning: to the sound of; to the rhythm of.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens while a sound is playing or accompanying it (music, radio, someone’s breathing, etc.). Often used with verbs like danser (to dance), s’endormir (to fall asleep), marcher (to walk). Literally “at the sound of.”
target_language_example: Je me suis réveillé au son des oiseaux.
native_language_example: I woke up to the sound of birds.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is located in the basement level of a building. Often with places like un parking (parking garage), la buanderie (laundry room), la cave (cellar). With feminine nouns you may also see: « à la cave » (in the cellar).
target_language_example: Les toilettes sont au sous-sol.
native_language_example: The restrooms are in the basement.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the subject or topic of what you’re talking about, often in slightly formal or neutral contexts (e.g., phone calls, emails, meetings). It’s similar to "à propos de" and "concernant". Followed by a noun or noun phrase: "au sujet de votre frère", "au sujet de ce rapport".
target_language_example: Je vous appelle au sujet de votre rendez-vous.
native_language_example: I'm calling you about your appointment.

meaning: at the supermarket; to the supermarket.
additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le". Use it with places (being there or going there): Je suis au supermarché (I’m at the supermarket) / Je vais au supermarché (I’m going to the supermarket). For a feminine place you’d use "à la" (e.g., à la boulangerie).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au supermarché à 18 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at the supermarket at 6 p.m.?

meaning: seriously (in « prendre … au sérieux » = “to take … seriously”).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with the verb « prendre »: « prendre quelqu’un/quelque chose au sérieux » (to take someone/something seriously). Very often appears in the negative: « ne pas prendre … au sérieux » (not to take … seriously).
target_language_example: Il faut prendre ce problème au sérieux.
native_language_example: We need to take this problem seriously.

additional_notes: Used to place something in a past era, often before a person, period, or generation: au temps de Napoléon, au temps de mes grands-parents. It often refers to 'back when' something was the case.
target_language_example: Au temps de mes grands-parents, il n'y avait pas d'internet.
native_language_example: In my grandparents' time, there was no internet.

additional_notes: Used with activities/sports after verbs like "jouer" and expressions of ability: "jouer au tennis" = "to play tennis"; "être bon/mauvais/médiocre au tennis" = "to be good/bad/mediocre at tennis". "Au" is the contraction of "à + le".
target_language_example: Je ne joue pas souvent au tennis, mais j’aime ça.
native_language_example: I don’t play tennis often, but I like it.

meaning: to the theater; at the theater.
additional_notes: "Au" is the contraction of "à + le" and is used with masculine singular places. With verbs of movement (aller, aller/venir), it often means "to the theater" (destination): « Je vais au théâtre. » With location/context, it can mean "at the theater": « Il y avait trop de monde au théâtre. » Note the past participle agreement in « aller » with "être": « ma femme et moi sommes allés » (mixed or all men) vs « sommes allées » (all women).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au théâtre à 19 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the theater at 7 p.m.

additional_notes: Used when asking for or stating the final sum/number after everything is counted or added up. Often placed at the end of a sentence: « Combien ça fait au total ? »
target_language_example: Nous avons trois tickets, donc ça fait 45 € au total.
native_language_example: We have three tickets, so that comes to €45 in total.

additional_notes: Most often means “at work” (being at your workplace or working): « Je suis au travail. » It can also be used after verbs like « se mettre au travail » to mean “to get to work / start working.”
target_language_example: Je suis au travail jusqu'à 18 h.
native_language_example: I’m at work until 6 p.m.

meaning: through; across (often through something, or via a medium).
additional_notes: Used to describe movement or passage from one side to the other (through a door, a city, a road), or seeing/understanding something via a “filter” (e.g., "au travers de ses yeux" = “through his/her eyes”). Often interchangeable with "à travers"; "au travers de" can sound a bit more emphatic about going through/around an obstacle or passing through something.
target_language_example: On est passé au travers de la forêt pour rentrer plus vite.
native_language_example: We went through the forest to get back faster.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is speaking/answering using a telephone. Often used with verbs like parler (à quelqu’un) au téléphone (to talk to someone on the phone) and répondre au téléphone (to answer the phone).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas parler maintenant, je suis au téléphone.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now, I’m on the phone.

additional_notes: Means someone is in the driver’s seat and controlling the vehicle. Commonly used with verbs like être (être au volant = to be driving) or to describe a person (le type au volant = the guy driving).
target_language_example: Je suis au volant, donc je ne peux pas répondre au téléphone.
native_language_example: I’m driving, so I can’t answer the phone.

additional_notes: A shouted warning/cry for help when you see someone stealing or running off with something. Often used with an exclamation mark: « Au voleur ! ».
target_language_example: Au voleur ! On m’a volé mon sac !
native_language_example: Thief! Someone stole my bag!

meaning: to the zoo / at the zoo.
additional_notes: "Au" is the contraction of "à + le". Use "au zoo" after verbs like aller (to go), être (to be), venir (to come), and emmener (to take/bring someone). The meaning can be "to the zoo" (direction) or "at the zoo" (location), depending on the verb and context.
target_language_example: On se retrouve au zoo à 14 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the zoo at 2 p.m.

additional_notes: Often used with people or organizations. It can mean being physically close to someone ("go be by/with him"), or dealing with/asking a person or institution for something ("from/with" them: e.g., demander un renseignement auprès de la mairie = ask the town hall for information).
target_language_example: J’ai pris des renseignements auprès de la mairie.
native_language_example: I got information from the town hall.

additional_notes: Future form of « avoir lieu » (literally “to have place”), used for scheduled or planned events (meetings, conferences, parties, competitions). It agrees with the subject: « l’événement aura lieu… ». Often followed by a time and/or place: « demain », « dimanche prochain », « à Tokyo », etc.
target_language_example: Le concert aura lieu samedi à 20 h.
native_language_example: The concert will take place on Saturday at 8 p.m.

additional_notes: Form of « devoir » in the conditional perfect: « il/elle/on » + « aurait dû » + infinitive (e.g., « On aurait dû partir plus tôt. »). Used to express regret, criticism, or that something was expected but didn’t happen. It can also indicate that something was supposed to happen or have an expected effect: « Ça aurait dû le tuer. »
target_language_example: On aurait dû téléphoner avant et réserver une table.
native_language_example: We should have called ahead and reserved a table.

meaning: as well as; just as well as.
additional_notes: Used for comparisons. (1) To say two things/people are included equally: « les adultes aussi bien que les enfants » = “adults as well as children.” (2) To say someone does something at the same level as someone else: « Elle skie aussi bien que son frère » = “She skis as well as her brother.” Often intensified with « tout » (tout aussi bien que = “just as well as”) or softened with « presque » (presque aussi bien que = “almost as well as”).
target_language_example: Il cuisine tout aussi bien que sa sœur.
native_language_example: He cooks just as well as his sister.

additional_notes: Used to compare speeds or how quickly two actions happen: aussi + adverb (vite) + que + the reference (a person, thing, or clause). It can mean equality ("as fast as") and often implies a limit with pouvoir: « aussi vite que je peux / que tu le peux » = "as fast as I/you can."
target_language_example: On va avancer aussi vite que possible.
native_language_example: We’ll move forward as fast as possible.

additional_notes: Used to say you will do something with maximum speed. It can stand alone as an instruction/request (“As quickly as possible.”). Often used after a verb: courir/venir/se préparer/répondre aussi vite que possible. You can also hear "le plus vite possible" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Envoyez-moi les documents aussi vite que possible, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please send me the documents as quickly as possible.

additional_notes: Introduces a time clause for something that happens immediately after another event. Use it with a conjugated verb: « aussitôt que tu arrives ». In instructions, it’s common with the imperative: « Téléphone-moi aussitôt que tu arrives ! ». Don’t confuse with « aussitôt que possible » = “as soon as possible / as quickly as possible.”
target_language_example: Aussitôt que j’ai fini, je te rappelle.
native_language_example: As soon as I’m done, I’ll call you back.

additional_notes: Used to talk about quantity/degree. Common patterns: (1) with a verb: "autant que tu veux/peux" = "as much as you want/can"; (2) in comparisons: "pas autant que" = "not as much as" (e.g., "La Lune ne brille pas autant que le Soleil" = "The Moon doesn’t shine as much as the Sun").
target_language_example: Prends autant que tu veux, il y en a assez pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: Take as much as you want; there’s enough for everyone.

meaning: as much as possible; as far as possible.
additional_notes: Used to say you should do something to the maximum extent you can. It often follows a verb (e.g., voir/lire/éviter autant que possible) or can be used alone as a short answer. With verbs, it means “as much as possible,” and in some contexts it can mean “as far as possible” (to the greatest extent feasible).
target_language_example: Parle français autant que possible pendant le cours.
native_language_example: Speak French as much as possible during class.

additional_notes: Used to talk about position or movement around something/someone: «autour de la table» (around the table), «passer autour de moi» (go past/around me). It can also be figurative: «tourner autour de» = to revolve around / be all about (often in «Le monde ne tourne pas autour de vous.»). With time/number/amount, it means approximately: «autour de 20 minutes» (about 20 minutes). Common with body language: «mettre/avoir le bras autour de quelqu’un» = put/have your arm around someone.
target_language_example: On se retrouve autour de 18 h autour du parc.
native_language_example: We’ll meet around 6 p.m. around the park.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or position around something masculine singular: autour du lac (= around the lake). With feminine singular, use "autour de la"; with a vowel sound, "autour de l'"; with plural, "autour des". Also common in set phrases like "autour du monde" (= around the world).
target_language_example: On s'est promenés autour du parc.
native_language_example: We went for a walk around the park.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a different thing. In questions, especially with vouloir or désirer, it often means "anything else?"
target_language_example: Je voudrais autre chose à boire.
native_language_example: I'd like something else to drink.

additional_notes: Used to say something should be done in a different place (similar to "ailleurs"). Watch out for the spelling/meaning difference: **autre part** = "elsewhere", but **une autre part** (with an article) usually means "another slice/portion" (e.g., of pie or cake).
target_language_example: On peut en parler autre part, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can we talk about it somewhere else, please?

additional_notes: Used in the pattern **(un/une) autre à + infinitive** or **(un/une) autre à + noun** to express an additional thing/person/task remaining to do/handle (e.g., *un autre à faire* = another thing to do). You may also see the plural **d’autres à...**. Note: for “other than,” French generally uses **autre que**, not *autre à*.
target_language_example: J’ai encore un appel, un autre à passer avant midi.
native_language_example: I still have a call—another one to make before noon.

additional_notes: Used to rephrase, clarify, or summarize what was just said (often at the start of a sentence). It can also be used alone as a question ("Autrement dit ?") to ask someone to rephrase or explain more clearly.
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas le temps aujourd’hui ; autrement dit, je ne peux pas venir.
native_language_example: I don’t have time today; in other words, I can’t come.

meaning: near; on the outskirts of; in the vicinity of.
additional_notes: Used to indicate something located close to a place, often just outside it or in the surrounding/approach area. More formal/descriptive than "près de" and often used in narration, reports, or signage. Typical patterns: "aux abords de la ville" (on the outskirts of the city), "aux abords de Saturne" (near Saturn).
target_language_example: Sa maison est aux abords de la ville.
native_language_example: His/Her house is on the outskirts of the city.

meaning: around; approximately; in the vicinity of.
additional_notes: Used to give an approximate time, age, number, etc. ("around midnight", "about 20"). It can also mean "near" a place ("in the area around the post office"). Common in everyday speech, slightly more formal than "vers" for time.
target_language_example: On se retrouve aux alentours de 18 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet around 6 p.m.?

meaning: at cards; playing cards (as a game).
additional_notes: Used after the verb jouer to mean “to play cards” (jouer aux cartes). The preposition à + les becomes aux. It refers to card games in general (e.g., poker, belote), not necessarily “at the cards” in a literal location sense.
target_language_example: Après le dîner, on joue souvent aux cartes.
native_language_example: After dinner, we often play cards.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is leading, running things, or in control of a situation (politics, a company, a project). Literally refers to being at the controls (like a vehicle or machine), and by extension means being the person in command.
target_language_example: Qui est aux commandes du projet ?
native_language_example: Who’s in charge of the project?

additional_notes: In food phrases, "aux + plural" means “with/featuring” that ingredient: *une tarte aux pommes* = apple pie, *une salade aux pommes* = a salad with apples. Note that "préférer X aux pommes" uses "à" to mean “prefer X to apples” (comparison), not an ingredient.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un gâteau aux pommes, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like an apple cake, please.

meaning: to the toilet/bathroom; to use the restroom.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (aller, entrer, se rendre) to say you’re going to the bathroom. Very common and neutral; in many contexts it means “to use the restroom.” You can also say "Je vais aux toilettes" on its own to excuse yourself.
target_language_example: Pardon, je vais aux toilettes.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going to the bathroom.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like « être » or « avoir » to describe a person/animal/police/bandits actively chasing someone: « La police est aux trousses de X » (The police are after X). « On a X aux trousses » means “X is after us / on our tail.” Often implies urgency or danger.
target_language_example: J’ai un chien aux trousses, il faut courir !
native_language_example: I’ve got a dog on my heels—we need to run!

meaning: in the eyes of; in someone’s view/opinion.
additional_notes: Used to express how something is judged or perceived by a person, group, or authority (e.g., Dieu, Rome, le public). Often means “according to” or “from the point of view of.” Note that related expressions include: « aux yeux de tous » (in everyone’s eyes) and « sauter aux yeux » (to be obvious, lit. “jump to the eyes”).
target_language_example: Aux yeux de ses collègues, il a fait le bon choix.
native_language_example: In his colleagues’ eyes, he made the right choice.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the game of chess in general (“In chess, …”) and after verbs like **jouer à**: **jouer aux échecs** = “to play chess.” **Aux** is the contraction of **à + les**. **Échecs** (plural) means “chess” here; don’t confuse it with English “checks.”
target_language_example: Aux échecs, il faut souvent penser plusieurs coups à l’avance.
native_language_example: In chess, you often have to think several moves ahead.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something someone had already said before another past moment. It’s formed with the imperfect of avoir (avait) + past participle (dit). Often appears with pronouns: « On m’avait dit… » = “I had been told…”, « Elle me l’avait dit » = “She had told me (it).”
target_language_example: Je croyais qu’il avait dit la vérité.
native_language_example: I thought he had told the truth.

additional_notes: Used with a singular subject (il/elle/on, or a singular noun) to talk about something that happened before another past event (plus-que-parfait). Very common in the passive voice: "avait été" + past participle = "had been" + past participle (e.g., "La porte avait été ouverte" = "The door had been opened"). For plurals, you’ll often see "avaient été".
target_language_example: Je croyais qu’il avait été informé.
native_language_example: I thought he had been informed.

additional_notes: This is the imperfect of avoir (avait) used with subject–verb inversion to ask a question: "avait-il… ?" = "had he…?" / "did he have…?" It’s relatively formal/written compared with just using intonation ("Il avait… ?"). The hyphen links the verb and the pronoun (il). Often appears with negatives: "N’avait-il pas… ?" = "Didn’t he have…?"
target_language_example: Avait-il déjà une idée en tête ?
native_language_example: Did he already have an idea in mind?

additional_notes: Imperfect past of « avoir besoin de » (“to need”). Use « avoir besoin de + noun/pronoun » to say someone needs something: « J’ai besoin de toi » (I need you). In the past: « Il/Elle avait besoin de… » (He/She needed…). Often implies necessity or dependence (e.g., help, money, something specific).
target_language_example: Elle avait besoin de repos après le voyage.
native_language_example: She needed rest after the trip.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of avoir: il/elle/on avait = “he/she/one had” or “was having/used to have.” Use "avait des + plural noun" to describe possession or something present/visible (e.g., des larmes, des numéros, des caméras, des tatouages). With body issues you often hear "avoir des + noun" (e.g., avoir des ampoules = to have blisters).
target_language_example: Quand il était jeune, il avait des cheveux très longs.
native_language_example: When he was young, he had very long hair.

additional_notes: Imperfect (third-person singular) of "avoir peur de" (to be afraid of). Used with "de" + noun/pronoun (avait peur de Marie, de son ombre) or "de" + infinitive (avait peur de faire une erreur, de mourir). Other common forms: present "a peur de"; passé composé "a eu peur de"; plural imperfect "avaient peur de".
target_language_example: Mary avait peur de faire une erreur.
native_language_example: Mary was afraid of making a mistake.

additional_notes: From the expression « avoir raison » = “to be right.” « avait » is the imperfect (past), used to describe a past situation, belief, or ongoing state. It does not mean “had a reason.” Typically used with a person as the subject: « Il/Elle avait raison », « Votre père avait raison ».
target_language_example: Malheureusement, Nancy avait raison.
native_language_example: Unfortunately, Nancy was right.

meaning: "had a" (past, third-person singular: he/she/it had a).
additional_notes: “Avait” is the imperfect tense of *avoir* (to have), used for ongoing states, descriptions, or background in the past. It’s followed by the masculine singular indefinite article *un* + a noun (for feminine nouns, use *avait une*).
target_language_example: Il avait un certain charme.
native_language_example: He had a certain charm.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of avoir ("to have") for il/elle/on: "avait" = "was having / had" in an ongoing, descriptive past. Used to describe possession or characteristics in the past. "Une" is the feminine form of "a/an" and is used before a feminine noun (une voix, une torche, une peau).
target_language_example: Quand j’étais petit, j’avais une peur bleue des chiens, et mon frère avait une grande patience avec moi.
native_language_example: When I was little, I was terribly afraid of dogs, and my brother had a lot of patience with me.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened two days ago. It can stand alone (Avant-hier.) or be followed by a time expression like "avant-hier soir" (the evening before last). Hyphenated in French: avant-hier.
target_language_example: On s'est vus avant-hier après-midi.
native_language_example: We saw each other the day before yesterday in the afternoon.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say that one action happens earlier than another: avant de partir, avant de manger. If the subject changes, French usually uses avant que instead.
target_language_example: Je me lave les mains avant de manger.
native_language_example: I wash my hands before eating.

additional_notes: Used to say an action should happen earlier than the moment of leaving. Often follows advice or instructions (e.g., do X avant de partir). Can refer to leaving a place now or departing for a trip.
target_language_example: Appelle-moi avant de partir, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Call me before you leave, please.

meaning: not for a long time; (sometimes) before long/soon.
additional_notes: Very common with negation: "ne… pas avant longtemps" = "not for a long time / not anytime soon". Without negation, it can mean "before long / soon" (often a bit formal or literary, and less common in everyday speech than "bientôt").
target_language_example: On ne se reverra pas avant longtemps.
native_language_example: We won’t see each other again for a long time.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause about an action/event that happens later: « avant que + subject + verb ». It’s very often followed by the subjunctive in French (e.g., « avant que les soldats viennent »). You may also see an extra « ne » (called *ne explétif*) after « avant que » (e.g., « avant que je ne sois diplômé »); it doesn’t mean “not”.
target_language_example: Ferme la fenêtre avant que la pluie n’entre.
native_language_example: Close the window before the rain comes in.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize priority or what matters most. Common at the start of a sentence (“Avant tout, …”) or alone as a short reply meaning “above all / first of all.” Can also be used in slogans like “Le devoir avant tout” (“Duty above all”).
target_language_example: Avant tout, je veux comprendre.
native_language_example: Above all, I want to understand.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/thing is accompanied by, has, or uses unspecified plural items: "avec des jouets" (with some toys), "avec des couverts" (using cutlery). It can also mean "together with" or "against" depending on context: "se battre avec des filles" (fight with/against girls). "des" is the plural of the indefinite article ("some" / "any").
target_language_example: Je suis venu avec des amis.
native_language_example: I came with some friends.

additional_notes: Used to say you are spending time in the company of friends. Often answers “Avec qui ?” (With whom?) or explains who you’re with: « Je suis avec des amis. » / « Je sors avec des amis. ». The first example (« Avec des amis comme vous… ») is an ironic set phrase meaning “With friends like you…”.
target_language_example: Ce soir, je dîne avec des amis.
native_language_example: Tonight, I’m having dinner with some friends.

additional_notes: Means being together/accompanying a female person ("her"). Very common after verbs like "sortir avec elle" (go out with her / date her), "parler avec elle" (talk with her), "être avec elle" (be with her). It’s the feminine form; compare "avec lui" = "with him".
target_language_example: Je veux parler avec elle après le cours.
native_language_example: I want to talk with her after class.

meaning: 'with them' (referring to a group of males or mixed gender).
additional_notes: Uses the stressed pronoun "eux" (not "les") after a preposition like "avec". Refers to a group (they/them) that is masculine or mixed; for an all-female group, use "avec elles". Often contrasts groups: "avec nous" vs "avec eux".
target_language_example: Tu peux venir avec eux si tu veux.
native_language_example: You can come with them if you want.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like attendre (to wait/expect) to show you’re really looking forward to something. Common pattern: attendre [something] avec impatience / attendre avec impatience de + infinitive.
target_language_example: J’attends avec impatience les vacances.
native_language_example: I’m looking forward to the vacation.

additional_notes: Composed of avec + le. Used before a masculine singular noun: avec le chien, avec le professeur. Unlike à + le or de + le, it does not contract.
target_language_example: Je parle avec le voisin.
native_language_example: I'm speaking with the neighbor.

meaning: over time; as time goes by.
additional_notes: Used to say that something changes gradually as time passes. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence as an introductory phrase (“Avec le temps, …”), but it can also come after the verb (“… avec le temps”). Not to be confused with “avec le beau temps” (with good weather).
target_language_example: Avec le temps, tu te sentiras mieux.
native_language_example: Over time, you’ll feel better.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “with the …”. It can express accompaniment (venir avec les amis), a relationship/connection (un lien avec les amis), comparison (comparer … avec les leurs), or something being associated/affected (un problème avec les freins). In set phrases: « Avec les compliments de… » = “With compliments from…”.
target_language_example: Je suis venu avec les enfants.
native_language_example: I came with the children.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together/spending time with children (your kids or other children), or doing something in their presence: rester avec les enfants (stay with the children), aller avec les enfants (go with the children), jouer/parler avec les enfants (play/talk with the children). "Les" is the plural definite article (“the”). Note: French "enfants" means “children,” not specifically “infants.”
target_language_example: Je reste à la maison avec les enfants ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm staying home with the children tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with a male person. After a preposition like avec, French uses the stressed pronoun lui, not il.
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma avec lui.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with him.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together/doing something in your sister’s company. In "Tom sort avec ma sœur", "sortir avec" often means "to date" (be in a relationship) rather than just "go out".
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma avec ma sœur ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with my sister tonight.

additional_notes: Used for being together with the speaker: physically near them, accompanying them, doing something jointly, or interacting with them. In some contexts, especially with être, it can also mean 'on my side' or 'following what I mean'.
target_language_example: Viens avec moi au marché.
native_language_example: Come with me to the market.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your brother or doing something alongside him. With some verbs (e.g., "se confondre"), it can mean "mistaken for my brother"; with "ça va/se passe bien", it asks how things are going between you and your brother.
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma avec mon frère ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with my brother tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone does something together with the speaker and their group. Common after verbs like venir, aller, rester, and travailler.
target_language_example: Tu peux dîner avec nous ce soir.
native_language_example: You can have dinner with us tonight.

additional_notes: Used to politely accept a request or offer help (often as a standalone reply, like “Sure!”). Also used in sentences to mean you did/will do something willingly and happily: “aider avec plaisir” = “to help gladly.”
target_language_example: Je peux vous aider, avec plaisir.
native_language_example: I can help you, with pleasure.

additional_notes: Used to indicate being accompanied by someone (doing something with someone): « aller avec quelqu’un », « venir avec quelqu’un », etc. With « être avec quelqu’un », it can also mean being in a romantic relationship with someone (“she’s seeing someone”). Often followed by « d’autre » to mean “someone else”: « avec quelqu’un d’autre ».
target_language_example: Elle est avec quelqu'un.
native_language_example: She’s with someone.

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask which person someone is with, talking to, competing with, going out with, etc. In everyday speech it often corresponds to “who … with?” (even though “whom” is more formal in English). Word order varies: “Avec qui parles-tu ?” or “Tu parles avec qui ?”.
target_language_example: Tu es avec qui ce soir ?
native_language_example: Who are you with tonight?

additional_notes: Used when the noun after it is feminine singular: avec sa langue (his/her tongue), avec sa classe (his/her class), avec sa main droite (his/her right hand). For a masculine singular noun, use "avec son"; for plural, "avec ses". It can also appear in "rompre avec sa ..." (“to break up with his/her ...”).
target_language_example: Il est venu avec sa sœur.
native_language_example: He came with his sister.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "avec" (with) + the possessive determiner "ses" before a plural noun: "ses talons", "ses clients". "Ses" means "his/her/their" depending on context, and it agrees with what is owned (plural), not with the owner’s gender.
target_language_example: Elle est venue avec ses amis.
native_language_example: She came with her friends.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together/spending time with their friends. "Ses" agrees with the person who has the friends (his or her), not with the friends themselves. Common with verbs like être, partir, discuter, boire, regarder, jouer, prendre un café.
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma avec ses amis ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with his/her friends tonight.

additional_notes: Used before a singular noun to mean that someone is with something that belongs to him or her. The exact English possessive depends on context, so son can also mean "its." Note that son is used with masculine singular nouns, and also before feminine singular nouns that begin with a vowel sound: avec son épée = "with her/his sword."
target_language_example: Il est venu avec son frère.
native_language_example: He came with his brother.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together/accompanied by their brother. It can describe doing an activity together (jouer avec son frère), coming with him (venir avec son frère), sharing something with him (partager… avec son frère), or being compared/confused with him (confondre… avec son frère). Note: it refers to a male person’s brother; for a female person, you’d usually say « avec son frère » as well (frère is masculine), but the possessor is shown by context or by using « son/sa » for the person being talked about.
target_language_example: Il est parti en vacances avec son frère.
native_language_example: He went on vacation with his brother.

meaning: “with your” (talking to one person; followed by a plural noun).
additional_notes: Used with the informal singular subject “tu” to refer to things that belong to the person you’re speaking to: “avec tes voisins” = “with your neighbors.” It’s common in complaints/insults: “avec tes …” can mean “with your stupid/dirty …,” depending on context and the adjective that follows. For feminine plural it becomes “avec tes …” as well; for singular: “avec ton” (masc.) / “avec ta” (fem.).
target_language_example: Arrête avec tes excuses !
native_language_example: Stop with your excuses!

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with, accompanying, or sharing something with the person spoken to. "toi" is the stressed form of "tu" used after a preposition like "avec"; for formal or plural "you," use "avec vous."
target_language_example: Je veux venir avec toi.
native_language_example: I want to come with you.

additional_notes: Used after an adjective or verb to say how someone behaves toward all people in general (not just one person). Common with être gentil(le), aimable, poli(e), parler avec, etc.
target_language_example: Il parle avec tout le monde à la fête.
native_language_example: He talks with everyone at the party.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun. It can mean being together with something/someone, or using something as a tool or means. Compare with "avec une" before a feminine singular noun.
target_language_example: Il ouvre la boîte avec un couteau.
native_language_example: He opens the box with a knife.

additional_notes: Used to say what tool/instrument you use to do an action. Often follows the verb (e.g., couper, manger). You can swap the noun: avec une fourchette (with a fork), avec une cuillère (with a spoon).
target_language_example: Ouvre le paquet avec un couteau, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Open the package with a knife, please.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is accompanied by or contains an object/feature. “Une” is the feminine form of “a/an,” so it’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., une douche, une bombe).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un café avec une pâtisserie, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a coffee with a pastry, please.

additional_notes: Question form of vous avez, made by inversion. It is used with vous for formal or plural 'you', especially in writing or careful speech.
target_language_example: Avez-vous le temps de parler ?
native_language_example: Do you have time to talk?

additional_notes: Inversion form used to ask a question with the verb acheter (to buy) in the passé composé: avez (have) + acheté (bought). Used with “vous” for one person formally or for multiple people. In everyday speech, French often uses “Vous avez acheté… ?” (rising intonation) instead.
target_language_example: Avez-vous acheté du pain ?
native_language_example: Did you buy any bread?

meaning: "did you say?" / "have you said?" (formal "you"), used to ask what someone said.
additional_notes: This is the inversion form of the passé composé: "avez" (have) + "vous" (you) + "dit" (said). It’s used in questions, often to confirm or clarify what someone said: "Avez-vous dit oui ?" (Did you say yes?) and in set phrases like "Qu’avez-vous dit ?" (What did you say?) and "Pardon, qu’avez-vous dit ?" (Sorry, what did you say?). With an object: "Que lui avez-vous dit ?" (What did you say to him/her?) and "Pourquoi lui avez-vous dit cela ?" (Why did you tell him/her that?).
target_language_example: Pardon, avez-vous dit quinze ou cinquante ?
native_language_example: Sorry, did you say fifteen or fifty?

additional_notes: Formal question form using inversion: "avez-vous" = "have you" (addressing one person politely, "vous"). "déjà" can mean "already" (something expected by now) or "ever" in questions about life experience, depending on context.
target_language_example: Avez-vous déjà visité Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever visited Paris?

additional_notes: "Avez-vous" is the formal/polite inversion form of "have you" (more common in writing or formal speech). "déjà" means "already" and, with questions like this, often corresponds to English "ever" (asking about past experience). Used to ask if someone has seen something before, or rhetorically to express surprise: "Have you ever seen anything like that?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous déjà vu un film aussi drôle ?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a movie that funny?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s past experiences. It’s the formal/inverted question form with vous. "déjà" = "ever/already"; "été" is the past participle of être (to be). Often followed by an adjective (amoureux), a past participle (licencié), or a situation/state (pris dans un accident). Agreement: "été" stays the same, but adjectives/past participles after it can agree (e.g., traitée for a woman).
target_language_example: Avez-vous déjà été à Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Paris?

additional_notes: This is the verb "entendre" (to hear) in the passé composé: "avez" + "entendu", used with inversion to form a question in a more formal style. It can mean hearing a sound/news (Avez-vous entendu la nouvelle… ?) or sometimes "Did you hear/understand me?" (M'avez-vous entendu ?). In everyday speech, you’ll often hear: "Vous avez entendu … ?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous entendu ce que le professeur a dit ?
native_language_example: Did you hear what the teacher said?

additional_notes: This is the formal, inverted question form of the passé composé of *avoir*: **vous avez eu** (“you had/you got”) → **avez-vous eu… ?**. It’s used to ask about something in the past, often meaning **had/received** (e.g., *des nouvelles* = news), **had/drank/eaten** (e.g., coffee), or **got/obtained** (e.g., a phone number, an item). In everyday speech, people often say **Vous avez eu… ?** instead of inversion.
target_language_example: Avez-vous eu le temps de lire mon message ?
native_language_example: Did you have time to read my message?

meaning: "have you done" / "did you do" (formal or polite question).
additional_notes: Inversion of verb + subject used to ask a question in a formal/polite way. Built from "avoir" (avez) + "vous" + past participle "fait" (from "faire"). Used to ask whether someone has done something (e.g., chores, homework) or what they did to someone: "Que lui avez-vous fait ?" = "What did you do to him/her?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous fait la réservation ?
native_language_example: Have you made the reservation?

additional_notes:
Used to ask if someone is done with an activity or task. This is the polite/formal question form with inversion ("avez-vous"), common in writing and formal speech. You can follow it with:
- "de" + infinitive: « Avez-vous fini de lire ? » (finished reading?)
- a noun: « Avez-vous fini votre repas ? » (finished your meal?)
You may also see « En avez-vous fini avec… ? » meaning “Are you done with …?” where « en » refers back to what you’re doing/using.
target_language_example: Avez-vous fini de remplir le formulaire ?
native_language_example: Have you finished filling out the form?

additional_notes: Formal question using inversion (avez-vous…). Used with a past participle after être to ask about someone’s past experience/state. In questions, "jamais" often means "ever" (not "never"). With être, the past participle agrees with the subject (e.g., été mariés / mariées; été seul / seule / seuls / seules).
target_language_example: Avez-vous jamais été à Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Paris?

additional_notes: "Avez-vous" is the formal (vous) way to ask a question using inversion. "lu" is the past participle of "lire" (to read), used with "avoir" in the passé composé. It can be followed by a noun (Avez-vous lu les instructions ?) or used with a direct object pronoun: "L’avez-vous lu ?" = "Have you read it?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous lu ce message ?
native_language_example: Have you read this message?

meaning: formal/inverted question form of «vous avez mis»: “did you put / did you place” or “how long did you take (to do something)” (with «mettre»).
additional_notes: «Avez-vous mis… ?» is the formal question form (inversion) of «Vous avez mis… ?». With a direct object (keys, sunscreen, etc.), «mettre» means “to put/place”: «Où avez-vous mis… ?» = “Where did you put…?”. With «combien de temps… pour + infinitive», it means “to take (time)”: «Combien de temps avez-vous mis pour… ?» = “How long did you take to…?”. Past participle agrees only with a preceding direct object pronoun (e.g., «les»).
target_language_example: Avez-vous mis du sucre dans le café ?
native_language_example: Did you put sugar in the coffee?

additional_notes: Formal inversion question using **vous** (often used with strangers, in interviews, with customers). Used to ask whether someone observed something: **avez-vous remarqué + noun** (Avez-vous remarqué sa robe ?) or **avez-vous remarqué que + clause** (Avez-vous remarqué que votre sac avait disparu ?). In everyday speech, you’ll also hear **Vous avez remarqué… ?**
target_language_example: Avez-vous remarqué que la porte était ouverte ?
native_language_example: Did you notice that the door was open?

additional_notes: Uses inversion (verb + “-vous”) for a polite/formal question in the passé composé. Often followed by a direct object: « Avez-vous reçu + noun ? ». In everyday speech you’ll also hear: « Est-ce que vous avez reçu… ? » or « Vous avez reçu… ? ».
target_language_example: Avez-vous reçu mon e-mail ?
native_language_example: Have you received my email?

additional_notes: Uses inversion (verb + hyphen + subject) to ask a question with "vous". It’s the passé composé of "trouver" (avez + trouvé), often used to ask whether someone has found something or what they thought of something (e.g., "Avez-vous trouvé ça utile ?" = "Did you find that useful?").
target_language_example: Avez-vous trouvé votre chemin jusqu’ici ?
native_language_example: Did you manage to find your way here?

additional_notes: Inversion question form of "vous avez vu" (you have seen). Used to ask if someone has seen a person/thing, or has noticed/witnessed something: "Avez-vous vu Tom ?" / "Avez-vous vu ce qu’il a fait ?" In casual speech you’ll often hear "Vous avez vu… ?" or "Est-ce que vous avez vu… ?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous vu mon sac quelque part ?
native_language_example: Have you seen my bag anywhere?

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of "être" with subject–verb inversion used in questions. It’s used with "vous" (either formal singular or plural). The past participle "été" can agree with the subject in gender/number in some contexts (e.g., "Avez-vous été blessée ?" to a woman; "blessé" to a man; "blessés/blessées" for plural). Often used to ask about past states or experiences: "avez-vous été en France ?" (have you been to France?), "avez-vous été malade ?" (have you been sick?).
target_language_example: Avez-vous été en France l’année dernière ?
native_language_example: Have you been to France last year?

additional_notes: Formal inversion of vous avez used to ask a question. Vous can mean plural "you" or formal singular "you." Often seen in polite speech, writing, and service interactions.
target_language_example: Avez-vous une réservation ?
native_language_example: Do you have a reservation?

meaning: "Do you have any …?" (formal; asking about plural items).
additional_notes: Uses subject–verb inversion (avez-vous) for a polite/formal question. Followed by "des" + a plural noun (or things thought of in the plural). Often translates as "any" in English: "Avez-vous des menus en anglais ?" → "Do you have any English menus?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous des chambres disponibles ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you have any rooms available tonight?

meaning: “Do you have a…?” (formal/polite, for one masculine item).
additional_notes: This is the formal inversion question form of « vous avez ». Use it in polite situations (shops, hotels, officials). « un » is used for a singular masculine noun (un passeport, un parapluie). For feminine nouns, use « avez-vous une… ? » (une réservation). For plural, « avez-vous des… ? ».
target_language_example: Bonjour, avez-vous un plan de la ville ?
native_language_example: Hello, do you have a city map?

additional_notes: Used to ask a question with inversion (verb + -vous). It’s followed by a feminine singular noun: Avez-vous une boutique… ? For masculine singular, use « avez-vous un… ? »; for plural, « avez-vous des… ? ». Common in shops, restaurants, and formal situations.
target_language_example: Avez-vous une table pour deux ?
native_language_example: Do you have a table for two?

meaning: a wanted notice; a police bulletin saying someone is wanted.
additional_notes: Used for an official notice (often from police) posted or broadcast to help find a person (suspect, missing person, escaped prisoner). You’ll see it on posters, in the news, or online: « Un avis de recherche a été lancé contre/pour… ». Not the same as a simple « annonce » or « avis » (review/opinion).
target_language_example: La police a lancé un avis de recherche pour retrouver le suspect.
native_language_example: The police issued a wanted notice to find the suspect.

additional_notes: Past infinitive of être. It is used to talk about a state or quality that existed before another moment, often after verbs like sembler, devoir, penser, dire, or croire: elle semble avoir été heureuse = she seems to have been happy.
target_language_example: Elle dit avoir été malade la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: She says she was sick last week.

additional_notes: Used with “à” + a place/thing/service: “avoir accès à Internet”, “avoir accès au bâtiment”. Often means you are allowed/able to use or enter something (permission, credentials, rights).
target_language_example: Est-ce que je peux avoir accès au Wi-Fi ici ?
native_language_example: Can I have access to the Wi‑Fi here?

meaning: to be dealing with; to have to do with.
additional_notes: Used with a person or a situation/thing: « avoir affaire à quelqu’un/quelque chose ». It often means you are confronted with or must handle someone/something (sometimes with a sense of difficulty: « Tu ne sais pas à qui tu as affaire ! »). Not related to an “affair” in the romantic sense.
target_language_example: Aujourd’hui, je vais avoir affaire à un client très exigeant.
native_language_example: Today, I’m going to be dealing with a very demanding client.

meaning: to do something in vain; to do something but with no result ("no matter how much...").
additional_notes: Used almost always as **avoir beau + infinitive**. It means that despite your efforts, the situation doesn’t change: *J’ai beau essayer…* = “I try and try, but… / No matter how much I try…”. It does **not** mean “to have something beautiful,” even though *beau* means “beautiful.”
target_language_example: Il a beau lui téléphoner, il ne répond jamais.
native_language_example: No matter how much he calls him, he never answers.

additional_notes: Used to express necessity or need. It is followed by a noun or by an infinitive: avoir besoin de quelque chose / avoir besoin de faire quelque chose. Literally, it is closer to 'to have need of.'
target_language_example: Tu pourrais avoir besoin de ceci.
native_language_example: You might need this.

meaning: to be right; to have guessed correctly.
additional_notes: Used mostly in some regional French (especially Switzerland/Belgium) or in older-style French. In standard French, you usually say « avoir raison » (to be right). Often appears in the past: « tu avais bon » = “you were right.”
target_language_example: Je crois que je vais avoir bon : il va pleuvoir.
native_language_example: I think I’m going to be right: it’s going to rain.

meaning: to look well; to look healthy (good complexion).
additional_notes: Used to comment on someone’s appearance (they look rested, healthy, or in good shape). Often said as a compliment, commonly in the present tense (e.g., « Tu as bonne mine ! »). The word « mine » here means someone’s face/appearance, not an actual mine.
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, tu sembles avoir bonne mine ; tu as bien dormi ?
native_language_example: Today, you seem to look well; did you sleep well?

meaning: to be hot; to feel warm (because of the temperature).
additional_notes: Literally “to have hot,” but in French you use avoir + adjective for physical sensations: avoir chaud (hot), avoir froid (cold). Common conjugations: j’ai chaud, tu as chaud, il/elle a chaud, nous avons chaud, vous avez chaud, ils/elles ont chaud. You can also use it in infinitive form after another verb: je vais avoir chaud, je commence à avoir chaud, je ne veux pas avoir chaud. You can add a cause: avoir chaud à cause du soleil. Note: “avoir chaud au cul” is vulgar slang meaning to feel “hot” in a sexual sense.
target_language_example: Tom doit avoir chaud.
native_language_example: Tom must be hot.

additional_notes: Often used with "en" + a person/thing: "avoir confiance en quelqu’un" = to trust someone; "avoir confiance en soi" = to be confident in yourself. Also common in the negative: "Je n’ai pas confiance" = I don’t trust (it/them).
target_language_example: Il faut avoir confiance en toi.
native_language_example: You have to trust yourself.

meaning: to be aware of; to know about (usually: "avoir connaissance de").
additional_notes: Most often used with "de" + noun: "avoir connaissance de quelque chose" = to have knowledge/awareness of something, often in a formal or official context (documents, information, facts). Related expression: "prendre/reprendre connaissance" means "to (re)gain consciousness" (medical sense), but that's a different phrase.
target_language_example: Je déclare avoir connaissance de ces faits.
native_language_example: I declare that I am aware of these facts.

meaning: to be aware (of); to realize; to be conscious (of).
additional_notes: Usually followed by "de" + noun/infinitive: "avoir conscience de + nom" (to be aware of something) or "avoir conscience de + infinitif" (to realize/understand that you are doing something). Also possible with "que" + clause: "avoir conscience que..." Often used for recognizing the seriousness or reality of a situation. Don’t confuse with English "conscience" (moral sense): French "conscience" can also mean "awareness/consciousness".
target_language_example: Je dois avoir conscience que ce sera difficile.
native_language_example: I have to be aware that it will be difficult.

meaning: to be in effect; to be valid; to apply (for a rule, law, practice).
additional_notes: Used for things like laws, rules, currencies, prices, customs, or ideas that are currently accepted or officially valid: «Cette loi a cours» = this law is in force. Don’t confuse with the classroom-related sense: French more commonly uses «avoir des cours» / «suivre des cours» for having/taking classes; «avoir cours» in the “be in effect” sense is different.
target_language_example: Cette règle n’a plus : avoir cours depuis 2020.
native_language_example: This rule has no longer been in effect since 2020.

meaning: to be lucky; to have luck.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is lucky in general or in a specific situation. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., « avoir de la chance de + infinitive » = “to be lucky to…”). You can also wish someone luck with « Bonne chance ! ».
target_language_example: Je suis content d’avoir de la chance d’avoir une place près de la fenêtre.
native_language_example: I’m happy to be lucky enough to have a seat near the window.

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck (in a given situation).
additional_notes: Common, fairly informal way to say someone has good luck, often about a particular situation. Frequently used as an exclamation: « Tu as de la veine ! » Literally « to have some vein », so it’s idiomatic rather than a literal translation.
target_language_example: On va peut-être rater le train, mais si on a de la veine, il y aura un autre départ dans dix minutes.
native_language_example: We might miss the train, but if we’re lucky, there’ll be another departure in ten minutes.

meaning: to have children (to be a parent; or to plan to become one).
additional_notes: Used both for already being parents (having children) and for wanting/trying/planning to have kids in the future. Very common with verbs like vouloir (to want), aimer (to like), envisager (to consider), s’imaginer (to imagine), and in questions (Voulez-vous… ?).
target_language_example: Ils veulent avoir des enfants l'année prochaine.
native_language_example: They want to have children next year.

meaning: to be educated; to be well-read.
additional_notes: A rather formal/old-fashioned expression. Here, « les lettres » refers to literature and the humanities (as in « un homme de lettres » = a man of letters), not actual letters in the mail. It implies having learning or a strong literary education.
target_language_example: Il semble avoir des lettres : il cite des auteurs classiques avec aisance.
native_language_example: He seems to be well-read: he quotes classic authors with ease.

meaning: to be entitled to; to have the right to (avoir droit à…).
additional_notes: Often used with **à**: **avoir droit à + noun** (something you’re entitled to) or **avoir droit de + infinitive** (more formal: the right to do something). Common in rules, benefits, permissions, and legal/official contexts. In everyday speech, **avoir le droit de** is also very common for permissions.
target_language_example: Vous pouvez avoir droit à une réduction si vous êtes étudiant.
native_language_example: You may be entitled to a discount if you’re a student.

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck.
additional_notes: Informal expression meaning you had good luck (often by chance). Commonly used in the present (« J’ai du bol ») or past (« J’ai eu du bol »).
target_language_example: On dirait qu’on va avoir du bol : le soleil revient juste à temps pour la balade.
native_language_example: Looks like we’re going to be lucky: the sun is coming back just in time for the walk.

meaning: to have some good points; to be beneficial in some way.
additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t perfect, but it has advantages or positive aspects. Common in general statements: « Ça peut avoir du bon » / « Avoir du bon, c’est… ». Close in meaning to « Il y a du bon (là-dedans) » (“there’s something good in it”).
target_language_example: Travailler à la maison peut avoir du bon : tu gagnes du temps.
native_language_example: Working from home can have its benefits: you save time.

meaning: to have trouble (doing something); to struggle.
additional_notes: Often used with "à" + infinitive: "avoir du mal à + verb" (to have difficulty doing something). It can mean something is hard, takes effort, or you’re not succeeding easily. In the negative, "ne pas avoir de mal à" means "to have no trouble".
target_language_example: Je vais avoir du mal à trouver le sommeil, maintenant.
native_language_example: I’m going to have trouble falling asleep now.

avoir du pain sur la planche

target_language_multi_word_term: avoir du pain sur la planche
meaning: to have a lot to do; to have plenty of work ahead of you.
additional_notes: Idiomatic and common in everyday speech. It conveys that you have many tasks waiting for you, often in the near future. Used in different tenses (e.g., « J’avais du pain sur la planche »).
target_language_example: Cette semaine, je vais avoir du pain sur la planche : je dois finir le rapport et préparer la présentation.
native_language_example: This week, I’m going to have a lot to do: I have to finish the report and prepare the presentation.

additional_notes: Informal/colloquial. Used to say someone has good luck (often in a specific situation). You can also use it as an exclamation: « Quel pot ! » = “What luck!”
target_language_example: Tu vas avoir du pot : il reste une dernière place !
native_language_example: You’re going to be lucky: there’s one last seat left!

avoir du sang sur les mains

target_language_multi_word_term: avoir du sang sur les mains
meaning: to have blood on your hands (to be responsible for someone’s death or serious harm).
additional_notes: Used to accuse someone of being guilty/responsible (directly or indirectly) for violence or a tragedy. Can be literal (actual blood) but is very often figurative (moral/legal responsibility). Common forms: « Il a du sang sur les mains. » / « Vous avez du sang sur les mains. »
target_language_example: Il affirme que le ministre peut avoir du sang sur les mains après cette décision.
native_language_example: He claims the minister may have blood on his hands after that decision.

meaning: to make sense; to be meaningful.
additional_notes: Used to say something is logical/understandable (often with « Ça/Cela » or « Ce que tu dis »): « Ça a du sens. » In the negative: « Ça n’a pas de sens. » It can also mean something has meaning or purpose: « Sa vie a du sens. »
target_language_example: Ça doit avoir du sens.
native_language_example: It has to make sense.

meaning: to have in mind; to remember; to keep in mind.
additional_notes: Used to express that you’re thinking about something (an idea, plan, intention) or that you’re keeping something present in your memory. Very common in everyday French. Often followed by a noun or clause: « avoir en tête une idée », « avoir en tête que… ».
target_language_example: J’ai avoir en tête une idée pour notre voyage.
native_language_example: I have an idea in mind for our trip.

additional_notes: Usually used as: « avoir envie de + noun » or « avoir envie de + infinitive ». It expresses a desire/craving in the moment (often softer than « vouloir »). In the negative: « je n’ai pas envie de… » = “I don’t feel like…”
target_language_example: Je vais avoir envie de prendre un café.
native_language_example: I’m going to feel like having a coffee.

additional_notes: Literally “to have hunger,” but it’s the standard way to say “to be hungry” in French. Use it after another verb like devoir (must) or commencer à (to start to): Il doit avoir faim = He must be hungry.
target_language_example: Il doit avoir faim.
native_language_example: He must be hungry.

additional_notes: Often followed by "en" + noun/pronoun: "avoir foi en Dieu" (to have faith in God), "avoir foi en toi" (to believe in you). Can be religious or more general (trust/confidence in a person, idea, or plan).
target_language_example: Tu dois avoir foi en toi : tu vas y arriver.
native_language_example: You have to believe in yourself: you’re going to make it.

additional_notes: French commonly uses "avoir" (to have) for physical sensations: "J’ai froid" = "I’m cold." You can also use it for predictions or assumptions: "Tu dois avoir froid" (You must be cold) / "Vous allez avoir froid" (You’re going to be cold). Common opposite: "avoir chaud" (to be hot/warm).
target_language_example: Tu dois avoir froid, prends mon pull.
native_language_example: You must be cold—take my sweater.

additional_notes: Used with avoir + noun (literally “to have shame”). Often followed by de + noun/verb to say what you’re ashamed of: avoir honte de son comportement (to be ashamed of one’s behavior), avoir honte de dire la vérité (to be ashamed to tell the truth). With devoir (tu/devrais) it can sound like a reproach: “You should be ashamed.”
target_language_example: Tu devrais avoir honte de ton comportement.
