meaning: 'this car is …' (used to describe or identify a specific car).
additional_notes: "Cette voiture" means "this car" (feminine singular). "Est" is the verb "to be" (he/she/it is). You typically follow it with an adjective (couleur, état: "noire", "comme neuve"), a noun phrase to identify/claim it ("la mienne", "la sienne"), or possession with "à + stress pronoun" ("à lui", "à elle").
target_language_example: Cette voiture est très pratique en ville.
native_language_example: This car is very practical in the city.

additional_notes: Used to point to specific items/people that are close in space/time or in the conversation. It replaces a noun (e.g., 'those books' → 'ceux-ci' if 'books' is already understood). Typically refers to masculine plural nouns; for feminine plural, use 'celles-ci'. Often contrasts with 'ceux-là' = 'those (ones)' farther away / the other ones.
target_language_example: Parmi tous les modèles, je préfère ceux-ci.
native_language_example: Among all the models, I prefer these ones.

meaning: “those (ones)”, referring to specific masculine plural items (not near the speaker).
additional_notes: Masculine plural demonstrative pronoun: ceux (ones) + -là (over there / the ones you mean). Used to point out or contrast items: « Ceux-ci …, ceux-là … ». For feminine plural, use « celles-là ». Often used with « de »: « un de ceux-là » = “one of those.”
target_language_example: Je préfère ceux-là, pas ceux-ci.
native_language_example: I prefer those (ones), not these.

meaning: "those who have" (the people who have done/experienced something).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people defined by what they have done or what has happened to them. It’s followed by a past participle (e.g., "ceux qui ont quitté", "ceux qui ont vécu"). You’ll often see it contrasted with "ceux qui n’ont pas…" (“those who haven’t…”). Feminine plural is "celles qui ont".
target_language_example: Je remercie ceux qui ont aidé pendant la crise.
native_language_example: I thank those who helped during the crisis.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people (plural) who share a characteristic: **ceux qui + verb** = “those who + verb.” Here **ont** is the present tense of **avoir** (“to have”). It’s for a masculine or mixed group; for an all-female group, say **celles qui ont**. Often followed by a noun phrase: **ceux qui ont des problèmes** (“those who have problems”).
target_language_example: Ceux qui ont des questions peuvent me demander maintenant.
native_language_example: Those who have questions can ask me now.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific group of people defined by what they are like or their condition/location, often followed by an adjective, a prepositional phrase, or a further description: « Ceux qui sont devant… », « ceux qui sont prêts… ». It contrasts with « ceux qui ont » (“those who have”) and can be feminine: « celles qui sont ».
target_language_example: Ceux qui sont en retard doivent s'excuser.
native_language_example: Those who are late have to apologize.

additional_notes: "Ceux-ci" is a demonstrative pronoun meaning “these ones” (plural, usually masculine or mixed group). It’s used to point out specific items close to you or in the current context, often contrasted with "ceux-là" (“those ones”). For a plural feminine group, use "celles-ci sont". In questions, invert: "Ceux-ci sont-ils… ?"
target_language_example: Ceux-ci sont mes chaussures, pas les tiennes.
native_language_example: These are my shoes, not yours.

meaning: "every man for himself" / "each person for themselves."
additional_notes: Said when people stop cooperating and everyone looks out for their own interests (often in a negative or resigned tone). Often heard as part of the proverb: « Chacun pour soi, Dieu pour tous » (“Every man for himself, God for everyone”).
target_language_example: Quand la nourriture a manqué, c'était chacun pour soi.
native_language_example: When the food ran out, it was every man for himself.

additional_notes: Used to describe the little bumps on your skin when you’re cold, scared, or moved (e.g., by music). Very common with the verb phrase "avoir la chair de poule" (to have goosebumps).
target_language_example: J'ai la chair de poule quand j'écoute cette chanson.
native_language_example: I get goosebumps when I listen to that song.

additional_notes: A more specific/neutral way to say “bedroom,” especially in contexts like describing a home or asking what’s in the room. In everyday speech, people also often just say “chambre.”
target_language_example: La chambre à coucher est au bout du couloir.
native_language_example: The bedroom is at the end of the hallway.

meaning: gas chamber (a room where people are killed with poison gas).
additional_notes: Used mainly in historical contexts (notably Nazi extermination camps during WWII) or to refer to a method of execution. Very heavy, sensitive term.
target_language_example: Pendant la Seconde Guerre mondiale, des prisonniers ont été tués dans une chambre à gaz.
native_language_example: During World War II, prisoners were killed in a gas chamber.

meaning: battlefield; (figuratively) a place of intense conflict.
additional_notes: Literally “field of battle.” Used for a real battlefield in war (“sur le champ de bataille” = on the battlefield). It’s also common figuratively to describe a chaotic or hostile situation (e.g., streets, politics, the workplace).
target_language_example: Après la manifestation, le centre-ville ressemblait à un champ de bataille.
native_language_example: After the protest, downtown looked like a battlefield.

additional_notes: Used for a person or team that has won the top international title in a sport or competition. Often used with an article (le champion du monde / la championne du monde) or as a title after the noun (Ayrton Senna, champion du monde). Feminine: championne du monde.
target_language_example: Il a le potentiel pour devenir un champion du monde.
native_language_example: He has the potential to become a world champion.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used in news, politics, and science to talk about long-term changes in the climate. Often used with verbs like parler de (talk about), agir contre (act against), être menacé par (be threatened by), and faire contre (do something about).
target_language_example: On doit réduire nos émissions pour lutter contre le changement climatique.
native_language_example: We need to reduce our emissions to fight climate change.

additional_notes: Used when someone revises a decision or opinion. The structure is: changer d’avis (no article). It often appears with verbs like pouvoir/devoir/faire: Tu peux changer d’avis (You can change your mind), Il a dû changer d’avis (He must have changed his mind), Je vais te faire changer d’avis (I’m going to make you change your mind).
target_language_example: Si tu veux, tu peux encore changer d'avis.
native_language_example: If you want, you can still change your mind.

additional_notes: Used with the verb changer: "changer d’avis" = to change your mind/opinion/decision. It’s the past participle "changé" + the preposition "de" (contracted to "d'" before a vowel) + "avis". In the passé composé, it is usually formed with "avoir" (e.g., "j'ai changé d'avis", "nous avons changé d'avis"). Neutral/polite in most contexts.
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai changé d'avis : je ne peux pas venir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I changed my mind: I can’t come.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens annually (a repeated habit or regular event). Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence: « Chaque année, … » / « … chaque année. ».
target_language_example: Nous visitons mes grands-parents chaque année.
native_language_example: We visit my grandparents every year.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a repeated situation or habit. It’s followed by a verb (often in the present for general habits, or in the past for repeated past events). The second clause can be separated by a comma in writing.
target_language_example: Chaque fois que je voyage, j’achète une carte postale.
native_language_example: Every time I travel, I buy a postcard.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens daily. Often goes at the end of the sentence (Je viens ici chaque jour), but it can also be placed earlier for emphasis.
target_language_example: Je fais du sport chaque jour.
native_language_example: I work out every day.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens each morning regularly or as a habit. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis ("Chaque matin, ..."), or after the verb ("Elle le salue chaque matin.").
target_language_example: Je fais du café chaque matin.
native_language_example: I make coffee every morning.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens weekly. « chaque » means “each/every” and is followed directly by a singular noun (chaque semaine, chaque jour, chaque année).
target_language_example: Je vais à la piscine chaque semaine.
native_language_example: I go to the pool every week.

additional_notes: Refers to someone paid a reward (une prime) to track down and capture/bring in a person (often a criminal). Often used with être: « Il est chasseur de primes. » Note: « prime » here means a reward/bonus, not “prime” (as in primary) or prime numbers.
target_language_example: Ils ont engagé un chasseur de primes pour le retrouver.
native_language_example: They hired a bounty hunter to track him down.

additional_notes: A feminine noun: une chauve-souris, des chauve-souris. Despite the literal parts ("bald" + "mouse"), it simply means the animal "bat" in everyday French. Often used when talking about caves, night, and hunting insects.
target_language_example: J’ai vu une chauve-souris voler près de la fenêtre.
native_language_example: I saw a bat flying near the window.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific channel you watch on TV (often numbered: la première/deuxième chaîne) or a broadcaster (locale/nationale). Often said as "une chaîne" when the context is TV.
target_language_example: Tu regardes quelle chaîne de télévision ce soir ?
native_language_example: Which TV channel are you watching tonight?

meaning: a masterpiece (a great work of art).
additional_notes: Used for an outstanding work (a painting, book, film, etc.). Often appears with articles: « un chef-d'œuvre » (a masterpiece), « le chef-d'œuvre de… » (the masterpiece of…). Can also be used more broadly for something exceptionally well done.
target_language_example: Ce film est un vrai chef-d'œuvre.
native_language_example: This film is a real masterpiece.

additional_notes: A common way to say “the railway/railroad” as a system/industry (often with "le"). Used in related phrases like "un pont de chemin de fer" (a railway bridge).
target_language_example: Elle travaille dans le chemin de fer depuis dix ans.
native_language_example: She has worked in the railway industry for ten years.

meaning: to try to; to seek to (do something).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive: « chercher à + infinitive ». It often implies making an effort or attempting to achieve something, sometimes with the idea of aiming for a result (not literally “searching”). Example: « Il cherche à comprendre » = he’s trying to understand.
target_language_example: Je vais chercher à améliorer mon français.
native_language_example: I’m going to try to improve my French.

meaning: "are you looking for…?" / "what are you looking for?" (formal question form).
additional_notes: This is the verb "chercher" (to look for/seek) with "vous" in inverted question order: "Cherchez-vous… ?" = "Are you looking for…?" It’s fairly formal; in everyday speech you often hear "Vous cherchez… ?" or "Qu’est-ce que vous cherchez ?". It can also mean "to seek" in a broader sense (e.g., "Que cherchez-vous à prouver ?" = "What are you trying to prove?").
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, cherchez-vous quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, are you looking for something?

additional_notes: Literally “white hair.” Used to talk about someone’s hair color (often with age). In expressions like « se faire des cheveux blancs » or « donner des cheveux blancs à quelqu’un », it means “to worry a lot” / “to make someone worry” (as if stress could make hair turn white).
target_language_example: Depuis qu’il a pris ce nouveau travail, il se fait des cheveux blancs.
native_language_example: Since he started this new job, he’s been worrying a lot.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s hair color. Often appears with "avoir" (Elle a les cheveux blonds) or after "aux" to mean "with" (le garçon aux cheveux blonds = the blond-haired boy). Note: "cheveux" is plural in French, so you usually say "les cheveux" or "des cheveux" (not *le cheveu* in this context).
target_language_example: J’ai les cheveux blonds, mais mon frère a les cheveux bruns.
native_language_example: I have blond hair, but my brother has brown hair.

additional_notes: A masculine noun: (un/le) chewing-gum. Used for the sweet you chew; common with the verbs mâcher (to chew) and vouloir (to want).
target_language_example: Tu as un chewing-gum à la menthe ?
native_language_example: Do you have a mint chewing gum?

meaning: at her place; to her place (her home).
additional_notes: “Chez” means “at/to someone’s place (home, office, etc.).” With “elle,” it refers to a female person: je vais chez elle (I’m going to her place), je suis chez elle (I’m at her place). Often used with verbs like aller (to go), rentrer (to go back/come home), rester (to stay), raccompagner (to escort back).
target_language_example: Je passe chez elle ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m stopping by her place tonight.

meaning: at their place / at their home; to their place (home).
additional_notes: Used with **chez + stressed pronoun** to talk about being **at someone’s house** or going **to someone’s house**. Here **eux** = “them” (for a group or for “they”). Common with verbs like **être** (to be), **vivre** (to live), **rentrer** (to go back/come home), **arriver** (to arrive), **travailler depuis** (to work from).
target_language_example: Après le dîner, on est allés chez eux.
native_language_example: After dinner, we went to their place.

meaning: at the hairdresser’s (salon); to the hairdresser’s.
additional_notes: "Chez" means "at/to someone’s place" or "at/to a business". "Le coiffeur" is the hairdresser (the person); in everyday French, "aller chez le coiffeur" means going to the hairdresser’s salon. Often used with verbs like aller (to go) and se faire couper les cheveux (to get your hair cut).
target_language_example: On se retrouve après, je vais d’abord chez le coiffeur.
native_language_example: Let’s meet up afterward; I’m going to the hairdresser’s first.

meaning: at the dentist’s (office); to the dentist.
additional_notes: Uses "chez" to mean "at/to someone’s place" (here: the dentist’s office). Very common with appointments: "J’ai rendez-vous chez le dentiste". You can also say "aller chez le dentiste" / "se rendre chez le dentiste" = "to go to the dentist".
target_language_example: Demain matin, je vais chez le dentiste pour un contrôle.
native_language_example: Tomorrow morning, I’m going to the dentist for a check-up.

meaning: at the doctor’s (office); to the doctor.
additional_notes: Uses "chez" to mean “at/to someone’s place,” so "chez le médecin" means at the doctor’s office (going there or being there). Common with verbs like "aller" (to go) and "avoir rendez-vous" (to have an appointment).
target_language_example: Je dois passer chez le médecin demain matin.
native_language_example: I have to stop by the doctor’s tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Uses "chez" + a stressed pronoun (lui = him) to mean "at/to someone’s home or place". Often refers to the person’s home, but can also mean their place in general (their apartment, house, office, etc.). You can change the pronoun: chez moi (my place), chez toi (your place), chez elle (her place), chez nous (our place), etc.
target_language_example: On va chez lui après le travail.
native_language_example: We’re going to his place after work.

additional_notes: Used with chez + a stressed pronoun to talk about someone's home or place. With verbs like être or rester, it means being at your place; with aller or venir, it can mean going to your place.
target_language_example: On peut dîner chez moi ce soir.
native_language_example: We can have dinner at my place tonight.

additional_notes: Means “at/to our home/our place.” With a verb of motion (aller, rentrer, venir), it often means “to our place”; with a verb describing where something happens (habiter, parler, manger), it means “at our place.” It can also mean “in our country/our region” in broader contexts (e.g., politics: « une armée chez nous » = “an army in our country”).
target_language_example: On se retrouve chez nous après le travail.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at our place after work.

meaning: at home; at one’s own place.
additional_notes: Uses the preposition chez (“at someone’s place”) + the reflexive stress pronoun soi (“oneself”) to mean being at your own home. Very common with verbs like être (to be) and rentrer (to go/come back): être chez soi, rentrer chez soi. It can also be used in general sayings/proverbs about “in one’s own home.”
target_language_example: Après le travail, je suis content d'être chez moi, chez soi c'est plus calme.
native_language_example: After work, I’m happy to be at my place; at home it’s calmer.

additional_notes: "Chez" means "at someone’s place / home." With "toi" it refers to the listener: "chez toi" = your home/your place. Often used with movement verbs: "Va chez toi" (go to your place), "Rentre chez toi" (go back home). It can also be used more generally to mean "in your home" or "with you" (in your personal life): "Je veux que tu te sentes chez toi" = I want you to feel at home.
target_language_example: Tu peux rester chez toi ce soir.
native_language_example: You can stay at your place tonight.

additional_notes: Means “at your home/house” or “to your home,” depending on the verb: with location verbs (être, rester, manger, etc.) it’s usually “at your place,” and with movement verbs (rentrer, aller, accompagner, etc.) it’s usually “to your home.” Can also be used more generally as “where you are/where you belong” (e.g., in a seat or role).
target_language_example: Je peux passer chez vous vers 18 h.
native_language_example: I can stop by your place around 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the Roman numeral system (I, V, X, L, C, D, M). You’ll see it in book chapters, centuries (le XXIe siècle), monarch names (Louis XIV), and sometimes clock faces. Singular: un chiffre romain; plural: des chiffres romains.
target_language_example: Dans ce livre, les chapitres sont numérotés en chiffre romain.
native_language_example: In this book, the chapters are numbered using Roman numerals.

additional_notes: A common food item. Usually used with the definite article: "le chocolat blanc". In preferences you’ll often see verbs like "aimer" (to like) and "préférer" (to prefer), e.g., "préférer le chocolat blanc" or "préférer le chocolat blanc au chocolat (noir)" (prefer white chocolate to (dark) chocolate).
target_language_example: Je prends une glace au chocolat blanc, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll have a white chocolate ice cream, please.

additional_notes: A common drink order. Often used with an article: "un chocolat chaud" (one hot chocolate) or "du chocolat chaud" (some hot chocolate). In a café, you can order by saying simply: "Un chocolat chaud, s'il vous plaît."
target_language_example: Je prendrai un chocolat chaud, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'll have a hot chocolate, please.

meaning: thing to do; the right/best/next thing to do.
additional_notes: Literally “thing to do.” Very common with an adjective and often with an article: la première/dernière/prochaine chose à faire (the first/last/next thing to do), la meilleure chose à faire (the best thing to do), la bonne chose à faire (the right thing to do). Used to talk about what action should be taken in a situation.
target_language_example: Avant de partir, la première chose à faire, c'est d'éteindre les lumières.
native_language_example: Before leaving, the first thing to do is to turn off the lights.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about tasks, errands, or activities you need to do. Often used with quantities like trop de (too many), plein de (lots of), and with time expressions (ce matin, aujourd’hui) to say when you have them to do.
target_language_example: J’ai encore deux ou trois choses à faire avant ce soir.
native_language_example: I still have two or three things to do before this evening.

additional_notes: Used for a castle-shaped structure made from sand, typically built by children on the beach. Often used with verbs like construire / faire (to build / make) and can be affected by the tide (la marée).
target_language_example: On a construit un château de sable près de l’eau.
native_language_example: We built a sandcastle near the water.

meaning: 'below' / 'down below' (in a document, page, or list).
additional_notes: Used mostly in writing/instructions to point the reader to information that appears later on the same page/screen (often right after). Common in forms, emails, manuals: « Voir/Voyez ci-dessous », « le texte ci-dessous », « le champ ci-dessous ».
target_language_example: Vous trouverez les détails ci-dessous.
native_language_example: You’ll find the details below.

meaning: 'this (one) here is…' (pointing to a specific nearby one).
additional_notes: “-ci” is added to a demonstrative (ce/cet/cette/ces) to emphasize the exact thing you mean: ce gâteau-ci, cet arbre-ci, cette boîte-ci. It’s often contrasted with “-là” (“that one over there”): cette boîte-ci est plus grande que celle-là. It’s written with a hyphen: ce …-ci.
target_language_example: Cette chaise-ci est plus confortable.
native_language_example: This chair here is more comfortable.

additional_notes: Used for durations of time ("for five years", "five years ago") and for age ("five years old"). Common patterns: « avoir cinq ans » = to be five; « il y a cinq ans » = five years ago; « depuis cinq ans » = for/since five years; « cela fait cinq ans que… » = it’s been five years since….
target_language_example: J'habite ici depuis cinq ans.
native_language_example: I've lived here for five years.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 500. When used by itself as a number, you usually pronounce the final -s in "cents" (unlike in "cinq cent un" where "cent" stays singular). In "cinq cents ans" it means "500 years (old)".
target_language_example: Le billet coûte cinq cents euros.
native_language_example: The ticket costs five hundred euros.

additional_notes: Used either to tell the time (Il est cinq heures = It’s five o’clock) or to talk about a duration (un voyage de cinq heures = a five-hour trip). With schedules, use "à cinq heures" (at five o’clock). After "dès", it means "as early as" (dès cinq heures).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à cinq heures ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at five o’clock?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a time duration. Very often used with "dans" to mean "in five minutes" (something will happen after five minutes).
target_language_example: Je reviens dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in five minutes.

meaning: “loud and clear” (radio/phone reception); literally “five out of five.”
additional_notes: Used to confirm that you can hear/receive someone perfectly, especially in radio communication (aviation, emergency services, walkie-talkies). Often follows verbs like « Je te/vous reçois… » or appears as « Reçu cinq sur cinq » (“Received loud and clear”).
target_language_example: Allô ? Je te reçois cinq sur cinq !
native_language_example: Hello? I hear you loud and clear!

additional_notes: The number 52. It’s often used in dates, especially years: « mille neuf cent cinquante-deux » (more formally: « mille neuf cent cinquante-deux » or with hyphens « mille-neuf-cent-cinquante-deux ») = 1952. « né / née » agrees with the speaker: a man says « Je suis né… », a woman says « Je suis née… ».
target_language_example: Il a cinquante-deux ans.
native_language_example: He is 52 years old.

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning the light of the moon (often in poetic or romantic contexts). Used in expressions like "au clair de lune" (by moonlight) or "un clair de lune" (a moonlit scene/night).
target_language_example: On s’est promenés au clair de lune.
native_language_example: We went for a walk by moonlight.

additional_notes: Refers to the social/economic group between the working class and the wealthy (upper class). Often used when talking about society, politics, jobs, income level, or lifestyle: « venir de la classe moyenne » (to come from a middle-class background), « être membre de la classe moyenne » (to be part of the middle class).
target_language_example: Beaucoup de familles de la classe moyenne ont du mal à payer le loyer.
native_language_example: Many middle-class families have trouble paying rent.

meaning: a wink; a nod to (a reference).
additional_notes: Literally “blink of an eye.” Most commonly means a wink (gesture). By extension, it can mean a subtle reference or inside joke (“un clin d'œil à …”). You’ll often see it with the verb faire: “faire un clin d'œil (à quelqu’un)”.
target_language_example: Il m’a fait un clin d'œil pour me dire que c’était une blague.
native_language_example: He winked at me to tell me it was a joke.

additional_notes: Common everyday noun for a portable storage device. Usually feminine: une clé USB. Often used with verbs like brancher (plug in), contenir (contain), copier (copy), mettre/enregistrer (save) and with prepositions like sur (on) or dans (in): sur la clé USB, dans une clé USB.
target_language_example: J'ai sauvegardé les photos sur une clé USB.
native_language_example: I saved the photos on a USB flash drive.

additional_notes: Used to refer specifically to the keys for your car (often a key or key fob). Common with possessives: mes/tes/ses clés de voiture. You can also say "les clés" when it’s clear you mean the car keys.
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mes clés de voiture à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot my car keys at home.

meaning: the (highway) traffic code; rules of the road.
additional_notes: Refers to the official set of traffic laws and signs taught for driving and tested on the French written driving exam ("l’examen du code"). Often used with verbs like "apprendre", "réviser", "connaître".
target_language_example: Je révise le code de la route pour passer l’examen.
native_language_example: I’m reviewing the traffic code to take the exam.

additional_notes: A sturdy, lockable metal box or cabinet used to protect valuables (money, jewelry, documents). Often found at home, in a hotel room, or in a bank (un coffre-fort de la banque).
target_language_example: Je laisse mon passeport dans le coffre-fort de l’hôtel.
native_language_example: I leave my passport in the hotel safe.

meaning: street corner; corner of a street.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a location at the corner where streets meet. Very often you’ll see it as **au coin de la rue** (“on/at the street corner”) or **au coin de [street name] et [street name]** (“at the corner of … and …”). You may also encounter the less common phrasing **au coin de rue** in some contexts.
target_language_example: Le café est au coin de rue.
native_language_example: The café is on the street corner.

additional_notes: Usually refers to an organized holiday stay where children/teens go away with supervisors (often during school holidays). You often use it with "partir en" (to go to) or "être en" (to be at). In sentence 1 it’s used humorously/ironically to mean “this isn’t a place to mess around/relax like a camp.”
target_language_example: Quand j’étais petite, j’allais souvent en colonie de vacances.
native_language_example: When I was little, I often went to summer camp.

additional_notes: Literal anatomy term for the spine (the bones running down your back). It can also be used in fixed expressions about feelings, especially with verbs like « parcourir » (to run through): « Un frisson parcourut ma colonne vertébrale » = “A shiver ran down my spine.”
target_language_example: J’ai mal à la colonne vertébrale depuis hier.
native_language_example: My spine has been hurting since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to ask the price of something. Followed by a noun (Combien coûte ce téléphone ?) or by “ça” (Combien ça coûte ?). “coûte” is the 3rd-person singular of “coûter” (to cost).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, combien coûte ce billet ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how much does this ticket cost?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the number of people. Often followed by a verb: « Combien de gens sont venus ? » (“How many people came?”). After a preposition like « avec », it becomes « avec combien de gens… ? » (“with how many people…?”).
target_language_example: Tu sais combien de gens vont venir ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you know how many people are going to come tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask (or report indirectly) the number of languages someone speaks/knows or that exist in a place. Often followed by a verb like parler (to speak): « Combien de langues parles-tu ? ». In indirect speech, it comes after verbs like demander/savoir: « Elle me demanda combien de langues je parlais. ».
target_language_example: Combien de langues parlez-vous ?
native_language_example: How many languages do you speak?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the number of books. "Combien de" + plural noun = “how many (of) …”. You often follow it with a verb: « Combien de livres as-tu ? » (How many books do you have?).
target_language_example: Combien de livres veux-tu acheter ?
native_language_example: How many books do you want to buy?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the number of words in something (a sentence, a list, an essay, etc.). Often followed by a noun or phrase like "anglais" (English), "dans cette phrase" (in this sentence), or "sur cette liste" (on this list). You can add "environ" to mean "about/approximately how many words".
target_language_example: Combien de mots dois-je écrire pour ce devoir ?
native_language_example: How many words do I have to write for this assignment?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a number of people. Often followed by a verb: « Combien de personnes viennent ? » (“How many people are coming?”). In other contexts it can follow « pour » to mean “for how many people”: « Pour combien de personnes… ? »
target_language_example: Combien de personnes sont dans la salle ?
native_language_example: How many people are in the room?

additional_notes: Used to ask about duration or the amount of time needed, left, or spent. Very common with verbs like durer (to last), rester (to remain), and prendre (to take).
target_language_example: Combien de temps faut-il pour y aller ?
native_language_example: How long does it take to get there?

meaning: “how long have you…” / “how long did you…” (asking about duration).
additional_notes: Used to ask how much time something took. It’s the start of a question and is typically followed by a past participle (passé composé): « Combien de temps as-tu attendu ? » (“How long did you wait?”). You can also use it with other past forms to ask about a duration in the past.
target_language_example: Combien de temps as-tu vécu à Paris ?
native_language_example: How long did you live in Paris?

meaning: "how many ... are there" (how many of something exist).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a number or quantity, usually with a plural noun: « Combien y a-t-il de + nom (pluriel) + lieu ? ». It’s an inverted, more formal version of « Il y a combien de… ? ». With a number, you often answer: « Il y en a … » (e.g., « Il y en a trois. »).
target_language_example: Combien y a-t-il de stations de métro à Paris ?
native_language_example: How many subway stations are there in Paris?

additional_notes: Used to ask the price of something. "Ça" often refers to the thing you’re looking at or talking about; you can also add it after: "Ça coûte combien ?" Polite version with "vous": "Vous savez combien ça coûte ?"
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, combien ça coûte ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how much does it cost?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a manner, appearance, or way of doing something that is clear from context. It can also describe something of that kind, as in « une voiture comme cela » = « a car like that ». « Comme ça » is the more common spoken variant.
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas vivre comme cela.
native_language_example: I don't want to live like that.

additional_notes: Informal abbreviation of « comme d'habitude ». Used to say something is happening the same way it normally does (routines, habits, typical situations). Often placed at the end of a sentence: « Il est en retard, comme d'hab. »
target_language_example: On se retrouve au café à 18 h, comme d'hab.
native_language_example: We'll meet at the café at 6 p.m., as usual.

additional_notes: Used to make a comparison: *comme* = “like/as”, *des* = “some” (plural). It’s often used in vivid expressions: *travailler comme des abeilles* (“work like bees”), *être comme des frères* (“be like brothers”), *presser comme des citrons* (“squeeze like lemons”). The noun after *des* is plural.
target_language_example: Après la pluie, les enfants couraient comme des fous dans la rue.
native_language_example: After the rain, the kids were running like crazy in the street.

additional_notes: Idiom used mainly with verbs like « se vendre » (to sell) or « partir » (to sell out/go quickly): « Ça se vend/Ça part comme des petits pains. » It means something is in high demand and sells extremely fast. Often used with « vraiment » for emphasis.
target_language_example: Les places pour le concert sont parties comme des petits pains.
native_language_example: The tickets for the concert sold like hotcakes.

meaning: like never before; more than ever.
additional_notes: Used to intensify an action or state: doing something to an extreme degree (often with an exclamation). It can also appear alone as a punchy emphasis (“Like never before.”). In sexual contexts it keeps the same meaning but the overall sentence may be explicit.
target_language_example: Je suis motivé comme jamais !
native_language_example: I’m more motivated than ever!

meaning: as if by magic; magically (as if it happened by itself).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens suddenly and surprisingly, as if without explanation or effort. Often follows a verb like disparaître, apparaître, marcher, se faire (e.g., « tout se fit silence »). Can be literal in a story about magic, but very often it’s just figurative.
target_language_example: Et puis, comme par magie, il a retrouvé ses clés.
native_language_example: And then, as if by magic, he found his keys again.

additional_notes: Informal, idiomatic intensifier used after a verb to mean “a lot/very much,” often for strong actions or weather: « travailler comme pas permis » (work like crazy), « pleuvoir comme pas permis » (rain like crazy). Literally it looks like “as not allowed,” but it’s not used that way.
target_language_example: Hier soir, il a plu comme pas permis.
native_language_example: Last night, it rained like crazy.

additional_notes: Informal intensifier used after a verb or adjective to mean “to an extreme degree.” Often used in speech: « Il travaille comme pas possible » = he works like crazy; « C’est cher comme pas possible » = it’s incredibly expensive.
target_language_example: Il a plu comme pas possible hier soir.
native_language_example: It rained like crazy last night.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone does something exceptionally well or in a unique way: « Il/Elle + verbe + comme personne ». Often implies “like no one else” rather than “like a person.”
target_language_example: Elle raconte des histoires comme personne.
native_language_example: She tells stories like nobody else.

meaning: “as with / just like (in the case of)”.
additional_notes: Used to compare one situation to another: it means that something works the same way or is done in a similar way as in the example that follows ("as with cigarettes…", "like for a ceremony"). It can also introduce a suggested parallel (often as a question): "Comme pour des poursuites… ?" = "Like for chases…?"
target_language_example: Comme pour les enfants, il faut être patient.
native_language_example: As with children, you have to be patient.

additional_notes: Used to say things are happening the way they were planned/anticipated. Often with verbs like « se passer » or « aller »: « Tout se passe comme prévu » (Everything is going as planned). Can also be used alone as a quick check or confirmation: « Comme prévu ? » = “As planned?”
target_language_example: On se retrouve à 18 h, comme prévu.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at 6 p.m., as planned.

additional_notes: Often used in conversation to ask someone to be more specific: « Comme quoi ? » = “Like what?” / “In what way?” It can also be used before a clause to introduce a conclusion or a slightly sarcastic takeaway: « Comme quoi, je dois tout deviner. » ≈ “So I’m supposed to guess everything.”
target_language_example: — Il faut que tu changes. — Comme quoi, par exemple ?
native_language_example: — You need to change. — Like what, for example?

additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to the person you’re speaking to (toi). It can follow a noun (“un garçon… comme toi” = “a boy… like you”) or a clause (“… comme toi” = “… like you do/are”). Often implies similarity; depending on tone it can be a compliment or an insult (e.g., “bête comme toi” = “as stupid as you”).
target_language_example: Je veux une amie comme toi.
native_language_example: I want a friend like you.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is the same as other people, or to appeal to what is normal/common (often meaning “like everyone else”). It can stand alone as a brief reply (“Of course—like everyone else.”) or be inserted at the start of a sentence (“Like everyone else, ...”).
target_language_example: Je veux juste être comme tout le monde.
native_language_example: I just want to be like everyone else.

meaning: really / very (an intensifier, especially after an adjective).
additional_notes: Commonly placed after an adjective to emphasize it: « contente comme tout », « poli(e) comme tout », « gentil(le) comme tout » = “really happy/polite/kind.” It’s fairly informal/colloquial. In « Comme tout à l'heure », it means “like earlier / as before.”
target_language_example: Il était fier comme tout de son dessin.
native_language_example: He was really proud of his drawing.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun. It often makes a comparison (comme un frère = like a brother) or indicates how someone/something is viewed or used (considéré comme un devoir = considered as a duty). Before a feminine noun, use comme une.
target_language_example: Elle chante comme un ange.
native_language_example: She sings like an angel.

meaning: like a child; like a kid.
additional_notes: Used with "comme" to compare someone’s behavior or feelings to those of a child. Often implies being immature or being treated as if you were a child (depending on context).
target_language_example: Arrête de te disputer comme un enfant !
native_language_example: Stop arguing like a child!

meaning: "like a man" / "as a man" (often: in a brave, responsible, or ‘manly’ way).
additional_notes: Literally means “like a man.” It’s commonly used in commands or encouragements (Agis/Bats-toi/Sors comme un homme) to tell someone to be brave, tough, or take responsibility—this can sound macho or old-fashioned. In other contexts it can be more neutral and simply mean “as a man,” e.g. considérer quelqu’un comme un homme honnête (“to consider someone an honest man”).
target_language_example: Il a assumé ses erreurs comme un homme.
native_language_example: He owned up to his mistakes like a man.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to a feminine singular noun ("une …"). Very common in similes: "rouge comme une betterave" (red like a beetroot), "nager comme une pierre" (swim like a stone). For masculine nouns, use "comme un"; for plural, "comme des".
target_language_example: Il est têtu comme une mule.
native_language_example: He’s as stubborn as a mule.

additional_notes: A very common phrase used to talk about manner, appearance, or state. It can mean "in that way," "as it is," or "in that state," depending on context: Continue comme ça = keep going like that; jolie comme ça = pretty as she is; il est comme ça = he's like that; c'est comme ça = that's the way it is. In everyday French, it often covers both English "like this" and "like that."
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu me regardes comme ça ?
native_language_example: Why are you looking at me like that?

meaning: properly; as it should be (also: respectable/proper).
additional_notes: Used to say something is done the right way or correctly: « Fais-le comme il faut. » It can also describe a person as respectable or socially “proper”: « un homme comme il faut ». Often implies doing things thoroughly or according to expectations/norms.
target_language_example: On va organiser la fête comme il faut.
native_language_example: We’re going to organize the party properly.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a common expression, proverb, cliché, or familiar way of putting something. It can appear at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end of a sentence, and often signals you’re quoting a well-known phrase rather than speaking literally.
target_language_example: Il faut se méfier des apparences, comme on dit.
native_language_example: You have to beware of appearances, as they say.

additional_notes: Used to compare with an unreal, hypothetical, or “pretend” situation. Very common in the pattern « faire comme si… » = “to act/pretend as if…”. Often followed by the imperfect or pluperfect in French (even when English uses “as if + past” too): « comme si tu savais tout » (as if you knew everything), « comme si rien ne s’était passé » (as if nothing had happened).
target_language_example: Il parle comme si tout était de sa faute.
native_language_example: He talks as if it were all his fault.

meaning: “as if it were yesterday” (said about a vivid memory).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you remember something very clearly, even if it happened a long time ago. Often follows verbs like « se souvenir de » / « s’en souvenir » (to remember) or « se rappeler » (to recall), or can be said alone as a reply.
target_language_example: Je me souviens de ce voyage comme si c'était hier.
native_language_example: I remember that trip as if it were yesterday.

additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) Exclamation with an adjective: « Comme tu es + adjective ! » = “How + adjective you are!” (e.g., « Comme tu es grande ! » = “How tall you are!”). (2) With verbs like aimer / accepter: « … comme tu es » = “...as you are” (accepting someone without wanting them to change).
target_language_example: Je t'apprécie comme tu es.
native_language_example: I appreciate you as you are.

additional_notes: Used to give someone freedom to choose (“call it whatever you want”, “do it however you want”), or to agree/accept someone’s choice (“OK, as you want”). Depending on tone, it can sound neutral and accommodating or slightly dismissive (“fine, whatever”).
target_language_example: On peut y aller maintenant ou plus tard, comme tu veux.
native_language_example: We can go now or later—whatever you want.

additional_notes: Used with a noun ("commence par un L") or with an infinitive to say the first step in a sequence ("Commence par faire..."). It can also mean that something begins with a certain cause or group: "Ça commence par nous" = "It starts with us."
target_language_example: Commence par ouvrir la fenêtre, puis on parlera.
native_language_example: Start by opening the window, then we'll talk.

meaning: "starts to" / "begins to" (followed by an infinitive verb).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about the start of an action or a change that is beginning: Commence à + infinitive (e.g., commencer à courir / préparer / étudier). It can also describe something that is starting to happen or become noticeable (La soupe commence à bouillir; Ça commence à faire beaucoup = “That’s starting to be a lot/too much”).
target_language_example: Je commence à comprendre.
native_language_example: I’m starting to understand.

additional_notes: Used with the verb commencer in the passé composé: avoir + commencé + à + infinitive (e.g., "j'ai commencé à..."). It introduces an action that started (and may or may not still be continuing). With être subjects: "elle a commencé à...", "ils ont commencé à...".
target_language_example: Nous avons commencé à travailler tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: We started working early this morning.

meaning: "How could I...?" (expressing shock, disbelief, or regret about something you did or didn’t do).
additional_notes: Used to question your own past action, often with a self-critical or astonished tone. Literally it’s "how have I been able," but in natural English it’s usually "How could I...?" The structure is: comment + ai-je (inverted "have I") + pu (past participle of pouvoir, "to be able to"), often followed by an infinitive: « Comment ai-je pu dire ça ? »
target_language_example: Comment ai-je pu dire une chose pareille ?
native_language_example: How could I say such a thing?

meaning: 'how are you going to…?' (asking how someone will do something).
additional_notes: In these examples, this is not the greeting “Comment allez-vous ?” (“How are you?”). It’s the question word comment (“how”) + aller in the near future: aller + infinitive (“to be going to” + verb). Used to ask about the method/plan: Comment allez-vous faire/payer/rembourser… ?
target_language_example: Comment allez-vous trouver une solution ?
native_language_example: How are you going to find a solution?

meaning: How are you? (formal / polite; to one person or to several people).
additional_notes: Uses the formal/plural pronoun « vous ». It can be used to address one person politely (a stranger, someone older, a customer) or to address multiple people (« vous tous »). Often used as a greeting, sometimes with extra context: « Comment allez-vous ces temps-ci ? » = “How have you been lately?”
target_language_example: Bonjour Madame, comment allez-vous aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: Hello ma’am, how are you today?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the way/method or plan to do something (often followed by an infinitive: entrer, faire, régler, etc.). In speech, it’s also common to say: « Comment va-t-on… ? » or more informally « Comment on va… ? ».
target_language_example: Comment allons-nous trouver une solution ?
native_language_example: How are we going to find a solution?

meaning: 'how could you…?' / 'how were you able to…?'.
additional_notes: Used to express shock, disbelief, or reproach about something someone did (or failed to do). It’s typically followed by an infinitive (Comment as-tu pu faire ça ?), or by a verb like être (Comment as-tu pu être aussi imprudente ?). The tense is passé composé of pouvoir (tu as pu), but in English it usually becomes 'how could you…?'
target_language_example: Comment as-tu pu oublier son anniversaire ?
native_language_example: How could you forget his birthday?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the way/method someone did something. "Avez-vous" is the formal or plural "have you" (passé composé) and is used here with inversion in questions. In everyday speech, you’ll also hear: "Comment vous avez… ?" (less formal) or "Comment as-tu… ?" (informal singular).
target_language_example: Comment avez-vous trouvé cet appartement ?
native_language_example: How did you find this apartment?

additional_notes: Used to question someone’s past action (passé composé of "pouvoir": "avez pu"). It often sounds accusatory or strongly emotional, like you can’t believe they did it. Very common with a verb after it (e.g., "comment avez-vous pu faire ça ?"), but it can also be left unfinished: "Comment avez-vous pu ?" The "vous" makes it formal or plural; with one person informally you’d say "Comment as-tu pu… ?"
target_language_example: Comment avez-vous pu partir sans prévenir ?
native_language_example: How could you leave without warning?

meaning: "How did you find ...?" / "What did you think of ...?"
additional_notes: Formal (vous) past tense of trouver. Depending on context it can mean (1) how you discovered/located something (e.g., a rare book, an address) or (2) your opinion after experiencing something (e.g., a film, a restaurant). Often followed by a noun: « Comment avez-vous trouvé le film ? » = “What did you think of the film?”
target_language_example: Comment avez-vous trouvé le restaurant ?
native_language_example: What did you think of the restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to ask or explain how something happens or works, with cela referring to a thing or situation already mentioned or understood from context. Cela is more formal than ça, so in everyday speech you will often hear comment ça... instead.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas comment cela s'est passé.
native_language_example: I don't know how that happened.

meaning: “How did you … it/him/her?” (question starter with inversion, usually in the passé composé).
additional_notes: Introduces a question about the way/method something happened. Structure: comment (how) + l’ (le/la = it/him/her) + as (avoir, 2nd person singular) + -tu (subject pronoun inversion used in questions). Typically followed by a past participle: « Comment l’as-tu + participe passé ? ». The « l’ » refers to someone/something already known from context. Note: not a false cognate; « comment » here means “how,” not “comment.”
target_language_example: Comment l'as-tu découvert ?
native_language_example: How did you discover it?

meaning: "How did you ... it/her?" (polite/formal question using inversion; often corresponds to "How did you ...?" / "How have you ...?").
additional_notes: Used to ask how someone obtained, learned, found, met, guessed, or managed to do something involving a direct object pronoun. Structure: comment (“how”) + l’ (“it” = le, or “her” = la; sometimes “him” in older/less careful usage) + avez-vous (inverted “have you,” used as a formal/polite way to ask in the passé composé). If l’ = la (feminine), the past participle may agree in writing: connue, rencontrée, trouvée, etc. Note: French comment means “how,” not the English noun “comment.”
target_language_example: Comment l'avez-vous trouvée ?
native_language_example: How did you find it/her?

meaning: "how to do it" / "how to do that."
additional_notes: Used to ask for or explain the method/steps for doing something already known from context. Often follows verbs like montrer (to show), dire (to tell), savoir (to know), apprendre/enseigner (to teach): « Montre-moi comment le faire » (Show me how to do it), « Je sais comment le faire » (I know how to do it). In speech, « le » refers back to the thing you’re doing (it/that).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas comment le faire, tu peux m’aider ?
native_language_example: I don’t know how to do it; can you help me?

meaning: "how do you/we do it?" / "how it’s done".
additional_notes: Uses "on" (often meaning "we" or informal "you" in French) with "faire" to ask about the method or way to do something. It can be a direct question ("Alors, comment on fait ?") or used inside another sentence ("Je vais te montrer comment on fait").
target_language_example: Tu peux m’expliquer comment on fait pour s’inscrire ?
native_language_example: Can you explain to me how you sign up?

additional_notes: A strong, often angry or shocked way to criticize someone for what they did or said. Usually followed by an infinitive (Comment oses-tu dire ça ?), but it can also be used alone: Comment oses-tu !
target_language_example: Comment oses-tu me parler comme ça ?
native_language_example: How dare you talk to me like that?

additional_notes: A strong, accusatory phrase used to express outrage or shock at what someone did or said. Uses the formal/plural address "vous"; with one person informally you can say "Comment oses-tu… ?". Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., "dire", "parler", "insulter") or a clause introduced by "…de".
target_language_example: Comment osez-vous me traiter comme ça ?
native_language_example: How dare you treat me like that?

meaning: "how can we/one…?" (asking how something is possible or how to do it).
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal subject on (“we/one/you/people in general”) and inversion (peut-on) for a neutral, often fairly formal question. It can be practical (“How can we remove…?”) or express surprise/judgment (“How can someone live like that?”). Often followed by an infinitive: Comment peut-on + verb…?
target_language_example: Comment peut-on trouver ce fichier ?
native_language_example: How can we find this file?

meaning: 'how can you...?' (often expressing surprise, disbelief, or criticism).
additional_notes: Used to question how someone is able or willing to do something. In conversation it’s often rhetorical, meaning you disapprove or can’t believe it (similar to “How could you…?”). Followed by an infinitive: « comment peux-tu + verbe » (e.g., faire, dire, vivre).
target_language_example: Comment peux-tu penser ça ?
native_language_example: How can you think that?

meaning: "how could I...?" / "how can I...?" (polite or rhetorical question).
additional_notes: Used to ask (often politely) how to do something: « Comment pourrais-je aider ? » (“How can I help?”). It can also be rhetorical to express disbelief or refusal: « Comment pourrais-je vous mentir ? » (“How could I lie to you?”). The verb is conditional (« pourrais » from « pouvoir »), which can sound more polite/soft than « comment puis-je ».
target_language_example: Comment pourrais-je vous aider aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: How can I help you today?

additional_notes: Used to ask how something is possible or acceptable. Often expresses surprise, disbelief, or criticism: « Comment pouvez-vous dire ça ? » = “How can you say that?” Uses the polite/formal « vous »; with friends you’d usually say « Comment peux-tu… ? ».
target_language_example: Comment pouvez-vous penser une chose pareille ?
native_language_example: How can you think such a thing?

additional_notes: Used to challenge or question someone’s certainty. It’s usually followed by an adjective like sûr/sûre/sûrs/sûres (“sure”) or certain/certaine (“certain”). The pronoun “en” means “of it/about it” and refers back to something already mentioned. You can intensify with words like “aussi” (so) or “tellement” (so/very).
target_language_example: Comment pouvez-vous en être si certain ?
native_language_example: How can you be so sure about it?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the way to do something, solve a problem, or offer help. It’s a more formal/inverted question form with the subject after the verb (pouvons-nous). In everyday speech you’ll also hear: "Comment est-ce qu’on peut… ?" or "Comment on peut… ?"
target_language_example: Comment pouvons-nous commencer ?
native_language_example: How can we start?

additional_notes: Used to ask for instructions or a solution in a polite, fairly formal way. It’s commonly followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., supprimer, terminer) and can be addressed to a person or used in written questions (emails, help forums).
target_language_example: Comment puis-je vous aider ?
native_language_example: How can I help you?

additional_notes: Used to ask about how an event, meeting, day, weekend, etc. went. It comes from the verb **se passer** (to happen / to go). Agreement note: the past participle can agree with the subject in some cases (**Comment s’est passée ta journée ?** with *journée* feminine; **Comment se sont passés vos examens ?** plural), but the fixed string **comment s'est passé** is commonly used before a masculine singular noun (**Comment s'est passé le travail ?**, **Comment s'est passé ton rendez-vous ?**). Also common: **Ça s’est bien passé ?** = “Did it go well?”
target_language_example: Comment s'est passé ton rendez-vous ?
native_language_example: How did your appointment go?

additional_notes: Used to ask how someone knows something or how they figured it out. Often followed by a clause introduced by “que” (comment sais-tu que…?) or by an indirect question word like “lequel/quel/quelle” (comment sais-tu lequel…?, comment sais-tu quel poids…?). You can make it formal by using “comment savez-vous…?”
target_language_example: Comment sais-tu qu’il dit la vérité ?
native_language_example: How do you know he’s telling the truth?

additional_notes: Used to ask how someone knows a fact or piece of information. It can be addressing one person formally (vous) or multiple people. Often followed by a clause (e.g., ce que…, quel/quelle…, lequel…) or by a noun (mon nom).
target_language_example: Comment savez-vous où j’habite ?
native_language_example: How do you know where I live?

meaning: "How come you…?" / "How is it that you…?"
additional_notes: Used to ask with surprise or curiosity about the reason something is true. Very often followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "comment se fait-il que tu connaisses…", "que tu saches…", "que tu aies vu…"). You can replace "tu" with another subject: "comment se fait-il que vous… / qu’il… / qu’elle…".
target_language_example: Comment se fait-il que tu sois déjà ici ?
native_language_example: How come you’re already here?

meaning: 'how come you…?' / 'how is it that you…?'.
additional_notes: Used to ask how or why something is the case, often expressing surprise or curiosity. It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., « comment se fait-il que vous connaissiez… ? »). The subject can change (« …que tu / qu’il / qu’elle / que nous », etc.).
target_language_example: Comment se fait-il que vous soyez déjà ici ?
native_language_example: How come you’re already here?

meaning: "What do you think of…?" (asking for someone’s opinion).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s impression or evaluation of something (a wine, a city, a book, an apartment, etc.). It’s a polite/formal phrasing because of "vous". Literally it’s "How do you find…?" but in English the natural meaning is "What do you think of…?"
target_language_example: Comment trouvez-vous ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: What do you think of this restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to start an informal question in spoken French, followed by a past participle (passé composé): "Comment tu l'as connu/rencontré/su/trouvé ?" Here, "l'" is a shortened form of "le" or "la" meaning "him / her / it / that" (the thing you’re asking about). More formal alternatives include "Comment l’as-tu … ?" or "Comment est-ce que tu l’as … ?"
target_language_example: Comment tu l'as appris ?
native_language_example: How did you find out (about it)?

meaning: "How can you…?" (often expressing disbelief or criticism).
additional_notes: Literally “how you can,” but used like “How can you…?” in everyday speech. It’s commonly said with an accusing or shocked tone: *Comment tu peux dire ça ?* (“How can you say that?”). In more formal French you might hear *Comment peux-tu… ?* (inversion) or *Comment est-ce que tu peux… ?*.
target_language_example: Comment tu peux rester calme dans une situation pareille ?
native_language_example: How can you stay calm in a situation like that?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone about their physical or emotional state. It’s common in conversation; in more formal French you may hear "Comment vous vous sentez ?" (vous = you, formal/plural). You can also say "Comment tu te sens ?" on its own or after something like "Dis-moi..." (Tell me...).
target_language_example: Après l’examen, comment tu te sens ?
native_language_example: After the exam, how do you feel?

additional_notes: Common informal way to ask how someone is doing. It uses the informal subject pronoun “tu” (you, singular). More formal: “Comment allez-vous ?”. Often used after “Salut” or “Et toi,”.
target_language_example: Salut ! Comment tu vas aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: Hi! How are you today?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone's state or how things are going. It is often followed by a name or noun: Comment va Ben ? / Comment va votre fille ? On its own, Comment va ? is a short, casual way of asking how things are going, similar to Comment ça va ?
target_language_example: Comment va ton frère aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: How is your brother doing today?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the condition of someone/something using the verb aller: « Comment va votre + noun ? ». « Votre » is the polite/formal form of “your” (to one person you don’t know well, or in formal situations). Make sure the verb agrees with the noun: « Comment vont vos enfants ? » (plural). Note: French « comment » usually means “how,” not “comment.”
target_language_example: Comment va votre père ?
native_language_example: How is your father?

meaning: “how are you going to…?” / “how will you…?” (addressing one person informally).
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s method, plan, or way of doing something. It’s built from comment (“how”) + vas-tu (inversion of tu vas, “you’re going”). Often followed by an infinitive: Comment vas-tu faire ? If you mean “How are you?” (greeting), you typically say Comment vas-tu ? (with no verb after).
target_language_example: Comment vas-tu y arriver sans voiture ?
native_language_example: How are you going to manage without a car?

additional_notes: Common greeting when speaking to one person you address as tu. Literally “how are you going?”, but used like “How are you doing?”. You can add time/context: ce matin (this morning), ces temps-ci (these days), par cette chaleur (in this heat). For a more formal/polite version, use « Comment allez-vous ? ».
target_language_example: Salut ! Comment vas-tu aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Hi! How are you today?

additional_notes: Used to ask how something happened to the person you’re speaking to, using inversion for a polite/formal question (vous + êtes-vous). It’s followed by a past participle (e.g., brûlé, fait, mis, rencontrés). Often used in contexts like accidents or explaining a situation.
target_language_example: Comment vous êtes-vous retrouvé ici si tard ?
native_language_example: How did you end up here so late?

additional_notes: Used in speech to ask for an explanation or react with surprise. In a normal question it can introduce “how does that…?”: « Comment ça se termine ? » = “How does it end?” With a surprised tone (often followed by a noun/adjective), it means “What do you mean?” / “How come?”: « Comment ça, fichu ? » = “What do you mean, ruined?”
target_language_example: Comment ça, tu pars déjà ?
native_language_example: What do you mean, you're leaving already?

additional_notes: Used to talk about how a system, process, machine, or situation functions. Often in questions: « Comment ça marche ? » (“How does it work?”). In statements like « Vous savez comment ça marche », it means “You know how it works” (i.e., you know the rules or procedure). « Ça » = “it/that” and « marche » literally means “works”.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, comment ça marche, ce distributeur ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how does this ATM work?

meaning: “How did it go?” / “How did it go (for you)?”
additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase **se passer** (“to happen/to go”), in the **passé composé** (**s'est passé**). Commonly used to ask how an event, meeting, exam, trip, etc. went. You can add a time or detail after it: *Comment ça s'est passé ce matin ?* / *Comment ça s'est passé avec le médecin ?*
target_language_example: Comment ça s'est passé ce matin ?
native_language_example: How did it go this morning?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a translation into another language. You add the language name after en (en anglais, en allemand, en espagnol, etc.). Often followed by the word/phrase you mean from context or you can point to it: Comment ça se dit en anglais ?
target_language_example: Comment ça se dit en français ?
native_language_example: How do you say it in French?

meaning: “how it goes” / “how it’s going” (how things happen or how a situation unfolds in practice).
additional_notes: Used to ask about or describe the way a situation unfolds (logistics, what happens next, how it turns out). Common after verbs like savoir (to know), voir (to see), attendre (to wait), or in prompts like Voyons… (“Let’s see…”). In the past you’ll often see: comment ça s’est passé (“how it went”).
target_language_example: On attend de voir comment ça se passe.
native_language_example: We’re waiting to see how it goes.

meaning: How are you? / How’s it going?
additional_notes: A very common greeting. Literally “how that goes,” but used to ask how someone is doing. Often followed by a name or friendly term: « Comment ça va, Marie ? ». A typical reply is « Ça va. » (I’m fine/It’s going OK) or « Ça va bien / Ça va mal. ».
target_language_example: Salut ! Comment ça va aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Hi! How’s it going today?

meaning: “How did you…?” / “How have you…?” (formal or plural “you”).
additional_notes: Used to ask how something happened or how someone achieved something, with subject–verb inversion. It’s typically followed by a past participle (arrivés, devenu, venus, parvenus, etc.) or by “parvenir à …” (“to manage to …”). Note: French “comment” means “how,” not an English “comment.”
target_language_example: Comment êtes-vous arrivé(e) à ce résultat ?
native_language_example: How did you get that result?

additional_notes: Past historic (passé simple) form of "commencer à" (he/she/it began to). Very common in written narratives and literature; in everyday speech you’ll usually see/hear the passé composé: "a commencé à".
target_language_example: À ce moment-là, il commença à comprendre la vérité.
native_language_example: At that moment, he began to understand the truth.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a commercial company that operates flights. Often appears with verbs like contacter/téléphoner à (to contact/call), réserver (to book), changer un billet (to change a ticket), and with issues like bagages (baggage) and retards (delays).
target_language_example: Je dois contacter la compagnie aérienne pour demander un remboursement.
native_language_example: I need to contact the airline to ask for a refund.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: it’s the negative form of "tu comprends" (you understand) with "ne" dropped (full form: "tu ne comprends pas"). Used to say you don’t understand something, or to ask "You don’t understand?"
target_language_example: Je comprends pas pourquoi il est en colère.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why he’s angry.

additional_notes: Inversion of the verb and subject pronoun: "comprenez" (you understand) + "vous" (you). Used in questions, often in more formal speech or writing. It can address one person politely (vous) or several people. With an object: "Comprenez-vous ce que je veux dire ?" = "Do you understand what I mean?" You can also say "Me comprenez-vous ?" = "Do you understand me?" In everyday speech, people often use "Vous comprenez ?" or "Tu comprends ?" (informal singular).
target_language_example: Comprenez-vous pourquoi je vous demande ça ?
native_language_example: Do you understand why I’m asking you that?

meaning: report; write-up; summary (often of a meeting/event).
additional_notes: Used for an account of what happened (facts, decisions, results). Common in professional/academic contexts: un compte-rendu de réunion (meeting minutes/report), un compte-rendu mensuel (monthly report), un compte-rendu oral (oral report). Often followed by "de" + topic/event: un compte-rendu de son voyage. Note: hyphenated noun; plural is "des comptes-rendus".
target_language_example: Je t’envoie le compte-rendu de la réunion cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I’m sending you the meeting report this afternoon.

additional_notes: Used for an account you hold at a bank (to keep money, receive a salary, pay bills, etc.). Often appears with verbs like avoir (to have), ouvrir (to open), fermer (to close), and vérifier/consulter (to check). Possessives are common: mon/ton/son/votre compte bancaire.
target_language_example: Je dois ouvrir un compte bancaire en France.
native_language_example: I need to open a bank account in France.

additional_notes: Used for an official or organized summary of what happened or what was discussed (e.g., a meeting, an intervention, an event). Common verbs: "faire un compte rendu" (to give/write a report), "rédiger un compte rendu" (to write up a report). Depending on context it can be like meeting minutes or a briefing.
target_language_example: Après la réunion, je dois rédiger un compte rendu pour l’équipe.
native_language_example: After the meeting, I have to write up a report for the team.

additional_notes: Used for a countdown before an event starts (a launch, a race, the start of a video, etc.). Often used with verbs like « commencer » (start) or « lancer » (launch/start), e.g. « Le compte à rebours a commencé ».
target_language_example: On lance le compte à rebours : 3, 2, 1… partez !
native_language_example: We start the countdown: 3, 2, 1… go!

meaning: a score to settle; unfinished business (often implying revenge or confrontation).
additional_notes: Most often used in the expression « avoir un compte à régler avec quelqu’un ». Literally it’s like “a bill to pay,” but in practice it means you have a personal grievance to deal with, and it can sound threatening depending on context.
target_language_example: Après ce qu’il m’a fait, j’ai un compte à régler avec lui.
native_language_example: After what he did to me, I have a score to settle with him.

meaning: to intend to do; to plan to do.
additional_notes: Used as « compter + infinitive » to express an intention or plan: « compter faire + [something] ». Note: « compter » here does not mean “to count” (numbers); it means “to intend/plan.”
target_language_example: Je compte faire un voyage en France cet été.
native_language_example: I plan to take a trip to France this summer.

meaning: to count for; to matter to; to mean (a lot) to.
additional_notes: Used either literally (a portion/weight in a total: « Ça compte pour 30 % de la note. ») or figuratively to express importance to someone (often with « beaucoup »).
target_language_example: Tu comptes pour beaucoup pour moi.
native_language_example: You mean a lot to me.

additional_notes: Used to say you trust someone/something will help or be dependable: compter sur + person/thing (Je peux compter sur toi/elle). It can also mean "to be counting on" in the sense of expecting something to happen: compter sur + noun/pronoun, and sometimes compter sur + infinitive (Je compte sur toi pour m'aider / Je compte sur venir demain).
target_language_example: Tu peux compter sur moi si tu as besoin d'aide.
native_language_example: You can count on me if you need help.

meaning: to count on you; to rely on you.
additional_notes: Used to say you trust someone to help, show up, or do what they promised. Common in questions (“Pouvons-nous compter sur toi ?” = “Can we count on you?”). You can swap the pronoun: compter sur moi / sur lui / sur elle / sur vous / sur eux / sur elles.
target_language_example: On peut compter sur toi ?
native_language_example: Can we count on you?

meaning: 'do you plan to…?' / 'are you intending to…?'
additional_notes: Inversion form of "tu comptes…" from the verb "compter". Very common in questions: "compter + infinitive" = "to plan/intend to" (not literally "to count"). Often used to ask about someone’s plans: Où comptes-tu aller ? (Where do you plan to go?).
target_language_example: Comptes-tu venir ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you plan to come tonight?

additional_notes: Formal question form with inversion (verb + vous), from "compter" meaning "to plan/intend" (often followed by an infinitive: « comptez-vous rester… ? »). It can also be used with « en »: « Que comptez-vous en faire ? » = “What do you plan to do with it?” Note: « compter » can also mean “to count,” so don’t confuse this planning/intending meaning with numbers.
target_language_example: Quand comptez-vous partir ?
native_language_example: When do you plan to leave?

meaning: "focus on" / "concentrate on" (telling one person to focus).
additional_notes: Imperative form of **se concentrer sur** addressed to **tu** (one person you’re speaking to informally). Used to tell someone to pay attention to a task, person, or moment. For formal/plural: **Concentrez-vous sur...**
target_language_example: Concentre-toi sur ta respiration.
native_language_example: Focus on your breathing.

additional_notes: Used for the general ability or act of driving a car. You can negate it with "ne pas" (e.g., "Je ne sais pas conduire une voiture"). Often mentioned with "le permis" (driver’s license): "avoir le permis" / "devoir avoir le permis".
target_language_example: Je sais conduire une voiture, mais je préfère prendre le bus.
native_language_example: I can drive a car, but I prefer taking the bus.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avoir" ("avoir confiance en moi" = "to have confidence in myself"). In questions like "Tu as confiance en moi ?", it means "Do you trust me?" (confidence in me), even though "moi" literally means "me"—context tells you whether it’s self-confidence (en moi = in myself) or trust (in me).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas beaucoup confiance en moi quand je parle français.
native_language_example: I don’t have much confidence in myself when I speak French.

additional_notes: Usually used with verbs like avoir (to have), construire/développer (to build/develop), and manquer de (to lack): « avoir confiance en soi », « construire sa confiance en soi », « manquer de confiance en soi ». Note: in correct French you normally say « Construis ta confiance en toi » / « Construisez votre confiance en vous » (agreement with the person).
target_language_example: Elle a gagné en confiance en soi après ses cours de français.
native_language_example: She gained self-confidence after her French classes.

additional_notes: Most often used in the structure **faire confiance à + person/thing**: *Je fais confiance à Tom* (“I trust Tom”). The **à** introduces who/what you trust (à moi, à toi, à elle, etc.). Don’t confuse **confiance** with English “confidence” in the sense of self-confidence; **faire confiance à** is about trusting someone/something.
target_language_example: Je fais confiance à mon médecin.
native_language_example: I trust my doctor.

additional_notes: Most often used with the verb **faire**: **(Ne) faire confiance à personne** = “to trust nobody.” In standard French you use the negative **ne … personne**: *Je ne fais confiance à personne.* In casual speech, **ne** is often dropped: *Je fais confiance à personne.* Can also be used as a warning/command: *Ne fais confiance à personne !*
target_language_example: Je ne fais confiance à personne ici.
native_language_example: I don't trust anyone here.

additional_notes: A formal meeting where a public figure or organization speaks to journalists and answers questions. Common with verbs like tenir (to hold), donner (to give), or commencer (to start).
target_language_example: Après la réunion, elle a tenu une conférence de presse.
native_language_example: After the meeting, she held a press conference.

additional_notes: Question form with inversion: verb + hyphen + subject pronoun (tu). It comes from the verb « connaître » (to know/be familiar with), used for people, places, and things you’re acquainted with (not for facts—use « savoir » for that). Often used like « Connais-tu Marie ? » = “Do you know Marie?”
target_language_example: Connais-tu ce quartier ?
native_language_example: Do you know this neighborhood?

additional_notes: Informal spoken French: this is the negative form of "(je/tu/il…) ne connais pas" with "ne" dropped. Used with "connaître" for knowing a person/place or being familiar with something (facts, rules, a topic). More formal/written: "je ne connais pas…" / "je ne vous connais pas".
target_language_example: Désolé, je connais pas ce quartier.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know this neighborhood.

additional_notes: Formal question form (inversion) of « vous connaissez…? ». Used to ask if someone is familiar with a person/thing/place (connaître). For knowing a fact or how to do something, French often uses « savoir » instead.
target_language_example: Connaissez-vous ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: Do you know this restaurant?

meaning: to know (someone) by sight; to recognize (someone) but not know them personally.
additional_notes: Used when you’ve seen someone before and you can recognize them, but you haven’t met them or don’t really know them. Often used with a person as the direct object: « Je le/la connais de vue. »
target_language_example: Je peux connaître de vue plusieurs personnes dans ce quartier, mais je ne leur ai jamais parlé.
native_language_example: I might recognize several people in this neighborhood (know them by sight), but I’ve never spoken to them.

meaning: to know the drill; to have heard it all before (same old story).
additional_notes: Idiomatic. Often used with the general subject « on » (e.g., « On connaît la chanson ! ») to mean “We know how this goes” or “Yeah, we’ve heard that one before,” sometimes with a skeptical or sarcastic tone (often about excuses, repeated promises, or a predictable situation).
target_language_example: Il dit qu’il va changer, mais on doit connaître la chanson.
native_language_example: He says he’s going to change, but we know the drill.

meaning: to know the drill; to know how things work.
additional_notes: Idiomatic, fairly informal expression meaning you already know the routine, the usual pattern, or what’s going to happen (often from experience). Common in the 3rd person (« Il connaît la musique »), but it also works with other persons as long as the exact phrase « connaître la musique » is present.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : je vais te l’expliquer, parce que toi, tu ne peux pas encore dire que tu vas connaître la musique.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll explain it to you, because you can’t yet say you know the drill.

additional_notes: Uses connaître (“to know, be acquainted with”) + la vérité (“the truth”). Often means finding out or being made aware of the truth in a situation, not just knowing someone/something. Common patterns: vouloir connaître la vérité (want to know the truth), finir par connaître la vérité (end up finding out the truth), laisser/empêcher quelqu’un de connaître la vérité (let/prevent someone from learning the truth).
target_language_example: Je veux connaître la vérité, même si c’est difficile à entendre.
native_language_example: I want to know the truth, even if it’s hard to hear.
