target_language_example: Allez, montre-moi ce que tu as dans le ventre !
native_language_example: Come on, show me what you’re made of!

meaning: "into the void"; also "blankly / into empty space" (without focus).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: into empty space (e.g., "regarder dans le vide" = to stare off into space; "pousser dans le vide" = to push into the void/off an edge). Figurative meaning: without being heard or listened to ("parler dans le vide" = to talk to no one / feel like you’re not being listened to).
target_language_example: J’ai l’impression de parler dans le vide quand personne ne répond.
native_language_example: I feel like I’m talking into the void when nobody answers.

additional_notes: Commonly means “in the” before a plural noun: dans les grottes (in the caves), dans les Alpes (in the Alps), dans les bouchons (in traffic jams). It can also express an approximate amount, especially with numbers: Ça coûte dans les trente euros. (“It costs around 30 euros.”).
target_language_example: On s’est rencontrés dans les rues de Paris.
native_language_example: We met in the streets of Paris.

meaning: in the woods / in the forest.
additional_notes: Indicates location within a wooded area (a forest). Often used with verbs of movement (aller: « Allons dans les bois. ») or to describe where something happens or someone lives (« Il vit seul dans les bois. »).
target_language_example: On s'est perdus dans les bois pendant la randonnée.
native_language_example: We got lost in the woods during the hike.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is close by or in the surrounding area. Common in questions about places and services (e.g., a hotel, ATM, pharmacy).
target_language_example: Il y a une boulangerie dans les environs ?
native_language_example: Is there a bakery nearby?

meaning: 'in every detail' / 'down to the last detail.'
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is described, planned, or explained very thoroughly, including even the smallest details. Often goes with verbs like décrire (to describe), expliquer (to explain), raconter (to tell), prévoir (to plan). You may also hear the longer form: « jusque dans les moindres détails » (“right down to the last detail”).
target_language_example: Explique-moi le problème dans les moindres détails.
native_language_example: Explain the problem to me in every detail.

additional_notes: Indicates location or direction toward a mountainous area. Used with verbs of movement (aller, partir, monter) for “into/up to the mountains,” and with location verbs (être, vivre, se cacher) for “in the mountains.”
target_language_example: On va faire une randonnée dans les montagnes ce week-end.
native_language_example: We’re going hiking in the mountains this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is in the vicinity, or that you’re looking for something close by. Very common in questions like « Y a-t-il… dans les parages ? » (“Is there… nearby?”). With a person, it often implies they’re around/lingering somewhere close (sometimes with a slightly suspicious “hanging around” feel depending on context).
target_language_example: Je cherche une pharmacie dans les parages.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a pharmacy nearby.

additional_notes: Used almost always with the verb tomber: tomber dans les pommes. It’s a common, informal idiom for suddenly losing consciousness (often from shock, heat, seeing blood, etc.). Usually said about someone else, or about yourself in the present/habitual: Je tombe dans les pommes. Not literal: it doesn’t mean being “in apples.”
target_language_example: Il faisait très chaud, et j’ai failli tomber dans les pommes dans le métro.
native_language_example: It was really hot, and I almost fainted on the subway.

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening out on public streets (outside, in town/city). Often describes events or situations spread across multiple streets (e.g., chaos, fighting, people out) or being out and moving around; you can also specify a place: « dans les rues de Nîmes ».
target_language_example: Il y avait beaucoup de monde dans les rues ce soir-là.
native_language_example: There were a lot of people in the streets that night.

meaning: properly; according to the rules/procedure (by the book).
additional_notes: Used to say something is done the correct, official way—following the required steps, rules, or social conventions (e.g., making a request through the proper channels, doing paperwork correctly, or doing a formal introduction “properly”). Often appears with verbs like faire (faire quelque chose dans les règles), revenir, or déposer/faire une demande.
target_language_example: On va le faire dans les règles, avec tous les documents nécessaires.
native_language_example: We’re going to do it properly, with all the necessary documents.

meaning: on time; within the planned schedule (also: in times past, depending on context).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say you’re not late and things are going according to schedule: « On est dans les temps », « On a fini dans les temps ». With an adjective like « anciens », it means “in ancient/old times” (« dans les temps anciens »). Often used with « être » or « finir ».
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, on est encore dans les temps pour attraper le train.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we’re still on time to catch the train.

additional_notes: Used literally for something physically in your eyes (shampoo, blood, etc.), and very commonly after verbs like regarder/fixer to mean “to look (someone) in the eyes” (often implying direct eye contact). You’ll also hear “droit dans les yeux” = “right/straight in the eyes.”
target_language_example: Regarde-moi dans les yeux quand tu me parles.
native_language_example: Look me in the eyes when you talk to me.

meaning: "in their" (inside/within something that belongs to them).
additional_notes: Used with the plural possessive determiner "leur" (= their) after the preposition "dans" (= in). "Leur" agrees with the thing possessed (singular), not with the number of owners; use "dans leurs" if the possessed noun is plural (e.g., "dans leurs maisons"). "Leur" can refer to either masculine or feminine singular nouns ("leur vie", "leur famille", "leur langue", "leur pays").
target_language_example: Ils ont gardé le secret dans leur groupe.
native_language_example: They kept the secret within their group.

meaning: in my room / into my room (my bedroom).
additional_notes: Means being located inside your room, or moving into it. With verbs of motion (venir, rentrer, entrer), it often implies “into my room.” The possessive agrees with the owner: dans mon/ma/mes… (e.g., dans mon appartement, dans ma chambre, dans mes affaires).
target_language_example: Je vais dans ma chambre pour me reposer.
native_language_example: I'm going to my room to rest.

additional_notes: Used to say something is inside one of your pockets (e.g., in your pants, jacket, or bag pocket). Often used with être (Les clés sont dans ma poche.) or with mettre/ranger (Je le mets dans ma poche.). You can specify which pocket with de + clothing: dans ma poche de veste.
target_language_example: Mon téléphone est dans ma poche.
native_language_example: My phone is in my pocket.

additional_notes: Used to talk about things or people that matter to you over the course of your life. Often appears after a noun phrase (e.g., « la personne la plus importante dans ma vie »). You can swap the possessive: « dans ta vie » (in your life), « dans sa vie » (in his/her life), etc.
target_language_example: Je n'ai jamais vu ça dans ma vie.
native_language_example: I've never seen that in my life.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "tenir" (to hold), "prendre" (to take/pull into your arms), "serrer" (to hug tightly), or "pleurer" (to cry) to show someone is physically in your embrace. You can change the possessive: "dans tes/ses/nos/vos/leurs bras".
target_language_example: Viens, je te garde dans mes bras.
native_language_example: Come here, I’ll hold you in my arms.

additional_notes: Used before a singular noun to show that something is inside your thing or goes into it. mon means "my" before masculine singular nouns, and also before feminine singular nouns that begin with a vowel or silent h (for example: dans mon urine). With verbs of movement or placement, it often translates as "into my."
target_language_example: J'ai laissé mes clés dans mon sac.
native_language_example: I left my keys in my bag.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is (or should go) inside the speaker’s office. Common with verbs like attendre (to wait), aller (to go), venir (to come), and passer (to stop by). “Dans” emphasizes being inside; compare “à mon bureau” (at my desk/office, more general location).
target_language_example: Je serai dans mon bureau à 15 h.
native_language_example: I’ll be in my office at 3 p.m.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located (inside your bag). Often appears in full sentences like « Il est dans mon sac » (“It’s in my bag”) or questions like « Tu as fouillé dans mon sac ? » (“Did you rummage through my bag?”). You can also use it with quantities: « J’en ai dans mon sac » (“I have some in my bag”).
target_language_example: Mon téléphone est dans mon sac.
native_language_example: My phone is in my bag.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to mean being inside/within something that belongs to or includes “us” (our city, our family, our room, our region, etc.). With verbs of movement (entrer, aller, mettre, etc.), it often means “into our …” rather than “in our …”: « Un oiseau est entré dans notre cage » = “A bird went into our cage.”
target_language_example: Il y a un café dans notre rue.
native_language_example: There’s a café on our street.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen a few days in the future, counting from the present moment. Often used for near-future predictions or plans. Similar idea: « d’ici quelques jours » (“within a few days”).
target_language_example: Je reviens dans quelques jours.
native_language_example: I'll be back in a few days.

additional_notes: Means someone/something is located inside the person’s room. "Sa" can mean "his" or "her" depending on who is being talked about (it agrees with "chambre," not with the person). Used with verbs of movement too: "entrer/aller/monter/retourner dans sa chambre" = to go into/to one’s room.
target_language_example: J’ai laissé mon sac dans sa chambre.
native_language_example: I left my bag in his/her room.

meaning: in his/her youth; when he/she was young.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a period earlier in someone’s life (childhood/teen years/young adulthood). The possessive changes with the person: dans ma jeunesse (in my youth), dans ta jeunesse, dans son/sa jeunesse, dans notre/votre/leur jeunesse.
target_language_example: Dans sa jeunesse, il jouait au football tous les jours.
native_language_example: In his youth, he played soccer every day.

additional_notes: Literally means something is inside someone’s pocket. The possessive changes with the person: dans ma poche (my), dans ta poche (your), dans sa poche (his/her), dans notre/votre/leur poche (our/your/their). Often used with verbs like mettre, glisser, fourrer, trouver.
target_language_example: Il a glissé un paquet de cigarettes dans sa poche avant de rentrer.
native_language_example: He slipped a pack of cigarettes into his pocket before going home.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition phrase "dans" (in/inside) + "sa" (his/her) + "voiture" (car). It can describe being inside the car (rester dans sa voiture), getting into it (entrer/monter dans sa voiture), or doing something while inside it (fumer dans sa voiture). Note: "sa" can mean either "his" or "her" depending on who owns the car; French uses "sa" because "voiture" is feminine.
target_language_example: Elle attend dans sa voiture.
native_language_example: She’s waiting in her car.

meaning: in his/her arms; held in an embrace.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically holding another person (often a baby/child) or hugging them. The possessive changes with the subject: dans ses bras (his/her), dans mes bras (in my arms), dans tes bras (in your arms), dans nos/vos/leurs bras. Common verbs: tenir/porter quelqu’un dans ses bras (to hold/carry someone in your arms), prendre quelqu’un dans ses bras (to take someone in your arms = hug), serrer quelqu’un dans ses bras (to hold someone tight in a hug).
target_language_example: Après la mauvaise nouvelle, il l’a prise dans ses bras.
native_language_example: After the bad news, he took her in his arms (hugged her).

additional_notes: A common, fully literal combination: dans means "in/inside" and son means "his," "her," or sometimes "its" depending on context. Son agrees with the noun that follows, not with the gender of the owner, so son can also refer to a female owner before a masculine noun (for example, dans son sac = "in her bag").
target_language_example: Elle a retrouvé ses lunettes dans son sac.
native_language_example: She found her glasses in her bag.

meaning: in his office (in his study/office room).
additional_notes: Literally “in his office.” Used to say someone is inside their office (a workplace office or a home office/study). The possessive adjective changes with the owner: dans mon bureau (my), dans ton bureau (your, informal), dans son bureau (his/her), dans notre/votre/leur bureau (our/your/their).
target_language_example: Je suis dans son bureau, mais il n’est pas là pour le moment.
native_language_example: I’m in his office, but he isn’t here at the moment.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something globally rather than focusing on details. Often placed at the start of a sentence to mean “overall” (“Dans son ensemble, …”), or after a noun (“la situation dans son ensemble” = “the situation as a whole”). The possessive changes with the noun: dans son ensemble (masc.), dans son entic38re (fem.), dans leur ensemble (plural).
target_language_example: Dans son ensemble, le projet s'est bien passc38, malgrc38 quelques problc38mes.
native_language_example: Overall, the project went well, despite a few problems.

additional_notes: Means something is happening or located in the person’s garden/yard at their home. The possessive changes with the owner: dans mon jardin (my), dans ton jardin (your), dans son jardin (his/her), dans notre/votre/leur jardin (our/your/their). Often used with gardening verbs like cultiver / faire pousser, or for events/objects kept in the yard.
target_language_example: Elle organise un barbecue dans son jardin.
native_language_example: She’s hosting a barbecue in her garden/yard.

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive (ta = your, to one person you address as tu). For formal/plural, use "dans votre chambre". Note: "ta" becomes "ton" before a vowel sound: "dans ton appartement".
target_language_example: Je suis dans ta chambre.
native_language_example: I’m in your room.

additional_notes: An aggressive taunt said to someone to humiliate them (often after you “win” or prove them wrong). Literally means “in your mouth,” but it’s used like English “in your face” or “take that.” Strongly informal/vulgar; avoid in polite situations. Often said alone (“Dans ta gueule !”) or with a verb like “Prends ça dans ta gueule !”.
target_language_example: Tu vois ? J’avais raison. Dans ta gueule !
native_language_example: See? I was right. In your face!

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s life in general (experiences over time) or their personal/romantic life (e.g., “Is there someone in your life?”). Can also mean “back into your life” when used with verbs like revenir/entrer.
target_language_example: Je ne veux plus de drame dans ta vie.
native_language_example: I don’t want any more drama in your life.

meaning: in your arms (i.e., in an embrace).
additional_notes: Used to talk about holding someone or hugging them. Often appears with verbs like « être » (to be), « (se) serrer » (to hold tight), « prendre » (to take/pull into one’s arms), and « tenir » (to hold). It’s literal (arms) but usually refers to a hug rather than just physical location.
target_language_example: Viens, je veux être dans tes bras.
native_language_example: Come here, I want to be in your arms.

meaning: “In your dreams!” (said to mean “no way” / “as if”).
additional_notes: Often used sarcastically to dismiss what someone says or wants (“Yeah right!”). You can also use it more literally in phrases like “mieux que dans tes rêves (les plus fous)” = “better than in your (wildest) dreams.” Variants: “dans ton rêve” (to one person with *tu*), “dans vos rêves” (formal/plural).
target_language_example: — Tu vas gagner ce match. — Dans tes rêves !
native_language_example: — You’re going to win this match. — In your dreams!

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun. It usually refers to being inside something ('in a'), but with verbs of movement it often means going inside something ('into a'). For feminine nouns, use 'dans une'.
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé mes clés dans un tiroir.
native_language_example: I found my keys in a drawer.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened as a result of a car crash/traffic accident. Often used with verbs like mourir (to die) or être blessé (to be injured). You can also say "dans un accident" when it’s clear what kind of accident it was.
target_language_example: Elle a été gravement blessée dans un accident de voiture.
native_language_example: She was seriously injured in a car accident.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone is/was going or where something is happening. It often follows verbs like aller (to go): « Ils sont allés dans un bar. ». You can add an adjective to specify the type of bar: « dans un bar gay ».
target_language_example: On se retrouve dans un bar à 20 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet in a bar at 8 p.m.?

meaning: in a corner; off to one side.
additional_notes: Used for a literal corner of a room (“dans un coin de la pièce”) or more generally for being tucked away/away from attention (“rester dans un coin”, “se cacher dans un coin”). Often suggests being out of the way or trying not to be noticed.
target_language_example: Le chat dort dans un coin du salon.
native_language_example: The cat is sleeping in a corner of the living room.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone/something is, or where you’re going, without naming the exact place. Often followed by an adjective (dans un endroit sûr = “in a safe place”, dans un endroit très éloigné = “in a very remote place”) or by a relative clause (dans un endroit dont on ne revient pas = “a place you don’t come back from”).
target_language_example: On va se retrouver dans un endroit tranquille.
native_language_example: We’re going to meet in a quiet place.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen shortly (in the next few seconds/minutes). Common with future tense: « ce sera… », « il/elle sera… », « j’arrive dans un instant ».
target_language_example: J’arrive dans un instant.
native_language_example: I'll be there in a moment.

additional_notes: Uses "dans" to say someone is inside/at a restaurant (location or where an action happens). Often with verbs like manger, travailler, être, aller/emmener. If you mean eating at a specific restaurant as an outing, you may also hear "au restaurant" (more general: going out to eat).
target_language_example: On se retrouve dans un restaurant près de la gare.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in a restaurant near the train station.

additional_notes: Used to qualify what you’re saying: it’s true from one point of view, or partly true. Often set off by commas and used at the beginning of a sentence as a softener (e.g., "Dans un sens, oui" = "In a way, yes"). Can also mean "in one direction" in other contexts, but in these examples it means "from one perspective."
target_language_example: Dans un sens, je suis d’accord, mais pas complètement.
native_language_example: In a way, I agree, but not completely.

additional_notes: Means “in/inside a” before a feminine singular noun ("une"). Used for being inside a place (dans une ville, dans une bibliothèque), within a time period (dans une année), or in an abstract situation (dans une misère profonde). It can sometimes translate as “into a” with verbs of movement depending on context.
target_language_example: Il travaille dans une petite entreprise.
native_language_example: He works in a small company.

additional_notes: Used to qualify a statement: something is partly true, partly done, or true only up to a point. Often implies limits or reservations (not completely). Can be placed at the start or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Je suis d'accord avec toi dans une certaine mesure, mais pas sur tout.
native_language_example: I agree with you to a certain extent, but not about everything.

additional_notes: Used with "dans" + a time amount to say something will happen after that amount of time from now (a delay), not at a specific clock time. Common in appointments, waiting, and service contexts.
target_language_example: Je finis dans une demi-heure, puis on peut partir.
native_language_example: I’ll finish in half an hour, then we can leave.

meaning: in an hour; one hour from now.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen one hour after the current moment (a delay from now), not at a specific clock time. For a specific time, French often uses "à" (e.g., "à 15 heures" = at 3 p.m.). You can swap in other time amounts: "dans deux heures", "dans dix minutes".
target_language_example: On se voit dans une heure.
native_language_example: See you in an hour.

additional_notes: Used with "dans" to indicate being inside a house/building. With motion verbs like "rentrer" (to go in/come home), it can mean going into a house: "rentrer dans une maison" = "to enter a house" (or "to go into a house").
target_language_example: Il y a trois chambres dans une maison typique ici.
native_language_example: There are three bedrooms in a typical house here.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen very soon. It can be literal (in 60 seconds) but often just means “shortly.” Common with future tense or near-future expressions: « On arrive dans une minute. »
target_language_example: Je te rappelle dans une minute.
native_language_example: I’ll call you back in a minute.

meaning: in a week; one week from now.
additional_notes: Used to express a deadline or a point in the future counting from now (about seven days). With durations like this, French uses "dans" for "in" (future): "dans une semaine" = one week from now. For "a week ago," use "il y a une semaine."
target_language_example: On se revoit dans une semaine.
native_language_example: We’ll see each other again in a week.

additional_notes: Means “in your” (inside/within your). Use **votre** with **vous**: it’s used for one person you’re addressing formally (e.g., a stranger, a customer) or for more than one person (“your” plural). It comes before a noun: *dans votre vie* (in your life), *dans votre hôtel* (in your hotel), *dans votre bureau* (in your office). For informal singular “your,” use *dans ton/ta/tes* instead.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous vérifier dans votre sac, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you check in your bag, please?

meaning: in your room / into your room.
additional_notes: Means “in your bedroom” or “into your room,” depending on the verb: with movement verbs like aller/retourner it often means “go into your room,” and with action verbs like faire le ménage it means “in your room.” Uses the formal/plural possessive votre (to one person politely, or to several people).
target_language_example: Je vais dans votre chambre pour vous parler un instant.
native_language_example: I’m going into your room to talk to you for a moment.

additional_notes: Used on forms and in official contexts to ask for or provide someone’s birth date. Often appears as a standalone prompt (e.g., on a form): « Date de naissance ? ». You may be asked « Quelle est votre date de naissance ? » (formal) or « Quelle est ta date de naissance ? » (informal).
target_language_example: Pour ouvrir un compte, j’ai besoin de votre date de naissance.
native_language_example: To open an account, I need your date of birth.

meaning: deadline; due date (the latest allowed date).
additional_notes: Used for a cutoff date by which something must be done or submitted. Often seen on forms, bills, and assignments: « date limite de dépôt » (submission deadline), « date limite de paiement » (payment due date).
target_language_example: La date limite pour envoyer le dossier est vendredi.
native_language_example: The deadline to send the file is Friday.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean “more (of something)”, often in comparisons: « davantage de … que … » (“more … than …”). It’s a bit more formal than « plus de » but very common in writing and polite speech.
target_language_example: J’aimerais davantage de temps pour finir ce travail.
native_language_example: I’d like more time to finish this work.

meaning: from A to Z; from start to finish (everything, in full detail).
additional_notes: Used to mean something is complete or covers every step/detail. Often follows verbs like savoir (to know), expliquer/raconter (to explain/tell), contrôler/gérer (to control/manage), or faire/créer (to do/create): « raconter l’histoire de A à Z ».
target_language_example: Explique-moi le plan de A à Z, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Explain the plan to me from A to Z, please.

additional_notes: Most often placed after a noun to mean “basic/fundamental”: principes de base (basic principles), données de base (baseline data), parfums de base (standard/basic scents). In more conversational French, it can also mean “basically / by default” (e.g., De base, je ne bois pas de café = Basically, I don’t drink coffee).
target_language_example: On va commencer par les notions de base.
native_language_example: We’re going to start with the basic concepts.

meaning: some beautiful (plural masculine) / beautiful (before a plural masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used before a plural masculine noun (beaux + noun): e.g., de beaux rideaux, de beaux châteaux, de beaux cheveux. It commonly appears after an expression of quantity like "de" (instead of "des"), and it agrees in gender/number: feminine plural is "de belles" (de belles idées). Note: in the idiom "être dans de beaux draps", it’s ironic and means "to be in a fine mess / in trouble".
target_language_example: Ils ont acheté de beaux cadeaux pour leurs amis.
native_language_example: They bought beautiful gifts for their friends.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something earlier than usual/expected (get up, go to bed, leave, arrive). It often implies “nice and early,” especially with le matin or demain matin. Not the same as de bonne humeur (“in a good mood”).
target_language_example: On partira de bonne heure pour éviter les embouteillages.
native_language_example: We’ll leave early to avoid traffic jams.

additional_notes: Used with the verb être (or seeming verbs like avoir l'air) to describe someone’s general mood at a moment: être de bonne humeur = to be in a good mood. Common opposite: être de mauvaise humeur (to be in a bad mood).
target_language_example: Je suis de bonne humeur aujourd'hui, alors on peut sortir.
native_language_example: I'm in a good mood today, so we can go out.

additional_notes: Used when announcing or hoping for positive information. Often comes after verbs like avoir (J’ai de bonnes nouvelles), apporter (Tu apportes de bonnes nouvelles), or espérer (J’espère que tu as de bonnes nouvelles). Note: nouvelles is plural in French, even though “news” is usually uncountable in English.
target_language_example: On a enfin de bonnes nouvelles : le train n’est pas annulé.
native_language_example: We finally have some good news: the train isn’t canceled.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “some good …” (e.g., de bons livres = some good books). It’s the plural form of bon (“good”) after de. You also see it in negatives: Je n’ai pas de bons amis ici. = I don’t have any good friends here. Sometimes it can stand alone to mean “good ones,” depending on context.
target_language_example: On a trouvé de bons restaurants près d’ici.
native_language_example: We found some good restaurants near here.

additional_notes: Means people who are friends and get along well; often implies a fairly close friendship. It uses the plural form: un bon ami / une bonne amie (singular) → de bons amis (plural). In French, you often say it with the verb être: Ils sont de bons amis.
target_language_example: On est de bons amis depuis l’école.
native_language_example: We’ve been good friends since school.

additional_notes: Literally “of (the) mouth.” Used mainly in set phrases to describe something done through the mouth or related to the mouth, e.g. « hygiène de bouche » (oral hygiene), « thermomètre de bouche » (oral thermometer), « respiration de bouche » (mouth breathing). On its own, « de bouche » is less common than these full expressions.
target_language_example: J’ai acheté un thermomètre de bouche.
native_language_example: I bought an oral thermometer.

additional_notes: Used with quantities or amounts: beaucoup de café (a lot of coffee), trop de café (too much coffee), plus/davantage de café (more coffee). After a negation, French often uses just "de" (not "du"): Je ne bois pas de café (I don’t drink coffee). It can also mean "of coffee" in noun phrases like "grains de café" (coffee beans).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas de café, mais je voudrais du thé.
native_language_example: I don't want any coffee, but I'd like some tea.

additional_notes: Usually means "of/from this/that" before a masculine singular noun. Here, ce means "this" or "that" depending on context, and de can mean things like "of," "from," or sometimes mark relation or topic. Before a masculine noun starting with a vowel sound, it becomes de cet; with feminine nouns, de cette; with plural nouns, de ces.
target_language_example: On a parlé de ce problème hier.
native_language_example: We talked about this problem yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to mean “of/from these” before a plural noun. The exact meaning depends on the verb/context: e.g., partir de ces pays = “leave these countries,” la(quel)le de ces… = “which of these…,” l’un de ces… = “one of these…”.
target_language_example: Je voudrais goûter l’un de ces desserts.
native_language_example: I’d like to try one of these desserts.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "de" + the demonstrative adjective "cette" (feminine singular) before a feminine noun: "de cette liste" (of/about this list). Often translates as "of this" (possession/description) or "about this" (topic). For masculine nouns you’ll usually use "de ce" / "de cet" (before a vowel sound).
target_language_example: On a parlé de cette idée hier.
native_language_example: We talked about this idea yesterday.

meaning: like this; in this way; like that (in that manner).
additional_notes: Used to describe the manner/way something is done or said. Often points to what you’re doing now ("like this") or to a behavior being criticized ("Don’t talk/treat him like that"). Similar to "comme ça" (more common in speech).
target_language_example: Ne me parle pas de cette façon, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to me like that, please.

meaning: in this way; like this (in this manner).
additional_notes: Used to describe the way someone does something or the way something is done/treated, often referring back to a specific behavior or attitude (sometimes with criticism: “talk to me like that”). Common with verbs like parler (to speak), traiter (to treat), penser (to think), faire (to do).
target_language_example: Ne me regarde pas de cette manière.
native_language_example: Don’t look at me like that.

additional_notes: Used to say someone must leave your home (or your place in general). Common after verbs like sortir, partir, dégager: « Sors de chez moi ! » = “Get out of my house!” « Chez moi » means “at my place”; adding « de » makes it “from/out of my place.”
target_language_example: Sors de chez moi tout de suite !
native_language_example: Get out of my place right now!

additional_notes: Placed after a noun to emphasize it. Common in set phrases like « une équipe de choc » (a crack team) or « un duo de choc » (an amazing duo). Depending on context, it can mean either “impressive/awesome” (often) or more literally “shocking/impactful.”
target_language_example: On a une équipe de choc pour ce projet.
native_language_example: We have a top-notch team for this project.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean something/someone is high-quality, distinguished, or specially chosen: "un vin de choix" (a fine wine), "des invités de choix" (distinguished guests). It’s fairly formal and often found in writing or polite speech.
target_language_example: Pour la cérémonie, ils ont invité des guests de choix.
native_language_example: For the ceremony, they invited distinguished guests.

additional_notes: Used to say people (or things) act at the same time and in a coordinated way: travailler/agir/réamer/sonner de concert. Don’t confuse with "un concert" (a music concert) as in "tickets de concert"—that’s a different word.
target_language_example: Les deux équipes doivent agir de concert pour finir le projet à temps.
native_language_example: The two teams have to work together (in coordination) to finish the project on time.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean “trusted” or “reliable”: une personne de confiance (a trustworthy person), un ami de confiance (a trusted friend), un homme de confiance (a trusted right-hand man). Very common in the phrase digne de confiance (“worthy of trust”). In negatives: pas de confiance = “no trust.”
target_language_example: Je cherche un médecin de confiance.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a doctor I can trust.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something’s color, often after verbs like changer (to change), peindre (to paint), or être (to be): changer de couleur (change color), de couleur bleue (blue-colored). It can also describe hair color: changer de couleur de cheveux. When used about people (e.g., une personne de couleur), it can mean “a person of color,” but this wording can sound dated or awkward; many speakers prefer personne racisée or refer to a specific background.
target_language_example: Je voudrais une chemise de couleur claire.
native_language_example: I’d like a light-colored shirt.

additional_notes: Used after a card rank to name the suit: *le valet de cœur* (the jack of hearts), *le quatre de cœur* (the four of hearts). Also appears in *en forme de cœur* (“heart-shaped”), describing the shape of something.
target_language_example: Tu as le roi de cœur ?
native_language_example: Do you have the king of hearts?

additional_notes: Used to express a quantity, size, or number with a noun: *épais de deux mètres* (two meters thick), *une maison de deux chambres* (a two-bedroom house). Also common in set phrases like *de deux façons / de deux manières* meaning “in two ways.”
target_language_example: On peut le faire de deux façons.
native_language_example: We can do it in two ways.

additional_notes: Used when a verb or noun is followed by "de" and then an infinitive, with the idea of becoming something (a job, a state, etc.). Common patterns include: "décider de devenir…" (decide to become…), "avoir pour but de devenir…" (have the goal of becoming…), "abandonner l’espoir de devenir…" (give up the hope of becoming…), and after "ce serait" to mean "to become" in a hypothetical situation.
target_language_example: Elle rêve de devenir pilote.
native_language_example: She dreams of becoming a pilot.

meaning: “to sleep” (infinitive introduced by *de*, often after another verb or expression).
additional_notes: Used when the verb *dormir* follows certain verbs/expressions that require *de* + infinitive, e.g. *empêcher de dormir* (“to keep [someone] from sleeping”), *avant de dormir* (“before going to sleep”), *faire semblant de dormir* (“to pretend to be asleep”), *il serait bon de dormir* (“it would be good to sleep”). In English it’s often translated as “to sleep / from sleeping / of sleeping,” depending on the structure.
target_language_example: J'essaie de ne pas boire de café avant de dormir.
native_language_example: I try not to drink coffee before going to sleep.

meaning: by right; legally (as a matter of law).
additional_notes: Used to say something is true or granted because of law or entitlement (not just in practice). Often contrasts with "de fait" (in fact / in practice). Can also mean "rightful" in phrases like "héritier de droit" (rightful heir).
target_language_example: Tu es, de droit, le propriétaire de cet appartement.
native_language_example: You are, by law/rightfully, the owner of this apartment.

additional_notes: Used to describe orientation or viewpoint: a person/thing seen from the front (photo, posture: « Les épaules de face »), someone standing or positioned facing you (« Vous étiez de face ? »), or something coming straight toward you like a headwind (« un vent de face »). Often contrasts with « de profil » (from the side).
target_language_example: Sur la photo, il est de face.
native_language_example: In the photo, he is facing forward (seen from the front).

additional_notes: Used after certain verbs or expressions to show that hunger is the cause of an action or state (e.g., crier de faim = cry from hunger, mourir de faim = die of starvation, trembler de faim = shake from hunger).
target_language_example: Après deux jours sans manger, ils tremblaient de faim.
native_language_example: After two days without eating, they were trembling from hunger.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: this is de + the infinitive faire. It often appears after verbs, adjectives, or nouns (for example libre de faire, risquer de faire, demander de faire). In English, it may translate as "to do/make" or sometimes "doing/making," depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Il a peur de faire une erreur.
native_language_example: He's afraid of making a mistake.

additional_notes: Used when an infinitive is introduced by **de** after certain verbs and expressions (e.g. **prévoir de…** = plan to…, **arrêter de…** = stop …ing, **être nécessaire de…** = be necessary to…). **Cela** means “that” (a bit more formal); in speech it’s often replaced by **ça** (“de faire ça”).
target_language_example: Tu devrais éviter de faire cela ici.
native_language_example: You should avoid doing that here.

additional_notes: Used after many verbs/adjectives that are followed by an infinitive introduced by **de** (e.g., *rêver de…*, *arrêter de…*, *être [adjective] de…*, *demander à quelqu’un de…*). **Faire** = “to do/make” and **ça** = “that/this” (informal for *cela*). Often expresses doing a specific action previously mentioned or understood from context.
target_language_example: Merci d’avoir accepté de faire ça.
native_language_example: Thanks for agreeing to do that.

meaning: in fact; indeed; as a matter of fact.
additional_notes: Used to introduce or confirm a statement as a factual reality (often at the beginning of a sentence): “De fait, …”. In writing it can feel slightly formal. Not to be confused with the legal expression “voies de fait” (acts of violence/assault), which is a different phrase.
target_language_example: De fait, il n’avait pas le choix.
native_language_example: In fact, he had no choice.

meaning: "of iron" (made of iron; or very strong/unyielding).
additional_notes: Used literally to describe something made of iron (un monstre de fer = an iron monster). Very common in fixed expressions like "une volonté de fer" meaning "an iron will" (a very strong determination). Also used with "fer" as a noun meaning the metal iron, especially in nutrition contexts.
target_language_example: Elle a une volonté de fer.
native_language_example: She has an iron will.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something that is in the background (musique de fond = background music), that is deep/serious and done thoroughly (travail de fond = thorough groundwork; article de fond = in-depth article), or that happens deep underground in mining (mineur de fond = underground miner). The exact meaning depends on the noun it follows.
target_language_example: On entendait de la musique de fond pendant le dîner.
native_language_example: We could hear background music during dinner.

additional_notes: Used after verbs to describe doing something using physical strength or power: « frapper la porte avec plus de force » (hit the door harder). It can also appear in expressions about having (or lacking) strength, e.g. « à bout de force » = exhausted/out of strength.
target_language_example: Il a poussé la porte de force.
native_language_example: He forced the door open.

meaning: makeshift / improvised; or (in finance) “wealth” (as in wealth management).
additional_notes: Placed after a noun to mean something made quickly with whatever is available: un abri de fortune (a makeshift shelter), une échelle de fortune (an improvised ladder), une table de fortune (a makeshift table). In formal/business contexts, especially banking, fortune can mean “wealth,” so gestion de fortune = wealth management.
target_language_example: On a installé un lit de fortune dans le salon.
native_language_example: We set up a makeshift bed in the living room.

additional_notes: Informal intensifier meaning something is extreme or impressive. Common after a noun: "un truc de fou" (something crazy), "une ambiance de fou" (an amazing/crazy vibe), "une chance de fou" (incredible luck). It can also be used with some adjectives/expressions in casual speech to mean "insanely": "c'est cher de fou" (it's insanely expensive).
target_language_example: Il y avait une ambiance de fou au concert.
native_language_example: There was a crazy/amazing atmosphere at the concert.

meaning: 'to smoke' / 'smoking' (used with verbs or nouns that take *de*).
additional_notes: French often uses *de* before an infinitive after certain verbs and expressions, e.g. *arrêter de* (to stop), *éviter de* (to avoid), *le fait de* (the fact of). So you’ll see *de fumer* meaning “to smoke” or “smoking” depending on the structure: *Arrête de fumer* = “Stop smoking”; *Le fait de fumer* = “The fact of smoking.” Note that *fumer* means “to smoke,” not English “to fume” (be angry).
target_language_example: J’essaie d’arrêter de fumer.
native_language_example: I’m trying to stop smoking.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean a service/provider is available outside normal hours: une pharmacie de garde (an on-call pharmacy), un médecin de garde (an on-call doctor). Used after "être" to mean someone is working a duty shift: Je suis de garde ce soir. Also common in negatives/conditions: Je ne suis pas de garde.
target_language_example: Le médecin de garde peut vous recevoir ce soir.
native_language_example: The on-call doctor can see you tonight.

additional_notes: Used after quantity expressions to talk about an (often unspecified) number of people: assez de gens (enough people), beaucoup/trop/plus de gens (many/too many/more people), peu/guère de gens (few/hardly any people), un flot de gens (a stream of people), etc. Note: "gens" is plural in meaning and normally takes plural agreement (e.g., "les gens sont...").
target_language_example: Il y avait trop de gens dans la rue.
native_language_example: There were too many people in the street.

additional_notes: Used after a noun or verb to show that an action or reaction is caused by joy (e.g., "crier de joie" = to shout with joy, "pleurer de joie" = to cry tears of joy, "sauter de joie" = to jump for joy).
target_language_example: Ils ont dansé de joie quand ils ont appris la bonne nouvelle.
native_language_example: They danced with joy when they heard the good news.

meaning: to play (used after certain expressions + “de” + infinitive).
additional_notes: French often uses “de + infinitive” after common expressions like: “C’est l’heure de… / Il est temps de…” (it’s time to…), “finir de…” (to finish …ing), “se contenter de…” (to be satisfied with …ing), and “à nous de…” (it’s up to us to…). Here, “de” doesn’t translate as “of” in natural English; you usually just translate the verb (“to play”, “playing”).
target_language_example: Après le dîner, c'est l'heure de jouer !
native_language_example: After dinner, it's time to play!

additional_notes: Used to say something happens in the daytime, often contrasted with « de nuit » (“at night”): « de jour ou de nuit », « de jour comme de nuit » (“day and night”). Common with verbs like « travailler », « être actif », « voyager ».
target_language_example: Je préfère conduire de jour.
native_language_example: I prefer to drive during the day.

meaning: day by day; more and more as each day passes.
additional_notes: Used to describe a gradual change over time (often getting better/worse) from one day to the next. Common with comparatives like "plus chaud/froid", and verbs like "empirer" (to get worse), "croître" (to increase), "changer" (to change).
target_language_example: Je me sens de jour en jour plus confiant.
native_language_example: I feel more confident day by day.

meaning: by a narrow margin; just barely.
additional_notes: Used to say something almost didn’t happen, or happened only at the last moment (a near miss) or with a very small difference (e.g., a vote or result). Common with verbs like échapper (to escape), manquer (to miss), survivre (to survive), and with approvals/wins: approuvé/gagné de justesse. Can be used alone as an exclamation: « De justesse ! » = “That was close!”
target_language_example: J’ai attrapé le bus de justesse.
native_language_example: I caught the bus just in time.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + le/la** before a vowel sound (including silent **h**): **de l’extérieur**, **de l’empire**, **de l’humanité**. It can mean **“of the”** (possession/description: *le bien de l’humanité*) or **“from the”** (origin/viewpoint: *vu de l’extérieur*).
target_language_example: C'est si différent, vu de l'extérieur.
native_language_example: It’s so different, seen from the outside.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like avoir/donner/prêter to refer to an unspecified amount of money. In negatives, it often becomes « d’argent »: « Je n’ai pas d’argent. » (note: « de » becomes « d’ » before a vowel). In questions, « de l’argent » is common: « As-tu de l’argent ? ».
target_language_example: As-tu de l'argent ?
native_language_example: Do you have any money?

meaning: on the other side; across (from here).
additional_notes: Used with a place or boundary: « de l'autre côté de + noun » = “on the other side of …” (de l'autre côté de la rue, du mur, de la colline). Used alone (« Il est de l'autre côté ») means “He’s on the other side / across (from here).” It can also be figurative, especially « se revoir de l'autre côté » = “see each other on the other side,” sometimes implying the afterlife depending on context.
target_language_example: Le café est de l'autre côté de la rue.
native_language_example: The café is on the other side of the street.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a location across from something (a street, river, wall, border, etc.). Often followed by a place or thing: « de l’autre côté de la rue / du fleuve / du mur ». You can also use it without « de » as « de l’autre côté » (“on the other side”).
target_language_example: La boulangerie est juste de l'autre côté de la rue.
native_language_example: The bakery is right across the street (on the other side of the street).

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (de + l’) to talk about an unspecified amount of an uncountable thing: Je veux de l'eau. In negatives it usually becomes just "d'eau" (Je ne veux pas d'eau). After a specific quantity, you typically use "d'eau" too: un verre d'eau. Note: it’s written "de l'eau" (with an apostrophe), not "de l’eau".
target_language_example: Vous voulez de l'eau ?
native_language_example: Do you want (some) water?

additional_notes: Used to talk about hope in general (an uncountable idea), not “a hope” as one specific wish. It often appears with expressions like « il reste de l'espoir » (there is hope left), « il y a encore/toujours de l'espoir » (there is still/always hope), or « avoir de l'espoir » (to have hope). You can also add « pour + noun/pronoun »: « de l'espoir pour toi » (hope for you).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il y a encore de l'espoir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there’s still hope.

meaning: to hear it / to hear him / to hear her.
additional_notes: Used with verbs or expressions that take **de + infinitive** (e.g., *être content/ravi de…*, *avoir besoin de…*). **l’** is a direct-object pronoun meaning “it / him / her,” referring to something already known from context: *Je suis content de l’entendre* = “I’m happy to hear it.”
target_language_example: J'étais soulagé de l'entendre.
native_language_example: I was relieved to hear it.

additional_notes: Combination of de + la, used before a feminine singular noun. It often shows relation or possession ('of the') or origin/source ('from the'). In some expressions, especially with faire, it may not translate word-for-word: faire de la randonnée = 'go hiking'.
target_language_example: Je reviens de la boulangerie.
native_language_example: I'm coming back from the bakery.

meaning: “of the Tower” (often used as part of a family name or place name).
additional_notes: Literally means “from/of the tower.” Most commonly seen as a name element (e.g., a surname like « de la Tour ») or in proper names of places/buildings. In names, it usually isn’t translated.
target_language_example: Je m'appelle Claire de la Tour.
native_language_example: My name is Claire de la Tour.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article "de la" to talk about an unspecified amount of a non-count noun (beer in general). In questions and negatives, you often switch to "de" (or "d'"), e.g. "Tu as de la bière ?" but "Je n'ai pas de bière."
target_language_example: On prend de la bière ou du vin ?
native_language_example: Shall we have some beer or some wine?

additional_notes: Literally “some of the good (kind)”. Often used with an implied feminine noun like *herbe* (“weed”) or *nourriture* (“food”): *Tu fumes toujours de la bonne ?* = “Do you still smoke the good stuff?” In neutral contexts it can simply mean “good” + a feminine noun you mention (e.g., *de la bonne nourriture* = “good food”), but used alone it commonly suggests cannabis.
target_language_example: Il a ramené de la bonne pour la soirée.
native_language_example: He brought some good weed for the evening.

additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb "avoir" to say you are lucky: "avoir de la chance" = "to be lucky" (literally "to have luck"). Often preceded by "de la" because "chance" is treated like an uncountable noun here (some luck).
target_language_example: Tu as de la chance d'avoir des amis comme ça.
native_language_example: You're lucky to have friends like that.

meaning: classy; (also) “of the class” (in a school group).
additional_notes: Common in the expression « avoir de la classe » = “to have class” (stylish, elegant, with good taste). It can also be literal after a noun to mean “of the class / in the class” when talking about students: « le plus grand de la classe » = “the tallest in the class.”
target_language_example: Même avec une tenue simple, elle a de la classe.
native_language_example: Even with a simple outfit, she has class.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (de la) to mean “some” in an uncountable sense: avoir de la compagnie = “to have company / not be alone.” Often used when someone is present or coming over: On a de la compagnie. / Veux-tu de la compagnie ? (Do you want someone to keep you company?). Note: compagnie can also mean a “company” (business), but this expression usually refers to companionship.
target_language_example: Je n'aime pas rester seul, j'aime avoir de la compagnie.
native_language_example: I don't like being alone; I like having company.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (de la) to talk about an unspecified amount of something uncountable: Je veux de la confiture. Also appears in the idiom « de la confiture pour les cochons » (“pearls before swine”), meaning something good is wasted on people who won’t appreciate it.
target_language_example: Tu veux de la confiture sur tes tartines ?
native_language_example: Do you want some jam on your toast?

additional_notes: Most often, "de la cuisine" means "from the kitchen" or "of the kitchen" (it uses "de" to show origin or location: "apporter… de la cuisine", "sortir de la cuisine", "la porte de la cuisine"). In another common use, "de la cuisine" can mean "(some) cuisine/cooking" in general: "manger de la cuisine japonaise" (eat Japanese food) or "faire de la cuisine" (do cooking).
target_language_example: Tu peux apporter une chaise de la cuisine ?
native_language_example: Can you bring a chair from the kitchen?

additional_notes: "De la" is a partitive article meaning “some” with an uncountable noun. With "drogue" (usually used as an uncountable noun), it often refers to illegal drugs in general. Common with verbs like "prendre" (to take/use) and "il y a" (there is/are): "prendre de la drogue" = to use drugs; "il y a de la drogue" = there are drugs.
target_language_example: Il a arrêté de prendre de la drogue.
native_language_example: He stopped using drugs.

meaning: in the family; one of the family.
additional_notes: Often used with the verb être: « Je suis de la famille » = “I’m family / I’m a family member.” It can also be used more loosely to mean “almost like family” (« presque/quasiment de la famille »). With verbs like dire du mal de…, it refers to the family as a group: « dire du mal de la famille » = “to speak badly about the family.”
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, il est de la famille.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, he’s family.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avoir" (to have): "avoir de la fièvre" = to have a fever. In questions you’ll often hear: "Tu as de la fièvre ?" (Do you have a fever?). You can also specify how high: "J’ai 39 de fièvre."
target_language_example: Je ne viens pas aujourd’hui, j’ai de la fièvre.
native_language_example: I’m not coming today; I have a fever.

additional_notes: Commonly used after a noun to describe something connected to the forest (e.g., "esprit de la forêt" = spirit of the forest) or to indicate where someone/something comes from (e.g., "le garçon de la forêt" = the boy from the forest). It’s also used after verbs of movement to show coming out of the forest ("sortir de la forêt" = to come out of the forest).
target_language_example: On entend des bruits étranges venir de la forêt.
native_language_example: We hear strange noises coming from the forest.

meaning: “from the train station” or “(of/near) the train station,” depending on context.
additional_notes: "La gare" means “the (train) station.” With "de" it often marks origin (where you come from): "Je viens de la gare" = “I’m coming from the station.” In questions like "proche de la gare" / "près de la gare," it means “near the station.”
target_language_example: On se retrouve près de la gare à 18h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet near the train station at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: In French, *la glace* can mean either “ice” or “ice cream,” depending on context. With *de la* it means “some” (a partitive), common when offering or asking for an amount: *Vous voulez de la glace ?* In food contexts like *manger de la glace*, it usually means “to eat ice cream.”
target_language_example: Après le dîner, on prend de la glace au chocolat.
native_language_example: After dinner, we’ll have chocolate ice cream.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify a connection to a particular war or to war in general (e.g., « victimes de la guerre » = war victims). Often appears with time expressions like « du temps de la guerre » (“during the war”). « de la » can change to « de l’ » before a vowel (e.g., « de l’Afghanistan » in « la guerre d’Afghanistan »).
target_language_example: Il garde des photos de la guerre dans une boîte.
native_language_example: He keeps photos from the war in a box.

meaning: 'the guitar' (used after jouer to mean 'to play the guitar').
additional_notes: In French you say jouer de + [instrument]. The partitive article agrees with the instrument: de la guitare (feminine), du piano (masculine), de l’accordéon (before a vowel), des percussions (plural). Used mainly with verbs like jouer: Il joue de la guitare = He plays the guitar.
target_language_example: Je joue de la guitare le soir.
native_language_example: I play the guitar in the evening.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like supprimer, retirer, rayer to say something/someone is removed from a list (often with the idea of being taken off, deleted, or crossed off). Often appears in passive forms: être supprimé/retiré de la liste.
target_language_example: J'ai été retiré de la liste des invités.
native_language_example: I was removed from the guest list.

additional_notes: Used with the partitive article "de la" to mean an unspecified amount of light (not "the light"). Often appears after expressions like "il y a..." (there is/are) or after verbs like "voir" (to see) and "émettre" (to emit). For "the light" in a specific sense, French often uses "la lumière" (e.g., "Éteins la lumière" = Turn off the light).
target_language_example: Il y a de la lumière dans la cuisine.
native_language_example: There is some light in the kitchen.

meaning: from the house/home; (in restaurants) on the house.
additional_notes: Often used after verbs of movement: partir/sortir de la maison = to leave the house, être viré de la maison = to be kicked out of the house. In set phrases like « avec les compliments de la maison », it means something is offered for free by the establishment (a free drink/dessert).
target_language_example: Il est sorti de la maison sans faire de bruit.
native_language_example: He left the house without making any noise.

meaning: from the sea; of the sea.
additional_notes: Used after another word to indicate origin or source (e.g., "le vent souffle de la mer" = the wind blows from the sea), distance/location relative to the sea ("loin de la mer" = far from the sea), or a taste/smell associated with the sea ("le goût de la mer" = a sea taste). Contrast: "à la mer" = to the sea; "en mer" = at sea/on the sea.
target_language_example: On entendait un bruit qui venait de la mer.
native_language_example: We could hear a sound coming from the sea.

additional_notes: Very vulgar and insulting. Literally refers to feces (often followed by an animal: de la merde de pigeon = pigeon poop). Figuratively, it means something is terrible/useless (C’est de la merde. = It’s crap.). It’s also used in aggressive insults like Va manger de la merde ! (“Go eat shit!”). Avoid in polite conversation.
target_language_example: J’ai acheté ce gadget, mais franchement, c’est de la merde.
native_language_example: I bought this gadget, but honestly, it’s crap.

meaning: "of death" / "death" (used to describe something linked to death).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify a connection with death (often dramatic or descriptive). Common set phrase: « le couloir de la mort » = death row. In English, this is often translated more naturally by turning it into an adjective or compound noun (e.g., « planète de la mort » → “death planet” / “planet of death”).
target_language_example: On a appris la nouvelle de la mort de son père.
native_language_example: We learned the news of his father's death.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like écouter / mettre / jouer to mean “some music” in general (not a specific piece): écouter de la musique, mettre de la musique, jouer de la musique. As a generic idea, French often uses de la with uncountable nouns like musique.
target_language_example: On peut mettre de la musique pendant le dîner ?
native_language_example: Can we put on some music during dinner?

meaning: of nature; natural (related to the natural world).
additional_notes: Used after nouns or in set phrases to mean “of nature” or “related to nature.” Common with expressions like "près de la nature" / "à proximité de la nature" (close to nature = in the countryside/outdoors). Also appears in phrases like "les caprices de la nature" (the whims/forces of nature) and job descriptions like "photographe de la nature" (nature photographer).
target_language_example: J’aime passer du temps dehors, près de la nature.
native_language_example: I like spending time outside, close to nature.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (de la) with an uncountable noun to mean an unspecified quantity. Common after weather verbs/expressions like « il y a / il y aura », « annoncer », « attendre »: « Il y aura de la neige. » In negative sentences, it often becomes « de »: « Il n’y a pas de neige. »
target_language_example: Demain matin, il pourrait y avoir de la neige sur les routes.
native_language_example: Tomorrow morning, there might be snow on the roads.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (de la) to mean an unspecified amount of an uncountable thing: “some food.” Often used after verbs like manger (to eat), donner (to give), avoir (to have), voler (to steal). For specific dishes or types, you can add an adjective: de la nourriture japonaise/coréenne. In everyday speech, people also often just say “à manger” or name the food directly.
target_language_example: Il n’y a plus de la nourriture dans le frigo.
native_language_example: There isn’t any food left in the fridge.

additional_notes: Used to say who a message, gift, thanks, or request comes from, or who you are speaking/acting on behalf of. Common in exchanges like: « C’est de la part de qui ? » (“Who is it from?”).
target_language_example: J’ai un message de la part de Marie.
native_language_example: I have a message from Marie.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article **de la** (for feminine singular nouns) to talk about an unspecified amount of something you eat or drink. Very common after verbs like **manger** (to eat) or **vouloir** (to want): *Tu veux de la pizza ?* In negatives, it often changes to **de**: *Je ne veux pas de pizza.*
target_language_example: Je voudrais de la pizza, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like some pizza, please.

meaning: (out) of the room; from the room.
additional_notes: Most often used with verbs of movement, especially sortir (to leave/go out): sortir de la pièce = “to leave the room.” It can also mean “in the room” when used with something like le plus petit de la pièce (“the smallest person in the room”). Note: pièce can mean “room” (not just “piece”).
target_language_example: Je suis sorti(e) de la pièce pour téléphoner.
native_language_example: I left the room to make a phone call.

additional_notes: Used with "il y a" or "avoir" to say there is enough space or available seats/capacity for a certain number of people or things. Common in offers/invitations and when checking availability: "Il y a de la place pour…" / "On a de la place pour…" / "Y a-t-il de la place pour… ?"
target_language_example: On a de la place pour toi dans la voiture.
native_language_example: We have room for you in the car.

meaning: (to be) in the police; a police officer.
additional_notes: Often used with the verb être: « Je suis de la police » = “I’m with the police / I’m a police officer.” In questions: « Vous êtes de la police ? » = “Are you with the police?” It also appears in set phrases like « entre les mains de la police » (“in the hands of the police”). Not translated literally as “of the police” in natural English.
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas : je suis de la police.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’m with the police.

additional_notes:
Used with **de** to link to **la porte** (“the door,” feminine singular). It often appears:
- after location phrases: **près de la porte** (near the door), **sur le pas de la porte** (on the doorstep)
- after verbs of moving away: **s’éloigner de la porte** (to move away from the door)
- to show what something belongs to: **la serrure de la porte** (the door lock).
target_language_example: Laisse ton sac près de la porte.
native_language_example: Leave your bag near the door.

meaning: of the river / from the river.
additional_notes: "De la" is the contraction of "de + la" (feminine singular). With "rivière" (a feminine noun), it often shows origin ("provenir de la rivière" = come from the river) or possession/description ("le niveau de la rivière" = the river’s level).
target_language_example: On entend le bruit de la rivière la nuit.
native_language_example: You can hear the sound of the river at night.

meaning: of the road; road/traffic-related (in some set phrases).
additional_notes: Most literally means “of the road” (de + la). Used to describe something connected to a road: e.g., "les deux côtés de la route" (both sides of the road), "près de la route" (near the road). In common fixed expressions like "un accident de la route", it means a road/traffic accident.
target_language_example: Il y a eu un accident de la route près de chez nous.
native_language_example: There was a road (traffic) accident near our place.

additional_notes: Used to describe something related to the street (sounds, side/end of the street, etc.). It also appears in set expressions like « l’homme de la rue » (= the average person) and in contexts like « une victime de la rue » (= a street victim, often implying homelessness or life on the streets).
target_language_example: On entend de la musique qui vient de la rue.
native_language_example: You can hear music coming from the street.

additional_notes: Used after a noun or expression to specify what it concerns (e.g., « au courant de la situation » = up to date on the situation; « maître de la situation » = in control of the situation). Often refers to the current circumstances or what’s going on.
target_language_example: Je t'expliquerai les détails de la situation demain.
native_language_example: I’ll explain the details of the situation to you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Means “of the” + “société.” In context, "la société" can mean a company/business (often in work/administrative contexts: président/directeur de la société) or society in general (family is the core of society, excluded/forgiven by society). The intended meaning depends on surrounding words.
target_language_example: Elle est la fondatrice de la société.
native_language_example: She is the founder of the company.

additional_notes: Used to describe the manner something is done or happens (often referring to what was just said or to a specific example): agir / se comporter / fonctionner de la sorte. In the fixed phrase "Rien de la sorte", it means "nothing like that" (not at all that kind of thing). More formal than "comme ça".
target_language_example: Ne lui parle pas de la sorte.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to him like that.

meaning: some soup (an unspecified amount of soup).
additional_notes: "De la" is the partitive article used with uncountable nouns to mean “some.” You use it when you’re having/eating/drinking soup in general, not a specific bowl. In a question like “De la soupe ?”, it often means “Some soup?” / “Soup?” as an offer or suggestion.
target_language_example: Tu veux de la soupe ?
native_language_example: Do you want some soup?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like enlever, retirer, débarrasser to show that something is removed from the surface of the table (taken off the table). It can also mean "from the (master’s) table" in the sense of leftovers/food coming from someone’s table (e.g., "les restes de la table du maître").
target_language_example: Peux-tu enlever ce livre de la table ?
native_language_example: Can you take this book off the table?

meaning: "with your head" / "of the head" (often used with gestures and in set expressions).
additional_notes: Most often seen in fixed phrases: «faire oui/non de la tête» = to nod/shake your head; «malade de la tête» = mentally ill / (informally) crazy; «ne pas savoir où donner de la tête» = to feel overwhelmed; «coûter les yeux de la tête» = to cost a fortune.
target_language_example: Elle a fait non de la tête.
native_language_example: She shook her head no.

meaning: from head to toe; all over.
additional_notes: Used to mean completely, covering the whole body. Common with being wet/dirty ("trempé/couvert… de la tête aux pieds") and with looking someone up and down ("regarder/examiner quelqu’un de la tête aux pieds").
target_language_example: Après la randonnée, j’étais sale de la tête aux pieds.
native_language_example: After the hike, I was dirty from head to toe.

additional_notes: Used with food to mean an unspecified quantity: "de la" + feminine noun (la viande). After a negation, it often becomes "de viande" (e.g., "Je ne mange pas de viande"). Can also be used in "avoir de la viande" meaning you have some meat (e.g., in your fridge or on your plate).
target_language_example: On achète de la viande pour le dîner.
native_language_example: We’re buying some meat for dinner.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that something is about life in general (e.g., le caractère ordinaire de la vie = “the ordinary nature of life”), or in set expressions like profiter de la vie (“enjoy life”). In au péril de la vie, it means “at the risk of one’s life” (very high danger).
target_language_example: Il veut profiter de la vie et voyager un peu.
native_language_example: He wants to enjoy life and travel a bit.

meaning: of the city; from/out of the city.
additional_notes: "De la" is a contraction of "de + la" (feminine singular). With "ville" it can mean (1) belonging to the city: "le moins cher de la ville" = the cheapest in the city; (2) movement/origin: "sortir/partir/venir de la ville" = to leave/come from the city; or (3) location relative to the city: "au nord de la ville" = north of the city.
target_language_example: On vient de la ville, mais on préfère vivre à la campagne.
native_language_example: We’re from the city, but we prefer living in the countryside.

meaning: (to) have visitors; company (someone has come to see you).
additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb "avoir": "J’ai de la visite" / "Tu as de la visite" / "Vous avez de la visite" meaning someone is here (or coming) to visit. It can be said as an announcement (“You have a visitor”). With "le début de la visite" or "le jour de la visite," "la visite" means “the visit” (e.g., a tour/appointment/visiting time), but "avoir de la visite" is specifically about receiving visitors.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas parler longtemps : j’ai de la visite.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk long: I have visitors.

meaning: “of the car” / “from the car” (depending on context).
additional_notes: "De la" is the contraction of "de + la" (feminine singular). With a noun like "la voiture" (the car), it can mean possession/relationship ("la porte de la voiture" = the car door) or movement from inside/out of ("sortir de la voiture" = to get out of the car).
target_language_example: Je prends mon sac de la voiture.
native_language_example: I’m taking my bag from the car.

additional_notes: Used with quantities/containers (une brique de lait, une bouteille de lait) and comparisons (plus de lait que de café). After negative expressions or amounts like peu, you often see "de lait" (Il reste peu de lait).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un café avec un peu de lait, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like a coffee with a little milk, please.

additional_notes: Made of **de** + infinitive (**dire**) with the object pronoun **le** (“it”). Common after expressions like **c’est facile pour toi de le dire** (“easy for you to say”), **il suffisait de le dire** (“you only had to say so”), **pardonnez-moi de le dire** (“forgive me for saying so”), or **à toi de le dire** (“you tell me / it’s for you to say”).
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû de le dire plus tôt.
native_language_example: You should have said it earlier.

additional_notes: Used after a verb or expression that requires "de" + infinitive (e.g. proposer de, essayer de, décider de). "le" is the direct-object pronoun meaning “it” and comes before the infinitive: "de le faire" = “to do it.”
target_language_example: Je vais essayer de le faire demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to try to do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used after verbs/adjectives that take **de + infinitive** (e.g., *promettre de...*, *désespérer de...*, *avoir la permission de...*). The direct object pronoun **le** (“him/it”) is placed **before** the infinitive: *le rencontrer* = “meet him.” (Not to be confused with *du* = *de + le* as an article.)
target_language_example: J'espère de le rencontrer bientôt.
native_language_example: I hope to meet him soon.

additional_notes: "De" + "leur" means "of/from their" and is used before a singular noun that belongs to them (3rd person plural: they/them). For plural nouns, use "de leurs" (e.g., "de leurs amis" = "of their friends"). The exact translation depends on context: possession ("the date of their wedding"), origin ("released from their cage"), or topic ("nothing about their plan").
target_language_example: Je ne sais rien de leur décision.
native_language_example: I don't know anything about their decision.

additional_notes: Used when an infinitive verb is introduced by "de" after certain verbs/expressions, e.g. "valoir la peine/le coup de" (to be worth), "continuer de" (to keep/continue), "finir de" (to finish), "arrêter de" (to stop). In English you usually just say "to read" without "of".
target_language_example: J'ai arrêté de lire parce que j'étais fatigué.
native_language_example: I stopped reading because I was tired.

additional_notes: Used with nouns after quantities or expressions like beaucoup/plus/trop/un nombre/un choix: "trois livres" (three books) but "plus de livres" (more books). After a negative, "des" usually becomes "de": "Je ne lis pas de livres" = "I don’t read any books." The full phrase varies with gender/number (de/d’, du/de la/des), but before plural nouns like "livres" you often see "de" in these patterns.
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas acheté de livres cette semaine.
native_language_example: I didn’t buy any books this week.

additional_notes: Two common uses: (1) distance: « de loin / vu de loin » = from far away, often about how something looks at a distance; can also mean coming from far away (« je viens de loin »). (2) emphasis/comparison: « de loin le meilleur » = by far the best. In « cousins, mais de loin », it means a distant relationship (not close).
target_language_example: De loin, on dirait un château, mais c’est juste un vieux bâtiment.
native_language_example: From far away, it looks like a castle, but it’s just an old building.

additional_notes: de + lui uses the stressed pronoun lui after the preposition de. It often follows verbs or adjectives that require de, as in parler de lui ('talk about him'), être fier de lui ('be proud of him'), or se moquer de lui ('make fun of him'). In phrases like faire de lui..., it means 'make ... of him.' In de lui avoir donné..., lui is instead the pronoun 'to him' before an infinitive, not the same fixed pattern.
target_language_example: On parle souvent de lui en classe.
native_language_example: People often talk about him in class.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something luxurious or top-quality: un hôtel de luxe, une voiture de luxe, un appartement de luxe. It can also be used alone as a short comment meaning “deluxe / fancy!”
target_language_example: On a réservé une chambre de luxe pour notre anniversaire.
native_language_example: We booked a deluxe/luxury room for our anniversary.

meaning: Contraction of "de le" / "de la" meaning "of the", "from the", or "some (of)" before a vowel or silent h.
additional_notes: Used before a noun that starts with a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u) or a silent h: de l’océan (of the ocean), de l’école (of the school), de l’orage (some storm / stormy weather). It can express possession/relationship ("habitudes de l’Ombre" = habits of the Shadow) or an indefinite amount, especially in expressions like "de l’orage" (some storm / thunderstorm).
target_language_example: On a parlé de l’hôtel près de la gare.
native_language_example: We talked about the hotel near the station.

additional_notes:
Used with a noun to show possession or a close relationship: 
- le copain de ma mère = my mom’s boyfriend
- les yeux de ma mère = my mother’s eyes
It also appears in strong oath expressions with sur ("on"), like Sur la tête de ma mère ! / Sur la vie de ma mère ! = “I swear on my mother’s life!” (very emphatic, often informal/colloquial).
target_language_example: La voiture de ma mère est garée devant la maison.
native_language_example: My mother's car is parked in front of the house.

meaning: "from me" / "on my behalf" (when sending greetings, thanks, congratulations, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to pass along a message or sentiment to another person (often with verbs like dire bonjour, saluer, remercier, féliciter). It agrees with the speaker: de ma part (from me), de ta part (from you), de sa part (from him/her), de notre part (from us), de votre part (from you formal/plural), de leur part (from them).
target_language_example: Remercie-les de ma part, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Thank them for me, please.

additional_notes: Literally means “of my life.” Common uses: (1) after superlatives to mean “in my life”: « le pire jour de ma vie » (“the worst day of my life”); (2) in phrases like « l'amour de ma vie » (“the love of my life”); (3) with verbs like « sortir / disparaître de ma vie » to mean “get out of my life” (more emotional/strong).
target_language_example: C'est le meilleur voyage de ma vie.
native_language_example: It’s the best trip of my life.

additional_notes: Often used with **faire**: **faire du mal à quelqu’un** = “to hurt someone,” **se faire du mal** = “to hurt yourself.” Also appears after negatives/indefinites like **rien de mal** (“nothing wrong”) and **quelque chose de mal** (“something wrong/bad”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, il n’y a rien de mal.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, there’s nothing wrong.

additional_notes: Very common in informal spoken French to emphasize how extreme something is (good or bad). Often used after a noun or adjective: « un truc de malade » (something insane), « c’est beau de malade » (it’s insanely beautiful). It doesn’t mean someone is literally sick in these uses.
target_language_example: Ce concert était bien de malade !
native_language_example: That concert was insanely good!

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something marked by bad luck or tragedy: un jour de malheur (an ill-fated day), des rumeurs de malheur (rumors of tragedy/bad news). With "plus que ta part de malheur", it means “more than your share of misfortune.”
target_language_example: Depuis ce jour de malheur, elle a perdu tout espoir.
native_language_example: Since that ill-fated day, she has lost all hope.
