additional_notes: Often used in phrases like **à la dernière minute** (“at the last minute”) or **de dernière minute** (“last-minute,” used like an adjective): *un changement de dernière minute* (“a last-minute change”).
target_language_example: On a décidé ça à la dernière minute.
native_language_example: We decided that at the last minute.

additional_notes: Refers to the most recent years before now. Often used with a number or a time marker: « ces dernières années » (these last few years), « dans les dernières années » (in recent years), « les dernières années de sa vie » (the final years of his life), « ces quatre dernières années » (these last four years).
target_language_example: Ces dernières années, j'ai beaucoup voyagé pour le travail.
native_language_example: In recent years, I've traveled a lot for work.

additional_notes: Used to say something (or someone) is located or hiding in the space on the other side of the door, often out of sight (e.g., to hang a coat or to hide). It describes position: "derrière" + a noun with the article ("la porte").
target_language_example: Le chat dort derrière la porte.
native_language_example: The cat is sleeping behind the door.

additional_notes: An idiomatic way to say someone is in prison or will be sent to prison. Often used with verbs like « être » (to be), « passer X ans » (to spend X years), or « mettre » (to put/send someone) + « derrière les barreaux ».
target_language_example: S'il continue comme ça, il finira derrière les barreaux.
native_language_example: If he keeps that up, he'll end up behind bars.

additional_notes: Uses "de" + "les" → "des" before "autres" (plural). Common after a noun or adjective to compare or distinguish: "différent des autres" = "different from the others". In questions like "Qu’en est-il des autres ?", it means "What about the others?".
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas être comme les autres : je veux être différent des autres.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be like the others: I want to be different from the others.

additional_notes: Used to compare or choose between exactly two options. Common after a superlative/comparative (e.g., « le plus … des deux » = “the most … of the two”) and in « l’un des deux » (“one of the two”).
target_language_example: Je préfère celui de gauche des deux.
native_language_example: I prefer the one on the left of the two.

additional_notes: "Des" is often the plural of "un/une" (= “some/any”), but after expressions like "autour de", "prendre soin de", or in "la chambre/jardin des …", it usually means "de + les" (= “of the / the”), referring to a specific group of children. So "s’occuper/prendre soin des enfants" usually means “take care of the children” (not just “some children”).
target_language_example: Ce soir, je garde des enfants.
native_language_example: Tonight, I’m babysitting some kids.

additional_notes: "Gens" means "people" (in general). "Des" is often the plural indefinite article, so "des gens" commonly means "some people" or just "people" in a general sense. Very often you’ll also see "les gens" = "people" / "the public" in general. Note that "gens" is usually masculine plural for agreement (e.g., "des gens heureux"), but if an adjective comes before it, it can be feminine (e.g., "de bonnes gens").
target_language_example: Il y a des gens qui parlent très vite.
native_language_example: There are people who speak very fast.

additional_notes: "Des" is an indefinite article meaning "some" (plural of "un/une"). You use "des amis" to talk about friends in general or an unspecified group: "Je suis avec des amis" (I’m with some friends). In speech, you may also hear "C’est des amis à moi" meaning "They’re friends of mine" (more formal: "Ce sont des amis à moi" or "Ce sont mes amis"). After a negative, "des" usually becomes "de": "Je n’ai pas d’amis" (I don’t have any friends).
target_language_example: Ce week-end, je sors avec des amis.
native_language_example: This weekend, I’m going out with some friends.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural indefinite article: it often means "some" or "(any)" in general statements. "Des animaux" can refer to animals in general (Je déteste voir des animaux souffrir.) or to unspecified animals (Ils ont des animaux.). In sentence 1, it’s also used to describe what something is: "Ce sont des animaux" = "They are animals."
target_language_example: Ils ont des animaux à la ferme.
native_language_example: They have animals on the farm.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration lasting many years, often to emphasize that something took a long time ("Ça fait des années", "Ça m'a pris des années", "pendant des années"). It can also mean "years of" in expressions like "des années de pratique" or "des années de données".
target_language_example: Ça fait des années que je veux apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I've been wanting to learn French for years.

additional_notes: Plural indefinite article (des) + armes. Often translated simply as “weapons” in English (“Il y a des armes…” = “There are weapons…”). Note the potential confusion with English “arms” (body parts): in French, « les bras » are your arms, while « des armes » are weapons.
target_language_example: La police a trouvé des armes dans la voiture.
native_language_example: The police found weapons in the car.

additional_notes: “Des” is the plural partitive/indefinite article, used to mean “some” or “(any)”. “Biscuits” in French usually refers to sweet cookies; you can specify the type (e.g., biscuits pour chiens = dog biscuits/treats). Common with verbs like apporter (bring), faire (make/bake), and in offers like « Veuillez vous servir… » (“Please help yourself…”).
target_language_example: Tu veux des biscuits avec ton café ?
native_language_example: Do you want some cookies with your coffee?

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb « faire »: « faire des cauchemars » = to have nightmares / to have bad dreams. Often appears with time expressions like « la nuit » (at night) or frequency words like « souvent » (often), « régulièrement » (regularly).
target_language_example: Depuis ce film, je fais des cauchemars.
native_language_example: Since that movie, I’ve been having nightmares.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a large number (in the hundreds) followed by a noun: « des centaines de livres/personnes/voitures ». Often also used loosely for emphasis, like English “hundreds of times” (« Je te l’ai dit des centaines de fois. »).
target_language_example: Il y a des centaines de messages dans ma boîte mail.
native_language_example: There are hundreds of messages in my inbox.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural of the indefinite article (like "some" or "(a few)"). "Des choses" is very common to talk about things in general or unspecified items/ideas: "Je sais des choses" (I know things), "Il cache des choses" (He’s hiding things). Often it can translate naturally as just "things" in English, without "some."
target_language_example: On a des choses à te dire.
native_language_example: We have things to tell you.

additional_notes: Used to say you have tasks/errands or obligations. Often with avoir (“to have”): « J’ai des choses à faire » = “I have things to do.” With « Il y a… » it means “There are things to do” (work remains). You can add words like « encore » (still) or a place like « ici » (here).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : j’ai des choses à faire ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have things to do tonight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the sound or occurrence of gunfire. Very common with verbs like entendre (to hear) and tirer (to fire): « On a entendu des coups de feu » / « Des coups de feu ont été tirés ». « Il y a des coups de feu » means “There are gunshots / There’s gunfire.”
target_language_example: J’ai entendu des coups de feu près de la gare.
native_language_example: I heard gunshots near the train station.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural indefinite article ("some"). Use "des enfants" when talking about children in general or an unspecified number (e.g., having kids: "On a des enfants"). In questions or exclamations, it can also mean simply "children?" / "There are children!" It can be used figuratively to mean "(you/they) are being childish" (e.g., "Mes amis sont vraiment des enfants").
target_language_example: Dans ce parc, il y a toujours des enfants qui jouent.
native_language_example: In this park, there are always children playing.

additional_notes: Most common in set phrases like **avoir des ennuis (avec …)** = “to be in trouble (with …)” (e.g., *avec la loi*, *avec ses parents*). You can also say **causer / créer des ennuis** = “to cause trouble” and **faire des ennuis à quelqu’un** = “to give someone trouble.” Note: French **ennui** can also mean “boredom,” but **des ennuis** often means “trouble/problems.”
target_language_example: J’ai des ennuis au travail en ce moment.
native_language_example: I’m having trouble at work right now.

additional_notes: Plural of "une erreur". Used with "faire des erreurs" (to make mistakes) and "commettre des erreurs" (to commit/make mistakes). Often means mistakes in general, not specific ones; to be specific you can say "ces erreurs" (these mistakes) or "des erreurs dans..." (mistakes in...).
target_language_example: J’ai fait des erreurs, mais j’apprends.
native_language_example: I made mistakes, but I’m learning.

additional_notes: Plural form of « une excuse » (an apology/an excuse). With verbs like « vouloir » and « devoir », it commonly means asking for or owing an apology: « vouloir des excuses » = to want an apology; « devoir des excuses (à quelqu’un) » = to owe someone an apology.
target_language_example: Je te présente des excuses pour mon retard.
native_language_example: I apologize to you for being late.

additional_notes: Plural of « une famille ». « des » is an indefinite plural article meaning “some” or “(a few)”, but in English it’s often just translated as “families.” In phrases like « Ils ont des familles », it can mean they have families/relatives (often implying responsibilities or dependents).
target_language_example: Ils ne peuvent pas partir, ils ont des familles à nourrir.
native_language_example: They can’t leave; they have families to feed.

additional_notes: “Des” is the plural indefinite article, usually meaning “some” or just indicating an unspecified plural (“women”). In general statements it can translate as “women” (e.g., “men and women”). Compare: “des femmes” = some/unspecified women; “les femmes” = women in general / the women (specific group).
target_language_example: Il y a des femmes dans la salle d’attente.
native_language_example: There are (some) women in the waiting room.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural of the indefinite article (roughly “some”), so "des films" can mean “some movies” (unspecified). In many everyday contexts it also just means “movies” generally, especially after verbs like regarder/voir/aimer: "regarder des films" = “watch movies.”
target_language_example: On peut regarder des films ce soir.
native_language_example: We can watch some movies tonight.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural of the indefinite/partitive article (often translated as “some”). You use "des fleurs" when you mean an unspecified number of flowers (buying, bringing, picking). Contrast: "les fleurs" = “the flowers” (specific/generic), "deux fleurs" = “two flowers.”
target_language_example: Je vais acheter des fleurs pour la fête.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy some flowers for the party.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech as a shorter, more informal alternative to « parfois ». It can be used at the beginning or end of a sentence. In questions like « …, des fois ? », it often means “by any chance?”
target_language_example: Des fois, je me couche tard.
native_language_example: Sometimes I go to bed late.

additional_notes: Common in spoken French and fairly informal. Often followed by the subjunctive: « Des fois qu’il pleuve… » = “in case it rains…”. You’ll also see it after an instruction/advice: « Prends ton parapluie, des fois qu’il pleuve. » A more neutral/formal equivalent is « au cas où ».
target_language_example: Prends un chargeur, des fois que ton téléphone n’ait plus de batterie.
native_language_example: Take a charger, just in case your phone runs out of battery.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural partitive/indefinite article, used to talk about an unspecified quantity or some items in general. You’ll often see it in shopping/eating contexts: acheter des fruits (buy some fruit), manger des fruits (eat fruit). In French it stays plural (des fruits), even though English often uses "fruit" as an uncountable noun.
target_language_example: Je prends des fruits pour le dessert.
native_language_example: I’m having some fruit for dessert.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural of "un/une" and often translates as "some" (or is left untranslated in English). "Gens" means "people" and is almost always plural. "Des gens" can mean specific people in a situation ("some people") or people in general depending on context.
target_language_example: Il y a des gens qui n'aiment pas le café.
native_language_example: There are some people who don't like coffee.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing a group of people. Very common after expressions like « il y a » / « il existe » / « je connais » / « nous avons ». It can be general (“there are people who…”) or refer to a specific group depending on context.
target_language_example: Il y a des gens qui parlent très vite.
native_language_example: There are people who speak very fast.

additional_notes: Refers to good times (des hauts) and bad times (des bas) in life, a situation, or a relationship. Often used with "il y a eu..." (there were...) or "on a eu..." (we had...) to describe a period with mixed experiences.
target_language_example: Notre relation a eu des hauts et des bas, mais on s'aime toujours.
native_language_example: Our relationship has had ups and downs, but we still love each other.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a long duration (“for hours”), often after verbs like durer, attendre, parler, pleuvoir. Common patterns: « pendant des heures », « durant des heures », and the literary/emphatic « des heures durant » (= “for hours on end”).
target_language_example: On a discuté des heures sans voir le temps passer.
native_language_example: We talked for hours without noticing the time go by.

meaning: stories; (also) nonsense or trouble (in some expressions).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: “some stories.” Often used in set expressions: « Raconte pas des histoires » = “Don’t make things up / Don’t give me that.” « Chercher des histoires » = “to look for trouble / pick a fight.” « Se raconter des histoires » = “to fool yourself / kid yourself.”
target_language_example: Raconte pas des histoires, je sais que tu mens.
native_language_example: Don’t make things up—I know you’re lying.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural indefinite article (like "some"). Use "des hommes" when you mean men in general or an unknown/unspecified set of men. It contrasts with "les hommes" (men in general / the men) and "d'hommes" after negation or certain expressions (e.g., "Je n'ai pas vu d'hommes").
target_language_example: Dans ce village, des hommes travaillent dans les champs.
native_language_example: In this village, some men work in the fields.

additional_notes: Plural indefinite article: "des" + "idées". Often used after "avoir": "avoir des idées" = to have ideas/thoughts/opinions (e.g., "des idées différentes" = different ideas/views). Can be modified to judge the ideas: "des idées pareilles" (ideas like that), "des idées tordues" (twisted/weird ideas).
target_language_example: J'ai des idées pour le projet, mais je ne suis pas sûr.
native_language_example: I have some ideas for the project, but I’m not sure.

meaning: some information; information (plural form in French).
additional_notes: In French, *information* is usually used in the plural (*des informations*) even when English would use uncountable “information.” Use it when asking for or giving details: *Je veux des informations*, *On a des informations pour vous*. In negative sentences, it often becomes *d’informations*: *Je n’ai pas d’informations*.
target_language_example: Pourriez-vous me donner des informations sur les horaires ?
native_language_example: Could you give me some information about the schedules?

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural indefinite article (roughly “some/any”). Use "des livres" when you mean an unspecified number of books, or just “books” in general (e.g., what someone reads). If you mean specific books, use "les livres" (“the books”). After a negation, it often becomes "de livres" (e.g., "Je ne lis pas de livres").
target_language_example: J’achète des livres pour le voyage.
native_language_example: I’m buying some books for the trip.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural indefinite article ("some"). "Lunettes" is usually used in the plural in French to mean eyeglasses. Common verbs: "porter des lunettes" (to wear glasses), "mettre des lunettes" (to put on glasses). You can add a type: "des lunettes de soleil" (sunglasses), "des lunettes de sécurité" (safety glasses).
target_language_example: Tu portes des lunettes ?
native_language_example: Do you wear glasses?

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural of the indefinite/partitive article (often translated as “some”), used before plural nouns when you mean an unspecified amount. In English you might just say “vegetables” without “some.” Common in food/shopping contexts (e.g., buying, eating, growing vegetables).
target_language_example: Je vais acheter des légumes pour la soupe.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy some vegetables for the soup.

additional_notes: Used to express a large number of people (at least 2,000, often meaning “very many”). It commonly appears as the subject of a sentence with a plural verb: « Des milliers de personnes sont/ont… ». You can swap the noun: « des milliers de visiteurs », « des milliers de fois », etc.
target_language_example: Des milliers de personnes ont assisté au concert.
native_language_example: Thousands of people attended the concert.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural partitive/article, meaning “some” (or just plural “-s” in English). "Des médicaments" is used for medicines in general or an unspecified quantity. With specific meds, French often uses "les médicaments" (the medicines) or names the medicine. Common with verbs like acheter (to buy), prendre (to take), and questions like "Prenez-vous des médicaments ?" (= Do you take any medications?).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'acheter des médicaments pour le rhume.
native_language_example: I need to buy some medicine for a cold.

additional_notes: Used to ask if you’ve heard from someone (“Tu as des nouvelles de… ?”) or to request an update (“Donne(z)-moi des nouvelles de…”). Often implies contact or information about how someone is doing. In questions, it can be shortened to just “Des nouvelles de … ?” meaning “Any news from … ?”.
target_language_example: Tu as des nouvelles de Julie ?
native_language_example: Have you heard from Julie?

additional_notes: Plural of « un ordre ». Used for official or military-style instructions (« recevoir des ordres », « agir selon des ordres »), or more generally to talk about telling people what to do (« donner des ordres »). In the set phrase « Tes désirs sont des ordres ! », it means “whatever you want, I’ll do it” (often polite, sometimes ironic).
target_language_example: On a reçu des ordres de ne pas entrer.
native_language_example: We received orders not to go in.

additional_notes: “Des” is the plural indefinite article meaning “some” (or it can be left untranslated in English). Used when talking about photos in general or an unspecified number: prendre des photos (to take photos), faire des photos (to take photos / do a photo shoot), j’ai des photos (I have some photos). In the negative, it usually becomes “de”: je ne prends pas de photos (I don’t take any photos).
target_language_example: On a pris des photos pendant le voyage.
native_language_example: We took some photos during the trip.

additional_notes: Used to say what the photos are of. "Des" is the plural indefinite article (some), and "de" introduces the subject of the photos. Often used with "avoir" (to have) or "prendre" (to take): "J’ai des photos de…", "Je prends des photos de…".
target_language_example: J’ai des photos de Paris sur mon téléphone.
native_language_example: I have some pictures of Paris on my phone.

additional_notes: Indefinite plural: used when talking about an unspecified amount of potatoes, often as a food you eat or buy. You’ll also see it without the article: “pommes de terre” = “potatoes” in general.
target_language_example: On achète des pommes de terre pour le dîner.
native_language_example: We’re buying some potatoes for dinner.

additional_notes: Plural of « une preuve » (“a piece of evidence/proof”). Often used with verbs like « avoir » (to have), « fournir / présenter » (to provide/show), « chercher » (to look for), or « dissimuler » (to hide). In legal or formal contexts, « des preuves » = evidence supporting a claim; in everyday speech it can also mean “proof” (e.g., proof that something is true).
target_language_example: On n'a pas encore des preuves suffisantes.
native_language_example: We don’t have enough evidence yet.

additional_notes: Plural of "un problème". Used with "avoir" (avoir des problèmes = to have problems/trouble) and "il y a" (il y a des problèmes = there are problems). Often followed by "avec" (problems with someone/something) or "de" (type of problem: des problèmes de circulation = traffic problems).
target_language_example: On a des problèmes de connexion aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: We’re having connection problems today.

additional_notes: Plural of "une question". "Des" is an indefinite article meaning "some" (or just plural "a/an"). Common in polite contexts: "Avez-vous des questions ?" = "Do you have any questions?" Also used after verbs like "poser" (to ask): "poser des questions" = "to ask questions".
target_language_example: Si vous avez des questions, je peux y répondre.
native_language_example: If you have any questions, I can answer them.

additional_notes: Literally “centuries.” Often used with "depuis" to mean “for centuries / for ages” (sometimes exaggerated in everyday speech: "Je suis ici depuis des siècles" = “I’ve been here forever”). Can also mean a duration (“vivre des siècles” = “to live for centuries”) or appear in time expressions like "des siècles plus tard" = “centuries later.”
target_language_example: On attend depuis des siècles !
native_language_example: We’ve been waiting for ages!

meaning: lots of; a ton of; loads of.
additional_notes: Means “a lot of / many” before a noun. Common in spoken French and casual writing. It works with countable nouns (des tas de gens = lots of people) and uncountable nouns too (des tas de choses = lots of things). Often implies a large quantity, like “loads of.”
target_language_example: Il y a des tas de choses à faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: There are loads of things to do today.

additional_notes: Very common, informal way to refer to things when you don’t want to be specific or don’t know the exact word. Often used for objects (“J’ai acheté des trucs”) or events (“Il s’est passé des trucs” = “some things happened”). In more formal French, prefer “des choses”.
target_language_example: J’ai encore des trucs à faire ce soir.
native_language_example: I still have some stuff to do tonight.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase using the partitive/indefinite plural article "des" to mean an unspecified quantity (“some”). Often used with verbs like "porter" (to wear) and can be followed by an adjective ("des vêtements noirs") or a description ("des vêtements qui sont passés de mode").
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’acheter des vêtements pour l’hiver.
native_language_example: I need to buy some clothes for the winter.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural indefinite article (often like “some” or just “(plural)”). It’s used when you’re talking about an unspecified quantity of eggs (shopping, what’s in a box, ingredients). After a negation, it often changes to "de" ("Je n’ai pas d’œufs").
target_language_example: On a acheté des œufs au marché.
native_language_example: We bought some eggs at the market.

additional_notes: Used for animated TV shows and movies; also in phrases like "personnage de dessin animé" (cartoon character). Often used with the article: "un/le dessin animé".
target_language_example: Je regarde le dessin animé !
native_language_example: I’m watching the cartoon!

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or an age difference. Common patterns: "depuis deux ans" = "for two years" (continuing until now); "il y a deux ans" = "two years ago"; "ça fait deux ans" = "it’s been two years"; "de deux ans plus/moins" = "(by) two years older/younger."
target_language_example: J’habite ici depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: I’ve been living here for two years.

additional_notes: Used to state the number 200. In counting, *cent* usually takes an -s (*deux cents*), but it drops the -s when another number follows (e.g., *deux cent un* = 201). In front of a noun, it stays the same: *deux cents personnes* (two hundred people).
target_language_example: Ça coûte deux cents euros.
native_language_example: It costs two hundred euros.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency or repetition: "deux fois par an" = "twice a year." It can also mean "double" in comparisons or quantities: "Il gagne deux fois mon salaire" = "He earns twice my salary" (i.e., double). With comparisons: "deux fois plus + adjective" = "twice as + adjective" (e.g., "deux fois plus grande" = "twice as big").
target_language_example: J’ai vérifié deux fois avant de partir.
native_language_example: I checked twice before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency. It’s usually followed by a time period: "deux fois par semaine" (twice a week), "deux fois par mois" (twice a month), "deux fois par an" (twice a year).
target_language_example: Je vais à la piscine deux fois par semaine.
native_language_example: I go to the pool twice a week.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens in a day. Often follows the verb or comes at the end of the sentence (e.g., Je prends ce médicament deux fois par jour).
target_language_example: Je prends ce médicament deux fois par jour.
native_language_example: I take this medicine twice a day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how often something happens. You can change the number: « une fois par semaine » (once a week), « trois fois par semaine » (three times a week). « Une ou deux fois par semaine » means “once or twice a week.”
target_language_example: Je vais à la salle de sport deux fois par semaine.
native_language_example: I go to the gym twice a week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or time interval. With prepositions it changes meaning: “dans deux heures” = in two hours (from now); “depuis deux heures” = for two hours/for the past two hours (starting two hours ago and continuing); “toutes les deux heures” = every two hours.
target_language_example: On se voit dans deux heures.
native_language_example: See you in two hours.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (pour deux jours = for two days), or a point in time relative to something else (deux jours après = two days later). With chaque: chaque deux jours = every two days (i.e., every other day).
target_language_example: Je serai à Paris pendant deux jours.
native_language_example: I’ll be in Paris for two days.

additional_notes: Literally means “two minutes,” but it’s commonly used to ask someone to wait briefly, similar to “give me a minute.” It can also be used more literally for a short amount of time (“in two minutes”).
target_language_example: Attends deux minutes, j’arrive.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m coming.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for two months), a time from now/past (in two months; two months ago), frequency (every two months), or a stage of pregnancy (two months pregnant). Common patterns: « dans deux mois » (in two months), « ça fait deux mois que… » (it’s been two months since…), « tous les deux mois » (every two months), « enceinte de deux mois » (two months pregnant).
target_language_example: Ça fait deux mois qu’on habite ici.
native_language_example: We’ve been living here for two months.

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate small number, often meaning “a couple” or “a few,” not necessarily exactly 2 or 3. It can refer to items (deux ou trois personnes / stylos) or frequency (deux ou trois fois par semaine). Often matches “something like two or three” / “about two or three.”
target_language_example: Je vais rester ici deux ou trois jours.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here for two or three days.

additional_notes: Used to count items that come in twos (shoes, socks, gloves, etc.). Often followed by "de" + a plural noun: "deux paires de chaussettes". Can also refer to the poker hand "two pair" ("deux paires").
target_language_example: Je vais prendre deux paires de chaussures, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll take two pairs of shoes, please.

additional_notes: Used to organize people or things into pairs (often for lining up: «En rang deux par deux»). It can also describe doing something two at a time or taking steps two at a time (e.g., climbing stairs quickly).
target_language_example: On entre dans la salle deux par deux.
native_language_example: We go into the room two by two (in pairs).

additional_notes: Often used to describe something that has two dot-like markings (e.g., a ladybug species: « la coccinelle à deux points » = the two-spot ladybug). In punctuation, « deux points » also means a colon (:).
target_language_example: Mets deux points avant la liste : pain, fromage, fruits.
native_language_example: Put a colon before the list: bread, cheese, fruit.

additional_notes: A basic time expression used to say a duration (pour deux semaines = for two weeks) or a point in the future (dans deux semaines = in two weeks). Can also be used as an exclamation/title for a trip: Deux semaines à Bali !
target_language_example: Je serai en vacances pendant deux semaines.
native_language_example: I’ll be on vacation for two weeks.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about being given another opportunity after a mistake or failure. Very common with verbs like donner/accorder (to give/grant) and mériter (to deserve), and in expressions like avoir droit à une deuxième chance (to have a right to a second chance).
target_language_example: Peux-tu me donner une deuxième chance ?
native_language_example: Can you give me a second chance?

meaning: “was supposed to be” / “must have been” (depending on context).
additional_notes:
Form of **devoir** (imparfait, il/elle/on) + **être**. It can express:
- **obligation/expectation/plan**: *Elle devait être là…* = “She was supposed to be there…”
- **deduction/likelihood about the past**: *Laura devait être malade.* = “Laura must have been sick.”
Often used with **ça** or **on** to comment on how something was expected or assumed to be.
target_language_example: Il devait être fatigué après le voyage.
native_language_example: He must have been tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "devant" (in front of) + "la porte" (the door) to describe a position/location. You can also use it with other places: "devant la maison" (in front of the house), "devant l’école" (in front of the school).
target_language_example: Attends-moi devant la porte, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Wait for me in front of the door, please.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective (difficile, populaire, fort, grande, compliqué) to show that something is changing over time and increasing in degree. It’s the 3rd-person singular of "devenir" (to become): "X devient de plus en plus + adjectif". You can also use other forms: "deviennent de plus en plus" (they are becoming) or past tense "est devenu(e) de plus en plus" (became more and more).
target_language_example: Avec le temps, ce travail devient de plus en plus stressant.
native_language_example: Over time, this job is becoming more and more stressful.

additional_notes: Used in conversation to introduce news or something surprising/funny. Often rhetorical (you’re not really asking the other person to guess), and it can be said with or without a question mark. You’ll also hear: « Et devine quoi… » (“And guess what…”) or « Mais devine quoi ? » (“But guess what?”).
target_language_example: Devine quoi ? J’ai retrouvé tes clés !
native_language_example: Guess what? I found your keys!

additional_notes: From the verb devoir ("to have to/must"). "Devons-nous… ?" is the inverted (more formal) way to ask a question; in everyday speech you often hear "On doit… ?" or "Est-ce que nous devons… ?". Used to ask about obligation or necessity.
target_language_example: Devons-nous partir tout de suite ?
native_language_example: Do we have to leave right away?

additional_notes: "Devraient" is the conditional of devoir (must/should). With "être" it expresses what is expected, recommended, or logically likely about a state or situation. Often used for opinions/advice (Les criminels devraient être punis.) or expectations (Ils devraient être là. = They should be there by now).
target_language_example: À cette heure-ci, ils devraient être à la maison.
native_language_example: By this time, they should be at home.

additional_notes: "Devrais-je" is a polite/formal way to ask what you should do. It’s the verb "devoir" (to have to / should) in the conditional ("devrais") with question inversion ("-je"). Common in offers and polite questions: "Devrais-je vous aider ?"
target_language_example: Devrais-je attendre ici ou revenir plus tard ?
native_language_example: Should I wait here or come back later?

additional_notes: Form of the verb devoir in the conditional (il/elle/on devrait) + être. Used to express what ought to be the case, what is recommended, or what is expected to be true. Can imply obligation (Cela devrait être fait immédiatement) or expectation/probability (Tom devrait être prêt à présent).
target_language_example: Ça devrait être assez facile.
native_language_example: That should be pretty easy.

additional_notes: Used to ask what would be the right thing to do: *Devrions-nous… ?* = “Should we…?” It’s formed with inversion (*devrions* + *nous*) and is a bit more formal than *On devrait… ?* or *Est-ce qu’on devrait… ?*. You can also use it for advice or recommendations in a group setting.
target_language_example: Devrions-nous partir maintenant ou attendre encore un peu ?
native_language_example: Should we leave now or wait a bit longer?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say an action is hard: « Difficile de + infinitif ». It’s a shortened form of « C’est difficile de… » and often appears as a stand-alone comment (e.g., « Difficile de résumer. »). You can also use it after « être »: « Il a été difficile de… ».
target_language_example: C'est difficile de choisir un restaurant ce soir.
native_language_example: It’s hard to choose a restaurant tonight.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something is hard to do: « (c’)est difficile à + infinitive » or « [noun] est difficile à + infinitive ». The adjective « difficile » agrees with the noun it describes (difficile / difficile(s)). Often corresponds to English “hard/difficult to” + verb.
target_language_example: Ce problème est difficile à résoudre.
native_language_example: This problem is hard to solve.

additional_notes: Uses the noun « adieu » (“farewell”). It can be emotional or final (leaving a place, ending a relationship, or not seeing someone again). You can also use it reflexively: « se dire adieu » = “to say goodbye to each other.” Common patterns: « dire adieu à + [person/place/thing] » and « venir dire adieu » (“to come say goodbye”).
target_language_example: Avant de partir, je suis passé dire adieu à mes collègues.
native_language_example: Before leaving, I stopped by to say goodbye to my coworkers.

additional_notes: Used when leaving or ending a conversation. Often appears with expressions like « il est temps de dire au revoir » (“it’s time to say goodbye”). You can also use the reflexive form « se dire au revoir » when people say goodbye to each other.
target_language_example: Je vais y aller, je dois dire au revoir à tout le monde.
native_language_example: I’m going to go; I have to say goodbye to everyone.

additional_notes: Used for taking leave of a person. The "à" introduces the person you’re saying goodbye to (dire au revoir à Marie). Often used with "aller" (aller dire au revoir à...) or in the imperative (Va dire au revoir à...).
target_language_example: Je dois dire au revoir à mes collègues avant de partir.
native_language_example: I have to say goodbye to my coworkers before leaving.

meaning: to speak badly of (someone); to badmouth; to say negative things about (someone).
additional_notes: Used with "de" + a person/thing: "dire du mal de quelqu’un/de quelque chose". Often implies criticizing, gossiping, or talking behind someone’s back. Common in advice or rules: "Ne dis pas du mal des autres."
target_language_example: Il a pour règle de ne jamais dire du mal des autres.
native_language_example: He has a rule never to speak badly of others.

additional_notes: Means to state what is true (not to lie). Often used after modal verbs like devoir/pouvoir (e.g., « Tu dois dire la vérité » = “You must tell the truth”) and with an indirect object for who you tell it to: « dire la vérité à quelqu’un » / « leur dire la vérité ».
target_language_example: Je vais te dire la vérité : je suis en retard.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you the truth: I’m late.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause after dire. Most often it means "say/tell that" (often as dire à quelqu’un que = "tell someone that"), but after verbs like vouloir it can mean "mean that". Very common for reporting information, opinions, or messages.
target_language_example: Je voulais te dire que je pars demain.
native_language_example: I wanted to tell you that I'm leaving tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common pattern with the verb "dire" (to say/tell) + a thing ("quelque chose"). Often used with an indirect object pronoun for who you’re speaking to: "nous/te/lui dire quelque chose" = "to tell us/you/him (or her) something."
target_language_example: Je dois te dire quelque chose.
native_language_example: I have to tell you something.

additional_notes: Common in spoken French, often as a short question showing surprise, confusion, or asking for clarification: « Dire quoi ? » = “Say what?” / “Say what exactly?”. It’s frequently used after another verb, with « quoi » left at the end: « Je viens de dire quoi ? » (What did I just say?) / « Tu allais dire quoi ? » (What were you going to say?). With « Tu veux dire quoi par là ? », it means “What do you mean by that?”. Sometimes « Je vais te dire quoi » is used informally like “I’ll tell you what…”, introducing an explanation.
target_language_example: Attends, tu veux dire quoi par là ?
native_language_example: Wait, what do you mean by that?

meaning: to always say; to keep saying.
additional_notes: Literally “to say always.” As written, *dire toujours* is an infinitive phrase, so it most naturally appears after a conjugated verb (e.g., *Je vais dire toujours…*, *Il veut dire toujours…*), though many speakers prefer rephrasing to place *toujours* after the conjugated verb (*Il dit toujours…*). It can express a habit (always saying something) or repetition (keeping saying the same thing).
target_language_example: Il va dire toujours la même chose.
native_language_example: He is going to always say the same thing.

meaning: to say a word; to say anything (often: to have a quick word).
additional_notes: Very common in the fixed phrase «sans dire un mot» = “without saying a word” (in silence). With an indirect object («te/vous dire un mot»), it often means “to have a quick word (with you),” sometimes suggesting a brief, private comment rather than literally one word.
target_language_example: Tu peux attendre deux minutes ? J’aimerais te dire un mot.
native_language_example: Can you wait two minutes? I’d like to have a quick word with you.

meaning: to say that / to say this.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific thing someone said (or is about to say). Often appears in questions and reactions: « Comment dire ça ? » = “How can I put it?”, « Qu’est-ce qui te fait dire ça ? » = “What makes you say that?”, « Tu ne peux pas dire ça » = “You can’t say that.” Object pronoun « ça » refers to “that/this” idea or statement.
target_language_example: Je suis désolé de dire ça, mais je ne suis pas d’accord.
native_language_example: I’m sorry to say this, but I don’t agree.

meaning: straight to bed; directly to bed.
additional_notes: Means going to bed immediately, without doing anything else first. Often used with verbs of movement like aller (to go) or partir (to leave/go off). Word order: verb + directement + au lit. Note: you usually say "aller au lit" (to go to bed) rather than *aller au lit* meaning getting into bed; "se coucher" is another common verb meaning "to go to bed / lie down to sleep."
target_language_example: Après le dîner, je suis allé directement au lit.
native_language_example: After dinner, I went straight to bed.

additional_notes: Imperative form of *dire* (“to say/tell”) + the direct object pronoun *le* (“it”), joined with a hyphen. Used to tell someone to say something out loud or to tell a piece of information. If you add an indirect object too, it becomes *dis-le-lui* (“tell it to him/her”).
target_language_example: Si tu sais la vérité, dis-le maintenant.
native_language_example: If you know the truth, say it now.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) with tu: dis = “tell/say”, le = “it” (direct object), moi = “to me”. In French imperatives, object pronouns come after the verb and are linked with hyphens. You can swap le for another direct object: Dis-la-moi (tell me it/her), Dis-les-moi (tell me them). Often used to urge someone to speak frankly: Dis-le-moi franchement.
target_language_example: Si tu sais la vérité, dis-le-moi.
native_language_example: If you know the truth, tell me.

additional_notes: Imperative form of dire addressed to one person (tu): dis = “tell/say”; leur = “to them.” It’s used to give an instruction like “Tell them to leave,” “Tell them what you know,” or “Tell them that…”. For a formal/plural command, use “Dites-leur.”
target_language_example: Dis-leur que j'arrive dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Tell them I’ll be there in five minutes.

additional_notes: Imperative form of *dire* (to say/tell) + the indirect object pronoun *lui* (to him/to her). Used to give an order: *Dis-lui de partir* (“Tell him/her to leave”). Can also stand alone as an encouragement/command: *Dis-lui !* (“Tell him/her!”). For more than one person, use *dites-lui* (formal/plural).
target_language_example: Dis-lui la vérité.
native_language_example: Tell him/her the truth.

additional_notes: Used to give an instruction that someone should pass on to another person: "Dis-lui de + infinitive". "Lui" can refer to either "to him" or "to her"; for more than one person, you’d use "Dis-leur de...".
target_language_example: Dis-lui de m’envoyer un message ce soir.
native_language_example: Tell him/her to send me a message tonight.

additional_notes: "Dis" is the informal (tu) command form of dire (to say/tell). "Lui" means “to him/to her” (an indirect object pronoun), and "que" introduces what you’re telling them. It’s used to pass on a message: Dis-lui que + full sentence. For a formal or plural command, use: Dites-lui que…
target_language_example: Dis-lui que je vais arriver en retard.
native_language_example: Tell him/her that I'm going to arrive late.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (informal/familiar: tu) to explain the way to do something or how something happened. Often followed by an infinitive (Dis-moi comment faire…) or a full clause (Dis-moi comment tu as fait…). You can also say it alone: Dis-moi comment !
target_language_example: Dis-moi comment tu as fait ça.
native_language_example: Tell me how you did that.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a location or place in an indirect question. Often followed by a clause (e.g., « Dis-moi où tu habites. »), and in formal written French you may also see inversion (e.g., « Dis-moi où es-tu né ? »). It can also be left hanging as « Dis-moi où. » when the rest is understood from context.
target_language_example: Dis-moi où tu as mis mes clés.
native_language_example: Tell me where you put my keys.

meaning: "hey" / "say" (to get someone’s attention, often with surprise or reproach).
additional_notes: Very common spoken interjection. Used to call someone (“Dis donc, toi !”), to react with surprise (“Dis donc, vous vous êtes levés tôt !”), or to scold/complain (“Dis donc, ça commence à faire…”). Often followed by a comma and said with emphasis. Informal.
target_language_example: Dis donc, tu pourrais au moins dire bonjour !
native_language_example: Hey, you could at least say hello!

additional_notes: Imperative form (tu) of dire: “dis” = “(you) tell/say.” Used to urge someone to be honest. You can also use “Dire la vérité” (infinitive) and other forms like “Je dis la vérité” (I’m telling the truth) or “Dis-moi la vérité” (Tell me the truth).
target_language_example: Dis la vérité, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Tell the truth, please.

additional_notes: Imperative form of *dire* (“to say/tell”) used to urge someone to speak (often because they’re being silent). Can sound impatient or pleading depending on tone (e.g., *Enfin !* = “Come on!/At last!”). Also: *Dites quelque chose* (formal/plural), *Dis-moi quelque chose* (“Tell me something”).
target_language_example: Dis quelque chose, je t'écoute.
native_language_example: Say something—I'm listening.

additional_notes: Used for a computer’s storage device. You’ll often see it with adjectives like externe (external) or plein (full), and with verbs like enregistrer (to save/record) and perdre des données (to lose data).
target_language_example: J’ai acheté un disque dur externe pour faire une sauvegarde.
native_language_example: I bought an external hard drive to make a backup.

additional_notes: Used to mean an automated bank machine where you withdraw cash. Often shortened in speech to "un distributeur". Common related phrases: "retirer de l’argent" (withdraw money), "Le distributeur est en panne" (The ATM is out of order), "Le distributeur a avalé ma carte" (The machine kept my card).
target_language_example: Je vais au distributeur de billets pour retirer de l’argent.
native_language_example: I’m going to the ATM to withdraw cash.

additional_notes: From the verb dire (to say/tell) + la vérité (the truth). In context you’ll usually change the verb form: il dit la vérité (he tells the truth), elle dit la vérité (she tells the truth), il a dit la vérité (he told the truth), merci de m’avoir dit la vérité (thanks for telling me the truth). Often used after verbs like croire (to believe): Je crois qu’il dit la vérité.
target_language_example: Je pense qu’elle dit la vérité, même si c’est difficile à entendre.
native_language_example: I think she’s telling the truth, even if it’s hard to hear.

additional_notes: "dit" is the 3rd-person singular form of the verb "dire" (to say/tell): "il/elle/on dit que…" = "he/she/one says that…". In stories and legends, "On dit que…" often means "They say that…". You can change the subject and tense: "je dis que" (I say that), "il a dit que" (he said that), etc.
target_language_example: On dit que ce restaurant est excellent.
native_language_example: They say that this restaurant is excellent.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken, informal French to ask what someone said: « Il/Elle t’a dit quoi ? » (= « Qu’est-ce qu’il/elle t’a dit ? »). You can also use it about yourself: « J’ai dit quoi ? / J’avais dit quoi ? » (= “What did I say?”). It often comes at the end of the question, after the verb « dire » and sometimes an object pronoun like « te » (to you).
target_language_example: Il t’a dit quoi exactement ?
native_language_example: What exactly did he tell you?

additional_notes: Past form of **dire** (“to say”), used to refer back to something someone said. Often appears in questions (**Ils ont dit ça ?** = “They said that?”) and in negation (**Tu n’as pas dit ça.** = “You didn’t say that.”). The informal contraction **T’as pas dit ça** is common in speech.
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu as dit ça ?
native_language_example: Why did you say that?

additional_notes: Imperative of dire ("to say/tell") + the direct object pronoun le ("it"). Used when telling one or more people what to say or to tell someone. Other pronouns can be added after it, e.g. Dites-le-moi ("Tell me"), Dites-le-lui ("Tell him/her"), Dites-le-nous ("Tell us").
target_language_example: Si vous êtes d’accord, dites-le clairement.
native_language_example: If you agree, say it clearly.

additional_notes: Imperative of dire (“to say/tell”) + indirect object pronoun leur (“to them”). Used to give an instruction to one person you address as vous (one person formally, or several people): Dites-leur de… (“Tell them to…”) / Dites-leur que… (“Tell them that…”) / Dites-leur qui… (“Tell them who…”).
target_language_example: Dites-leur que j'arrive dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Tell them I’ll be there in five minutes.

additional_notes: Imperative of **dire** (“to say/tell”) + indirect object pronoun **lui** (“to him/to her”). Used to tell someone what to say to a third person. With **lui**, it can mean either “him” or “her” (context makes it clear). For an informal singular command, you’d say **dis-lui**.
target_language_example: Dites-lui de me rappeler ce soir.
native_language_example: Tell him/her to call me back tonight.

additional_notes: "Dites" is the vous-form imperative of dire (used for politeness or when speaking to more than one person). "-lui" means “to him/her” (indirect object). It’s followed by "de" + infinitive: dites-lui de + verb (e.g., venir, attendre, appeler).
target_language_example: Dites-lui de revenir demain matin.
native_language_example: Tell him/her to come back tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Polite (vous) command form of dire (“to say/to tell”), used to ask someone for information. Often followed by a question word (qui, quoi, où, etc.). In writing, it’s usually hyphenated: dites-moi. (Informal version: dis-moi.)
target_language_example: Dites-moi où vous habitez.
native_language_example: Tell me where you live.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (with vous = polite or plural “you”) to say what they have/think/want/decide, etc. It’s an imperative: dites-moi = “tell me,” followed by ce que = “what/that which.” Often completed by a verb (avez, pensez, voulez, décidez…).
target_language_example: Dites-moi ce que vous cherchez.
native_language_example: Tell me what you’re looking for.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (politely or formally, with "vous") for a location or place. It’s the imperative of "dire" (dites) + "moi" (to me) + "où" (where), and is usually followed by a clause like "elle est" (she is) or "je peux le/la trouver" (I can find him/her/it).
target_language_example: Dites-moi où se trouve la gare, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Tell me where the train station is, please.

additional_notes: Literally “say, then,” but used as an interjection. Often placed at the start of a sentence to call someone’s attention (“Dites donc, Monsieur…”) or to react with surprise/admiration/annoyance (“Mais dites donc !”, “Enfin, dites donc !”). It uses the polite/plural imperative of *dire* (dites).
target_language_example: Dites donc, vous avez vu l’heure ?
native_language_example: Hey, have you seen what time it is?

additional_notes: The number 18. Used for counting, giving ages, prices/amounts, results in math, and in phone numbers (often said digit by digit). Hyphenated in French: dix-huit.
target_language_example: J'ai dix-huit ans.
native_language_example: I am eighteen years old.

additional_notes: Used for the number 19 (age, counting, etc.). In time expressions with "heures", it means 19:00 (7 p.m.) in the 24-hour clock: "dix-neuf heures". Note the hyphen in spelling.
target_language_example: Il a dix-neuf ans aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: He is nineteen years old today.

additional_notes: The number 17. Often used for age ("J'ai dix-sept ans" = "I'm seventeen") or in times/durations ("quatre heures et dix-sept minutes" = "4 hours and 17 minutes"). Hyphenated in French: "dix-sept".
target_language_example: J'ai dix-sept ans aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I turn seventeen today.

additional_notes: Used to express a duration of time (for ten years / ten years ago: « Il a vécu là dix ans », « Ça fait dix ans ») or someone’s age (« un fils de dix ans » = a ten-year-old son). With age, it can appear after a noun: « une fille de dix ans ».
target_language_example: Ça fait dix ans que j’habite ici.
native_language_example: I’ve been living here for ten years.

additional_notes: Used to tell the time (à dix heures = at ten o’clock) or a duration/quantity of time (pendant dix heures = for ten hours; dix heures par jour = ten hours per day). Often appears with prepositions like à (at), pendant (for), and par (per).
target_language_example: Le train part à dix heures.
native_language_example: The train leaves at ten o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (depuis dix minutes = for ten minutes; après dix minutes de marche = after ten minutes of walking) or a time difference (dix minutes en avance = ten minutes early; ma montre avance de dix minutes = my watch is ten minutes fast).
target_language_example: Attends-moi dix minutes, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Wait for me ten minutes, please.

additional_notes: Formal question form of « je dois » (from « devoir », to have to/must). It uses inversion (verb + -je) and is common in written French or formal speech. In everyday conversation you’ll also hear « est-ce que je dois… ? » or « je dois… ? »
target_language_example: Dois-je remplir ce formulaire maintenant ?
native_language_example: Do I have to fill out this form now?

additional_notes: Used when **devoir** (to have to / must) is followed by a **reflexive verb** in the infinitive. The pattern is: **je dois + me + infinitive** (e.g., *je dois me reposer* = I have to rest). The **me** refers back to the subject “I” and goes right before the infinitive.
target_language_example: Je dois me dépêcher, on est en retard.
native_language_example: I have to hurry, we’re late.

additional_notes: Usually heard as part of "je dois y aller" (= "I have to go / I need to leave"). The "y" replaces a place ("there"), but in this expression it often just means you have to leave/end the conversation. In casual speech, "je" is often shortened: "J'dois y aller."
target_language_example: Désolé, j'dois y aller, il est tard.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go, it’s late.

additional_notes: Usually expresses a deduction or strong probability in sentences like these, not an obligation. It is the 3rd-person singular form of devoir + être.
target_language_example: Ce bruit doit être le vent.
native_language_example: That noise must be the wind.

additional_notes: Used with a plural subject to express obligation or necessity. Very often followed by a past participle to make a passive meaning: "doivent être + past participle" = "must be + past participle" (e.g., doivent être changées = must be changed; doivent être rendus = must be returned).
target_language_example: Les documents doivent être signés avant demain.
native_language_example: The documents must be signed before tomorrow.

additional_notes: Imperative form of *donner* + indirect object pronoun *lui* (“to him/to her”). Used to tell someone to give something to a person: *Donne-lui le livre.* = “Give him/her the book.” *Lui* can refer to either “him” or “her” (singular), based on context. Often followed by a direct object (*donne-lui une chance*) or by *en* (“some/any”): *Donne-lui en.* = “Give him/her some.”
target_language_example: Donne-lui ce livre, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give him/her this book, please.

meaning: "give me your" (to one person; for a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: "Donne" is the informal (tu) command form of *donner* (to give). "Moi" means "to me." "Ton" means "your" before a masculine singular noun (e.g., *ton numéro*, *ton manteau*) and also before some feminine nouns that start with a vowel sound (e.g., *ton amie*). This phrase can sound like an order; to make it more polite, you can add *s'il te plaît*.
target_language_example: Donne-moi ton adresse, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me your address, please.

meaning: to entitle (to); to give the right to.
additional_notes: Often used with **à**: **donner droit à + noun** or **donner droit à + infinitive**. Common in administrative/legal contexts to say someone is eligible for a benefit, discount, access, or permission.
target_language_example: Cette carte va vous donner droit à une réduction de 10 %.
native_language_example: This card will entitle you to a 10% discount.

meaning: to make (someone) want to; to make (someone) feel like (doing something).
additional_notes: Often used as **donner envie de + infinitive** (to make you want to do something): *Ça me donne envie de voyager.* It can also be used with a noun: **donner envie de + noun** (to make you want something): *Ça me donne envie de chocolat.* Usually takes an indirect object pronoun like **me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur**: *Ça lui donne envie de…* Note: **envie** means “desire/craving,” not “envy” (which is **jalousie**).
target_language_example: Cette photo me donne envie de donner envie aux autres de voyager.
native_language_example: This photo makes me want to make others want to travel.

meaning: to hold someone’s hand; to give someone your hand (e.g., to help them up).
additional_notes: Often used with an indirect object: « donner la main à quelqu’un ». In everyday French, a handshake is more commonly « serrer la main (à quelqu’un) » (to shake hands). « Donner la main » is frequently about holding hands (walking together) or offering your hand to help someone.
target_language_example: Tu veux me donner la main pour traverser la rue ?
native_language_example: Do you want to hold my hand to cross the street?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone (or an animal) having a baby: « donner naissance à un enfant ». In a broader, figurative sense, it can mean “to give rise to / lead to” an idea, movement, or event: « donner naissance à un projet / un mouvement ».
target_language_example: Elle va donner naissance à une petite fille en mai.
native_language_example: She is going to give birth to a baby girl in May.

meaning: to say (someone) is right; to agree with (someone).
additional_notes: Most often used as "donner raison à quelqu’un" (to side with someone / acknowledge they’re right). Past tense is very common: "Je t’ai donné raison" (I agreed with you / I admitted you were right).
target_language_example: Je vais te donner raison : tu avais raison depuis le début.
native_language_example: I’ll admit you’re right: you were right from the start.

meaning: to face / overlook / open onto (a view, street, courtyard, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to describe where a room, window, balcony, building, etc. has its view or opens. Common patterns: « La chambre donne sur la mer. » (has a sea view), « La fenêtre donne sur la cour. » (faces the courtyard). It does not mean “to give on.”
target_language_example: Notre appartement va donner sur une rue calme.
native_language_example: Our apartment is going to face a quiet street.

meaning: to give a hand; to help out.
additional_notes: Common, friendly way to offer or ask for help, especially with a task. Often used with an indirect object (me/te/nous/lui/leur): « Je vais te donner un coup de main. » It can be used in requests: « Tu peux / pourrais-tu me donner un coup de main ? »
target_language_example: Tu peux me donner un coup de main avec les valises ?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand with the suitcases?

meaning: to teach someone a lesson (often: to punish or reprimand to make them learn).
additional_notes: Used when you want someone to learn from a mistake, often with the idea of disciplining, scolding, or "showing them" so they won’t do it again. Can be serious or threatening depending on tone ("Je vais te/vous donner une leçon"). Also used more neutrally for actually giving instruction, but in everyday speech it often implies punishment.
target_language_example: Il faut lui donner une leçon pour qu’il arrête de mentir.
native_language_example: He needs to be taught a lesson so he’ll stop lying.

additional_notes: Imperative of donner + indirect object pronoun lui (“to him/to her”). Used to tell someone politely (vous) or to address multiple people: Donnez-lui + [thing]. In writing it’s hyphenated. Without a noun after it (“Donnez-lui !”), the “something” is understood from context.
target_language_example: Donnez-lui ce livre, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please give him/her this book.

additional_notes: "Donnez" is the imperative (command/request) form of "donner" (to give) used with "vous" (formal singular or plural). Add the thing you want after it: "Donnez-moi votre nom." It can sound like a polite request depending on tone/context, but it’s still a direct form. Not the same as English "donate" (which is more specific, like giving to a charity).
target_language_example: Donnez-moi une minute, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Give me a minute, please.

additional_notes: Uses the imperative of donner addressed to vous (a polite or plural "you"). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun (un + noun): Donnez-moi un chocolat / un baiser. For a feminine noun, use "Donnez-moi une..."; for plural, "Donnez-moi des...". "Donnez-moi un anneau" can also mean "Give me a ring" (call me).
target_language_example: Donnez-moi un café, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Give me a coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to hand over something or provide information. It uses the imperative of "donner" (donnez) with "moi" (to me) and "votre" (your). "Donnez" is also used for "vous" (polite singular or plural), so it can sound polite but still quite direct depending on context (e.g., a request from staff, or a firm instruction).
target_language_example: Donnez-moi votre passeport, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Give me your passport, please.

meaning: to sleep very soundly (to sleep like a baby).
additional_notes: Common idiom used to say you slept extremely well, often through the night without waking up. Conjugate the verb dormir as needed: « J’ai dormi comme un bébé » (I slept like a baby).
target_language_example: Après la randonnée, dormir comme un bébé a été facile.
native_language_example: After the hike, sleeping like a baby was easy.

meaning: To sleep very deeply (to be fast asleep).
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression: literally “to sleep with clenched fists,” but it means you’re sleeping so soundly that nothing wakes you up. Used in everyday spoken and written French; not slang.
target_language_example: Après le long voyage, il semblait dormir à poings fermés.
native_language_example: After the long trip, he seemed to be fast asleep.

meaning: a cold shower; (figuratively) a harsh shock / rude awakening.
additional_notes: Often used literally with the verb « prendre »: « prendre une douche froide » = “to take a cold shower.” Figuratively, « une douche froide » means disappointing news or a sudden setback that brings you back to reality (similar to “a cold shower” or “a rude awakening” in English).
target_language_example: Apprendre qu’on a perdu le contrat a été une vraie douche froide.
native_language_example: Finding out we lost the contract was a real shock.

meaning: “Good Lord!” / “Jesus!” (an exclamation of shock, surprise, or exasperation).
additional_notes: Used as a standalone interjection (often with “Oh”) to react emotionally—similar to invoking Jesus in English. It can sound dramatic or old-fashioned, and some people may find it rude or blasphemous because it uses a religious name as an exclamation.
target_language_example: Doux Jésus, j’ai oublié mon passeport !
native_language_example: Good Lord, I forgot my passport!

meaning: red flag; (in racing) a red-flag stoppage.
additional_notes: Literally “red flag.” Used for an actual red flag (e.g., waved by a marshal/official). In motorsports, being “sous drapeau rouge” means the session/race is stopped or suspended for safety (accident, debris, bad weather, etc.). Often shouted as a warning: « Drapeau rouge ! »
target_language_example: On est sous drapeau rouge, la course est interrompue.
native_language_example: We’re under red flag; the race has been stopped.

meaning: the right path; the right way (to behave/live).
additional_notes: Used literally for a correct route, but very often figuratively meaning a morally correct or sensible way of living/behaving. Common with verbs like «rester sur» (stay on), «se remettre dans» (get back on), and «montrer» (show).
target_language_example: Après ses erreurs, il essaie de revenir sur le droit chemin.
native_language_example: After his mistakes, he’s trying to get back on the right path.

meaning: straight to the point; directly to the goal.
additional_notes: Used with the verb « aller »: « aller droit au but » means to speak or act without wasting time, skipping extra details and getting to what matters. Common in requests or announcements like « Je vais aller droit au but » or « Peux-tu aller droit au but ? ».
target_language_example: On va droit au but : je n’ai plus de budget pour ce projet.
native_language_example: Let’s get straight to the point: I don’t have any more budget for this project.

additional_notes: Used to say you want something said plainly and without unnecessary details. Literally “straight to the goal,” so you may also hear it in sports contexts to mean playing/acting very directly.
target_language_example: Je vais aller droit au but : je ne suis pas intéressé.
native_language_example: I’ll get straight to the point: I’m not interested.

meaning: the right to vote; voting rights.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the legal right/permission to vote in an election. Often appears with verbs like avoir (to have), exercer (to exercise/use), donner (to give/grant), retirer (to take away), and with "le" or "son" (le droit de vote, son droit de vote).
target_language_example: Dans ce pays, on a le droit de vote à dix-huit ans.
native_language_example: In this country, you have the right to vote at eighteen.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to comment that something feels unusual, unexpected, or questionable: « une drôle de façon », « un drôle de goût ». Often expresses mild criticism or surprise. It agrees with the noun: « un drôle de… » (masc.) / « une drôle de… » (fem.).
target_language_example: C'est drôle de dire ça maintenant.
native_language_example: That's a strange time to say that.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + le Sud**. Use **venir du Sud** = “to come from the South,” and **quelque chose du Sud** = “something from/of the South” (southern food, a southern name, the men of the South, southern seas, etc.). Often refers to a southern region within a country or a broadly defined “the South,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Elle vient du Sud de la France.
native_language_example: She comes from the south of France.

additional_notes: Literally “from the sky/heaven” (de + le ciel → du ciel). Common in fixed expressions like « tomber du ciel » (“to fall from the sky”), often used to say someone seems to appear out of nowhere or to react as if they don’t know what’s going on. Also used in phrases like « pirates du ciel » (“sky pirates/air pirates”), « êtres du ciel » (“beings from the sky/heaven”), and « un signe du ciel » (“a sign from heaven”).
target_language_example: Il a reçu une aide du ciel au dernier moment.
native_language_example: He got help from heaven at the last moment.

meaning: nearby; local; from around here (the area).
additional_notes: Often used with a place or shop: « le café / le supermarché du coin » = the nearby/local one (the one around the corner). With people: « Être du coin » means to be from the local area/around here.
target_language_example: On va au café du coin après le travail.
native_language_example: We’re going to the café nearby (around the corner) after work.

meaning: "of the body" (sometimes "of the corpse/body" depending on context).
additional_notes: “du” = “de + le” and usually means “of the” or “some.” With “corps,” it most often refers to the (living) body: *une partie du corps*, *un organe du corps*, *les mouvements du corps*. In crime/death contexts, *le corps* can mean “the body/corpse,” as in *se débarrasser du corps*. Also note the fixed phrase *garde(s) du corps* = “bodyguard(s).”
target_language_example: Le cerveau est une partie du corps.
native_language_example: The brain is a part of the body.

meaning: on the side of; from the side of (someone/somewhere).
additional_notes: Used to indicate (1) which “side” or viewpoint you support in a disagreement (“être/se tenir du côté de …”), or (2) which family branch someone comes from (“du côté de mon père” = “on my father’s side”). It can also mean “toward/on the side of” a place (“du côté de Paris” = “toward Paris/in the Paris area”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Dans ce débat, je suis du côté des étudiants.
native_language_example: In this debate, I'm on the students' side.

additional_notes: Rather formal. It introduces the cause/reason and is followed by a noun or noun phrase: du fait de + nom (e.g., du fait de la pluie). With a full clause, French often uses "du fait que" + indicatif.
target_language_example: Le match a été reporté du fait de la pluie.
native_language_example: The game was postponed because of the rain.

additional_notes: "Du" is the contraction of "de + le". So "du feu" often appears after prepositions or phrases that use "de" (e.g., "près du feu" = near the fire, "à distance du feu" = away from the fire). It can also mean “some fire” in other contexts (partitive), but in these examples it refers to a specific fire.
target_language_example: On s'est assis près du feu.
native_language_example: We sat near the fire.

meaning: overnight; all of a sudden (very quickly, unexpectedly).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens very fast, sometimes unexpectedly—almost from one day to the next. Often with verbs like changer, devenir, perdre. Can also be used in negative statements to mean “it won’t happen overnight” (it will take time).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : on ne peut pas tout apprendre du jour au lendemain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you can’t learn everything overnight.

meaning: of the lake / from the lake.
additional_notes: "Du" is the contraction of "de + le". You use "du" before a masculine singular noun like "lac" (lake) to mean "of the" or "from the" (e.g., "près du lac" = near the lake; "la profondeur du lac" = the depth of the lake).
target_language_example: La vue du lac est magnifique.
native_language_example: The view of the lake is magnificent.

meaning: “in the morning” / “of the morning” (used with a time or thing from the morning).
additional_notes: Used after an exact time to mean “in the morning”: « à six heures du matin » = “at 6 a.m.” Also used after a noun to mean “the morning [noun]”: « le journal du matin » = “the morning newspaper,” « le premier train du matin » = “the first train in the morning.” Often contrasts with « du soir » (in the evening).
target_language_example: J'ai un rendez-vous à huit heures du matin.
native_language_example: I have an appointment at 8 a.m.

meaning: from morning to night; all day long.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something lasts the whole day, from the morning until the evening/night. Often used with verbs like travailler (to work) or se plaindre (to complain). It can describe a habit (present/imparfait) or a one-time situation (passé composé).
target_language_example: Je suis en réunion du matin au soir aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I'm in meetings from morning to night today.

meaning: "at least" / "or rather" (to correct or soften what you just said).
additional_notes: Used to qualify a statement: you add a limitation, correction, or weaker version of what you just said (often after a pause). Common pattern: “..., du moins, ...” or at the start of a sentence to mean “at least, anyway”.
target_language_example: Il va venir demain — du moins, il l’a dit hier.
native_language_example: He’s coming tomorrow—or at least, that’s what he said yesterday.

additional_notes: Literally combines de + le + monde. It often means "of the world" after a noun (les régions du monde), but after a superlative it is usually translated as "in the world" (le plus grand du monde). It also appears in expressions like tout le temps du monde = "all the time in the world."
target_language_example: C'est le plus beau château du monde.
native_language_example: It's the most beautiful castle in the world.

meaning: from (all over) the whole world; worldwide.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say where people/things come from or that something is known everywhere (e.g., des touristes du monde entier = tourists from all over the world; connu du monde entier = known worldwide). Often follows plural nouns like gens/personnes/touristes.
target_language_example: Des étudiants du monde entier viennent étudier à Paris.
native_language_example: Students from all over the world come to study in Paris.

additional_notes: “Du” = “de + le” (of the / from the). With “pays” (country), it often means something is national in scope: *les journaux du pays* (the country’s newspapers), *les amateurs de sport du pays* (sports fans in the country), *la situation économique du pays* (the country’s economic situation), or superlatives like *la plus heureuse du pays* (the happiest in the country).
target_language_example: C’est l’un des meilleurs restaurants du pays.
native_language_example: It’s one of the best restaurants in the country.

additional_notes: Most often, this is the contraction of **de + le = du**, meaning **“of the”**: *la chaleur du soleil* (“the heat of the sun”), *la planète la plus proche du soleil* (“the planet closest to the sun”). In other contexts, **du** can also mean **“some”** with an uncountable noun (e.g., *avoir du soleil* = “to have some sun/sunshine”).
target_language_example: On a besoin de la lumière du soleil pour que les plantes poussent.
native_language_example: We need sunlight for plants to grow.

meaning: of the village; from the village.
additional_notes: "Du" is the contraction of "de + le". With "village," it most often means (1) belonging to the village (les enfants du village = the village’s children) or (2) coming from the village (un homme du village = a man from the village). In directions, it can also mean "of/from" the village area (au sud-ouest du village = southwest of the village). It can also be used after a verb like "parler de": parler du village = to talk about the village.
target_language_example: La fête du village a lieu ce week-end.
native_language_example: The village festival is happening this weekend.

additional_notes: Used with an uncountable noun in the partitive form (du = de + le) to mean “some butter” or “any butter,” especially in questions and statements about ingredients or availability. In negatives, it often becomes “de beurre” (e.g., Je n’ai pas de beurre.).
target_language_example: Je voudrais du beurre, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like some butter, please.

meaning: good work; a job well done.
additional_notes: Uses the informal noun "boulot" (work/job). "Faire du bon boulot" = to do good work; it’s often said to praise someone’s results (like “Nice work!”).
target_language_example: Merci, vous avez fait du bon boulot !
native_language_example: Thanks, you did a great job!

additional_notes: Usually used with verbs like « passer » (passer du bon temps = to have a good time) or « se payer » (se payer du bon temps = to treat yourself to some fun). « Du » is the partitive article here, meaning “some,” so it often translates naturally as “a good time” rather than word-for-word “some good time.”
target_language_example: On a passé du bon temps ensemble hier soir.
native_language_example: We had a good time together last night.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (du = “some”) with bon (“good”). Often used to say there is something positive in a situation or in a person: « Il y a du bon en lui » (“There’s some good in him”). Also common with « avoir du bon » to mean “to have its good points”: « Le changement a du bon ». In « C’est du bon », it’s a more colloquial way to say “That’s good stuff / That’s good.”
target_language_example: Même si c’est difficile, il y a du bon dans cette expérience.
native_language_example: Even if it’s hard, there’s something good in this experience.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article "du" ("some") with an uncountable noun: "boire du café" (drink coffee), "faire/refaire du café" (make more coffee). In questions/offers, it often means "would you like some coffee?"
target_language_example: On prend du café après le déjeuner ?
native_language_example: Shall we have some coffee after lunch?

additional_notes: Used as a short interjection to tell someone (or a group) to relax, stop panicking, or lower their voice. Often preceded by “Hé/Eh” (“Hey”) and followed by a comma and an instruction (e.g., “Du calme, laisse-le faire.”). Literally “some calm,” but in English you’d usually translate it as an imperative.
target_language_example: Du calme, tout va bien.
native_language_example: Calm down, everything is fine.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French to connect what was just said to the next idea (often like filler: “so…/and so…”). It can be placed at the start (“Du coup, …”) or at the end (“…, du coup.”). In more formal writing, you’ll more often see "donc", "alors", or "par conséquent" instead.
target_language_example: Il pleuvait, du coup on est rentrés tôt.
native_language_example: It was raining, so we went home early.

meaning: a hard time; something difficult to deal with.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like « donner » (to give) or « avoir » (to have): « donner du fil à retordre à quelqu’un » = to give someone a hard time / be a tough challenge for them; « avoir du fil à retordre » = to have a lot to deal with. It’s a common idiom (not usually translated word-for-word).
target_language_example: Ce problème nous a donné du fil à retordre.
native_language_example: This problem gave us a hard time.
