additional_notes: Used to say someone (or something living, like plants) continues to be alive up to now. Often appears in questions ("Est-il encore en vie ?") or to express surprise ("Je suis impressionné que tu sois encore en vie"). You can swap the subject: "Je suis encore en vie", "Mes plantes sont encore en vie".
target_language_example: Après l'accident, il est miraculeusement encore en vie.
native_language_example: After the accident, he is miraculously still alive.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize repetition (often to show something is persistent, annoying, or relentless). It can modify an action (Il a essayé… encore et encore) or be said on its own as an exasperated comment (“Again and again.”).
target_language_example: Je relis ce message encore et encore, mais je ne comprends toujours pas.
native_language_example: I reread this message again and again, but I still don’t understand.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something hasn’t left or changed position. In questions like « Qu’est-ce que tu fais encore là ? », it often expresses surprise or annoyance (“Why are you still here?”). « là » can mean “here” or “there” depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu es encore là ? Je croyais que tu étais parti(e).
native_language_example: You’re still here? I thought you had left.

meaning: "even less" / "let alone" (to emphasize that something is even less possible/likely).
additional_notes: Used to strengthen a negative or limitation: you state one thing that’s already not possible/true, then add a second thing that’s even more impossible/less true. Often follows a negation (ne… pas, ne… jamais) or an idea like “not enough money/time.” It can also be used alone as a short reply meaning “(them) even less,” e.g., « Rubens, encore moins. » = “Rubens, even less so.”
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas sortir ce soir, encore moins aller au cinéma.
native_language_example: I can’t go out tonight, let alone go to the movies.

additional_notes: Used to increase the degree/amount compared to what was already mentioned. Often follows a comparison ("plus ...") or is used on its own as a short reply meaning “even more.” You can also use it to intensify an adjective/adverb ("encore plus intéressant") or an expression like "et peut-être encore plus" (“and perhaps even more”).
target_language_example: Avec cette réduction, tu vas économiser encore plus.
native_language_example: With this discount, you’re going to save even more.

additional_notes: Used when *encore* (“still”) modifies a verb like *croire, vouloir, penser*, and *que* introduces what follows (a clause). Very common pattern: *croire encore que…* (“to still believe that…”) or *vouloir encore que…* (“to still want [someone] to…”). Don’t confuse with *encore* alone (“again / more”) or with the other meaning of *encore que* as “although/however” in more formal contexts.
target_language_example: Il pense encore que tout va s’arranger.
native_language_example: He still thinks everything will work out.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or offer a bit more of something (food, drink, time, etc.). In questions like « Encore un peu ? », it often means “More?” or “A little more?”. Note: French « encore » usually means “again” or “more,” which is different from English “encore” (a repeat performance).
target_language_example: Tu veux encore un peu de gâteau ?
native_language_example: Do you want a little more cake?

meaning: again; once again; one more time.
additional_notes: Used to ask for a repetition (e.g., say/do something again) or to emphasize that something is being repeated, often with a tone like “once again”/“yet again.” It can appear at the start of a sentence (“Encore une fois, désolé !”) or after the verb (“Je te le demande encore une fois.”).
target_language_example: Tu peux répéter encore une fois, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you repeat one more time, please?

meaning: a spoiled child; a spoiled brat.
additional_notes: Used to criticize someone (a child or even an adult) who acts entitled, demanding, or used to getting everything they want. Often appears with "un/une" (un enfant gâté / une enfant gâtée), and you may also hear it as an exclamation: "Quel enfant gâté !".
target_language_example: Il ne supporte pas qu’on lui dise non : c’est un enfant gâté.
native_language_example: He can’t stand being told no: he’s a spoiled brat.

meaning: Only child (a child with no brothers or sisters).
additional_notes: Used with être: « Je suis / Il est / Elle est enfant unique ». With the indefinite article in a question or description: « un enfant unique » (male) / « une enfant unique » (female). Note: « unique » agrees in number (unique/uniques) but is the same for masculine and feminine singular.
target_language_example: Je suis enfant unique, donc je n'ai pas de frères ni de sœurs.
native_language_example: I'm an only child, so I don't have any brothers or sisters.

additional_notes: Often refers to hearing voices that aren’t there (auditory hallucinations), especially in a mental-health context. It can also be used jokingly/figuratively to suggest someone is imagining things or “going crazy,” depending on tone.
target_language_example: Depuis quelques jours, il dit qu’il va finir par entendre des voix.
native_language_example: For the past few days, he says he’s going to end up hearing voices.

meaning: to hear that…; to hear it said (that…).
additional_notes: Used to report information you heard from someone else (a rumor or second-hand info), very often in the form: « J’ai entendu dire que… » (= “I heard that…”). You can also use it with a direct object: « J’ai entendu dire ça » (“I heard that said / I heard that”).
target_language_example: J’ai entendu dire que ce restaurant est très bon.
native_language_example: I heard that this restaurant is very good.

meaning: to hear (it) said that; to hear that (as a rumor/second-hand information).
additional_notes: Used to report information you heard indirectly (not something you witnessed yourself). Very common in the past tense: « J’ai entendu dire que… » (= I heard that…). Often introduces rumors, news, or what people say.
target_language_example: J’ai entendu dire que le musée est gratuit le dimanche.
native_language_example: I heard that the museum is free on Sundays.

additional_notes: Most often used as **entendre parler de + something/someone** = “to hear about.” With the pronoun **en**, it replaces “de + thing/person” already mentioned: **en entendre parler** = “to hear about it/them.” Very common in the negative to mean “don’t mention it / I don’t want to hear about it anymore”: **Je ne veux plus en entendre parler.**
target_language_example: Tu as dû entendre parler de moi.
native_language_example: You must have heard about me.

additional_notes: Used with a person or thing: « entendre parler de quelqu’un/quelque chose ». It means you’ve heard information, rumors, or people talking about it (not necessarily that you heard it directly). Often appears in negatives and questions: « Tu as déjà entendu parler de… ? » / « Je n’en ai jamais entendu parler. »
target_language_example: Tu as déjà entendu parler de ce film ?
native_language_example: Have you ever heard of this movie?

additional_notes: Used mainly in the pattern « avoir entendu parler de + [something/someone] » = “to have heard about/of.” Very often you’ll see « en » to replace « de + noun »: « J’en ai entendu parler » = “I’ve heard about it.”
target_language_example: J’ai déjà entendu parler de ce restaurant, mais je n’y suis jamais allé.
native_language_example: I’ve already heard about this restaurant, but I’ve never been there.

additional_notes: A celebration for the groom-to-be with friends, usually shortly before the wedding. Often shortened to “EVG” in messages. The feminine version is “enterrement de vie de jeune fille” (bachelorette party).
target_language_example: On organise un enterrement de vie de garçon pour Julien samedi soir.
native_language_example: We’re organizing a bachelor party for Julien on Saturday night.

meaning: 'in the meantime' / 'meanwhile' (during the time between two events).
additional_notes: Used to say what happens in the interval before something else happens or while waiting. Often placed at the start of a sentence followed by a comma: « Entre-temps, ... ». Can also be used in a question: « Que s’est-il passé entre-temps ? ».
target_language_example: Le train a du retard ; entre-temps, on peut prendre un café.
native_language_example: The train is delayed; in the meantime, we can have a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a non-exhaustive list: you mention one or more examples, but there are more items not named. It can come after what you name ("Il a fait ça, entre autres") or at the start ("Entre autres, ..."). You may also see "entre autres choses" = "among other things".
target_language_example: J’ai visité Paris et Lyon, entre autres.
native_language_example: I visited Paris and Lyon, among other places.

additional_notes: Used to describe interaction or communication within a group (a reciprocal action): Ils parlent entre eux (they talk to each other/among themselves). Often appears as "d’entre eux" meaning "(of) them" in expressions like "certains d’entre eux" = "some of them."
target_language_example: Ils se sont mis d’accord entre eux avant la réunion.
native_language_example: They agreed among themselves before the meeting.

additional_notes: Used with "entre" to locate something in the space separating two things/people ("entre les deux maisons / villes") or to talk about a choice ("choisir entre les deux"). It can also appear alone as a short answer meaning "between them". In expressions like "entre les deux yeux," it means "between the two eyes."
target_language_example: Je suis assis entre les deux fenêtres.
native_language_example: I'm sitting between the two windows.

meaning: between us; (confidentially) between you and me.
additional_notes: Often used at the start of a sentence to introduce a confidential remark or personal opinion: « Entre nous, ... » (“Between you and me, ...”). It can also be literal, describing a relationship or situation between two people: « de la haine entre nous » (“hatred between us”).
target_language_example: Entre nous, je n’aime pas trop ce restaurant.
native_language_example: Between you and me, I don’t really like this restaurant.

additional_notes: Used literally to mean text inside round brackets: ( ... ). It can also introduce a side remark, like “by the way / as an aside”: « Entre parenthèses, … ». Common with the verb « mettre »: « mettre … entre parenthèses » (to put … in parentheses; also figuratively, to set something aside for now).
target_language_example: Entre parenthèses, je pense que tu as raison.
native_language_example: As an aside, I think you’re right.

meaning: to come into play; to become relevant (or start having an effect).
additional_notes: Used when a factor, rule, person, or element starts to matter in a situation. Common with abstract nouns: « Quand X entre en jeu, ... » (= when X comes into play).
target_language_example: À partir de ce moment-là, la météo peut entrer en jeu.
native_language_example: From that moment on, the weather can come into play.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb avoir: "avoir envie de" + infinitive (J’ai envie de dormir. = I feel like sleeping) or + noun/pronoun (J’ai envie de café. = I feel like a coffee; J’ai envie de toi. = I want you / I desire you). Not the same as English "envy" (which is "envie" in the sense of wanting what someone else has); in everyday speech "avoir envie de" often just means "to feel like / to want."
target_language_example: J’ai envie de sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: I feel like going out tonight.

additional_notes: Question form of tu es, made by inversion. It is common in standard written French and more formal speech. In everyday spoken French, tu es ... ? is also very common.
target_language_example: Es-tu prêt ?
native_language_example: Are you ready?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone is doing right now, at this moment (action in progress). Often followed by an infinitive: « Es-tu en train de + verbe ? ». In questions like « Qu'es-tu en train de dire ? », it can also express surprise/criticism ("What are you saying?").
target_language_example: Es-tu en train de regarder la télé ?
native_language_example: Are you watching TV (right now)?

additional_notes: Used to ask if a state or situation continues up to now. Built from "es-tu" ("are you", informal singular) + "encore" ("still"). Often followed by an adjective (amoureux, en colère, jaloux), or a place/status expression (chez toi, debout, sous la douche). For formal "you" use "êtes-vous encore… ?"
target_language_example: Es-tu encore au travail ?
native_language_example: Are you still at work?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is available (not busy) at a certain time. Common in invitations and planning. It’s the inverted-question form of "tu es libre ?" and is slightly more formal; with someone you don’t address as "tu", use "êtes-vous libre ?" (or "libre" → "libres" for plural).
target_language_example: Es-tu libre ce soir pour prendre un café ?
native_language_example: Are you free tonight to grab a coffee?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is ready/willing to do something. It’s the inverted question form of "tu es prêt à…" (you are ready to…). "Prêt" agrees with the person: "es-tu prêt" (to a male), "es-tu prête" (to a female). Often followed by an infinitive verb: "es-tu prêt(e) à partir ?"
target_language_example: Es-tu prêt à commencer ?
native_language_example: Are you ready to start?

additional_notes: Used to ask for confirmation about a fact or situation. It’s the inversion form of the question (es-tu), common in writing or more formal speech; in everyday conversation you’ll often hear: « Tu es sûr que… ? » or « T’es sûr que… ? ». « Sûr » agrees with who you’re talking to (sûre for a woman).
target_language_example: Es-tu sûr que tu as fermé la porte ?
native_language_example: Are you sure you locked the door?

additional_notes: Used to ask if something is still true at the present moment. It’s the inverted question form of « tu es… ? » (verb–subject order): « Es-tu toujours + adjective/location/status ? ». « Toujours » can also mean “always,” but in questions like these it often means “still.” You can also use the more common spoken order: « Tu es toujours… ? ».
target_language_example: Es-tu toujours en vacances ?
native_language_example: Are you still on vacation?

additional_notes: Used to question or challenge what someone says, often showing doubt or surprise. It’s the inverted question form of "tu es" + "vraiment". Very common with adjectives or descriptions: "Es-tu vraiment sûr ?", "Es-tu vraiment italien ?"
target_language_example: Es-tu vraiment prêt à partir maintenant ?
native_language_example: Are you really ready to leave now?

additional_notes: Used right before a noun as an insult or put-down: « espèce de + noun ». Often becomes « espèce d’ » before a vowel (e.g., « espèce d’idiot »), but the core pattern is « espèce de ». Literally “species of,” but in everyday speech it’s a fixed insulting construction meaning something like “you …!” or “you so-called …!”. Very informal; can be vulgar depending on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Espèce de crétin, tu as encore perdu tes clés !
native_language_example: You idiot, you lost your keys again!

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive. In the examples, "essaie" is the "tu" imperative (command) form of "essayer": "Essaie de faire mieux" = "Try to do better." It can also appear in other forms (e.g., "il essaie de" = "he tries to"). With negation, French often uses "essaie de ne pas" + infinitive: "Essaie de ne pas être en retard" = "Try not to be late."
target_language_example: Essaie de comprendre avant de répondre.
native_language_example: Try to understand before answering.

meaning: 'Try not to…' (giving advice or a warning).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to avoid doing something. It’s the tu (informal singular) command form of essayer de + infinitive, with negation: ne pas + verb. Often followed by a verb in the infinitive: « Essaie de ne pas + [verbe] ».
target_language_example: Essaie de ne pas faire de bruit pendant le film.
native_language_example: Try not to make noise during the movie.

additional_notes: « essaya » is the passé simple (literary past) form of « essayer ». You’ll mostly see it in books, stories, or formal writing; in everyday speech people usually say « a essayé de » (passé composé). It is followed by an infinitive verb: « essayer de + infinitif ».
target_language_example: Elle essaya de rester calme.
native_language_example: She tried to stay calm.

meaning: "try to" (telling one person to do something).
additional_notes: "Essaye" is the informal singular (tu) command form of "essayer". It’s followed by "de" + an infinitive: "Essaye de rester" (Try to stay), "Essaye de dormir" (Try to sleep). For the formal/plural command, use "Essayez de".
target_language_example: Essaye de parler plus lentement, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Try to speak more slowly, please.

additional_notes: Used before another infinitive to say that someone makes an effort to do something: essayer de faire = to try to do. Very common in everyday French.
target_language_example: Tom va essayer de vous contacter.
native_language_example: Tom is going to try to contact you.

meaning: to always try; to keep trying.
additional_notes: Literally “try always.” In everyday French you’ll more often hear the adverb placed before the verb: « toujours essayer (de…) » or, with a conjugated verb, « j’essaie toujours de… » (“I always try to…”). Used to encourage persistence.
target_language_example: Il faut essayer toujours de faire de son mieux.
native_language_example: You have to always try to do your best.

meaning: to try and see (what happens / whether it works).
additional_notes: Informal/colloquial shortening of "essayer de voir" (or "essayer et voir"). Often used when suggesting a quick test or when you’re not sure of the result: "On peut essayer voir" = "We can try and see." In more standard French, prefer "essayer de voir".
target_language_example: On peut essayer voir si ça marche.
native_language_example: We can try and see if it works.

meaning: 'try to' (imperative: telling someone to try to do something).
additional_notes: From the verb **essayer de + infinitive** (“to try to do”). **Essayez de** is the command form for **you** (plural) or **formal you** (vous): “Try to…”. Before a vowel or silent h, it becomes **essayez d’**: *Essayez d’imaginer…*
target_language_example: Essayez de parler plus lentement, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Try to speak more slowly, please.

additional_notes: Literally "is it/this." Used at the start of a yes/no question to ask whether something is the case, especially before a noun, adjective, or short phrase. It also appears in the longer question pattern est-ce que.
target_language_example: Est-ce normal ?
native_language_example: Is that normal?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question with extra emphasis or a slightly formal/literary tone. The added là points to the thing/idea being referred to (roughly “that/this”), often in phrases like “Est-ce là ce que… ?” (“Is that what… ?”) or “Est-ce là tout… ?” (“Is that all… ?”).
target_language_example: Est-ce là ce que tu voulais dire ?
native_language_example: Is that what you meant?

additional_notes: Used to form a yes/no question with the subject "il" (he/it): est-ce qu'il + verb. Common in spoken and written French and more neutral/polite than just using intonation (e.g., "Il dort ?"). In formal writing you may also see inversion instead ("Dort-il ?").
target_language_example: Est-ce qu'il vient ce soir ?
native_language_example: Is he coming tonight?

meaning: “can we…?” / “is it possible for us to…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask a yes/no question politely. "Est-ce que" is a question frame; "on" often means "we" (or informal "people/you"), and "peut" is "can" (from "pouvoir"). Frequently followed by an infinitive verb: "Est-ce qu'on peut + verbe… ?"
target_language_example: Est-ce qu'on peut commencer maintenant ?
native_language_example: Can we start now?

additional_notes: common question marker used to form yes/no questions in neutral spoken and written French. It goes at the beginning of the sentence: Est-ce que tu viens ? = Are you coming? Literally it comes from something like "is it that," but it usually isn't translated word-for-word in English.
target_language_example: Est-ce que vous comprenez la question ?
native_language_example: Do you understand the question?

additional_notes: Used to form a yes/no question: "Est-ce que" + a statement word order. "Cela" means "that/it" and refers to something already mentioned or obvious from context (often interchangeable with "ça" in casual speech). You then add the verb and the rest: "Est-ce que cela signifie… ?"
target_language_example: Est-ce que cela marche ici ?
native_language_example: Does that work here?

additional_notes: Used to form a yes/no question with « je » (I) when the verb has « te » (you) as an object. « Est-ce que » is a very common way to ask questions without inverting the subject and verb. « te » goes before the verb: « Est-ce que je te dérange ? » (“Am I bothering you?”).
target_language_example: Est-ce que je te dois quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Do I owe you something?

meaning: “Do you like…?” (asking someone if they like something).
additional_notes: A very common way to form a yes/no question: “Est-ce que” + subject + verb. Here, “tu aimes” = “you like.” You can follow it with a noun (“cette cravate”), a pronoun (“ça”), or an infinitive to ask about enjoying an activity (“écrire”).
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu aimes la cuisine italienne ?
native_language_example: Do you like Italian food?

meaning: “Do you have…?” / “Did you…?” (question form with “you have”).
additional_notes: Used to ask a yes/no question with tu (informal “you”), followed by avoir (“to have”) or the passé composé with avoir (e.g., est-ce que tu as fermé…? = “Did you close…?”). It’s a very common, neutral way to form questions. In speech, you may also hear the shorter form: “T’as…?”
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu as du temps ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you have time tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask a yes/no question with "tu" (informal singular "you"). It’s built from the question marker "est-ce que" + "tu as" (you have). Follow it with a noun ("un stylo", "ton passeport"), or sometimes with something like "faim" (hungry) or an age ("plus de 18 ans"). In more casual spoken French you may also hear "T’as… ?"
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu as du temps ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you have time tonight?

meaning: “Do you know…?” (asking if someone is familiar with a person/thing).
additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone knows or is familiar with someone or something. Often followed by a name or a noun: « Est-ce que tu connais Adam ? » / « Est-ce que tu connais cette fille ? ». In French, « est-ce que » is a common question marker (neutral/polite), and « tu connais » uses the informal “you” (tu).
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu connais ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: Do you know this restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to ask a yes/no question with the verb "être" (tu es = you are). It’s the "est-ce que" question structure + subject (tu) + verb (es). Very common in speaking and writing. You can add an adjective, a noun, or a longer phrase after it: « Est-ce que tu es prêt ? » (Are you ready?), « Est-ce que tu es étudiant ? » (Are you a student?).
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu es prêt à partir ?
native_language_example: Are you ready to leave?

meaning: "do you speak" / "are you talking" (a question to "tu parles").
additional_notes: Used to form a question with the verb parler (tu = informal singular "you"). Often followed by a language (Est-ce que tu parles italien ?) meaning "Do you speak Italian?". With "de" + something, it means "to talk about" (Est-ce que tu parles de moi ? = "Are you talking about me?"). In "Mais de quoi est-ce que tu parles ?", it means "What are you talking about?" (often expressing surprise or confusion).
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu parles anglais ?
native_language_example: Do you speak English?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or belief. It’s a common, neutral way to form a yes/no question in French: "Est-ce que" + statement word order. "Tu penses que" introduces what you think, and it’s followed by a full clause (often in the present or future). In more informal speech you can also hear "Tu penses que…?" without "est-ce que".
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu penses que ça va marcher ?
native_language_example: Do you think it will work?

meaning: “can you…?” (polite way to ask someone to do something).
additional_notes: Used to form a yes/no question with "est-ce que" + subject (tu) + verb (peux). Often used for requests: "Est-ce que tu peux + infinitive… ?" (Can you + verb…?). You can make it more polite with "s’il te plaît" (please) or more formal with "Est-ce que vous pouvez… ?"
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu peux m’aider avec ça, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you help me with that, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone politely to do something. It’s formed with the question marker “est-ce que” + “tu pourrais” (you could). Often followed by an infinitive: “Est-ce que tu pourrais + verb… ?” You can make it even softer with “s’il te plaît”.
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu pourrais m’aider avec ça, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Could you help me with that, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has information. Often followed by a question word (ce que/quoi = what, où = where, pourquoi = why, qui = who) or by “quelque chose” (something). In conversation it can also mean “you know…” as a quick check before asking a question.
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu sais à quelle heure il arrive ?
native_language_example: Do you know what time he’s arriving?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone what they want or if they want to do something. Very common in questions; often followed by an infinitive (Est-ce que tu veux venir ?) or a noun (Est-ce que tu veux un café ?). You can make it more formal/polite with « Est-ce que vous voulez… ? ».
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu veux prendre un café avec moi ?
native_language_example: Do you want to have a coffee with me?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone can see or notice something. It’s a yes/no question: "Est-ce que" + subject (tu) + verb (vois). Can also be used to check if someone understands (similar to "Do you see what I mean?").
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu vois la sortie d'ici ?
native_language_example: Do you see the exit from here?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (vous) if they like something or like doing something. "Est-ce que" is a common way to form yes/no questions; "vous aimez" is the polite or plural form of "you like".
target_language_example: Est-ce que vous aimez voyager en France ?
native_language_example: Do you like traveling in France?

additional_notes: Used to form a yes/no question with the subject "vous" (you = polite singular or plural). Follow it with a past participle to ask about a past action: "Est-ce que vous avez compris ?" = "Did you understand?" It can also introduce "have" in the sense of possession when followed by a noun: "Est-ce que vous avez une voiture ?" = "Do you have a car?"
target_language_example: Est-ce que vous avez une question ?
native_language_example: Do you have a question?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask if someone has something, or if they have time/ideas/a quality (like a good memory). "Est-ce que" makes a yes/no question, and "vous avez" is the formal/plural "you have". Very common in shops and everyday requests; you can add a noun after it (e.g., "du lait", "le temps").
target_language_example: Est-ce que vous avez une carte de crédit ?
native_language_example: Do you have a credit card?

additional_notes: Used to ask a polite question with "vous" (formal or plural "you"). Common for requests: "Est-ce que vous pouvez + infinitive" (e.g., attendre, remplir, traduire). Often interchangeable with "Pouvez-vous...?" (more formal) and "Est-ce que tu peux...?" (informal, singular). In spoken French, you may also hear "Vous pouvez...?" (less formal).
target_language_example: Est-ce que vous pouvez parler plus lentement, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you speak more slowly, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (one person politely, or multiple people) what they want. It’s made of the question marker "est-ce que" + "vous voulez" (you want). Often followed by an infinitive ("…boire ?" = to drink) or a noun ("…cette chemise ?" = this shirt). In everyday speech you may also hear "Vous voulez… ?" without "est-ce que".
target_language_example: Est-ce que vous voulez un café ?
native_language_example: Would you like a coffee?

additional_notes: A polite way to ask someone (or several people) if they can see something. Uses the question pattern “est-ce que” + subject + verb. In speech it’s often followed by a noun or pronoun: “Est-ce que vous voyez ça ?”
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, est-ce que vous voyez ce panneau ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you see that sign?

additional_notes: Used to start a yes/no question with the polite or plural subject "vous". It’s the question form of "vous êtes" (“you are”). It can be followed by an adjective ("… capable"), a place/state ("… en train de …"), or a past participle with "être" ("… allé"), which agrees in gender/number: allé / allée / allés / allées.
target_language_example: Est-ce que vous êtes prêt à commencer ?
native_language_example: Are you ready to start?

meaning: "does it/that…?" (a common way to start a yes/no question with “it/that”).
additional_notes: Used to form a question: **Est-ce que + subject + verb…?** Here the subject is **ça** (= “it/that/this,” often referring to a situation or thing already known). Very common in spoken and written French. Often translates naturally as “Does it…?”, “Is it…?”, “Will it…?”, etc., depending on the verb tense.
target_language_example: Est-ce que ça marche ?
native_language_example: Does it work?

meaning: “does that … to you?” / “would that … bother you?” (start of a question before a verb).
additional_notes:
Used to ask a question about how something affects the person you’re speaking to. It’s typically followed by a verb: 
- est-ce que ça te dérange…? = does it bother you…?
- est-ce que ça te semble…? = does it seem… to you?
- est-ce que ça te suffit…? = is it enough for you?
- est-ce que ça te va…? = is it OK with you…?
“te” is the informal “to you” (singular). With “vous”: est-ce que ça vous…
target_language_example: Est-ce que ça te convient si on se retrouve demain matin ?
native_language_example: Does it work for you if we meet tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: A very common question to check on someone’s well-being. Literally it’s a question form (est-ce que) + “that goes” (ça va). Depending on context and tone, it can mean a casual “How’s it going?” (Salut, ça va ?) or a concerned “Are you alright?” (Ça va maintenant ?). Often followed by a name or term of address: « Tom, est-ce que ça va ? »
target_language_example: Est-ce que ça va, ou tu as besoin d’aide ?
native_language_example: Are you OK, or do you need help?

meaning: "is it a" (question form, before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask a yes/no question: "Est-ce un + noun ?" = "Is it a + noun?" Use **est-ce une** before a feminine singular noun, and **est-ce des** for plural. Often shortened in speech to "c'est un...?" but "est-ce" is the more standard question form.
target_language_example: Est-ce un bon plan ?
native_language_example: Is it a good deal?

meaning: 'is it a...?' (yes/no question, before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask a yes/no question. "Est-ce" is a common question marker meaning "is it that…"; "une" is the feminine form of "a/an". Use "est-ce un" with a masculine noun (e.g., "Est-ce un problème ?"). In speech, it’s often followed by a noun phrase: "Est-ce une bonne idée ?"
target_language_example: Est-ce une bonne idée ?
native_language_example: Is it a good idea?

meaning: "Is this/that your …?" (asking if something belongs to you).
additional_notes: Used to ask a yes/no question: "Est-ce" + noun with "votre" (your, singular). Often followed by a noun: « Est-ce votre chat ? » You can also say more casually: « C’est votre chat ? » If you’re addressing more than one person, use « est-ce votre » with the plural sense of « votre » (your = belonging to you all), or use « est-ce vos … » before a plural noun.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, est-ce votre sac ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is this your bag?

additional_notes: Question form of "elle est" using subject-verb inversion, common in formal writing and careful speech. It usually means "is she"; before a past participle, it can help form a past tense, often translating as "has she" or sometimes "did she."
target_language_example: Où est-elle maintenant ?
native_language_example: Where is she now?

additional_notes: Formal or careful yes/no question form using inversion of être + il. It can mean "is he" when referring to a person, or "is it" when referring to a thing, idea, or clause. After a noun subject, French often repeats the subject with -il: for example, "Ce mur est-il... ?"
target_language_example: Le film est-il intéressant ?
native_language_example: Is the movie interesting?

meaning: "has he gone" / "did he go" (formal question word order).
additional_notes: This is the verb inversion used to form a question in more formal French: **est** (auxiliary *être*) + **-il** (he) + **allé** (past participle of *aller*). It’s the **passé composé** of *aller* and usually translates as “Has he gone…?” or “Did he go…?” depending on context. With other subjects, it changes (e.g., *est-elle allée ?* for “has she gone?”) and *allé* agrees in gender/number with the subject when using *être*.
target_language_example: Est-il allé au magasin ?
native_language_example: Did he go to the store?

meaning: 'did he/it go by?' / 'has he/it gone?' (question form of "il est passé").
additional_notes: This is inversion used to form a question in the passé composé: "Il est passé" (He/It passed / went by) → "Est-il passé ?" (Did he/it pass? / Has he/it gone by?). Common with "Où est-il passé ?" meaning “Where did he go?” or “Where has he gone?” In "Que s’est-il passé ?", it’s part of "se passer" = “to happen” (literally: “What happened?”).
target_language_example: Où est-il passé ? Je l’attends depuis dix minutes.
native_language_example: Where did he go? I’ve been waiting for him for ten minutes.

additional_notes: Passé composé of aller with a singular masculine subject (for example il/Tom). It is formed with être, so the past participle agrees: est allée (feminine), sont allés/allées (plural). Often used for movement to a place: à, chez, dans, etc.
target_language_example: Il est allé au marché ce matin.
native_language_example: He went to the market this morning.

meaning: 'went to' (for a male subject + a masculine singular place).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of **aller**: **il est allé** = “he went”. **Au** is the contraction of **à + le** (“to the” before a masculine singular noun): *au Canada, au musée*. With a female subject: **elle est allée au...** (extra -e). With a feminine place: **à la** (*elle est allée à la banque*). With plural places: **aux** (*ils sont allés aux États-Unis*).
target_language_example: Il est allé au restaurant après le travail.
native_language_example: He went to the restaurant after work.

meaning: 'went to' (with certain places) or 'went by' (with a mode of transport).
additional_notes:
This is the passé composé of *aller* (to go): **il/elle est allé(e)** + **en**.
- **en + transport** (no article) = “by” that transport: *en bus, en bicyclette, en voiture*.
- **en + place** is used with many **feminine countries** and **continents**: *en Inde, en Amérique, en Australie* (but: *au Canada*, *aux États-Unis*).
Agreement: **allé** (masc.) / **allée** (fem.) depending on the subject.
target_language_example: Monsieur White est allé en Inde.
native_language_example: Mr. White went to India.

additional_notes: Past tense of "aller à" (to go to), using passé composé with the helper verb "être": "il/elle est allé(e) à ...". The past participle "allé" agrees with the subject (add -e for feminine: "elle est allée"). Used before a place or destination introduced by "à" (e.g., "à Paris", "à un club").
target_language_example: Il est allé à la bibliothèque après le travail.
native_language_example: He went to the library after work.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of aller with être. Used with a feminine singular subject (elle, ma mère, etc.), so the past participle agrees: allé (masc.), allée (fem.), allés (masc. pl.), allées (fem. pl.). Often followed by a destination (à Paris), the pronoun y (“there”), or an infinitive to show purpose (elle est allée manger = she went to eat).
target_language_example: Elle est allée au marché ce matin.
native_language_example: She went to the market this morning.

additional_notes: Passé composé of arriver with être. It often means "arrived" or "has arrived" for a person or thing reaching a place, and it can also mean "happened" in expressions like ce qui est arrivé. It is often followed by à, au, à la, or à l' for the destination. In writing, the past participle agrees with the subject: arrivée, arrivés, arrivées.
target_language_example: Le colis est arrivé ce matin.
native_language_example: The package arrived this morning.

meaning: 'arrived' / 'has arrived' (for a feminine subject); also 'happened' (to someone).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *arriver* with **être**. *Arrivée* agrees with the subject: **il est arrivé** (masc.), **elle est arrivée** (fem.). With an indirect object, it can mean “to happen to someone”: *Une chose terrible lui est arrivée* = “Something terrible happened to her/him.”
target_language_example: Elle est arrivée en retard à la réunion.
native_language_example: She arrived late to the meeting.

additional_notes: "Est" is "is" (from être). "Assez" often means "quite/pretty" before an adjective: "c'est assez simple" = "it's quite simple." It can also mean "enough" (sufficient), often with "pour" + infinitive: "il est assez grand pour…" = "he is tall/old enough to…" In sayings, "X est assez" can mean "X is enough."
target_language_example: C'est assez pour aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: That's enough for today.

meaning: 'is aware' / 'knows about it' / 'is up to date (on something)'.
additional_notes: From « être au courant (de ...) » = to be aware of / informed about something. Commonly used to check whether someone knows a piece of information: « Est-ce qu'il est au courant ? » You can specify what they're aware of with « de »: « Il est au courant de la situation. »
target_language_example: Est-ce qu'il est au courant de la réunion de demain ?
native_language_example: Is he aware of tomorrow’s meeting?

additional_notes: Used with être: "je suis au courant, tu es au courant, il/elle est au courant, on est au courant". Often followed by de (about): "être au courant de quelque chose" or que + clause: "être au courant que...". Common in conversation to confirm someone knows information (often news, a situation, an incident).
target_language_example: Le monde entier est au courant.
native_language_example: The whole world knows about it.

additional_notes: Used to compare size or height: **[subject] + est + aussi + adjective + que + [comparison]**. With **grand**, it often means “tall” for people and “big/large” for things. You can swap in other adjectives (e.g., *est aussi rapide que* = “is as fast as”). Note: **grand** agrees in gender/number (e.g., *grande, grands, grandes*), but this entry focuses on the exact masculine singular form **est aussi grand que**.
target_language_example: Ken est aussi grand que Bill.
native_language_example: Ken is as tall as Bill.

additional_notes: Used with adjectives/adverbs in comparisons, often followed by "que" (than): "est beaucoup plus + adjective/adverb + que...". Example: "beaucoup plus long" = "much longer". You’ll also see it with other verbs (not only "être"): "c’est beaucoup plus...", "il travaille beaucoup plus...".
target_language_example: Cette ville est beaucoup plus grande que mon village.
native_language_example: This city is much bigger than my village.

additional_notes: With être, bien can mean 'well' or 'properly' before a participle or adjective (est bien protégé = 'is well protected'). It can also act as an intensifier meaning 'really', 'quite', or 'much' (est bien plus grande = 'is much bigger'). In expressions like on est bien, it means 'to feel good/comfortable'.
target_language_example: Ton sac est bien lourd !
native_language_example: Your bag is really heavy!

additional_notes: Used to strongly intensify a comparison, most often in the pattern **être bien plus + adjective/adverb + que** (“to be much more … than”). Here **bien** means “really/quite” (an intensifier), not “well.”
target_language_example: Ce film est bien plus intéressant que le premier.
native_language_example: This movie is much more interesting than the first one.

additional_notes: Literally means "is good." With à or en before an activity or subject, it often means "is good at" something (est bon au foot, est bon en plongée). With pour, it means "is good for" (est bon pour lui). This form is masculine singular; feminine singular is est bonne.
target_language_example: Paul est bon en maths.
native_language_example: Paul is good at math.

additional_notes: Used to say that an activity, habit, or thing benefits health. Often followed by a noun or infinitive as the subject (e.g., "Le sport est bon pour la santé" / "Rire est bon pour la santé"). You can change the subject and the verb to match: "sont bons pour la santé" (plural), and "bon/bonne" agrees with the subject (masc./fem.). It’s also commonly used in negatives or irony (e.g., "Fumer est bon pour la santé" is usually meant sarcastically).
target_language_example: Manger des légumes est bon pour la santé.
native_language_example: Eating vegetables is good for your health.

meaning: "is able to / can" (is capable of doing something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s ability or capacity to do something. Common pattern: "être capable de" + infinitive. In the 3rd-person singular present it becomes "il/elle/on est capable de" (also used with a name: "Adam est capable de…"). With "de tout", it means "capable of anything" (sometimes implying someone might do something extreme).
target_language_example: Le bébé est capable de marcher.
native_language_example: The baby can walk.

additional_notes: Used with être (“to be”) + complètement to strongly emphasize an adjective or state: *est complètement différent* (“is completely different”), *est complètement nu* (“is completely naked”). The form of *être* changes with the subject (*je suis*, *tu es*, *il/elle est*, *nous sommes*, etc.).
target_language_example: Ce film est complètement incroyable.
native_language_example: This movie is completely incredible.

additional_notes: Used with être (in whatever tense) + de retour to say someone or something has come back or is back again. Common with people (Tom est de retour) and also situations or events (La guerre est de retour en Europe = war is back/has returned in Europe).
target_language_example: Tom est de retour.
native_language_example: Tom is back.

additional_notes: Past form of devenir, used with a singular masculine subject. It expresses a change of state, role, or condition: someone or something became something else. With jobs or roles, French often uses no article: est devenu médecin, est devenu soldat.
target_language_example: Mon frère est devenu professeur l'année dernière.
native_language_example: My brother became a teacher last year.

meaning: has gone crazy / has become mad.
additional_notes: Past tense of « devenir » (to become): « il est devenu fou » = “he became/has become crazy.” Often used both literally (someone loses their mind) and figuratively (someone acts irrationally; “the world has gone crazy”). Adjectives agree: « elle est devenue folle », « ils sont devenus fous », « elles sont devenues folles ».
target_language_example: Il a perdu son travail et il est devenu fou.
native_language_example: He lost his job and he went crazy.

additional_notes: From the verb **devenir** (“to become”). Used to describe a change or transformation: **[subject] est devenu un + masculine noun**. For a feminine noun, use **est devenue une** (with -e if the subject is feminine). In the negative: **n’est pas devenu un/une**.
target_language_example: Avec le temps, ce quartier est devenu un endroit très calme.
native_language_example: Over time, this neighborhood became a very quiet place.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of **devenir**: **être** + past participle **devenu/devenue**. It agrees with the subject: **il est devenu**, **elle est devenue**, **ils sont devenus**, **elles sont devenues**. In questions like **Qu'est devenue… ?**, it often means **“What happened to…?” / “What became of…?”**.
target_language_example: Depuis, elle est devenue médecin.
native_language_example: Since then, she has become a doctor.

additional_notes: Uses the verb « être » (to be) + the adjective « difficile ». It can be followed by « à » + infinitive to say something is hard to do: « C’est difficile à comprendre » (It’s hard to understand). When talking about a person (« Il/Elle est difficile »), it often means they are hard to please / picky / difficult to deal with (depending on context).
target_language_example: Ce problème est difficile à résoudre.
native_language_example: This problem is difficult to solve.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say something is hard to do or hard to understand: « C’est/Il/Elle est difficile à + infinitive ». Often followed by verbs like comprendre (understand), apprendre (learn), estimer (estimate), trouver (find).
target_language_example: Cette règle est difficile à retenir.
native_language_example: This rule is hard to remember.

additional_notes: A common combination of est (from être) + déjà. Most often it means "is already" before a place, adjective, or state: Il est déjà là. In forms with a past participle, it can correspond to English "has already": Ça t'est déjà arrivé ? = Has that already happened to you?
target_language_example: Il est déjà trop tard.
native_language_example: It's already too late.

meaning: is in good health; is healthy.
additional_notes: Used with the verb être to say someone is healthy (not sick). You can change the subject and tense: « Je suis en bonne santé », « Elle était en bonne santé », « Ils seront en bonne santé ». Often used when talking about someone’s condition now or in general.
target_language_example: Après l'opération, il est en bonne santé.
native_language_example: After the operation, he is healthy.

additional_notes: Used with être: « être en colère » = to be angry/mad. You can add « contre » or sometimes « avec » to specify who you’re angry at (e.g., « Il est en colère contre moi. », « Elle est en colère avec moi. »). Note that « est en colère » is 3rd-person singular (he/she/it is angry).
target_language_example: Je comprends pourquoi Tom est en colère.
native_language_example: I understand why Tom is angry.

additional_notes: Used with a subject + être (conjugated): « Je suis en danger », « Il/Elle est en danger », « Nous sommes en danger », etc. Means someone/something is threatened and could be harmed; often used to stress urgency.
target_language_example: Dépêche-toi : il est en danger !
native_language_example: Hurry up: he's in danger!

meaning: is at stake; is on the line.
additional_notes: Used with the verb « être » to say that something important could be won, lost, or seriously affected. Common with big consequences: « Sa vie est en jeu » (His/Her life is at stake), « Son avenir est en jeu » (Their future is on the line). You’ll also often see « ce qui est en jeu » = “what’s at stake / what’s on the line.”
target_language_example: Dans cette décision, tout est en jeu.
native_language_example: In this decision, everything is at stake.

additional_notes: Used with a machine, vehicle, or device that has stopped working (often temporarily). You can change the verb for other subjects/tenses: "être en panne" → "Je suis en panne" (my car/device is down), "Le bus était en panne" (the bus broke down).
target_language_example: Désolé, l'ascenseur est en panne.
native_language_example: Sorry, the elevator is out of order.

additional_notes: Used with "être" to say someone or something isn’t on time or is delayed. You can add "de + duration" to specify how late (e.g., "est en retard de 30 minutes"). It can also describe something running behind schedule (a season, work, a project).
target_language_example: Notre avion est en retard de trente minutes.
native_language_example: Our plane is thirty minutes late.

meaning: is safe; is in a safe place (not in danger).
additional_notes: Used with the verb être + en sécurité to say someone/something is safe or secure. It can describe people (not in danger) or things (protected/secure), often followed by a place: « en sécurité ici/dans une banque ».
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, ton passeport est en sécurité à l'hôtel.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, your passport is safe at the hotel.

meaning: is (in the process of) / is currently (doing)
additional_notes: Used as: (conjugated form of « être ») + « en train de » + infinitive to emphasize an action happening right now (similar to the English present continuous). The exact form « est en train de » is specifically 3rd person singular present (« il/elle/on est en train de… »). Often optional in French—the simple present can also describe what’s happening now, but « en train de » adds emphasis (“right now / in the middle of”).
target_language_example: Mon épouse est en train de cuisiner, je te rappelle plus tard.
native_language_example: My wife is cooking right now; I'll call you back later.

meaning: "is (in the middle of) doing" (action happening right now).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that an action is in progress at the moment of speaking. It’s the present tense of "être en train de" + infinitive (faire / manger / travailler, etc.). Often translates to the English present continuous ("is doing"), but French can also use the simple present without it; this phrase adds emphasis like “right now.”
target_language_example: Il est en train de faire ses devoirs, je te rappelle plus tard.
native_language_example: He’s doing his homework right now; I’ll call you back later.

additional_notes: Used with the 3rd-person singular of être to say that a state or condition continues. In these examples, encore means "still" rather than the English noun "encore." With other subjects, the form of être changes: suis encore, es encore, sont encore, etc.
target_language_example: Le magasin est encore fermé.
native_language_example: The store is still closed.

additional_notes: Passé composé of "entrer" (to enter), formed with "être" + past participle. The past participle usually agrees with the subject: "il est entré", "elle est entrée", "ils sont entrés", "elles sont entrées". Often followed by "dans" (into) or "par" (through/by) to show where/how someone entered.
target_language_example: Il est entré dans le bureau sans dire bonjour.
native_language_example: He came into the office without saying hello.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something matches a description perfectly. It’s commonly followed by a clause with a verb: « C’est exactement ce que + subject + verb » (e.g., « C’est exactement ce que je veux »). Note: « est » changes with the subject (c’est / c’était / ce serait / ce sont, etc.).
target_language_example: C’est exactement ce que je voulais dire.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I meant.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say something/someone is easy to do/use/find/understand, etc.: « C'est facile à + infinitive ». With people, it can mean “easy to live/work with” (pleasant, not difficult): « facile à vivre ».
target_language_example: Ce logiciel est facile à installer.
native_language_example: This software is easy to install.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not open/accessible (a shop, a door, a building, etc.). It can also be figurative: "mon monde t'est fermé" = "my world is closed off to you" / "you can't access or understand my world." Agreement changes with the subject: "il est fermé", "elle est fermée", "la porte est fermée", "les magasins sont fermés". In questions you may see "C’est fermé ?" (= "Is it closed?").
target_language_example: Désolé, le magasin est fermé aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, the store is closed today.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has ended or is completed. It’s the verb "être" ("is") + the past participle "fini" (from "finir"). Very often you’ll also hear "c’est fini" (= "it’s over/it’s finished").
target_language_example: Le film est fini.
native_language_example: The movie is over.

meaning: “is finished / is over” (for a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with **être + fini(e)** to say something has ended or is completed. **Finie** agrees with the noun it describes: **il est fini** (masc.), **elle est finie** (fem.), **ils sont finis** (masc. pl.), **elles sont finies** (fem. pl.). Often used for events/activities: *La leçon est finie* = “Class is over.”
target_language_example: La réunion est finie, on peut partir.
native_language_example: The meeting is over; we can leave.

additional_notes: "est important" is the 3rd-person singular form of "être" (to be) + "important". It’s used to say something/someone is important, significant, or matters. Very common patterns: (1) "Il est important de + infinitive" = "It’s important to..." (2) "Il est important que + subjunctive" = "It’s important that..." (e.g. "que vous soyez..."). It can refer to a thing, a person, or a factor ("important pour" = "important for").
target_language_example: Il est important de bien dormir.
native_language_example: It’s important to sleep well.

additional_notes: Used to state that a city is the capital city of a country or region. Structure: [City] + est la capitale de la + [country/region]. The place name after "de la" is usually feminine singular (e.g., la Jordanie, la Grèce, la Syrie, la Suède). With other places you may need: "du" (de + le) for masculine singular (Paris est la capitale du Portugal), "des" for plural (… des États-Unis), or "de l’" before a vowel or silent h (… de l’Italie).
target_language_example: Amman est la capitale de la Jordanie.
native_language_example: Amman is the capital of Jordan.

meaning: “is the capital of” (for a masculine country).
additional_notes: Used to state that a city is the capital of a place. "Est" = “is”, "la capitale" = “the capital”, and "du" is the contraction of "de + le" (“of the”). Use "est la capitale de la" for feminine countries (ex. "Paris est la capitale de la France") and "est la capitale des" for plural places (ex. "Bruxelles est la capitale des Pays-Bas").
target_language_example: Rabat est la capitale du Maroc.
native_language_example: Rabat is the capital of Morocco.

additional_notes: Used to say that a feminine noun (e.g., histoire, série, équipe) is the best. It’s the superlative of bon: bonne → la meilleure. With a masculine noun you say “est le meilleur”; with plural you say “sont les meilleurs / les meilleures.” Often used for comparisons: “mais la leur est la meilleure” = “but theirs is the best.”
target_language_example: Cette option est la meilleure pour nous.
native_language_example: This option is the best for us.

additional_notes: A very common combination of est ("is") and le ("the"). It is used before a masculine singular noun or title: Mars est le dieu de la guerre. You also see it with superlatives like est le plus..., and in price questions such as À combien est le kilo... ? = "how much is a kilo... ?"
target_language_example: Le vrai problème est le manque de temps.
native_language_example: The real problem is the lack of time.

additional_notes: Used with the verb être ("to be") to say someone/something is the best. It changes for gender and number: il est le meilleur, elle est la meilleure, ils sont les meilleurs, elles sont les meilleures. Often followed by a noun or description: "le meilleur juge" (the best judge), "le meilleur employé" (the best employee), or "le meilleur … que je connais" (the best … that I know).
target_language_example: Ce film est le meilleur de l'année.
native_language_example: This movie is the best of the year.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the best among a category: **[subject] + est le/la meilleur(e) des + plural noun**. The adjective agrees with the subject (**meilleur** masc., **meilleure** fem.). Very common in sayings and proverbs (e.g., “Time is the best medicine”).
target_language_example: Le temps est le meilleur des remèdes.
native_language_example: Time is the best medicine.

meaning: “is the biggest / largest; is the greatest.”
additional_notes: Used to form the superlative with "le plus" + adjective: "X est le plus grand" = “X is the biggest.” Agreement matters: grand → grande (fem.), grands (masc. pl.), grandes (fem. pl.). Often followed by a group introduced by "de"/"du"/"de la"/"des": "le plus grand lac de Suisse" (the biggest lake in Switzerland), "le plus grand de la classe" (the tallest/biggest in the class), "le plus grand de tous" (the greatest of all). Meaning can be literal size (biggest/tallest) or figurative (greatest).
target_language_example: Cet immeuble est le plus grand de la ville.
native_language_example: This building is the biggest in the city.

additional_notes: Means “is (located) there/here” or “is present.” Often answers the question « Où est… ? » (Where is…?). « là » is a general “there/here” (context-dependent); « ici » is more specifically “here (right where I am).”
target_language_example: Ton sac est là, sur la chaise.
native_language_example: Your bag is there, on the chair.

additional_notes: "Est" is the "he/she/it is" form of être. "Là-bas" points to a place away from the speaker ("over there"), often with a gesture or something visible at a distance. It can refer to a person, place, or thing; in "X est là-bas pour...", it means "X is there to...".
target_language_example: Mon téléphone est là-bas, sur la table.
native_language_example: My phone is over there, on the table.

additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to you or is your preferred thing. It’s made of **est** (he/she/it is) + **ma** (my, feminine singular). Use **ma** before most feminine singular nouns: *La physique est ma matière favorite.* (But **ma** becomes **mon** before a feminine noun starting with a vowel or silent h: *C’est mon amie.*)
target_language_example: Cette voiture est ma voiture.
native_language_example: This car is my car.

additional_notes: Used with the verb être (to be) to say someone is sick/ill: il/elle est malade. The adjective malade agrees in number: il/elle est malade; ils/elles sont malades. Depending on context it can also mean someone feels unwell.
target_language_example: Écoutez, il est malade.
native_language_example: Listen, he is sick.

additional_notes: Used to compare something (masculine singular) to something that belongs to you. "Meilleur" is the comparative of "bon" (good) and agrees with the noun being described: "est meilleur" (masc. singular), "est meilleure" (fem. singular), "sont meilleurs" (masc. plural), "sont meilleures" (fem. plural). "Le mien" means "mine" (masc. singular); variants: "la mienne" (fem.), "les miens" (masc. plural), "les miennes" (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Ton français est meilleur que le mien.
native_language_example: Your French is better than mine.

additional_notes: A straightforward combination of est (“is”) + mon (“my”). Used with a singular subject to say that something is the speaker’s. mon is used before masculine singular nouns, and also before feminine singular nouns that begin with a vowel sound, as in mon épouse.
target_language_example: Ce livre est mon préféré.
native_language_example: This book is my favorite.

additional_notes: Common past form of mourir for a singular subject (he/she/it or a singular noun). Literally it looks like "is dead," but in sentences like these it usually means "died" or "has died." With a feminine subject, it becomes est morte.
target_language_example: Le vieil arbre est mort après la tempête.
native_language_example: The old tree died after the storm.

additional_notes: From the verb *mourir* (to die) in the compound past tense (*passé composé*) with *être*. With *être*, the past participle agrees with the subject: masculine *il est mort*, feminine *elle est morte*; plural *ils sont morts*, *elles sont mortes*. Used to state that a female person/animal has died (often translated either “she died” or “she is dead” depending on context).
target_language_example: Sa mère est morte quand il avait onze ans.
native_language_example: His mother died when he was eleven.

additional_notes: Used to say something belongs to or is associated with “us” (a group including the speaker): « X est notre + nom ». « notre » is the singular “our” and is used before a singular noun (both masculine and feminine): « notre devoir », « notre famille ». For plural nouns, use « nos »: « Ce sont nos amis. »
target_language_example: Ce jardin est notre petit coin de paradis.
native_language_example: This garden is our little corner of paradise.

additional_notes: Past form of "naître" (to be born). Use it with "être": "il/elle est né(e)". Add -e for a female: "elle est née". Common with time ("il y a deux mois" = two months ago) and place ("à Londres", "aux États-Unis").
target_language_example: Ma sœur est née en 2001.
native_language_example: My sister was born in 2001.

additional_notes: Used to indicate location or direction, often while pointing. Common when giving directions, especially in buildings. Frequently heard with « C’est par là. » (“It’s that way.”). The phrase is compositional: « est » (is) + « par là » (that way/over there, in that direction).
target_language_example: La sortie est par là.
native_language_example: The exit is that way.

additional_notes: Usually means someone or something has gone away or left. It is the passé composé of partir with être, so it changes for gender and number: est parti / est partie / sont partis / sont parties. With a destination, it can mean "left for" (Tom est parti pour Boston). In fixed expressions like c'est parti, it can mean "here we go" or "it's started."
target_language_example: Mon frère est parti très tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: My brother left very early this morning.

additional_notes: Used with **être** + **parti** (passé composé of *partir*) to say someone **has left / went** with a following phrase introduced by **en**. Common uses: **destination** (*est parti en Australie* = went to Australia), **means of transport** (*est parti en vélo* = left by bike), or **type of activity/trip** (*est parti en randonnée / en expédition* = went on a hike / an expedition). Note: **partir en fumée** is an idiom meaning “to go up in smoke” (something is lost/destroyed).
target_language_example: Tom est parti en Australie le lendemain de Noël.
native_language_example: Tom left for Australia the day after Christmas.

meaning: 'has left' / 'is gone' (said about a feminine subject).
additional_notes: Passé composé of partir with être. It agrees with the subject: feminine singular est partie; masculine singular est parti; plural sont partis/parties. Used both for someone leaving (Ta femme est partie.) and for something that has gone away/disappeared (La douleur est partie.).
target_language_example: Elle est partie il y a cinq minutes.
native_language_example: She left five minutes ago.

additional_notes: Passé composé of passer used with être. Depending on context, it can mean 'went,' 'passed/went by,' or 'came by/stopped by.' In expressions like le pire est passé, it means 'is over.' In the reflexive form s'est passé, it means 'happened.'
target_language_example: Le train est passé il y a cinq minutes.
native_language_example: The train passed five minutes ago.

meaning: "has passed" / "went by" / "stopped by" (feminine singular past of *passer* with *être*).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular subjects ("elle", "la crise", etc.). Meaning depends on context: time/events "are over" (La crise est passée.), someone "came by/stopped by" (Ma tante est passée me voir.), or something "went past" (Une voiture est passée...). For masculine singular: *est passé*; plural: *sont passés / sont passées*.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : la tempête est passée.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: the storm has passed.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty about a situation or a guess: "Il est peut-être…" = "He might be…". In French, "peut-être" often comes right after the verb ("il est peut-être malade") but can also be placed elsewhere for emphasis (e.g., "Peut-être qu'il est malade").
target_language_example: Elle est peut-être déjà partie.
native_language_example: She might have already left.

meaning: is full of / is filled with.
additional_notes: Used with a singular subject: "X est plein de Y". "Plein" agrees with the subject (e.g., feminine: "est pleine de"; plural: "sont pleins/pleines de"). Often followed by a plural noun: "plein de possibilités" = "full of possibilities".
target_language_example: Votre avenir est plein de possibilités.
native_language_example: Your future is full of possibilities.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular subject (e.g., « la grotte », « la ville », « la vie », « ton étagère »). It’s the feminine form of « est plein de ». If the subject is plural: « sont pleins de / sont pleines de ». Followed by a noun (often with an article like « de + les → des »: « pleine de chauve-souris », « pleine de livres »).
target_language_example: La salle est pleine de monde.
native_language_example: The room is full of people.

meaning: is bigger/larger than; is taller than.
additional_notes: Comparative form of the adjective « grand » (“big/tall”). Pattern: « X est plus grand que Y ». With people it most often means “taller than”; with places/objects it often means “bigger/larger than.” Note: « grand » normally agrees with the subject (e.g., « elle est plus grande que… », « ils sont plus grands que… »), but the fixed term here is the masculine singular form « est plus grand que ».
target_language_example: Tom est plus grand que Dan.
native_language_example: Tom is taller than Dan.

meaning: "is for you" (meant for you; addressed to you; intended for you).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is intended for the person you’re talking to. Common with gifts (Cette rose est pour toi.), items/food (Le thé est pour toi.), messages/letters (Cette lettre est pour toi.), or when assigning someone a turn/question/task (La première question est pour toi.). You can change the verb for gender/number (sont pour toi) and the person (est pour moi / pour vous).
target_language_example: J’ai un cadeau : il est pour toi.
native_language_example: I have a gift: it’s for you.

additional_notes: Most commonly used in the full phrase « c'est pour ça que … » to introduce a reason/explanation, followed by a clause: « C'est pour ça que je viens. » (= That's why I'm coming.)
target_language_example: C'est pour ça que je suis ici.
native_language_example: That's why I'm here.

additional_notes: Used with être ("to be") to say something is close to happening/being true: "C'est presque…" (It's almost…). "Presque" usually comes after the verb (est presque) and before the adjective/adverb or phrase it modifies: "est presque fini" (is almost finished), "est presque toujours" (is almost always), "est presque de la famille" (is practically family). You can change "est" to match the subject (je suis presque, on est presque, ils sont presque, etc.).
target_language_example: Le repas est presque prêt.
native_language_example: The meal is almost ready.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is ready. This is the 3rd-person singular form; with a feminine subject it becomes est prête. You can also use it with pour + noun (ready for) or à + infinitive (ready to do something).
target_language_example: Le café est prêt.
native_language_example: The coffee is ready.

additional_notes: "Rentrer" means to return (to a place). "Être rentré" is the past tense (passé composé with être) and agrees with the subject: il est rentré, elle est rentrée, ils sont rentrés, elles sont rentrées. Often used with a time (à neuf heures) or a reason/occasion (pour Noël).
target_language_example: Thomas est rentré à la maison.
native_language_example: Thomas came home.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *rester* for **il/elle/on**: *il est resté / elle est restée*. It often describes (1) staying in a place (*il est resté ici* = he stayed here) or (2) continuing in a state with an adjective (*il est resté calme* = he remained calm). With *être* in the passé composé, *resté* agrees in gender/number: *restée, restés, restées*.
target_language_example: Elle est restée à la maison toute la journée.
native_language_example: She stayed at home all day.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « revenir » (to come back/return). It uses « être » as the auxiliary verb. Often means simply “is back” in context. With « être », the past participle agrees with the subject: « elle est revenue », « ils sont revenus », « elles sont revenues ». Note: « revenu » can also mean “income” as a noun (« un revenu »), and it can look like English “revenue” but here it’s the verb form.
target_language_example: Il est revenu tard hier soir.
native_language_example: He came back late last night.

additional_notes: Passé composé of **sortir** with **être** (literally “is out,” but usually means “went out/has gone out,” i.e., left). It can mean leaving a place (Il est sorti par la fenêtre = he got out through the window) or going out to do an activity (sortir faire des achats = go out shopping). The past participle agrees with the subject: **il est sorti**, **elle est sortie**, **ils sont sortis**, **elles sont sorties**.
target_language_example: Elle est sortie acheter du pain.
native_language_example: She went out to buy some bread.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located: **être** (to be) + **sur** (on) + **la table** (the table). This exact form (**est**) is 3rd-person singular present tense (il/elle/on). It changes with the subject (e.g., *sont sur la table* = are on the table) and can take other nouns/places (e.g., *est sur le bureau* = is on the desk).
target_language_example: La boîte est sur la table.
native_language_example: The box is on the table.

meaning: is about to (do something); is on the verge of.
additional_notes: Used to say something is going to happen very soon. The full expression is usually "être sur le point de" + infinitive. This entry shows the 3rd-person singular form "est" (il/elle/on). Other forms: je suis / tu es / nous sommes / vous êtes / ils sont / elles sont.
target_language_example: Ma batterie est sur le point de mourir.
native_language_example: My battery is about to die.

additional_notes: Used with the verb être (il/elle/on/c’/ça + est) to say something has ended or is completed. Common for events or periods of time (Le rendez-vous est terminé. Octobre est terminé.), work/tasks (Notre travail est terminé.), or a situation (Leur calvaire est terminé.). Agreement: terminé (masc. singular), terminée (fem. singular), terminés/terminées (plural).
target_language_example: Désolé, la réunion est terminée.
native_language_example: Sorry, the meeting is over.

additional_notes: Passé composé of tomber, used for a completed action. It is formed with être, so the past participle agrees with the subject: est tombé / est tombée / sont tombés / sont tombées.
target_language_example: Mon téléphone est tombé dans l'eau.
native_language_example: My phone fell in the water.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *tomber* with the auxiliary *être*. It agrees with the subject: **il est tombé** (masc.), **elle est tombée** (fem.), **ils sont tombés**, **elles sont tombées**. Used for things physically falling (a coin fell), for night coming (**La nuit est tombée** = night fell), for precipitation (**La neige est tombée**), and for numbers/temperature decreasing (**La température est tombée**).
target_language_example: Elle est tombée dans les escaliers.
native_language_example: She fell on the stairs.

additional_notes: With être, toujours can mean either 'still' for a situation that continues, or 'always' for something habitual or generally true. The surrounding context shows which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: La porte est toujours fermée.
native_language_example: The door is still closed.

meaning: is always (in the middle of) doing.
additional_notes: Built from the structure « être en train de + infinitive » (the French progressive: “to be in the process of doing”). « toujours » adds “always/constantly” and can suggest irritation depending on context. Conjugate « être » to match the subject: « je suis toujours en train de… », « elle est toujours en train de… », « ils sont toujours en train de… ».
target_language_example: Il est toujours en train de se plaindre.
native_language_example: He’s always complaining.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm or emphasize a statement about someone/something: *être + tout à fait + adjective* (e.g., *tout à fait correct, tout à fait capable*). With an adjective, it can mean “completely/entirely,” and in some contexts it’s closer to “quite” (stronger than *très* for agreement: *C’est tout à fait vrai* = “That’s absolutely true”).
target_language_example: Ce plan est tout à fait réaliste.
native_language_example: This plan is completely realistic.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone or something is NOT the adjective/noun that follows. Structure: [subject] + est + tout sauf + adjective/noun. Often strong/critical in tone: « Sa chambre est tout sauf propre » = it’s definitely not clean.
target_language_example: Ce film est tout sauf ennuyeux.
native_language_example: This movie is anything but boring.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or adverb to say something is excessively so: est trop + adjective/adverb. Here est is the 3rd-person singular of être, so with other subjects it changes: je suis trop..., ils sont trop.... Often followed by pour to say 'too ... for/to'.
target_language_example: Ce sac est trop lourd pour moi.
native_language_example: This bag is too heavy for me.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something doesn’t have the required age/maturity for an action. Pattern: [subject] + être (conjugated) + trop jeune + pour + verb (infinitive). You can change the subject and the form of être (e.g., "je suis trop jeune pour…", "ils sont trop jeunes pour…").
target_language_example: Elle est trop jeune pour rester seule à la maison.
native_language_example: She is too young to stay home alone.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something as having a strong quality: est is the 3rd-person singular form of être, so this exact phrase is used with il/elle/on or a singular noun. The word très intensifies an adjective or adverb.
target_language_example: Ce livre est très utile.
native_language_example: This book is very useful.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "être" to describe how something (or someone) looks. "Beau" agrees with what it describes: masculine singular "il est très beau"; feminine singular "elle est très belle"; plural "ils/elles sont très beaux/belles". For people, it can mean "handsome" (masc.) or "beautiful" (fem.).
target_language_example: Ce pont est très beau.
native_language_example: This bridge is very beautiful.

additional_notes: Used to describe a feminine noun (e.g., une fleur, la lune) as very beautiful. It’s the verb être in the present tense (est = “is”) + très (“very”) + belle (“beautiful,” feminine singular). For a masculine noun, use « est très beau »; for plural, « sont très beaux / très belles » depending on gender.
target_language_example: Cette robe est très belle.
native_language_example: This dress is very beautiful.

additional_notes: Used to say something has high importance. It’s the verb être ("to be") in the 3rd-person singular (est) + très ("very") + important. Change est to sont for a plural subject: « Ces détails sont très importants. » You can also change the adjective for gender/number: importante (fem. singular), importants (masc. plural), importantes (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Pour réussir, la pratique est très importante.
native_language_example: To succeed, practice is very important.

meaning: 'is very pretty' (said of a feminine person/thing).
additional_notes: Uses the verb être ("to be") + très ("very") + the adjective joli/jolie ("pretty"). Jolie is the feminine form, used with feminine nouns (une fille, une maison, une montre, la vue) or with "elle" / a woman’s name. For masculine, use "est très joli" (e.g., "Il est très joli.").
target_language_example: Cette robe est très jolie.
native_language_example: This dress is very pretty.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is liked by many people. Changes with the subject: "sont très populaires" (they are very popular). "Populaire" agrees in gender/number: populaire (m/f singular), populaires (plural).
target_language_example: Cette chanteuse est très populaire en France.
native_language_example: This singer is very popular in France.

additional_notes: Used to identify or classify someone or something with a masculine singular noun: for example, Tom est un jockey. It is made of est ("is") + un ("a"). In some contexts, un may instead belong to another expression, like un peu ("a little").
target_language_example: Mon frère est un médecin.
native_language_example: My brother is a doctor.

additional_notes: Used with **il/elle** or a noun to state that someone or something is an animal: **X est un animal**. Often followed by an adjective or a relative clause: **un animal nocturne**, **un animal puissant**, **un animal qui vit en mer**. It can also be used **figuratively** about a person (often jokingly or as an insult) to mean they’re behaving like an animal or are very rough/uncivilized.
target_language_example: Ce chat est un animal très calme.
native_language_example: This cat is a very calm animal.

meaning: “is an art” (a skill or practice requiring talent, technique, or finesse).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is a true art form (dance, sculpture, etc.) or that doing it well takes special skill and subtlety (often in proverbs like « Écouter est un art »). You can also use it ironically for habits: « Remettre à plus tard est un art. »
