additional_notes: Expression used to give advice or a warning. Very commonly used in the conditional (« tu/il/elle/on ferait mieux de + infinitif »), but the base form « faire mieux de » is the dictionary form. It’s typically followed by an infinitive.
target_language_example: Il vaut parfois mieux faire mieux de partir tôt pour éviter les embouteillages.
native_language_example: Sometimes it’s better to leave early to avoid traffic jams.

additional_notes: Used to encourage someone (sometimes teasingly or reproachfully) to improve their effort or performance. Commonly said with "tu peux" (“you can”) or as an imperative: "Fais mieux que ça !"
target_language_example: Je sais que tu es fatigué, mais tu peux faire mieux que ça.
native_language_example: I know you’re tired, but you can do better than that.

additional_notes: Used mainly in the impersonal expression « Il fait noir » meaning “It’s dark (outside).” Often refers to nighttime or when it has gotten dark after sunset. Common variants include « Il commence à faire noir » (It’s starting to get dark) and « Il va faire noir bientôt » (It’ll be dark soon).
target_language_example: Il commence à faire noir, allume la lumière.
native_language_example: It’s starting to get dark—turn on the light.

meaning: to get dark; to be night (nighttime).
additional_notes: Used with impersonal « il »: « il fait nuit » = it’s dark/it’s nighttime; « il commence à faire nuit » = it’s starting to get dark; « il va bientôt faire nuit » = it will soon be dark. (Like other weather/time expressions with « faire »: il fait froid, il fait jour, etc.)
target_language_example: Dépêche-toi : il va bientôt faire nuit.
native_language_example: Hurry up: it’ll soon be dark.

meaning: to serve as; to act as; to function as.
additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone plays the role of something else, often as a substitute or temporary solution. Common pattern: « X fait office de Y » (X serves as Y). Note: it’s sometimes mistakenly understood literally as “to do office of,” but the idiomatic meaning is “to serve as.”
target_language_example: Cette caisse va faire office de table.
native_language_example: This crate is going to serve as a table.

meaning: to share; to inform; to let someone know (about something).
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object (me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur) + « faire part de + noun/idea ». In questions, « en faire part » means “to let (someone) know about it / to inform them of it.” Common in more formal or careful speech, especially for decisions, news, or feelings.
target_language_example: Je dois lui faire part de la nouvelle.
native_language_example: I have to tell him/her the news.

meaning: to be part of; to belong to; to be included in
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is a member of a group or is included in something larger. Common pattern: « faire partie de + [group/thing] » (de becomes d’ before a vowel): « faire partie d’une équipe », « faire partie du projet ». Conjugates with « faire »: je fais partie, tu fais partie, il/elle fait partie, etc.
target_language_example: Voulez-vous faire partie de mon équipe�?
native_language_example: Do you want to be part of my team?

meaning: to put/let something or someone through; to pass on; to administer (a test/exam).
additional_notes: Very common pattern: "faire + infinitive" = "to make/have someone do something". So "faire passer" often means (1) to administer or conduct a test/exam/analysis/interview: « Je vais vous faire passer un test. »; (2) to get an idea/message across: « faire passer le message » = "to pass on/communicate the message"; (3) to get something accepted or included (e.g., in a book, a plan): « difficile à faire passer » = "hard to get across / to get approved"; (4) sometimes "to slip/pass something to someone" (even secretly): « la faire passer furtivement ».
target_language_example: Le professeur va nous faire passer un examen demain.
native_language_example: The teacher is going to give us an exam tomorrow.

additional_notes: Often used with an indirect object: « faire peur à quelqu’un » = to scare someone. Also common with an object pronoun: « me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur faire peur ». « Ça fait peur » means “it’s scary” / “it frightens (me).” Can also imply trying to intimidate someone.
target_language_example: Tu veux me faire peur ?
native_language_example: Do you want to scare me?

additional_notes: Common, informal/euphemistic way to say you need to urinate, often used with children. Used with "avoir envie de" (to feel like/need to): "J’ai envie de faire pipi." More formal alternatives: "uriner" (medical/formal) or "aller aux toilettes" (neutral).
target_language_example: Attends une minute, je vais faire pipi.
native_language_example: Wait a minute, I’m going to go pee.

meaning: to be pitiful / to inspire pity (often: to look pathetic).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something makes you feel sorry for them, and very often to criticize something as pathetic or embarrassingly bad (e.g., « Ça fait pitié ! » = « That’s pathetic! »). It can sound harsh/judgmental depending on context.
target_language_example: Avec cette excuse, tu vas faire pitié.
native_language_example: With that excuse, you’re going to look pathetic.

meaning: to make room; to step aside (make way).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to move so there’s space: « Faites place ! ». Often appears as « faire place à + noun » meaning “to make room for / give way to” (e.g., one thing replaces another). Conjugates like a normal verb phrase: je fais place, nous faisons place, etc.
target_language_example: Pardon, pouvez-vous faire place ?
native_language_example: Sorry, could you make room?

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object: faire plaisir à quelqu’un / lui faire plaisir (“to please them”). You can also use it without saying who: Ça fait plaisir ! (“That’s nice to hear / That makes me happy”). Common in phrases like pour te/vous/me faire plaisir (“to make you/me happy”).
target_language_example: Je t’ai acheté ton gâteau préféré pour te faire plaisir.
native_language_example: I bought your favorite cake to make you happy.

meaning: to do for; to do in order to; to make an effort to (depending on context)
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- « Qu’est-ce que je peux faire pour toi/vous ? » = offering help/service (“What can I do for you?”).
- « faire (tout) pour + infinitive » = making an effort toward a goal (“do everything to…”): « On va tout faire pour vous faire plaisir. »
- « Que faire pour + noun ? » = asking what action to take about something (“what to do about…”): « Que vais-je faire pour le reste ? »
Note: In « faire pour + infinitive », the idea is often effort/trying rather than a literal “do for.”
target_language_example: On va tout faire pour vous faire plaisir.
native_language_example: We’re going to do everything we can to make you happy.

meaning: to put pressure on; to pressure (someone).
additional_notes: Used when you try to influence or push someone to do something (by insisting, urging, threatening consequences, lobbying, etc.). Often followed by “sur” + person/group: “faire pression sur quelqu’un”. You can also say “continuer à faire pression” = “keep applying pressure”.
target_language_example: Les employés tentent de faire pression sur la direction pour obtenir une augmentation.
native_language_example: The employees are trying to put pressure on management to get a raise.

additional_notes: Usually followed by "de" + a noun: "faire preuve de patience/de courage/de persuasion". It’s used for personal qualities or attitudes (patience, courage, tact), often in advice or formal contexts. Common pattern: "Il faut faire preuve de…" = "You have to show…".
target_language_example: Dans ce travail, il faut faire preuve de rigueur.
native_language_example: In this job, you have to show rigor/thoroughness.

meaning: to keep a low profile; to lie low.
additional_notes: Used when someone tries not to attract attention, often after a mistake, a conflict, or when they want to avoid trouble. Common with advice like « Il vaut mieux faire profil bas » (“It’s better to keep a low profile”). Conjugates with « faire »: je fais / tu fais / il fait / nous faisons, etc.
target_language_example: Après l’incident, il a préféré faire profil bas pendant quelques semaines.
native_language_example: After the incident, he preferred to keep a low profile for a few weeks.

additional_notes: Common, flexible phrase with "faire" (to do/make) + "quelque chose" (something). Often used to ask for action or for a solution: "Tu peux y faire quelque chose ?" = "Can you do something about it?" When you replace the object with a pronoun, it often becomes "le" or "en": "Tu veux faire quelque chose ? Fais-le." (Do it.)
target_language_example: On peut faire quelque chose pour t'aider ?
native_language_example: Can we do something to help you?

additional_notes: Used to ask or tell someone to do you a favor/help you. The verb "faire" changes with the subject and tense (peux-tu faire…, tu dois faire…, tu vas faire…, voudriez-vous faire…). You can swap "moi" for other people: "pour toi" (for you), "pour lui/elle" (for him/her), "pour nous" (for us).
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu pourrais faire quelque chose pour moi, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Could you do something for me, please?

additional_notes: A colloquial, spoken way to ask what someone is doing, going to do, supposed to do, or should do. It often comes after another verb, as in "je dois faire quoi ?" = "what should I do?" More formal French often uses structures like "que faire ?" or "qu'est-ce que je dois faire ?"
target_language_example: On va faire quoi ce soir ?
native_language_example: What are we going to do tonight?

meaning: to be all the rage; to be very popular (said of a trend, especially in fashion).
additional_notes: Refers to something currently extremely popular or trendy (often clothing, colors, products, or a craze). It’s idiomatic: literally “to make rage,” but the natural English rendering is “to be all the rage.” A close synonym is “faire fureur.” In actual sentences it’s commonly conjugated (e.g., “fait rage,” “faisait rage”), but the expression is “faire rage.”
target_language_example: En ce moment, les baskets blanches font rage : tout le monde en porte.
native_language_example: Right now, white sneakers are all the rage: everyone is wearing them.

meaning: to bring in; to make (someone/something) come in/go back in.
additional_notes: Uses the causative verb faire + rentrer (“to go/come in”), so it means you cause someone or something to go inside or return inside. Common with people (faire rentrer les enfants), animals, or objects (faire rentrer la voiture au garage).
target_language_example: Je vais faire rentrer les enfants, il fait froid.
native_language_example: I’m going to bring the kids inside; it’s cold.

meaning: 'to refer to' (to mention or point to something).
additional_notes: Often followed by "à" + a person/thing: "faire référence à..." (= refer to...). Used in formal or neutral contexts (writing, explanations). Example conjugations: present "je fais référence", past "j’ai fait référence".
target_language_example: Dans ce rapport, je vais faire référence à une étude récente.
native_language_example: In this report, I am going to refer to a recent study.

additional_notes: Used with an object introduced by **sans** to mean managing or carrying on without something you normally have or need: **faire sans + noun/pronoun** (e.g., *faire sans argent*, *faire sans ton aide*). Often used in questions or statements about whether something is possible without that thing.
target_language_example: On va devoir faire sans voiture pendant une semaine.
native_language_example: We’re going to have to do without a car for a week.

meaning: to blow up; to make explode; (electricity) to trip/blow (a fuse/breaker).
additional_notes: Construction: faire sauter + direct object. Common meanings: (1) cause something to explode/destroy suddenly: faire sauter un pont / une porte. (2) electricity: faire sauter un fusible, faire sauter les plombs (= trip the fuse/breaker). Can be used in casual speech for dramatic effect (e.g., faire sauter la baraque).
target_language_example: Ils vont faire sauter le pont.
native_language_example: They’re going to blow up the bridge.

additional_notes: Often used with an object pronoun: le/la/les (it/them) or lui/leur (to him/her/them): « Je voulais te le faire savoir » (I wanted to let you know). Very common in polite requests and emails: « Merci de me le faire savoir… » / « Veuillez me faire savoir si… ». Structure: faire savoir + [information], or faire savoir à + [person] + [information].
target_language_example: Je voulais simplement te le faire savoir.
native_language_example: I just wanted to let you know.

meaning: to pretend; to act as if something were true.
additional_notes: Often followed by **de + infinitive**: *faire semblant de ne pas comprendre* (pretend not to understand). It can suggest faking feelings, opinions, or actions (sometimes to avoid conflict or embarrassment).
target_language_example: Il va faire semblant de ne pas avoir entendu.
native_language_example: He’s going to pretend he didn’t hear that.

meaning: to pretend to; to act as if.
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive: faire semblant de + verb (e.g., faire semblant de dormir). It means you behave as though something is true or you are doing something, even though it isn’t true (often to hide something or as a joke).
target_language_example: Il va faire semblant de ne pas comprendre.
native_language_example: He is going to pretend not to understand.

meaning: to signal (to someone), e.g. with a gesture or wave.
additional_notes: Often used with "à" + person: "faire signe à quelqu’un" = to gesture to someone to come closer, to get their attention, or to indicate something (often without speaking). Can also be used without an object when the person is understood from context.
target_language_example: Je vais faire signe au serveur pour avoir l’addition.
native_language_example: I’m going to signal to the waiter to get the bill.

meaning: to keep it simple; to make it simple.
additional_notes: Used when you choose a simple solution or want to avoid unnecessary complexity. Often follows verbs like "on va" or "je vais" ("On va faire simple" = "We’ll keep it simple"). Can also be used as a suggestion or instruction.
target_language_example: On va faire simple : on se retrouve à 18 h devant la gare.
native_language_example: Let’s keep it simple: we’ll meet at 6 p.m. in front of the train station.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone (informal singular “tu”) to complete their schoolwork. The verb “faire” (to do/make) + “tes devoirs” (your homework). In commands you’ll often see “Fais tes devoirs !” (Do your homework!). It can also appear in the causative structure “faire faire” (have someone else do it): “Fais faire tes devoirs par ta mère !” = “Have your mom do your homework!”
target_language_example: Tu dois faire tes devoirs avant de dîner.
native_language_example: You have to do your homework before dinner.

meaning: to stand up to; to resist; to withstand (most often used as: "faire tête à").
additional_notes: Most often used with "à" + a person/thing you oppose: "faire tête à quelqu’un/quelque chose" = resist it, face it without backing down. Used for opponents, problems, pressure, competition, etc. (e.g., "faire tête à la concurrence", "faire tête aux difficultés").
target_language_example: Elle a dû faire tête à la pression et continuer malgré tout.
native_language_example: She had to withstand the pressure and keep going despite everything.

meaning: (Informal) to have been a long time; “it’s been a while.”
additional_notes: Most often used in the fixed expression **Ça fait un bail (que...)** = “It’s been a long time (since...)”. Literally, **un bail** is a **lease/rental contract**, and **faire/sign(er) un bail** can also mean “to draw up/sign a lease,” but the “long time” meaning is the common everyday idiom.
target_language_example: On n’a pas fait un bail depuis la dernière fois qu’on s’est vus ?
native_language_example: Hasn’t it been a while since the last time we saw each other?

meaning: (idiomatic, informal) “to spell it out” / “to make it really obvious.”
additional_notes: Often used as a rhetorical question to show impatience: « Je dois te faire un dessin ? » / « Faut te faire un dessin ? » = “Do I have to draw you a picture?” meaning “Do I really have to explain this in super simple terms?” You can also say « Pas la peine de me faire un dessin » to mean “No need to spell it out (I get it).”
target_language_example: Je comprends, pas la peine de me faire un dessin.
native_language_example: I understand—no need to spell it out.

meaning: To be a big hit; to be very successful.
additional_notes: An idiom often used for a show, movie, song, product, or event that gets a lot of enthusiasm or sells extremely well. Common in spoken French and the media.
target_language_example: Son nouveau film va faire un tabac au cinéma.
native_language_example: His new movie is going to be a huge hit at the cinema.

meaning: to go for a walk / to take a stroll; to have a look around.
additional_notes: Very common for suggesting going out for a short walk or outing, often with no specific destination (e.g., in the neighborhood, in town, around a park). It can also mean doing a quick round/loop or going somewhere briefly. Often used in invitations: « Tu viens faire un tour ? », « On va faire un tour. »
target_language_example: Après le dîner, on peut faire un tour dans le quartier.
native_language_example: After dinner, we can go for a walk around the neighborhood.

meaning: to do such a thing (often: something shocking/unacceptable).
additional_notes: Used to express surprise, disapproval, or disbelief about an action. Very common in questions like « Comment as-tu pu faire une chose pareille ? » (How could you do such a thing?) or « Qui a pu faire une chose pareille ? » (Who could have done such a thing?). « Une chose pareille » means “such a thing / something like that.”
target_language_example: Comment as-tu pu faire une chose pareille ?
native_language_example: How could you do such a thing?

meaning: to make a cross (✝) / to put an X (as a mark); also (in « faire une croix sur … ») to give up on something / write it off.
additional_notes: Literal sense: draw a cross or put an X as a mark (e.g., on a form, to sign with an X). Very common figurative use: « faire une croix sur + [something] » = to stop hoping for it, to abandon it, to write it off (e.g., « Il faut faire une croix sur ce projet. »).
target_language_example: Il faut faire une croix sur ce projet.
native_language_example: We have to give up on that project.

meaning: to take a break; to pause.
additional_notes: Used when you want to stop an activity for a short rest (work, studying, driving, etc.). Very common with verbs like vouloir (want), pouvoir (can), devoir (should/must), and avoir besoin de (need).
target_language_example: On peut faire une pause de cinq minutes ?
native_language_example: Can we take a five-minute break?

meaning: to go for a walk; to take a stroll.
additional_notes: Used for a leisure walk (often outside). Very common with "aller" (aller faire une promenade = go for a walk). You can add where you’ll walk with "dans" or "le long de" (e.g., dans la campagne, le long du fleuve).
target_language_example: Après le dîner, on va faire une promenade dans le parc.
native_language_example: After dinner, we're going to go for a walk in the park.

additional_notes: Used to react to or question an action seen as surprising, shocking, or hard to understand. "Une telle" means "such a" (often with emphasis). You can swap in other nouns: "faire une telle erreur" (make such a mistake).
target_language_example: Pourquoi voudrais-tu faire une telle chose ?
native_language_example: Why would you want to do such a thing?

meaning: to use; to make use of.
additional_notes: A fairly formal way to say "utiliser" or "se servir de." Often followed by "de" + a noun: "faire usage de" (make use of / use). Common in polite requests (e.g., asking permission to use something).
target_language_example: Vous pouvez faire usage de cette salle si vous en avez besoin.
native_language_example: You can use this room if you need it.

meaning: to send for / have someone (or something) come.
additional_notes: Uses the causative pattern **faire + infinitive** to mean you cause someone to do something. With **faire venir**, you arrange for someone to come (often by calling, asking, or requesting). Common with professionals: **faire venir un médecin** = call a doctor. It can also be used for getting something delivered or brought: **faire venir une pizza / un taxi**.
target_language_example: Je vais faire venir un taxi.
native_language_example: I’m going to call a taxi.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object: « faire voir quelque chose à quelqu’un » = “to show someone something.” In the fixed expression « aller/se faire voir » (or « qu’il aille se faire voir »), it’s an informal/rude way to say “get lost / go to hell.”
target_language_example: Tu peux me faire voir ta carte d’identité, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you show me your ID, please?

meaning: to make/take a vow (a solemn promise).
additional_notes: Often used for formal or religious promises: e.g. *faire vœu de silence* (take a vow of silence), *faire vœu de pauvreté* (take a vow of poverty). In everyday French you may also hear *faire un vœu* meaning “to make a wish,” but without an article (*faire vœu*) it usually means “to vow” (a serious commitment).
target_language_example: Il a décidé de faire vœu de silence pendant un mois.
native_language_example: He decided to take a vow of silence for a month.

additional_notes: A very common everyday phrase for carrying out an action that is already known from context. In spoken French, ça often means "that" or "it". Depending on context, it can refer to something specific someone just mentioned.
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas faire ça aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I can't do that today.

meaning: to team up; to work as a team (with someone).
additional_notes: Often used with "avec" to say who you’re teaming up with: "faire équipe avec quelqu’un". It can describe agreeing to partner up for a task, game, or project. In casual speech you’ll also hear "On fait équipe ?" / "On va faire équipe."
target_language_example: Tu veux faire équipe avec moi pour ce projet ?
native_language_example: Do you want to team up with me for this project?

additional_notes: Command form (imperative) of "faire" for "tu" + the direct object pronoun "le" (= it). The pronoun comes after the verb in affirmative commands and is linked with a hyphen: "Fais-le !" (Do it!). For a negative command, the pronoun goes before the verb: "Ne le fais pas."
target_language_example: Fais-le maintenant, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Do it now, please.

additional_notes: Imperative of faire ("to do/make") + indirect object pronoun moi ("to me"). Common in requests: fais-moi savoir ("let me know"), fais-moi connaître ("tell me/let me know"), fais-moi une faveur ("do me a favor"), fais-moi une offre ("make me an offer"). Often said as Fais-moi... or with politeness: S'il te plaît / je te prie.
target_language_example: Fais-moi savoir quand tu arrives.
native_language_example: Let me know when you arrive.

additional_notes: An informal/neutral command using the tu form: fais (from faire) + moi (me). Used to reassure someone or ask them to rely on you. For a more formal/polite version, say: « Faites-moi confiance. ». Note: « confiance » looks like English “confidence,” but here it usually means “trust.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, fais-moi confiance.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, trust me.

meaning: "do you...?" / "are you doing...?" (question form of *faire* with *tu*).
additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of *tu fais* (“you do/you’re doing”). It’s used in more formal or written questions: *Que fais-tu ?* (“What are you doing?”). In everyday speech, French often uses *Tu fais quoi ?* or *Qu’est-ce que tu fais ?* instead. It can also mean “do you…?” in expressions like *faire confiance* (“to trust”): *Me fais-tu confiance ?* (“Do you trust me?”).
target_language_example: Pourquoi fais-tu ça ?
native_language_example: Why are you doing that?

additional_notes: Informal singular imperative of « faire attention ». Used to warn someone or tell them to be cautious; can stand alone (“Fais attention !”) or be followed by « en + -ant » (Fais attention en traversant…), « où » (Fais attention où…), or a situation (sur la route, la prochaine fois).
target_language_example: Fais attention, c’est glissant ici.
native_language_example: Be careful, it’s slippery here.

additional_notes: A common goodnight phrase. It uses the informal singular imperative ("fais")—said to one person you address as "tu" (a friend, child, partner). For a more formal or plural version, you can say: "Faites de beaux rêves." Often paired with "Bonne nuit" (good night). Depending on tone, it can be affectionate ("ma princesse") or sarcastic/insulting if followed by an insult.
target_language_example: Bonne nuit, fais de beaux rêves !
native_language_example: Good night, sweet dreams!

additional_notes: Informal imperative of « faire gaffe ». Used to warn someone or tell them to pay attention (to danger, a mistake, or how they speak). Often followed by « à + noun » (Fais gaffe à la marche !).
target_language_example: Fais gaffe en traversant la rue !
native_language_example: Watch out when crossing the street!

additional_notes: Informal spoken negative imperative of *faire* (“to do/make”). In careful/written French you usually say **ne fais pas ça**; in speech, **ne** is often dropped: **fais pas ça**. Often used to stop someone, protest, or beg (“Please, don’t do that”).
target_language_example: Fais pas ça, tu vas te blesser.
native_language_example: Don’t do that—you’re going to hurt yourself.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French as a shortened, informal question (often in: « Je fais quoi ? »). Used when you’re unsure what to do next or what someone expects you to do. More formal: « Qu’est-ce que je fais ? » or « Que dois-je faire ? »
target_language_example: Bon, j’ai fini le dossier… je fais quoi maintenant ?
native_language_example: Okay, I’ve finished the file… what do I do now?

additional_notes: Imperative of « faire voir » (tu form). Used to ask someone to show something (an object, a document, what they can do, etc.). Often sounds casual and a bit pushy depending on tone; you can soften it with « Fais voir, s’il te plaît » or use « Montre-moi… ».
target_language_example: Fais voir ton ticket, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Let me see your ticket, please.

meaning: "do that" / "do this" (telling someone to do something).
additional_notes: Uses the verb *faire* (to do/make) with *tu*: **fais** is the present/imperative form for "you" (informal singular). Often used as a command: *Fais ça !* (“Do that!”). In questions about the past you’ll usually see **fait** (past participle): *Pourquoi as-tu fait ça ?* (“Why did you do that?”).
target_language_example: Fais ça avant de partir.
native_language_example: Do that before leaving.

meaning: “does he do / is he doing” (question form of *il fait*).
additional_notes: Used in questions with subject–verb inversion: *il fait* → *fait-il ?* It’s the verb *faire* (“to do/make”), so the meaning depends on context (doing something, making something, or “what is he doing?”). Written with a hyphen in inversion.
target_language_example: Pourquoi fait-il ça ?
native_language_example: Why is he doing that?

meaning: (has/have) done what needed to be done; did the right thing.
additional_notes: Used to say someone took the necessary/proper action in a situation. Often implies responsibility or reassurance ("we did what we had to do"). Can be used on its own ("On a fait ce qu'il fallait") or followed by an infinitive for emphasis ("ce qu'il fallait faire").
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : on a fait ce qu'il fallait.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we did what needed to be done.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **faire des progrès** = “to make progress.” It’s commonly used with **en + subject/skill** (e.g., *faire des progrès en anglais*) or with an adjective like *rapides*, *remarquables*. Tense changes with the subject (e.g., *je fais*, *tu fais*, *il/elle fait*, *nous faisons*, *vous faites*, *ils/elles font*; past: *a fait*, *ont fait*).
target_language_example: Tu as fait des progrès en français depuis le début de l’année.
native_language_example: You’ve made progress in French since the beginning of the year.

meaning: (has) done a good job; (has) done good work.
additional_notes: Used to praise someone’s work. It’s the past tense with avoir: "j’ai fait du bon boulot" (I did a good job), "tu as fait…", "il/elle a fait…", "nous avons fait…", "vous avez fait…", "ils/elles ont fait…". In speech you’ll also hear the present: "Tu fais du bon boulot" (You’re doing a good job).
target_language_example: Bravo, tu as fait du bon boulot sur ce projet !
native_language_example: Well done, you did a good job on this project!

meaning: (has) done good work; did a good job.
additional_notes: Used to praise someone’s performance or the quality of what they did. Often appears as "Tu as fait du bon travail" (you did a good job) or "Vous avez fait du bon travail" (you did a good job—formal/plural). With a name/subject: "Il/Tom fait du bon travail" = he/Tom does good work. Note: agreement happens on "toutes" when addressing a group of women ("Vous avez toutes fait...").
target_language_example: Merci pour ton aide : tu as fait du bon travail.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help: you did a good job.

additional_notes: Past tense of « faire le bon choix » (“to make the right choice”). Used to say someone chose correctly; often appears with « j’ai/tu as/on a fait le bon choix ». You can also say « faire le bon choix » in general statements: « Il faut faire le bon choix. »
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : tu as fait le bon choix.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you made the right choice.

additional_notes: Used with a person as the indirect object (me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur): « Ça me fait mal » = “It hurts (me).” In questions about pain: « Qu’est-ce qui vous fait mal ? » (“What hurts?”) or « Quelle dent/jambe vous fait mal ? » (“Which tooth/leg hurts?”). Past: « Ça vous a fait mal ? » = “Did it hurt?”
target_language_example: Ça me fait mal au dos.
native_language_example: My back hurts.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is included in a group, organization, set, or whole. It’s the 3rd-person singular present of "faire partie de" (to be part of). You’ll also see changes like "font partie de" (they are part of) and forms with "de la / de l’ / des" depending on the noun: "fait partie du club" (of the club), "fait partie de la famille" (of the family), "fait partie des membres" (of the members).
target_language_example: Cette rue fait partie du centre-ville.
native_language_example: This street is part of the city center.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "faire peur (à quelqu’un)" = “to scare someone.” It agrees with the subject (fait / font / faisait / a fait, etc.). The person who is scared is often introduced with an indirect object: "Ça me fait peur" (It scares me), "Les chiens nous ont fait peur" (The dogs scared us).
target_language_example: Ce film me fait peur, alors je préfère regarder une comédie.
native_language_example: This movie scares me, so I’d rather watch a comedy.

meaning: "does/did what?" → used to ask what someone is doing/did (casual spoken French)
additional_notes: Common in spoken French as a fairly direct, informal question built from **faire** + **quoi**. Meaning depends on context/tense: **il/elle fait quoi ?** = “what is he/she doing?”, **tu as fait quoi ?** = “what did you do?”. In **ça te fait quoi ?**, it means “how does that make you feel?” (literally “what does that do to you?”).
target_language_example: Elle fait quoi, là ?
native_language_example: What’s she doing there/now?

additional_notes: From the verb « faire » (to do/make) + « ça » (that/it). « fait » is the present tense form used with il/elle/on (he/she/one). Often used to talk about a repeated habit: « Des fois, il fait ça » = “Sometimes he does that.”
target_language_example: Pourquoi est-ce qu'il fait ça ?
native_language_example: Why does he do that?

additional_notes: Imperative (command) with **vous** form of *faire* (“to do/make”) + the direct object pronoun **le** (“it/him”), joined with a hyphen. Often means **“do it”** (e.g., *Faites-le sans attendre.*). With an infinitive, it can be the causative *faire*: **faites-le + infinitive** = “make him/it + verb” (e.g., *Faites-le parler* = “Make him talk”).
target_language_example: Si tu es prêt, faites-le maintenant.
native_language_example: If you’re ready, do it now.

additional_notes: Imperative of **faire** for **vous** (“faites…”) + the direct object pronoun **les** (“them”). Very often used in the causative pattern **faites-les + infinitive**: *Faites-les entrer* (“Have them come in”), *Faites-les taire* (“Make them be quiet”). The pronoun **les** comes before the infinitive it affects.
target_language_example: Faites-les attendre ici, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Have them wait here, please.

additional_notes: From the polite command form of *faire* (“faites”) + *moi* (“me”). It’s often followed by an infinitive or set phrases: **faites-moi connaître** = “let me know”, **faites-moi part de…** = “tell me / share… with me”, **faites-moi voir** = “show me”. You can also add **s’il vous plaît** for extra politeness.
target_language_example: Faites-moi savoir quand vous arrivez, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please let me know when you arrive.

additional_notes: This is the verb "faire" (vous form: "faites") with inversion "-vous" to form a question in formal/polite French: "Faites-vous… ?" = "Do you…?" It can also appear with pronouns: "Comment le faites-vous ?" (How do you do it?) and with a reflexive verb: "Où vous faites-vous coiffer ?" (Where do you get your hair done?). In a command, "Faites-vous plaisir" means "Treat yourself" (literally "Make yourself pleasure").
target_language_example: Que faites-vous ce soir ?
native_language_example: What are you doing tonight?

additional_notes: Imperative (vous form) of « faire attention ». Often followed by « à » + noun or clause: « Faites attention à la voiture » (Watch out for the car) or « Faites attention à ce que vous dites » (Be careful what you say). Used both as a warning and as advice to be mindful.
target_language_example: Faites attention en traversant la rue.
native_language_example: Be careful when crossing the street.

additional_notes: Fixed expression said by a dealer or announcer in gambling contexts (casino, roulette, etc.) to invite players to bet. It uses the formal/plural command form (faites = “do/make” to you all / to a customer). Not used much outside betting contexts.
target_language_example: Au casino, le croupier a dit : « Faites vos jeux ! »
native_language_example: At the casino, the dealer said, “Place your bets!”

meaning: to have to; to be necessary that
additional_notes: Usually appears in conjugated forms such as il faut que or il va falloir que, followed by a subjunctive verb. It expresses necessity, obligation, or something that needs to be done.
target_language_example: Il va falloir que tu finisses tes devoirs.
native_language_example: You’re going to have to finish your homework.

additional_notes: Used with the verb faire: faire une fausse couche = to have a miscarriage. It’s a sensitive medical/personal topic; in everyday conversation, people may also say "perdre le bébé" (lose the baby) or use medical terms like "interruption spontanée de grossesse".
target_language_example: Elle a fait une fausse couche l’année dernière.
native_language_example: She had a miscarriage last year.

additional_notes: This is the question form (inversion) of "il faut" ("it’s necessary / we need"). It’s often used in real questions (e.g., asking what’s needed) and also in rhetorical questions expressing doubt or surprise ("Faut-il…?" = "Do we really have to…?").
target_language_example: Faut-il réserver à l’avance ?
native_language_example: Do we need to book in advance?

meaning: “(Well,) you have to / it has to be done” (resigned necessity).
additional_notes: Short for spoken/written informal "(il) faut bien". Used to express that there’s no real choice: something is necessary even if you don’t like it. Often followed by "que" + subjunctive: "Faut bien que je parte" (“I have to go”). Can also stand alone: "Faut bien." / "Oui, il faut bien." (“Well, you have to.”).
target_language_example: Faut bien que j’y aille, demain je travaille tôt.
native_language_example: I have to go—tomorrow I start work early.

additional_notes: Used to explain what happens because something is missing or because you didn’t manage to do something. Common patterns: **faute de + noun** (for lack of something): *Faute de temps…*; **faute de + infinitive** (failing to do something): *Faute de comprendre…*. Not the same as **une faute** (= a mistake/error).
target_language_example: Faute de preuves, la police a classé l’affaire.
native_language_example: For lack of evidence, the police closed the case.

additional_notes: Means a wheelchair (a chair with wheels used by someone who has difficulty walking). Often used with the verb "être" (to be) or with "en" to mean being transported in one: "être dans un fauteuil roulant", "être évacué en fauteuil roulant". You may also hear "chaise roulante" (more common in Canada).
target_language_example: Après l’accident, il se déplace en fauteuil roulant.
native_language_example: After the accident, he gets around in a wheelchair.

meaning: a figure of speech; (also) someone’s way of speaking.
additional_notes: Often used to correct or soften what you just said: « C’était / Ce n’était qu’une façon de parler » = “I didn’t mean it literally; it was just an expression.” You can also use it parenthetically: « Il est, façon de parler, un robot » (“so to speak”). In a more literal sense, « sa façon de parler » means “his/her way of speaking / manner of speaking.”
target_language_example: Je dis ça, mais c’est une façon de parler : je ne le pense pas vraiment.
native_language_example: I say that, but it’s just a figure of speech—I don’t really mean it.

additional_notes: Used to describe how someone (or a group/culture) typically thinks or approaches ideas. Often followed by a possessive adjective: « ma/ta/sa/notre/votre/leur façon de penser ».
target_language_example: Sa façon de penser a beaucoup changé depuis l'année dernière.
native_language_example: His/Her way of thinking has changed a lot since last year.

meaning: a housewife; a stay-at-home woman who runs the household.
additional_notes: Used to describe a woman whose main activity is managing the home (housework, childcare, etc.), rather than having paid work outside the home. Often used after être: « Je suis femme au foyer » (no article). With an article it’s treated like a noun: « une femme au foyer », « les femmes au foyer ».
target_language_example: Depuis la naissance de son bébé, elle est femme au foyer.
native_language_example: Since her baby was born, she has been a stay-at-home mom.

additional_notes: Refers to a woman who cleans and tidies rooms and may bring items (soap, towels) in a hotel or private household. Historically it can also mean a lady’s maid/maidservant for a wealthy woman. Plural: femmes de chambre.
target_language_example: La femme de chambre passera tout à l’heure pour refaire la chambre.
native_language_example: The chambermaid will come by later to make up the room.

additional_notes: Refers to a woman whose job is cleaning (in a home, hotel, office, etc.). It does not mean “housewife” (a woman who manages her own household). In some contexts it can sound a bit old-fashioned; you may also hear more neutral terms like « agent(e) d’entretien ».
target_language_example: La femme de ménage arrive tous les lundis matin.
native_language_example: The cleaner comes every Monday morning.

meaning: 'will you do...?' / 'will you make...?' (formal question form of *faire*).
additional_notes: This is the **future tense** of *faire* (“to do/make”) with **inversion** (*verbe + -vous*) to ask a question: *Ferez-vous… ?* = “Will you…?” It’s more **formal** than *Vous ferez… ?* or *Est-ce que vous ferez… ?*. It can mean “do” (*Que ferez-vous ?* = “What will you do?”) or “make” (*Me ferez-vous une faveur ?* = “Will you do me a favor?”).
target_language_example: Ferez-vous le ménage demain matin ?
native_language_example: Will you do the cleaning tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: Informal and aggressive command telling someone to stop talking. Literally means “close it,” where “la” refers to the mouth; often written with a hyphen in the imperative: « Ferme-la ! ». Avoid in polite situations; use « Tais-toi » / « Taisez-vous » for a less harsh “be quiet.”
target_language_example: Ferme-la et laisse-moi finir.
native_language_example: Shut up and let me finish.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) of the verb *fermer* (“to close”) + *la porte* (“the door”). Often used to tell one person to close a specific door. Use *Fermez la porte* for “close the door” to more than one person or as the polite/formal form. Can be softened with *s’il te plaît* (“please”) or *je te prie* (“please/I beg you”).
target_language_example: Il fait froid : ferme la porte, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: It’s cold: close the door, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask or tell someone to shut a window. Common in polite requests: "Veuillez fermer…" (please, formal) and "Voudriez-vous…?" (would you…?, very polite). In everyday speech you might also say: "Ferme la fenêtre."
target_language_example: Tu peux fermer la fenêtre, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you close the window, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to close a door. Very common with polite requests: « Peux-tu… ? » (Can you…?), « Pourrais-tu… ? » (Could you…?), « Veuillez… » (Please…; formal), « …, je vous prie » (…, please; polite). « Fermer la porte derrière toi » means “close the door behind you.”
target_language_example: Tu peux fermer la porte, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you close the door, please?

meaning: to close your eyes; (figuratively) to ignore/turn a blind eye (to something).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: physically close your eyes. Figuratively, often used with « sur/ là-dessus » to mean “to overlook something” or “to pretend not to notice,” especially in requests like « Pourrais-tu fermer les yeux là-dessus ? » (“Could you let it slide?”).
target_language_example: Je vais fermer les yeux sur cette erreur, mais pas la prochaine fois.
native_language_example: I’ll overlook this mistake, but not next time.

meaning: to lock (with a key); to lock up.
additional_notes: Used when you close something and secure it with a key (a door, a window, a suitcase, etc.). Often used in the imperative: « Ferme à clé ! » (= Lock it!). You can specify what you’re locking: « Fermer la porte à clé ».
target_language_example: Pense à fermer à clé avant de partir.
native_language_example: Remember to lock up before leaving.

additional_notes: Imperative of *fermer* (“to close”) + *la* (“it”), used as an abrupt command for someone to stop talking. Commonly felt as aggressive/insulting; in polite contexts prefer *Taisez-vous.* (formal) or *Tais-toi.* (informal).
target_language_example: Fermez-la et laissez-moi parler !
native_language_example: Shut up and let me talk!

additional_notes: This is the imperative of "fermer" addressed to "vous". Use it when speaking politely to one person (e.g., a stranger, customer, older person) or to several people. For an informal command to one person, you’d say: "Ferme la porte." You can soften it with "s’il vous plaît" or "je vous prie".
target_language_example: Fermez la porte, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Close the door, please.

meaning: “closed the door” (past tense of “to close the door”).
additional_notes: Uses the past participle fermé of fermer (“to close”), typically with avoir to form the passé composé: j’ai/tu as/il a/nous avons fermé la porte. Often followed by details like de + place (la porte de sa chambre) or derrière nous (“behind us”).
target_language_example: J’ai fermé la porte, mais la fenêtre est restée ouverte.
native_language_example: I closed the door, but the window stayed open.

additional_notes: A fire made outdoors (often while camping, sometimes on a beach) for warmth, light, or cooking. Used with faire/allumer/construire un feu de camp (“make/light/build a campfire”).
target_language_example: On a fait un feu de camp pour se réchauffer.
native_language_example: We made a campfire to warm up.

additional_notes: Used when giving directions or talking about driving rules. In French you often say “au feu rouge” (at the red light) or “après le feu rouge” (after the red light). “Griller un feu rouge” means “to run a red light.”
target_language_example: Arrêtez-vous au feu rouge, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Stop at the red light, please.

additional_notes: Used literally for traffic lights (au feu vert = when the light is green) and figuratively for authorization (donner/avoir le feu vert = to give/get the go-ahead). Often used alone as a short confirmation: « Feu vert. »
target_language_example: On attend le feu vert avant de commencer.
native_language_example: We’re waiting for the green light before starting.

additional_notes: Very informal and rude. Used as an order to make someone leave (similar to "dégage !" or "va-t’en !"). Also used with other forms: "Je fiche le camp" = "I’m getting out of here / I’m leaving," and "Il faut fiche le camp" = "We/you need to get out (leave)."
target_language_example: Fiche le camp, je ne veux plus te voir ici.
native_language_example: Get lost, I don’t want to see you here anymore.

meaning: to leave (someone) alone; to stop bothering (someone).
additional_notes: Usually used to tell someone to stop annoying you: « Fiche-moi la paix ! » = “Leave me alone!” It’s informal and can sound rude/angry depending on tone. You can also use it with a third person: « Fiche-lui la paix » (Leave him/her alone). Similar to « laisser tranquille » (a bit more neutral).
target_language_example: Je voudrais que tu arrêtes de me déranger et que tu me laisses ficher la paix.
native_language_example: I’d like you to stop bothering me and leave me alone.

meaning: to clear off; to get lost; to run off.
additional_notes: Informal (can sound rude depending on tone). Used to tell someone to leave (often as an imperative: « Fiche le camp ! ») or to say that someone/something left suddenly (« Il/Elle a fiché le camp. »). Similar to « foutre le camp » (usually stronger/more vulgar).
target_language_example: Quand il a vu la police, il a fiché le camp.
native_language_example: When he saw the police, he cleared off.

additional_notes: Used to praise or encourage someone you address as “tu.” “Fier” agrees with the speaker: a man says “je suis fier de toi,” a woman says “je suis fière de toi.” You can also use it with other people: “fier de lui/elle,” “fiers/fières de vous/eux/elles.”
target_language_example: Je suis très fier de toi pour ton travail !
native_language_example: I'm very proud of you for your work!

additional_notes: Used for thin metal wire, often for practical uses like making cages, fixing things, crafting, or tying items. With materials you’ll often see it after en (“made of”): en fil de fer. With quantities it’s usually du fil de fer (“some wire”).
target_language_example: On a réparé la clôture avec du fil de fer.
native_language_example: We repaired the fence with some wire.

additional_notes: Most literally means a red wire (or thread), especially when talking about electronics or instructions ("Cut the red wire"). Figuratively, it can also mean a “common thread” or main theme linking parts of a story or argument ("le fil rouge de l’histoire").
target_language_example: Coupe le fil rouge, pas le fil vert.
native_language_example: Cut the red wire, not the green one.

additional_notes: Usually used with "en" ("en file indienne") to tell people to line up one behind another, often in school or when moving through a narrow space. Related verb phrase: "se mettre en file indienne" = to line up single file.
target_language_example: Pour entrer dans le musée, mettez-vous en file indienne.
native_language_example: To enter the museum, line up single file.

additional_notes: Means a girl who has no brothers or sisters. Used without an article after the verb être: « Je suis fille unique. » For a male only child, say « fils unique ».
target_language_example: Ma sœur est fille unique, donc elle n'a pas de frères ni de sœurs.
native_language_example: My sister is an only child, so she has no brothers or sisters.

meaning: A very vulgar insult: “son of a bitch / you bastard.”
additional_notes: Extremely offensive and aggressive (stronger than many common insults). Used to insult someone directly ("Tu es un fils de pute") or to talk about someone ("ce fils de pute"). In the plural: "fils de pute" / "fils de putes". Literal meaning is “son of a whore,” but the closest natural English equivalent is usually “son of a bitch.” Avoid in polite or everyday situations.
target_language_example: C'est un fils de pute, il m'a volé mon téléphone.
native_language_example: He’s a son of a bitch—he stole my phone.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has no brothers (and no sisters if you mean they are the only child overall). Feminine: « fille unique » (only daughter). If someone is an only child (no siblings at all), you can also say « enfant unique ».
target_language_example: Il est fils unique, donc il n'a pas de frères.
native_language_example: He’s an only son, so he doesn’t have any brothers.

additional_notes: Very common in Canadian French (especially Quebec) for “weekend”; in France you’ll often hear “week-end”. Used with or without an article: « une bonne fin de semaine », « chaque fin de semaine », « en fin de semaine » (= on the weekend). « une longue fin de semaine » = a long weekend.
target_language_example: On se voit en fin de semaine ?
native_language_example: See you this weekend?

additional_notes: Used literally for an apocalypse/disaster ("la fin du monde") or more loosely to exaggerate a situation ("Ce n’est pas la fin du monde" = “It’s not the end of the world”). You’ll often see it with an article: "la fin du monde".
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas la fin du monde si on est en retard.
native_language_example: It’s not the end of the world if we’re late.

meaning: "ended up" / "eventually" (after some time, effort, or events).
additional_notes: Used as the verb phrase "finir par" + infinitive: "Il/Elle a fini par comprendre" = "He/She ended up understanding." It often suggests a result that happens after a process (waiting, trying, changing, repeated actions). You’ll commonly see it in past tenses (passé composé: "a fini par"; plus-que-parfait: "avait fini par").
target_language_example: On a fini par trouver un restaurant ouvert.
native_language_example: We eventually found a restaurant that was open.

meaning: proud of you (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone you’re proud of them. Agreement matters: a woman says « fière »; a man says « fier ». « de toi » is informal singular “of you”; with « vous », it’s « fier/fière de vous ».
target_language_example: Je suis fière de toi, tu as vraiment bien travaillé.
native_language_example: I’m proud of you—you really worked hard.

meaning: “times a year” (how many times per year).
additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency over a year. Often comes after a number or after “combien de” in a question: “deux fois par an” (twice a year), “Combien de fois par an… ?” (How many times a year…?). Similar patterns: “fois par mois” (times a month), “fois par semaine” (times a week).
target_language_example: Je vais à la salle de sport trois fois par an.
native_language_example: I go to the gym three times a year.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency (how often something happens within a month), often after a number: « deux fois par mois » (twice a month). In questions you’ll often see « Combien de fois par mois… ? » (How many times per month…?).
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma une fois par mois.
native_language_example: I go to the movies once a month.

meaning: to burst into tears (to suddenly start crying).
additional_notes: Used when someone begins crying abruptly due to strong emotion (sadness, relief, shock, etc.). Conjugate « fondre » to match the subject and tense (e.g., « elle fondre en larmes » is incorrect; use « elle fond en larmes », « elle a fondu en larmes », etc.).
target_language_example: Quand il a annoncé son départ, elle a fondu en larmes.
native_language_example: When he announced he was leaving, she burst into tears.

additional_notes: "Font-ils" is the inverted question form of "ils font" (they do / they are doing). It’s used in formal or written questions, often after a question word: « Que font-ils ? » (What are they doing?), « Pourquoi font-ils… ? » (Why do they…?). In everyday speech, people often say « Qu’est-ce qu’ils font ? » or « Ils font quoi ? ».
target_language_example: Que font-ils ce week-end ?
native_language_example: What are they doing this weekend?

additional_notes: Used to specify the sport (as opposed to football = soccer in many French-speaking contexts). Often appears after prepositions like jouer au / faire du (to play) and in comparisons like préférer X au Y (to prefer X to Y).
target_language_example: Je regarde le football américain le dimanche.
native_language_example: I watch American football on Sundays.

meaning: (formal) “it must be admitted / it is necessary” (often: “force est de + infinitive”).
additional_notes: Used in formal writing to express an unavoidable conclusion or obligation. Very common in the set phrase “Force est de constater que…” (= “We/one must admit/acknowledge that…”). Usually followed by “de” + infinitive, or by “que” + clause.
target_language_example: Force est de constater que les prix ont augmenté.
native_language_example: We have to admit that prices have gone up.

meaning: to pressure someone into doing something; to twist someone’s arm.
additional_notes: Used when someone is trying to push you to agree or act against your will (e.g., insisting, guilt-tripping, not taking no for an answer). Often appears with an indirect object pronoun: « me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur forcer la main ». Can be used in the imperative: « Arrête de me forcer la main ! » (to one person) / « Arrêtez de me forcer la main ! » (formal or plural).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas, alors n’essaie pas de me forcer la main.
native_language_example: I don’t want to, so don’t try to pressure me into it.

additional_notes: Usually refers to elite military units trained for high-risk missions (often used with the definite article: « les forces spéciales »). In conversation it can also be used jokingly or as a nickname to address someone acting like a commando: « Eh, les forces spéciales ! »
target_language_example: Il rêve d'entrer dans les forces spéciales.
native_language_example: He dreams of joining the special forces.

additional_notes: Used with être (or devenir) to say someone is extremely happy about something: « être fou de joie ». You can add a reason with « en + verbe » (e.g., « en apprenant la nouvelle » = “on hearing the news”). Note agreement: « fou » → « folle » for a woman (e.g., « Elle est folle de joie »).
target_language_example: Il est devenu fou de joie en apprenant la nouvelle.
native_language_example: He became overjoyed when he heard the news.

additional_notes: Used with "être" or "devenir" to say someone is extremely angry. You can use it as an exclamation ("Fou de rage !") or in a sentence ("Il est fou de rage").
target_language_example: Quand il a appris la nouvelle, il est devenu fou de rage.
native_language_example: When he heard the news, he became furious.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is "crazy" in a very emphatic way (often as an insult or harsh judgment). Literally "crazy to be tied up"—as if they’d need to be restrained. It agrees with the person: fou (masc. sing.), folle (fem. sing.), fous/folles (plural).
target_language_example: Arrête de conduire comme ça, tu es fou à lier !
native_language_example: Stop driving like that, you’re completely crazy!

meaning: to mess up / ruin (something); to blow up (destroy).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar because of « foutre » (roughly like “to screw up” / “to fuck up”). Used for ruining plans (« foutre en l’air un projet »), messing something up (« foutre en l’air tout le travail »), or sometimes literally destroying/blowing something up. In polite contexts, prefer: « gâcher », « bousiller » (informal), or « ruiner ».
target_language_example: J’ai foutre en l'air ma présentation en oubliant mes notes.
native_language_example: I screwed up my presentation by forgetting my notes.

meaning: to leave (someone) alone; to stop bothering (someone).
additional_notes: Informal and somewhat rude/strong (because of “foutre”). Used to tell someone to stop annoying you, or to say you want to be left alone. Common in the imperative (e.g., “Fous-moi la paix !”), but can also be used with verbs like “laisser” (e.g., “Laisse-moi foutre la paix.”). A more neutral option is “Laisse-moi tranquille.”
target_language_example: Laisse-moi foutre la paix, je travaille.
native_language_example: Leave me alone, I’m working.

meaning: to scare the hell out of (someone); to really frighten.
additional_notes: Very informal (and a bit vulgar because of "foutre"). Usually used with an indirect object pronoun: "Ça m’a foutre la trouille" / "Il lui a foutre la trouille" (in practice you’ll most often hear the past participle form: "a foutu la trouille"). Used for a sudden, strong fright.
target_language_example: Ce film va te foutre la trouille.
native_language_example: That movie is going to scare the hell out of you.

meaning: to get out / leave (very informal, can be rude: “clear off!”).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French but vulgar because of the verb « foutre ». Often used to tell someone to leave (as an order, typically conjugated: « Fous le camp ! » / « Foutez le camp ! »), but it can also describe a situation that’s falling apart or going wrong: « Tout a commencé à foutre le camp » = “Everything started to go to hell / fall apart.”
target_language_example: Il me semble que vous devriez foutre le camp.
native_language_example: It seems to me that you should get out / leave.

meaning: to really scare (someone); to freak (someone) out.
additional_notes: Very informal and a bit vulgar because of "foutre". Commonly used with an indirect object pronoun: "Tu me fous les jetons" (You’re freaking me out) / "Ça me fout les jetons" (That really scares me). Stronger and slangier than "faire peur".
target_language_example: Ce film va te foutre les jetons !
native_language_example: That movie is going to really freak you out!

additional_notes: Used with a subject (often “quelqu’un”) to say there is a knock at the door. You can also ask “Qui frappe à la porte ?” (“Who’s knocking at the door?”). The verb is *frapper* (“to knock/strike”), and *à la porte* means “at the door.”
target_language_example: Quelqu’un frappe à la porte : tu peux ouvrir ?
native_language_example: Someone’s knocking at the door: can you open it?

additional_notes: Common idiom used to emphasize that it’s extremely cold (often said about the weather or a place). It’s informal/colloquial and is often used with « Il fait un froid de canard ! » or as an exclamation: « Quel froid de canard ! ».
target_language_example: Mets ton manteau : dehors, c’est un froid de canard !
native_language_example: Put on your coat—it's freezing cold outside!

additional_notes: Means cheese made from goat’s milk. Often used after verbs like aimer/détester/préférer, or when listing types of cheese (du fromage de chèvre). You can compare it with other cheeses: fromage de vache (cow’s cheese) / fromage de lait de vache (cheese made from cow’s milk).
target_language_example: Je prends une salade avec du fromage de chèvre.
native_language_example: I’ll have a salad with goat cheese.

additional_notes: Most often used in the plural: « fruits de mer ». Common on menus and in expressions like « plateau de fruits de mer » (a seafood platter). It generally refers to shellfish (oysters, mussels, shrimp, etc.) rather than fish.
target_language_example: Ce fruit de mer est très frais.
native_language_example: This seafood item is very fresh.

meaning: seafood (shellfish and other things from the sea).
additional_notes: Usually used as an uncountable category in French: manger des fruits de mer = “to eat seafood.” Often includes shellfish like shrimp, mussels, oysters, etc. Common with partitives/articles like des, les, and with acheter/vendre/manger.
target_language_example: On a commandé des fruits de mer au restaurant.
native_language_example: We ordered seafood at the restaurant.

additional_notes: Means your siblings as a group. It’s also used as a form of address to a group (often in religious contexts): « Bien chers frères et sœurs ! » = “Dear brothers and sisters!” (like “dear friends”).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas de frères et sœurs, je suis enfant unique.
native_language_example: I don't have any brothers or sisters; I'm an only child.

meaning: livelihood; the work that provides your income.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the job or activity that lets someone earn a living. Often appears with possessives (mon/son/leur gagne-pain) and in the plural when many people lose their source of income (perdre son gagne-pain / perdre ses gagne-pain).
target_language_example: Il ne veut pas changer de métier : c’est son gagne-pain.
native_language_example: He doesn’t want to change jobs: it’s his livelihood.

meaning: To save time; to buy yourself time.
additional_notes: Literally “to win time.” Very common with "faire" ("faire gagner du temps à quelqu’un" = to save someone time). You can also use it on its own: "On va gagner du temps" (We’ll save time).
target_language_example: Si on prend le métro, on va gagner du temps.
native_language_example: If we take the metro, we’ll save time.

meaning: to gain ground; to make progress (often by getting an advantage).
additional_notes: Used literally (e.g., an army advancing) or figuratively (an idea becoming more popular, a business increasing market share, someone improving in a competition). Often followed by "sur" + someone/something (gagner du terrain sur ses concurrents).
target_language_example: Notre équipe commence à gagner du terrain sur ses concurrents depuis le début de la saison.
native_language_example: Our team has started to gain ground on its competitors since the start of the season.

meaning: to earn a living; to make a living.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone supports themselves financially (usually through a job). Often appears with verbs like « devoir » (must), « pouvoir » (can), or questions like « Que fais-tu pour gagner ta vie ? ». The possessive changes with the subject: gagner ma/ta/sa/notre/votre/leur vie.
target_language_example: Elle travaille la nuit pour gagner sa vie.
native_language_example: She works at night to earn a living.

meaning: wardrobe; closet; (by extension) your clothes (your wardrobe).
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a closet/wardrobe where you store clothes: «dans la garde-robe». It can also mean your whole collection of clothes: «toute ma garde-robe». In some contexts (e.g., theater/film), «la garde-robe» can also refer to the costume/wardrobe department.
target_language_example: Je dois ranger ma garde-robe ce week-end.
native_language_example: I have to tidy up my closet/wardrobe this weekend.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a person whose job is to protect someone (often a celebrity, politician, etc.). Gender/number can vary: un garde du corps (most common), une garde du corps (also used, especially if the bodyguard is a woman), des gardes du corps (plural). Often used with possessives: mon/ton/son garde du corps.
target_language_example: Le chanteur se déplace toujours avec un garde du corps.
native_language_example: The singer always travels with a bodyguard.

meaning: police custody; being held by the police for questioning.
additional_notes: Used in legal/police contexts. Most often you’ll see it with être en garde à vue (to be in police custody) or être placé en garde à vue (to be taken/placed into police custody). It refers to a temporary measure during an investigation, not a prison sentence.
target_language_example: Elle a été placée en garde à vue après son interrogatoire.
native_language_example: She was taken into police custody after her questioning.

meaning: to keep watch; to keep an eye out.
additional_notes: Means staying alert and watching for something. In modern usage, more common forms are « garder l’œil ouvert » (stay alert/keep your eyes open) and « garder un œil sur + [quelqu’un/quelque chose] » (keep an eye on). « garder l'œil » on its own may sound a bit incomplete without context.
target_language_example: Quand tu es à la terrasse, garde l'œil sur ton sac.
native_language_example: When you’re sitting at the café terrace, keep an eye on your bag.

meaning: To keep a cool head; stay calm under pressure.
additional_notes: Used to say someone stays calm and thinks clearly in a stressful or tense situation. Often used as advice: « Garde la tête froide. »
target_language_example: Pendant l'examen, j'essaie de garder la tête froide.
native_language_example: During the exam, I try to keep a cool head.

meaning: 'to stay on course' / 'to stay on track' (keep pursuing the same goal).
additional_notes: Used both literally (a boat/plane keeps its heading) and figuratively (keep the same direction/plan despite difficulties). Often used with "il faut" or "on doit" to encourage perseverance: "Il faut garder le cap."
target_language_example: Malgré les difficultés, on doit garder le cap.
native_language_example: Despite the difficulties, we have to stay on track.

meaning: to keep quiet; to remain silent.
additional_notes: Used for staying silent on purpose (not speaking). Common with rules/requests (e.g., in class) and can also mean not speaking about something or to someone ("à mon égard" = "toward me / with me").
target_language_example: Merci de garder le silence dans la bibliothèque.
native_language_example: Please keep quiet in the library.

additional_notes: Means not telling other people confidential information. Often used after pouvoir (can) or savoir (know how/know how to) to say you are able to keep something confidential: « Je peux garder un secret » / « Je sais garder un secret ». In questions, « Tu peux… ? » is informal (to a friend) and « Pouvez-vous… ? » is more formal/polite.
target_language_example: Je peux garder un secret.
native_language_example: I can keep a secret.

additional_notes: A job title for someone who supervises inmates in a prison. You can also hear "surveillant (de prison)" in France in more official contexts.
target_language_example: Le gardien de prison ouvre la porte de la cellule.
native_language_example: The prison guard opens the cell door.

additional_notes: Used for the main place where long-distance and regional buses depart/arrive (a bus terminal). Not the same as a "gare" for trains ("gare ferroviaire"), though in some cities the bus and train stations are next to each other.
target_language_example: Les bus pour Lyon partent de la gare routière.
native_language_example: Buses to Lyon leave from the bus station.

meaning: tomboy (a girl who behaves in ways seen as boyish).
additional_notes: Used to describe a girl or woman who has interests, clothing, or behavior traditionally associated with boys/men (e.g., rough-and-tumble, sports, fighting). It can sound old-fashioned or judgmental depending on context, so use with care. Grammar note: the word "garçon" stays masculine in the expression; you still use feminine agreement for the person (e.g., "Elle est un garçon manqué").
target_language_example: Quand elle était petite, elle était un vrai garçon manqué : elle passait ses journées dehors à jouer au foot.
native_language_example: When she was little, she was a real tomboy: she spent her days outside playing soccer.

additional_notes: "Gentil" means kind/nice. With "être" (il est/était/a été), it describes someone’s behavior toward you. "Avec moi" specifies who they’re being kind to. You can change the pronoun: "gentil avec toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux". For a woman, use the feminine form: "gentille avec moi".
target_language_example: Merci, tu es vraiment gentil avec moi.
native_language_example: Thanks, you’re really kind to me.

additional_notes: Used for a flotation device worn on a boat or for water activities. You’ll also hear "gilet de sauvetage" in safety instructions. Note: "gilet" = vest, "sauvetage" = rescue.
target_language_example: N'oubliez pas de mettre votre gilet de sauvetage avant de monter dans le bateau.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to put on your life jacket before getting in the boat.

additional_notes: Used mostly with negation (ne… pas / ne… plus / ne… jamais) to mean “not much / not a lot” (e.g., ne pas servir à grand-chose = “to not be of much use”, il ne reste plus grand-chose = “there isn’t much left”). Without negation, it can mean “a lot,” but that use is less common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas appris grand-chose aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I didn’t learn much today.

additional_notes: A family word used when talking about or addressing a man who is your mother’s or father’s uncle. Often used with a possessive: « mon grand-oncle », « son grand-oncle ». The feminine form is « grand-tante » (great-aunt).
target_language_example: Mon grand-oncle habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My great-uncle lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: Means a grandparent (grandmother or grandfather). Often used in the plural: « les grands-parents ». You’ll also see « grand-mère » (grandmother) and « grand-père » (grandfather). The hyphen is common; plural adds -s: « des grands-parents ».
target_language_example: Mon grand-parent habite près de Lyon.
native_language_example: My grandparent lives near Lyon.

additional_notes: Usually means an older brother in the family (as opposed to a younger brother: « petit frère »). It can also be used directly to address someone like “big bro/brother,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Mon grand frère habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My older brother lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: Used for a special, significant date or event (often a wedding, an exam, a move, a launch, etc.). Common in questions like « C’est quand le grand jour ? » and announcements like « Le grand jour est arrivé ! ».
target_language_example: Demain, c’est le grand jour : je passe mon examen.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is the big day: I’m taking my exam.

meaning: department store (a large store with many sections).
additional_notes: Used with an article (le/un/ce) to talk about a big retail store that sells many kinds of products (clothes, home goods, etc.). You can also mention services inside, like a restaurant or food court: « manger au grand magasin ».
target_language_example: On se retrouve au grand magasin après le travail.
native_language_example: We'll meet at the department store after work.

additional_notes: Used to describe something fully open (a door, window, mouth, eyes, etc.). It agrees with the noun: masculine singular grand ouvert, feminine singular grande ouverte, masculine plural grands ouverts, feminine plural grands ouverts (masc.), feminine plural grandes ouvertes. Often placed after the noun: « la porte grande ouverte », « les yeux grands ouverts ».
target_language_example: J’ai laissé le portail grand ouvert toute la nuit.
native_language_example: I left the gate wide open all night.

meaning: big screen; the movie screen / cinema.
additional_notes: Used literally for a large display (TV, projector, presentation screen): « sur le grand écran » = “on the big screen.” Also used idiomatically to mean the world of cinema/films: « une star du grand écran » = “a movie star.” Often appears with « sur » (on) or « du » (of the).
target_language_example: Ce film est encore mieux sur grand écran.
native_language_example: This movie is even better on the big screen.

additional_notes: Very informal and often insulting, because *gueule* is a rough word for “mouth” (also used for animals). Common in **avoir une grande gueule** (“to be a loudmouth / to talk big”), and in **fermer sa grande gueule** (“shut your big mouth”). Can describe someone who talks a lot, talks too boldly, or brags.
target_language_example: Arrête de faire ta grande gueule et écoute un peu.
native_language_example: Stop being a loudmouth and listen a bit.

meaning: an adult; a tall/big person (depending on context).
additional_notes: Often means “grown-up/adult” (especially in childlike speech: « Je suis une grande personne. »). It can also be literal and mean a physically tall or large person (« une très grande personne »). Agreement changes with gender/number: « un grand monsieur », « une grande dame », « de grandes personnes ». Note: « grand/grande » can mean “great/important” with some nouns, but with « personne » it’s usually about size or being grown-up.
target_language_example: Laisse-moi faire, je suis une grande personne maintenant.
native_language_example: Let me do it, I’m a grown-up now.

additional_notes: Used for the large rotating wheel at a fair/carnival or in a city (like the London Eye). Often used with the article: « la grande roue ».
target_language_example: On monte dans la grande roue après le dîner ?
native_language_example: Shall we go on the Ferris wheel after dinner?

additional_notes: A masculine noun (un gratte-ciel). Often used when talking about city skylines; it can be singular or plural (des gratte-ciel). Literally “scrapes the sky,” but in English you say “skyscraper.”
target_language_example: Ils construisent un nouveau gratte-ciel dans le centre-ville.
native_language_example: They’re building a new skyscraper downtown.

additional_notes: Used with the definite article: « le grec ancien ». Often contrasted with « le grec moderne » (Modern Greek). You can use it after verbs like « parler » (to speak) or « connaître » (to know).
target_language_example: Elle étudie le grec ancien à l’université.
native_language_example: She studies Ancient Greek at university.

meaning: Modern Greek (the Greek language used today).
additional_notes: Used to distinguish today’s Greek from older forms like "grec ancien" (Ancient Greek). Usually appears in language-learning, translation, and comparison contexts (e.g., "traduire en grec moderne").
target_language_example: J'apprends le grec moderne depuis six mois.
native_language_example: I've been learning Modern Greek for six months.

additional_notes: A noun for the kitchen appliance that toasts bread. Often used with "dans" (in) or with verbs like "casser" (to break), "être coincé" (to be stuck), and "lâcher" (to give out/stop working): "Le pain est coincé dans le grille-pain."
target_language_example: Je vais mettre du pain dans le grille-pain.
native_language_example: I’m going to put some bread in the toaster.

meaning: plain old common sense; sound judgment.
additional_notes: Uses "gros" as an intensifier (like "real" / "good" in English), to stress that something is obvious and practical. Often said to suggest a simple solution rather than something complicated.
target_language_example: Avec un peu de gros bon sens, on peut régler ce problème rapidement.
native_language_example: With a bit of plain old common sense, we can solve this problem quickly.

meaning: a tough guy; a bully; a strongman (also literally: “big arms”).
additional_notes: Often used informally/ironically to talk to or about someone acting tough or trying to intimidate others ("jouer/faire le gros bras" = to act like a tough guy). It can also be literal: "avoir de gros bras" = to have big/muscular arms. Frequently used in the plural to refer to a group: "les gros bras" (the tough guys / the muscle).
target_language_example: Arrête de faire le gros bras, ça ne m'impressionne pas.
native_language_example: Stop acting like a tough guy—it doesn’t impress me.

additional_notes: "Gros" means "big/large" (often implying size or heaviness) and agrees with the noun: masculine singular "un gros chien"; feminine would be "une grosse…". With "avoir peur de", it often becomes "avoir peur du gros chien" (= de + le). Can also be used as an exclamation: "Quel gros chien !"
target_language_example: On a vu un gros chien dans le parc.
native_language_example: We saw a big dog in the park.

additional_notes: Used especially for lotteries, contests, or a big prize (“gagner/toucher/décrocher le gros lot”). It can also be used figuratively to mean someone “hit the jackpot” (got very lucky, found something great).
target_language_example: Avec ce billet, elle a touché le gros lot.
native_language_example: With that ticket, she hit the jackpot.

meaning: a swear word; a rude word.
additional_notes: Used to refer to profanity or rude language, often in a mild/child-friendly way (e.g., telling someone not to swear). Commonly used with verbs like dire (“to say”) or employer (“to use”): « Ne dis pas de gros mots. »
target_language_example: Ne dis pas de gros mots devant les enfants.
native_language_example: Don’t say swear words in front of the children.

additional_notes: Literally “big toe.” It’s the main toe on your foot; commonly used with body-part possessives like "mon/ton/son gros orteil" or with "le" when the person is clear from context (e.g., medical instructions: "Bouge le gros orteil").
target_language_example: J'ai un pansement sur mon gros orteil.
native_language_example: I have a bandage on my big toe.

meaning: a big fish; (figuratively) a “big fish” (an important person/major catch).
additional_notes: Often literal (a large fish you catch), but also used figuratively for an important/valuable person or target. Common idiom: « On a un plus gros poisson à frire » = “We have bigger fish to fry” (something more important to deal with).
target_language_example: Ils veulent attraper un gros poisson dans cette affaire.
native_language_example: They want to catch a big fish in this case.

meaning: a crude insult: “you big lump / you slob” (often implying “fat idiot”).
additional_notes: Used to insult someone directly (vocative), often intensified as “gros tas de merde” (“piece of shit”). It’s very rude and aggressive; avoid using it except to recognize it.
target_language_example: Arrête de te moquer, gros tas !
native_language_example: Stop making fun of me, you big slob!
