additional_notes: Used in newspapers, magazines, and online news for the main headline. Often appears in the expression « faire les gros titres » = “to make headlines.”
target_language_example: Cette affaire a fait les gros titres pendant des jours.
native_language_example: This case made the headlines for days.

meaning: “fat cow” (a very rude insult, usually aimed at a woman).
additional_notes: Literally means “big/fat cow,” but it’s used as an insulting name for someone (often implying they’re unpleasant and/or overweight). Very offensive; avoid in polite conversation. Can be used about someone (“cette grosse vache…”) or shouted as an insult (“Grosse vache !”).
target_language_example: Il l’a traitée de grosse vache, et elle s’est mise à pleurer.
native_language_example: He called her a fat cow, and she started crying.

additional_notes: Used in medical or emergency contexts to identify your blood classification (e.g., A, B, AB, O, and Rh +/−: « A positif », « O négatif »). Often asked as a question: « Quel est votre groupe sanguin ? »
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas mon groupe sanguin.
native_language_example: I don't know my blood type.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the person or thing that made something possible. Often has a positive or appreciative tone (like “thanks to”), but can sometimes be neutral. Followed by a noun/pronoun (grâce à moi, grâce à son travail) or an infinitive phrase with a subject (grâce à travailler dur).
target_language_example: Grâce à ton aide, j'ai fini le projet à temps.
native_language_example: Thanks to your help, I finished the project on time.

additional_notes: Used to give credit for a positive result ("thanks to you"), but it can also be ironic/blaming in context ("thanks to you, we’re in trouble"). Followed by a noun, name, or stressed pronoun: grâce à moi/toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux/elles.
target_language_example: Grâce à vous, j’ai trouvé mon chemin.
native_language_example: Thanks to you, I found my way.

meaning: civil war (a war within the same country/group).
additional_notes: Used for an internal conflict between groups from the same country/empire/organization (often political or military). It can also be used figuratively for a serious internal dispute (e.g., within a team or department).
target_language_example: Après des années de guerre civile, le pays a finalement signé un accord de paix.
native_language_example: After years of civil war, the country finally signed a peace agreement.

additional_notes: A historical event (1955–1975). In French, wars are often expressed as "la guerre de/du + place": here "du" = "de + le" because "Vietnam" is treated as masculine in this expression. Often used with "pendant" (during), "contre" (against), and verbs like "manifester" (to protest) or "être opposé à" (to be opposed to).
target_language_example: Mon grand-père a servi pendant la guerre du Vietnam.
native_language_example: My grandfather served during the Vietnam War.

additional_notes: Informal/common in spoken French. Used with avoir: "J’ai la gueule de bois" (not *je suis*). You can also ask: "T’as la gueule de bois ?" (= Tu as…). Literally means something like “wooden mouth,” but it doesn’t translate word-for-word in English.
target_language_example: Après la soirée, j’avais la gueule de bois toute la matinée.
native_language_example: After the party, I had a hangover all morning.

additional_notes: Usually means a person who shows visitors around ("un/une guide touristique"), often used as a job title: « Elle est guide touristique. ». It can also mean a travel guidebook, depending on context: « rédiger un guide touristique » = to write a travel guide.
target_language_example: Nous avons engagé une guide touristique pour visiter la ville.
native_language_example: We hired a tour guide to visit the city.

additional_notes: Used with a place to say where someone lives. Common with cities/countries (J'habite à Paris), and with a specific location you can also hear it as “lives at” (Elle habite à cette adresse). For “next door/nearby,” French often uses “à côté” (J'habite à côté).
target_language_example: J'habite à Montréal depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in Montreal for two years.

additional_notes: Used to show you don’t know, don’t care, or can’t do anything about a situation. Often implies indifference or resignation. Common in narration with the subject: « Il/Elle a haussé les épaules. »
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas quoi te dire, alors je vais hausser les épaules.
native_language_example: I don’t know what to tell you, so I’m going to shrug.

additional_notes: Usually a device that plays sound out loud (a loudspeaker). In phone contexts, « sur haut-parleur » means the call is on speakerphone: « Mets-le / Mettez-le sur le haut-parleur » = put it on speaker; « Tu es sur haut-parleur » = you’re on speaker.
target_language_example: Je te rappelle : je suis sur haut-parleur.
native_language_example: I’ll call you back: I’m on speaker.

additional_notes: Used as an adjective after a noun (e.g., un hôtel haut de gamme) to describe something upscale, premium, or luxury. It can also be used on its own as a short description/label (e.g., Haut de gamme.). Often contrasts with entrée de gamme (entry-level) or milieu de gamme (mid-range).
target_language_example: On cherche une voiture haut de gamme, mais pas trop chère.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a high-end car, but not too expensive.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who holds an important job or has a lot of authority (often in government, business, the military, etc.). It usually comes after the noun: « un responsable haut placé », « un fonctionnaire haut placé ».
target_language_example: La police a interrogé un responsable haut placé.
native_language_example: The police questioned a high-ranking official.

meaning: moment of glory; time to shine.
additional_notes: Used to talk (often playfully or dramatically) about a brief moment when someone gets attention, praise, or success. It’s commonly said with "C’est mon/ton heure de gloire" to mean “This is my/your moment.”
target_language_example: Allez, vas-y : c’est ton heure de gloire !
native_language_example: Go on—this is your moment of glory!

meaning: rush hour; peak time (when traffic/public transport is busiest).
additional_notes: Used for the busiest commuting times (often morning and late afternoon/evening). You can also see the plural: « aux heures de pointe ». Common with transport/traffic words like « trafic », « métro », « embouteillages ».
target_language_example: Évite de prendre le métro à l’heure de pointe.
native_language_example: Avoid taking the subway during rush hour.

meaning: the morning hours; (at) … o’clock in the morning.
additional_notes: Used to specify a time during the morning, especially very early (e.g., 2–6 a.m.). Often used after a number: « à trois heures du matin » = “at three in the morning.” You can also say « dans la matinée » for “during the morning” (less specific).
target_language_example: Je me suis réveillé à cinq heures du matin.
native_language_example: I woke up at five in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to express a daily rate or amount of time, usually with a number: « X heures par jour ». Common in schedules, work/study routines, habits, and recommendations. Often paired with verbs like travailler (to work), dormir (to sleep), étudier (to study), faire de l’exercice (to exercise).
target_language_example: Je travaille huit heures par jour.
native_language_example: I work eight hours per day.

additional_notes: Used when you work beyond your normal scheduled hours. Often appears with faire: « faire des heures supplémentaires » (= to work overtime), or with demander/souhaiter: « quelques heures supplémentaires » (= a few extra hours, often to finish something).
target_language_example: Cette semaine, on a fait des heures supplémentaires pour terminer le projet.
native_language_example: This week, we worked overtime to finish the project.

additional_notes: Used when greeting someone you’ve met before. "Vous" makes it polite/formal (one person formally or multiple people). Common variants: "Je suis (très) heureux/heureuse de vous revoir"; "Nous sommes heureux/heureuses de vous revoir". Agree "heureux" with the speaker(s): a man says "heureux", a woman says "heureuse", a mixed/masc. group "heureux", an all-female group "heureuses".
target_language_example: Je suis très heureux de vous revoir après toutes ces années.
native_language_example: I’m very happy to see you again after all these years.

additional_notes: Used to politely express pleasure at seeing someone you address as "vous" (one person formally, or more than one person). Often appears with "Je suis…" or "Nous sommes…" and can be intensified: "très/si heureux de vous voir". Feminine form: "heureuse de vous voir".
target_language_example: Nous sommes très heureux de vous voir ce soir.
native_language_example: We’re very happy to see you this evening.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened during the afternoon of the previous day. "Hier" = yesterday; "après-midi" = afternoon. Often used with past tenses (passé composé, imparfait).
target_language_example: On s'est parlé hier après-midi.
native_language_example: We talked yesterday afternoon.

additional_notes: Means “yesterday evening / last night,” referring to the evening of the previous day. Common in casual questions about what happened: “Et toi, hier soir ?” = “So, last night?”
target_language_example: On s'est vus hier soir au cinéma.
native_language_example: We saw each other last night at the movie theater.

meaning: “ancient history” (figuratively: something from the past that’s no longer important).
additional_notes: Often used as a set phrase: « C’est de l’histoire ancienne » = “That’s ancient history / That’s all in the past / Water under the bridge.” It can be said alone (« De l’histoire ancienne. ») to brush off a topic and move on.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas pour notre dispute : c’est de l’histoire ancienne.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about our argument: it’s all in the past.

meaning: “a story/history of …” or “just to / in order to …” (histoire de + infinitive).
additional_notes: 1) With a noun: "une histoire de + nom" = a story/history about something (often: “it’s a matter of …”, “it’s a family story”). 2) With an infinitive: "histoire de + infinitif" expresses purpose in a casual way: “just to…”, “so as to…”, “in order to…”. It often implies it’s not a big, serious goal, just a reason for doing something.
target_language_example: Je suis passé te voir, histoire de dire bonjour.
native_language_example: I stopped by to see you, just to say hi.

additional_notes: Refers to a man whose work involves business, commerce, or managing/owning a company. Plural: « des hommes d'affaires ». Feminine equivalent: « femme d'affaires ».
target_language_example: C'est un homme d'affaires très connu à Paris.
native_language_example: He's a very well-known businessman in Paris.

meaning: the right person for the job (the one who can handle the situation).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is particularly suited to solve a problem or manage a difficult moment. It’s a fixed expression; in modern usage you may also hear the more gender-neutral "la personne de la situation". Often used with "être" (e.g., "Il/Elle est l’homme/la personne de la situation").
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : Marie est l’homme de la situation, elle va trouver une solution.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: Marie is the right person for the job—she’ll find a solution.

meaning: caveman; a very primitive/old-fashioned man (often as an insult).
additional_notes: Literally “man of the caves.” Can refer to a prehistoric caveman, but it’s often used figuratively to say someone is backward, uncultured, or stuck in the past (and can sound mocking). You can also say “un homme préhistorique.” Feminine: “une femme des cavernes.”
target_language_example: Arrête de penser comme un homme des cavernes !
native_language_example: Stop thinking like a caveman!

meaning: an honest man; a decent/respectable man.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone with good morals who tells the truth and behaves correctly. In modern French you’ll also often hear the more gender-neutral "une personne honnête" (an honest person).
target_language_example: C'est un honnête homme : tu peux lui faire confiance.
native_language_example: He’s an honest man: you can trust him.

meaning: An appetizer; a starter (small dish served before the main meal).
additional_notes: Used on restaurant menus or when hosting: plural is usually "des hors-d'œuvre" (often pronounced like "or-derv"). It can refer to one item or a selection of small bites (cold or hot) served before the meal.
target_language_example: Pour commencer, je vais prendre les hors-d'œuvre.
native_language_example: To start, I’ll have the appetizers.

additional_notes: Used on menus or when serving food to refer to small dishes eaten before the main meal. In French it literally means “outside of the work/course,” but in everyday use it simply means “appetizer.”
target_language_example: Pour commencer, nous allons prendre des hors d'oeuvre.
native_language_example: To start, we’re going to have some appetizers.

additional_notes: Often expresses being outside something (a place, a situation, a category): « hors de l’eau » = out of the water; « hors de ça » = out of this / not involved in this. Common set phrases: « hors de moi / hors de lui » = beside myself/himself (very angry or upset); « hors de service » = out of order / not working (phone, machine, etc.).
target_language_example: Le distributeur est hors de service, donc je suis allé ailleurs.
native_language_example: The ATM is out of order, so I went somewhere else.

additional_notes: Used to say a person, situation, machine, emotions, etc. are no longer under control (can mean dangerous, chaotic, or impossible to manage). Often used with "être" (C'est/Il est/La situation est hors de contrôle) and can be intensified: "complètement" / "totalement" / "vraiment" hors de contrôle.
target_language_example: Après la panne, tout est devenu hors de contrôle.
native_language_example: After the breakdown, everything got out of control.

additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb être to say that someone is no longer in immediate risk (often after an accident, illness, or emergency). You can use it for one person or a group: Il/Elle est…, Nous sommes…, On est….
target_language_example: Après l'opération, il est enfin hors de danger.
native_language_example: After the operation, he's finally out of danger.

meaning: Out of reach; beyond one's means.
additional_notes: Used for things that can’t be reached physically (too far away) or can’t be obtained because they’re not accessible/affordable. Often followed by "pour moi/toi/nous" to mean something is not within someone’s budget or possibilities: "C’est hors de portée pour moi."
target_language_example: Ce restaurant est hors de portée pour nous cette année.
native_language_example: That restaurant is beyond our means for us this year.

additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t fit the subject or situation. Can be said alone as a sharp dismissal (“Hors de propos.”). Often follows nouns like remarque/question/commentaire: « une remarque hors de propos ».
target_language_example: Désolé, c’est hors de propos ici.
native_language_example: Sorry, that’s off-topic here.

meaning: out of the question; no way.
additional_notes: Used to strongly refuse or say something is impossible/forbidden. Often followed by “de” + infinitive: “Il est hors de question de…” (It’s out of the question to…). Can also be said alone as a firm “No way.”
target_language_example: Pour moi, il est hors de question de mentir à mes amis.
native_language_example: For me, it’s out of the question to lie to my friends.

additional_notes: Used mostly for machines, equipment, or services that are currently not functioning (e.g., air conditioning, vending machines, elevators, websites). Often seen on signs: « Appareil hors service » (Device out of order). With être: « C’est/Il est hors service ».
target_language_example: Désolé, l’ascenseur est hors service aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, the elevator is out of order today.

meaning: a hot dog (sausage in a bun).
additional_notes: Common loanword in French, used like in English. You may also see it written without a hyphen: "hot dog". Plural: "des hot-dogs".
target_language_example: Je prends un hot-dog avec de la moutarde, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll have a hot dog with mustard, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about age (Il a huit ans.), an amount of time in the past (il y a huit ans = eight years ago), or a duration (depuis/ça fait huit ans = for eight years). You also see it in comparisons: huit ans de plus/moins que… = eight years older/younger than…
target_language_example: Ça fait huit ans que j'habite ici.
native_language_example: I've lived here for eight years.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 800. When "cent" is multiplied and not followed by another number, it takes -s: "huit cents" (800). If another number follows, no -s: "huit cent un" (801).
target_language_example: Ça coûte huit cents euros.
native_language_example: It costs eight hundred euros.

additional_notes: Can mean a time on the clock (usually 8:00) or a duration (8 hours). With durations, you often add context like "par jour" (per day) or "de … à …" (from … to …). In work schedules, "minuit–huit heures" means “midnight to 8 a.m.”.
target_language_example: Le cours commence à huit heures.
native_language_example: The class starts at eight o’clock.

meaning: “hey, hey!” (to get attention, react, or gently warn someone).
additional_notes: Often said to stop someone, calm things down, or express mild surprise/interest (like “hey, wait” / “hold on” / “hey there”). Common in speech; punctuation and repetition can vary: “Hé, hé !”, “Hé !”, etc.
target_language_example: Hé, hé ! Attends une seconde, je n’ai pas fini.
native_language_example: Hey, hey! Wait a second, I’m not finished.

additional_notes: Used to say someone will be in this place later today (in the evening). Very common with verbs like être (to be), dormir (to sleep), rester (to stay), and with commands (e.g., “Sois ici ce soir.”).
target_language_example: Je serai ici ce soir, vers huit heures.
native_language_example: I’ll be here tonight, around eight o’clock.

meaning: "here for a long time" / "have been here for a long time".
additional_notes: Used to say someone has been in this place for a long time. Often appears in questions like « Vous êtes ici depuis longtemps ? » (“Have you been here long?”). With « depuis », French commonly uses the present tense to describe something that started in the past and is still true now (e.g., « J’habite ici depuis longtemps. »). It can also be used with past tenses to describe a long period in the past (e.g., « Ils ont vécu ici depuis longtemps. »).
target_language_example: Je suis ici depuis longtemps, mais je connais encore peu de monde.
native_language_example: I’ve been here for a long time, but I still don’t know many people.

meaning: here and there; in various places.
additional_notes: Used to mean “in different places,” often implying a scattered or occasional presence (e.g., looking/searching in several spots, threats happening in some places). Can also be a short answer to “Where?” meaning “around / in a few places.”
target_language_example: On a vu des affiches ici et là dans la ville.
native_language_example: We saw posters here and there around the city.

additional_notes: Used to say why someone/something is here (purpose/reason). Often followed by an infinitive: "ici pour + verb" ("here to + verb") or by a noun: "ici pour + noun" ("here for + noun/reason"). With time expressions it can also mean duration, e.g. "ici pour un moment" = "here for a while."
target_language_example: Je suis ici pour apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I'm here to learn French.

additional_notes: Usually means "he has" on its own. Very often it is also used as the auxiliary in the passé composé, followed by a past participle: for example, "il a appris" = "he learned" or "he has learned."
target_language_example: Il a oublié son sac.
native_language_example: He forgot his bag.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of accepter: il (he) + a (has) + accepté (accepted). Use it when a man/boy accepts an offer, proposal, job, invitation, etc. You’ll often add what he accepted with a direct object: « Il a accepté notre offre. » You can also add an adverb like « tout de suite » (right away) or « à contrecœur » (reluctantly).
target_language_example: Il a accepté l’invitation sans hésiter.
native_language_example: He accepted the invitation without hesitating.

meaning: "he bought a" / "he has bought a" (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of acheter: il + a (has) + acheté (bought). The object usually follows and can be any masculine singular noun starting with a consonant sound: un journal, un poulet, un terrain. For a feminine noun, use « il a acheté une… ». For plural, « il a acheté des… ».
target_language_example: Il a acheté un cadeau pour sa mère.
native_language_example: He bought a gift for his mother.

additional_notes: Used to describe when rain begins. Very common with time markers like soudain (suddenly), dès que (as soon as), peu après (shortly after), or with amounts like un peu (a little) / en abondance (heavily). Also appears in other tenses: il commence à pleuvoir (it’s starting to rain), il a commencé à pleuvoir (it started raining).
target_language_example: On venait juste d’arriver, et il a commencé à pleuvoir.
native_language_example: We had just arrived, and it started to rain.

meaning: he disappeared; he went missing; he's gone.
additional_notes: "Il" means "he" (or "it" for a masculine thing). "a disparu" is the past tense (passé composé) of "disparaître". Use it for someone/thing vanishing from sight ("dans la foule", "dans la nuit") or for someone going missing (often with "sans laisser de trace").
target_language_example: On ne l'a pas revu : il a disparu sans laisser de trace.
native_language_example: We didn’t see him again: he disappeared without a trace.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *dire* (“to say”). Common in reported speech, often followed by **que** + a clause (*Il a dit que...* = “He said that...”), or followed by an infinitive for indirect reporting (*Il a dit être...* = “He said (that) he was...”).
target_language_example: Il a dit qu’il viendrait demain.
native_language_example: He said he would come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man/boy said, introducing an indirect statement. Very often triggers backshifting in French (present → imperfect, future → conditional): « Il a dit qu'il allait bien » (He said he was fine), « Il a dit qu'il viendrait » (He said he would come). In speech, « que + il » contracts to « qu'il ».
target_language_example: Il a dit qu'il viendrait bientôt.
native_language_example: He said he would come soon.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an action he chose to do. It’s the passé composé of « décider » (decided). Pattern: « il a décidé de + infinitive » (e.g., louer, vendre, se mettre…). You can swap « il » for another subject: « j’ai décidé de… », « elle a décidé de… », « ils ont décidé de… ».
target_language_example: Il a décidé de partir plus tôt ce soir.
native_language_example: He decided to leave earlier tonight.

meaning: “he had to” or “he must have” (in the past).
additional_notes:
From the verb **devoir**. In the **passé composé** (**il a dû + infinitive**), it can express:
- **obligation/necessity**: *Il a dû vendre sa voiture.* = “He had to sell his car.”
- **a logical guess about the past** (deduction): *Il a dû faire froid.* = “It must have been cold.”
Context usually tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Il a dû partir tôt, parce qu’il avait un rendez-vous.
native_language_example: He must have left early because he had an appointment.

meaning: he tried to / he attempted to.
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb to say that a man (il) made an effort to do something. It’s the passé composé of essayer (j’ai essayé, il a essayé). In everyday speech you may also hear: « Il a essayé d’en parler » (de + en → d’en).
target_language_example: Il a essayé de m’appeler hier soir, mais je n’ai pas répondu.
native_language_example: He tried to call me last night, but I didn’t answer.

additional_notes: Passé composé of faire. It usually means 'he did' or 'he made', depending on what comes after it. Because faire is very flexible, it can also mean things like 'he caused' or be part of set expressions such as faire référence. With weather expressions like il a fait beau or il a fait chaud, il is impersonal and the whole phrase means 'it was' (for example, 'it was nice' or 'it was hot').
target_language_example: Il a fait ses devoirs avant le dîner.
native_language_example: He did his homework before dinner.

additional_notes: Past tense of the impersonal verb falloir (“to be necessary”). Used to say that something was required, or that it took some time/effort for something to happen. Pattern: il a fallu + noun (Il a fallu du temps/des efforts) or il a fallu que + subjunctive (Il a fallu que je + verb).
target_language_example: Il a fallu trois semaines pour finir le projet.
native_language_example: It took three weeks to finish the project.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *laisser*. It can mean (1) leaving something/someone behind (*Il a laissé sa mère en France* = he left his mother in France) or (2) letting something happen: **laisser + infinitive** (*Il a laissé le moteur tourner* = he let the engine run) or leaving something in a state (*Il a laissé la fenêtre ouverte* = he left the window open). In the common expression **laisser tomber**, it means “to drop” or “to give up” (*Il a laissé tomber* = he gave up).
target_language_example: Il a laissé son téléphone sur la table.
native_language_example: He left his phone on the table.

meaning: 'he took' (it took him) [time] to do something.
additional_notes: Used with a duration + "à" + infinitive: "Il a mis trois ans à écrire" = he spent/took three years writing. This is the passé composé of "mettre" used to talk about how long something took someone (not about placing/putting something).
target_language_example: Il a mis dix minutes à trouver ses clés.
native_language_example: It took him ten minutes to find his keys.

additional_notes: Weather expression using an impersonal subject: **il** doesn’t mean “he” here. Uses **passé composé** of *neiger* (avoir + neigé) to talk about snow that happened/has happened (often with a time period like *de lundi à vendredi*, *toute la journée*, or a place like *sur le balcon*).
target_language_example: Cette nuit, il a neigé, alors les routes sont glissantes.
native_language_example: It snowed last night, so the roads are slippery.

additional_notes: Common pattern with the passé composé of perdre (to lose): il a perdu + a noun. Son means “his” (also “her/its” depending on context) and is used before a masculine singular noun (son billet, son emploi) or before a vowel sound even if the noun is feminine (son amie).
target_language_example: Il a perdu son téléphone dans le métro.
native_language_example: He lost his phone on the subway.

additional_notes: Past tense of the verb *pleuvoir* (to rain). French uses a dummy subject *il* (“it”) for weather: *il pleut* (it’s raining), *il a plu* (it rained/has rained). Often followed by a duration with *pendant*: *Il a plu pendant trois jours* (It rained for three days).
target_language_example: Hier, il a plu toute la journée.
native_language_example: Yesterday, it rained all day.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of prendre: il (he) + a (has) + pris (taken). It’s used with a direct object, and the meaning depends on what follows. Common set phrases: prendre la fuite = run away; prendre part à = take part in; prendre le petit-déjeuner = have breakfast; prendre de la drogue = take drugs.
target_language_example: Il a pris le train pour rentrer chez lui.
native_language_example: He took the train to go home.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man (il) did not agree or chose not to do something. Followed by an infinitive (refuser de faire, refuser de venir). For other subjects: j’ai refusé de (I refused to), elle a refusé de (she refused to), ils/elles ont refusé de (they refused to).
target_language_example: Il a refusé de répondre aux questions.
native_language_example: He refused to answer the questions.

meaning: he managed to / he succeeded in.
additional_notes: "Réussir à" is followed by an infinitive (réussir à faire, réussir à escalader) and means achieving something, often despite difficulty. In the passé composé, "il a réussi à" refers to a completed success in the past. For passing an exam, French typically says "réussir un examen" (or "réussir à un examen"), not *"avoir son examen"* (though you may hear it).
target_language_example: Il a réussi à terminer le projet à temps.
native_language_example: He managed to finish the project on time.

meaning: he tried to / he attempted to.
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "tenter de" + infinitive. Used to say that a man tried to do something, often with a sense of effort and not necessarily success. Note the false friend: French "tenter" usually means "to try/attempt," not "to tempt" (that’s "tenter" only in the sense of "to tempt" someone, but many common uses mean "to attempt").
target_language_example: Il a tenté de l’appeler, mais il n’a pas répondu.
native_language_example: He tried to call him, but he didn’t answer.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « trouver » (to find). Often followed by what he found (il a trouvé la boîte), but can also be used alone when the object is understood: « Il a trouvé. » = “He found it” / “He figured it out.”
target_language_example: Après quelques minutes, il a trouvé ses clés.
native_language_example: After a few minutes, he found his keys.

additional_notes: Passé composé of écrire (to write): il (he) + a (has) + écrit (written). Used for a completed action in the past; often translates as simple past (“he wrote”) in English. It can take a direct object (Il a écrit un livre) or be followed by à for writing to someone (Il a écrit à ses parents).
target_language_example: Hier, il a écrit un e-mail à son professeur.
native_language_example: Yesterday, he wrote an email to his teacher.

additional_notes: Literally means "he/it has been," but very often appears before a past participle or adjective to make a passive or resulting-state meaning: "he/it was ..." The pronoun "il" can mean either "he" or "it," depending on context.
target_language_example: Il a été surpris par la nouvelle.
native_language_example: He was surprised by the news.

additional_notes: Present-tense form of avoir with il. Used to say that a male person, or a masculine noun referred to by il, possesses something or has a quality/state.
target_language_example: Il a deux frères.
native_language_example: He has two brothers.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy needs something. Follow it with a noun (Il a besoin de temps.) or with an infinitive verb (Il a besoin de changer de travail.). Before a vowel sound, de becomes d’ (Il a besoin d’aide.). You can change the subject: j’ai besoin de (I need), elle a besoin de (she needs), etc.
target_language_example: Il a besoin de repos après le travail.
native_language_example: He needs rest after work.

meaning: 'he has' (with a plural noun: 'he has some/any').
additional_notes: Used with a plural noun to say that a man/boy possesses something or has certain qualities/traits. "des" is the plural of the indefinite article (like "some"), and in many cases it’s not translated in English: "Il a des dents blanches" = "He has white teeth." You can swap the subject: "j’ai des", "elle a des", "on a des", etc.
target_language_example: Il a des amis en France.
native_language_example: He has friends in France.

meaning: “he looks / he seems” (talking about appearance or impression).
additional_notes: Literally “he has the air,” but it’s used to describe how someone appears or comes across. Very common with an adjective: « il a l'air sympa / fatigué / content ». In questions like « De quoi il a l'air ? », it means “What does he look like?” (often implying “What’s he like / what does he look like right now?”). Can also be used for things with « ça/elle/il »: « Ça a l'air neuf. »
target_language_example: Il a l'air très sympa.
native_language_example: He looks very nice.

additional_notes: Used to agree with what a man/boy has said or to say his opinion is correct. You can add details like "là-dessus" (about that) or "à mon avis" (in my opinion). Feminine: "elle a raison" (she is right). Plural: "ils ont raison" / "elles ont raison" (they are right).
target_language_example: Je pense qu'il a raison, mais ce n'est pas facile.
native_language_example: I think he’s right, but it’s not easy.

additional_notes: 'a' is the third-person singular of avoir ('to have'). 'un' is the masculine singular indefinite article, so this pattern is used before a masculine singular noun.
target_language_example: Il a un chien très calme.
native_language_example: He has a very calm dog.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir to talk about possession or something someone has. It can also introduce fixed expressions where avoir + noun expresses a feeling or state (e.g., il a une peur bleue = he’s terribly afraid). The feminine article une is used before a feminine singular noun.
target_language_example: Il a une voiture rouge.
native_language_example: He has a red car.

additional_notes: "Il" means "he" and "aime" is the present tense of "aimer" (to like/to love). Use it with a noun ("il aime la musique" = he likes music) or with an infinitive ("il aime vivre ici" = he likes living here). Depending on context, "aimer" can be as strong as "to love".
target_language_example: Il aime regarder des films le soir.
native_language_example: He likes watching movies in the evening.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens occasionally (not always). It’s impersonal and is followed by the subjunctive: Il arrive que + subject + verb (subj.). Example: Il arrive qu’il soit en retard. Similar in meaning to « il se peut que » (“it may be that”).
target_language_example: Il arrive que je sois fatigué le lundi.
native_language_example: Sometimes I’m tired on Mondays.

meaning: "he should have" / "he ought to have" (something he didn’t do, often with regret or criticism).
additional_notes: This is the past form of devoir used to talk about a missed obligation or a better choice in the past. Structure: il (he) + aurait (would have) + dû (had to/should have) + infinitive (e.g., acheter, travailler, être). Negative can wrap the infinitive: « Il aurait dû ne pas le faire » = “He should not have done it.”
target_language_example: Il aurait dû partir plus tôt.
native_language_example: He should have left earlier.

meaning: he could have (done); he might have (done).
additional_notes: Past conditional of pouvoir ("to be able to"): il + aurait (would have) + pu (been able). Used for a missed possibility in the past ("He could have finished earlier") or for something that might have happened (often a warning/regret: "Something could have happened to him"). Often followed by an infinitive: "il aurait pu finir / aider / se contenter de…" It can also stand alone: "Il aurait pu." = "He could have."
target_language_example: Il aurait pu venir, mais il était trop fatigué.
native_language_example: He could have come, but he was too tired.

meaning: “he had” / “he used to have” (imperfect of avoir); also “he had” in the pluperfect (plus-que-parfait).
additional_notes: Used to describe a past state or repeated situation (imperfect): Il avait faim. = He was hungry / He used to be hungry. Very commonly, it’s also the auxiliary verb for the pluperfect: il avait + past participle = “he had done” (something happened before another past moment), e.g., il avait perdu = he had lost. The feminine form is elle avait (“she had”).
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il avait déjà fini son travail.
native_language_example: When I arrived, he had already finished his work.

additional_notes: "Il avait" is the imperfect past of "avoir" (to have). It’s used for background descriptions in the past (states, possessions, feelings, ongoing situations) or habitual actions: "Il avait complètement tort" (He was completely wrong), "Il avait un certain charme" (He had a certain charm). In the pattern "il avait à + infinitive", it often means "he had to" / "he needed to": "Il a fait ce qu’il avait à faire" (He did what he had to do).
target_language_example: Quand j’étais petit, il avait toujours une histoire à raconter.
native_language_example: When I was little, he always had a story to tell.

additional_notes: Used to describe what someone had in the past (a possession, relative, idea, quality, etc.), often as background/description. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (une assurance, une cousine, une idée, une position, une voix).
target_language_example: Quand il était jeune, il avait une vieille voiture.
native_language_example: When he was young, he had an old car.

meaning: “he should be” / “he is supposed to be” (likely/expected).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of devoir (devrait) + infinitive être to express expectation, probability, or what is considered appropriate. Often followed by a place/time/state: il devrait être ici (he should be here), il devrait être en prison (he ought to be in prison), il devrait être arrivé… (he should have arrived…).
target_language_example: Il devrait être à la maison maintenant.
native_language_example: He should be at home by now.

additional_notes: From devoir. It can express obligation or necessity ("has to / must"), a strong guess ("must be / must come from"), or what is expected or appropriate (sometimes "should"). Because il can mean both "he" and "it," the exact English translation depends on context.
target_language_example: Il doit être fatigué après le voyage.
native_language_example: He must be tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Used to express a strong assumption or conviction that something exists or is the case. Often followed by a noun or pronoun: « Il doit bien y avoir une solution / quelqu’un / quelque chose ». « bien » adds emphasis like “surely / really”.
target_language_example: Il doit bien y avoir une solution, on va la trouver.
native_language_example: There’s got to be a solution—we’re going to find it.

additional_notes: Used to express that you believe something exists or is true (a strong guess), often based on logic or clues. Built from "il doit" (it must) + "y avoir" (there to be). Commonly followed by a noun or "quelque chose": "Il doit y avoir une raison" (There must be a reason), "Il doit y avoir quelque chose à faire" (There must be something to do).
target_language_example: Il doit y avoir une erreur dans le message.
native_language_example: There must be a mistake in the message.

meaning: "there must be a" / "there should be a" (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to express assumption or strong probability that something exists. Built from: il doit (it must) + y avoir (there to be). The following noun is feminine singular; with a masculine noun you’d say "il doit y avoir un"; with plural "il doit y avoir des".
target_language_example: Il doit y avoir une solution plus simple.
native_language_example: There must be a simpler solution.

additional_notes: Used with "devoir" (must/probably) + "y en avoir" (to be some/any of it/them). It expresses an estimate or assumption about existence/quantity, often followed by a number/amount: "Il doit y en avoir des milliers" (There must be thousands). "y" refers to a place/context (there), and "en" replaces the thing being counted (some/any of them).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il doit y en avoir d’autres au magasin.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there must be others at the store.

meaning: 'he must be' / 'he has to be' (often a deduction).
additional_notes: Uses the verb devoir + infinitive (être) to express a strong guess based on evidence: “He must be…” It can also mean obligation depending on context, but in many everyday sentences it’s about deduction. Can be used with other subjects too (je dois être, ça doit être, ils doivent être).
target_language_example: Il doit être fatigué après le voyage.
native_language_example: He must be tired after the trip.

meaning: "he has (some/of it/of them)" (with "en" replacing something introduced with de).
additional_notes: "En" is a pronoun that usually replaces "de + noun" (or "des + noun"). With "avoir", it’s very common when you mention a quantity or an unspecified amount: "Il en a trois" = "He has three (of them)." It can also appear in set expressions like "en avoir après quelqu’un" (to be after someone / hold a grudge against someone) and "en avoir pour longtemps" (to take a long time / to have a lot left to do). What "en" refers to is understood from context.
target_language_example: Il en a deux, mais j’en veux trois.
native_language_example: He has two, but I want three.

additional_notes: Uses the pronoun "en" to mean "some/any of it/them" and "reste" from "rester" (to remain). Very common when talking about quantities: "Il en reste deux" = "There are two left." You can add "encore" to mean "still": "Il en reste encore."
target_language_example: Tu veux un biscuit ? Il en reste trois.
native_language_example: Do you want a cookie? There are three left.

additional_notes: Basic combination of il + est. It usually means "he is" when talking about a male person, but it can also mean "it is" when referring to a thing or situation from context.
target_language_example: Il est très gentil.
native_language_example: He is very kind.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "aller" (to go). It uses "être" as the helping verb, and the past participle "allé" agrees with the subject (e.g., "elle est allée", "ils sont allés", "elles sont allées"). Often followed by an infinitive to show purpose: "il est allé + infinitive" = "he went to + verb" (e.g., "il est allé dire..." = "he went to say...").
target_language_example: Il est allé chercher du pain à la boulangerie.
native_language_example: He went to get bread at the bakery.

additional_notes: Past tense of aller (to go) with être: il est allé. Used before a place introduced by à (a city, a place name, etc.). You can swap il (he) for other subjects: elle est allée à…, je suis allé(e) à…, ils/elles sont allé(e)s à….
target_language_example: Il est allé à Paris la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: He went to Paris last week.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "arriver" using the auxiliary "être". Often used with a place or time: "Il est arrivé ici avant midi." In questions it can mean “How did he get there?” (how he ended up there). You can also add details like "dix minutes en avance" (ten minutes early) or "sans encombre" (safely, without problems).
target_language_example: Il est arrivé à l’aéroport très tôt.
native_language_example: He arrived at the airport very early.

meaning: 'he is good' (at something) / 'is it good?' (about food).
additional_notes: Used with a person to say they’re good at an activity: « Il est bon au basket / au foot ». With a noun (often without a preposition) it can describe a quality: « Il est bon conducteur » (“He’s a good driver”). With food, « C’est bon ? » is more common than « Il est bon ? », but you may still hear « Il est bon, le tofu ? » meaning “Is tofu good?” (often with « le + noun » as a topic).
target_language_example: Il est bon en maths, mais il n'aime pas ça.
native_language_example: He’s good at math, but he doesn’t like it.

meaning: 'he is in' / 'he is inside' (in a place, object, or situation).
additional_notes: Used as **il est dans + noun phrase** to say where something/someone is: *Il est dans le bâtiment / dans mon sac.* It can also be figurative to mean being involved or part of something: *Il est dans une affaire* (“he’s involved in something”), or in idioms like *Il est dans mes petits papiers* (“he’s in my good books”).
target_language_example: Il est dans la cuisine.
native_language_example: He is in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *devenir* (“to become”), used to describe a change of state or identity. It’s commonly followed by an adjective (*Il est devenu dingue*), a noun with an article (*Il est devenu un acteur célèbre*), or sometimes a nationality/status (*Il est devenu algérien*).
target_language_example: Après l’accident, il est devenu très prudent.
native_language_example: After the accident, he became very cautious.

additional_notes: Impersonal structure: **il est + adjective + de + infinitive**. It’s used to make a general statement (not specifically about “he”). Often followed by a verb in the infinitive: *il est difficile de comprendre / faire / parler à quelqu’un*.
target_language_example: Il est difficile de rester calme dans cette situation.
native_language_example: It’s difficult to stay calm in this situation.

meaning: 'he is (in the middle of) doing' / 'he is currently (doing)'.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that an action is happening right now (the French way to express the English present continuous "he is doing"). It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « il est en train de + infinitive ». You can change the subject: « je suis en train de… », « elle est en train de… », « ils/elles sont en train de… ».
target_language_example: Il est en train de préparer le dîner.
native_language_example: He’s making dinner (right now).

additional_notes: Used to say someone is still present or something is still true at the moment. Often followed by an adverb of place like « là » (here/there): « Il est encore là. » Note: « encore » can also mean “again” in other contexts, but here it means “still.”
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, il est encore là.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, he’s still here.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb (il est impossible de + infinitif) to say something cannot be done or is not possible. It’s a neutral/formal structure (impersonal "il"); you can also use the more direct but similar "c’est impossible de" or "c’est impossible à" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Il est impossible de tout prévoir.
native_language_example: It’s impossible to predict everything.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy is present or has arrived. "Là" can mean either "here" or "there" depending on the situation (where the speaker is pointing/looking). It’s often repeated for emphasis ("Il est là, il est là") when you’ve found someone or want to draw attention to their presence.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, il est là.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, he’s here.

additional_notes: Used to state that a man has died. With time expressions: « Il est mort il y a cinq ans » (he died five years ago). With causes: « Il est mort dans un accident » (he died in an accident), « Il est mort de mort naturelle » (he died of natural causes). With « pour » it can mean dying for a cause or purpose: « Il est mort pour son pays » (he died for his country).
target_language_example: Il est mort hier soir à l’hôpital.
native_language_example: He died last night at the hospital.

meaning: "he was born" / "he is born" (used for birth).
additional_notes: Used to say where/when someone was born. In French, birth is expressed with the verb "naître" and the auxiliary "être" in the past tense: "il est né" (he was born), "elle est née" (she was born), "ils sont nés" (they were born), "elles sont nées" (they were born). The past participle agrees with the subject (né/née/nés/nées). Often followed by "à" + city and "aux"/"en"/"dans" + country/region.
target_language_example: Il est né en France, mais il a grandi au Canada.
native_language_example: He was born in France, but he grew up in Canada.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of « partir » with « être » as the helping verb. Used when someone has left a place, often with a destination (e.g., « il est parti en vacances / pour New York »). In some contexts it can be a gentle/euphemistic way to say someone has passed away (the tone depends on context).
target_language_example: Il est parti tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: He left early this morning.

meaning: "it is likely that" / "it is probable that".
additional_notes: Used to say something is probably true, but not 100% certain. It often introduces a clause with the subjunctive (especially in more formal French): « Il est probable qu’il vienne. » In everyday speech you may also hear the indicative, especially when the speaker feels fairly sure: « Il est probable qu’il vient demain. »
target_language_example: Il est probable que nous arrivions en retard.
native_language_example: It’s likely that we’ll arrive late.

additional_notes: Common spoken word order for asking the time. Often used with a question mark: « Il est quelle heure ? ». A more formal/standard version is « Quelle heure est-il ? ».
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, il est quelle heure ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time is it?

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *rester* with *être*: *il est resté*. Used for staying in a place (*il est resté au Japon / chez moi / dehors*) and also for remaining in a state or position (*il est resté couché, debout, muet, fidèle à...*). The feminine form is *elle est restée* (often with an extra -e), and in plural: *ils sont restés / elles sont restées* (agreement in writing).
target_language_example: Il est resté à la maison toute la journée.
native_language_example: He stayed at home all day.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *revenir* with **être**: *il est revenu* (he came back). The feminine form is *elle est revenue*. Often followed by a place with **à/chez/ici** (*il est revenu chez lui*), or by an origin with **de** (*il est revenu de France*).
target_language_example: Il est revenu trop tard pour le dîner.
native_language_example: He came back too late for dinner.

additional_notes: Used to say that the right moment has arrived to do an action. It is followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., partir, voter, dire, découvrir).
target_language_example: Il est temps de partir, on est en retard.
native_language_example: It's time to leave; we're late.

meaning: "it’s time for you to…" / "it’s about time you…"
additional_notes: Used to say someone should do something now (often as advice, a push, or impatience). It’s normally followed by the subjunctive: « Il est temps que tu grandisses. » If you want the simple infinitive structure instead, you can also say: « Il est temps de + infinitive » (e.g., « Il est temps de partir. »).
target_language_example: Il est temps que tu fasses tes devoirs.
native_language_example: It’s time for you to do your homework.

meaning: 'he fell' (or, in 'tomber malade', 'he got sick / fell ill').
additional_notes: Passé composé of *tomber* uses **être**: *il est tombé*. It can be literal (physically falling: *dans la rivière*) or part of common expressions like **tomber malade** = “to fall ill / get sick.” (Feminine: *elle est tombée*; plural: *ils sont tombés*, *elles sont tombées*.)
target_language_example: Il est tombé et il s'est fait mal au genou.
native_language_example: He fell and hurt his knee.

additional_notes: Used to describe a habitual or constant situation. With a person, it often comes before an adjective (Il est toujours ponctuel = He’s always punctual) or before a place/time expression (Il est toujours à l’hôpital = He’s still/always at the hospital). In patterns like « Il est toujours + adjective + de + infinitive » (Il est toujours bon de…), « il » is impersonal and means “it” (“It’s always good to…”).
target_language_example: Il est toujours important de vérifier l’adresse.
native_language_example: It’s always important to check the address.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective to say someone is excessively something. Very often followed by an infinitive with « pour »: « Il est trop + adjectif + pour + verbe » (e.g., “too big to run fast”). In everyday spoken French, « trop » is also often used informally to mean “really/so” (e.g., « Il est trop malin ! » = “He’s so smart!”), depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Il est trop fatigué pour sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: He’s too tired to go out tonight.

additional_notes: Used to describe a male person (or masculine noun) with an adjective: "Il est très + adjective" (e.g., "Il est très connu" = "He is very well-known"). For a female person: "elle est très". For things/ideas you often use "c'est très" ("It's very").
target_language_example: Il est très content aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: He is very happy today.

additional_notes: Past tense of "venir" (to come), using the passé composé with "être": il + est + venu. In English it can be "he came" or "he has come" depending on context. "Venu" agrees with the subject (il → venu; elle → venue; ils → venus; elles → venues). Often followed by an infinitive to say why he came: "il est venu me voir" (he came to see me).
target_language_example: Il est venu me voir hier soir.
native_language_example: He came to see me last night.

additional_notes:
Used with different meanings depending on what comes after:
- être à + place = location: « Il est à Paris » = “He’s in Paris.” « Il est à son bureau » = “He’s at his office/desk.”
- être à + person/pronoun = possession (“it’s someone’s”): « il est à vous » = “it’s yours.”
- être à + infinitive (often passive meaning) = “to be to … / to be for …”: « Il est à blâmer » = “He is to blame.”
target_language_example: Si vous le trouvez, il est à vous.
native_language_example: If you find it, it’s yours.

additional_notes: Imperfect of faire (“to do/make”). Very common in the impersonal pattern il faisait + adjective/noun for weather or conditions: il faisait froid/chaud (“it was cold/hot”), il faisait nuit (“it was nighttime / it was already dark”). In questions like Qu’est-ce qu’il faisait ? it usually means “What was he doing?” Also appears in the expression faire partie de (“to be part of”): il faisait partie de… (“he was part of…”).
target_language_example: Hier soir, il faisait très froid, alors je suis resté à la maison.
native_language_example: Last night, it was very cold, so I stayed at home.

additional_notes: Present tense of faire with il. Usually refers to a male person: 'he does' or 'he makes'. In impersonal expressions about weather or general conditions, il does not mean a person: il fait chaud / froid = 'it's hot / cold'.
target_language_example: Il fait ses devoirs après l'école.
native_language_example: He does his homework after school.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal weather expression "il fait + adjective" (literally “it makes/does + adjective”). You can add a place with "à" (Il fait froid à Boston.) or use "quand" to mean “when it’s cold.”
target_language_example: Ferme la fenêtre : il fait froid dans l’appartement.
native_language_example: Close the window: it’s cold in the apartment.

additional_notes: Imperfect of "il faut" (to be necessary). Used to talk about a necessity or obligation in the past, often in a general/ongoing way. Very commonly followed by "que" + subjunctive: "Il fallait que je parte" = "I had to leave" (literally: "it was necessary that I leave"). In casual speech, "Il fallait pas" means "You/I shouldn’t have" or "It wasn’t necessary."
target_language_example: Il fallait que je rentre tôt, alors je suis parti.
native_language_example: I had to get home early, so I left.

additional_notes: Impersonal form of devoir in the future tense (from "il faut"). Used to say something will be required or unavoidable. Often followed by an infinitive: "il faudra + verb" (il faudra apprendre). Can also be used with "bien" to mean 'we really will have to' / 'we’d better' (il faudra bien y aller), or with "se faire à" to mean 'get used to it' (il faudra vous y faire).
target_language_example: Il faudra partir tôt demain.
native_language_example: We’ll have to leave early tomorrow.

additional_notes: An impersonal expression used to talk about necessity or obligation. Literally it means something like "it is necessary," but in everyday English it is usually translated as "must" or "have to." It is often followed by an infinitive: il faut partir = we/you have to leave.
target_language_example: Il faut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: We have to leave now.

additional_notes: Built with the impersonal expression **il faut** + infinitive. It means “it’s necessary to…,” and often translates as “you have to…” or “we need to…,” depending on context. It’s commonly followed by a place/direction (**aller à… / par là / ici**) or by another infinitive idea like **aller le/la chercher** (“go get him/her/it”).
target_language_example: Il est tard : il faut aller à la maison.
native_language_example: It’s late: we have to go home.

meaning: "you have to / you need to" + "some (of it/them)" or "about it/them".
additional_notes: “Il faut” expresses necessity (“one must/it’s necessary”). “En” is the pronoun that usually replaces something introduced by de (de + noun), and it can mean “some (of it/them)” or “of it/them/about it/them,” depending on the verb or expression. Common patterns: Il faut en acheter un/une (“You need to buy one (of them)”), il faut en tenir compte (“You have to take it into account”), il faut en profiter (“You have to take advantage of it”). Note: “prendre compte” is not standard; it’s usually “tenir compte de …”.
target_language_example: On n’a plus de pain : il faut en acheter.
native_language_example: We don’t have any bread left: we need to buy some.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression: it doesn’t refer to a specific “he.” Used to say something is necessary/required. Common pattern: « il faut + infinitive » (here, « faire »), often followed by what needs doing: « Il faut faire vite » (We have to be quick). Can also take a direct object: « Il faut faire quelque chose » (Something must be done).
target_language_example: Il faut faire attention quand on traverse la rue.
native_language_example: You have to be careful when crossing the street.

additional_notes: "Il faut" is an impersonal way to say something is necessary/required. "La" is a direct object pronoun meaning "her" or "it" for a feminine singular person/thing previously mentioned (e.g., la table → il faut la réparer; Mélanie → il faut la croire). This pattern is usually followed by an infinitive: il faut la + verb (inf.).
target_language_example: La voiture est en panne : il faut la faire réparer.
native_language_example: The car is broken down: we have to get it repaired.

meaning: “You have to do it / it must be done.” (Also: “Can you believe it?!” as an exclamation.)
additional_notes: Built on **il faut** (“it’s necessary / you must”) + **le faire** (“do it”). Used to express necessity or obligation: *Il faut le faire manuellement.* = “You have to do it manually.” With an exclamation (**Il faut le faire !**), it can express strong surprise, admiration, or indignation (similar to “You’ve got to be kidding!” / “I can’t believe it!”), depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Il faut le faire aujourd’hui, sinon ce sera trop tard.
native_language_example: You have to do it today, otherwise it’ll be too late.

meaning: 'they must be' / 'we (you) need to' + them (before a verb).
additional_notes: "Il faut" is an impersonal way to say something is necessary/required. It’s usually followed by an infinitive (Il faut + verb). "Les" is a direct object pronoun meaning "them" and it comes before the infinitive: Il faut les ouvrir = "We/You have to open them." Often translates as "we have to" or "you have to" depending on context.
target_language_example: Il faut les nettoyer avant de partir.
native_language_example: We/You have to clean them before leaving.

additional_notes: Used with the impersonal expression **il faut** (“it’s necessary”) followed by a **reflexive verb** starting with **se**: *il faut se comprendre* (“we/you have to understand each other”), *il faut se dire* (“you have to tell yourself”). The subject is general (people in general, we, you, one) and depends on context.
target_language_example: Il faut se calmer avant de parler.
native_language_example: You have to calm down before speaking.

meaning: we/you have to go; we/you need to leave.
additional_notes: Used to say it’s necessary to leave or get going. "Il faut" is an impersonal way to mean "it’s necessary" (often said as "we/you have to" in English). "Y" refers to the place/activity you’re going to, so in this phrase it usually just means "go/leave" without naming the destination. Often used as a prompt, sometimes urgently: "Vite, il faut y aller !"
target_language_example: On est en retard, il faut y aller !
native_language_example: We’re late—we have to go!

meaning: "you have to be" / "one must be" (it’s necessary to be).
additional_notes: Impersonal expression ("il" doesn’t refer to a person). Used to express necessity or a requirement. Commonly followed by an adjective (Il faut être prudents.), a noun phrase (Il faut être médecin pour faire ça.), or a complement like "à + infinitive" (Il faut être deux pour porter ça.). Can be general advice/rules or what’s needed for something to work.
target_language_example: Pour réussir, il faut être patient.
native_language_example: To succeed, you have to be patient.

additional_notes: An impersonal expression used to say that something is necessary, required, or needed. Common patterns are il faut + noun (Il faut du temps. = Time is needed / It takes time.), il faut + infinitive (Il faut partir. = We/you must leave.), and il faut que + subjunctive to say what a specific person must do (Il faut que tu viennes. = You have to come.).
target_language_example: Il faut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: We need to leave now.

meaning: "he has to / it’s necessary that he" (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity, obligation, or something required about “he” (il). The verb after "qu'il" is normally in the subjunctive: "il faut qu'il parle" (he must speak). Can also mean “it’s important that he… / he needs to…” depending on context.
target_language_example: Il faut qu'il vienne demain.
native_language_example: He has to come tomorrow.

meaning: “we have to / we need to” (literally: “it’s necessary that we…”).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation for a group including the speaker. It is followed by the subjunctive in French: il faut qu'on + verb (ex: qu'on aille, qu'on appelle, qu'on discute). "Qu'on" is the contraction of "que" + "on" (here, "on" often means "we" in everyday French).
target_language_example: il faut qu'on discute.
native_language_example: We need to talk.

meaning: "We need to talk" / "We have to talk."
additional_notes: Literally "it’s necessary that we talk." Very common to introduce an important (sometimes serious) conversation. After "il faut que", French uses the subjunctive: "qu’on parle". Often followed by "de + [topic]" (il faut qu’on parle de ça) or "en privé" (in private).
target_language_example: Il faut qu'on parle après le dîner.
native_language_example: We need to talk after dinner.

meaning: “I have to go” / “I need to go.”
additional_notes: Built from the impersonal expression “il faut” (“it’s necessary”) + “que” + the subjunctive of “aller” (“j’aille” = “I go”). Used to express that you must go somewhere or go do something; often followed by a destination (e.g., “au lycée”, “à l’hôpital”) or by an infinitive/verb phrase (e.g., “bosser”, “travailler”, “le voir”).
target_language_example: Il faut que j'aille au lycée.
native_language_example: I have to go to high school.

meaning: "I have to go" / "I need to go" (I must leave).
additional_notes: Used to say you have an obligation/need to leave. Built from: "il faut" (it’s necessary) + "que" + subjunctive "j’aille" (that I go). "y" means “there/to it” and often just refers to leaving in general. Common with softeners like "écoute(z)", "OK ?", "je crois que...".
target_language_example: Désolé, il faut que j'y aille : j'ai un rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go: I have an appointment.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is necessary for the speaker to do. It is followed by a verb in the subjunctive: il faut que je + subjunctive. Literally, it means "it is necessary that I..."
target_language_example: Il faut que je parte maintenant.
native_language_example: I have to leave now.

meaning: "I have to" / "I need to" (followed by a verb).
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal expression "il faut" (it is necessary) + "que" + subjunctive: "je fasse" (from "faire"). It expresses necessity/obligation (from strong need to a requirement). Often followed by what you must do: "Il faut que je fasse + [noun/verb phrase]". Question form: "Qu'est-ce qu'il faut que je fasse ?" = "What do I have to do?".
target_language_example: Il faut que je fasse mes devoirs avant ce soir.
native_language_example: I have to do my homework before tonight.

meaning: "I have to / I need to (myself)…" (starting a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used to say something is necessary: **il faut que + subject + verb** (usually in the **subjunctive**). Here, **je me** shows the next verb is **reflexive** (an action you do to yourself): *je me cache* (I hide), *je me coiffe* (I do my hair), *je me tire* (I get out of here / I leave—informal).
target_language_example: Il faut que je me dépêche.
native_language_example: I have to hurry.

il faut que je te parle

target_language_multi_word_term: il faut que je te parle
meaning: I need to talk to you / I have to talk to you.
additional_notes: Common way to introduce an important or urgent conversation. Literally “it’s necessary that I talk to you,” using the expression il faut que + subjunctive (je parle). Often followed by de + topic (de ça, d’un truc) or en privé (“in private”). Can sound serious depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Il faut que je te parle ce soir, c’est important.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you tonight; it’s important.

meaning: "we need to / we have to" (it’s necessary that we…).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation. After "il faut que", French uses the subjunctive: "nous commencions", "nous parlions", "nous partions", etc. Often translates as "we have to" or "we must" in English.
target_language_example: Il faut que nous fassions attention.
native_language_example: We have to be careful.

additional_notes: Used to say something is necessary/required. Literally: “it’s necessary that you…”. It’s built with the verb falloir (impersonal: il faut) + que + a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., il faut que tu comprennes / que tu rentres…). Often used for advice, instructions, or requirements.
target_language_example: Il faut que tu sois à l’heure demain.
native_language_example: You have to be on time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation. After « il faut que », French uses the subjunctive: « que vous compreniez / laissiez / parliez / sachiez / travailliez / voyiez ». « vous » can mean either 'you' (formal singular) or 'you all' (plural).
target_language_example: Il faut que vous soyez à l’heure demain.
native_language_example: You need to be on time tomorrow.

additional_notes: A formal/literary past tense mainly used in written French (stories, history). In everyday speech, you usually use "il a été" (completed past: he was/has been) or "il était" (ongoing past: he was).
target_language_example: Il fut très heureux d'apprendre la nouvelle.
native_language_example: He was very happy to hear the news.

meaning: “he has it / he did it” (il + l’ + a).
additional_notes: Very common structure: **il** (he) + **l’** (short for *le* or *la*, meaning “it/him/her”) + **a** (has, from *avoir*). Used with the **passé composé** before a past participle: *Et il l'a trouvé* = “And he found it.” If followed by **été**, it can mean “he was/has been (that)”: *Il l'a été* = “He was (that).”
target_language_example: Et il l'a trouvé.
native_language_example: And he found it.

additional_notes: Very common past tense using the passé composé: il + l’ (short for "le" or "la" = "it") + a fait ("has done/did"). The l’ refers to something already mentioned or understood from context. Often followed by a reason or purpose: "Il l’a fait pour toi" (He did it for you), or with emphasis like "exprès" (on purpose) and "lui-même" (himself).
target_language_example: Il l'a fait hier soir, mais il ne veut pas en parler.
native_language_example: He did it last night, but he doesn’t want to talk about it.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression with falloir. Uses "le" to refer to "it" (the action/situation). Common in set phrases like "s’il le faut" (if necessary) and "quand il le faut" (when necessary).
target_language_example: Je viendrai te chercher à minuit, s’il le faut.
native_language_example: I’ll come pick you up at midnight, if necessary.

additional_notes: Common chunk in the passé composé: subject + direct object pronoun (les = “them”) + auxiliary avoir (a). In English, you usually translate it as “he + past tense verb + them” (e.g., “he beat them / he drew them”). With a direct object pronoun placed before avoir, the past participle often agrees in gender/number with les: Il les a battues (them = feminine plural), Il les a tirés (them = masculine plural).
target_language_example: Il les a déjà vues.
native_language_example: He has already seen them.

additional_notes: "Il" usually means "he" (or "it" in impersonal expressions). "Lui" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him" or "to her" (same form for both). "A" is the auxiliary verb "avoir" in the passé composé (past tense): it’s followed by a past participle (e.g., "il lui a montré" = "he showed him/her"). In impersonal phrases like "il lui a été difficile…", it means "it was difficult for him/her…".
target_language_example: Il lui a dit la vérité.
native_language_example: He told him/her the truth.

additional_notes: Very common pattern in the passé composé: "il" (he) + "m'" (= me, short for "me") + "a" (has, from "avoir") + past participle. It means “he did [something] to/for me” or “he [verb]ed me.” The "m'" goes before the verb (before "a"). Used before a vowel or silent h (otherwise it’s "il m’a" vs "il me + consonant").
target_language_example: Il m'a appelé hier soir.
native_language_example: He called me last night.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. il means 'he' or 'it', and me is the object pronoun 'me' placed before the verb. With some verbs, English translates this as 'to me' or even changes the structure completely: il me reste... literally means 'it remains to me', but in natural English it's usually 'I have ... left'.
target_language_example: Il me parle souvent.
native_language_example: He talks to me often.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of falloir (impersonal verb). It often expresses necessity in the past (a need/obligation that existed then): Il me fallait + infinitive (“I had to…”). With a noun/pronoun: C’est exactement ce qu’il me fallait (“That’s exactly what I needed”).
target_language_example: Après le travail, il me fallait rentrer tout de suite.
native_language_example: After work, I had to go home right away.

additional_notes: "Il me faut" is a common way to say you need something (often in a more formal or firm way than "j’ai besoin de"). It literally means “it is necessary for me.” The thing needed comes after it: "il me faut un/une + noun" (e.g., "il me faut une carte"). You can also change the person: "il te faut..." (you need), "il lui faut..." (he/she needs), "il nous faut..." (we need), etc.
target_language_example: Pour m’inscrire, il me faut un passeport.
native_language_example: To register, I need a passport.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something: literally “it is necessary to me.” The word after "une" must be a feminine noun (une adresse, une signature). For a masculine noun, use "il me faut un...". Often sounds a bit more formal/insistent than "j’ai besoin d’une...".
target_language_example: Il me faut une minute pour finir.
native_language_example: I need a minute to finish.

additional_notes: Used to say what remains for you (time, things to do, pages, money, etc.). The verb is **rester** (“to remain”), and **me** indicates it’s remaining *for me*. It’s often followed by a quantity: **Il me reste trois pages (à lire)**, **Il me reste combien de temps ?** You can add **encore** (“still”) for emphasis: **Il me reste encore...**.
target_language_example: Il me reste dix minutes avant de partir.
native_language_example: I have ten minutes left before leaving.

meaning: “it seems to me that…” / “I think (that)…” (not completely certain).
additional_notes: Used to give your personal impression or opinion, often with some uncertainty (like “I feel like…” or “I think…”). It’s commonly followed by the indicative: « Il me semble que tu as raison. » You can also use it without « que »: « Il me semble que oui / non. »
target_language_example: Il me semble que le train est en retard.
native_language_example: I think the train is late.

additional_notes: Contraction of **il me a**: **m’** = “me” and **a** is the present of *avoir* used to form the passé composé. It’s followed by a past participle: *Il m’a remercié* (“He thanked me”), *Il m’a accompagné* (“He accompanied me”). Note: in **il m’a fallu + time/number**, the meaning is impersonal: “it took me …” (e.g., *Il m’a fallu trois jours* = “It took me three days”).
target_language_example: Il m’a appelé hier soir.
native_language_example: He called me last night.

additional_notes: Basic negation with the verb être (“to be”): **il + ne + est + pas**. **Il** can mean “he” (a person) or “it” (a thing/idea), depending on context. Often followed by an adjective (**il n'est pas normal**), an adverb (**il n'est pas loin**), or a prepositional phrase (**il n'est pas à toi**). In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: **Il est pas…** (more informal).
target_language_example: il n'est pas loin.
native_language_example: It isn’t far.

meaning: “there is no / there are no” (there isn’t any).
additional_notes: Negative form of “il y a” (“there is/there are”), used to say something doesn’t exist or isn’t present. It’s followed by a noun; even with plural nouns it uses “de” (not “des”): “Il n'y a pas de fenêtres.” If the noun starts with a vowel or silent h, “de” becomes “d’”: “Il n'y a pas d’eau.”
target_language_example: Il n'y a pas de soldats ici.
native_language_example: There are no soldiers here.

additional_notes: Used to express limitation or exclusivity (“only”). Often followed by a noun (Il n’y a que des enfants), a pronoun (Il n’y a que lui), or a relative clause with "qui" (Il n’y a que lui qui sache = only he knows). With people you can list: Il n’y a que toi et moi (only you and me). Note the verb agreement in the relative clause: Il n’y a que toi qui comptes (because "toi" = you, so "tu comptes").
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, il n'y a que nous ici.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s only us here.

additional_notes: Usually not complete on its own: ne is the first part of a negative pattern and is normally followed later by pas, plus, jamais, or que. il can mean 'he', but in impersonal expressions it can also correspond to 'it' or sometimes 'there' in English.
target_language_example: Il ne mange pas de viande.
native_language_example: He doesn't eat meat.

meaning: “you/it shouldn’t have (done that)” or “it wasn’t necessary.”
additional_notes: From the impersonal verb falloir (“to be necessary”). In the imperfect tense (il fallait), it often looks back on something: il ne fallait pas + infinitive = “you/it shouldn’t have + verb” / “you weren’t supposed to + verb” (e.g., Il ne fallait pas changer. = “You shouldn’t have changed.”). On its own (Il ne fallait pas.), it means “You/it shouldn’t have.” With Merci…, it’s a polite formula meaning “Oh, you shouldn’t have!” (said when someone gives you a gift or does something nice).
target_language_example: Oh merci pour le cadeau, il ne fallait pas !
native_language_example: Oh thanks for the gift, you shouldn’t have!

additional_notes: Impersonal expression based on « il faut » (= “it is necessary”). With « ne … pas », it becomes a negative rule or advice: “one must not / you shouldn’t.” Often used for general instructions, warnings, or prohibitions (not about a specific person). You can add an infinitive after it: « Il ne faut pas + verbe » (e.g., parler, y aller).
target_language_example: Il ne faut pas oublier ton passeport.
native_language_example: You mustn’t forget your passport.

il ne manquait plus que ça

target_language_multi_word_term: il ne manquait plus que ça
meaning: “That’s just what we needed!” / “As if things weren’t bad enough.” (usually ironic)
additional_notes: Used to react to a new problem on top of existing ones. Literally it means “only that was missing,” but in real life it’s said sarcastically: another annoyance has happened and it’s the last straw.
target_language_example: J’ai raté mon train, et maintenant il pleut : il ne manquait plus que ça !
native_language_example: I missed my train, and now it’s raining—just what we needed!

additional_notes: Negative form of the verb pouvoir ("can/to be able to"): il + ne ... pas + peut. Depending on context, il can mean a specific "he" or an impersonal "it" (as in "Il ne peut pas y avoir..." = "There can't be..."). In speech, ne is often dropped: "il peut pas".
target_language_example: Il ne peut pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: He can't come tonight.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of pouvoir (pouvait), often describing an ongoing inability or repeated situation in the past ("he couldn’t sleep", "he couldn’t walk any farther"). It’s followed by an infinitive: il ne pouvait pas + verb (dormir, ouvrir, marcher, etc.).
target_language_example: Il ne pouvait pas venir ce soir-là.
native_language_example: He couldn’t come that evening.

additional_notes: Used to say that everything else is gone or already taken, and only the thing(s) after que remain. It’s often followed by a noun or pronoun: Il ne reste que toi (Only you are left). You can also use other forms like "ne ... que" for "only," but here it’s specifically with "rester" (to remain).
target_language_example: Il ne reste que deux places.
native_language_example: There are only two seats left.

meaning: “he doesn’t …” used before a reflexive verb (ne + se + verb).
additional_notes: This is the start of a negative sentence with a reflexive verb: Il ne se + verb… (e.g., il ne se trompe pas = he isn’t mistaken). In everyday spoken French, “ne” is often dropped: Il se trompe pas. With adverbs like jamais/presque jamais/plus, the second negative word comes after the verb: Il ne se met presque jamais en colère.
target_language_example: Il ne se réveille pas tôt le week-end.
native_language_example: He doesn’t wake up early on weekends.
