additional_notes: A common pronoun combination. il is usually "he", but it can also be impersonal "it". nous means "us" or "to us", and in French object pronouns come before the verb: Il nous aide = "He helps us." In expressions like Il nous tarde de..., il is impersonal and the whole phrase means something like "we can't wait to...".
target_language_example: Il nous écrit chaque semaine.
native_language_example: He writes to us every week.

additional_notes: A very common start to a sentence in the passé composé: **il** (he) + **nous** (us/to us) + **a** (has). The verb’s past participle usually comes after: *Il nous a aidés* (“He helped us”). **Nous** is an object pronoun placed before the verb. In the fixed pattern **il nous a fallu + time/thing + pour + infinitive**, **falloir** is impersonal and means “we needed / we had to”: *Il nous a fallu une heure pour partir.*
target_language_example: Il nous a appelés après le cours.
native_language_example: He called us after class.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression with the verb "falloir" ("to be necessary"). "Il nous faut + infinitive" = “we need to / we must …” (Il nous faut partir. = We need to leave.). It can also be followed by a noun: "Il nous faut du temps" = “we need time.”
target_language_example: Il nous faut partir tout de suite.
native_language_example: We need to leave right away.

meaning: “we need to” (used before a reflexive verb: “we need to [do something] ourselves/to ourselves”).
additional_notes: This is the start of the structure **Il nous faut + infinitive** = “We need to / We have to…”. Here, the next verb is reflexive, so you add **nous** again as the reflexive pronoun: **Il nous faut nous + verb** (e.g., *il nous faut nous dépêcher*). In everyday speech, people often say **On doit…** or **Il faut qu’on…** instead.
target_language_example: Il nous faut nous dépêcher si on veut arriver à l’heure.
native_language_example: We need to hurry if we want to arrive on time.

meaning: we need; we have to (it is necessary for us).
additional_notes: Impersonal structure with falloir: literally “it is necessary to us.” Used to say something is needed or required. It’s followed by a noun (Il nous faut du sommeil.) or an infinitive (Il nous faut partir maintenant. = We have to leave now.). You can change the indirect object pronoun: il me/te/lui/vous/leur faut.
target_language_example: Il nous faut partir tout de suite.
native_language_example: We have to leave right away.

additional_notes: Built on the verb phrase « il faut » (impersonal: “it is necessary”). « Il nous faut un + noun » means “we need a + noun.” The object pronoun changes with who needs it: « il me faut… » (I need…), « il te faut… » (you need…), « il lui faut… » (he/she needs…), « il leur faut… » (they need…).
target_language_example: Pour ce travail, il nous faut un ordinateur.
native_language_example: For this job, we need a computer.

meaning: "we have ... left" / "there is ... left for us" (remaining).
additional_notes: Used with a noun or quantity to say what remains: Il nous reste une heure (We have an hour left). With "à + infinitive" it means what is left to do: Il nous reste à faire ... (We still have to do ...). "Il" is an impersonal/dummy subject here; "nous" is the indirect object (for us).
target_language_example: Il nous reste trois minutes avant le départ.
native_language_example: We have three minutes left before departure.

additional_notes: Used to report information you heard (a rumor or something not confirmed), often without saying who told you. Common in conversation; can introduce either bad or good news. Similar to “on dit que…” (“they say that…”).
target_language_example: Il paraît que le train est en retard.
native_language_example: Apparently the train is late.

additional_notes: "Il" means "he" and "parle" is the present tense of "parler" (to speak/to talk). Use it for speaking a language (Il parle français / Il parle le français) or talking about a topic, often with "de": "De quoi est-ce qu'il parle ?" = "What is he talking about?" You can add an adverb like "bien" (well) or "trop vite" (too fast).
target_language_example: Il parle de son travail.
native_language_example: He's talking about his job.

additional_notes: Third-person singular of pouvoir. Used to talk about ability, possibility, or permission depending on context, and it is often followed by an infinitive: il peut venir = 'he can come.'
target_language_example: Il peut le faire demain.
native_language_example: He can do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weather. French uses the impersonal subject "il" (like English "it") with weather verbs: "il pleut" = "it’s raining". Often combined with time expressions such as "depuis" (since/for): "Il pleut depuis hier" = it has been raining since yesterday.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne viens pas : il pleut trop.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m not coming: it’s raining too much.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of pleuvoir (“to rain”) to describe ongoing/background weather in the past, often setting the scene or describing a repeated situation (e.g., “It was raining when…”, “It used to rain every day”). The “il” is an impersonal “it” (not a real subject).
target_language_example: Quand je suis sorti, il pleuvait encore.
native_language_example: When I went out, it was still raining.

additional_notes: Often used impersonally to mean “there is/are … left”: « Il reste du pain. » = “There’s some bread left.” With quantities: « Il reste peu de lait. » = “There’s little milk left.” It can also mean someone “stays/remains” in a state: « Il reste calme. » = “He stays calm.” In the pattern « il reste que + clause », it means “the fact remains that / still”: « Il reste qu’on t’a tiré dessus. » = “The fact remains that you were shot at.”
target_language_example: Il reste deux minutes, dépêche-toi !
native_language_example: There are two minutes left—hurry up!

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or a final point after what was just said. Often followed by a full clause (il reste que + subject + verb). Close to: « pourtant », « néanmoins », « malgré tout »; slightly formal/neutral.
target_language_example: On a beaucoup travaillé ; il reste que le résultat n’est pas parfait.
native_language_example: We worked a lot; still, the result isn’t perfect.

meaning: 'it’s about…' / 'it’s a matter of…' / 'this is…' (used to introduce or specify what/who something concerns or is).
additional_notes: Impersonal, fairly formal phrase used to identify or specify the topic/subject. Common in explanations, presentations, and official contexts. Typically followed by a noun/pronoun (Il s’agit de mon fils. = This is my son.) or an infinitive (Il s’agit de comprendre. = The point is to understand.). Less common in casual everyday speech.
target_language_example: Il s'agit de mon fils.
native_language_example: This is my son.

meaning: 'he has' (used with reflexive/pronominal verbs in the past: “he …ed himself/got …”).
additional_notes: This is the start of a reflexive verb in the passé composé: il + se → s’ + être (s’est). It’s followed by a past participle: il s’est excusé (he apologized), il s’est évanoui (he fainted), il s’est disputé (he argued), il s’est moqué (he made fun), il s’est occupé de… (he took care of…). In English you often don’t translate the “se” literally; it just marks the verb as pronominal.
target_language_example: Il s'est levé tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: He got up early this morning.

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to say an event occurred (often implying it was important, unexpected, or unclear). Uses the impersonal subject "il" + the verb "se passer" in the past (passé composé). It can be followed by details: "ici" (here), "d'autre" (something else), or "entre nous / entre vous" (something happened between us/you—often suggesting a personal, romantic, or tense situation).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas tout expliquer, mais il s'est passé quelque chose hier soir.
native_language_example: I can’t explain everything, but something happened last night.

additional_notes: From the verb "savoir" ("to know" facts/information). Often followed by a question word or clause: "il sait où..." (he knows where...), "il sait qui..." (he knows who...), "il sait que..." (he knows that...). For knowing a person or being familiar with a place/thing, French usually uses "il connaît" instead.
target_language_example: Il sait que tu es là.
native_language_example: He knows that you are here.

additional_notes: Used before a reflexive or pronominal verb. se is the third-person singular reflexive pronoun. It can sometimes mean "himself," but very often you translate the whole verb expression instead, not se by itself.
target_language_example: Il se lève tôt tous les jours.
native_language_example: He gets up early every day.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal "il" (it) with "se passer" (to happen). Often used when you suspect something is happening, sometimes something unusual or important. You can add a place with "ici / à la maison / entre vous".
target_language_example: Je pense qu'il se passe quelque chose dans le bureau.
native_language_example: I think something is going on in the office.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It is followed by the subjunctive (e.g., « il se peut que je sois… », « il se peut qu’il vienne… »). Often interchangeable with « il est possible que », though « il se peut que » is very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Il se peut que nous soyons en retard à cause du trafic.
native_language_example: We might be late because of traffic.

meaning: "it might be that" / "it could be that" (expresses possibility).
additional_notes: Used to say something is possible but not certain. It’s fairly formal/neutral, and it is normally followed by the subjunctive: « Il se pourrait que ce soit… », « …que tu aies… », « …que vous soyez… ».
target_language_example: Il se pourrait que le train ait du retard.
native_language_example: The train might be late.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective (bien, fatigué, heureux, faible, blessé) or sometimes with a noun phrase to talk about someone’s physical or emotional state. It comes from the reflexive verb « se sentir » (to feel). In English you usually just say “he feels …”.
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, il se sent mieux.
native_language_example: Today, he feels better.

meaning: "he was standing" / "he was positioned" (was staying in a certain posture or place).
additional_notes: Imperfect of the verb "se tenir" (reflexive). Used to describe someone’s posture or where they were located for a period of time. It’s often followed by details like "debout" (standing up), "contre" (against), or a place/distance: "à quelques mètres de moi" (a few meters from me).
target_language_example: Il se tenait près de la porte et attendait en silence.
native_language_example: He was standing near the door and waiting in silence.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a fact (often unexpected or relevant to the situation), similar to “it so happens that…”. It’s followed by a clause with que: « Il se trouve que + [subject] + [verb] ». It can also be used as a short reply: « Il se trouve que oui/non » (“It turns out yes/no”).
target_language_example: Il se trouve que j’ai déjà réservé une table.
native_language_example: It turns out I already booked a table.

additional_notes: Used to express an impression or conclusion based on what you see/know, not full certainty. Often followed by the subjunctive in more formal French (e.g., « Il semble que Jeanne ait… »), but in everyday speech you may hear the indicative (« Il semble que Jeanne a… »). Can also be shortened to « Il semble que oui/non » (“it seems so/not”).
target_language_example: Il semble que le train ait du retard.
native_language_example: It seems that the train is delayed.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a future state/identity/quality: *Il sera là* (he’ll be there), *Il sera un bon mari* (he’ll be a good husband). With negation, standard French is *Il ne sera pas…* (often spoken as *Il sera pas…*). Also appears in impersonal/passive-style phrases like *Il sera exigé de vous…* = “You will be required to…”.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il sera prêt demain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’ll be ready tomorrow.

meaning: "you just need to" / "all you have to do is".
additional_notes: Used to say that something is enough to achieve a result, often implying it’s easy or requires only that one action. Structure: il suffit de + infinitive (Il suffit d’appeler). Can also be followed by "pour" + infinitive to state the purpose: Il suffit d’appuyer ici pour commencer.
target_language_example: Pour ouvrir la porte, il suffit de tourner la clé.
native_language_example: To open the door, you just have to turn the key.

additional_notes: Contraction of "il te a" → "il t'a" before a vowel sound. Common in the passé composé: "il t'a parlé" = "he spoke to you" / "he has spoken to you"; "il t'a fait quelque chose ?" = "did he do something to you?" The meaning depends on the past participle that follows (parlé, posé, fait, etc.).
target_language_example: Il t'a envoyé un message hier soir.
native_language_example: He sent you a message last night.

additional_notes: Impersonal structure with falloir. Pattern: “Il te faut + infinitive” = “You need to / You have to …” (often sounds like advice, instruction, or necessity). You can also use it with a noun: “Il te faut un stylo” = “You need a pen.”
target_language_example: Il te faut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: You need to leave now.

additional_notes: From the impersonal verb « falloir » (necessity): literally “it is necessary for you.” Used to say someone needs something (Il te faut du repos), or to ask how much/how long is needed (Il te faut combien ? / Il te faut combien de temps ?). Often followed by a noun; with a verb you use « il te faut + infinitive » (e.g., Il te faut partir).
target_language_example: Pour demain, il te faut ton passeport.
native_language_example: For tomorrow, you need your passport.

additional_notes: Present tense of « travailler ». Depending on context, it can mean a general habit/job (“he works at a hospital”) or what he’s doing right now (“he’s working”). Note: « travailler » means “to work,” not “to travel.”
target_language_example: Il travaille aujourd'hui, donc il ne peut pas venir.
native_language_example: He's working today, so he can't come.

additional_notes: Usually followed by an infinitive to express the near future: il va partir = 'he's going to leave'. Here il can mean 'he' or an impersonal 'it'. In il va y avoir, the full expression means 'there is/are going to be'.
target_language_example: Il va pleuvoir ce soir.
native_language_example: It's going to rain tonight.

meaning: "he/it is going to do/make"; also "the weather is going to be" (talking about weather).
additional_notes: This is the futur proche: aller (il va) + infinitive (faire) to talk about something that’s going to happen soon. "Il" can mean "he" (about a person) or an impersonal "it" (especially with weather: "Il va faire quel temps ?" = "What’s the weather going to be like?"). In questions you’ll often see: "Il va faire quoi ?" (What’s he going to do?) and "Il va faire quel temps ?" (What will the weather be like?).
target_language_example: Demain, il va faire beau, alors on va sortir.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, it’s going to be nice out, so we’re going to go out.

meaning: "we're going to have to" / "it will be necessary to" (soon).
additional_notes: Impersonal expression using the near future of falloir ("to be necessary"). It means that something must be done, often implying obligation or necessity. Common patterns: il va falloir + infinitive (Il va falloir attendre.) and il va falloir que + subjunctive (Il va falloir que tu viennes.).
target_language_example: Il va falloir partir maintenant.
native_language_example: We’re going to have to leave now.

additional_notes: Used to predict upcoming rain. Very common with a time marker like "demain" (tomorrow), "ce soir" (tonight), or "dans la soirée" (later in the evening). "Il" here is an impersonal subject (it doesn’t refer to a person).
target_language_example: Prends un parapluie : il va pleuvoir.
native_language_example: Take an umbrella: it’s going to rain.

additional_notes: An impersonal expression used to give advice or say what is preferable. Often followed by an infinitive (Il vaut mieux partir.) or by "que" + subjunctive (Il vaut mieux que je reste.).
target_language_example: Il vaut mieux que tu prennes un taxi.
native_language_example: You’d better take a taxi.

additional_notes: From vouloir. Used to say what a man or boy wants, plans, or wishes for. It is often followed by an infinitive verb (il veut partir = he wants to leave) or by que + another clause (il veut qu'on vienne = he wants us to come).
target_language_example: Il veut apprendre le français.
native_language_example: He wants to learn French.

additional_notes:
From the verb « venir » (to come). It can be followed by:
- a place/person: « Il vient d'une ferme » = “He comes from a farm”; « Il vient me voir » = “He comes to see me / He visits me.”
- a direction: « Il vient droit vers le pont » = “He’s coming straight toward the bridge.”
Common related pattern: « il vient de + infinitive » means “he has just (done something)” (recent past): « Il vient d'entrer » = “He just came in.”
target_language_example: Il vient avec nous ce soir.
native_language_example: He’s coming with us tonight.

meaning: "he comes from" or "he has just (done something)".
additional_notes: 1) With a place/person/thing after it, it means origin: « Il vient de Gênes. » = he comes from Genoa. 2) With an infinitive (verb) after it, « venir de + infinitif » expresses the recent past: « Il vient de prier. » = he just prayed / he has just prayed. The subject can change (je/tu/il/elle/on/nous/vous/ils) but the structure stays the same.
target_language_example: Il vient de finir ses devoirs.
native_language_example: He has just finished his homework.

additional_notes: Used to say where a man/boy lives (permanent or current situation): il vit en ville (he lives in the city), il vit encore avec ses parents (he still lives with his parents). In other contexts, "il vit" can also mean "he sees" (from "voir"), but with places like "dans / en" it almost always means "he lives".
target_language_example: Il vit près de la gare.
native_language_example: He lives near the train station.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (imparfait): it often describes an ongoing desire in the past, a repeated wish, or a background intention. Very common in questions like « Qu’est-ce qu’il voulait ? » (“What did he want?”) and « Qu’est-ce qu’il voulait dire ? » (“What did he mean?”). With « que + subjunctive »: « Il voulait que… » = “He wanted (that) …”.
target_language_example: Il voulait que je vienne avec lui.
native_language_example: He wanted me to come with him.

additional_notes: From the verb falloir (“to be necessary”). It’s an impersonal structure meaning something is necessary for you. Used with an infinitive: il vous faut + verb (e.g., il vous faut pratiquer). “Vous” can be plural (“you all”) or formal singular (“you,” polite). More common in speech: il faut que vous + subjunctive, or simply vous devez (“you must / have to”).
target_language_example: Il vous faut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: You need to leave now.

additional_notes: Built with the impersonal verb « falloir »: « il faut » = “it is necessary / you must”. « Il vous faut… » is a polite/formal way to tell someone what they need to do. It’s typically followed by an infinitive (« être ») and then « plus » + an adjective. The adjective agrees with the person you’re talking to: organisée/patiente/polie (feminine singular), patient/poli (masculine singular), patientes/polies (feminine plural), patients (masculine plural or mixed group).
target_language_example: Pour ce travail, il vous faut être plus attentifs.
native_language_example: For this job, you need to be more attentive.

additional_notes: From the verb "falloir" (impersonal: "il faut"). Used with an object: "il vous faut + noun" = "you need + noun". "vous" is formal singular or plural; informal singular would be "il te faut". Often expresses a requirement or necessity.
target_language_example: Pour entrer, il vous faut une pièce d’identité.
native_language_example: To get in, you need an ID.

meaning: “there was a” / “there has been a” (something happened).
additional_notes: Used to say that an event occurred in the past. It’s the past tense of “il y a” (“there is/are”). Often followed by an event noun (un accident, un mariage, un scandale, un silence). With a specific time expression, it typically means simple past (“there was”); without one, it can translate as “there has been.”
target_language_example: Hier soir, il y a eu un accident sur l’autoroute.
native_language_example: Last night, there was an accident on the highway.

additional_notes: Very common fixed expression. Most often it introduces something that exists or is present: il y a un livre sur la table = there is a book on the table. It is used for both singular and plural. Before a length of time, it means 'ago': il y a deux ans = two years ago.
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup de monde ici.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people here.

additional_notes: Used to add another item to a list or mention an extra thing that exists/is available. Often followed directly by a noun phrase (Il y a aussi un cadeau...), and it can refer to something in a specific place when you add a location (Il y a aussi mes photos, chez ma mère).
target_language_example: Il y a aussi une boulangerie près d'ici.
native_language_example: There’s also a bakery near here.

additional_notes: Used with "il y a" (= "there is/there are") to say there’s an additional thing, fact, or issue to mention or check. Often followed by "que..." to add details: "Il y a autre chose que tu devrais savoir." In a question ("Il y a autre chose ?"), it means “Is there anything else?”
target_language_example: Il y a autre chose dont je dois m'occuper ?
native_language_example: Is there anything else I need to take care of?

additional_notes: Used with "il y a" (there is/there are) + "beaucoup de" (a lot of) to say there are many things/people or a large amount of something. Before a plural noun: "il y a beaucoup de touristes" (a lot of tourists). Before an uncountable noun: "il y a beaucoup de place" (a lot of space). "De" usually stays the same (not "des") after "beaucoup".
target_language_example: Dans ce café, il y a beaucoup de monde le matin.
native_language_example: In this café, there are a lot of people in the morning.

meaning: 'there is indeed / surely there is' (or, with time: '... ago (really/a long time)').
additional_notes: Built on **il y a** (“there is/are” or “... ago”) plus **bien** to add emphasis/assurance. Often used to confirm something exists (**Il y a bien un problème.**) or in a confirming question (**Il y a bien un service de livraison ?** = “There *is* a delivery service, right?”). With time expressions it intensifies the duration: **il y a bien longtemps** = “a very long time ago.”
target_language_example: Il y a bien une solution, ne t’inquiète pas.
native_language_example: There is definitely a solution, don’t worry.

additional_notes: Used to say that more alternatives exist. It’s typically followed by a plural noun: « Il y a d'autres options. » (There are other options.) You can also use it without a noun when it’s understood from context: « Il y en a d'autres. » (There are others.)
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : il y a d'autres possibilités.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there are other possibilities.

additional_notes: Used to say that many things exist/are present. "De nombreuses" agrees with a feminine plural noun (e.g., chansons, explications, façons, rivières). With masculine plural nouns, use "il y a de nombreux" (e.g., de nombreux problèmes).
target_language_example: Il y a de nombreuses raisons de partir tôt.
native_language_example: There are many reasons to leave early.

additional_notes: Used to say that many of something exist or are present. It’s the phrase "il y a" (there is/are) + "de nombreux" (many) before a plural noun. "De nombreux" agrees with the noun: masculine plural "de nombreux" (parcs), feminine plural "de nombreuses" (animaux → masculine, but "de nombreuses choses").
target_language_example: Il y a de nombreux restaurants dans ce quartier.
native_language_example: There are many restaurants in this neighborhood.

additional_notes: Used to say that some people/things exist or are present. It’s the expression "il y a" (there is/there are) + "des" (some) for a plural noun: "il y a des + noun". For a singular noun you usually use "il y a un/une"; for an uncountable noun, "il y a du/de la/de l’".
target_language_example: Il y a des touristes dans le musée.
native_language_example: There are (some) tourists in the museum.

meaning: years ago; a long time ago.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened several years in the past, often to emphasize that it was quite a long time ago. It can stand alone (Il y a des années !) or be followed by de cela / de ça (“ago / back then”).
target_language_example: On s’est rencontrés il y a des années, mais je me souviens encore de toi.
native_language_example: We met years ago, but I still remember you.

il y a des gens qui

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a des gens qui
additional_notes: Used to introduce the idea that some people do a certain thing or have a certain belief. Very common for general statements; it’s followed by a verb clause (e.g., il y a des gens qui + verb). Often implies “some people” rather than all people.
target_language_example: Il y a des gens qui n’aiment pas le café.
native_language_example: Some people don’t like coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It often comes at the beginning or end of a sentence. The full pattern is "il y a + duration" (e.g., il y a trois jours = three days ago).
target_language_example: J'ai commencé ce travail il y a deux ans.
native_language_example: I started this job two years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It can come at the end of the sentence (Elle a disparu il y a deux jours.) or at the beginning (Il y a deux jours, ...).
target_language_example: On s'est vus il y a deux jours.
native_language_example: We saw each other two days ago.

additional_notes: Used to say that some amount of something is present. It’s the phrase “il y a” (“there is/are”) + the partitive article: du (masc. singular), de la (fem. singular), de l’ (before a vowel/h), or des (plural). Often used for things you can’t easily count (work, fog, noise, sun, frost, movement, etc.).
target_language_example: Aujourd’hui, il y a du vent.
native_language_example: Today, there is some wind.

additional_notes: Used to say something still exists/is present, or that there are additional things left. Often followed by a noun: "Il y a encore des problèmes" (There are still problems). In questions like "Qu'est-ce qu'il y a encore ?", it means "What is it now?/What else is there?" depending on context.
target_language_example: Il y a encore du travail à faire.
native_language_example: There’s still work to do.

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate number, amount, distance, or time. With a quantity: « Il y a environ 30 personnes » = there are about 30 people. With a time expression: « Il y a environ une heure/un an » = about an hour/a year ago.
target_language_example: Il y a environ vingt minutes, j’ai envoyé un message.
native_language_example: About twenty minutes ago, I sent a message.

meaning: a long time ago; for a long time (in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the structure "il y a + time" to mean "... ago" (e.g., il y a deux jours = two days ago). With "longtemps", it often means "a long time ago" and can also suggest something should have happened earlier ("You should have told me a long time ago").
target_language_example: Je ne l’ai pas vu depuis longtemps : je l’ai rencontré il y a longtemps.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen him in a long time: I met him a long time ago.

meaning: "there is no / there are no" (there isn’t any).
additional_notes: Informal spoken form of "il n’y a pas de" (dropping "ne"). Used to say something doesn’t exist or isn’t available. It’s followed by a noun without an article: "Il y a pas de budget" = “There’s no budget.” In more careful French (writing, formal situations), use "Il n’y a pas de…".
target_language_example: Désolé, il y a pas de place pour ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, there are no seats left for tonight.

additional_notes: Used to suggest a possibility that something exists. "Il y a" means "there is/are"; adding "peut-être" softens it to an uncertain guess ("maybe"). Often followed by a noun phrase like "quelque chose", "une solution", "un meilleur moyen".
target_language_example: Il y a peut-être une erreur dans ce document.
native_language_example: There might be a mistake in this document.

meaning: 'there are lots of' / 'there is plenty of'.
additional_notes: Uses the structure "il y a" (there is/are) + "plein de" (lots of/plenty of) + noun. Very common in spoken French to mean "a lot of"; can sound a bit informal compared with "beaucoup de". The noun after "de" is usually plural ("plein de choses"), but you can also use it with an uncountable idea like "plein de place" (plenty of space).
target_language_example: Il y a plein de bons restaurants dans ce quartier.
native_language_example: There are lots of good restaurants in this neighborhood.

meaning: 'there are more than' / 'there is more than'.
additional_notes: Used to say a quantity is greater than another quantity ("plus de + noun") or greater than a number ("plus de + number"). Often followed by "que" for comparisons: "Il y a plus de X que de Y" (more X than Y).
target_language_example: Il y a plus de trente personnes dans la salle.
native_language_example: There are more than thirty people in the room.

additional_notes: Used to say that more than one thing exists or is available. Often followed by a plural noun ("Il y a plusieurs possibilités") or by a plural noun + relative clause ("Il y a plusieurs étoiles qui..."). Note: "Il y a plusieurs années" can mean "several years ago" (time ago), depending on context.
target_language_example: Il y a plusieurs restaurants près d'ici.
native_language_example: There are several restaurants near here.

additional_notes: Uses the common structure "il y a" (there is/there are) + "quelqu'un" (someone). In a question (often said like "Il y a quelqu’un ?"), it can mean "Is anyone there?" or "Is someone here?". You can add a place (là-bas, à l’intérieur) or a clause ("qui arrive" = "who is arriving").
target_language_example: Je crois qu'il y a quelqu'un.
native_language_example: I think there’s someone.

il y a quelque chose que

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a quelque chose que
additional_notes: Used to introduce an unspecified “something” followed by a relative clause with que. Often followed by verbs like devoir/devrait (“must/should”) or pouvoir (“can”). In a question, it can mean “Is there something I can do?” (often implying “to help”).
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose que je dois te dire.
native_language_example: There’s something I have to tell you.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It can come at the end of the sentence (Elle est partie il y a quelques années.) or at the beginning as a time marker (Il y a quelques années, ...). Built from il y a (“there is/there are”) + quelques (“a few”) + années (“years”).
target_language_example: J’ai commencé le français il y a quelques années.
native_language_example: I started French a few years ago.

additional_notes: Used with the expression "il y a" (there is/are) plus "toujours" (always) to say something is always present or always happens. The noun that follows determines whether English uses "is" or "are" (e.g., "de la place" → "there is"; "des armes" → "there are").
target_language_example: Il y a toujours une solution.
native_language_example: There is always a solution.

meaning: "there is always a..." (with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Built from the common structure "il y a" = "there is/there are" + "toujours" = "always" + "une" = "a" (feminine). It’s often used to express a general truth or reassurance: "There’s always a solution/way out/possibility." Change "une" to "un" for masculine nouns ("il y a toujours un..."), or to "des" for plurals ("il y a toujours des...").
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : il y a toujours une solution.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there’s always a solution.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It’s built from "il y a" ("there is/are" but used for time = "ago") + a time expression ("trois ans"). Often placed at the end of the sentence: "Je suis arrivé il y a trois ans." You can also use it alone as a short answer to “When?”
target_language_example: J’ai commencé le français il y a trois ans.
native_language_example: I started French three years ago.

additional_notes: Used with a past event to say how long ago it happened. The pattern is: [past tense verb] + il y a + [time]. Example: « Je suis parti(e) il y a deux heures » = “I left two hours ago.”
target_language_example: J'ai commencé ce travail il y a trois jours.
native_language_example: I started this job three days ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It typically goes after the verb (often in the past tense): « J’ai déménagé il y a trois mois. » You can swap the time amount: « il y a deux jours / une semaine / un an ».
target_language_example: J'ai commencé ce travail il y a trois mois.
native_language_example: I started this job three months ago.

meaning: there are too many / too much (of).
additional_notes: Used to say there is an excessive amount or number of something. Follow it with a noun: il y a trop de + nom. With plural countable nouns: « trop de + nom pluriel » (trop de villages). With uncountable nouns: « trop de + nom singulier » (trop de bruit). Often expresses complaint or frustration.
target_language_example: Il y a trop de monde dans le métro ce matin.
native_language_example: There are too many people on the subway this morning.

additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is present somewhere. In this phrase, un is the masculine singular article, so before a feminine noun you would say il y a une, and for plural nouns il y a des.
target_language_example: Il y a un chat dans le jardin.
native_language_example: There is a cat in the garden.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. Very common with past tenses: « C’était il y a un an », « La maison a été construite il y a un an ». You can add precision with words like « environ » (about), or extend it: « il y a un an et demi » (a year and a half ago).
target_language_example: J’ai commencé ce travail il y a un an.
native_language_example: I started this job a year ago.

additional_notes: "Il y a" is the common way to say "there is/there are" in French. Add a place after it (e.g., "à la porte" = at the door, "dans le jardin" = in the garden, "ici" = here, "dehors" = outside). Often used to point out someone’s presence, sometimes with an adjective: "Il y a un homme bizarre…" = "There’s a strange man…".
target_language_example: Il y a un homme devant la maison.
native_language_example: There’s a man in front of the house.

additional_notes: Uses the common structure "il y a" (“there is/there are”) to point out that something is wrong. Often followed by "avec…" to specify what has an issue ("Il y a un problème avec les freins" = “There’s a problem with the brakes”). You can also say it on its own as a warning or to introduce bad news.
target_language_example: Il y a un problème avec la connexion internet.
native_language_example: There’s a problem with the internet connection.

additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is present. "Une" is the feminine singular article (use it before feminine nouns: une porte, une voiture, une procédure). For a masculine noun: "il y a un". For plural: "il y a des". In the negative: "il n’y a pas de" (e.g., Il n’y a pas de solution).
target_language_example: Il y a une erreur dans le document.
native_language_example: There is an error in the document.

additional_notes: Used to say that another person/thing exists or is available. It must be followed by a noun (e.g., "Il y a une autre porte"). "Une autre" is feminine; for a masculine noun use "il y a un autre …" and for plural "il y a d’autres …".
target_language_example: Il y a une autre solution.
native_language_example: There is another solution.

il y a une chose que

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a une chose que
meaning: “There is one thing that …” / “There’s something that …”
additional_notes: Used to introduce a specific thing (often important) followed by a relative clause with que. Very common pattern: Il y a une chose que + subject + verb (e.g., je dois faire / tu dois savoir). You can swap une chose for quelque chose (“something”).
target_language_example: Il y a une chose que je veux te dire.
native_language_example: There’s one thing I want to tell you.

additional_notes: Used to say how much time has passed since an event happened. The pattern is: [past tense] + il y a + duration (e.g., il y a deux minutes / trois jours). Note that "il y a" literally means "there is/are" but here it means "ago".
target_language_example: Je t’ai envoyé un message il y a une heure.
native_language_example: I sent you a message an hour ago.

meaning: “a week ago” (one week in the past).
additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It often comes at the end of the sentence: « Il est parti il y a une semaine. ». You can add « environ » to mean “about”: « il y a une semaine environ ».
target_language_example: On s’est vus il y a une semaine.
native_language_example: We saw each other a week ago.

meaning: "there will be" / "there is going to be".
additional_notes: Future tense of « il y a » (“there is/are”). Used to announce that something will exist or happen in the future. Very common with quantities and events: « Il y aura un contrôle demain » (There will be a test tomorrow), « Il y aura des problèmes » (There will be problems).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, il y aura assez de temps pour tout faire.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, there will be enough time to do everything.

additional_notes: Imperfect past form of "il y a". Used to say that something existed/was present in the past, often for background description (people/things in a place, a situation at that time). Same form for singular and plural: "il y avait une voiture" / "il y avait des voitures".
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait beaucoup de monde.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there were a lot of people.

additional_notes: Used to say that several people/animals/things existed or were present in the past. It’s the imperfect tense of « il y a » and is followed by a plural noun: « Il y avait des + nom (pluriel) ».
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait des gens devant la porte.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there were people in front of the door.

additional_notes: Past-tense form of "il y a". Used to describe what existed or was present in a place or situation in the past. Often followed by a noun: "Il y avait un drapeau..." (= there was a flag), "Il y avait un hic" (= there was a problem/catch), "Il y avait un total de..." (= there was a total of...). You can change the article/number as needed (une / des) and it can also be negative: "il n’y avait pas de...".
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait un chat devant la porte.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there was a cat in front of the door.

additional_notes: Imperfect form of "il y a". Used to describe that something existed/was present at a place or at a time in the past, often as background description (people, things, events: "il y avait une vue", "il y avait une fête"). With plural: "il y avait des..."
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait une longue file d’attente.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there was a long line.

additional_notes: Used to say that a certain quantity exists/is available, often followed by a number or an expression like "trop" (too many/too much), "beaucoup" (a lot), "assez" (enough). It combines "il y a" (there is/there are) with the pronoun "en" (= some/any of it/them, referring back to something already mentioned).
target_language_example: Des biscuits ? Oui, il y en a encore.
native_language_example: Cookies? Yes, there are still some.

il y en a des qui

target_language_multi_word_term: il y en a des qui
additional_notes: Used to introduce a general statement about a subset of people or things. Built from **il y en a** (“there are/there is”) + **des… qui** (“some… who/that”). Common in spoken French; often followed by a verb describing what those people do or are like.
target_language_example: Il y en a des qui pensent que c’est facile, mais ce n’est pas vrai.
native_language_example: Some people think it’s easy, but that’s not true.

meaning: "there’s enough (of it) for…" / "it will last for…"
additional_notes: Used with a duration or a group to say how long something lasts or that there’s enough to cover someone/something. Common patterns: « Il y en a pour tout le monde » = there’s enough for everyone; « Il y en a pour une seconde / deux jours » = it lasts one second / two days (often about battery life, time, money, food, etc.). « en » refers to the thing you’re talking about (some of it), and « il y a » is an impersonal way to say “there is/are.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il y en a pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there’s enough for everyone.

additional_notes: Used to say that one exists or is available. Built on **il y a** (“there is/are”) + **en** (“some/any/of them,” replacing a noun mentioned or understood) + **un** (“one”). Often answers a question like *Tu en as un ?* (“Do you have one?”) → *Oui, il y en a un.*
target_language_example: Tu cherches un chargeur ? Il y en a un sur la table.
native_language_example: Are you looking for a charger? There’s one on the table.

meaning: "There is one" / "There’s one (of them)" (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used when you mean “one of it/them” and the thing has already been mentioned or is understood. « en » replaces “of it/them” (a previously mentioned noun), and « une » shows it’s ONE and feminine (for a masculine noun, you’d say « il y en a un »). Common in counts or comparisons: « Il y en a une de moins » = “There’s one less.”
target_language_example: Tu as des piles ? Oui, il y en a une dans le tiroir.
native_language_example: Do you have batteries? Yes, there’s one in the drawer.

additional_notes: Imperfect past form of "il y en a". Used when "en" replaces a previously mentioned noun (meaning "some" or "(some) of it/them"): *Il y en avait beaucoup* = "There were a lot (of them)." You often add a quantity after it (beaucoup, un, deux, etc.).
target_language_example: Dans le frigo, il y en avait encore.
native_language_example: There were still some in the fridge.

additional_notes: Imperfect form of être with il. Usually used for descriptions, states, or background/ongoing situations in the past. In context, il can mean either "he" or "it".
target_language_example: Il était très content de te voir.
native_language_example: He was very happy to see you.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past tense (était) to describe an ongoing state in the past: where/ how someone was sitting, often as background description. Frequently followed by a place or position: "sur une chaise" (on a chair), "par terre" (on the floor), "entre X et Y" (between X and Y), "avec les bras/jambes croisés" (with arms/legs crossed).
target_language_example: Quand je suis entré, il était assis près de la fenêtre.
native_language_example: When I came in, he was sitting near the window.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (était) to describe an ongoing state, feeling, or characteristic in the past (background description). "Il" usually means "he," but it can also mean "it" (e.g., talking about a movie: "Il était très long"). Typically followed by an adjective: "Il était très content/fatigué."
target_language_example: Quand il était jeune, il était très timide.
native_language_example: When he was young, he was very shy.

meaning: "Once upon a time there was a..." (storybook opening).
additional_notes: Used at the start of fairy tales and stories to introduce a character. It’s the imperfect tense of être (il était = “he/it was”), followed by une fois (“once”), then un/une + noun. You can change un to une depending on the noun: « Il était une fois une princesse… »
target_language_example: Il était une fois un chat qui voulait devenir roi.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a cat who wanted to become king.

additional_notes: Set phrase used to begin fairy tales and stories. It’s in the imperfect tense (était) to set the scene in the past. Often followed by a character or setting: « il était une fois un roi… »
target_language_example: Il était une fois une princesse qui vivait dans une grande forêt.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a princess who lived in a big forest.

additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine plural, or mixed group). "Aiment" is the present tense (3rd person plural) of "aimer". It can mean "to like" (Ils aiment ça. = They like that.) or "to love" (Ils aiment leurs enfants. = They love their children.). You can follow it with a noun (ils aiment leurs enfants), an infinitive (ils aiment se plaindre = they like to complain), or a pronoun like "ça" (they like that).
target_language_example: Ils aiment regarder des films le soir.
native_language_example: They like watching movies in the evening.

additional_notes: Used to describe an ongoing state, repeated situation, or background in the past (the imperfect). Common patterns: « ils avaient peur de… » = “they were afraid to/of…”, « ils avaient besoin de… » = “they needed…”. Often appears in reported speech after « ils ont dit que… » (they said that…).
target_language_example: Quand ils étaient jeunes, ils avaient toujours peur du noir.
native_language_example: When they were young, they were always afraid of the dark.

meaning: “They say that…” (people say; it’s said that).
additional_notes: Used to report what people in general are saying (rumors, common beliefs, hearsay). It often doesn’t refer to a specific group of men; “ils” can mean “they/people.” You’ll also hear similar forms like “on dit que …” (“they say/it’s said that …”) and other subjects: “elle dit que…” (“she says that…”), “ils ont dit que…” (“they said that…”).
target_language_example: Ils disent que ce restaurant est le meilleur du quartier.
native_language_example: They say this restaurant is the best in the neighborhood.

meaning: “they must / they have to” (they are required to).
additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (a group of males, or a mixed group). "Doivent" is the present tense of "devoir" (to have to / must). It’s used to express obligation or necessity, and is followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "ils doivent partir"). In the negative: "ils ne doivent pas..." = "they must not / they aren’t supposed to...".
target_language_example: Ils doivent partir maintenant.
native_language_example: They have to leave now.

meaning: 'they must be' / 'they have to be' (or 'they must be' = 'they’re probably…').
additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine or mixed group). "Doivent" is the present tense of "devoir" (must/should/have to). With "être" it can express either (1) obligation/requirement: "They have to be replaced", or (2) a logical guess/probability: "They must be tired" (= they’re probably tired).
target_language_example: Ils doivent être en retard, il y a beaucoup de trafic.
native_language_example: They must be late; there’s a lot of traffic.

additional_notes: Present tense of the verb « faire » (to do/to make) with « ils » (they). Very common and used broadly: doing an action (« Ils font un test. »), making/producing something (« Ils font tout le nécessaire. »), or “doing” an activity (« Ils font ça depuis… »). In informal speech you may hear « Ils font pas… » (missing « ne ») instead of the more formal « Ils ne font pas… ».
target_language_example: Ils font ça tous les jours.
native_language_example: They do that every day.

meaning: "they have" + "it/him/her" (used to form the past tense: "they ...ed it/him/her").
additional_notes: « Ils » = « they ». « l’ » is a direct object pronoun meaning “it,” “him,” or “her,” used before a verb that starts with a vowel (like « ont »). « ont » is the present tense of « avoir » (they have) and is used to build the passé composé: ils l’ont + past participle (fait, pris, emmené, etc.) → “they did it / they took him/her/it / they brought him/her, etc.” With « avoir », the past participle can agree in gender/number when the direct object pronoun comes before it: « Ils l’ont pris » (masc. “him/it”), « Ils l’ont prise » (fem. “her/it”).
target_language_example: Ils l'ont emmené à l'hôpital.
native_language_example: They took him/it to the hospital.

additional_notes: Used to start a negative sentence with “they” (ils). In standard French, “ne” is paired with a second negative word: most often ne … pas (“not”), ne … rien (“nothing”), ne … plus (“no longer”), etc. In everyday spoken French, “ne” is often dropped: “Ils savent pas.”
target_language_example: Ils ne veulent pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: They don’t want to come tonight.

additional_notes: From the verb *pouvoir* (“to be able to / can”) in the present tense: *ils peuvent* (“they can”). The standard French negation is *ne … pas*: *ils ne peuvent pas* (“they can’t”). In casual spoken French, *ne* is often dropped: *ils peuvent pas*.
target_language_example: Ils ne peuvent pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: They can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: This is the negative form of **ils sont** (“they are”) with **ne … pas** placed around the verb **être**: **ils ne sont pas + adjective / prepositional phrase / past participle**. In casual spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: **ils sont pas**.
target_language_example: Ils ne sont pas prêts pour le départ.
native_language_example: They aren’t ready to leave.

meaning: 'they have' / 'they did' (talking about what they did to us).
additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the passé composé: ils (they) + nous (to us) + ont (have). The object pronoun nous goes before the verb. In sentences like « Ils nous ont oubliés / saluées », the past participle can agree with nous (forgotten us / greeted us) in gender/number when nous refers to the direct object.
target_language_example: Ils nous ont aidés à trouver un hôtel.
native_language_example: They helped us find a hotel.

additional_notes: Composed of ils + ont (from avoir). It can mean possession, but it is also very commonly used as the auxiliary in the passé composé. In that case, English often translates it with a simple past: ils ont dormi = “they slept.”
target_language_example: Ils ont déjà fini.
native_language_example: They've already finished.

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of *dire* with *ils* (they): *ils* + *ont* (have) + *dit* (said). Used for something they said in the past, often translated simply as “they said.” Common in reported speech: *Ils ont dit qu’ils…* (“They said that they…”).
target_language_example: Ils ont dit qu’ils viendraient demain.
native_language_example: They said they would come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Past of devoir ("to have to" / "must"). It can express (1) obligation in the past: « Ils ont dû partir » = “They had to leave.” It can also express a deduction (very common): « Ils ont dû avoir un accident » = “They must have had an accident.” With deduction about a completed action, you’ll often see « ont dû » + infinitive (or + avoir/être + past participle).
target_language_example: Ils ont dû oublier l'adresse.
native_language_example: They must have forgotten the address.

additional_notes: "Ils ont eu" is the passé composé of avoir (ils + ont + eu) and talks about a completed past event. Depending on context, it can mean they possessed something (Ils ont eu plusieurs enfants = they had several children), they got/received something (Ils ont eu ce qu’ils voulaient = they got what they wanted), or they experienced something (Ils ont eu de la chance = they were lucky). In "ils ont eu raison", it’s part of the fixed phrase "avoir raison" = 'to be right'.
target_language_example: Ils ont eu beaucoup de succès cette année.
native_language_example: They had a lot of success this year.

additional_notes: This is the **passé composé** of *faire* for **ils** (“they”): *ils* + *ont* (have) + *fait* (done/made). It’s used for completed actions in the past. *Faire* can mean **do** or **make** depending on context: *Ils ont fait une pause* (“They took a break”), *Ils ont fait le tour du monde* (“They travelled around the world”), *Ils ont fait de leur mieux* (“They did their best”).
target_language_example: Ils ont fait la cuisine hier soir.
native_language_example: They cooked last night.

meaning: 'they put/placed' (past tense of mettre); also 'they took (time)' and in fixed phrases like 'they put an end (to)'
additional_notes: "Ils ont mis" is the passé composé of mettre (they put/placed). Common patterns: (1) mettre + object + place: « Ils ont mis mon nom dans la Coupe » = they put my name in the Goblet. (2) mettre + object (meaning install/add): « Ils ont mis un portail » = they installed/put in a gate. (3) mettre + duration + à + infinitive: « Ils ont mis deux ans à construire… » = it took them two years to build… (4) mettre fin à + noun: « Ils ont mis fin au… » = they put an end to…
target_language_example: Ils ont mis trois heures à arriver.
native_language_example: It took them three hours to arrive.

additional_notes: Passé composé of prendre (to take). Used for many common meanings: taking/grabbing something (Ils ont pris de la nourriture), having a meal/drink (Ils ont pris leur petit-déjeuner = they had breakfast), taking a risk (Ils ont pris un gros risque), taking someone away (can imply kidnapping depending on context), and choosing a route (Qu’est-ce qu’ils ont pris comme rues ? = Which streets did they take?).
target_language_example: Ils ont pris le bus pour aller au centre-ville.
native_language_example: They took the bus to go downtown.

meaning: “they all have” / “they have all” (all of them).
additional_notes: Used with the subject pronoun ils (“they”) + avoir (“have”), with tous emphasizing that every person in the group did the action. In the passé composé, tous is commonly placed between the auxiliary verb ont and the past participle: Ils ont tous changé (“They all changed”). Can also mean “they all have (something)” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ils ont tous compris la question.
native_language_example: They all understood the question.

additional_notes: "Ils" = they. "Ont tué" is the passé composé of "tuer" (to kill). Used to describe a completed action in the past; the object usually follows (e.g., "Ils ont tué Bob").
target_language_example: Ils ont tué le dragon dans l'histoire.
native_language_example: They killed the dragon in the story.

meaning: “they were / they have been” (passé composé of être; often used to form the passive).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a past participle to make the passive voice: ils ont été + participe passé (e.g., attaqués, surpris). The past participle usually agrees with ils (masculine plural: -s).
target_language_example: Ils ont été invités à la fête, mais ils n’ont pas pu venir.
native_language_example: They were invited to the party, but they couldn’t come.

additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" and "ont" is the present tense of "avoir" (to have) for "they". Very common in set expressions where English often uses "to be": "ils ont raison" (they’re right), "ils ont peur" (they’re afraid), and for age: "ils ont dix ans" (they’re ten).
target_language_example: Ils ont peur de perdre leur travail.
native_language_example: They’re afraid of losing their job.

additional_notes: “Avoir besoin de” means “to need.” After it, use a noun (Ils ont besoin de vacances) or an infinitive verb (Ils ont besoin de s’inspirer…). “De” may contract with articles: de + les → des, de + le → du, de + l’ stays de l’.
target_language_example: Ils ont besoin de temps pour réfléchir.
native_language_example: They need time to think.

additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine or mixed group). "ont" is the present tense of "avoir" (to have). "des" is the plural indefinite article meaning "some" (often not translated in English). Used to say that they possess or have something available: "Ils ont des armes" = "They have weapons"; "Ils ont des bonnes nouvelles ?" = "Do they have any good news?"; "Ils ont des jumelles" = "They have binoculars."
target_language_example: Ils ont des amis à Paris.
native_language_example: They have friends in Paris.

additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine or mixed group). "Parlent" is the present tense of "parler". It can mean speaking a language (often with no preposition: "Ils parlent français") or talking about something (use "de": "Ils parlent de musique"), and it can also be used as a question: "Ils parlent ?" = "Are they speaking/talking?"
target_language_example: Ils parlent de toi en ce moment.
native_language_example: They’re talking about you right now.

meaning: “they can / they are able to” (sometimes “they may”).
additional_notes: "Ils" = “they” (masculine or mixed group). "Peuvent" is the present tense of "pouvoir" (to be able to / can). It’s used for ability (“They can speak French”), possibility (“They can maybe start…”), or permission depending on context. In questions, it often means “Can they…?” ("Ils peuvent faire ça ?").
target_language_example: S’ils veulent, ils peuvent venir demain.
native_language_example: If they want, they can come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Present tense of the verb **savoir** (to know a fact / to know that…). **Ils** = “they” (usually a group of men, or a mixed group). Often used before **que** (“that”): *Ils savent que…* In speech, **ils** is often not strongly pronounced, and there is a liaison: *ils savent* → sounds like **[il sav]**.
target_language_example: Ils savent que c’est important.
native_language_example: They know that it’s important.

additional_notes: "Se" is a pronoun that goes before the verb. With "ils" (they), it usually marks a reflexive action (they do it to themselves) or a reciprocal action (they do it to each other). Common in many verbs: "ils se battent" (they fight each other), "ils se détendent" (they relax), "ils se disent" (they say to each other).
target_language_example: Quand ils se voient, ils se parlent longtemps.
native_language_example: When they see each other, they talk for a long time.

additional_notes: Used to form the passé composé of reflexive ("se") verbs with the subject "ils" (they). Structure: ils + se + sont + past participle. Many reflexive verbs translate as "they got ..." or "they ... themselves" in English, depending on the verb (e.g., ils se sont levés = they got up). The past participle often agrees in plural: ils se sont levés / ils se sont noyés.
target_language_example: Ils se sont réveillés tôt.
native_language_example: They woke up early.

meaning: they got married / they married (each other).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the reflexive verb se marier (“to get married”). Used to say that a couple married at a specific time (often with il y a…, quand…, récemment, etc.).
target_language_example: Ils se sont mariés en juin.
native_language_example: They got married in June.

additional_notes: Used to talk about where people will be or what they will be like in the future: Ils seront là dans quelques minutes. It can also express a guess/assumption about the present (“they must be…”), especially from context: Ils seront déjà partis. In your example « ils seront rentrés », the helper verb is in the future (« ils seront ») + past participle (« rentrés ») to form the futur antérieur (“they will have come back / they must have come back”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : ils seront prêts demain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: they will be ready tomorrow.

additional_notes: Present-tense form of être used with ils for a masculine or mixed-gender plural subject. For an all-female group, use elles sont.
target_language_example: Ils sont très contents aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: They are very happy today.

meaning: “they went” / “they have gone” (masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of aller with être: ils (they) + sont (are) + allés (gone). Use for a group of males or a mixed group; for all-female, say « elles sont allées » (with -es). Often followed by a place with « à/dans/au/à la/aux » or an activity: « aller + infinitive » (e.g., « allés voir » = went to see).
target_language_example: Après le travail, ils sont allés au restaurant.
native_language_example: After work, they went to the restaurant.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of arriver with être: ils + sont + arrivé(s). The -s on arrivés agrees with ils (masculine plural; for an all-female group you’d write elles sont arrivées). Used for arriving at a place (à + city, en + country) and also figuratively in “arriver à la conclusion” = “to come to the conclusion.”
target_language_example: Ils sont arrivés à Paris hier soir.
native_language_example: They arrived in Paris last night.

meaning: they are (currently) / they are in the middle of (doing).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize an action happening right now (French version of the English present continuous). Structure: être (conjugated) + en train de + infinitive. Here: ils sont en train de + infinitive = “they are currently …”.
target_language_example: Ils sont en train de préparer le dîner.
native_language_example: They are preparing dinner (right now).

additional_notes: Used to point out that a group of males or a mixed group is present. Depending on context, “là” can mean either “here” (near the speaker) or “there” (at a specific place). Often said when noticing or locating someone/something: “Regarde, ils sont là.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, ils sont là pour t’aider.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, they’re here to help you.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *mourir* (to die) with the auxiliary *être*. *Ils sont morts* can describe (1) the event of dying (“they died”) or (2) the resulting state (“they’re dead”). In writing, you may also see it used in a time clause: *Quand ils sont morts, …* (“When they died, …”).
target_language_example: Ils sont morts il y a dix ans.
native_language_example: They died ten years ago.

additional_notes: Past tense with the verb "être" (passé composé) of "partir" = to leave/go away. "Ils" refers to a group of males or a mixed group. Often followed by time ("il y a une heure"), purpose/duration ("pour le week-end"), direction ("par là"), or a destination ("pour Paris").
target_language_example: Ils sont partis sans dire au revoir.
native_language_example: They left without saying goodbye.

additional_notes: Used to say that every person in a (masculine or mixed-gender) group is in a certain state or place. "tous" agrees with "ils" (masculine plural). For an all-female group, you say "elles sont toutes". In questions, you’ll often hear it as "Où sont-ils tous ?" (more standard word order) or "Où ils sont tous ?" (more conversational).
target_language_example: Ils sont tous à la maison.
native_language_example: They’re all at home.

meaning: "they are very" (used to describe a group of males or a mixed group).
additional_notes: “Ils” = “they” (for a group of men/boys, or a mixed-gender group). “Sont” is the verb “être” (to be) for “they are.” “Très” means “very” and usually comes right before an adjective (très forts, très généreux). The adjective that follows generally agrees in number (plural) with “ils.”
target_language_example: Ils sont très gentils.
native_language_example: They are very nice.

meaning: 'they came' / 'they have come' (masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of venir with être: venir → ils sont venus. Used for arriving/coming to a place (chez moi, à mon appartement), coming from somewhere (depuis le Brésil), or coming at a time (la semaine passée, le lundi). Agreement: venus (masc. plural); if the group is all female: elles sont venues.
target_language_example: Ils sont venus tôt pour m’aider.
native_language_example: They came early to help me.

additional_notes: "Ils" means "they" (for a group of males or a mixed group). "Veulent" is the present tense of "vouloir" (to want) for "ils/elles". Often followed by an infinitive: "ils veulent partir" (they want to leave). It can also be followed by "que" + subjunctive to express what they want someone to do: "ils veulent que je vienne" (they want me to come).
target_language_example: Ils veulent aller au cinéma ce soir.
native_language_example: They want to go to the movies tonight.

additional_notes: Present tense of venir (to come) with ils (they). It can describe movement toward someone/somewhere (Ils viennent vers nous. = They’re coming toward us.) or be used in the near past with venir de + infinitive (Ils viennent juste de la sortir… = They just took her out…).
target_language_example: Ils viennent ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are they coming tonight?

additional_notes: From the verb aller (“to go”). Very often used with an infinitive (ils vont + infinitive) to express the near future: “they’re going to …”. On its own, ils vont can also mean “they go/they are going”.
target_language_example: Ils vont partir bientôt.
native_language_example: They’re going to leave soon.

meaning: “they’re going to … us” (near future with “nous” = us).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about something that’s about to happen: Ils vont + infinitive. The pronoun “nous” (us) is placed before the infinitive: « Ils vont nous voir » = “They’re going to see us.” Depending on the verb, “nous” can be a direct object (see us) or indirect object (talk to us).
target_language_example: Cache-toi : ils vont nous entendre !
native_language_example: Hide: they’re going to hear us!

additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine or mixed group). "Voulaient" is the imperfect past tense of "vouloir" (to want), used for an ongoing/recurring desire in the past, background context, or what someone wanted at the time. Often followed by a noun ("ils voulaient des excuses") or by "que" + subjunctive for what they wanted someone to do ("ils voulaient que je vienne").
target_language_example: Quand ils étaient plus jeunes, ils voulaient voyager partout.
native_language_example: When they were younger, they wanted to travel everywhere.

additional_notes: "Ils" means "they" (for a group with at least one male, or mixed gender). "Étaient" is the imperfect past tense of "être" (to be). It’s used for describing a past state/condition, ongoing situation, or background description (not a single completed event). For an event like "they arrived," French usually uses "ils sont arrivés" (passé composé), not "ils étaient arrivés" unless it’s in a past-before-past context.
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, ils étaient déjà là.
native_language_example: When I arrived, they were already there.

additional_notes: Used to say that every person in a group of males or mixed gender was in the same situation/state. "Ils" = they (masc./mixed), "étaient" = were (imperfect of être), and "tous" = all. "Tous" here is an adverb meaning “all (of them)” and typically goes right after the verb: « Ils étaient tous + adjective/past participle/noun phrase » (e.g., « en uniforme », « partis »).
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, ils étaient tous déjà là.
native_language_example: When I arrived, they were all already there.

additional_notes: Used to say an action won’t help or isn’t worth doing. Very common in the full form: « Il est inutile de + infinitive » (“It’s pointless to…”). In speech and writing it’s often shortened to « Inutile de + infinitive » (“No point in…”).
target_language_example: Inutile de t'inquiéter, tout va bien.
native_language_example: No point in worrying, everything is fine.

additional_notes: Means you like something (or someone) a lot. Used with a noun ("j'adore ce nom" = "I love that name") or with an infinitive to say you love doing something ("j'adore faire…" = "I love doing…"). "J'" is the shortened form of "je" before a vowel sound.
target_language_example: J'adore cette chanson !
native_language_example: I love this song!

meaning: “I love this …” (referring to a singular feminine thing).
additional_notes: Used to express strong liking/love for something. It must be followed by a noun: **j'adore cette + nom**. **cette** is the feminine singular form of “this,” used with feminine nouns (and also before a vowel sound or *h* muet: *cette amie*). For masculine nouns, use **ce/cet** (*j'adore ce film / j'adore cet endroit*).
target_language_example: j'adore cette idée.
native_language_example: I love this idea.

additional_notes: Contraction of je ai. It is the 1st-person singular form of avoir and is used both for possession/state (for example, j'ai un livre = I have a book) and as an auxiliary before a past participle to form a very common past tense, often translated as the simple past in English.
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon téléphone.
native_language_example: I forgot my phone.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of appeler: j’ + ai + appelé. Use it to say you called someone or called a place. With time expressions you can specify when: « J’ai appelé … il y a deux jours » = “I called … two days ago.”
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai appelé trop tard.
native_language_example: Sorry, I called too late.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *apprendre* with *je*: **j'ai appris**. It can mean (1) you learned something (a skill/knowledge): *j'ai appris le français* (“I learned French”), or (2) you found out/heard some information: *j'ai appris la nouvelle* (“I found out/heard the news”). It’s commonly followed by **que** (“that”) or **ce qui** (“what”): *j'ai appris que…*, *j'ai appris ce qui s’est passé*.
target_language_example: j'ai appris hier que tu étais ici.
native_language_example: I found out yesterday that you were here.

additional_notes: Past tense of attendre (“to wait”), using the passé composé: j’ + ai + attendu. Often followed by a duration (des heures, toute la journée, très longtemps) or by pour + infinitive (“in order to / to”): J’ai attendu toute ma vie pour le dire.
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai attendu longtemps, mais tu n'es pas venu.
native_language_example: Sorry, I waited a long time, but you didn’t come.

additional_notes: Past tense of comprendre (“to understand”), used to say you understood something just explained. In conversation it often means “Got it/OK, I understand,” and can sound firm depending on tone (e.g., "Ouais, j'ai compris" = “Yeah, I got it”).
target_language_example: D'accord, j'ai compris : on se retrouve à 18 h devant la gare.
native_language_example: Okay, I got it: we’re meeting at 6 p.m. in front of the station.

additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of *croire* to report what you believed at that moment, often implying you later realized it was wrong or it turned out differently (surprise, fear, misunderstanding). It’s followed by a full clause with its own verb tense: *j’ai cru que + imparfait / plus-que-parfait / conditionnel*, etc. Example nuance: *J’ai cru que tu étais parti/partie* (agreement with the person addressed: *parti* to a man, *partie* to a woman).
target_language_example: J'ai cru que c'était un voleur.
native_language_example: I thought it was a burglar.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « dire » (to say/tell). Used to report something you said in the past (often like English simple past “I said”). Can also be used to insist or repeat an instruction: « J'ai dit ! » = “I said so!/That’s what I said!”
target_language_example: Hier, j'ai dit que je viendrais demain.
native_language_example: Yesterday, I said that I would come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what you previously said, followed by a full clause. After « que », French commonly uses backshifting (e.g., conditional/past forms) in reported speech: « J'ai dit que je le ferais » (“I said I would do it”). In casual speech you may also hear no backshift: « J'ai dit que je le ferai » (“I said I will do it”), though it’s less standard in careful French.
target_language_example: J'ai dit que je le ferais.
native_language_example: I said that I would do it.

meaning: "I had to" / "I needed to"; sometimes "I must have" (probably).
additional_notes: Passé composé of devoir (to have to). It often expresses a past obligation/necessity: « J'ai dû partir » = “I had to leave.” In some contexts it expresses a logical guess about the past: « J'ai dû m'évanouir » = “I must have fainted” (I probably fainted). The form « dû » (with the accent) can look like English “due” but it’s a different word.
target_language_example: J'ai dû annuler le rendez-vous.
native_language_example: I had to cancel the appointment.

additional_notes: Passé composé of entendre (“to hear”). Used for (1) something you heard at a specific moment (J'ai entendu l'appel; J'ai entendu ça à la radio) or (2) information/rumors you learned by hearing (J'ai entendu dire que…; J'ai entendu de bonnes choses sur…). Often translates as either “I heard” or “I’ve heard” depending on context.
target_language_example: J'ai entendu ça à la radio.
native_language_example: I heard that on the radio.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: « j'ai failli + infinitif » = you came very close to doing something, but it didn’t happen (often a near miss). Despite looking like English “failed,” « faillir » means “to almost (do)” in this structure.
target_language_example: J'ai failli avoir un accident en venant.
native_language_example: I almost had an accident on my way here.

additional_notes: Used to say you carried out whatever follows—often what you thought was right/necessary, or what someone told/asked you to do. It’s typically followed by another clause (e.g., "j’ai pu" = I could; "j’avais à faire" = I had to do; "tu as dit" = you said; "vous avez demandé" = you asked).
target_language_example: J'ai fait ce que j'ai pu.
native_language_example: I did what I could.

additional_notes: Passé composé of "faire" with "avoir": "j'ai fait" = "I did" / "I have done." Used to state you did something; can also express emphasis, disbelief, or defensiveness in questions (e.g., "J'ai fait ça, moi ?"). "Ça" refers to something already known from context.
target_language_example: Vous pensez que j'ai fait ça ?
native_language_example: Do you think I did that?

additional_notes: With a direct object, it means you completed something: « J'ai fini mon service. » = “I finished my shift.” Used with a place (often with « ici », « au… », « dans… »), « finir » can mean “to end up”: « J'ai fini ici. » = “I ended up here.”
target_language_example: J'ai fini trop tard, alors j'ai pris un taxi.
native_language_example: I finished too late, so I took a taxi.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *lire* with *avoir*: **j'** (je) + **ai** (have) + **lu** (read). Used to say you read something (a file, report, article). Often translates to English simple past (“I read…”) or present perfect (“I have read…”), depending on context.
target_language_example: J'ai lu ton message ce matin.
native_language_example: I read your message this morning.

additional_notes: Past tense of oublier (“to forget”) using the passé composé: j’ai + oublié. Often used alone as an apology (“Sorry, I forgot.”) or followed by what was forgotten: j’ai oublié + noun (j’ai oublié les paroles) or j’ai oublié ce que… (“I forgot what…”).
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon mot de passe, je ne peux pas me connecter.
native_language_example: I forgot my password, I can’t log in.

additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t do an action because you forgot. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « j’ai oublié de + infinitive » (e.g., j’ai oublié de fermer la porte). Can also introduce something you forgot to mention: « Oh, j’ai oublié de te dire… ».
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai oublié de répondre à ton message.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot to reply to your message.

meaning: “I don’t have / I didn’t / I haven’t” (informal negative form of « j’ai »).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: it drops « ne » from the standard negative « je n’ai pas … ». Used either with a noun (« J'ai pas le temps » = I don’t have time) or before a past participle (« J'ai pas compris » = I didn’t understand / I haven’t understood). In careful writing or formal situations, use « je n’ai pas ».
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai pas le temps aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have time today.

meaning: “I had / I spent a …” (talking about time, like a day or an evening).
additional_notes: Used with a time period (une journée, une soirée, une semaine, etc.) to describe how your time was. It’s the passé composé of *passer*: *j’ai passé* + adjective + time word. Even though it looks like English “I passed,” here it usually means “I spent” or “I had.”
target_language_example: J'ai passé une semaine incroyable à Paris.
native_language_example: I had an incredible week in Paris.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed/assumed about someone (often as an explanation). It’s the passé composé of penser (j’ai pensé = “I thought”), followed by que + a clause starting with tu. What follows can be in the imperfect/conditional/etc. depending on the meaning: e.g., "J’ai pensé que tu aurais faim" = “I thought you would be hungry.”
target_language_example: J'ai pensé que tu étais déjà parti.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

additional_notes: Passé composé of prendre (je prends → j'ai pris). Very common and flexible depending on what follows: it can mean you took/grabbed something (j'ai pris de quoi manger), took notes (j'ai pris des notes), had food/drinks (j'ai pris deux verres de vin), answered a call (j'ai pris l'appel), made a decision (j'ai pris ma décision), made an appointment (j'ai pris rendez-vous), or took care of someone (j'ai pris soin de toi). The most natural English translation depends on the object/complement.
target_language_example: J'ai pris des notes pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: I took notes during the meeting.

meaning: 'I was able to' / 'I could' / 'I managed to' (in the past).
