additional_notes: Past tense of "pouvoir" (passé composé). It often means you had the ability or the opportunity to do something and succeeded: "J'ai pu faire…" = "I was able to do…". In questions, it can express surprise/regret: "Comment j'ai pu… ?" = "How could I…?". Common with comparisons/time: "aussi vite que j'ai pu" (as fast as I could), "autant que j'ai pu" (as much as I could), "dès que j'ai pu" (as soon as I could).
target_language_example: Je suis parti dès que j'ai pu.
native_language_example: I left as soon as I could.

additional_notes: Literally "I have always wanted." Used to talk about a long-standing desire up to now. Often followed by an infinitive (j'ai toujours voulu + verb: "j'ai toujours voulu voyager") or by a noun ("j'ai toujours voulu un fils"). In more formal/written French, you may also see "j'ai toujours voulu dire" for "I've always wanted to say," but everyday speech often uses "j'ai toujours voulu te dire…".
target_language_example: J'ai toujours voulu apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I've always wanted to learn French.

additional_notes: Often used at the start of a sentence with a past participle (passé composé): **J'ai tout + past participle** = “I … everything” (e.g., *J'ai tout essayé* = “I tried everything”). On its own, **J'ai tout** can mean “I have everything / I’ve got everything,” depending on context.
target_language_example: J'ai tout préparé pour ce soir.
native_language_example: I prepared everything for tonight.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *trouver* with **avoir**. Used when you located/discovered something (*j'ai trouvé une solution*), found/obtained something (*j'ai trouvé du travail*), or to express an opinion with **j'ai trouvé que + clause** (“I thought / I found that…”, e.g., *j'ai trouvé ça tout à fait normal* / *j'ai trouvé que c'était normal*). It can also be used alone to mean “I’ve got it!” / “Found it!” (*Voilà, j'ai trouvé.*).
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé une solution.
native_language_example: I found a solution.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « voir » (to see). Depending on context, can mean “I saw” (past event) or “I’ve seen” (present relevance). In conversation, « C’est bon, j’ai vu » can mean “OK, I saw” → “OK, I get it / I understand.”
target_language_example: C'est bon, j'ai vu.
native_language_example: OK, I saw / OK, I get it.

additional_notes: Literally "I have seen that" (passé composé of voir). Used to say you saw something (on TV, in the news, online, etc.) or that you’ve already seen it before. In casual speech you may also hear just "Vu ça" or "J’ai déjà vu ça" (I’ve already seen that).
target_language_example: T'inquiète, j'ai vu ça sur Internet.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I saw that on the Internet.

additional_notes: Passé composé of être (je + ai + été). Often used (1) with an adjective to describe how you were/you felt: « J'ai été content/ravi. », and (2) to form the passive voice: « J'ai été acquitté » = “I was acquitted.” In many everyday contexts it translates to English simple past (“I was”), even though the literal form is “I have been.”
target_language_example: J'ai été très fatigué hier soir.
native_language_example: I was very tired last night.

additional_notes: Contraction of je ai, from the verb avoir. Very common in everyday French for possession and in many set expressions: j'ai faim = I'm hungry, j'ai 20 ans = I'm 20 years old, j'ai rendez-vous = I have an appointment.
target_language_example: J'ai une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I have a good idea.

meaning: "I need a" (followed by a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you need something or someone. It’s the most common way to express need in French. Change the article depending on the noun: j’ai besoin d’une + feminine noun; j’ai besoin de + plural/uncountable (e.g., j’ai besoin de temps); j’ai besoin d’ + vowel sound (e.g., j’ai besoin d’un avocat).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un stylo, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I need a pen, please.

meaning: “I need a/an …” (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or requirement. "J'ai besoin de" = "I need"; it becomes "d'une" before a feminine singular noun (e.g., une autorisation, une signature). For a masculine noun, use "j'ai besoin d'un"; for a plural, use "j'ai besoin de" + plural noun (e.g., "j'ai besoin de clés"). Note the apostrophe: "j'ai" is the contraction of "je ai".
target_language_example: j'ai besoin d'une autorisation.
native_language_example: I need an authorization/permission.

additional_notes: Used to say that you need something or need to do something. It is followed by de + a noun (j'ai besoin de détails) or de + an infinitive (j'ai besoin de partir). This form is specifically for 'I need'.
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de parler avec toi.
native_language_example: I need to talk with you.

additional_notes: Used to say you need someone’s help, support, or presence. "J’ai besoin de" is followed by a person (toi/vous/lui/elle) or a thing (ex. "J’ai besoin d’aide" = I need help). You can add a place or time: "J’ai besoin de toi là-bas" (I need you there) or "quand j’ai besoin de toi" (when I need you).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de toi maintenant, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I need you now, please.

additional_notes: Used to say you possess or have something in general, before a plural noun: j’ai + des + noun (e.g., des projets, des infos). "J’ai" is the contraction of "je ai". "Des" often means "some" or simply marks an unspecified plural in French.
target_language_example: J'ai des questions pour toi.
native_language_example: I have some questions for you.

meaning: "I still have" / "I have ... left" (also "I have more").
additional_notes: Used to say something remains to do/ask, time remains, or that you can add something else. Common patterns: "j'ai encore + noun" (j'ai encore du travail = I still have work), "j'ai encore + infinitive" (j'ai encore des choses à faire = I still have things to do), and "j'ai encore le temps" (I still have time). In "j'ai encore mieux", it means "I have something even better".
target_language_example: j'ai encore quelques questions à vous poser.
native_language_example: I still have a few questions to ask you.

additional_notes: Used to express a desire or urge. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « j'ai envie de + infinitive » (j'ai envie de sortir, j'ai envie de marcher). It can be a light preference (“I feel like…”) or a stronger desire depending on context. In a negative or rhetorical question, it can imply reluctance or annoyance: « Tu crois que j'ai envie de faire ça ? » (“Do you think I want to do that?”).
target_language_example: J'ai envie de rentrer chez moi.
native_language_example: I feel like going home.

additional_notes: A very common way to express hunger in French. Literally “I have hunger” (avoir + noun): j'ai faim (I’m hungry), tu as faim (you’re hungry), il/elle a faim (he/she is hungry), nous avons faim (we’re hungry), vous avez faim (you’re hungry/formal), ils/elles ont faim (they’re hungry).
target_language_example: J'ai faim, on peut manger maintenant ?
native_language_example: I'm hungry—can we eat now?

additional_notes:
Common everyday way to say you feel fear. Often followed by:
- "de" + infinitive: "J'ai peur de tomber." (I’m afraid of falling.)
- "que" + subjunctive: "J'ai peur qu'il soit en retard." (I’m afraid he might be late.)
You can also use it alone as a reaction: "J'ai peur !"
target_language_example: J'ai peur de parler en public.
native_language_example: I'm afraid of speaking in public.

additional_notes: Used to say you have something (an object, a problem, or something intended for someone). Often followed by extra info: **dans** + body part (j'ai quelque chose dans l'œil = something is in my eye), **pour** + person (j'ai quelque chose pour lui = I have something for him), or a relative clause **qui…** (j'ai quelque chose qui t'est destiné = I have something meant for you). Note: the contraction **j'ai** is very common in writing; you may also see **j’ai** with a typographic apostrophe.
target_language_example: J'ai quelque chose pour toi.
native_language_example: I have something for you.

additional_notes: Literally “I have reason,” but it means “I’m right.” Often used in conversation to confirm you’re correct: “J’ai raison, pas vrai ?” (“I’m right, aren’t I?”). In the pattern “J’ai raison ou j’ai raison ?”, it’s a rhetorical way of saying “I’m right, obviously.”
target_language_example: Tu vois ? J'ai raison, pas vrai ?
native_language_example: See? I’m right, aren’t I?

additional_notes: From the verb **avoir** (to have): **j'ai** = “I have.” It’s used to introduce something you possess or want to say, especially with announcements or information: **J’ai une annonce / une question / une idée.** The **j’** is a shortened form of **je** before a vowel sound. Use **un** instead of **une** with a masculine noun (**j’ai un problème**).
target_language_example: J'ai une question à te poser.
native_language_example: I have a question to ask you.

additional_notes: Used when the noun is feminine and is either mentioned just before or understood from context (e.g., une théorie, une faveur, une question). If you explicitly say the noun, you can add it after « autre »: « J’ai une autre théorie. » For a masculine noun, use « j’ai un autre … » (e.g., « J’ai un autre problème. »).
target_language_example: J'ai une autre théorie à vous soumettre.
native_language_example: I have another theory to put to you.

additional_notes: Used to get someone’s attention before asking something. Often followed by a detail: « pour toi » (for you), « à propos de… » (about…), or « à poser » (to ask). In more formal settings you can also say « J’aurais une question » (“I have a question” / “I’d like to ask a question”).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, j'ai une question : où est la gare ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a question: where is the train station?

meaning: "I have to do (something)" / "I have things to do."
additional_notes: From the structure **avoir à + infinitive**, which expresses that you have something to do (often an obligation or task). It can be left incomplete in context (**j'ai à faire**) to mean “I have things to do / I’m busy,” but it’s more common to specify the verb: **J’ai à faire mes devoirs**. Often similar in meaning to **je dois + infinitive** (“I must / I have to”), with **avoir à** sounding a bit more formal or administrative.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : j'ai à faire ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have things to do tonight.

additional_notes: From aimer. The apostrophe appears because je becomes j' before a vowel or silent h. Use it to say you like or love something, someone, or doing an action: j'aime le café, j'aime danser.
target_language_example: J'aime lire le soir.
native_language_example: I like reading in the evening.

additional_notes: Common, everyday way to say you like something without it sounding as strong or intense as “j’adore” (I love it). Often used to express a positive opinion or preference: “J’aime bien ça” (I like that), “J’aime bien cet endroit” (I quite like this place). Can also be used on its own to mean “I like it” or “I’m fine with it”: “Moi, j’aime bien.”
target_language_example: J'aime bien ce film, surtout la musique.
native_language_example: I quite like this movie, especially the music.

additional_notes: Common polite way to say what you want or would like to do. Used with an infinitive (j’aimerais + verb): “J’aimerais y aller” = “I’d like to go there.” It can also be followed by a noun: “J’aimerais un café” = “I’d like a coffee.” Often sounds softer/more polite than “je veux” (I want).
target_language_example: J'aimerais un verre d'eau, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like a glass of water, please.

meaning: “I was going” / “I was going to” (was about to).
additional_notes: Contraction of « je » + « allais » (imparfait of « aller »). Very common for the near future in the past: « j'allais + infinitive » = “I was going to / I was about to …” (often something planned or almost happening: « J'allais t'appeler. »). It can also mean simple past movement: “I was going (somewhere)”.
target_language_example: J'ai cru que j'allais m'évanouir.
native_language_example: I thought I was going to faint.

additional_notes: This is the past conditional of "aimer" and is used to express that you would have wanted something, but it didn’t happen (or you regret it). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive ("j'aurais aimé rester") or by "que" + subjunctive ("j'aurais aimé que tu m’en parles"). It can also sound like a gentle reproach meaning "I wish you had…".
target_language_example: j'aurais aimé que tu m'en parles plus tôt.
native_language_example: I would have liked you to tell me about it earlier.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you did NOT do in the past and now think it was the right thing to do (often expressing regret, criticism, or a missed opportunity). It’s formed with the conditional of "avoir" + "dû" (past participle of "devoir") and is usually followed by an infinitive: "j'aurais dû + infinitive" (e.g., "j'aurais dû venir").
target_language_example: J'aurais dû te prévenir plus tôt.
native_language_example: I should have warned you earlier.

meaning: “I could have” / “I would have been able to.”
additional_notes: This is the past conditional of pouvoir (“can/to be able to”): j’ (je) + aurais (would have) + pu (been able). It’s used for missed possibilities, regrets, or hypothetical past situations. It’s usually followed by an infinitive (e.g., j'aurais pu le faire = I could have done it), but it can also stand alone when the action is understood from context (J'aurais pu. = I could have.)
target_language_example: J'aurais pu te le dire, mais j'ai oublié.
native_language_example: I could have told you, but I forgot.

meaning: “I had” / “I used to have” / “I was (having)” — imperfect past of « avoir »; also used to form the past perfect (plus-que-parfait): « j'avais + participe passé » = “I had + past participle”.
additional_notes: « j'avais » is « je » + « avais » (imperfect of « avoir », to have). It expresses past states, habitual actions, or ongoing situations (“I had/used to have/was having”). It also serves as the auxiliary for the plus-que-parfait: « j'avais compris » = “I had understood”. In informal speech/writing, French often drops « ne » in negation: « j'avais pas » = “I didn’t have / I hadn’t”.
target_language_example: C'est ce que j'avais compris.
native_language_example: That’s what I had understood.

additional_notes: Contraction of "je avais" → "j'avais". It’s the imperfect past of "avoir" (to have), used for ongoing states/habits in the past and for giving your age in the past: "J'avais huit ans" = "I was eight (years old)".
target_language_example: Quand j'avais dix ans, j'avais un chien.
native_language_example: When I was ten, I had a dog.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of "avoir besoin de" (to need). Use it for ongoing/repeated needs in the past or to set background: "I needed...". Followed by a noun (besoin de compagnie), an infinitive (besoin de réfléchir), or a person/object + infinitive (besoin de te voir). In more formal French, say "j'avais besoin d'argent" instead of "de fric".
target_language_example: J'avais besoin de repos, alors je suis resté chez moi.
native_language_example: I needed some rest, so I stayed home.

additional_notes: Used with the pronoun "en" to replace something introduced with "de" (or an amount/quantity). It often means “some” or “(some) of it/them.” Common patterns: "j'en ai" + past participle (e.g., "j'en ai mangé" = I ate some), and "j'en ai assez" + past participle (e.g., "j'en ai assez vu/entendu" = I’ve seen/heard enough).
target_language_example: Tu veux des biscuits ? J'en ai acheté.
native_language_example: Do you want cookies? I bought some.

additional_notes: Passé composé form built from **j’ + en + ai + eu** (avoir). **En** typically replaces something previously mentioned introduced with **de / du / de la / des**, especially an amount, number, or “some of it/them.” It’s commonly completed by a quantity or fixed expression: **j'en ai eu deux/une** (“I had two/one (of them)”), **j'en ai eu assez / marre** (“I’ve had enough / I’m fed up”). On its own (**J'en ai eu.**), it means “I had some/it,” with the context understood.
target_language_example: Tu veux encore du gâteau ? — Non merci, j'en ai eu assez.
native_language_example: Do you want more cake? — No thanks, I’ve had enough.

additional_notes: en replaces something already mentioned, often an unspecified quantity or something introduced with de. So j'en ai commonly means 'I have some/any' or 'I have it/them' depending on context. In certain set expressions, the full English translation changes, for example j'en ai l'intention = 'I intend to' and qu'est-ce que j'en ai à faire ? = 'what do I care?'.
target_language_example: Tu as du pain ? Oui, j'en ai.
native_language_example: Do you have any bread? Yes, I have some.

additional_notes: From "avoir besoin de" (to need). "En" replaces something introduced with "de" (de ça, de lui/d’elle, du pain, etc.) and means “of it/of them/some.” Used when what you need is already known from context.
target_language_example: Je n'ai plus de café : j'en ai besoin pour rester éveillé.
native_language_example: I don't have any coffee left: I need it to stay awake.

meaning: “It’ll take me…” (a certain amount of time).
additional_notes: Used to say how long something will take you. It’s part of the expression « en avoir pour + duration »: « J'en ai pour deux minutes » = “I’ll be two minutes / It’ll take me two minutes.” You can also ask: « J'en ai pour combien de temps ? » (“How long will it take me?”).
target_language_example: J'en ai pour cinq minutes.
native_language_example: It’ll take me five minutes.

additional_notes: Uses the pronoun "en" to mean "of it" / "of them" (replacing something introduced with de, du, de la, des, or a quantity). "Un" agrees with the item you mean: j'en ai un (masc.), j'en ai une (fem.), j'en ai deux/trois, etc. Often answers "Tu en as un ?" / "Vous en avez un ?"
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, j'en ai un de rechange.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I have a spare one.

additional_notes: Uses the pronoun "en" to replace something previously mentioned (often introduced with "de"/"des"), and "une" because the thing you have is feminine singular. For a masculine noun you’d say "j’en ai un"; for more than one: "j’en ai deux / j’en ai plusieurs". Common with "avoir" to avoid repeating the noun: « Tu as une voiture ? — Oui, j’en ai une. »
target_language_example: Tu as une question ? Oui, j'en ai une.
native_language_example: Do you have a question? Yes, I have one.

meaning: "I am (one)" / "I’m at that point" / "I’m (almost) sure (of it)" (with *en* = “of it/of them”).
additional_notes: *En* replaces something introduced with **de** ("of it/of them"). So **j'en suis** can mean “I’m one (of them)” (*J'en suis un/une aussi.*) or “I’m at that stage/point” depending on context. With adjectives like **sûr/sûre**, it commonly expresses certainty about something previously mentioned: *J'en suis (presque) sûr(e).*
target_language_example: J'en suis presque sûre.
native_language_example: I’m almost sure of it.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you hope is true about a man or boy. It’s the start of a longer sentence: J’espère (que) + clause. After que, il often becomes qu’il (elision). With espérer, French usually uses the indicative (e.g., j’espère qu’il sait…), not the subjunctive.
target_language_example: J'espère qu'il sait ce qu'il fait.
native_language_example: I hope he knows what he’s doing.

additional_notes: Used to express hope about a situation. It’s followed by a full clause: "j'espère que + subject + verb". In French it commonly takes the indicative (e.g., "j'espère qu'il va bien"). In English, “that” is often optional: “I hope (that) …”.
target_language_example: j'espère que tu as de bonnes nouvelles.
native_language_example: I hope you have good news.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you’re hoping will happen. “Ça” is a very common pronoun meaning “it/that/this” (often referring to a situation or what was just mentioned). It’s typically followed by a verb clause: “j'espère que ça va”, “j'espère que ça t'ira”, “j'espère que ça vous aidera”.
target_language_example: j'espère que ça vous aidera.
native_language_example: I hope that will help you.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb: j'essaie de + infinitive (e.g., j'essaie de comprendre). It expresses effort, not guaranteed success. The full form is "j'essaie de"; "j'" is short for "je" before a vowel sound (essaie).
target_language_example: J'essaie de parler français tous les jours.
native_language_example: I’m trying to speak French every day.

additional_notes: Used to express an assumption or a likely conclusion, often based on what you know (but not with complete certainty). Very common in conversation. Typically followed by a clause introduced by "que": "j'imagine que tu as raison." You may also hear/write the more informal "j'imagine que t'as..." (= "tu as").
target_language_example: j'imagine que tu as raison.
native_language_example: I guess you’re right.

additional_notes: Very common informal spoken form of « je ne sais pas ». In casual speech, « ne » is often dropped (« je sais pas »), and « je » is contracted to « j’ » before a vowel sound (« j’sais » = « je sais »). Avoid in formal writing.
target_language_example: J'sais pas, peut-être demain.
native_language_example: I don't know, maybe tomorrow.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: contraction of « je (ne) sais pas quoi ». Often used when you can’t name or specify something (« Il a dit j'sais pas quoi » = “He said something or other”) or when you’re unsure what exactly (« On peut faire j'sais pas quoi ce soir » = “We can do… I don’t know, something tonight”). « ne » is usually dropped in speech.
target_language_example: Il m'a demandé j'sais pas quoi, mais j'ai pas compris.
native_language_example: He asked me something or other, but I didn’t understand.

additional_notes: "j'y" is "je" + the pronoun "y". "Y" usually replaces a place ("there") or something introduced with "à" ("to it/that"). It comes before the verb: "J'y pense" = "I’m thinking about it." "J'y vais" = "I’m going there." "Je" becomes "j'" before a vowel sound.
target_language_example: J'y vais demain.
native_language_example: I’m going there tomorrow.

additional_notes: This is a common chunk in the passé composé: j' (je) + y (pronoun meaning “there” or “to it/that”) + ai (have). Use y to replace something introduced with à (à Paris → j'y…, à ça → j'y…), or a place already known from context. It comes before the auxiliary: J'y ai pensé. (not *J'ai y pensé*).
target_language_example: J'y ai déjà été une fois.
native_language_example: I've already been there once.

additional_notes: “Y” replaces a place (there) or something introduced with à (to it/at it). In ordinary contexts, j'y suis often means “I’m there” (at that place). It also appears in the set expression “Allez/Va voir ailleurs si j'y suis”, a dismissive, fairly informal way to say “Get lost / Go away.”
target_language_example: Tu me cherches ? Je suis dans le salon : j'y suis.
native_language_example: Are you looking for me? I’m in the living room: I’m there.

additional_notes: Uses the pronoun **y** to mean “there” (to a place already mentioned or understood). **J'y vais** can mean you’re going to that place (“I’m going there”) or that you’re leaving/heading out now (“Okay, I’m going”). Often appears with time or decision markers: *alors* (then), *de toute façon* (anyway), *il est tard* (it’s late), etc.
target_language_example: D'accord, j'y vais, on se voit demain.
native_language_example: Okay, I'm heading off—see you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of « être » (j’étais) + « là » (“there”). Used to state that you were present at a time in the past, often as background information or to explain how you knew something. Very common in clauses with « que »: « Il savait que j’étais là » (“He knew I was there”).
target_language_example: Comment as-tu su que j'étais là ?
native_language_example: How did you know I was there?

additional_notes: Used as an emphatic, often exclamatory way to refuse or disagree—stronger than just « non ». It can stand alone, or be reinforced with « mais » ("Mais jamais de la vie !").
target_language_example: — Tu veux lui demander pardon ? — Jamais de la vie !
native_language_example: — Do you want to apologize to him? — No way!

additional_notes: Usually appears with **ne ... jamais ... rien** to mean someone **never says/does/understands anything**. Word order can change with pronouns: **Elle n’en a jamais rien dit** (“She never said anything about it”), **Vous ne me dites jamais rien** (“You never tell me anything”).
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais rien compris à ce jeu.
native_language_example: I never understood anything about this game.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never seen something/someone. Often appears with avoir in the past participle form: «(je) n'ai jamais vu…» = “I have never seen…”. In casual spoken French, «ne» is often dropped: «J'ai jamais vu ça.» You can also add «encore» for emphasis: «Je ne l'ai encore jamais vu.» = “I still haven’t ever seen him/it.”
target_language_example: Je n'ai jamais vu un film aussi long.
native_language_example: I have never seen a movie that long.

additional_notes: Used when you’re searching for something/someone (often followed by a noun): « Je cherche mon chat. » It can also introduce what you’re trying to figure out: « Je cherche quelle phrase écrire. » In « Je cherche mes mots », it means you’re struggling to find the right words ("I’m searching for words / I can’t find my words").
target_language_example: Je cherche un café pas trop cher près d’ici.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a café that’s not too expensive near here.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (verb in the “to ___” form): je commence à comprendre, je commence à m’y habituer. It expresses that something is beginning, often gradually. You can change the subject (tu commences à…, il/elle commence à…, etc.) and the tense (j’ai commencé à… = “I started to…”).
target_language_example: Je commence à parler français un peu mieux.
native_language_example: I’m starting to speak French a little better.

additional_notes: Used to say you understand what someone is saying, a situation, or how someone feels. Often followed by a clause: "je comprends que..." (= “I understand that...”). Can also be used alone as a response: "Je comprends." (= “I understand / I see.”).
target_language_example: Je comprends, mais je ne suis pas d'accord.
native_language_example: I understand, but I don't agree.

additional_notes: From connaître. Used with people and nouns to say you know someone or are familiar with something (a place, expression, type of person, etc.). French often uses savoir instead for knowing a fact or knowing how to do something.
target_language_example: Je connais bien ce quartier.
native_language_example: I know this neighborhood well.

additional_notes: Used to express worry or to politely introduce bad news or a negative answer. It is typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., « Je crains que ton plan ne fonctionne pas. »). You may also see an extra « ne » after « que » (the *ne explétif*), which is common in formal French and doesn’t mean “not” by itself. It can also be used alone as « Je crains que non. » = “I’m afraid not.”
target_language_example: Je crains que nous soyons en retard.
native_language_example: I’m afraid we’re late.

additional_notes: Used to express confidence or faith in a person, group, idea, or thing. Often followed by a noun or stressed pronoun: moi/toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux/elles (e.g., « Je crois en toi »). It can mean moral support/trust (« I believe in you ») or belief/faith (« I believe in that/God ») depending on context.
target_language_example: Je crois en toi, tu vas y arriver.
native_language_example: I believe in you—you’re going to make it.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or what you believe about a man/boy ("il" = "he/it"). In everyday French, "je crois que" often means "I think" (a bit uncertain), not necessarily a strong belief. It’s followed by a full clause: "Je crois qu'il + verb..."
target_language_example: Je crois qu'il va rentrer bientôt.
native_language_example: I think he’s going to come home soon.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion or guess. "Je crois que" = "I think/believe that"; before a vowel it becomes "qu'". "On" often means "we" in everyday French, but it can also mean "people" or an unspecified "they," depending on context.
target_language_example: Je crois qu'on est en retard.
native_language_example: I think we're late.

additional_notes: A common way to introduce an opinion, belief, or guess. In everyday English, it is often translated as "I think" rather than the more literal "I believe." The "that" is often omitted in English.
target_language_example: Je crois que tu as raison.
native_language_example: I think you're right.

additional_notes: Used to express a guess or belief about something. Often followed by a noun, pronoun, adjective, or prepositional phrase (e.g., « pour moi », « à toi », « prêt »). In speech, it’s commonly shortened to « je crois que c’est… ».
target_language_example: Je crois que c'est la bonne adresse.
native_language_example: I think it's the right address.

additional_notes: Used to express a belief or guess about something you did or that happened (often with a past action: *j’ai + past participle*). It sounds a bit unsure/soft, like “I think I…” rather than a firm statement. Often followed by verbs like *vu* (seen), *compris/pigé* (understood), *changé* (changed), *oublié* (forgotten), etc.
target_language_example: Je crois que j'ai oublié mes clés.
native_language_example: I think I forgot my keys.

meaning: "I think I am" / "I believe I am".
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or a personal belief about your own state/identity/feelings, often followed by an adjective or noun phrase: « Je crois que je suis fatigué(e) », « Je crois que je suis amoureux/amoureuse ». The word for “in love” agrees with the speaker: « amoureux » (typically masculine) / « amoureuse » (typically feminine). You’ll often add « de toi » (“with you”) or « encore » (“still”).
target_language_example: Je crois que je suis perdu(e).
native_language_example: I think I’m lost.

meaning: "I think I’m going to…" (I think I will… soon).
additional_notes: Used to express an intention or something you expect will happen in the near future. It’s typically followed by an infinitive: « Je crois que je vais partir » (I think I’m going to leave). In speech, you may hear it shortened: « J’crois que j’vais… ».
target_language_example: Je crois que je vais prendre un café.
native_language_example: I think I’m going to have a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or belief about a situation. “Ça” usually refers to something general (“it/that”), like a result, an idea, or a situation: Je crois que ça a marché (“I think it worked”). In everyday speech, you’ll also hear “Je crois que…” without “ça,” or “Je crois que ça…” followed by a verb like plaît, a plu, a fonctionné, etc.
target_language_example: Je crois que ça va être difficile.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to be difficult.

meaning: I think I know / I believe I know.
additional_notes: Used to express that you *probably* know something, but you’re not 100% sure. Often followed by an indirect question (ce que…, où…, pourquoi…, comment…, etc.). More cautious than “je sais” (I know).
target_language_example: Je crois savoir comment on peut t’aider.
native_language_example: I think I know how we can help you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you believed before, often implying surprise or disappointment that it isn’t true. The imperfect (croyais) suggests an earlier belief. "On" can mean "we" (very common in speech) or "people/one" depending on context.
target_language_example: Je croyais qu'on avait le temps, mais le train part dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I thought we had time, but the train leaves in five minutes.

meaning: "I thought (that)…" (often: I used to think / I was under the impression that).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect (croyais) to describe a past belief or assumption, often one that turned out to be wrong or was later corrected. It’s followed by a full clause: je croyais que + subject + verb (in a past or conditional tense depending on meaning).
target_language_example: Je croyais que tu étais déjà parti(e).
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

meaning: “I thought it was …” (often implying: I was mistaken / I had assumed).
additional_notes: Used to state a past belief or assumption, often when correcting yourself or realizing you were wrong. It’s in the imperfect (je croyais), which can sound softer/more tentative than “j’ai cru” (a more sudden/one-time “I thought”). You typically complete it with a noun/adjective/pronoun: “Je croyais que c’était fait / la femme / le mien / pour moi / réglé / vous.”
target_language_example: Je croyais que c'était réglé.
native_language_example: I thought it was settled.

additional_notes: Used to say you had an assumption about what “you” (tu) did or was doing, often implying you were mistaken or surprised. Literally “I believed that you…”. The verb is in the imperfect (croyais), so it often corresponds to English “I thought (at the time)…”. It’s typically followed by another verb clause: “je croyais que tu + avais/étais/allais…”.
target_language_example: Je croyais que tu venais ce soir.
native_language_example: I thought you were coming tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say your belief/assumption in the past, often when you’ve just learned it’s not true. The verb is in the imperfect (je croyais) because it describes an ongoing state of belief in the past. Followed by a clause with “tu étais” + an adjective (d’accord, occupé/occupée, retraité), a past participle (parti/partie), or an expression (à la retraite). Adjectives and past participles may change for gender: occupé/occupée, parti/partie. “Être retraité” and “être à la retraite” both mean “to be retired.”
target_language_example: Je croyais que tu étais en vacances cette semaine.
native_language_example: I thought you were on vacation this week.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of devoir ("to have to / must"). It’s used to talk about an obligation, necessity, or expectation in the past, often followed by an infinitive: je devais partir (I had to leave). Depending on context, it can mean either something you were required to do (had to) or something planned/expected (was supposed to).
target_language_example: Je devais appeler ma mère, mais j’ai oublié.
native_language_example: I was supposed to call my mom, but I forgot.

additional_notes: "Je devrais" is the conditional form of "devoir" (to have to / must). It’s commonly used to give softer advice or express what you think is the right thing to do (less strong than "je dois" = I must / I have to). Often followed by an infinitive: "je devrais partir" (I should leave).
target_language_example: Je devrais prendre rendez-vous chez le médecin.
native_language_example: I should make an appointment with the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to make a cautious suggestion about your own actions (a polite, tentative way to say what you think is the right thing to do). It’s the conditional of devoir (je devrais = I should/ought to) + peut-être (maybe). Often followed by an infinitive: je devrais peut-être partir (maybe I should leave).
target_language_example: Je devrais peut-être appeler ma mère ce soir.
native_language_example: Maybe I should call my mom tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say what you think is the right thing, expected thing, or advisable situation for you. It often expresses obligation, duty, or regret (that you aren’t in that situation). Built from the conditional of devoir (je devrais = I should) + infinitive être (to be), and it can be followed by a place (au lit, là-bas) or a state/feeling (heureuse).
target_language_example: Je devrais être plus prudent.
native_language_example: I should be more careful.

additional_notes: From dire. Used when stating an opinion, reporting words, or giving instructions: je dis que... = 'I say/I'm saying that...'; fais ce que je dis = 'do what I say.' Depending on context, dire can also translate as 'tell' in English.
target_language_example: Je dis la vérité.
native_language_example: I'm telling the truth.

additional_notes: First-person singular of devoir. It is usually followed by an infinitive and expresses obligation, necessity, or something you need to do. In other contexts, je dois can also mean "I owe."
target_language_example: Je dois finir mes devoirs ce soir.
native_language_example: I have to finish my homework tonight.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "devoir" (je dois) + an infinitive to express obligation/necessity. Often followed by a place/activity with "aller": "je dois aller chez le dentiste" (I have to go to the dentist), "je dois aller travailler" (I have to go to work). In questions you may also see the more formal word order "où dois-je aller ?"
target_language_example: Désolé, je dois aller maintenant.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go now.

meaning: I have to go to… / I need to go to…
additional_notes: Used to say you’re obligated to go somewhere (a place or an event). Follow with a city/country (Je dois aller à Paris) or with an event/activity using an article (Je dois aller à une réunion). For feminine destinations, you often use en instead of à (Je dois aller en France).
target_language_example: Désolé, je dois aller à l'aéroport maintenant.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go to the airport now.

additional_notes: Used to say you are obliged/required to do something. Very common in questions like « Qu'est-ce que je dois faire ? » (What do I have to do?) or « Comment je dois faire ? » (How should I do it?/How do I go about it?). You can also add an object after it: « je dois faire mes devoirs » (I have to do my homework).
target_language_example: Je dois faire les courses avant de rentrer.
native_language_example: I have to do the grocery shopping before going home.

meaning: "I have to do it" / "I must do it."
additional_notes: Uses the verb "devoir" (to have to / must): "je dois" = "I have to". "Le" is an object pronoun meaning "it" (referring to something already mentioned). Often expresses obligation or necessity; in context it can sound like a strong requirement ("must") or a simple need ("have to").
target_language_example: Désolé, je dois le faire aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to do it today.

meaning: "I have to / I must" + "me" (used before a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used when you need to say you must do something to yourself (a reflexive verb). Structure: "Je dois me" + verb (infinitive). Examples: "Je dois me cacher" (I have to hide), "Je dois me changer" (I have to get changed), "Je dois me reposer" (I have to rest). With a vowel or silent h, "me" becomes "m'": "Je dois m'habiller" (I have to get dressed).
target_language_example: Je dois me dépêcher.
native_language_example: I have to hurry.

additional_notes: Used to say you have an obligation or need to speak with someone. Follow with a person (name, family member, etc.). You can add what you need to talk about with “de …” (e.g., parler à Tom de quelque chose = talk to Tom about something).
target_language_example: Je dois parler à mon professeur après le cours.
native_language_example: I have to talk to my teacher after class.

meaning: “I have to leave / I need to go.”
additional_notes: Used to say you must leave (often for a reason or obligation). You can add a time: « Je dois partir dans dix minutes » (in ten minutes) or « tout de suite » (right away). In speech, « je dois » is often pronounced quickly, like “j’dois.”
target_language_example: Je suis désolé, je dois partir maintenant.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I have to leave now.

meaning: "I have to go home" / "I need to head back."
additional_notes: Used when you must return to your home or to the place you’re staying. "Rentrer" means "to go back/come back" and often implies going back home; the time can be added (e.g., "dimanche après-midi") and it’s often followed by an action with an infinitive ("rentrer faire mes devoirs" = go home to do my homework).
target_language_example: Désolé, je dois rentrer maintenant.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go home now.

meaning: "I need to know" / "I have to know."
additional_notes: Used to express necessity/urgency about knowing information. Often followed by a question word + clause (ce que, qui, pourquoi, quand, où, comment): « Je dois savoir ce que tu as vu. » It can also be used in questions like « Y a un truc que je dois savoir ? » (= “Is there something I should know?”).
target_language_example: Je dois savoir où tu étais hier soir.
native_language_example: I need to know where you were last night.

meaning: "I have to / I must / I should" + "you" (to you), before a verb.
additional_notes: Used with the verb devoir (dois = “(I) must/have to”) followed by te (“you” as an object, meaning “to you”). It’s normally followed by an infinitive: je dois te prévenir (I have to warn you), je dois te remercier (I should thank you). Depending on context and tone, it can sound like a strong obligation (“I must…”) or a softer polite duty (“I should…”).
target_language_example: Je dois te parler après le cours.
native_language_example: I have to talk to you after class.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity: je dois (I must / I have to) + infinitive trouver (to find). It’s followed by what you need to find (a person, object, solution, etc.): Je dois trouver + [noun/pronoun]. In speech, it often sounds like "j’dois".
target_language_example: Je dois trouver une solution avant demain.
native_language_example: I have to find a solution before tomorrow.

meaning: "I have to / I must" (speaking to you formally or to more than one person).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb to say you are obligated or need to do something: « Je dois vous + infinitif » (e.g., laisser, parler, rappeler). « vous » is the object pronoun meaning “you” (formal singular or plural). In English you usually don’t translate « vous » separately here; you translate the whole phrase as “I have to…” or “I need to…”.
target_language_example: Je dois vous poser une question.
native_language_example: I need to ask you a question.

meaning: “I really have to / I really must.”
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize necessity/obligation (often with reluctance, annoyance, or urgency). In questions ("Je dois vraiment ?" / "Je dois vraiment le faire ?"), it can mean “Do I really have to?”—often rhetorical, as if hoping the answer is no.
target_language_example: Je dois vraiment partir maintenant.
native_language_example: I really have to leave now.

meaning: "I have to go" / "I need to leave."
additional_notes: Common, polite way to say you need to leave. "dois" is from "devoir" (to have to). "y" replaces a place or situation already known from context (roughly “there”), so it’s like “I have to go (there/now).” Often used with apologies or to end a conversation: « Désolé, je dois y aller. »
target_language_example: Il est tard, je dois y aller.
native_language_example: It’s late, I have to go.

meaning: "I must be" / "I have to be" (sometimes "I must be" = "I must be (probably)").
additional_notes: Used with an adjective, noun, or place to express obligation or necessity: « Je dois être impartial » (I have to be impartial), « Je dois être à Boston… » (I have to be in Boston…). It can also express a strong guess/deduction about a situation: « Je dois être en train de rêver » (I must be dreaming).
target_language_example: Je dois être au travail à huit heures.
native_language_example: I have to be at work at eight o’clock.

additional_notes: Present tense of *dormir* with **je**. It can describe a general habit (*Je dors huit heures*) or what’s happening now/around now depending on context (*Dis-lui que je dors*). For a near-future plan, French often still uses the present (*Je dors ici ce soir* = “I’m sleeping here tonight”).
target_language_example: Je dors mal quand il fait trop chaud.
native_language_example: I sleep badly when it’s too hot.

meaning: "I doubt that..." (I don't think it's true/likely).
additional_notes: Very often followed by the subjunctive: « Je doute qu’il soit… / qu’elle ait… ». You may also see an extra « ne » after « que » (called *ne explétif*): « Je doute que Tom ne soit occupé »—it does not mean "not" here; it’s still "I doubt Tom is busy."
target_language_example: Je doute que ce soit une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I doubt that it's a good idea.

additional_notes: First-person singular of détester in the present tense. It expresses strong dislike and can be followed by a person, thing, or an infinitive verb: Je déteste ce bruit. / Je déteste attendre.
target_language_example: Je déteste me lever tôt.
native_language_example: I hate getting up early.

additional_notes: Used to express strong dislike of a general category of things or people in the plural. It’s followed by a plural noun, often with the definite article “les” (e.g., les insectes). In polite conversation, “je n’aime pas…” is softer than “je déteste…”.
target_language_example: Je déteste les embouteillages.
native_language_example: I hate traffic jams.

additional_notes: First-person singular of faire in the present tense. It is used for doing actions in general, making things, and with many activities. With sports or hobbies, English may use a different verb: je fais du tennis often means "I play tennis."
target_language_example: Je fais un gâteau pour ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm making a cake for tonight.

meaning: "I do that" / "I’m doing that" (I do this).
additional_notes: "Je fais" is the present tense of "faire" (to do/to make). "Ça" means "that/this" in everyday speech. Use it to talk about an action you do in general or right now; often followed by details like "pour..." (in order to/for), "pendant..." (during), or "tout le temps" (all the time).
target_language_example: Je fais ça pour apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I do it to learn French.

meaning: "I was doing/making" or "I used to do" (imperfect of *faire*).
additional_notes: This is the *imparfait* (imperfect) form of **faire** for **je**. Use it for an action that was ongoing in the past ("I was doing"), a repeated/habitual past action ("I used to do"), or background description. It’s also common after a past reporting verb in indirect speech: *Il a dit que je faisais...* ("He said I was doing...").
target_language_example: Quand tu as appelé, je faisais la vaisselle.
native_language_example: When you called, I was doing the dishes.

additional_notes: Simple future form of the verb « faire » (to do / to make). Used to say you will do something in the future, often as a promise or decision: « Je ferai ça » = “I’ll do that.” With an adverb it can mean how you’ll do it: « Je ferai vite » = “I’ll do it quickly / I’ll be quick.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je ferai le nécessaire.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll do what’s necessary.

additional_notes: Used to promise effort and goodwill (often in response to a request). Literally “I will do of my best,” but the natural English is “I’ll do my best.” You can add a purpose with pour + infinitive: « Je ferai de mon mieux pour + verbe » (“I’ll do my best to + verb”).
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas, je ferai de mon mieux pour être à l’heure.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll do my best to be on time.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of faire (je ferais) to give advice or express what you think is the best choice, often with a slight warning or urgency. It’s followed by an infinitive: « Je ferais mieux de partir. » You can change the subject: « Tu ferais mieux de… », « Il/Elle ferait mieux de… », etc.
target_language_example: Je ferais mieux de t'appeler demain.
native_language_example: I’d better call you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used mainly in literature and formal narration (especially writing) to talk about a completed past event. In everyday speech, people usually say “j’ai été” or “j’étais,” depending on the meaning.
target_language_example: Je fus surpris par la nouvelle.
native_language_example: I was surprised by the news.

additional_notes: l’ is a shortened form of le or la before a vowel or silent h, so it can mean it, him, or her. In sentences with a past participle, je l’ai often translates as "I [past verb] it/him/her" rather than literally "I have it."
target_language_example: Je l'ai vu hier.
native_language_example: I saw him yesterday.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *faire*: **je + l’ (le/la) + ai + fait**. **l’** replaces a thing already mentioned (“it”). Can be followed by an infinitive to mean “I had/made it done”: *Je l’ai fait enlever* (“I had it removed”), *Je l’ai fait entrer* (“I made him/it come in”).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je l'ai fait hier.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I did it yesterday.

meaning: "I did it for" (someone / something; for the purpose of).
additional_notes: Used to give the reason, beneficiary, or goal of an action. "l'" is a direct object pronoun meaning “it/this/that” (the thing you did). Often followed by a person (pour elle/eux/toi), a noun (pour l'argent), or an infinitive (pour te protéger = “to protect you”).
target_language_example: Je l'ai fait pour toi, pas pour moi.
native_language_example: I did it for you, not for me.

additional_notes: This introduces a sentence in the passé composé: je + l’ (direct object pronoun meaning “it/him/her”) + ai (have) + toujours (always) + past participle. It’s used to say you have always done/thought/felt/had something: « Je l’ai toujours fait » = “I’ve always done it.” Note: l’ is used instead of le/la before a vowel sound or silent h. Spelling requires an apostrophe: « Je l’ai toujours … ».
target_language_example: Je l'ai toujours fait.
native_language_example: I've always done it.

meaning: "I found it" / "I found him" (depending on what "l'" refers to).
additional_notes: Passé composé of "trouver" (to find). "l'" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it/him/her" (singular), used when the thing/person has already been mentioned or is understood from context. In English you usually translate it as simple past ("I found it"), even though the French is literally "I have found it."
target_language_example: Je l'ai trouvé près de la porte.
native_language_example: I found it near the door.

additional_notes: Passé composé of voir (“to see”) with avoir: je + l’ (direct object pronoun) + ai + vu. l’ replaces le/la and can mean “him,” “her,” or “it,” depending on context. Often used when the object has already been mentioned or is obvious.
target_language_example: Je l'ai vu hier au cinéma.
native_language_example: I saw him/her/it yesterday at the movie theater.

additional_notes: Past tense with avoir (passé composé): "j'ai vu(e)" = "I saw / I have seen". "l'" is a direct object pronoun meaning "her" (or "it" if referring to a feminine noun). Because the direct object pronoun comes before the verb, the past participle agrees in gender/number: vu → vue (feminine singular).
target_language_example: Je l'ai vue hier soir dans la rue.
native_language_example: I saw her last night in the street.

meaning: "I have it" / "I've got it" (sometimes: "I got it" = I understand).
additional_notes: “L’” is a direct-object pronoun meaning “it” (or “him/her” depending on context). “Je l’ai” is often followed by extra information: location/possession (“Je l’ai sur moi.” = I have it on me), keeping an eye on something (“Je l’ai à l’œil.” = I’m keeping an eye on it/him), or confirming you have found/received something (“Je l’ai, c’est bon.” = I’ve got it, all good). Note: “ai” can also be the auxiliary in the past tense, but then you add a past participle (e.g., “Je l’ai vu.” = I saw him/it).
target_language_example: Je l'ai sur moi.
native_language_example: I have it on me.

meaning: I loved him/her/it; I liked him/her/it (in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense ("j'aimais") to describe an ongoing feeling or a habitual past situation ("I used to love/like..."). "l'" is a direct object pronoun (short for "le" or "la") and can mean "him," "her," or "it" depending on context; it becomes "l'" before a vowel sound (aimer). Often contrasts with "je l'ai aimé" (past completed action/feeling at a specific time).
target_language_example: Quand j'étais enfant, je l'aimais bien, mais maintenant on ne se parle plus.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I liked him/her, but now we don’t talk anymore.

meaning: I love him/her/it; I like him/her/it.
additional_notes: "L’" is a direct object pronoun meaning "him," "her," or "it" (you choose from context). It goes before the verb: je l’aime. With people, "aimer" often means "to love"; with things/activities it can mean "to like". You can add adverbs like "encore" (still), "toujours" (always), "énormément" (a lot).
target_language_example: Je l'aime beaucoup, mais je ne sais pas s'il m'aime aussi.
native_language_example: I love him/her a lot, but I don’t know if he/she loves me too.

meaning: "I had it / I had him / I had her" ("I" + "had" + a direct object).
additional_notes: This is the imperfect of "avoir" (j'avais = "I had") with the direct object pronoun "l'" (= le/la, meaning "him/her/it") placed before the verb. It’s commonly used in the pluperfect (plus-que-parfait) with a past participle: "je l’avais dit / remarqué / vu" = "I had said/noticed/seen it (him/her)". "L'" is used before a vowel sound (otherwise you’ll see "je le..." or "je la...").
target_language_example: Je l'avais déjà oublié.
native_language_example: I had already forgotten it.

additional_notes: "Je" means "I" and "la" is a direct object pronoun meaning "her" or "it" (referring to a feminine noun). "La" usually goes before the verb: "Je la vois" = "I see her/it." It can refer to a woman/girl/person (“her”) or to a feminine thing/idea (“it”). (If the next word starts with a vowel or silent h, "la" can shorten to "l'": "Je l'aime".)
target_language_example: Je la connais bien.
native_language_example: I know her well.

additional_notes: Used with the verb connaître for knowing a person (or being familiar with a place/thing). La is a direct object pronoun meaning “her” (replacing a feminine person, e.g., Marie → je la connais). In the negative you’ll often hear je la connais pas (informal spoken French) or je ne la connais pas (more formal/written). Don’t confuse connaître (know someone / be familiar with) with savoir (know a fact / know how).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je la connais depuis longtemps.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ve known her for a long time.

meaning: "I see her" / "I’m seeing her" (female direct object).
additional_notes: “La” is a direct object pronoun meaning “her” (or “it” for a feminine noun). It goes before the verb: je la vois = I see her. Depending on context it can mean right now (“I see her!”) or in general/scheduled (“I’m seeing her tomorrow” = I’ll see her tomorrow). With “ne… plus” it becomes “Je ne la vois plus” = “I don’t see her anymore.”
target_language_example: Je la vois ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m seeing her tonight.

additional_notes: "Le" here is the direct-object pronoun, not the article "the." In French it usually comes before the verb, so je le crois means "I believe him/it." Depending on context, le can refer to a person, a thing, or even an idea already mentioned; with être (je le suis), it can mean "so" or refer to a description already understood.
target_language_example: Je le vois tous les jours.
native_language_example: I see him every day.

additional_notes: Used with the verb « connaître » to say you know someone/something (you’re familiar with them/it). « le » is the direct object pronoun (often “him,” but it can also mean “it” for a masculine noun). Common extensions: « je le connais bien / très bien » (I know him/it well), « je le connais de quelque part » (I know him from somewhere), « je le connais de vue » (I recognize him), « je le connais à peine » (I barely know him), « je le connais seulement de nom » (I only know him by name), « je le connais par cœur » (I know it by heart, e.g., a text/song).
target_language_example: Je le connais, mais je ne me souviens plus de son nom.
native_language_example: I know him, but I don’t remember his name anymore.

meaning: "I do it" / "I’m doing it" (sometimes: "I’ll do it").
additional_notes: "Le" is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” (the thing you already mentioned or that’s clear from context). "Je le fais" is often used with adverbs like beaucoup/rarement/quotidiennement. In questions like « Tu lui dis ou je le fais ? », it can imply a suggestion or mild threat: “Are you going to tell him, or should I / or I will?”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : je le fais ce soir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll do it tonight.

additional_notes: "Ferai" is the simple future of "faire" (to do/to make). "Le" is a pronoun meaning "it" (or sometimes "him"), referring to something already understood from context: "Je le ferai" = "I’ll do it." It can sound like a promise, reassurance, or a firm/defiant response depending on tone (e.g., "Oh, je le ferai." = "Oh, I will."). In the pattern "je le ferai + infinitive" (e.g., "je le ferai venir"), "faire" is often used in a causative sense: "I’ll have him/it come" / "I’ll make him come."
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je le ferai demain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of faire (ferais) to talk about a hypothetical situation, something you would do under certain conditions, or to sound more polite/less direct. "Le" is an object pronoun meaning "it" (replacing whatever action/thing was mentioned). Often used with "si": "Je le ferais si je pouvais" (I’d do it if I could).
target_language_example: Je le ferais, mais je n’ai pas le temps.
native_language_example: I would do it, but I don’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to strongly insist that what you’re saying is true or that you didn’t do something. "Le" is a pronoun meaning “it/that” (the thing you’re talking about). You can intensify it with "Je le jure sur..." (“I swear on...”), e.g. "sur ma tête" (on my head) or "sur la tombe de..." (on someone’s grave).
target_language_example: Je te promets que je ne mens pas, je le jure.
native_language_example: I promise you I’m not lying, I swear.

additional_notes: Means “I know it,” with **le** = “it” (referring to something already mentioned or understood). Often used on its own to reassure someone or stop them repeating information: “Je le sais.” You can add words like **déjà** (“already”) for emphasis: “Je le sais déjà.”
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je le sais.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I know.

additional_notes: Used to say you already knew something. "le" means “it/that” (the fact or information), and "savais" is the imperfect of "savoir" (to know), often implying you knew it already or for some time. Common with emphasis like "Bien sûr que je le savais" (“Of course I knew it”) or "je le savais déjà" (“I already knew that”).
target_language_example: Je le savais : tu allais arriver en retard.
native_language_example: I knew it: you were going to be late.

additional_notes: Used when you have a feeling or intuition about something (often without proof): *Il va se passer quelque chose, je le sens.* The pronoun **le** refers to “it” (the situation/thing you’re talking about). It can also be literal/physical (feeling something in your body), depending on context.
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas l'expliquer, mais je le sens : il va appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I can't explain it, but I feel it: he's going to call tonight.

additional_notes: "Je le vois" means “I see it/him.” Here, "le" is a direct object pronoun that replaces a masculine noun (a thing = “it”, or a man/boy = “him”) and it comes before the verb: je + le + vois. It’s often followed by extra info like "bien" (clearly/well) or "dans ses yeux" (in his/her eyes).
target_language_example: Je le vois sur la photo.
native_language_example: I see it in the photo.

additional_notes: "Je les ai" is "I" + the direct object pronoun "les" (them) + the auxiliary "ai" (have) used in the passé composé. It must be followed by a past participle: "Je les ai aidés" (I helped them), "Je les ai prévenus" (I warned them). With "avoir," the past participle often agrees in gender/number with a direct object pronoun placed before the verb: "Je les ai suivis" (them = masculine/mixed plural), "Je les ai entendues" (them = feminine plural), "Je les ai faites" (them = feminine plural, e.g., the tasks).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : je les ai déjà envoyés.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I already sent them.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *voir* (to see): **j’ai vu** = “I saw.” The direct object pronoun **les** (“them”) comes **before** the auxiliary (**ai**). The past participle **vu** agrees with **les** because it comes before the verb: **vus** for a masculine/mixed group; **vues** for an all-female group (*Je les ai vues*).
target_language_example: Je les ai vus hier au marché.
native_language_example: I saw them yesterday at the market.

additional_notes: "Les" is the direct object pronoun meaning "them" (for masculine plural or mixed groups; also used for feminine plural in direct object position). It comes before the verb: je les aime = "I like/love them." You can add adverbs like "aussi" (also), "beaucoup" (a lot), "tous" (all). In "un/une ... comme je les aime", it means "a (man/woman) the way I like them" / "just how I like them".
target_language_example: Je les aime tous, ils sont très gentils.
native_language_example: I like them all; they’re very nice.

meaning: 'I ... to them' (I have/ did ... to them).
additional_notes: "Je" = I. "leur" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to them" (to those people). "ai" is the present of "avoir" used to form the passé composé, so it’s followed by a past participle: "Je leur ai dit" (I told them), "Je leur ai parlé" (I spoke to them), "Je leur ai laissé" (I left them). Used with verbs that take an indirect object (often with "à"): dire à, parler à, demander à, laisser à, mentir à.
target_language_example: Je leur ai envoyé un message hier soir.
native_language_example: I sent them a message last night.

additional_notes: Present tense of the verb *lire* (to read). In French the present can mean a general habit (*I read novels*) or something happening now (*I’m reading right now*), depending on context (e.g., *je lis encore* = “I’m still reading”). Pronunciation: *je lis* sounds like “zhuh lee”.
target_language_example: Je lis un livre en français pour m’entraîner.
native_language_example: I’m reading a book in French to practice.

additional_notes: Start of a passé composé clause: je + lui + ai + past participle. lui means 'to him' or 'to her' and comes before the auxiliary ai. It is used with verbs that take an indirect object, and English often translates it as just 'him/her' without 'to' (for example, je lui ai dit = 'I told him/her').
target_language_example: Je lui ai envoyé un message ce matin.
native_language_example: I sent him/her a message this morning.

additional_notes: Used to report a request you made to someone. Structure: "Je" (I) + "lui" (to him/her) + "ai demandé" (asked) + "de" + infinitive verb. For more than one person, use "leur": "Je leur ai demandé de …". In the negative: "Je lui ai demandé de ne pas …" (I asked him/her not to …).
target_language_example: Je lui ai demandé de m'aider demain.
native_language_example: I asked him/her to help me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of dire: "j’ai dit" = "I said/told." "Lui" is the indirect object pronoun meaning "to him" or "to her" (you don’t say *je l’ai dit* here because that would mean "I said it" / "I told it"). Often followed by what you said (e.g., "que..." = "that...") or an instruction with "de" + infinitive ("je lui ai dit de venir" = "I told him/her to come").
target_language_example: Je lui ai dit que j'arriverais en retard.
native_language_example: I told him/her that I would arrive late.

additional_notes: Used to report an instruction or advice you gave to someone. "lui" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him" or "to her" (gender is not shown). It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb: "Je lui ai dit de partir" (I told him/her to leave). In the negative, you may hear "de ne pas" (more standard) or "de pas" (more casual): "Je lui ai dit de ne pas le faire."
target_language_example: Je lui ai dit de m’appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I told him/her to call me tonight.

additional_notes: Past tense of donner (to give) with an indirect object pronoun. "lui" means “to him” or “to her” (you often can’t tell which without context). Structure: je + lui + ai + donné + (direct object). Used for giving someone something: a number, a key, a chance, your word, etc. (In spoken French this can also mean a recent past: “I’ve just given…”.)
target_language_example: Je lui ai donné mon adresse.
native_language_example: I gave him/her my address.

additional_notes: Used in the causative structure **faire + infinitive** to say you cause someone to do an action or you get someone to do it for you: **Je lui ai fait + infinitive**. Here **lui** = “to him/to her” (the person who does the action), and the verb after **fait** stays in the infinitive (balayer, laver, ouvrir, réparer…). Often translated as “I made him/her…” or “I had him/her…/I got him/her to…”.
target_language_example: Je lui ai fait préparer le dîner.
native_language_example: I had him/her prepare dinner.

meaning: I spoke to him/her (I talked to him/her).
additional_notes: "lui" is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him” or “to her” (you often need context to know which). "ai parlé" is the past tense (passé composé) of "parler". Used for talking to someone (in person, on the phone, etc.), often followed by a detail like "au téléphone", "hier", "pendant une heure".
target_language_example: Je lui ai parlé, mais il/elle n'était pas d'accord.
native_language_example: I spoke to him/her, but he/she didn’t agree.

meaning: "I have it / I did it" (I + "l’" + have), used with the passé composé.
additional_notes: “Je l’ai” = “je” (I) + “l’” (short for “le” or “la”, meaning him/it or her/it) + “ai” (have). It’s very common before a past participle: “je l’ai promis” (I promised it), “je l’ai vu/faite” (I saw/did it). In speech and writing, “le/la” becomes “l’” before a vowel or silent h. With passé composé and “avoir”, the past participle can agree with the direct object pronoun when it comes before the verb: “Je l’ai entendue” (I heard her).
target_language_example: Je l’ai déjà dit.
native_language_example: I already said it.

additional_notes: Standard way to introduce yourself and say your name. It uses the verb "s’appeler" (to be called) with a reflexive pronoun: "je" + "m’" + "appelle". You can also use it as a question: « Je m’appelle comment ? » (“What’s my name again?”).
target_language_example: Bonjour, je m'appelle Nadia.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Nadia.

additional_notes: "Je m'en" is a pronoun combo used before many verbs: "je" + "me" (to/for myself) + "en" (replaces something introduced by "de" or means "some of it/them"). It doesn’t translate as a fixed phrase by itself; the meaning comes from the verb: e.g. "je m'en souviens" (I remember it), "je m'en sers" (I use it), "je m'en rends compte" (I realize it), "je m'en réjouis" (I’m happy about it), "je m'en lasse" (I get tired of it).
target_language_example: Je m'en souviens très bien.
native_language_example: I remember it very well.

meaning: I'll take care of it / I’ll handle it.
additional_notes: From "s'occuper de" = "to take care of / to deal with." The pronoun "en" replaces "de + [thing]" (e.g., "Je m'occupe du dossier" → "Je m'en occupe"). Often used to reassure someone or accept a task; you can add politeness or emphasis: "Je m'en occupe, monsieur/chef"; "Je m'en occupe moi-même" (I’ll do it myself); "de suite" (right away).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je m'en occupe tout de suite.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take care of it right away.

additional_notes: From the verb "se souvenir de" = "to remember". The "en" replaces something introduced with "de" (de ça, de cette histoire, de ce jour-là): "Tu te souviens de ce film ?" → "Oui, je m'en souviens." Often intensified with "très bien" (I remember very well) or used after "Ça y est" to mean “That’s it, I remember now.” Note: French "souvenir" is a false friend—English "souvenir" is a keepsake, but "se souvenir" is "to remember".
target_language_example: Je m'en souviens maintenant : on s'est rencontrés à Paris.
native_language_example: I remember it now: we met in Paris.

meaning: "I (myself) have … (of it / from it / about it)" — the start of a reflexive passé composé construction with the pronoun "en"; it must be followed by a past participle or complement to be complete.
additional_notes:
This sequence isn’t a standalone sentence: it’s a common pronoun + auxiliary pattern used before what comes next. Breakdown: "je" (I) + "me" → "m’" (myself) + "en" (of it / about it / from it) + "suis" (am, used as the auxiliary for reflexive verbs in the passé composé). The meaning depends on the verb/phrase that follows, e.g.: 
- Je m'en suis bien sorti(e). = I got through it / handled it well.
- Je m'en suis occupé(e) (moi-même). = I took care of it (myself).
- Je m'en suis remis(e). = I got over it / recovered from it.
- Je m'en suis rendu compte. = I realized it.
- Je m'en suis voulu. = I blamed myself for it.
Agreement note: in some cases the past participle agrees with the subject (sorti/sortie, occupé/occupée, remis/remise).
target_language_example: Je m'en suis rendu compte trop tard.
native_language_example: I realized it too late.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase « s’en aller » (to leave, to go away). « Je m’en vais » is very common in spoken French to announce that you’re about to leave (often right now). You can add a time word like « maintenant » (now) or « tout de suite » (right away).
target_language_example: Désolé, je m'en vais tout de suite.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm leaving right away.

meaning: "I take care of" / "I handle" / "I’m in charge of".
additional_notes: Used to say you will look after someone (care for them) or deal with something (take responsibility, manage it). It’s the verb "s’occuper de"; with "je" it becomes "je m'occupe de" ("I take care of..."). Often followed by a person or a thing: "je m'occupe de lui" (I’ll take care of him) / "je m'occupe de ça" (I’ll handle that).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je m'occupe de ça.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll handle that.

additional_notes: "Je" means "I" and "mange" is the present tense of "manger" (to eat). Use it to say what you eat in general or what you are eating now, depending on context. Often followed by "des" (some) or "de" in expressions like "beaucoup de" (a lot of).
target_language_example: Je mange une pomme tous les jours.
native_language_example: I eat an apple every day.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question starting with “what.” It’s followed by a normal sentence word order (no inversion), e.g. “Je me demande ce que ça veut dire” (“I wonder what that means”). Often used with the present (“je me demande”), but the verb after can be in different tenses depending on meaning (present, past, conditional, etc.).
target_language_example: Je me demande ce que tu penses de cette idée.
native_language_example: I wonder what you think about this idea.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question about a place or location. It’s followed by normal statement word order (subject + verb), not question word order: « Je me demande où il est » (NOT « où est-il »). You can use it for past, present, or future depending on the verb tense that follows.
target_language_example: Je me demande où se trouve la gare.
native_language_example: I wonder where the train station is.

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or puzzlement about a reason. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb): « Je me demande pourquoi il/elle… », « …pourquoi il y a… ». In speech, it can also be used on its own as a complete thought: « Je me demande pourquoi… ».
target_language_example: Je me demande pourquoi tu es en retard.
native_language_example: I wonder why you're late.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question about a person. It’s often followed by a full clause (e.g., « Je me demande qui c’est. »). Literally it’s closer to “I’m asking myself who…”. Note: « demander » usually means “to ask” (not “to demand”).
target_language_example: Je me demande qui a laissé la porte ouverte.
native_language_example: I wonder who left the door open.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unsure and you’re asking yourself a yes/no question. It introduces an indirect question with "si" (= whether/if): "Je me demande si…" + statement word order (no inversion). Often corresponds to English "I wonder if…" or "I’m not sure whether…". You can also say "je me demande ce que/qui/où…" for indirect questions with what/who/where.
target_language_example: Je me demande si on a le temps de passer au supermarché.
native_language_example: I wonder if we have time to stop by the supermarket.

meaning: 'I was thinking (to myself)' / 'I was telling myself.'
additional_notes: Imperfect of *se dire* (“to say to oneself”), used for an ongoing or repeated thought in the past. Often used to react to someone else: *C’est exactement ce que je me disais* (“That’s exactly what I was thinking”), or alone as *Je me disais bien…* (“I knew it / I had a feeling…”). It’s usually followed by **que + clause**: *Je me disais que…* (“I told myself that…”).
target_language_example: Je me disais que tu allais appeler, mais je me suis trompé.
native_language_example: I thought you were going to call, but I was wrong.

additional_notes: From the verb *se lever* (reflexive). Commonly used for getting out of bed in the morning (*Je me lève à sept heures*), but it can also mean standing up from a sitting/lying position (*C’est pire quand je me lève*). Often followed by a time (à + heure) or a frequency (tous les jours, généralement).
target_language_example: Je me lève tôt demain pour prendre le train.
native_language_example: I’m getting up early tomorrow to catch the train.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb *se rappeler* to talk about remembering someone or something. You can follow it with a noun (*Je me rappelle ce type*), an infinitive about a past action (*Je me rappelle lui avoir donné la clé*), or sometimes **de** + noun (*Je me rappelle de son nom*—common in speech, though often taught without *de*). Don’t confuse it with *rappeler* (non‑reflexive), which usually means “to remind” or “to call back.”
target_language_example: Je me rappelle de cette histoire.
native_language_example: I remember that story.

additional_notes: From the verb « se rendre »: « je me rends à/chez… » is a slightly formal way to say you go somewhere (similar to « je vais… »). Use « à » with places (je me rends à la bibliothèque) and « chez » when going to someone’s place or a professional (je me rends chez le dentiste / chez le coiffeur). Don’t confuse with « je me rends compte (de…) », which means “I realize / I notice.” Also, « je me rends ! » can mean “I surrender!”, but that’s a different context.
target_language_example: Je me rends au travail en bus.
native_language_example: I go to work by bus.

additional_notes: First-person singular of se sentir. Used to talk about how you feel physically or emotionally, often followed by an adjective or by bien/mal: je me sens fatigué(e), je me sens bien. If an adjective follows, it agrees with the speaker's gender.
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, je me sens un peu fatigué.
native_language_example: Today, I feel a little tired.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how you feel physically or emotionally. The verb is reflexive: « se sentir » (je me sens, tu te sens, etc.). « Bien » means “well” (not « bon », which is “good” for things like food: « C’est bon »). You can intensify it with « mieux »: « je me sens bien mieux » = “I feel much better.”
target_language_example: Après un bon repas, je me sens bien.
native_language_example: After a good meal, I feel good.

additional_notes: Used to describe how you feel by comparing it to a state, impression, or identity. Often followed by an adjective (fatigué, malade), a noun phrase (un homme nouveau), or an expression like "en rêve". In everyday French, "Je me sens..." (without "comme") is more common with adjectives; "comme" adds a comparison/“as if” nuance.
target_language_example: Je me sens comme si j'avais couru toute la journée.
native_language_example: I feel as if I’d been running all day.

meaning: I feel unwell / I feel bad.
additional_notes: Used to say you feel physically sick (nauseous, ill) or emotionally bad (sad, guilty, uneasy). You can add details with “de + noun” or “à propos de …” (about): “Je me sens mal à propos de ça.”
target_language_example: Je me sens mal depuis ce matin, je crois que je vais rentrer chez moi.
native_language_example: I’ve been feeling unwell since this morning; I think I’m going to go home.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb *se sentir* to talk about how you feel. It’s usually followed by an adjective (e.g., *heureux/heureuse, gêné/gênée, stupide*) or by *bien/mal/mieux*. Remember agreement: *Je me sens tellement jolie* (speaker is female), *Je me sens tellement joli* (male).
target_language_example: Je me sens tellement fatigué aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I feel so tired today.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective to describe how you feel physically or emotionally (e.g., malade, seul, optimiste). The verb is reflexive: se sentir → je me sens. You can swap out "très" for other intensifiers like "assez" (quite) or "vraiment" (really).
target_language_example: Je me sens très fatigué aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I feel very tired today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your physical or emotional state. Often followed by an adjective (déprimé, fiévreux, frustré, responsable) or a comparative like "mieux" (better). "Je me sens" = "I feel" (about how you feel), not "I feel that…" (opinion), which is usually "je pense que" / "j’ai l’impression que".
target_language_example: Je me sens un peu fatigué aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I feel a little tired today.

meaning: "I really feel" / "I truly feel" (to express how you feel).
