additional_notes: Used with an adjective or phrase to say how you feel: je me sens vraiment bien/mal, je me sens vraiment désolé(e), je me sens vraiment idiot(e). The adjective often agrees with the speaker (désolé/désolée, idiot/idiote). You can also use it to introduce an honest statement about your feelings: « comment je me sens vraiment » = “how I really feel.”
target_language_example: Je me sens vraiment fatigué aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I really feel tired today.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (imparfait) to describe an ongoing state/feeling in the past, often setting the scene (how you felt at that time). It comes from the reflexive verb "se sentir" (to feel). Don’t confuse "sentir" with English "to scent"—"je me sentais" is about how you felt, not smelling something.
target_language_example: Pendant le voyage, je me sentais fatigué.
native_language_example: During the trip, I felt tired.

additional_notes: Passé simple of « se sentir » (to feel). Mostly used in novels, stories, and formal writing; in everyday speech you usually say « je me suis senti(e) » (passé composé). With adjectives, add -e if the speaker is female: « Je me sentis idiote. »
target_language_example: Quand j’entrai dans la salle, je me sentis nerveux.
native_language_example: When I entered the room, I felt nervous.

meaning: “I remember having…” (I remember that I did…).
additional_notes: Used to say you remember a past action or experience. It’s followed by an infinitive (avoir demandé, avoir vu, avoir entendu, avoir lu, avoir rendu), which emphasizes that the action happened before the moment you’re remembering it. In everyday speech, you can also say: « Je me souviens que j’ai… » (“I remember that I…”).
target_language_example: Je me souviens avoir rencontré son frère l’année dernière.
native_language_example: I remember having met his brother last year.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **se souvenir de** = “to remember.” It’s reflexive (uses **me/te/se/nous/vous/se**) and it normally takes **de** before what you remember: **Je me souviens de cette nuit**. With a verb idea, you often use **de + ce qui...** (“what/that which...”), e.g. **Je me souviens de ce qui s'est passé**. Note: English **souvenir** (a memento) is related in origin but **se souvenir** is a verb meaning “to remember.”
target_language_example: Je me souviens de ton nom.
native_language_example: I remember your name.

additional_notes: Used before a past participle to form the past tense (passé composé) of a reflexive/pronominal verb: je me suis levé, je me suis trompé. The me is part of the verb and may correspond to 'myself' in English, but English often just uses a normal past verb, as in 'I bathed' or 'I made sure.'
target_language_example: Je me suis brossé les dents après le dîner.
native_language_example: I brushed my teeth after dinner.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of s’asseoir (“to sit down”). Uses the reflexive pronoun (me) and the auxiliary être: je me suis assis (male speaker) / je me suis assise (female speaker). Common with place phrases: sur (on), dans (in), à (at), à côté de (next to), derrière (behind).
target_language_example: Je me suis assis près de la fenêtre pour attendre.
native_language_example: I sat down near the window to wait.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the reflexive verb s’asseoir (“to sit down”). It uses être as the helping verb: je me suis… The past participle agrees with the subject: assise (feminine singular). A man would usually say: je me suis assis. Common with places using prepositions like au/à (at), sur (on), à côté de (next to).
target_language_example: Je me suis assise près de la fenêtre.
native_language_example: I sat down near the window.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the reflexive verb *se couper* (to cut oneself). Often followed by **avec** to say what you cut yourself with (*Je me suis coupé avec un rasoir*), or by **en + verb** to explain how it happened (*Je me suis coupé en me rasant*). With body parts, French usually uses **le/la/les** (not *mon/ma/mes*): *Je me suis coupé la main.*
target_language_example: Je me suis coupé le doigt en cuisinant.
native_language_example: I cut my finger while cooking.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of s’endormir (“to fall asleep”). Used for the moment you doze off, often with en + activity (“en lisant” = “while reading”) or sur + place/person (“sur son épaule” = “on his/her shoulder”). For a woman: je me suis endormie.
target_language_example: Je me suis endormi pendant le film.
native_language_example: I fell asleep during the movie.

meaning: I fell asleep / I went to sleep (past tense, said by a woman).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of the reflexive verb s’endormir (“to fall asleep”). With être in the passé composé, the past participle agrees with the subject: endormie (female speaker) vs endormi (male speaker). Often used when you unintentionally dozed off: Je me suis endormie en classe = “I fell asleep in class.”
target_language_example: Désolée, je me suis endormie pendant le film.
native_language_example: Sorry, I fell asleep during the movie.

meaning: "I got" / "I had" (something happen to me or done to me).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of **se faire** (to get/make something happen to oneself). Very common with **mal**: *Je me suis fait mal* = “I hurt myself.” It can also be used to mean “I got/had something done” (*Je me suis fait couper les cheveux* = “I got my hair cut”) or “I got [something] stolen/robbed” (*Je me suis fait voler mon sac*).
target_language_example: Je me suis fait couper les cheveux hier.
native_language_example: I got my hair cut yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the reflexive verb *se lever* (“to get up / to stand up”). It usually means getting out of bed (*se lever tôt*) but can also mean standing up from a chair. Uses *être* as the helping verb: *je me suis...* The past participle agrees with the speaker: a woman says *je me suis levée*. Often followed by a time: *je me suis levé à 5 heures*.
target_language_example: Je me suis levé trop tard et j’ai raté le bus.
native_language_example: I got up too late and I missed the bus.

meaning: “I got up / I got out of bed” (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of se lever (“to get up”). Use levée (with -e) when the speaker is female; a man says je me suis levé. Often used with a time (à sept heures) or how long ago (il y a une heure), and can imply “I woke up and got up.”
target_language_example: Je me suis levée tôt pour prendre le train.
native_language_example: I got up early to catch the train.

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of the verb phrase « se mettre à » = “to start/begin to.” It’s used with an infinitive: « Je me suis mis à vomir » (I started to vomit). It agrees with the subject (e.g., « je me suis mise à… » for a woman; « nous nous sommes mis/mises à… »). Don’t confuse it with « mis à jour » (as in « je me suis mis à jour »), which is a different expression meaning “updated” or “caught up.”
target_language_example: Je me suis mis à rire sans raison.
native_language_example: I started laughing for no reason.

meaning: "I found myself" / "I ended up" (in a situation).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the reflexive verb « se retrouver ». It’s used when you end up somewhere or in some state—often unexpectedly: « je me suis retrouvé là » = “I ended up there.” It’s built with « être » in the passé composé: je me suis retrouvé(e) (add -e if the speaker is female).
target_language_example: Après le concert, je me suis retrouvé dans une rue que je ne connaissais pas.
native_language_example: After the concert, I found myself on a street I didn’t know.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of se réveiller (to wake up). Uses être as the auxiliary verb and a reflexive pronoun (me). The past participle usually agrees with the speaker: je me suis réveillé (male), je me suis réveillée (female). Often followed by a time phrase (ce matin, soudainement) or what happened next.
target_language_example: Je me suis réveillé en retard et j’ai raté le bus.
native_language_example: I woke up late and I missed the bus.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the reflexive verb "se réveiller" (to wake up). The subject pronoun is "je" and the reflexive pronoun is "me". The past participle agrees with the speaker: "réveillée" (female), "réveillé" (male). Often followed by time or place expressions: "à cinq heures", "au milieu de la nuit", "sur le canapé", etc.
target_language_example: Je me suis réveillée très tôt et je n’arrivais plus à me rendormir.
native_language_example: I woke up very early and I couldn’t fall back asleep.

additional_notes: From the verb *se sentir* (“to feel”). This is the passé composé form, used to talk about how you felt at a specific moment in the past. The adjective usually agrees with the speaker: *je me suis senti* (male), *je me suis sentie* (female). Common patterns: *je me suis senti(e) + adjective* (seul(e), mal, trahi(e), en sécurité) and *je me suis senti(e) + adjective + pour + someone* (*désolé(e) pour toi/vous*).
target_language_example: Après l’entretien, je me suis senti plus confiant.
native_language_example: After the interview, I felt more confident.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of se sentir (“to feel”), with the reflexive pronoun me. Sentie agrees with a female speaker; a male speaker says je me suis senti. Often followed by an adjective: je me suis sentie coupable / heureuse.
target_language_example: Après l’examen, je me suis sentie soulagée.
native_language_example: After the exam, I felt relieved.

additional_notes: From the verb "se tromper" (to be mistaken). Often used to admit you may be wrong or to check what you think: "Je me trompe peut-être" (I may be mistaken). You can also hear "Je me trompe ?" meaning "Am I wrong?"
target_language_example: Je me trompe peut-être, mais il arrive à 18 h.
native_language_example: I may be wrong, but he’s arriving at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has never happened to you up to now. It uses the negation pattern "ne ... jamais" (“never”) around the verb; here it’s with "avoir" in the passé composé: "je n'ai jamais + past participle" (e.g., "je n'ai jamais compris"). In casual spoken French, "ne" is often dropped: "j'ai jamais compris".
target_language_example: Je n'ai jamais compris ça.
native_language_example: I’ve never understood that.

additional_notes: Negative form of "j'ai" (I have): "ne" comes before the verb (n' before a vowel sound) and "pas" comes after it: "je n'ai pas". Very often used with a past participle to make the negative passé composé: "je n'ai pas dit" = "I didn't say / I haven't said". It can also be used on its own: "je n'ai pas" = "I don't have (any)".
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas compris la question.
native_language_example: I didn't understand the question.

meaning: "I have/I've got nothing"; often "I didn't do/see/find/decide anything."
additional_notes: This is the negative pattern ne + verb + rien (“nothing”). In speech and informal writing, ne is often dropped: « J’ai rien décidé / J’ai rien fait ». With another verb (like décider, faire, voir, trouver), it usually translates as “I didn’t … anything” rather than literally “I have nothing …”.
target_language_example: Désolé, je n'ai rien compris.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn't understand anything.

meaning: "I don’t have any" / "I have no" (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have something. It’s the negative of « j’ai » (I have). With negation, « un/une/des » usually becomes « de »: « J’ai un mari » → « Je n’ai pas de mari ». Often shortened in speech: « J’ai pas de… ». Note: the full spelling uses apostrophes (« je n’ai pas de »), but the term here is given without them as « je n'ai pas de ».
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas de plan.
native_language_example: I don’t have a plan.

meaning: "I don’t have any (of it/them)." / "I don’t have one."
additional_notes: "En" replaces something previously mentioned or something introduced with "de" (often a quantity): "J’ai des stylos" → "J’en ai"; "Je n’en ai pas" = "I don’t have any." It’s used to avoid repeating the noun. You can specify: "Je n’en ai pas d’autre" = "I don’t have another one"; "Je n’en ai pas d’autres" = "I don’t have any others." With "besoin": "Je n’en ai pas besoin" = "I don’t need it/any (of it/them)."
target_language_example: Je n'en ai pas d'autres.
native_language_example: I don’t have any others.

additional_notes: Used with je as the first part of a negative sentence. In standard French, ne usually goes with another negative word after the verb, such as pas, jamais, plus, rien, or personne. In casual spoken French, ne is often dropped: je ne sais pas → je sais pas.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas.
native_language_example: I don't understand.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t understand what someone said, how something works, or a situation in general. Often followed by a clause (ce que…, comment…, pourquoi…) or a direct object (ça, votre anglais). In everyday speech, the “ne” is often dropped: « Je comprends pas. »
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne comprends pas : vous pouvez répéter ?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t understand: can you repeat?

additional_notes: Uses connaître (“to be familiar with/know”) for people, places, and things you’re acquainted with (e.g., someone, a city, the rules). For information or facts you’ve learned, French often uses savoir instead (e.g., Je ne sais pas la vérité = “I don’t know the truth”). On its own, Je ne connais pas. can mean “I don’t know.”
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne connais pas cette personne.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know this person.

additional_notes: Used to express disbelief or doubt. Often followed by: (1) a preposition + noun: "je ne crois pas à/en ..." (I don’t believe in ...); (2) an infinitive: "je ne crois pas pouvoir ..." (I don’t think I can ...); or (3) "que" + verb for an opinion about a fact. In careful French it’s "je ne crois pas qu’il t’ait entendu" (subjunctive), but in speech you may hear the indicative.
target_language_example: Je ne crois pas que ce soit une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s a good idea.

meaning: “I’m not saying…” / “I don’t say …” (often to soften or qualify what you mean).
additional_notes:
Used in several common patterns:
- **Je ne dis pas (que) + clause**: “I’m not saying (that) …” (you’re not making a claim; often followed by *mais…*).
- **Je ne dis pas mot**: “I don’t say a word.”
- **Je ne dis pas non**: literally “I don’t say no,” meaning “I’m not opposed / I wouldn’t say no (if you insist).”
- **Je ne dis pas le contraire**: “I’m not saying the opposite / I’m not disagreeing.”
target_language_example: Je ne dis pas que c’est une mauvaise idée, mais c’est cher.
native_language_example: I’m not saying it’s a bad idea, but it’s expensive.

additional_notes: This is the negative form of "je fais" (I do / I make). It’s usually followed by what you don’t do: a noun (Je ne fais pas les règles. = I don’t make the rules.), an activity/field (Je ne fais pas dans les armes. = I’m not in the weapons business.), or part of a longer expression like "je ne fais pas partie de…" (I’m not part of…). With an amount, it can mean "I don’t do much" (Je ne fais pas beaucoup de choses…).
target_language_example: Je ne fais pas de sport le matin.
native_language_example: I don’t do sports in the morning.

additional_notes: Uses the restrictive pattern **ne … que** (“only”) with **faire**: **je ne fais que + infinitive / noun**. It downplays or limits what you’re doing: *Je ne fais que passer* (“I’m just passing through”), *Je ne fais que regarder* (“I’m only looking”), *Je ne fais que ça* (“That’s all I do”). In casual speech, **ne** is often dropped: *Je fais que passer.*
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne fais que mon travail.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m just doing my job.

additional_notes: Uses the pattern "ne ... que" (= "only") in the imperfect tense ("faisais"), often to downplay or justify an action: "I was just asking / joking / doing my job." It’s followed by an infinitive ("je ne faisais que demander") or a noun phrase ("je ne faisais que mon boulot"). In speech, "ne" is often dropped: "je faisais que..."
target_language_example: Je ne faisais que t’aider, je ne voulais pas t’embêter.
native_language_example: I was only trying to help you; I didn’t mean to bother you.

additional_notes: Common negative pattern in the passé composé: ne + object pronoun (l’ = le/la) + auxiliary (ai) + jamais + past participle. l’ refers to “him,” “her,” or “it” depending on context. With avoir, the past participle can agree with l’ when it stands for a direct object: Je ne l’ai jamais touché (him/it), Je ne l’ai jamais touchée (her).
target_language_example: Je ne l'ai jamais vu(e) en vrai.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen him/her in real life.

additional_notes: Common start of a negative sentence in the passé composé. It uses **ne … pas** around the helping verb **ai** (avoir), and **l’** is an object pronoun meaning **“it / him / her”** placed before the verb: *Je ne l'ai pas appelé.* Often *ne* is dropped in casual speech (*Je l'ai pas appelé*).
target_language_example: Je ne l'ai pas appelé.
native_language_example: I didn’t call him/her/it.

meaning: "I don’t ... her" / "I don’t ... it" (feminine object pronoun in a negative sentence).
additional_notes: "La" replaces a feminine direct object (a woman/girl, or a feminine noun like *la voiture*). In negatives, French commonly uses *ne ... pas/jamais/plus*, and the object pronoun comes before the verb: *Je ne la connais pas* (I don’t know her/it), *Je ne la reverrai jamais* (I’ll never see her/it again). In everyday speech, *ne* is often dropped: *Je la connais pas*.
target_language_example: Je ne la vois plus.
native_language_example: I don’t see her/it anymore.

additional_notes: This is the start of a negative sentence with the direct object pronoun le ("him" or "it") placed before the verb. A verb must follow, and the tense comes from that verb, so it can also mean "I didn't ..." or "I won't ..." depending on context. The negative is often completed later by pas, plus, jamais, personne, etc.
target_language_example: Je ne le vois pas aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I don't see him today.

additional_notes: Used to deny or contradict a description of yourself. The pronoun **le** replaces what was just mentioned (often an adjective or noun phrase): *— Tu es prêt ? — Non, je ne le suis pas.* In casual speech, **ne** is often dropped: *Je le suis pas.*
target_language_example: — Tu es d’accord ? — Non, je ne le suis pas.
native_language_example: — Do you agree? — No, I don’t.

additional_notes: This is a common negative pattern in the passé composé (past): **Je ne les ai pas + past participle** (e.g., *appelés, invités, pris*) = “I didn’t call/invite/take them.” Here **les** is a direct object pronoun meaning “them,” placed before **ai**. Without a past participle (e.g., **Je ne les ai pas !**), it usually means “I don’t have them!”
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne les ai pas trouvés.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t find them.

additional_notes: Used to start a negative sentence with a reflexive verb (a verb used with a pronoun like me/te/se). The full negation is usually "je ne me ... pas" (I don't), but you can also see other negative words: "je ne me ... jamais" (never), "je ne me ... plus" (no longer), "je ne me ... que" (only). The reflexive pronoun "me" comes before the verb (or before the helping verb in compound tenses): "je ne me cache pas"; "je ne me suis pas réveillé(e)".
target_language_example: Je ne me rappelle pas son nom.
native_language_example: I don't remember his/her name.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or adverb to describe your state or feelings: Je ne me sens pas bien (I don’t feel well), Je ne me sens pas en confiance (I don’t feel confident). It’s the negative form of « je me sens » (I feel), with « se sentir » meaning “to feel” and « me » referring to yourself.
target_language_example: Aujourd’hui, je ne me sens pas prêt à parler.
native_language_example: Today, I don’t feel ready to talk.

meaning: "I have never" (about yourself, using the past).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs in the passé composé to say you’ve never done/been/ felt something: ne + (reflexive pronoun) + auxiliary être + jamais + past participle. Example pattern: « Je ne me suis jamais + participe passé ». With être, the past participle can agree: « amusé » (masc.) / « amusée » (fem.). Often followed by words like « autant » (so much), « aussi » (as), or « de ma vie » (in my life) for emphasis.
target_language_example: Je ne me suis jamais levé aussi tôt pour aller travailler.
native_language_example: I have never gotten up so early to go to work.

meaning: “I didn’t …” (negative form with a reflexive verb in the passé composé).
additional_notes: Used to negate a past action that you did to yourself or that happened to you (reflexive verb): je + ne + me + suis + pas + past participle. You often see it with verbs like se réveiller (to wake up), s’endormir (to fall asleep), s’ennuyer (to be bored), se noyer (to drown). The past participle may agree with the subject when using être: réveillé (male) / réveillée (female). In casual speech, “ne” is often dropped: « Je me suis pas réveillé(e). »
target_language_example: Je ne me suis pas trompé.
native_language_example: I didn’t make a mistake.

additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t expect something or weren’t thinking about it. Often followed by **que** + a clause: *Je ne pensais pas que…* (“I didn’t think that…”). It can also be followed by **à** to mean “I wasn’t thinking about”: *Je ne pensais pas à ça.*
target_language_example: Je ne pensais pas que ce serait si difficile.
native_language_example: I didn’t think it would be so difficult.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt or a negative opinion. Often followed by an infinitive: « Je ne pense pas pouvoir venir. » (“I don’t think I can come.”) or by « que » + subjunctive: « Je ne pense pas qu’il revienne. » (“I don’t think he’ll come back.”). In casual speech, « ne » is often dropped: « Je pense pas… ».
target_language_example: Je ne pense pas que ce soit une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I don't think it's a good idea.

additional_notes: Standard way to say you cannot do something. It uses pouvoir (“to be able to / can”) in the first person. In everyday spoken French, the ne is often dropped: je peux pas.
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I can't come tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re no longer able to do something, often because of exhaustion, limits, or a situation that has become unbearable. It’s the negative of pouvoir (to be able to) with plus meaning “anymore.” You can add an infinitive: « Je ne peux plus parler » (I can’t speak anymore), or use it alone: « Je ne peux plus ! » (I can’t take it anymore!). With « rien »: « Je ne peux plus rien faire » (I can’t do anything anymore).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux plus t'aider aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't help you anymore today.

meaning: “I won’t be able to / I can’t” (future).
additional_notes: Uses the future tense of pouvoir (je pourrai) with negation (ne…pas). It means you won’t be able to do something later (often “tomorrow,” “next week,” etc.). In casual speech, people often drop ne: « Je pourrai pas. »
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne pourrai pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I won’t be able to come tonight.

meaning: "I could never" / "I would never be able to."
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of pouvoir (pourrais) to express an impossible or unthinkable action, often with a strong emotional/moral sense ("I could never do that"). You can use it alone as an emphatic reply (Je ne pourrais jamais.) or followed by an infinitive: je ne pourrais jamais + faire/oublier/devenir…
target_language_example: Je ne pourrais jamais te mentir.
native_language_example: I could never lie to you.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of "pouvoir" (je pouvais) with negation (ne…pas). It often describes an ongoing inability in the past, repeated situations, or inability due to circumstances (heat, noise, etc.). In casual spoken French, "ne" is often dropped: "je pouvais pas."
target_language_example: Je ne pouvais pas venir hier soir parce que j'étais malade.
native_language_example: I couldn't come last night because I was sick.

additional_notes: Literal meaning is “I don’t know,” but with an infinitive it often means “I don’t know how to…” (ability): Je ne sais pas nager = I can’t swim / I don’t know how to swim. You can add adverbs for emphasis: bien (well), du tout (at all).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne sais pas comment ça marche.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't know how it works.

additional_notes: A very common fixed expression for saying you don't know something. It is often followed by a question word or clause, like quoi, qui, où, comment, or ce que. In everyday spoken French, the ne is often dropped: je sais pas.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas où il habite.
native_language_example: I don't know where he lives.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know the method/way to do something: « Je ne sais pas comment répondre / lui parler ». It can also stand alone (« Je ne sais pas comment. ») or be followed by « mais… » to mean “I don’t know how, but…” (often implying you’ll find a way).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas comment t'aider, mais je vais essayer.
native_language_example: I don't know how to help you, but I'll try.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect yes/no question (uncertainty): *Je ne sais pas si + subject + verb…* It often corresponds to “I’m not sure if…” in natural English. You can add *ou non* (“or not”): *Je ne sais pas si nous avons gagné ou non.*
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas si elle vient ce soir.
native_language_example: I don’t know if she’s coming tonight.

meaning: “I don’t know anymore” / “I can’t remember anymore.”
additional_notes: Used when you used to know (or thought you knew) but you no longer do—often because you forgot or you’re unsure now. Common before an indirect question: « je ne sais plus ce que/qui/où/quand… ». It can also stand alone as « Je ne sais plus. » meaning “I don’t know anymore / I don’t remember.”
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne sais plus où j’ai mis mes clés.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t remember where I put my keys.

additional_notes: Used to say you have no knowledge/information about something or someone. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun (de cela, de vous, de sa famille) or by a clause introduced with ce que (de ce que + verb). You’ll also see the shortened spoken form: « Je sais rien de… » (dropping ne).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne sais rien de cette histoire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't know anything about this story.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (je savais) to talk about a past state of not knowing, often used for background information or when describing what you knew at the time. Often followed by a question word (où, pourquoi, comment…) or by "que" + a full clause: "Je ne savais pas que…".
target_language_example: Je ne savais pas qu’il parlait français.
native_language_example: I didn’t know he spoke French.

additional_notes: Future tense (futur simple) of être with negation: je serai = “I will be”, so je ne serai pas = “I won’t be.” Often followed by an adjective or past participle in the passive: Je ne serai pas jugé. (“I won’t be judged.”) It can also be used in the common expression Je ne serai pas long/longue (“I won’t be long”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je ne serai pas long.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I won’t be long.

meaning: "I am never" / "I have never" (with a past participle).
additional_notes: Used for negation with "ne ... jamais" ("never"). With "être" in the present, it means "I am never" (a habit/state): "Je ne suis jamais à la maison." With a past participle (e.g., allé(e), venu(e)), it means "I have never" done/been somewhere: "Je ne suis jamais allé(e) ..." Note: in casual spoken French, "ne" is often dropped: "Je suis jamais allé(e) ..." (still means "I've never...").
target_language_example: Je ne suis jamais allé en Italie.
native_language_example: I have never been to Italy.

additional_notes: Negative form of je suis ('I am'). Used to say what you are not, such as with adjectives, identity, age/status, or location. In casual spoken French, ne is often dropped: je suis pas.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas prêt.
native_language_example: I'm not ready.

meaning: "I am not a…" (before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to deny an identity or role: je + ne + suis + pas + un + [noun]. The noun that follows is masculine singular. With a feminine noun, use "je ne suis pas une". In everyday French, with professions/nationalities/religions you often drop the article: "Je ne suis pas médecin" (not "un médecin"), but "un/une" is common when the noun is described (e.g., "un bon médecin") or when emphasizing the category.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas un expert, mais je peux t’aider.
native_language_example: I'm not an expert, but I can help you.

meaning: "I am not a…" (said by a woman, before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to deny being someone/something: Je ne suis pas une + noun (often a job/role or label). Because the speaker is female and the noun is feminine, it uses une. For masculine nouns you use je ne suis pas un (e.g., Je ne suis pas un médecin). In informal spoken French, ne is often dropped: Je suis pas une…
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas une experte, mais je peux t'aider.
native_language_example: I’m not an expert, but I can help you.

additional_notes: Used to say that a previous state is no longer true. Built from the negative "ne … plus" (= no longer) with "je suis" (I am). The "ne" is often dropped in speech: "Je suis plus…" (but in writing, keep "ne"). "Plus" is pronounced [ply] here (not [plys]).
target_language_example: Je ne suis plus prêt à partir.
native_language_example: I’m not ready to leave anymore.

additional_notes: Common sentence start meaning “I do not … you” (or “I won’t … you”). **je** = “I”; **te** is the object pronoun meaning “you” (to you / you as the object). It’s usually followed by a verb, and often completed with French negation: **ne … pas** (not), **ne … jamais** (never), etc. Examples: *Je ne te crois pas* = “I don’t believe you”; *Je ne te pardonnerai jamais* = “I will never forgive you.”
target_language_example: Je ne te comprends pas.
native_language_example: I don’t understand you.

meaning: I won’t let you / I won’t allow you (to).
additional_notes: Future tense of "ne pas laisser" with an indirect object pronoun: "te" = "you" (to you). It’s followed by an infinitive to say what you won’t allow: "Je ne te laisserai pas partir" (I won’t let you leave). In everyday speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Je te laisserai pas…". With strong verbs like "crever" (to die, very informal/harsh), the whole sentence can sound very intense.
target_language_example: Je ne te laisserai pas conduire si tu as bu.
native_language_example: I won’t let you drive if you’ve been drinking.

additional_notes: Negative form of **aller** with **ne … pas**. Very often used with an infinitive to make the near future (**aller + infinitive**) in the negative: *Je ne vais pas répondre* = “I’m not going to answer.” It can also be the simple present meaning “I don’t go” (usually followed by a place): *Je ne vais pas dehors* = “I don’t go outside.” In casual speech, **ne** is often dropped: *Je vais pas…*.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne vais pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m not going to come tonight.

additional_notes: Used to refuse or say you don’t want to do something. It’s the negative form of "je veux" (I want): "ne ... pas" wraps around the verb "veux". Often followed by an infinitive ("je ne veux pas jouer" = I don’t want to play) or by "de" + noun ("je ne veux pas de ça" = I don’t want that). In casual spoken French, "ne" is often dropped: "je veux pas".
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne veux pas sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t want to go out tonight.

meaning: I don’t want any / I don’t want (some).
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t want a thing (or any amount of it). It’s followed by a noun: Je ne veux pas de + nom. In negative sentences with an indefinite/partitive idea, French uses “de” (often meaning “any”), e.g., Je ne veux pas de détails = I don’t want any details. With a specific, identified item, you’d often use “Je ne veux pas du/de la/de l’/des …” instead (e.g., Je ne veux pas du micro, if you mean that specific microphone). In casual speech, “ne” is often dropped: Je veux pas de…
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas de café, merci.
native_language_example: I don’t want any coffee, thanks.

additional_notes: Used to refuse or express that you don’t want to become a certain person/thing or be in a certain state. Often followed by a noun (je ne veux pas être policière), an adjective (je ne veux pas être différent), or a past participle to express something happening to you (je ne veux pas être dérangé = I don’t want to be disturbed). In speech, the “ne” is often dropped: je veux pas être…
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas être en retard demain.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be late tomorrow.

meaning: "I don't want (it) anymore" / "I no longer want (to)".
additional_notes:
Used to say you’ve stopped wanting something or you don’t want it from now on. Often followed by:
- a noun: « Je ne veux plus de ça. » (note « de » after negation)
- an infinitive: « Je ne veux plus vivre ici. »
- « rien » (nothing) or « jamais » (ever again): « Je ne veux plus rien. », « Je ne veux plus jamais… »
target_language_example: Je ne veux plus attendre.
native_language_example: I don’t want to wait anymore.

meaning: “I don’t see” (often: “I don’t understand / I don’t get it”).
additional_notes: Literally means you don’t see something, but very commonly used figuratively to say you don’t understand something or don’t see the point/difference. Often followed by a question word: « Je ne vois pas de quoi… » (what you’re talking about), « Je ne vois pas où… » (where someone is going with this). As a short reply (« Non, je ne vois pas. »), it means “No, I don’t (see/understand).”
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne vois pas ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t see what you mean.

meaning: “I wouldn’t like to / I wouldn’t want to” (often: “I’d rather not”).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of *vouloir* (*je voudrais*) with negation to sound more polite, hesitant, or indirect than *je ne veux pas* (“I don’t want”). Common for soft refusals, avoiding something, or saying you don’t want to cause a problem: *Je ne voudrais pas te déranger.*
target_language_example: Je ne voudrais pas te déranger, mais j’ai une question.
native_language_example: I wouldn’t want to bother you, but I have a question.

meaning: "I didn't want to" / "I wasn't intending to".
additional_notes: Literally "I not wanted (imperfect) not". Uses the imperfect (voulais) to express an ongoing state in the past, often used to soften or explain (e.g., "I didn’t mean to say that", "I wasn’t trying to hurt you"). Typically followed by an infinitive (je ne voulais pas dire/aller) or a noun with de/d’ (je ne voulais pas de ce travail). You can also use it alone: "Je ne voulais pas." = "I didn’t want to."
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne voulais pas te faire peur.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t mean to scare you.

additional_notes: This is the start of a negated verb phrase. Use it with a verb after it: “je ne vous + verbe + pas” = “I don’t + verb + you” when speaking to one person formally (vous) or to several people. Example pattern: « je ne vous vois pas » = “I don’t see you.”
target_language_example: Je ne vous comprends pas.
native_language_example: I don’t understand you.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never done something involving the person(s) you’re addressing. It’s the perfect tense negative pattern: "je" + "ne" + "vous" (to you / you as object) + "ai" (have) + past participle + "jamais" (ever/never). In speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Je vous ai jamais..." (though in careful/formal writing it stays). The past participle may agree with "vous" if it’s a direct object placed before the verb: "Je ne vous ai jamais vus" (to men/mixed group), "...vues" (to women), "...oubliés/oubliées".
target_language_example: Je ne vous ai jamais vu(e) auparavant.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen you before.

meaning: “I haven’t / I didn’t … you” (negative in the past with “vous”).
additional_notes: This is the start of a negative sentence in the passé composé. Word order: **Je + ne + vous (object pronoun) + ai (avoir) + pas + past participle**. **Vous** can mean “you” (formal singular) or “you” (plural). The sentence is completed by adding the past participle (e.g., *vu, entendu, acheté*). In speech, **ne** is often dropped: *Je vous ai pas…*
target_language_example: Je ne vous ai pas oubliés.
native_language_example: I haven’t forgotten you.

additional_notes: Uses the French negative pattern **ne … jamais** (“never”) with **avoir** in the present to make the **passé composé**: **je n’ai jamais + past participle** (e.g., *je n’ai jamais dit*, *je n’ai jamais réussi*). In casual speech, **ne** is often dropped: *j’ai jamais…*
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais visité Paris.
native_language_example: I’ve never visited Paris.

additional_notes: Used to say you do not have something: "je n’ai pas de + noun" (no/any), or "je n’ai pas + noun with article" (e.g., "je n’ai pas le temps"). Before a vowel or silent h, "de" becomes "d’" ("je n’ai pas d’argent"). Often in speech, "ne" is dropped: "j’ai pas".
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas de temps aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to make a confident guess or assumption based on what you think is likely. Often followed by a full clause (Je parie que tu as raison.) and can be used alone as a reply: Je parie que si. In casual speech, you may hear shortened/contracted forms (Je parie qu’t’es…).
target_language_example: Je parie que tu as oublié tes clés.
native_language_example: I bet you forgot your keys.

additional_notes: Used with a language to mean "I speak" ("Je parle chinois"). With de, dont, or de qui, it often means "I'm talking/about" ("Je parle de vous", "Tu sais de qui je parle").
target_language_example: Je parle anglais avec mes collègues.
native_language_example: I speak English with my coworkers.

meaning: “I speak a little / I speak a bit.”
additional_notes: Use it to say you have basic ability in a language: « Je parle un peu + [langue] » (usually without an article: « Je parle un peu français. »). You may also hear « Je parle un peu le français », but it’s less common and can sound more like “I speak a bit of the French language.”
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je parle un peu français.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I speak a little French.

additional_notes: From the verb "partir" (to leave/depart). Used when you’re leaving a place or setting off on a trip. In casual spoken French, the negation is often shortened: "je pars pas" = "je ne pars pas" (I’m not leaving). Often followed by "pour" + a destination/time/purpose: "je pars pour Bruxelles" (I’m leaving for Brussels), "je pars dans une heure" (I’m leaving in an hour).
target_language_example: Désolé, je pars maintenant.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm leaving now.

additional_notes: Used to say you had an assumption or belief in the past, often one that turned out to be wrong. It’s built with the imperfect tense: « je pensais » (I was thinking / I thought) + « que » (that) + « c’était » (it was). Often followed by a person (« moi », « vous »), a thing, or a whole clause.
target_language_example: Je pensais que c'était ton frère.
native_language_example: I thought it was your brother.

additional_notes: Used to express what you believed in the past (often implying you were mistaken or surprised). It uses the imperfect tense: « je pensais » (I was thinking / I thought) + « que » + « nous étions » (we were). The adjective or past participle that follows often agrees with « nous »: « heureuses » (all women), « heureux » (mixed group or all men).
target_language_example: Je pensais que nous étions d’accord, mais apparemment non.
native_language_example: I thought we agreed, but apparently not.

additional_notes: Used to say what you believed about someone in the past (often an assumption that may have been wrong). It’s commonly followed by a place, an activity/state, or an opinion: *Je pensais que tu étais au travail / contre… / sérieuse.* Grammar: **je pensais** (imparfait of *penser*) + **que** + **tu étais** (imparfait of *être*).
target_language_example: Je pensais que tu étais déjà parti.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

additional_notes: Used to say your earlier belief or assumption about someone/something was different from what you now know. It’s in the imperfect (je pensais) + que + imperfect (vous étiez), a very common pattern for past assumptions. "Vous" can mean one person you’re being polite to, or several people. After "vous étiez", the adjective/noun usually agrees with the person/people (e.g., blessés/blessées; parti/partie/partis/parties).
target_language_example: Je pensais que vous étiez déjà au courant.
native_language_example: I thought you already knew.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you believed or expected in the past (often an assumption that turns out to be wrong). "Je pensais" is the imperfect tense, common for background thoughts/beliefs. It’s typically followed by a clause with "ça" (= it/that), e.g. "je pensais que ça allait..." (I thought it was going to...).
target_language_example: Je pensais que ça serait plus facile.
native_language_example: I thought it would be easier.

meaning: "I was thinking about" / "I was thinking of."
additional_notes: Imperfect of *penser à* (to think about/of), used for an ongoing background thought or something you had in mind. It can be followed by a noun (*je pensais à la clé*), an infinitive (*je pensais à acheter...* = I was thinking of buying...), or a clause (*je pensais à ce que tu m'as dit*).
target_language_example: Je pensais à toi en rentrant chez moi.
native_language_example: I was thinking of you on my way home.

meaning: "I thought I was" / "I believed I was".
additional_notes: Used to talk about a past belief or assumption about yourself that may turn out to be wrong. It’s the imperfect tense of penser + infinitive être, often followed by an adjective or noun: je pensais être gentil(le), seul(e), trop jeune, votre cadet, etc. Gender agreement happens on adjectives (heureuse, seul/seule).
target_language_example: Je pensais être en retard, mais je suis arrivé à l’heure.
native_language_example: I thought I was late, but I arrived on time.

meaning: “I think so / I guess so” (often: “yes, indeed”).
additional_notes: Used to agree or confirm what was just said, often with emphasis (similar to “you bet” or “of course”). Depending on tone, it can also sound ironic or annoyed (like “Yeah, sure I do”). In casual speech you’ll also hear: “Je pense bien que oui !” or “Je pense bien !”.
target_language_example: — Tu vas venir demain ? — Je pense bien !
native_language_example: — Are you coming tomorrow? — You bet / Of course!

meaning: "I think I can" / "I think I’ll be able to".
additional_notes: Used to express a belief about your ability to do something. It’s followed by another verb in the infinitive (e.g., je pense pouvoir venir = I think I can come). In negatives: je ne pense pas pouvoir… = I don’t think I can…
target_language_example: Je pense pouvoir venir demain.
native_language_example: I think I can come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or belief about what a man/boy (“il”) does or what is true. Very often followed by a verb in the present or past: « Je pense qu’il a raison. » You can also drop “que” in casual speech (« Je pense qu’il… » is standard; « Je pense il… » is not).
target_language_example: Je pense qu'il va arriver bientôt.
native_language_example: I think he’s going to arrive soon.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or guess, followed by a clause. "On" often means "we" in everyday French (instead of "nous"), but it can also mean "people" or an informal "you" depending on context. Common with verbs like: "Je pense qu'on a fini" (we’re done), "Je pense qu'on peut le faire" (we can do it), "Je pense qu'on y est" (I think we’re there).
target_language_example: Je pense qu'on peut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: I think we can leave now.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion, guess, or personal judgment. In English, "that" is often omitted, but in French "que" is normally kept here.
target_language_example: Je pense que c'est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I think it's a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or belief about something. It’s followed by an adjective, a noun, or a clause: “Je pense que c’est + adjective” (Je pense que c’est important), or “Je pense que c’est + finished/over/etc.” (Je pense que c’est terminé). Often translates naturally as “I think it’s…” in English.
target_language_example: Je pense que c'est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I think it's a good idea.

meaning: "I think it would be" (giving your opinion about a hypothetical).
additional_notes: Used to politely give your opinion or suggestion about a possible situation. "Ce serait" is the conditional of "c’est" (= "it is"), so it often introduces an idea like "it would be (better/smarter/nicer/too risky)". Very common before adjectives or phrases like "une bonne idée de…".
target_language_example: Je pense que ce serait mieux d’attendre un peu.
native_language_example: I think it would be better to wait a bit.

additional_notes: Used to express a plan, intention, or guess about what you’ll do very soon. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb (garder, partir, porter, vomir). "Je vais" is the near-future form (aller + infinitive), and adding "je pense que" makes it less certain/polite ("I think" / "I guess").
target_language_example: Je pense que je vais prendre un café.
native_language_example: I think I’m going to have a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to give an opinion or suggestion. "Je pense que" = "I think that" and "nous devrions" is the conditional of "devoir" ("we should / we ought to"). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive: "Je pense que nous devrions partir" (I think we should leave).
target_language_example: Je pense que nous devrions partir tout de suite.
native_language_example: I think we should leave right away.

additional_notes: Used to express your opinion/suggestion that a group (“we”) is able to do something. Often followed by an infinitive (aller, faire, gérer) or by “le faire.” You can soften it with “Je pense qu’on peut…” in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Je pense que nous pouvons résoudre ce problème ensemble.
native_language_example: I think we can solve this problem together.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or make a recommendation. Follow it with an infinitive verb (e.g., aller, attendre, faire). In negatives, use: « Je pense que tu ne devrais pas... » (“I think you shouldn’t…”).
target_language_example: Je pense que tu devrais te reposer un peu.
native_language_example: I think you should rest a bit.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or make a suggestion in a polite, somewhat indirect way. The subject is "vous" (you, formal or plural). After "devriez" (conditional of devoir), use an infinitive verb: "je pense que vous devriez partir". You can soften it further with "peut-être" (maybe) or "vraiment" (really).
target_language_example: Je pense que vous devriez réserver à l’avance.
native_language_example: I think you should book in advance.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or guess about what follows. It’s very common in conversation, and you typically continue with a verb phrase (e.g., "je pense que ça dépend", "je pense que ça va plaire"). In more formal French you may also hear "je pense que cela…" (cela = a more formal "that/it").
target_language_example: Je pense que ça va être difficile.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to be difficult.

meaning: "I’m thinking about" / "I’m thinking of" (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition **à** before a person or thing you have in mind (**penser à + noun/pronoun**). It can mean thinking about something in general, or thinking of someone (they come to mind). For opinions, French usually uses **je pense que...** (I think that...).
target_language_example: Je pense à toi quand j’écoute cette chanson.
native_language_example: I think of you when I listen to that song.

additional_notes: First-person singular of pouvoir in the present tense. It is usually followed by another verb in the infinitive: je peux voir, je peux parler. Object pronouns often come before the infinitive phrase: je peux la voir, je peux lui parler.
target_language_example: Je peux t'aider demain.
native_language_example: I can help you tomorrow.

meaning: “can I go” (am I allowed to go).
additional_notes: Often used to ask for permission to go somewhere and do something: « Je peux aller + infinitive ? » (Je peux aller jouer ?). You can also add a place: « Je peux aller jouer dans ma chambre ? ».
target_language_example: Je peux aller aux toilettes, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can I go to the bathroom, please?

meaning: "Can I have…?" / "May I have…?" (to ask for something).
additional_notes: Used to make a polite request for an item, some help, someone’s contact info, or a moment of their time. Common in cafés/shops/restaurants (often followed by a noun: « Je peux avoir un café ? »). You can make it more polite by adding « s’il vous plaît » or using the question form « Est-ce que je peux avoir… ? ».
target_language_example: Je peux avoir l’addition, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can I have the bill, please?

additional_notes: "Je peux" means "I can" (from "pouvoir"), and it’s usually followed by an infinitive like "faire" (to do / to make). Used to say you’re able/allowed to do something (context decides), or as a question: "Je peux faire… ?" = "Can I do…?" / "May I do…?" You can add an object after it: "je peux faire le travail" (I can do the work), "je peux faire ça" (I can do that).
target_language_example: Je peux faire ça maintenant, ou plus tard.
native_language_example: I can do that now, or later.

additional_notes: Used to express ability/capability, possibility, or willingness. You can expand it with details: time (Je peux faire ça en moins de dix minutes. = in under 10 minutes), comparison (plus vite que toi = faster than you), help (pour toi = for you), or independence (tout seul = by myself). In questions, it often means “How can I do that?” (Comment est-ce que je peux faire ça ?) or “Do you really think I can do that?” (Est-ce que tu penses vraiment que je peux faire ça ?).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je peux faire ça ce soir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I can do that tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you are able to do something. "Le" (“it”) refers to an action or task already mentioned or understood from context. You can add details like how or for whom: "Je peux le faire pour vous" (for you), "Je peux le faire toute seule" (all by myself), "Je peux le faire par mes propres moyens" (on my own / with my own resources). "Ça, je peux le faire" puts emphasis on "ça" (“that”), meaning “That, I can do.”
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : je peux le faire.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I can do it.

additional_notes: Informal spoken French version of « je ne peux pas » (dropping « ne »). Common in everyday speech: « Je peux pas venir » = “I can’t come.” In writing or formal situations, prefer « je ne peux pas ».
target_language_example: Je peux pas venir ce soir, je travaille.
native_language_example: I can’t come tonight, I’m working.

additional_notes: Literally “I can take,” but often used as a polite way to ask permission or offer a service. Common with a direct object: *Je peux prendre votre commande ?* (“May I take your order?”) or *Je peux prendre votre place ?* (“Can I take your seat/spot?”). Intonation (a rising tone) or adding *s’il vous plaît* makes it sound more like “may I…?” than ability.
target_language_example: Je peux prendre votre manteau ?
native_language_example: May I take your coat?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say you are able to do something for someone, or to ask permission: « Je peux te + infinitive ? ». « te » means “you” in the informal singular (tu) form, so it’s used with friends, family, kids, etc. For more formal/polite, use « je peux vous + infinitive ? ».
target_language_example: Je peux te montrer quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Can I show you something?

meaning: “Can I talk to you?” / “Can I speak to you?”
additional_notes: Used to ask permission to talk to someone, often to have a quick or private chat. You can add a time (“une seconde”, “une minute”) or a place (“dehors”) to soften the request: “Je peux te parler une seconde ?” / “Je peux te parler dehors ?”. In more formal situations, you’d usually say “Est-ce que je peux vous parler ?” (vous).
target_language_example: Je peux te parler deux minutes après le cours ?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you for two minutes after class?

additional_notes: Literally 'I can see.' Used to say you are able to see something (often with comparisons like 'aussi bien que' = 'as well as'). As a question ('Je peux voir ?'), it commonly means 'Can I see?' / 'May I take a look?' (e.g., asking to see something someone has).
target_language_example: Je peux voir ton billet, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can I see your ticket, please?

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb + the object pronoun "vous" (you, formal or plural): "Je peux vous + infinitive". Common for asking permission or making an offer/help: "Je peux vous appeler… ?" (May/Can I call you…?) or "Je peux vous aider" (I can help you). Word order: "je peux" + object pronoun (vous) + infinitive.
target_language_example: Je peux vous aider avec ça ?
native_language_example: Can I help you with that?

meaning: "I can help you" / "Can I help you?" (formal/polite).
additional_notes: Literally "I can help you." Used with "vous" to be polite or to address more than one person. Often used as a question in service situations: "Je peux vous aider ?" You can add "à" + infinitive to say what you can help with: "Je peux vous aider à rentrer" (I can help you get home).
target_language_example: Bonjour, je peux vous aider à trouver quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Hi, can I help you find something?

additional_notes: Used to offer to give someone something in a polite/formal way. "Vous" is the formal or plural "you". In casual situations with one person, you often say "je peux te donner".
target_language_example: Je peux vous donner une couverture si vous avez froid.
native_language_example: I can give you a blanket if you’re cold.

additional_notes: Literally “I can speak to you,” but most often used as a polite way to ask permission to talk to someone (often in a private or serious way). Commonly followed by a time phrase: « un instant / un moment » (“for a moment”). « vous » is the formal/plural “you”; with friends you’d usually say « Je peux te parler ? ». Can also be extended with a language: « Je peux vous parler en anglais » (“I can speak to you in English”).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je peux vous parler deux minutes ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I speak to you for two minutes?

meaning: "Can I go there?" / "I can go there."
additional_notes: Means being allowed to go, or being able to go. "y" replaces a place previously mentioned (there). In questions (often with rising intonation or "Alors,"), it can mean asking permission: "Alors, je peux y aller ?" = "So, can I go (there)?" It can also be used to say you’re able/allowed to go: "Je peux y aller" = "I can go." You can add details: "aussi" (too), "avec toi" (with you), "toute seule" (all by myself), or "comment" (how) in "Savez-vous comment je peux y aller ?"
target_language_example: Si tu veux, je peux y aller demain avec toi.
native_language_example: If you want, I can go there tomorrow with you.

additional_notes: Used to say you can do something only with great difficulty or only just enough (often because it’s hard, limited, or almost impossible). Structure: "je peux à peine" + verb (e.g., comprendre, payer, respirer, entendre). In polite/formal speech with "vous": "Je peux à peine vous entendre."
target_language_example: Je peux à peine marcher après l’opération.
native_language_example: I can barely walk after the operation.

additional_notes: From the verb *pouvoir* (to be able to). Often followed by an infinitive: *je peux venir* (I can come). It can also stand alone to mean “I can do that” (*Ça, je peux.*). In *Si je peux…* it means “If I’m able to / If I can…”.
target_language_example: Je peux te rappeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I can call you back tonight.

meaning: “I will be able to” / “I can” (in the future).
additional_notes: Future tense (futur simple) of *pouvoir* (“to be able to / can”). Usually followed by an infinitive: *je pourrai venir* (“I’ll be able to come”). It can also stand alone when the verb is understood from context: *Je pourrai ?* (“Will I be able to?”).
target_language_example: Je pourrai t’aider demain.
native_language_example: I’ll be able to help you tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Je pourrais" is the conditional form of "pouvoir" (to be able to / can). Use it to talk about a possibility or hypothetical action ("I could... / I might...") or to sound more polite/less direct when offering or suggesting something (similar to "I could..." in English). Often followed by an infinitive: "je pourrais + verbe".
target_language_example: Je pourrais t'aider demain si tu veux.
native_language_example: I could help you tomorrow if you want.

additional_notes: Imperfect of pouvoir: describes an ability, possibility, or what you were able to do in the past (often as background or ongoing). Common in phrases like « je pouvais voir/entendre » (= “I could see/hear”). In reported speech after « a dit que… », it often means “I could / would be able to.”
target_language_example: Je pouvais enfin respirer après l'examen.
native_language_example: I could finally breathe after the exam.

meaning: “I could barely / I was hardly able to.”
additional_notes: Used to say you almost couldn’t do something (because it was difficult, painful, tiring, dark, etc.). The tense is imperfect (pouvais), often for background or ongoing past situations. You can change the subject and tense: je peux à peine (I can barely), il/elle pouvait à peine, nous pouvions à peine, etc. Also common: à peine + infinitive (e.g., à peine voir = barely see).
target_language_example: Après la randonnée, je pouvais à peine marcher.
native_language_example: After the hike, I could barely walk.

additional_notes: First-person singular present of prendre. It is very common and can be used for physically taking something, using transport (je prends le train = I take the train), or taking over/continuing something (je prends la suite). In English, it can translate as either the simple present or present progressive depending on context.
target_language_example: Je prends le bus tous les matins.
native_language_example: I take the bus every morning.

additional_notes: First-person singular of préférer. It can be followed by a noun or pronoun (je préfère celle-ci = I prefer this one) or by an infinitive (je préfère voyager seul = I prefer to travel alone / I'd rather travel alone). With plutôt que, it can mean 'rather than'.
target_language_example: Je préfère rester à la maison ce soir.
native_language_example: I'd rather stay home tonight.

additional_notes: Used to express a preference for plural things. Often followed by "à/au/aux" to compare: "Je préfère les X aux Y" = "I prefer X to Y." Without a comparison, it just states what you like better in general: "Je préfère les matériaux simples."
target_language_example: Je préfère les films en français aux films doublés.
native_language_example: I prefer movies in French to dubbed movies.

meaning: I plan to / I’m planning to (I intend to).
additional_notes: Used to say you have an intention or plan. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (je prévois de + infinitive): Je prévois de partir demain. More formal/neutral than "je compte"; close to "j’ai l’intention de". Conjugates like prévoir: je prévois, tu prévois, il/elle prévoit, nous prévoyons, vous prévoyez, ils/elles prévoient.
target_language_example: Je prévois de commencer le français ce week-end.
native_language_example: I’m planning to start French this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to firmly say you will not do something, accept something, or allow something to happen. Structure: "Je refuse de" + infinitive verb (je refuse de répondre, de rester, de laisser...). For refusing a specific object, you often use "Je refuse" + noun (e.g., je refuse cette proposition) instead.
target_language_example: Je refuse de signer ce contrat.
native_language_example: I refuse to sign this contract.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *rentrer* to say you’re going back, often back home: *Je rentre tard.* You can specify how/when/where: *Je rentre par avion lundi matin* (by plane), *Je rentre du boulot* (I’m coming back from work), or *Je rentre pour son anniversaire* (I’m coming back for his/her birthday). In *il faut que je rentre*, it means “I have to go (home/back).” *Rentrer au bercail* is a more folksy/idiomatic way to say “go back home.”
target_language_example: Désolé, je rentre maintenant.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m heading home now.

additional_notes: Used with the verb rentrer (“to go back/return”) + chez moi (“to my place/home”). It often implies returning to where you live (from work, school, out in town, etc.). In questions, it can mean “How do I get home?” (Comment je rentre chez moi ?).
target_language_example: Après le dîner, je rentre chez moi.
native_language_example: After dinner, I’m going home.

additional_notes: Future tense of "revenir". It can mean coming back to a place (physical return) or coming back to a topic: "Je ne reviendrai pas là-dessus" = "I won’t go back to that / I won’t bring that up again." Often used with time expressions: "un peu plus tard" (a bit later).
target_language_example: Je reviendrai demain matin.
native_language_example: I’ll come back tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Literally “I come back.” Often used in the present tense to mean a near-future return: “I’ll be back (soon).” It can also mean you’re returning to do something specific, like pick something up (e.g., “je reviens prendre le reste” = “I’m coming back to get the rest”).
target_language_example: Attends ici, je reviens dans deux minutes.
native_language_example: Wait here, I’ll be back in two minutes.

meaning: "I know, I…" (acknowledging something, then adding what you’re doing/going to do).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to show you’ve understood or already knew, and to reassure the other person by immediately stating your action or response (often: je sais, je m’en occupe / je sais, je regarde / je sais, je viens de…). Depending on tone, it can also sound a bit impatient (“Yes, I know!”).
target_language_example: Je sais, je te rappelle dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I know, I’ll call you back in five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to acknowledge what someone just said (“I know”) and then introduce an objection, question, or exception (“but…”). Common in conversation; the comma is often optional in speech.
target_language_example: Je sais, mais on n’a pas assez de temps.
native_language_example: I know, but we don’t have enough time.

meaning: “I know what he…” / “I know what it…”
additional_notes: Used to start a sentence where you say you know what a man (“il” = he) does/wants/needs, or what an inanimate/impersonal subject (“il” = it, e.g., in *il va se passer*) is going to do. The key part is **ce qu’il** = “what he/it…”, with elision of *que il → qu’il*. It must be followed by a verb phrase (e.g., *Je sais ce qu'il veut*, *Je sais ce qu'il va faire*, *Je sais ce qu'il lui faut*).
target_language_example: Je sais ce qu'il va se passer.
native_language_example: I know what’s going to happen.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause about a specific thing you know. It’s usually followed by a subject + verb: “je sais ce que tu fais” (I know what you’re doing). Often contrasted with “je ne sais pas ce que…” (I don’t know what…).
target_language_example: Je sais ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: I know what you mean.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect clause with *ce que* (“what/that which”) + *tu* + a verb: *Je sais ce que tu faisais* (“I know what you were doing”), *Je sais ce que tu traverses* (“I know what you’re going through”). Often implies the speaker is aware of the other person’s actions/feelings/situation.
target_language_example: Je sais ce que tu penses, mais je ne suis pas d’accord.
native_language_example: I know what you think, but I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Used when what you “know” is followed by a clause where the unknown thing is the subject of the verb: Je sais ce qui est bon… (“I know what is good…”). If “what” is the object of the verb, you usually use « je sais ce que… » instead: Je sais ce que tu veux (“I know what you want”).
target_language_example: Je sais ce qui va t’aider.
native_language_example: I know what will help you.

additional_notes: Used to say you know how to do something or you understand the manner in which something happens. It’s typically followed by: (1) an infinitive: « Je sais comment m’en servir. » (I know how to use it.) or (2) a full clause: « Je sais comment c’est arrivé. » (I know how it happened.) In conversation it can imply confidence or reassurance: « Je sais comment tu te sens. » (I know how you feel.)
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je sais comment faire.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I know how to do it.

additional_notes: Used to say you know the location of someone/something or where an action will happen. Often followed by a full clause (e.g., “Je sais où ils vont.” = “I know where they’re going.”). It can also be used alone as a short answer (“Je sais où.”) meaning “I know where (it is/that is).”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je sais où est la gare.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I know where the train station is.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a fact or statement the speaker knows. It is the first-person form; with a different subject, it changes (for example: tu sais que, il sait que).
target_language_example: Je sais que tu as raison.
native_language_example: I know that you're right.

meaning: “I know that it’s / that it is.”
additional_notes: Used to state that you know a fact or identify something/someone. It’s made of: « je sais » (I know) + « que » (that) + « c'est » (it is/it’s). Often followed by a noun, a person/thing, or a description: « je sais que c'est ton ami », « je sais que c'est difficile ». Note: written here with a straight apostrophe (c'est) as provided; in French typography you may also see « c’est ».
target_language_example: Je sais que c'est une grande décision.
native_language_example: I know it’s a big decision.

additional_notes: Used to express confidence/certainty about your ability to do something. It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., *je sais que je peux venir* = “I know I can come”). *Je peux* is from *pouvoir* (“to be able to / can”). You can also add words like *toujours* (“always”) or a pronoun like *y* in *je sais que je peux y arriver* (“I know I can do it / make it”).
target_language_example: Je sais que je peux réussir si je m’entraîne.
native_language_example: I know I can succeed if I practice.

additional_notes: Used to state that you’re sure about something concerning the person you’re talking to. It’s followed by a verb (often in the present or future): “je sais que tu apprends… / je sais que tu apprendras…”. Often, “que” can be translated as “that,” but in English it’s frequently omitted: “I know you…”.
target_language_example: Je sais que tu as raison.
native_language_example: I know you’re right.

additional_notes: Used to state that you know the other person possesses something or is experiencing a state. "Je sais" = "I know"; "que" = "that"; "tu as" = "you have" ("avoir" is also used for some feelings/conditions like "avoir faim" = "to be hungry"). Often followed by a noun ("des problèmes", "une petite amie") or an expression with "avoir".
target_language_example: Je sais que tu as besoin d'aide.
native_language_example: I know that you need help.

additional_notes: Used to say you know what someone wants or intends to do. It’s often followed by an infinitive: « Je sais que tu veux aider / venir / rentrer… ». « que » = “that.” You can also add an object before the infinitive: « Je sais que tu veux m’aider » (“I know you want to help me”).
target_language_example: Je sais que tu veux partir tôt.
native_language_example: I know you want to leave early.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement you know to be true about the person(s) you’re addressing. « vous » is the formal or plural “you”. The verb « êtes » is the present tense of « être » (to be) for « vous ». Often followed by a noun/adjective: « je sais que vous êtes professeur / fatigué(e) ». With a past action, you’ll typically switch to a past tense: « Je sais que vous êtes parti(e) » (I know you left).
target_language_example: Je sais que vous êtes très occupé aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I know that you are very busy today.

meaning: 'I know who …' (I know the person’s identity).
additional_notes: Used before an indirect question with **qui**. After **qui**, French keeps normal word order: **Je sais qui elle est** (not *je sais qui est-elle*). You can add a noun/clause after it: **Je sais qui tu es**, **Je sais qui il est**, etc.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je sais qui tu es.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I know who you are.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you already knew about a man (or "it" if referring to a masculine noun). After "qu'il", you typically use the imperfect/past or conditional to talk about what you knew would happen: "Je savais qu'il viendrait" (I knew he would come).
target_language_example: Je savais qu'il allait appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I knew he was going to call tonight.

additional_notes: "Je savais que" uses the imperfect (savais) of "savoir" to express knowledge you had in the past (often as background information). In the present, you’d usually say "je sais que" (I know that). It’s followed by a full clause: "je savais que + [subject] + [verb]".
target_language_example: Je savais que tu avais raison.
native_language_example: I knew you were right.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause about what you (already) knew someone was going to do. "Je savais" is the imperfect of *savoir* (to know), often used for background knowledge, expectations, or something you suspected/anticipated. It can sound satisfied (“I knew it!”) or reproachful depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Je savais que tu finirais par appeler.
native_language_example: I knew you’d end up calling.

additional_notes: Used to say you already knew something about someone you’re addressing politely or in the plural ("vous" = "you" formal or "you all"). "Je savais" is the imperfect past of "savoir" and often implies a continuing state in the past ("I knew / I had known"). It’s followed by "que" + a full clause (e.g., "que vous viendriez").
target_language_example: Je savais que vous étiez en train de préparer une surprise.
native_language_example: I knew you were preparing a surprise.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you knew or expected in the past, followed by a full clause (often with a verb like "allait" or "devait"). "Je savais" is the imperfect tense (ongoing/background past). "Ça" refers to something general (“it/that”), like an event or situation.
target_language_example: Je savais que ça finirait par arriver.
native_language_example: I knew it would eventually happen.

additional_notes: Future tense of "être" (to be). Used to say what you will be/do in the future: "Je serai sur scène" (I’ll be on stage). Often appears in time expressions like "quand je serai..." (when I am / when I’m ... in the future).
target_language_example: Demain, je serai à la maison toute la journée.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, I will be at home all day.

meaning: "I'll be there" / "I'll be here" (future: I will be present).
additional_notes: Literally “I will be there.” Used for future presence at a place/time (Je serai là demain.) or to reassure someone you’ll be available to help/support them (Je serai là si tu as besoin de moi.). Context decides whether “là” is best translated as “there” or “here.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je serai là pour toi.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll be there for you.

additional_notes: A fairly formal/polite way to express a wish, desire, or request (often used in writing, emails, or official contexts). Common patterns: "je souhaite + infinitive" (je souhaite partir = I wish to leave) or "je souhaite que + subjunctive" (je souhaite que vous veniez = I wish that you would come). In everyday conversation, people often use "je veux" (more direct) or "je voudrais" (polite).
target_language_example: Je souhaite prendre rendez-vous.
native_language_example: I would like to make an appointment.

additional_notes: First-person singular of être. Use it to talk about who you are, how you feel, or what you are like: je suis heureux, je suis intelligent. In other contexts, the same spelling can also mean "I follow" from suivre, but here it means "I am."
target_language_example: Je suis prêt pour le voyage.
native_language_example: I am ready for the trip.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of « aller » with « être »: « je suis allé(e) ». Add -e if the speaker is female (« je suis allée »). Used for going to a place (« je suis allé au supermarché »), doing an activity (« je suis allé nager »), or in common patterns like « je suis allé voir… » = “I went to see/check…”.
target_language_example: Je suis allé au cinéma hier soir.
native_language_example: I went to the movie theater last night.

meaning: "I went to" (to a place, often a country/continent).
additional_notes: Past tense of aller (passé composé) with être: je suis allé (masc.) / je suis allée (fem.). Use en before continents and most feminine countries (en Europe, en Inde). For masculine countries use au (au Canada), and for plural places use aux (aux États-Unis).
target_language_example: Je suis allé en France l'année dernière.
native_language_example: I went to France last year.

additional_notes: Past tense of "aller" (to go) with "être": je suis allé (masc.) / je suis allée (fem.). Use "à" before a place or event: a city (à Paris), a store (à ce magasin), a concert (à un concert). Often followed by extra info like transport (en train) or purpose (voir Tom).
target_language_example: Je suis allé à Montréal l'année dernière.
native_language_example: I went to Montreal last year.

additional_notes: Past tense of "aller" (to go) in the passé composé: "je" + "être" (suis) + past participle "allé(e)". Add -e because the speaker is feminine (male: "je suis allé"). Often followed by a place with "à" (au/à la/à l’/aux), or by a person’s place with "chez" (e.g., "chez lui").
target_language_example: Je suis allée à la bibliothèque hier.
native_language_example: I went to the library yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *arriver* (to arrive). It uses **être** as the helping verb: *je suis + arrivé*. The past participle agrees with the subject: **je suis arrivé** (male speaker) / **je suis arrivée** (female speaker). Often used to announce you’ve just gotten somewhere: *Je suis arrivé !* = “I’m here / I’ve arrived!”
target_language_example: Salut ! Je suis arrivé à la gare.
native_language_example: Hi! I arrived at the station.

meaning: "I’m fine / I feel good"; also "Am I really…? / Am I in the right…?" (with a question).
additional_notes: With no extra complement, it often means you feel well or comfortable: « Je suis bien, et toi ? » / « Je suis bien là où je suis. » With a question and a place or situation, « bien » adds emphasis and asks for confirmation (similar to “really/indeed”): « Je suis bien à la poste ? » = “I’m at the post office, right?” It can also intensify an adjective: « bien décidé » = “really determined.”
target_language_example: Je suis bien ici, merci.
native_language_example: I feel good here, thanks.

additional_notes: Means you’re pleased/satisfied about something. Common patterns: « je suis content de + infinitive » (Je suis content de te voir. = I’m happy to see you) and « je suis content que + subjunctive » (Je suis content que tu sois là. = I’m glad you’re here). If the speaker is female, you usually say « je suis contente » (with -e).
target_language_example: Je suis content de t'aider.
native_language_example: I’m happy to help you.

je suis content que tu sois

target_language_multi_word_term: je suis content que tu sois
meaning: “I’m happy that you are …” / “I’m glad you’re …”
additional_notes: Used to express happiness or relief about the other person’s state or situation. After **content que**, French requires the **subjunctive**: **que tu sois** (not *que tu es*). **Content** agrees with the speaker: **je suis content** (male speaker) / **je suis contente** (female speaker). Note that French **content** usually means “happy/glad,” not the English sense of “content” (satisfied/calm).
target_language_example: Je suis content que tu sois mon ami.
native_language_example: I’m happy you’re my friend.

meaning: I’m happy / I’m glad (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to express happiness or satisfaction. “Contente” agrees with the speaker: a man says “Je suis content”; more than one woman: “Je suis contentes”; mixed/men: “Je suis contents.” Common patterns: “Je suis contente de + infinitive” (Je suis contente de te revoir), “Je suis contente pour + person” (happy for someone), and “Je suis contente que + subjunctive” (Je suis contente que tu sois venu).
target_language_example: Je suis contente qu’on puisse se voir ce week-end.
native_language_example: I’m glad we can see each other this weekend.

je suis contente que tu sois

target_language_multi_word_term: je suis contente que tu sois
