additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question with **qui** (“who”). Typically followed by a verb clause: **Je veux savoir qui a fait ça** (“…who did that”) or **Je veux savoir qui sont vos amis** (“…who your friends are”). With **qui** as the subject, the verb comes right after (**qui a donné…**).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir qui a pris mes clés.
native_language_example: I want to know who took my keys.

additional_notes: Used to express a simple or limited desire (often to soften what you’re asking for). Word order: "Je veux seulement + noun/infinitive". You can also say "Je veux juste..." (more common in speech).
target_language_example: Je veux seulement te poser une question.
native_language_example: I just want to ask you a question.

additional_notes: Used to soften or simplify what you’re asking for: you’re saying your desire is basic/only that. Often followed by an infinitive (je veux simplement partir) or by que + subjunctive (je veux simplement que tu sois heureuse).
target_language_example: Je veux simplement rentrer à la maison.
native_language_example: I just want to go home.

meaning: “I just want to be …” / “I simply want to be …”
additional_notes: Used to express a simple wish about a state or identity. It’s followed by the infinitive être (“to be”) plus an adjective (différente, seul) or past participle used like an adjective (aimé = loved). Word order is fixed: Je veux simplement être + (adjective/description).
target_language_example: Je veux simplement être heureux.
native_language_example: I just want to be happy.

additional_notes:
Often used to introduce a topic you want to discuss. It can sound serious or important depending on context. You can add details with:
- « au sujet de / à propos de + noun » = “about (a topic)”
- « de + noun » = “about”
You can also specify privacy: « Je veux te parler seule. » = “I want to talk to you alone / in private.”
target_language_example: Je veux te parler après le cours.
native_language_example: I want to talk to you after class.

meaning: “I want to see you.” (also: “I want to watch you” do something).
additional_notes: Used to say you want to see someone (meet them) or see them doing an action. Often followed by an infinitive to mean “I want to see you + verb” (e.g., je veux te voir danser = I want to see you dance). Context decides whether it means meeting in person (“I want to see you in my office”) or watching (“I want to see you laugh”).
target_language_example: Je veux te voir ce soir, si tu es libre.
native_language_example: I want to see you tonight, if you’re free.

additional_notes: Used to express a desire or plan to live somewhere (je veux vivre en Italie / dans une ville / à la campagne) or to live in a certain way (je veux vivre en paix). With a direct object, vivre can also mean “to experience” (je veux vivre de beaux moments / une vie heureuse).
target_language_example: Je veux vivre près de la mer un jour.
native_language_example: I want to live near the sea one day.

additional_notes: Uses the verb pattern « vouloir + infinitive »: « je veux » (I want) + « voir » (to see). Often followed by what you want to see (a person/thing) or by a clause with « ce que… » (what…). Can also be said on its own (« Je veux voir. ») meaning “I want to see (for myself).”
target_language_example: Je veux voir si tu as raison.
native_language_example: I want to see if you’re right.

additional_notes: Uses **vous** (formal “you” to one person, or “you” to several people). Often followed by **de + noun** or **à propos de + noun** to say what you want to talk about (e.g., *Je veux vous parler de ce rapport*). You can add **seul(e)** to mean “in private/alone” (*Je veux vous parler seul*).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je veux vous parler un instant.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I want to talk to you for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a strong desire or intention. Often followed by an infinitive (je veux vraiment partir) or a direct object (je veux vraiment ça). Word order can vary for emphasis (Vraiment, je veux vraiment ça).
target_language_example: Je veux vraiment apprendre le français cette année.
native_language_example: I really want to learn French this year.

additional_notes: Used to say what you want to become or what state you want to be in. Follow it with a noun (Je veux être guitariste), an adjective (Je veux être intelligent), or a past participle to express wanting to be in a resulting state, often in the passive (Je veux être invité(e) = “I want to be invited”; Je veux être promu = “I want to be promoted”). You can change the subject: tu veux être…, il/elle veut être…, nous voulons être…, etc.
target_language_example: Je veux être prêt pour demain.
native_language_example: I want to be ready for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Future tense of venir (to come). Use it to say you’ll come somewhere in the future (often with time words like demain, plus tôt, vers six heures). It can also mean “I’ll come (to do something)” before an infinitive: Je viendrai te chercher = I’ll come pick you up.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je viendrai te voir ce week-end.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll come see you this weekend.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to express the recent past: “venir de + infinitive” = having done something a moment ago. It conjugates like venir: je viens de…, tu viens de…, il/elle vient de…, etc. (Example 1 contains a vulgar verb, but the structure itself is neutral.)
target_language_example: Je viens de rentrer à la maison.
native_language_example: I just got home.

additional_notes: This uses the recent past construction: **venir de + infinitive** to say something happened a moment ago. Here it’s **je viens de** (I’ve just) + **faire** (do/make). If **faire** is followed by another verb (e.g., *faire nettoyer*, *faire peindre*), it often means **to have something done** (to get something cleaned/painted). You can change the subject: *tu viens de faire*, *il/elle vient de faire*, *nous venons de faire*, etc.
target_language_example: Je viens de faire mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I just did my homework.

additional_notes: Uses the recent past construction: venir de + infinitive. Here it’s conjugated as "je viens" + "de" + "voir" to say you saw something very recently. You can swap the subject and verb to fit the situation (e.g., "tu viens de voir…", "il/elle vient de voir…", "nous venons de voir…").
target_language_example: Je viens de voir une voiture passer très vite.
native_language_example: I just saw a car go by really fast.

additional_notes: First-person singular of venir. It can mean movement toward a place or person ("je viens avec toi" = "I'm coming with you"). With de, it often changes meaning: "je viens de + infinitive" means "I have just...", and "je viens de + place" can mean "I come from...".
target_language_example: Je viens avec vous si vous voulez.
native_language_example: I'll come with you if you want.

additional_notes: Two common uses: (1) origin: “Je viens de + place” = “I’m from / I come from …”. (2) very recent action: “Je viens de + infinitive” = “I just … / I’ve just …” (something that happened moments ago). In speech, you’ll also hear other subjects: “tu viens de…”, “il/elle vient de…”, “nous venons de…”.
target_language_example: Je viens de finir mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I just finished my homework.

meaning: "I just" / "I’ve just" (I did something very recently).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to express the very recent past: "venir de" = "to have just done"; adding "juste" emphasizes how recent it was. In speech it’s often shortened to "je viens de". Example pattern: "Je viens (juste) de + infinitive" (e.g., "Je viens juste de finir").
target_language_example: Je viens juste de prendre le bus.
native_language_example: I just took the bus.

additional_notes: "Je vis" is the present tense of "vivre" (to live) for "je" (I). It’s used for where you live (Je vis en Australie / à Paris), who you live with (Je vis avec ma mère), or more generally how you live (Je vis ici). For cities use "à"; for most countries use "en" (feminine or starting with a vowel) or "au" (masculine); for "chez" + person/people to mean 'at someone's place' (Je vis chez mes parents).
target_language_example: Je vis à Montréal, mais je travaille à distance.
native_language_example: I live in Montreal, but I work remotely.

additional_notes: Uses the verb *vivre* (“to live”). *À* is commonly used before cities (Je vis à Paris) and also some islands/places (Je vis à Tahiti, à Malte). For most countries you use **en** (en France) or **au/aux** (au Canada, aux États-Unis) instead of *à*.
target_language_example: Je vis à Lyon depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in Lyon for two years.

additional_notes: Literally means seeing with your eyes, but very often also means understanding or realizing something from context. With "que" or "ce que," it often means "i see that..." or "i see what...".
target_language_example: Ah, je vois ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: Ah, I see what you mean.

additional_notes: Used to say you notice or realize something based on what you observe or learn. Often followed by a full sentence with que.
target_language_example: Je vois que tu as compris.
native_language_example: I see that you understood.

additional_notes: A polite way to say what you want, especially when making a request or ordering something. It is softer and more courteous than je veux (“i want”). Literally, it is based on vouloir (“to want”) in the conditional.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like a coffee, please.

additional_notes: From the imperfect form of vouloir. It often expresses a past wish or intention, and can also sound softer and more polite than je veux when introducing a request or reason for speaking.
target_language_example: Je voulais te remercier pour ton aide.
native_language_example: I wanted to thank you for your help.

meaning: "I meant" / "what I was trying to say" (literally: "I wanted to say").
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of vouloir (voulais) to soften or qualify what you’re saying. Common when clarifying your meaning, correcting a misunderstanding, or adding precision: « Je voulais dire que… » = “I meant that…” / “What I was trying to say is…”.
target_language_example: Je voulais dire que je viendrai un peu plus tard.
native_language_example: I meant that I’ll come a little later.

meaning: "I wanted to talk to you" / "I meant to talk to you."
additional_notes: Common opener to introduce a topic you want to discuss. Uses the imperfect (voulais) to express an intention or something you had in mind (often polite/soft). Often followed by a topic: « Je voulais te parler de… » (I wanted to talk to you about…).
target_language_example: Je voulais te parler de demain : tu es libre ?
native_language_example: I wanted to talk to you about tomorrow—are you free?

additional_notes: je means "I" and vous means "you". vous can refer to one person formally or to several people. In French, object pronouns like vous usually come before the verb: je vous conseille = "I advise you," je vous parle = "I speak to you."
target_language_example: Je vous appelle ce soir.
native_language_example: I'll call you tonight.

additional_notes: A common sentence starter in the passé composé. It means "I" + a completed past action + "you." The word "vous" can mean one person formally or several people, and in English it may come out as "you," "for you," or "to you" depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Je vous ai laissé un message.
native_language_example: I left you a message.

meaning: I brought you (formal/plural) / I've brought you.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "apporter" (to bring) in the passé composé: "j'ai apporté" = I brought / I have brought. "Vous" can mean "you" (formal singular) or "you" (plural). Often followed by a direct object: "Je vous ai apporté de l'eau" (I brought you some water).
target_language_example: Je vous ai apporté votre commande.
native_language_example: I brought you your order.

additional_notes: Used to remind or insist that you previously gave an instruction. "Vous" is either formal "you" (one person) or plural "you" (several people). It’s followed by an infinitive verb (de + infinitive): "Je vous ai dit de vous asseoir". In speech, the negative is: "Je ne vous ai pas dit de …".
target_language_example: Je vous ai dit de fermer la porte.
native_language_example: I told you to close the door.

meaning: "I made you / I had you" (do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive after it: « je vous ai fait + infinitif » expresses the causative idea of causing/forcing/arranging for someone to do something (e.g., « Je vous ai fait marcher… » = I made you walk). « vous » is the object pronoun (“you” formal/plural). In speech it can also imply “let you” depending on context.
target_language_example: Je vous ai fait attendre dix minutes, désolé.
native_language_example: I made you wait ten minutes, sorry.

additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of voir: « j’ai vu » (“I saw / I’ve seen”). « vous » is used for one person in a formal/polite situation or for more than one person (“you all”). « vu » can agree in gender/number in some cases (e.g., « Je vous ai vue » to a woman; « Je vous ai vus/vues » for several people), but « vu » is often seen as the default form.
target_language_example: Je vous ai vu à la réunion ce matin.
native_language_example: I saw you at the meeting this morning.

meaning: 'I saw you' / 'I’ve seen you' (addressing 'you' as a woman, or a group with at least one woman).
additional_notes: "Vous" is the formal 'you' (one person) or 'you all' (plural). In the passé composé, the past participle of "voir" is "vu". It becomes "vue" when the direct object pronoun (vous) comes before the verb and refers to a feminine person (or feminine/mixed plural). If you're addressing a man (singular), you would say: "Je vous ai vu."
target_language_example: Je vous ai vue hier au restaurant.
native_language_example: I saw you yesterday at the restaurant.

additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of voir: "j’ai vu" = "I saw / I have seen." "Vous" can mean "you" (formal singular) or "you" (plural). Because "vous" is the direct object and it comes before the verb, the past participle can agree: "vus" (masculine plural or mixed group) / "vues" (feminine plural). With one person (formal singular), you’ll often see "je vous ai vu" (to a man) or "je vous ai vue" (to a woman).
target_language_example: Je vous ai vus tous les deux à la sortie du cinéma.
native_language_example: I saw both of you when you came out of the movie theater.

additional_notes: Used with vous to address one person formally (polite/distant, e.g., someone you don’t use tu with) or to say “I love you” to more than one person (“I love you all / both”). For “I love you” to one person informally, use Je t’aime. In French, Je vous aime can be romantic in formal contexts, but it’s also common for family/close relationships when speaking to a group.
target_language_example: Je vous aime tous, merci d’être là.
native_language_example: I love you all, thank you for being here.

additional_notes: Used to insist on what you’re saying or to introduce what comes next. The pronoun "vous" (to you) comes before the verb: "Je vous dis que..." (I’m telling you that...), "Je vous dis de..." (I’m telling you to...). It can also be used in set phrases like "Je vous dis au revoir" (I say goodbye to you).
target_language_example: Je vous dis la vérité.
native_language_example: I’m telling you the truth.

additional_notes: Used when you owe someone money (often said to a cashier/server: « Je vous dois combien ? » / « Combien je vous dois ? ») or when you owe something more figurative (an explanation, a favor, gratitude). It’s typically followed by an amount (« Je vous dois 12 euros ») or a noun (« Je vous dois une explication »).
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide, je vous dois une explication.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help, I owe you an explanation.

meaning: “I give you” / “I’m giving you” (formal or plural “you”).
additional_notes: Used when handing something to someone or granting something (e.g., permission). “Vous” is used for one person formally or for more than one person. In the past or future you’ll see the same pattern with other tenses: « Je vous ai donné… » (I gave you…), « Je vous donnerai… » (I will give you…).
target_language_example: Je vous donne ce document tout de suite.
native_language_example: I’m giving you this document right away.

additional_notes: Often used as a polite, formal way to say “please” when asking or urging someone to do something (often like “please, do…” or “please, come in”). It can also be used after someone thanks you to mean “you’re welcome” (literally closer to “I beg you / don’t mention it”).
target_language_example: Asseyez-vous, je vous en prie.
native_language_example: Please have a seat.

meaning: I beg you / I implore you.
additional_notes: A very strong, polite way to plead with someone (formal/polite because of "vous"). Used to express urgency or desperation, often at the beginning or end of a sentence. You can also say "je t’en supplie" when speaking informally to one person you know well.
target_language_example: Je vous en supplie, aidez-moi !
native_language_example: I beg you, help me!

additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of *dire* (to say/tell): *j’ai dit*. *vous* is formal “you” or plural “you (all)”. *l’* (“it”) refers to what was said before (the thing you told them). Often used to insist or remind someone: “I told you (already) / I told you so.”
target_language_example: Je vous l'ai dit, je ne peux pas venir demain.
native_language_example: I told you, I can’t come tomorrow.

meaning: “I’ll leave you” / “I’ll let you …” / “I’ll leave (something) with you.”
additional_notes:
Common, polite phrase with several uses depending on what follows:
- To end a conversation: « Faut que je vous laisse. » = “I have to go / I’ll let you go.”
- To allow someone to do something: « Je vous laisse décider. » = “I’ll let you decide.”
- To leave something with someone: « Je vous laisse ma carte. » = “I’ll leave you my card.”
- To give time or privacy: « Je vous laisse un moment. » / « Je vous laisse seule. » = “I’ll leave you for a moment / I’ll leave you alone.”
target_language_example: Bon, je vous laisse. À tout à l’heure.
native_language_example: Well, I’ll let you go. See you later.

additional_notes: Future tense of dire (“to tell/say”). Je = I, vous = you (formal or plural), le = it (the thing you’re talking about). Often used to postpone giving information: “later / in a moment / in two months.” Can also sound like a promise or condition (“Let me go and I’ll tell you”).
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas : je vous le dirai dès que je saurai la vérité.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll tell you as soon as I know the truth.

additional_notes: Very polite, somewhat formal way to soften a request or instruction, often placed at the end of a sentence (like “..., please.”). It can feel old-fashioned or very courteous in everyday speech; in many situations, "s’il vous plaît" is more common. Also appears in set phrases like "je vous en prie" (“you’re welcome” / “please, go ahead”).
target_language_example: Fermez la porte, je vous prie.
native_language_example: Close the door, please.

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to make a request, often used in official speech, letters, announcements, or serious contexts. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « Je vous prie de + infinitive » (e.g., « Je vous prie de patienter »). In everyday conversation, people more often say « s’il vous plaît » or « je vous demande de ».
target_language_example: Je vous prie de bien vouloir fermer la porte.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

meaning: “I present to you / I offer you / let me introduce…” (formal).
additional_notes: Used in polite/formal situations with **vous**. Common patterns: **Je vous présente mes condoléances** (“Please accept my condolences”), **Je vous présente mes excuses** (“I apologize”), and **Je vous présente [quelqu’un]** (“Let me introduce [someone]”). You can also say **Permettez que je vous présente…** (“Allow me to introduce…”).
target_language_example: Je vous présente mon collègue, Paul.
native_language_example: Let me introduce my colleague, Paul.

additional_notes: Uses the formal/polite object pronoun vous (“you” singular formal or plural). Often followed by de + infinitive to thank someone for doing something (Je vous remercie d’être venu), or de/pour + noun to thank for something (Je vous remercie de votre aide / pour votre aide). Can be strengthened with Du fond du cœur (“from the bottom of my heart”) and can address a group (Je vous remercie tous).
target_language_example: Je vous remercie pour votre aide.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help.

additional_notes: Used to express good wishes to one or more people, or to someone you address formally (vous). It’s commonly followed by a noun phrase like bon voyage, bonne chance, une bonne journée/soirée, or something like tout le bonheur du monde. With an infinitive, it can also mean “I hope you will…” (e.g., Je vous souhaite de réussir).
target_language_example: Je vous souhaite un bon séjour en France.
native_language_example: I wish you a nice stay in France.

meaning: to take a quick look (at); to glance (at).
additional_notes: Very common fixed expression meaning “to glance.” Typically followed by "à" + something: "jeter un coup d’œil à". You’ll often see it written without the ligature in plain text: "un coup d'oeil". Note the elision: "coup d’" before a vowel ("œil").
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un coup d' œil à mon message ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at my message?

meaning: To take a quick look; to have a glance.
additional_notes: A very common, neutral expression for looking briefly at something (a document, a screen, an item in a store, etc.). Often used to ask permission politely: « Je peux jeter un coup d'oeil ? » / « Vous voulez jeter un coup d'oeil ? ». You can also say « jeter un coup d'oeil à + noun » (e.g., « jeter un coup d'oeil à ce dossier »).
target_language_example: Je peux jeter un coup d'oeil ?
native_language_example: Can I take a quick look?

meaning: to take a quick look (to have a look).
additional_notes: Very common, informal-neutral expression meaning to look briefly at something. Often used as a suggestion or invitation: "Tu peux jeter un coup d'œil ?" (Can you take a look?). You can add what you’re looking at with "à": "jeter un coup d'œil à ce document".
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un coup d'œil à mon CV ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at my résumé?

meaning: to take a look; to have a quick look.
additional_notes: Common, everyday expression meaning to look at something briefly (often as a favor or to check something). Usually used with "à": "jeter un oeil à" + thing/person. Conjugates like "jeter" (je jette, tu jettes, il/elle jette). Often written with the ligature: "jeter un œil".
target_language_example: Je peux jeter un oeil à ton CV ce soir.
native_language_example: I can take a look at your résumé tonight.

meaning: to take a quick look; to have a look.
additional_notes: A very common, friendly way to ask or suggest looking at something briefly (e.g., a document, a message, a problem). Often used with a pronoun object: « jeter un œil à … » (jeter un œil à ce fichier / à ton téléphone).
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un œil à ce mail, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at this email, please?

additional_notes: Common, casual way to ask someone to look at something briefly (most often as an imperative: « Jette un œil ! », « Jette un œil là-dessus. »). It implies a quick glance, not a long, careful examination. Note: the same idiom also appears in other forms like « jeter un œil » (infinitive) or « je jette un œil » (present tense).
target_language_example: Jette un œil à mon devoir avant que je l’envoie.
native_language_example: Take a quick look at my homework before I send it.

meaning: a piece of cake; very easy.
additional_notes: Used (often with « C’est / Ça va être… ») to say something is very easy to do. Literally “a child’s game.” Common in present, past, or future: « C’était… », « Ce sera… ».
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : avec un bon plan, ce sera un jeu d'enfant.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: with a good plan, it’ll be a piece of cake.

meaning: a deck of cards (a pack of playing cards).
additional_notes: Used for the set of playing cards you use for card games. In everyday speech, it most often means the whole deck (not a single card). You can also say "un paquet de cartes" for "a pack/deck of cards."
target_language_example: On a acheté un jeu de cartes pour jouer au poker.
native_language_example: We bought a deck of cards to play poker.

meaning: a pun; a play on words.
additional_notes: Used when someone makes a word-based joke (often with a double meaning or similar sounds). You can comment on it with “C’est un jeu de mots.” To say you’re not intending one: “Sans jeu de mots.” To apologize for a possibly bad one: “Sans mauvais jeu de mots.”
target_language_example: Désolé, c’était un jeu de mots !
native_language_example: Sorry, that was a pun!

additional_notes: Usually masculine: un jeu vidéo. Plural: des jeux vidéo. Often followed by specifics like en ligne (online) or the genre/platform. Common related phrases: joueur/joueuse de jeu vidéo (video game player).
target_language_example: Fortnite est un célèbre jeu vidéo en ligne.
native_language_example: Fortnite is a famous online video game.

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to refer to a woman (often roughly in her late teens to early 30s) when you don’t know her name or want to describe her by age. It’s often used with an article (une/la jeune femme). The adjective usually comes before the noun here: jeune + femme.
target_language_example: Une jeune femme m’a demandé son chemin dans la rue.
native_language_example: A young woman asked me for directions in the street.

meaning: a young girl; (often) a young woman.
additional_notes: Literally “young girl.” Used to refer to a female person who is young (teen to young adult). It can sound old-fashioned or a bit patronizing if used to address an adult woman directly (“Jeune fille !”, “Merci, jeune fille.”). Also note the different meaning in “ma plus jeune fille” = “my youngest daughter” (comparative of jeune).
target_language_example: Qui est cette jeune fille ?
native_language_example: Who is that young woman?

additional_notes: Means a male person who is young (roughly a teenager or young adult). Often used with an article (un jeune homme) to describe someone, or as a direct form of address (Jeune homme !) in a polite but slightly formal tone.
target_language_example: Ce jeune homme cherche son téléphone.
native_language_example: That young man is looking for his phone.

additional_notes: Literally “young married (man)”. Used for a man who has just gotten married. The feminine form is « jeune mariée » (newlywed wife), and the plural « les jeunes mariés » often refers to the newlywed couple.
target_language_example: Le jeune marié a remercié tous les invités.
native_language_example: The groom thanked all the guests.

meaning: young people (young men; or youths in general).
additional_notes: A somewhat formal way to refer to young people as a group. Grammatically masculine plural, but it can be used generically (mixed group). Often appears with an article: « les jeunes gens » (the young people) or « ces jeunes gens » (these young people).
target_language_example: Ces jeunes gens cherchent du travail.
native_language_example: These young people are looking for work.

additional_notes: An idiom used when someone has difficulty covering basic expenses with the money they have. Often used with “avoir du mal à…” (to have trouble) or “essayer de…” (to try).
target_language_example: Depuis qu'il a perdu son travail, il a du mal à joindre les deux bouts.
native_language_example: Since he lost his job, he’s having trouble making ends meet.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "jouer à" + a sport/game. With "golf" it becomes "jouer au golf" (à + le = au). Conjugation changes with the subject (e.g., je joue, tu joues, il/elle joue, nous jouons).
target_language_example: Le week-end, elle joue au golf avec ses amis.
native_language_example: On weekends, she plays golf with her friends.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **jouer à** + a sport/game. With **tennis** (masculine), it contracts to **au** (= à + le): **jouer au tennis**. Conjugation: **je joue**, **tu joues**, **il/elle joue**, **nous jouons**, **vous jouez**, **ils/elles jouent**.
target_language_example: Mon frère joue au tennis le week-end.
native_language_example: My brother plays tennis on the weekend.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **jouer de** + an instrument: *jouer de la guitare / du piano / du violon*. With a person, you conjugate **jouer**: *je joue, tu joues, il/elle joue, nous jouons...* To ask “Who plays the guitar?”, say: *Qui joue de la guitare ?*
target_language_example: Elle joue de la guitare tous les soirs.
native_language_example: She plays the guitar every evening.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "jouer" + "de" + an instrument: "jouer du piano" (piano), "jouer de la guitare" (guitar). The form "joue" is the present tense for il/elle/on; for "I play the piano" you say "je joue du piano".
target_language_example: Mon frère joue du piano depuis cinq ans.
native_language_example: My brother has been playing the piano for five years.

additional_notes: Used with the verb jouer + à + the sport: jouer au football, jouer au tennis, jouer au basket. In many French-speaking contexts, football means “soccer” (not American football).
target_language_example: On va jouer au football après l'école.
native_language_example: We’re going to play soccer after school.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the activity/sport. With sports and games in French, you usually say "jouer à" + the sport/game, which contracts to "jouer au" before a masculine singular noun like "tennis" (à + le = au).
target_language_example: On peut jouer au tennis après le travail ?
native_language_example: Can we play tennis after work?

additional_notes: Used to talk about playing card games in general (e.g., poker, bridge, etc.). With games you use "jouer à"; here it becomes "jouer aux" because "les cartes" is plural (à + les = aux).
target_language_example: Je veux jouer aux cartes.
native_language_example: I want to play cards.

additional_notes: Used with "jouer à" + a game/sport. "Aux" = "à + les" because "échecs" is plural. Examples: "Je sais jouer aux échecs" (I know how to play chess) and "Je joue aux échecs" (I play chess / I’m playing chess).
target_language_example:
Savez-vous jouer aux échecs
?
native_language_example: Do you know how to play chess?

additional_notes: Used to invite someone to play (a game, with toys, etc.). Depending on tone/context, it can also mean “Are you messing with me / kidding me?” especially in questions like « Tu es en train de jouer avec moi ? » or « Tu croyais jouer avec moi ? ». With a child or friendly situation, it’s usually literal.
target_language_example: Tu veux venir jouer avec moi après l’école ?
native_language_example: Do you want to come play with me after school?

additional_notes: Used with musical instruments: you say « jouer de » + the instrument (e.g., jouer du piano, jouer de la batterie). In questions, you can invert the verb: « Savez-vous jouer de la guitare ? »
target_language_example: Il sait jouer de la guitare.
native_language_example: He knows how to play the guitar.

meaning: to play tricks (on someone); to prank someone.
additional_notes: Means to prank or trick someone, usually in a playful way (though it can be annoying). Common pattern: « jouer des tours à quelqu’un » (to play tricks on someone) or with an indirect pronoun: « me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur jouer des tours ». Example imperative: « Arrête de me jouer des tours ! » = “Stop playing tricks on me!”
target_language_example: Arrête de me jouer des tours !
native_language_example: Stop playing tricks on me!

additional_notes: Used with musical instruments: jouer + de/du/de la/de l’ + instrument. Here it’s "du" because "piano" is masculine singular (de + le = du). You can also use it after verbs like apprendre à ("learn to") or pouvoir ("can").
target_language_example: J'aime jouer du piano après le travail.
native_language_example: I like to play the piano after work.

meaning: to play along; to cooperate (do what’s expected).
additional_notes: Used when someone agrees to go along with rules, a plan, or a situation (sometimes even if they don’t really like it). Can also mean to act fairly or honestly in a negotiation or competition. Often used with “Je vais/On va jouer le jeu” (“I’ll/We’ll play along”).
target_language_example: D’accord, je vais jouer le jeu et suivre les règles.
native_language_example: Okay, I’ll play along and follow the rules.

meaning: day after day; day by day.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize something happening repeatedly or gradually over time (often a change that continues little by little). It can be placed at the start of a sentence ("Jour après jour, ...") or after the verb.
target_language_example: Jour après jour, elle reprend confiance.
native_language_example: Day by day, she's regaining confidence.

additional_notes: Used to talk about which weekday it is (lundi, mardi, mercredi, etc.) or to ask for it: « On est quel jour de la semaine ? ». You’ll often see it with numbers or order: « le premier/deuxième/troisième jour de la semaine ».
target_language_example: Le mardi est le deuxième jour de la semaine.
native_language_example: Tuesday is the second day of the week.

meaning: day and night; all the time (continuously).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens continuously, without stopping. Often with verbs like travailler (to work), vivre (to live), surveiller/espionner (to watch/spy on). It can be literal (daytime and nighttime) or more generally mean “24/7.”
target_language_example: Il étudie jour et nuit pour son examen.
native_language_example: He studies day and night for his exam.

meaning: a public holiday (a day off officially recognized).
additional_notes: Used to talk about an official holiday when many businesses, schools, and offices may be closed. Often used with verbs like être ("C’est un jour férié"), tomber ("Le jour férié tombe un lundi"), or to ask about schedules ("C’est férié demain ?").
target_language_example: Lundi, c’est un jour férié, donc la banque est fermée.
native_language_example: Monday is a public holiday, so the bank is closed.

meaning: logbook; record of events/activities (often on a ship or plane).
additional_notes: Used for an official written record kept day by day (e.g., "journal de bord du capitaine" = the captain’s logbook). Can also be used more generally for a personal or project “log” where you note what happened and what you did.
target_language_example: Le capitaine a noté l’incident dans le journal de bord.
native_language_example: The captain noted the incident in the logbook.

additional_notes: A private notebook where someone writes personal thoughts, feelings, and events. Often used with verbs like "tenir un journal intime" (to keep a diary) and "écrire dans son journal intime" (to write in one’s diary).
target_language_example: Elle écrit dans son journal intime tous les soirs.
native_language_example: She writes in her diary every evening.

additional_notes: Refers to the scheduled news program on TV (often at a fixed time, e.g., evening news). You can say "regarder le journal télévisé" (to watch the news) or "passer/être au journal télévisé" (to be shown/on TV news). In France it’s very commonly shortened to "le JT".
target_language_example: On a appris la nouvelle au journal télévisé de 20 heures.
native_language_example: We heard the news on the 8 p.m. TV news.

additional_notes: A common Christmas greeting said on Christmas Day and during the Christmas season. You can use it alone (Joyeux Noël !) or add who you’re addressing with à + person (Joyeux Noël à vous / à ta famille). Use « vous » for formal or plural, and « toi »/a name for informal (Joyeux Noël, papa !).
target_language_example: Joyeux Noël à toi et à ta famille !
native_language_example: Merry Christmas to you and your family!

additional_notes: Used to wish someone a happy birthday. You can say it directly with the person’s name ("Joyeux anniversaire, Marie !") or with "à" + the person ("Joyeux anniversaire à toi !", "… à ta femme !"). You can also use the feminine form "Joyeuse anniversaire", but in practice most people say "Joyeux anniversaire".
target_language_example: Joyeux anniversaire, papa !
native_language_example: Happy birthday, Dad!

meaning: all the way; to the end (to see something through).
additional_notes: Often used to express determination to continue and finish something, even if it’s difficult: "aller jusqu'au bout" = to go all the way / not give up. Can be used alone as a short, motivational phrase ("Jusqu'au bout." = "All the way." / "To the end.").
target_language_example: On a commencé ce projet, alors on ira jusqu'au bout.
native_language_example: We started this project, so we’ll see it through to the end.

additional_notes: Used to mark an end point in time (jusqu'à lundi, jusqu'à demain), or a limit/endpoint more generally (jusqu'à la fin). It can also mean “as far as” with places (jusqu'à Paris). Before a clause, it’s usually "jusqu'à ce que" + subjunctive: "jusqu'à ce qu'on vous relève" (“until someone relieves you”).
target_language_example: Attendez ici jusqu'à ce que je revienne.
native_language_example: Wait here until I come back.

additional_notes: Introduces a time limit that lasts up to the moment an event occurs. It’s followed by a verb (often in the subjunctive): « jusqu’à ce que ce soit fini » (until it’s finished). Often used with commands/instructions: « Reste ici jusqu’à ce que je t’appelle. »
target_language_example: Attends ici jusqu'à ce que je revienne.
native_language_example: Wait here until I come back.

meaning: until then; up to that point; that far.
additional_notes: Used for time ("up to then") or distance/extent ("that far"). Often placed at the start of a sentence to mean "up to that point" (Jusque-là, ...). Can also be used alone as an exclamation meaning something like "Up to there!/So far!" depending on context.
target_language_example: Jusque-là, tout allait bien, puis il a commencé à pleuvoir.
native_language_example: Up to that point, everything was going well, then it started to rain.

meaning: up to then; until then; up to there (that point).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a limit or endpoint in time ("until then" / "up to that time") or in space/extent ("up to there" / "up to that point"). Often refers to a specific moment, distance, or level that’s understood from context (e.g., food won’t last until then; hair was long up to that point on the body).
target_language_example: On peut marcher jusque là, mais pas plus loin.
native_language_example: We can walk up to there, but not farther.

additional_notes: Used to point out a precise location. Often said while giving directions or showing where something/someone is. Can also imply someone was there a moment ago ("He was just there").
target_language_example: Mets ton sac juste là, près de la porte.
native_language_example: Put your bag right there, near the door.

meaning: just now; right now (at this exact moment).
additional_notes: Often means something happened a moment ago ("just now"), or emphasizes that something is happening at precisely this moment ("right now"), especially when it feels sudden or inconvenient. It can be used as a short standalone reply ("Juste maintenant.") to mean "Just now." / "Right now."
target_language_example: Je suis occupé juste maintenant, je te rappelle dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I’m busy right now; I’ll call you back in five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to wait briefly or to say you only need a very short amount of time. Common with wait/hold on verbs like « attends/attendez ». In questions like « Je peux te parler juste une seconde ? », it softens the request by suggesting it won’t take long (even if it might be a bit longer in practice).
target_language_example: Juste une seconde, je finis ce message.
native_language_example: Just a second, I’m finishing this message.

additional_notes: Contraction of « je » + « ai » (present tense of avoir). Used to talk about possession (j’ai un livre = I have a book) and very often as the auxiliary verb in the passé composé to talk about past actions: « j’ai fait / j’ai attendu / j’ai vu » = “I did / I waited / I saw.”
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mes clés.
native_language_example: I forgot my keys.

meaning: 'I was' / 'I have been' (passé composé of être).
additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the passive voice, especially to say something happened to you: « J’ai été cambriolé / frappé / mordu » = “I was robbed/hit/bitten.” With the passive, the past participle usually agrees with the subject (e.g., « J’ai été cambriolé » masculine; « J’ai été cambriolée » feminine). It can also mean “I went” in some contexts (« J’ai été à Paris » = “I went to Paris”), but in these examples it’s passive “I was…”.
target_language_example: J’ai été blessé au bras.
native_language_example: I was injured in the arm.

additional_notes: Used to say you have/experience something. Often used for health issues (J’ai une bronchite / une douleur), possessions or things you’ve got (J’ai une meilleure image), or a state/condition (J’ai une pêche d’enfer = “I feel great”). If the noun is masculine, use “j’ai un”.
target_language_example: J’ai une question.
native_language_example: I have a question.

additional_notes: From the verb aimer (“to like/love”) in the present tense: j’ + aime (je becomes j’ before a vowel). Use it to say you like something (J’aime le café.), love someone/something (Je t’aime.), or enjoy doing an activity with an infinitive (J’aime voyager.). Often strengthened with adverbs like bien (“quite/pretty much”) or vraiment (“really”).
target_language_example: J’aime bien ce film, mais je préfère le livre.
native_language_example: I quite like this movie, but I prefer the book.

additional_notes: Contraction of « je » + « étais » (imparfait of « être », “to be”). Used to describe a state in the past, background information, or something habitual (“used to”). Often sets the scene rather than describing a single completed action.
target_language_example: Quand j’étais petit, j’étais souvent malade.
native_language_example: When I was little, I was often sick.

additional_notes: Used as a masculine noun in French: "le kung-fu". It commonly refers to Chinese martial arts in general, and by extension to kung-fu movies ("des films de kung-fu").
target_language_example: Il adore les films de kung-fu.
native_language_example: He loves kung-fu movies.

additional_notes: Most often seen in the expression avoir l'air, which means 'to look' or 'to seem.' Avoir l'air + adjective describes how someone or something appears: il a l'air fatigué. With en, it refers back to something already mentioned: tu en as l'air = 'you seem like it.'
target_language_example: Il a l'air fatigué aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: He looks tired today.

additional_notes: Definite form of "amour" (love), used for love in general or a specific love in context. Common in expressions like "de l'amour" (some love) and "Il y a de l'amour dans l'air" (There’s love in the air). Note: "faire l'amour" means "to make love" (to have sex).
target_language_example: Pour moi, l'amour, c'est du respect.
native_language_example: For me, love is respect.

additional_notes: Refers to money in general or a specific sum previously mentioned ("the money"). It is the noun "argent" with the definite article "le"; it becomes "l'" before a vowel sound. Common in set phrases like "pas pour l'argent" ("not for the money").
target_language_example: Tu as pris l'argent ?
native_language_example: Did you take the money?

additional_notes: Used for the time when the sun is just rising. Common in set phrases like « jusqu'à l'aube » (“until dawn”). Figuratively, it can mean “the beginning” of something: « l'aube d'une ère nouvelle » (“the dawn of a new era”).
target_language_example: On partira à l'aube pour éviter la circulation.
native_language_example: We’ll leave at dawn to avoid traffic.

meaning: the other day; recently (a few days ago).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a recent past day without specifying which one. Common when recalling something that happened recently or apologizing (e.g., « Excuse-moi pour l'autre jour »). It can be translated literally as “the other day,” but in practice it often simply means “recently.”
target_language_example: Je voulais m'excuser pour l'autre jour.
native_language_example: I wanted to apologize for the other day.

additional_notes: “L’” is the shortened form of “la” or “le” used before a vowel sound. So “l’eau” = “la eau” (not said) = “the water.” It can mean water in general, water in a specific place (e.g., in a pool/river), or the water you’re talking about in context.
target_language_example: Je vais dans l'eau, elle est chaude.
native_language_example: I'm going into the water; it's warm.

additional_notes: Often used for what you’re thinking about or what comes to you mentally: « venir à l’esprit » = “to come to mind”; « s’occuper l’esprit » = “to keep your mind busy / take your mind off things.” With « l’ » because « esprit » starts with a vowel sound.
target_language_example: C'est ce qui me vient à l'esprit.
native_language_example: That’s what comes to mind.

additional_notes: Used with the definite article (la → l’ before a vowel sound): l’histoire. In everyday conversation, it often means “the story” (what happened, the whole situation): Je connais toute l’histoire = “I know the whole story.” It can also mean “history” as a subject or the past in general: l’histoire de France = “the history of France.”
target_language_example: Tu peux me raconter l'histoire ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me the story?

additional_notes: "L'" is the shortened form of "le" used before a vowel sound (elision), so "l'homme" = "le homme" (not used). It can refer to a specific man ("Est-ce l'homme que vous avez vu ?" = "Is he the man you saw?") or to humans in general ("la santé de l'homme" = "human health").
target_language_example: L'homme que j'ai rencontré hier est médecin.
native_language_example: The man I met yesterday is a doctor.

additional_notes: “L’” is the shortened form of “le” before a vowel sound: l’hôpital. Often used with prepositions like “à l’hôpital” (at/in the hospital) or “de l’hôpital” (from the hospital).
target_language_example: Il est à l'hôpital depuis hier.
native_language_example: He has been in the hospital since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used for orderliness (organization, maintaining order) and for an order as a command. Common phrases: « donner l'ordre » = to give the order; « recevoir l'ordre » = to receive the order; « qui a donné l'ordre ? » = who gave the order? Also used in lists of abstract nouns: « l'ordre et la paix » (order and peace).
target_language_example: Qui a donné l'ordre ?
native_language_example: Who gave the order?

meaning: one after the other; one by one.
additional_notes: Used to describe things happening in sequence (not at the same time). Often follows a verb: Ils entrent l'un après l'autre. You can also say "les uns après les autres" for plural groups (e.g., the students).
target_language_example: Les clients sont entrés l'un après l'autre.
native_language_example: The customers came in one after the other.

meaning: one of them (one of those people/men).
additional_notes: Used to pick out a single person from a group. It agrees with the gender/number of the group: "l'un d'eux" = one of them (masculine or mixed group), "l'une d'elles" = one of them (feminine group). Common after "c'est", "je suis", "tu es" ("It's/I'm/you're one of them").
target_language_example: Je pense que l'un d'eux a menti.
native_language_example: I think one of them lied.

additional_notes: Reciprocal expression used when two people/things do the same action to one another. It often follows a verb (sometimes with a reflexive pronoun like se): Ils se regardent l'un l'autre. For two feminine nouns/people, use l'une l'autre; for more than two, you can also see les uns les autres / les unes les autres.
target_language_example: Ils s'aident l'un l'autre quand ça va mal.
native_language_example: They help each other when things are going badly.

additional_notes: Refers to school as an institution or the place students go. Common in set phrases like "à l'école" (at school), "de l'école" (from school), "rentrer de l'école" (to come home from school), and in questions like "Et l'école ?" (How’s school?/And school?). Also used for school-related things: "le journal de l'école" (the school newspaper).
target_language_example: Je rentre de l'école à cinq heures.
native_language_example: I’m coming home from school at five o’clock.

meaning: said it / told it (him/her/it, depending on context)
additional_notes: "l'" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (or "him/her" depending on what it refers to). "a dit" is the passé composé of "dire" (to say/tell): "a" (has) + "dit" (said). Common patterns: "il l'a dit" = "he said it / he told him/her"; "elle me l'a dit" = "she told me (it)". Word order: subject + object pronoun(s) + a dit.
target_language_example: C'est lui qui l'a dit.
native_language_example: He's the one who said it.

additional_notes: Passé composé of "faire" with the direct object pronoun "l'" (= "it/him/her" depending on context). Often used to confirm that someone carried out an action: "Elle l'a fait" = "She did it." If the object is plural, you’ll see "les a faits/faites" (agreement in writing).
target_language_example: Je ne pensais pas qu'il réussirait, mais il l'a fait.
native_language_example: I didn’t think he would succeed, but he did it.

additional_notes: Common spoken form of "ne ... pas": in casual speech, "ne" is often dropped ("Elle l'a pas dit" = "Elle ne l'a pas dit"). "l'" is the direct object pronoun "le" ("it") before "a". You can add an indirect object pronoun: "Elle me l'a pas dit" = "She didn't tell me (it)". In questions: "Il te l'a pas dit ?" = "He didn't tell you?".
target_language_example: Il te l'a pas dit ?
native_language_example: He didn’t tell you?

meaning: to call him/her/it; to name him/her/it.
additional_notes: "l'" is the direct object pronoun "le" (him/it) or "la" (her/it), shortened before a vowel or silent h. So "l'appeler" means "to call him/her/it" (e.g., on the phone) or "to call/name him/her/it" (i.e., what you will name something). The verb tense changes the meaning in time: "je dois l'appeler" (I have to call him/her), "je vais l'appeler" (I’m going to call him/her).
target_language_example: Je vais l'appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to call him/her tonight.

additional_notes: Here l' is the shortened form of le, used as a neutral pronoun to refer back to an adjective or noun phrase already mentioned. For example, Tu es prêt ? Je vais l'être. In English, this is often translated with just 'be' or 'be one' rather than a separate word like 'so'.
target_language_example: Tu n'es pas encore prêt, mais tu vas l'être bientôt.
native_language_example: You're not ready yet, but you will be soon.

additional_notes: “La pêche” most often means the activity of fishing (especially in phrases like “aller à la pêche” = to go fishing). It can also mean the fruit “a peach” in food contexts. Context usually makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Dimanche, on va à la pêche.
native_language_example: On Sunday, we're going fishing.

meaning: "the fourth wife" (a specific wife, identified by her rank/number).
additional_notes: Uses the ordinal number « quatrième » (fourth) with a feminine noun « épouse » (wife). In context it can function like a title or label for a person; the capitalization (« Quatrième ») suggests a specific character or role (e.g., in a story).
target_language_example: Je dois parler à la Quatrième épouse.
native_language_example: I have to talk to the fourth wife.

additional_notes: Refers to a female monarch (a queen regnant) or the wife of a king (queen consort). Often used with set phrases like « Vive la Reine ! » (“Long live the Queen!”) or « Que Dieu sauve/protège la Reine ! » (“God save/protect the Queen!”). Capitalizing « Reine » is common when talking about a specific queen as a title.
target_language_example: La Reine arrive au palais ce soir.
native_language_example: The Queen is arriving at the palace tonight.

additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: in sports/play it’s a ball ("Lance la balle !"); with weapons/shooting it can mean a bullet ("La balle atteignit sa cible"). Often used as "une balle" (a ball / a bullet).
target_language_example: La balle a rebondi contre le mur.
native_language_example: The ball bounced off the wall.

meaning: the battle; a fight (often a war battle).
additional_notes: Usually refers to a specific battle (often in war/history), but it can also be used more generally for a major fight or struggle. Common with verbs like gagner/perdre (to win/lose) and expressions like lors de la bataille (during the battle). In French you normally keep the article: la bataille.
target_language_example: Ils ont perdu la bataille, mais pas la guerre.
native_language_example: They lost the battle, but not the war.

additional_notes: Means a public or school/university place where you can read, study, or borrow books. Note: in French, "une bibliothèque" can also mean a bookcase/bookshelf (a piece of furniture), but in these examples it clearly means "library" as a building/place.
target_language_example: Je vais à la bibliothèque pour étudier.
native_language_example: I'm going to the library to study.

additional_notes: A common drink noun; feminine singular (la). You can also say: une bière (a beer), de la bière (some beer). In restaurants/bars you might order: « Je voudrais la bière, s’il vous plaît. » (if a specific beer has been chosen/pointed out).
target_language_example: Les Allemands adorent la bière et les saucisses.
native_language_example: Germans love beer and sausages.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to mean “the right/correct” one: la bonne direction (the right direction), la bonne réponse (the correct answer), la bonne chose à faire (the right thing to do). It agrees with the noun’s gender/number: le bon (masc. sing.), la bonne (fem. sing.), les bons / les bonnes (plural).
target_language_example: Je crois que c’est la bonne solution.
native_language_example: I think it’s the right solution.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific piece of positive news. Very common with verbs like annoncer (to announce), dire (to tell), and apprendre (to learn/hear). Often followed by a clause introduced by que: « la bonne nouvelle, c’est que… ».
target_language_example: Marie a appelé sa mère pour lui annoncer la bonne nouvelle.
native_language_example: Marie called her mother to announce the good news.

additional_notes: Used when talking about answering a question (quiz, test, interview, etc.). Often follows verbs like "c'est" (it’s), "choisir" (to choose), and "deviner" (to guess). Feminine singular: "la" + "bonne" + "réponse".
target_language_example: Si tu hésites, relis la question et choisis la bonne réponse.
native_language_example: If you’re hesitating, reread the question and choose the correct answer.

additional_notes: Used for the physical mouth (speaking, eating, kissing): « sur la bouche » = on the mouth/lips. Common expressions include « avoir la bouche sèche » (to have a dry mouth) and the idiom « Vous m’enlevez les mots de la bouche » (“You took the words right out of my mouth,” i.e., you said exactly what I was about to say).
target_language_example: Ouvre la bouche, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Open your mouth, please.

additional_notes: Refers to a bottle/container for liquids (milk, water, wine, etc.). Often used with "dans" (in the bottle) or in phrases like "cacher la bouteille" (hide the bottle, sometimes implying alcohol). Plural: "les bouteilles".
target_language_example: Il reste un peu de lait dans la bouteille.
native_language_example: There’s a bit of milk left in the bottle.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a box or container you can open/close (e.g., a cardboard box, a tin). In other contexts, "une boîte" can also mean a company (informal) or a nightclub (informal), but those meanings depend on context. Common related phrase: "la boîte aux lettres" = the mailbox.
target_language_example: J'ai mis les clés dans la boîte.
native_language_example: I put the keys in the box.

additional_notes: La caisse can mean a physical container (a box/crate) that you can carry and put things in (e.g., books). In shops/supermarkets, la caisse is the checkout area/cash register, so faire la queue devant la caisse means “to line up at the checkout.” Context usually makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la caisse, j’ai oublié mon porte-monnaie.
native_language_example: Meet me at the checkout; I forgot my wallet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about rural places (fields, villages, farms), often in contrast with the city (la ville). With prepositions you’ll often hear: « à la campagne » = in the countryside; « de la campagne » = from the countryside / rural.
target_language_example: Le week-end, on va souvent à la campagne pour se reposer.
native_language_example: On weekends, we often go to the countryside to rest.

additional_notes: Used for a device that records photos or video (a real camera, a phone camera, or a video/TV camera). Common with verbs like allumer/éteindre (turn on/off) or couper (cut/turn off), and in expressions like à travers la caméra (“through the camera”). Feminine noun: la caméra.
target_language_example: Tu peux allumer la caméra, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you turn on the camera, please?

additional_notes: Used to name the main city of a country/region. Structure: « la capitale de + [country/region] ». With a feminine country you usually get « de la » (la Finlande), with a masculine country « du » (le Japon), with a plural country « des » (les États-Unis), and with a vowel/h muet « de l’ » (l’Italie).
target_language_example: Bienvenue à Helsinki, la capitale de la Finlande.
native_language_example: Welcome to Helsinki, the capital of Finland.

additional_notes: Used to name a capital city. "du" = "de + le" and is used before masculine singular nouns (often masculine country names like le Japon, le Sénégal, le Burundi). For feminine countries, use "la capitale de la" (ex: la capitale de la France). For plural names, use "la capitale des" (ex: les États-Unis).
target_language_example: La capitale du Canada est Ottawa.
native_language_example: The capital of Canada is Ottawa.

meaning: the card; the menu; the map.
additional_notes: The meaning depends on context. In shops/restaurants, "la carte" often means a payment card ("payer par carte", "accepter la carte"). In restaurants, "la carte" can also mean the menu; "la carte des vins" is the wine list. In other contexts, "la carte" can mean a map (e.g., "une carte routière").
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, on peut avoir la carte, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can we have the menu, please?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "avoir" (J'ai la chair de poule / J'en ai la chair de poule) or "donner" (Ça me donne la chair de poule / Tu me donnes la chair de poule) to express that something makes you get goosebumps.
target_language_example: Quand j'entends cette chanson, j'ai la chair de poule.
native_language_example: When I hear that song, I get goosebumps.

additional_notes: Common word for a (usually simple) chair. Used with prepositions like sur (on), sous (under), and sometimes dans (in) depending on context. Note: English "chaise" usually refers to a lounge chair (as in "chaise longue"), so it can be misleading—French "chaise" is typically just a regular chair.
target_language_example: Le sac est sur la chaise.
native_language_example: The bag is on the chair.

meaning: heat; warmth (from the weather, sun, or something hot).
additional_notes: Used to talk about physical heat in general (often the heat of the sun or hot weather): la chaleur du soleil, la chaleur de l’été. It can also describe the warmth given off by something (e.g., a fire) or the warmth of a place (la chaleur de la pièce).
target_language_example: Je n’aime pas trop la chaleur en été.
native_language_example: I don’t really like the heat in summer.

meaning: the bedroom; the room (esp. a hotel room)
additional_notes: Usually means a bedroom in a home/apartment. In hotels, it commonly means “room” (hotel room). If you want to be extra clear about a bedroom, you can also say "la chambre à coucher".
target_language_example: La lumière du soleil illumine la chambre.
native_language_example: The sunlight lights up the bedroom.

additional_notes: Often means “luck” in general (good or bad): « La chance est aveugle. » It can also mean an opportunity you should take: « saisir la chance » = “to seize the opportunity.” Common phrases: « avoir de la chance » (to be lucky), « bonne chance ! » (good luck!).
target_language_example: Tu as de la chance : tu as encore une chance de réussir.
native_language_example: You're lucky: you still have a chance to succeed.

additional_notes: Used for a physical target (shooting, archery, aiming at something) or a figurative one (the goal, or the intended audience in marketing: « la cible » = “target audience”). Often appears with verbs like « viser » (to aim at), « toucher » (to hit), « atteindre » (to reach).
target_language_example: Je n'arrive pas à viser la cible.
native_language_example: I can’t manage to aim at the target.

meaning: traffic; road traffic (the flow of vehicles).
additional_notes: Often refers to how heavy or light traffic is (Il y a de la circulation / la circulation est faible). Used in set phrases like accident de la circulation (traffic accident) and fermé/ouvert à la circulation (closed/open to traffic). Can also mean traffic rules: les règles de la circulation.
target_language_example: À cause de la circulation, on est arrivés en retard.
native_language_example: Because of the traffic, we arrived late.

meaning: the classroom; the class (group of students).
additional_notes: Usually refers either to the physical room where students learn ("dans la classe", "entrer dans la classe") or to the group of students as a whole ("toute la classe", "la classe a été divisée en groupes"). Context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Toute la classe écoute le professeur.
native_language_example: The whole class is listening to the teacher.

additional_notes: Literally the object used to open a lock: « la clé de la porte » (“the key to the door”). It’s also used figuratively to mean the main point/solution: « la clé de cette affaire » (“the key to this case/matter”). Often followed by « de » + noun to say “the key to/for …” (e.g., « la clé du succès »).
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas la clé de la voiture.
native_language_example: I don’t have the car key.

additional_notes: A feminine noun used for a natural rise in the land (smaller than a mountain). Common with verbs like monter (go up), descendre (go down), and grimper (climb): monter/descendre/grimper la colline. Plural: les collines.
target_language_example: Vous devez monter la colline.
native_language_example: You have to go up the hill.

additional_notes:
Common meanings:
- **A business/transport provider**: *la compagnie* can mean a company/firm (e.g., a perfume company, a bus/airline company).
- **People’s presence**: *la compagnie de quelqu’un* = being with someone / someone’s company.
- In greetings, **« Bonsoir, la compagnie ! »** is a friendly way to say “Good evening, everyone!” (addressing the group).
target_language_example: J’aime bien la compagnie, mais je dois rentrer maintenant.
native_language_example: I like the company, but I have to go home now.

additional_notes: Refers to a physical rope or cord. Used with common action verbs like couper (to cut), lâcher (to let go of), attraper/saisir (to grab/hold). Note: in some contexts, "corde" can also mean a string on a musical instrument, but the examples here are about a rope.
target_language_example: Tiens bien la corde !
native_language_example: Hold the rope tight!

meaning: the court (especially a court of law).
additional_notes: In legal contexts, "la cour" refers to the court/judges as an institution (similar to “the court” in English). Depending on context, "la cour" can also mean a courtyard (e.g., "la cour de l’école") or a royal court (historical).
target_language_example: La cour rendra sa décision demain.
native_language_example: The court will deliver its decision tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used for sporting competitions where people (or vehicles) race (running race, bike race, etc.). In everyday speech, it can also mean “the shopping/errands,” but in these examples it clearly means a race (e.g., win the race = remporter/gagner la course; start of the race = le départ de la course).
target_language_example: Elle s'entraîne tous les jours pour la course de dimanche.
native_language_example: She trains every day for Sunday’s race.

additional_notes: Often refers to the room (the kitchen): « Nettoie la cuisine. » It can also mean the activity of cooking, especially in « faire la cuisine » (to do the cooking) or « être à la cuisine » (to be in the kitchen / busy cooking). In restaurants, « fermer la cuisine » means the kitchen stops serving food.
target_language_example: Ce soir, c'est moi qui fais la cuisine.
native_language_example: Tonight, I'm the one doing the cooking.

meaning: the lady (a polite way to refer to a woman).
additional_notes: Used for an adult woman, often to sound polite, respectful, or slightly formal (e.g., to a stranger or customer). In everyday speech it can also sound a bit distant compared to "la femme" (the woman) or "la fille" (the girl).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, la dame au comptoir peut vous aider.
native_language_example: Excuse me, the lady at the counter can help you.

meaning: the date (day/month/year); also a deadline or scheduled day for an event.
additional_notes: Used to talk about when something happens (la date du mariage, la date du voyage) or to ask/check the date (La date ? / Regarde la date.). Common with prepositions: la date de + noun (the date of...), à la date du… (on the date of…).
target_language_example: On doit choisir la date de la réunion.
native_language_example: We have to choose the date of the meeting.

additional_notes: Time expression meaning the most recent time something happened. Often used alone (Je l’ai fait la dernière fois. = I did it last time) or in questions (Quand… la dernière fois ? = When… last time?). In “C’est la dernière fois”, it often means “This is the last time” as a warning/firm decision. You can also use it with a clause: “la dernière fois que + subject + verb” (the last time that…).
target_language_example: Je ne l’ai vu qu’une seule fois, et la dernière fois, c’était en juin.
native_language_example: I only saw him once, and the last time was in June.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the most recent occasion when something happened. Common patterns: "la dernière fois que + verb" (e.g., "la dernière fois que je l’ai vu"), and in questions: "C’était quand la dernière fois que… ?" (= "When was the last time…?"). In the past, French often uses the imperfect in the main clause to set the scene: "C’était la dernière fois que je le voyais."
target_language_example: La dernière fois que je suis venu ici, il pleuvait.
native_language_example: The last time I came here, it was raining.

meaning: the difference (a distinction; what is not the same).
additional_notes: Used to compare two or more things: “voir la différence” = to notice the difference; “Quelle est la différence ?” = What’s the difference? It can also mean a difference in amount (e.g., the price difference).
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas la différence entre ces deux mots.
native_language_example: I don’t know the difference between these two words.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things: « la différence entre A et B ». Common with verbs like « faire la différence entre » (to tell the difference between) or « expliquer la différence entre » (to explain the difference between).
target_language_example: Peux-tu m’expliquer la différence entre « depuis » et « pendant » ?
native_language_example: Can you explain the difference between “depuis” and “pendant”?

additional_notes: Most often refers to a feeling of pain or suffering. Common with verbs like "avoir" (to have): "J’ai une douleur au dos" (I have back pain), "ressentir" (to feel), "apparaître" (to appear), and "partir" (to go away). Can also mean emotional pain: "la douleur de la perte" (the pain of loss).
target_language_example: Après quelques jours, la douleur a diminué.
native_language_example: After a few days, the pain decreased.

meaning: drugs (illegal drugs); drugs as a substance.
additional_notes: Usually refers to illegal narcotics in everyday speech, especially in contexts like trafficking, possession, or addiction. In French, it’s often used as a mass noun ("la drogue"), even when English would say "drugs."
target_language_example: La police a trouvé de la drogue dans la voiture.
native_language_example: The police found drugs in the car.

additional_notes: Refers to your family/relatives or family unit (parents, children, close relatives). Often used in set phrases like «dans la famille» (“in the family”). «Famille» is also used in expressions about family support/benefits (e.g., «aide à la famille»).
target_language_example: Je vais passer le week-end avec la famille.
native_language_example: I’m going to spend the weekend with the family.

additional_notes: Usually means "the woman." In context, especially in phrases like "la femme de...", it can also mean "the wife of...".
target_language_example: La femme de Marc travaille ici.
native_language_example: Marc's wife works here.

additional_notes: Includes the definite article la, so it refers to a specific window. In context, it can also appear in expressions like à la fenêtre, meaning 'at the window'.
target_language_example: La fenêtre est fermée.
native_language_example: The window is closed.

additional_notes: Literally “the open window,” but it’s often used after a verb like laisser (“to leave”) or dormir (“to sleep”) to mean someone left the window open while doing something: dormir la fenêtre ouverte = sleep with the window open. Agree with the noun: la fenêtre ouverte (fem.), la porte ouverte; les fenêtres ouvertes (plural).
target_language_example: Je dors souvent la fenêtre ouverte en été.
native_language_example: I often sleep with the window open in summer.

additional_notes:
Most commonly, **la ferme** is the noun phrase “the farm” (a place with animals/crops): *Les chevaux sont dans la ferme.*

As an interjection, **La ferme !** is an informal, rude way to tell someone to be quiet (like “Shut it!” / “Shut up!”). It’s often said on its own or followed by a name: *La ferme, Malefoy.*
target_language_example: La ferme ! J’essaie de dormir.
native_language_example: Shut up! I’m trying to sleep.

additional_notes: Can mean either 'girl' or 'daughter' depending on context. In family expressions like la fille de mon frère or la fille de votre père, it means 'daughter'; otherwise it often means 'girl'.
target_language_example: La fille de Paul habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: Paul's daughter lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: Means “the end” of something (a story, a movie, a line, an event, a period of time). Common patterns: “à la fin” = “at the end / in the end”; “jusqu’à la fin” = “until the end”; “la fin de …” = “the end of …”. In phrases like “Le meilleur pour la fin”, it means “save the best for last.”
target_language_example: Je garde le dessert pour la fin.
native_language_example: I’m saving dessert for last.

meaning: 'the end of' (a period, event, or thing).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to mark the ending point of something: *la fin de la journée* (end of the day), *la fin de l'année* (end of the year). Often followed by an article: *la fin du* (de + le) and *la fin des* (de + les). Can also be used in a dramatic sense: *la fin de tout* (“the end of everything”).
target_language_example: On se voit à la fin de la semaine.
native_language_example: See you at the end of the week.

meaning: “the end of the world.” (often: “it’s not the end of the world!” / “it’s a disaster!”)
additional_notes: Literal meaning: the apocalypse/end of the world. Very commonly used figuratively to exaggerate how bad a situation feels (“C’est la fin du monde !”), or in questions to downplay something (“Est-ce la fin du monde ?” = “Is it really that bad?”). You may also see it used literally in jokes or dramatic statements (“La fin du monde approche.”).
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas la fin du monde si on arrive en retard.
native_language_example: It’s not the end of the world if we arrive late.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like: **avoir la foi** (to have faith), **garder la foi** (to keep faith / keep believing), **perdre la foi** (to lose faith). It can refer to religious faith or more generally to trusting in something/someone.
target_language_example: Même quand c’est difficile, j’essaie de garder la foi.
native_language_example: Even when it’s hard, I try to keep the faith.

additional_notes: Used for physical strength (la force maximale), inner strength (la force du cœur), or the use of force/violence (utiliser la force). It can also describe the intensity or magnitude of something like an earthquake (la force du tremblement de terre). In pop culture, « Que la force soit avec toi » means “May the Force be with you.”
target_language_example: Il a utilisé la force pour ouvrir la porte.
native_language_example: He used force to open the door.

additional_notes: Means a forest/woods (a large area covered with trees). It’s a feminine noun, usually used with an article: "la forêt" (the forest), "une forêt" (a forest). Often appears with prepositions like "dans la forêt" (in the forest), "derrière la forêt" (behind the forest).
target_language_example: On se promène dans la forêt après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: We go for a walk in the forest after lunch.

meaning: the crowd; a mass of people.
additional_notes: Refers to a large group of people gathered in the same place (e.g., at a concert, in the street). It’s grammatically singular in French (la foule est…), even though it describes many people. Common verbs: applaudir (applaud), crier (shout), contrôler (control), se frayer un passage dans la foule (push through the crowd).
target_language_example: Il y avait tellement de monde que je me suis perdu dans la foule.
native_language_example: There were so many people that I got lost in the crowd.

additional_notes: Used for an official boundary between countries or regions. Common with verbs like "traverser" (to cross) and in phrases like "à la frontière" (at the border) and "la frontière entre X et Y" (the border between X and Y).
target_language_example: On a attendu une heure à la frontière.
native_language_example: We waited an hour at the border.

additional_notes: Refers to a social event or celebration. Depending on context, fête can also mean a festival or holiday celebration, but in these examples it means an event that takes place and then ends.
target_language_example: La fête commence à huit heures.
native_language_example: The party starts at eight o'clock.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a train station (often "la gare" or "la gare SNCF"). Common in directions with prepositions like "près de" (near), "en face de" (opposite/across from), and "pour" (to/for) + a destination.
target_language_example: On se retrouve devant la gare à 18 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet in front of the station at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: “La glace” can mean frozen water (ice) or ice cream; context makes it clear. With verbs like “fondre” (to melt), “céder / se rompre” (to give way / break), it means ice. With flavors (“au chocolat”, “à la vanille”) or verbs like “aimer / manger”, it usually means ice cream. Related: “un glaçon” = an ice cube.
target_language_example: Attention, la glace est fine ici.
native_language_example: Careful, the ice is thin here.

additional_notes: Can refer to war in general or to a specific war, depending on context. French often uses the definite article where English may simply say "war" in a general sense.
target_language_example: La guerre n'est jamais une solution.
native_language_example: War is never a solution.

meaning: slang/vulgar for “mouth” or “face” (often in insults or set expressions).
additional_notes: Very informal and often rude. Literally refers to an animal’s mouth/jaw, but in everyday slang it can mean a person’s mouth or face. Common in fixed phrases like « casser la gueule (à quelqu’un) » = “to beat someone up” and « se saouler la gueule » = “to get really drunk.” Not used in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Si tu cries, je te casse la gueule.
native_language_example: If you shout, I’ll beat you up.

additional_notes: Usually means “shame” (a painful feeling of being dishonored or humiliated), often used with de ("la honte de..." = "the shame of..."). It can also be an exclamation in everyday speech: "La honte !" = "How embarrassing!" / "So lame!" In informal French you may hear "foutre la honte (à quelqu’un)" = "to embarrass someone" / "to make someone look bad."
target_language_example: J’ai dit son nom de travers devant tout le monde… la honte !
native_language_example: I said his name wrong in front of everyone… so embarrassing!

additional_notes: Refers to a person’s leg. Common with body-related phrases: « à la jambe » (in the leg, e.g., injured), « le long de la jambe » (along the leg), and in instructions like « Lève la jambe » (Lift your leg).
target_language_example: J’ai mal à la jambe depuis hier.
native_language_example: My leg has been hurting since yesterday.

additional_notes: Literally “the young girl.” Used for a girl/young woman (often a teenager). It can sound a bit formal or old-fashioned compared with "la fille" in everyday speech. Feminine singular: "la" + "jeune" + "fille".
target_language_example: La jeune fille attend le bus devant l'école.
native_language_example: The young girl is waiting for the bus in front of the school.

additional_notes: Often refers to the day as a span of time or how the day went/feels (duration, experience): «passer la journée», «la journée a été longue», «la journée est presque finie».
