additional_notes: A common noun for a clothes-washing machine. Often used with an article: "un/mon/le lave-linge". You may also see "machine à laver" with the same meaning. Frequent with phrases like "tomber en panne" (to break down) and "hors-service" (out of order).
target_language_example: Je mets les draps dans le lave-linge.
native_language_example: I’m putting the sheets in the washing machine.

additional_notes: A noun for the appliance that washes dishes. Commonly used with articles: un/une/le/mon lave-vaisselle. You’ll often hear phrases like mettre la vaisselle dans le lave-vaisselle (“put the dishes in the dishwasher”).
target_language_example: Le lave-vaisselle est en panne, donc on va laver à la main.
native_language_example: The dishwasher is broken, so we’re going to wash by hand.

meaning: "Dr" = "Doctor" (a medical doctor, or someone with a doctorate).
additional_notes: Written abbreviation of "docteur". Used before a person’s name or by itself when the person is understood from context (often in hospitals/clinics). In speech you typically say "le docteur"; in writing you often see "le Dr" (feminine: "la Dre" in some usage).
target_language_example: Le Dr Martin vous recevra à 15 h.
native_language_example: Dr. Martin will see you at 3 p.m.

meaning: the ball (e.g., for sports); also a balloon.
additional_notes: Most often means a ball used in sports or games (soccer, basketball, etc.). It can also mean a balloon, but in that context you may hear “un ballon de baudruche” or just “un ballon” when it’s clear. Note the pronunciation: the final “n” is nasal and the final “on” is not pronounced like an English ‘on’.
target_language_example: On a perdu le ballon dans le jardin.
native_language_example: We lost the ball in the garden.

additional_notes: Refers to a vessel that travels on water. In everyday French, it can mean either a small “boat” or a larger “ship,” depending on context. Common with prepositions like "dans le bateau" (in the boat) and "sur le bateau" (on the boat).
target_language_example: On monte sur le bateau à 9 heures.
native_language_example: We get on the boat at 9 o’clock.

additional_notes: A masculine noun used to talk about the Berber language (often called “Tamazight” in some regions). It’s typically used with the definite article: « le berbère ». You can use it with verbs like apprendre (to learn), parler (to speak), and être (to be): « J’apprends le berbère. »
target_language_example: Je parle un peu le berbère, mais je veux progresser.
native_language_example: I speak a little Berber, but I want to improve.

meaning: the right choice; the good choice.
additional_notes: Used to say a decision was correct or a good one. Often appears with the verb faire (faire le bon choix = to make the right choice).
target_language_example: Je pense que c'est le bon choix pour toi.
native_language_example: I think it’s the right choice for you.

additional_notes: A common noun meaning “happiness” in general or a happy state. Often used with verbs like souhaiter (to wish): « Je te/vous souhaite le bonheur » or « tout le bonheur du monde » (“all the happiness in the world”). Also used in general statements: « Le bonheur ne vient pas que de… » (“Happiness doesn’t only come from…”).
target_language_example: Pour moi, le bonheur, c’est passer du temps avec ma famille.
native_language_example: For me, happiness is spending time with my family.

additional_notes: Refers to the arm (from shoulder to hand). Common in everyday phrases like: « sous le bras » (tucked under the arm), « tendre/allonger le bras » (to stretch out/reach with your arm), and « mettre le bras autour de quelqu’un » (to put your arm around someone).
target_language_example: Elle a un livre sous le bras.
native_language_example: She has a book under her arm.

additional_notes: "Le bruit" is a masculine noun meaning a noise or the sound made by something. Common patterns: "Désolé pour le bruit" (Sorry about the noise), "le bruit de + nom" (the sound of...), and "faire du bruit" (to make noise).
target_language_example: Désolé pour le bruit, on finit tout de suite.
native_language_example: Sorry about the noise, we'll finish right away.

additional_notes: Most often means an office (the workplace or office room): « quitter le bureau » = to leave the office. It can also mean a desk (the piece of furniture), especially with location words like « sous le bureau » (under the desk). Context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Elle a déjà quitté le bureau, mais une pièce a roulé sous le bureau.
native_language_example: She has already left the office, but a coin rolled under the desk.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific bus, or to buses in general depending on context. Common with verbs like attendre (to wait for), prendre (to take/catch), rater (to miss). Note: for the mode of transport, French more often uses « en bus » (by bus) rather than « par le bus », but « le bus » is required when referring to the bus as a concrete, identifiable vehicle.
target_language_example: J’ai attendu le bus pendant dix minutes.
native_language_example: I waited for the bus for ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used for a (usually large) constructed building or facility (office building, school building, etc.). In French, "bâtiment" can also mean a ship, but in everyday contexts like these examples it means a building. Gender: masculine (le bâtiment).
target_language_example: Le bâtiment est fermé aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: The building is closed today.

additional_notes: Refers to a very young child (a baby). Often used for babies and toddlers; you can also hear it used affectionately for someone (e.g., a partner: « mon bébé »). In « faire le bébé », it means “to act like a baby” (to whine/behave immaturely).
target_language_example: Le bébé dort dans sa poussette.
native_language_example: The baby is sleeping in his/her stroller.

additional_notes: Usually refers to coffee as a drink in general (e.g., liking coffee) or a specific coffee being discussed (e.g., the coffee on the table). When ordering, French often uses "un café" for one serving, but "le café" is common for general statements or when the context identifies the coffee.
target_language_example: Elle aime le café.
native_language_example: She likes coffee.

additional_notes: A masculine noun used for a large vehicle that transports goods. Often used with verbs like charger (to load) or décharger (to unload).
target_language_example: Le camion arrive dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: The truck arrives in five minutes.

additional_notes: Literally means “camp” (a campsite/encampment). Very common in set phrases: **lever le camp** = “to break camp / pack up and leave” (neutral). **foutre le camp** / **fous le camp !** = “to get out!/go away!” and is **very informal** and can sound rude.
target_language_example: Allez, on lève le camp !
native_language_example: Come on, let’s pack up and leave!

additional_notes: A masculine noun used for a sofa in a living room. Common with location prepositions: sous le canapé (under the couch), derrière le canapé (behind the couch).
target_language_example: On peut s’asseoir sur le canapé ?
native_language_example: Can we sit on the couch?

additional_notes: Usually used with the definite article: avoir le cancer = “to have cancer.” You can specify the type with “cancer de + body part” (e.g., cancer de la peau = skin cancer).
target_language_example: Ma tante a eu le cancer il y a dix ans.
native_language_example: My aunt had cancer ten years ago.

meaning: the captain; the person in charge (or the team captain).
additional_notes: Used for the leader of a sports team, a ship/plane, or more generally someone with authority. Often followed by de + noun: « le capitaine de l’équipe » (the team captain).
target_language_example: Le capitaine a décidé de changer la stratégie.
native_language_example: The captain decided to change the strategy.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is (or isn’t) true in a particular situation. Very common in phrases like « C’est le cas » (That’s the case / That’s true), « ce n’est pas le cas » (That’s not the case), and « si c’est le cas » (if that’s the case). Often refers back to something just mentioned.
target_language_example: Si c’est le cas, on peut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: If that’s the case, we can leave now.

additional_notes: A straightforward phrase made of the definite article le ("the") and chat ("cat"). Used for a specific cat, or for "the cat" in a general sense.
target_language_example: Le chat dort sur le canapé.
native_language_example: The cat is sleeping on the sofa.

meaning: "the cat has" / "the cat did" (with a past participle).
additional_notes: "Le chat" = "the cat." "a" is the 3rd-person singular of "avoir" (to have). On its own it means "has" (present tense): "Le chat a une souris" = "The cat has a mouse." Very often it’s used as the helping verb in the passé composé to talk about a completed past action: "Le chat a couru" = "The cat ran / has run."
target_language_example: Le chat a mangé sa nourriture.
native_language_example: The cat ate its food.

additional_notes: Used to describe the cat’s state, size, or location, usually followed by an adjective (grand, petit, en sécurité) or a place phrase (sur la chaise, sous la chaise). In questions you’ll often see it inside “Est-ce que … ?” → “Est-ce que le chat est … ?” (“Is the cat …?”). Note: French *chat* (cat) can look like English “chat” (conversation), but it’s a different word/meaning.
target_language_example: Le chat est sous la table.
native_language_example: The cat is under the table.

additional_notes: Meaning depends on context. With "de" + group ("chef de classe", "chef de section"), it means the person in charge (leader/head). In a restaurant or kitchen context, "le chef" commonly means the chef (the cook). Feminine form: "la cheffe" (also sometimes "le chef" for a woman in some contexts).
target_language_example: C'est le chef qui décide.
native_language_example: The boss is the one who decides.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a path/track or the route to get somewhere (often in directions: « montrer le chemin » = “show the way”). It can also be used more figuratively to mean someone’s journey or approach in life (e.g., « le chemin est le but » = “the journey is the goal”). Masculine noun: « le chemin », « un chemin ».
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, quel est le chemin le plus court pour aller au centre-ville ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what’s the shortest way to get to downtown?

additional_notes: A straightforward phrase: le means "the" with a masculine singular noun, and chien means "dog." It can refer to a specific dog, and in some contexts French also uses the definite article for animals in a general sense.
target_language_example: Le chien dort sous la table.
native_language_example: The dog is sleeping under the table.

meaning: "the dog has" / "the dog did" (start of the past tense with "avoir").
additional_notes: Used before a past participle to talk about what the dog did in the past (passé composé): « Le chien a aboyé » = the dog barked. In English you usually translate it as simple past (“did”), not literally “has.”
target_language_example: Le chien a mangé sa nourriture.
native_language_example: The dog ate his food.

additional_notes: Used to describe the dog (adjective), its state (“comme mort” = almost dead), a quality (“fidèle”), or to say who it belongs to (“à nous” = ours). This is simply “le chien” (the dog) + the verb “être” in the present tense (“est” = is).
target_language_example: Le chien est très gentil.
native_language_example: The dog is very nice.

additional_notes: A masculine noun used with the definite article "le" to talk about chocolate in general (e.g., likes/dislikes). For a specific chocolate, you might say "un chocolat" (a chocolate) or "ce chocolat" (this chocolate).
target_language_example: J'adore le chocolat noir.
native_language_example: I love dark chocolate.

meaning: the choice; a choice/option (having a say).
additional_notes: Means “choice” or “options,” often in the set phrases: « A-t-on le choix ? » / « Avais-je le choix ? » = “Do we/I have a choice?”; « Je n’ai plus le choix » = “I have no choice anymore / I have no other option.” Also used generally: « Vous aurez le choix » = “You’ll have a choice / options.”
target_language_example: On peut partir maintenant, mais tu as le choix : on peut aussi attendre demain.
native_language_example: We can leave now, but you have a choice: we can also wait until tomorrow.

additional_notes: Most often means “the sky” (what you see above you). It can also mean “heaven,” especially in expressions or a religious sense. Common pattern: "le ciel est..." (the sky is...).
target_language_example: Ce soir, le ciel est plein d'étoiles.
native_language_example: Tonight, the sky is full of stars.

meaning: the trunk (of a car); a chest/safe (a locked storage box).
additional_notes: Commonly refers to a car’s trunk: Ferme(z) le coffre. It can also mean a locked box or safe for valuables (coffre-fort = safe). Context usually makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: J’ai mis les valises dans le coffre.
native_language_example: I put the suitcases in the trunk.

additional_notes: A masculine noun. Used for a strong, lockable metal box/cabinet where you store valuables (cash, passports, jewelry). Common verbs: ouvrir/fermer (open/close), laisser ouvert (leave open), verrouiller (lock). Plural: les coffres-forts.
target_language_example: J'ai mis mon passeport dans le coffre-fort de l'hôtel.
native_language_example: I put my passport in the hotel safe.

additional_notes: A masculine noun used for a live music performance. Common with verbs like aller à / assister à (go to/attend), commencer (start), être (be: bon, horrible), and with phrases like billets pour (tickets for) and afficher complet (to be sold out).
target_language_example: Comment était le concert ?
native_language_example: How was the concert?

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that is the opposite of something else, often with "de": "le contraire de + noun/pronoun" (the opposite of…). You can also use it alone to correct or disagree: "Pas le contraire" (Not the opposite / Not the other way around).
target_language_example: Fais le contraire de ce qu’il dit.
native_language_example: Do the opposite of what he says.

meaning: the contract; an agreement in writing.
additional_notes: Used for a formal agreement (often written) between people/companies. Common with verbs like signer (to sign), lire/regarder (to read/look over), respecter (to follow), rompre (to break), and phrases like dans le contrat (in the contract).
target_language_example: On doit signer le contrat demain.
native_language_example: We have to sign the contract tomorrow.

meaning: the body; also a professional/organized body (e.g., medical corps).
additional_notes: Most commonly means the physical body ("le corps humain"). In some contexts, it can refer to an organized body of people ("le corps médical" = the medical profession/medical corps). Watch out for the English look-alike "corpse": French for "a corpse" is usually "un cadavre" (also "un corps" in some contexts, e.g., in crime reports).
target_language_example: Le corps humain est composé de milliards de petites cellules.
native_language_example: The human body is made up of billions of tiny cells.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for the sun going down in the evening. Use it with verbs like voir (to see), regarder (to watch), or filmer (to film). You’ll also often hear: « au coucher du soleil » (“at sunset”).
target_language_example: On va à la plage pour regarder le coucher de soleil.
native_language_example: We're going to the beach to watch the sunset.

additional_notes: Very common word with several idiomatic uses depending on the verb/context. 1) Physical or emotional “hit”: « encaisser le coup » = “take the blow / handle the shock.” 2) An attempt: « tenter le coup » = “give it a try.” 3) A move/trick/typical thing to do: « le coup classique » = “the classic move/trick.” 4) With « valoir »: « ça valait/vaut le coup » = “it was/is worth it,” and « ça vaut pas le coup » = “it’s not worth it.”
target_language_example: On peut tenter le coup, mais je ne sais pas si ça vaut le coup.
native_language_example: We can give it a try, but I don’t know if it’s worth it.

additional_notes: Very vulgar slang. Often used in insults and set phrases: « Bouge-toi le cul / Magne-toi le cul » = “get your ass moving / hurry up”; « baiser/lécher le cul (de quelqu’un) » = “kiss/lick someone’s ass” (to flatter or show contempt); « dans le cul » is a crude “up your ass / in the ass.” Avoid in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Allez, bouge-toi le cul, on va être en retard !
native_language_example: Come on, get your ass moving, we’re going to be late!

additional_notes: Literal: the physical heart. Very often figurative for emotions, especially love and sadness. Common expressions: « briser le cœur (à quelqu’un) » = to break someone’s heart; « le cœur guérira » = the heart will heal (you’ll feel better). With adjectives: « avoir le cœur dur » = to be hard-hearted/unkind; « avoir le cœur lourd » = to feel heavy-hearted/sad.
target_language_example: Après leur séparation, il a eu le cœur lourd pendant des semaines.
native_language_example: After their breakup, he felt heavy-hearted for weeks.

additional_notes: Used to express deep sadness, usually after a breakup, rejection, or loss. Most often appears with the verb "avoir": "avoir le cœur brisé" = "to be heartbroken" (literally "to have a broken heart"). You can also say "le cœur brisé" as an adjective phrase after a noun: "un homme au cœur brisé" (a heartbroken man).
target_language_example: Après la rupture, elle avait le cœur brisé.
native_language_example: After the breakup, she was heartbroken.

additional_notes: Used for the final or most recent person, thing, or event, depending on context. It can come before a noun (le dernier vol = the last flight) or stand alone (je suis le dernier = I'm the last one). It changes for gender and number: la dernière, les derniers, les dernières.
target_language_example: Je prends le dernier train pour Paris.
native_language_example: I'm taking the last train to Paris.

additional_notes: Used when talking about the final scheduled train you can catch; often with verbs like "rater" or "manquer" (to miss) and time pressure like "juste à temps" (just in time).
target_language_example: On doit partir maintenant, sinon on va rater le dernier train.
native_language_example: We have to leave now, otherwise we'll miss the last train.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens on Sundays in general (a habit). With days of the week, French often uses “le” to mean “on (that day) / on (that day) in general”. For one specific upcoming/previous Sunday, you can also say “dimanche” without “le” (e.g., “Dimanche, je travaille.”).
target_language_example: Le dimanche, on prend un café en terrasse.
native_language_example: On Sundays, we have a coffee on a patio.

meaning: the director; the manager; the head (male).
additional_notes: Used for a man who is in charge of an organization (company, school, department, etc.). In everyday contexts it often corresponds to “manager” or “principal” in English. Feminine form: « la directrice ». You can specify what he leads with « le directeur de … » (e.g., « le directeur de la société »).
target_language_example: Je veux voir le directeur de la société.
native_language_example: I want to see the director of the company.

additional_notes: Means “the doctor” (a medical doctor). In everyday French, you can also say "le médecin". Used when talking about a specific doctor already known in the situation (e.g., your doctor, the doctor on call).
target_language_example: Le docteur va te recevoir à 15 h.
native_language_example: The doctor will see you at 3 p.m.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the back part of a person’s body. Common in set expressions: « tourner le dos (à quelqu’un) » = to turn your back (on someone) / to face away; « le dos au mur » = with your back to the wall (cornered, under pressure); « se casser le dos » = to hurt your back badly / to break your back (often also used figuratively for working extremely hard).
target_language_example: Le soleil lui a brûlé le dos.
native_language_example: The sun burned his/her back.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is entitled to be informed (often about reasons, facts, or decisions): « avoir le droit de savoir ». It’s a formal/common expression in contexts like privacy, work, government, or relationships.
target_language_example: J’ai le droit de savoir ce qui s’est passé.
native_language_example: I have the right to know what happened.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the first moment/part of something (an event, a game, a visit, a period). Very common in phrases like « le début de + nom » (the beginning of …) and « avant le début » (before the start).
target_language_example: C'est le début de quelque chose de merveilleux.
native_language_example: It's the beginning of something wonderful.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to lunch, but in some regions (especially parts of France/Belgium) it can mean “breakfast.” Usually used with an article (le déjeuner).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à midi pour le déjeuner ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at noon for lunch?

additional_notes: Refers to the main meal in the evening (common meaning in France). In some regions/families, it can be used for the midday meal instead—context tells you which meal. Common verbs with it: préparer / faire le dîner (make dinner), cuire le dîner (cook dinner), le dîner est prêt (dinner is ready).
target_language_example: Je fais le dîner ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm making dinner tonight.

meaning: 'the fact that' (that something is true; the idea that).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause as a fact/point being discussed. Often followed by the subjunctive when it expresses doubt, insistence, or emotion (e.g., « Je doute le fait que… », « insister sur le fait que… »). With « malgré le fait que », it means “despite the fact that” and is commonly followed by the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Je suis surpris par le fait que tu sois venu si tôt.
native_language_example: I'm surprised by the fact that you came so early.

additional_notes: Usually means literal fire/flames (a building fire, a campfire). Common related phrases: « le feu prend » = “the fire catches/starts (spreads)”; « allumer le feu » = “to light the fire”; « par le feu » can mean “by fire” (burning) and, in military contexts, can also refer to “by gunfire.”
target_language_example: Attention, il y a le feu dans la cuisine !
native_language_example: Watch out, there’s a fire in the kitchen!

additional_notes: "Le" means "the" for a masculine singular noun, so "le film" usually refers to a specific movie/film. In everyday French, "un film" / "le film" often means "a movie" / "the movie." With verbs like "accélérer", it can mean speeding up/fast-forwarding the video (e.g., "accélérer le film" = fast-forward the movie).
target_language_example: On regarde le film ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we watching the movie tonight?

additional_notes: Used to describe a movie in the past. "était" is the imperfect past of "être" (to be), often used for descriptions (e.g., long, boring, good) or background information. In questions you may see inversion: "Le film était-il… ?" or "Est-ce que le film était… ?"
target_language_example: Le film était trop long, mais la fin était super.
native_language_example: The movie was too long, but the ending was great.

additional_notes: Used to state who someone’s parent(s) are: « X est le fils de Y ». With two parents you can say « le fils de [mother] et de [father] ». Agree the gender: « le fils de » (son) vs « la fille de » (daughter).
target_language_example: Paul est le fils de Sophie.
native_language_example: Paul is Sophie’s son.

additional_notes: Refers to the French language. In French, language names often take the definite article after verbs like parler, apprendre, enseigner, and comprendre, even though English usually just says "French" without "the." Also note the spelling difference: français = the language/adjective, while Français (capitalized) can mean a French person.
target_language_example: Je comprends un peu le français, mais je ne le parle pas bien.
native_language_example: I understand a little French, but I don't speak it well.

additional_notes: Informal/common short form of « le réfrigérateur ». Used in everyday speech. Often appears with « sur le frigo » (on the fridge), e.g., for notes, calendars, magnets, photos, etc.
target_language_example: J’ai mis le lait dans le frigo.
native_language_example: I put the milk in the fridge.

additional_notes: Means the time that hasn’t happened yet (what will come later). Often used with pour (plans for the future), dans (in the future), and in questions/speculation about what will happen.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce que le futur nous réserve.
native_language_example: I don’t know what the future holds for us.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific boy. Le is the masculine singular form of 'the', so this phrase is for one identifiable male child or young man in context.
target_language_example: Le garçon joue dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The boy is playing in the garden.

meaning: "the boy has" / "the boy" + past tense (passé composé).
additional_notes: Used as the subject (le garçon = the boy) followed by the present tense of avoir (a = has). Very often, "a" introduces the passé composé: "Le garçon a dormi" = "The boy slept/has slept." Note: "garçon" can also mean "waiter" in restaurants, but in these sentences it means "boy."
target_language_example: Le garçon a oublié son sac à l'école.
native_language_example: The boy forgot his bag at school.

additional_notes: Refers to the people/institutions that run a country (the state leadership/administration). Often used when talking about politics, laws, public services, or what the state does or doesn’t do. In sentence 3, “est à chier” is very vulgar slang meaning “is really terrible.”
target_language_example: Le gouvernement a annoncé de nouvelles mesures.
native_language_example: The government announced new measures.

additional_notes: A masculine noun used for cakes and many sweet baked desserts (e.g., birthday cake, apple cake). Often followed by "à la/aux" to say the flavor or main ingredient: "gâteau à la pomme" (apple cake), "gâteau au chocolat" (chocolate cake), "gâteau aux fraises" (strawberry cake).
target_language_example: On va manger le gâteau après le dîner.
native_language_example: We’re going to eat the cake after dinner.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article (le) to talk about the Japanese language in general: apprendre le japonais, parler le japonais. (Japanese nationality would be "un/une Japonais(e)"; as an adjective: "japonais/japonaise".)
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu apprends le japonais en ce moment ?
native_language_example: Are you learning Japanese right now?

additional_notes: Refers to a garden or yard area (often behind/around a house). Used with the definite article: "le" (the). You’ll also see it without an article after some prepositions, e.g. "dans le jardin" (in the garden).
target_language_example: Les enfants jouent dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The children are playing in the garden.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for a male who is young (teen/young adult). Feminine equivalent: « la jeune femme » (young woman) or, for a younger girl, « la jeune fille ». Plural: « les jeunes hommes ».
target_language_example: Le jeune homme parle avec sa sœur.
native_language_example: The young man is talking with his sister.

additional_notes: Usually means a specific day or occasion, as in le jour de... ('the day of...') or le jour où... ('the day when...'). When contrasted with la nuit or used with durant, it can mean 'daytime'.
target_language_example: Je travaille le jour et je me repose la nuit.
native_language_example: I work during the day and rest at night.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to specify a particular day or event: le jour de Noël (Christmas Day), le jour de mon anniversaire (on my birthday). Often answers “when?” and can refer either to the calendar day (“Christmas Day”) or to the exact date an event happens (“the day of the wedding”).
target_language_example: On se voit le jour de ton départ.
native_language_example: We’ll see each other on the day you leave.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific day, often followed by a clause with a verb: « le jour où je suis né » (“the day I was born”). It can mean a literal calendar day or a more general “the moment when something happens” (often about an important or expected event).
target_language_example: Le jour où tu arrives, on fait une fête.
native_language_example: The day you arrive, we’ll have a party.

meaning: the following day; the next day.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the day after a previously mentioned day or event. It can come after the time reference (e.g., "le lundi… le jour suivant") or at the start of a sentence ("Le jour suivant, ..."). Also commonly said as "le lendemain".
target_language_example: On s’est vus mardi, et le jour suivant il est parti.
native_language_example: We saw each other on Tuesday, and the next day he left.

additional_notes: Most often means a newspaper (the physical paper or the newspaper as an organization). For a personal diary, French usually says "un journal intime" or "un carnet". It can also be used in expressions like "le journal de l’école" (the school newspaper) or "le journal télévisé" (the TV news).
target_language_example: J’achète le journal tous les matins.
native_language_example: I buy the newspaper every morning.

additional_notes: Used for a judge in a court/legal setting. In direct address, you often say « Monsieur le juge » (Sir/Judge) or « Madame le juge » (Ma’am/Judge), and it can be abbreviated in writing as « M. le juge ». Plural: « les juges ».
target_language_example: Le juge a rendu son verdict.
native_language_example: The judge delivered his verdict.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (un lac). Used for a lake as a body of fresh (or sometimes salt) water. With places, you’ll often see: le lac + name (e.g., le lac Léman). Common prepositions include sur le lac (on the lake), au bord du lac (by the lake), and autour du lac (around the lake).
target_language_example: Il y avait quelques bateaux sur le lac.
native_language_example: There were a few boats on the lake.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (le lait). Used with the definite article “le” when talking about milk in general (Tu aimes le lait ?) or a specific milk understood in context. Common expression: “Le lait a tourné” = the milk has gone sour/spoiled.
target_language_example: Le lait a tourné.
native_language_example: The milk has gone sour.

additional_notes: This is a possessive pronoun used to replace a noun already understood from context: *le leur* = “their one” / “theirs” (for a masculine singular thing). Variations: *la leur* (fem. sg.), *les leurs* (plural). Often used after *c'est / ce sont*: *C'est le leur.*
target_language_example: Ce stylo est le leur.
native_language_example: This pen is theirs.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (un lit). Used for sleeping, or sometimes figuratively/technically (e.g., a riverbed: le lit d’une rivière). In everyday speech, "faire le lit" means "to make the bed."
target_language_example: Je vais me coucher : je suis déjà dans le lit.
native_language_example: I’m going to bed: I’m already in bed.

additional_notes: A basic noun phrase: livre means "book," and it is masculine, so the singular definite form is le livre. In connected speech, le often becomes l' before a vowel sound, but not here.
target_language_example: Où est le livre que tu lis ?
native_language_example: Where is the book that you're reading?

additional_notes: Used to describe the book (with an adjective) or to say where it is (often with a location phrase like “sur / dans / sous …”). “Le” is “the” for a masculine singular noun; “est” is “is” (from être).
target_language_example: Le livre est sur la table.
native_language_example: The book is on the table.

meaning: along; alongside (following the length of something).
additional_notes: Used to describe movement or position that follows the edge/length of something (a street, road, beach), or something moving down/up a body part (e.g., tears down cheeks, something climbing up a leg). Often used with verbs like aller, marcher, se promener, serpenter, tomber, grimper.
target_language_example: Nous avons marché le long de la rivière.
native_language_example: We walked along the river.

additional_notes: Used to describe movement or something positioned following the length of something (a leg, the coast, a cliff, a hull, etc.). Often goes with verbs like monter/grimper (up along), descendre (down along), marcher/courir (run/walk along), naviguer (sail along).
target_language_example: Nous avons marché le long de la rivière pendant une heure.
native_language_example: We walked along the river for an hour.

additional_notes: Used to describe something located or moving next to the river, following its edge or course. The core pattern is **le long de + [place]** (“along + [place]”), e.g. *le long de la route* (along the road).
target_language_example: On a pique-niqué le long de la rivière.
native_language_example: We had a picnic along the river.

additional_notes: Refers to a (physical) store/shop where you buy things. Common in phrases like "le magasin de fleurs" (the flower shop) and "dans le magasin" (in the store).
target_language_example: Ceci est le magasin le moins cher de la ville.
native_language_example: This is the cheapest store in the city.

additional_notes: Refers to the elected head of a town/city (the local government official). Often followed by “de + place” to say where: “le maire de notre ville” (the mayor of our town).
target_language_example: Le maire de la ville va faire un discours ce soir.
native_language_example: The city’s mayor is going to give a speech tonight.

additional_notes: Used with avoir: « avoir le mal du pays » = to feel homesick, especially when you’re away from your country/region/home. Informal speaking often drops "ne" and uses "t'as" instead of « tu as ».
target_language_example: Depuis que je suis à l'étranger, j'ai le mal du pays.
native_language_example: Since I’ve been abroad, I’ve been homesick.

meaning: the market (marketplace; also a market/sector, including the stock market).
additional_notes: Used for a physical place to shop (a market), or more generally for the market as an economic system/sector: "le marché des valeurs mobilières" = the stock market; "le marché a repris" = the market picked up/recovered; "inondé de produits" = flooded with products. In expressions like "C'est le marché", it means “that’s how the market works / that’s the way things are.”
target_language_example: Ce produit est moins cher sur le marché.
native_language_example: This product is cheaper at the market.

additional_notes: Can mean the institution/commitment of being married (“marriage”) or the ceremony/event itself (“a wedding”). Often used with: "annuler le mariage" (cancel the wedding), "avant le mariage" (before marriage), "le mariage de + name" (someone’s wedding), and "avoir lieu" (to take place).
target_language_example: Ils veulent un petit mariage, mais le mariage aura lieu en été.
native_language_example: They want a small wedding, but the wedding will take place in the summer.

additional_notes: Used for a sports match/game (soccer, baseball, etc.). Common with de + sport (un match de baseball) or between teams (un match France–Angleterre). You can talk about the result (gagner/perdre le match), timing (avant/après le match), or changes (le match a été reporté = postponed).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au stade avant le match.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the stadium before the match.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the morning in general or as a regular time of day. Often follows a verb to mean “in the morning” (Je travaille le matin = I work in the morning / in the mornings). With a specific day, it can mean “the next morning / that morning” (Le matin suivant = the following morning).
target_language_example: Le matin, je bois un café avant de partir.
native_language_example: In the morning, I drink a coffee before leaving.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to mark the superlative: le meilleur moyen = the best way. Meilleur is the irregular form related to bon ('good'). It changes for gender and number: la meilleure, les meilleurs, les meilleures. If the noun is omitted, le meilleur can mean 'the best one.'
target_language_example: C'est le meilleur choix pour nous.
native_language_example: It's the best choice for us.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the best option or outcome. Often appears with verbs like vouloir/chercher/choisir: « Nous voulons le meilleur pour toi » (“We want the best for you”). It agrees with gender/number in other forms: « la meilleure » (f.), « les meilleurs / les meilleures » (pl.).
target_language_example: C'est le meilleur restaurant du quartier.
native_language_example: It's the best restaurant in the neighborhood.

meaning: the message (a written or spoken note/information).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a message you received or want to check (text, voicemail, note, email, etc.). In conversation, “Le message ?” can mean “What does the message say?” or “Which message?” depending on context. “Prends le message” commonly means “take the message” (i.e., write it down/pass it on).
target_language_example: Tu peux prendre le message et le lui donner ?
native_language_example: Can you take the message and give it to him?

additional_notes: Possessive pronoun used to avoid repeating a masculine singular noun already mentioned or understood from context. It agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner: for example, livre → le mien. Related forms are la mienne, les miens, and les miennes.
target_language_example: Ton manteau est sur la chaise, et le mien est dans la voiture.
native_language_example: Your coat is on the chair, and mine is in the car.

additional_notes: A masculine noun for an object with a reflective surface. Common with verbs like « montrer » (to show), « prendre » (to take), « tenir » (to hold), and « réfléchir » (to reflect).
target_language_example: Je me regarde dans le miroir avant de partir.
native_language_example: I look at myself in the mirror before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize even the smallest amount or detail, especially in questions and negative statements: "pas le moindre..." = "not the slightest / not any...". It agrees with the noun: "le moindre" (masc. sing.) and "la moindre" (fem. sing.). Common with nouns like "sens", "doute", "sou", "argent", "indice", "intérêt".
target_language_example: Ce que je dis a-t-il le moindre sens ?
native_language_example: Does what I'm saying make the slightest sense?

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened during the previous month. It often goes at the end of the sentence (e.g., « J’ai voyagé le mois dernier. »), but it can also be placed earlier for emphasis.
target_language_example: Je l’ai vu le mois dernier.
native_language_example: I saw him last month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the month after the current one. Often placed at the end of the sentence as a time expression, but it can also be used alone as a short answer.
target_language_example: On commence le nouveau travail le mois prochain.
native_language_example: We start the new job next month.

additional_notes: Means a specific point in time (“the moment”), often used to talk about when something should happen: “le moment de + infinitive” (the time to do something), “le moment présent” (the present moment), “ce n’est pas le moment” (it’s not the right time), “le moment est venu” (the time has come), “le moment opportun” (the right/appropriate time).
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas le moment de parler de ça.
native_language_example: This isn’t the right time to talk about that.

meaning: when the time comes; when the moment arrives.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen later, at the appropriate time. Often placed at the end of a sentence as a set phrase, and can be used alone (“Le moment venu.”) to mean “When the time comes.”
target_language_example: Je te dirai la vérité le moment venu.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you the truth when the time comes.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the world in general: the planet, life on earth, or human society. In some contexts, it can also suggest people in general.
target_language_example: Je veux voyager et voir le monde.
native_language_example: I want to travel and see the world.

additional_notes: Literally “the entire world.” Used to emphasize that something is known, involved, or affected worldwide, or (more loosely) that everybody knows/does something. Often used with verbs like savoir (to know), être au courant (to be aware), or in emotional statements like détester le monde entier (to hate everyone/the whole world).
target_language_example: Il a posté la vidéo, et le monde entier l’a vue.
native_language_example: He posted the video, and the whole world saw it.

additional_notes: Used to describe what the world is like (often with an adjective or noun phrase): « le monde est compliqué », « le monde est un endroit dangereux ». Note: « le monde » usually means “the world,” but it can also refer to “people/society” in general depending on context. Don’t confuse it with « tout le monde est » = “everyone is.”
target_language_example: Parfois, le monde est injuste.
native_language_example: Sometimes, the world is unfair.

additional_notes: Said when you run into someone unexpectedly, discover a surprising connection, or realize people/places are linked in an unexpected way. Often used as an exclamation: « Comme/Que le monde est petit ! » (similar to “How small the world is!”). « hein ? » can be added to seek agreement (“right?”).
target_language_example: On se retrouve encore ici ? Le monde est petit !
native_language_example: We end up here again? It’s a small world!

additional_notes: Used to say something is common knowledge. In everyday French, "tout le monde sait" is much more common than "le monde sait" on its own.
target_language_example: Tout le monde sait que Paris est la capitale de la France.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that Paris is the capital of France.

additional_notes: This isn’t really a complete set phrase on its own: it’s usually the start of a sentence before a reflexive verb (a verb that uses *se*, like *se lever*, *se souvenir*, *se rencontrer*). *Le monde* can mean “the world,” but it can also mean “people/everyone” depending on context (more commonly you’ll see *tout le monde* = “everyone”).
target_language_example: Le monde se souvient de ce moment.
native_language_example: People remember that moment.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s mood/mental state, especially when it’s high or low. Common patterns: « avoir le moral » (to be in good spirits), « remonter le moral (à quelqu’un) » (to cheer [someone] up / lift [someone’s] spirits), and the idiom « avoir le moral dans les chaussettes » (to feel very down).
target_language_example: Après une mauvaise journée, j’écoute un podcast pour me remonter le moral.
native_language_example: After a bad day, I listen to a podcast to lift my spirits.

additional_notes: Used for a computer/account password or a secret code to access something. Often appears with verbs like changer (to change), demander (to ask for), oublier (to forget), or entrer/saisir (to enter/type).
target_language_example: J'ai oublié le mot de passe, je dois le réinitialiser.
native_language_example: I forgot the password; I have to reset it.

additional_notes: Refers to an engine in a vehicle or machine. Common with verbs like tourner (run), fonctionner (work), être bruyant (be noisy), and éteindre (turn off/shut down).
target_language_example: Le moteur de la voiture démarre enfin.
native_language_example: The car’s engine finally starts.

additional_notes: A masculine noun: (un) mur. Used for a wall in a building (inside or outside), or a barrier/fortification (e.g., a stone wall). Plural: les murs. Common phrases: contre le mur (against the wall), sur le mur (on the wall).
target_language_example: Il y a une fenêtre dans le mur.
native_language_example: There is a window in the wall.

additional_notes: Means “the doctor” (male doctor or doctor in general). Common with verbs like appeler (call) and consulter (see/consult a doctor): « Appelle le médecin » = “Call the doctor”; « consulter le médecin » = “to see the doctor.”
target_language_example: J'ai rendez-vous chez le médecin demain matin.
native_language_example: I have an appointment at the doctor's tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to say that two or more people or things are identical in some way. It often comes before a noun, as in le même livre ('the same book'), and changes for gender and number: la même, les mêmes. It is often followed by que to compare: le même ... que ('the same ... as').
target_language_example: Nous avons le même professeur de français.
native_language_example: We have the same French teacher.

additional_notes: A more formal/general word for a ship than "bateau". Often used in news, history, and nautical contexts. Common with verbs like "couler" (to sink), "abandonner" (to abandon), and phrases like "être à flot" (to be afloat).
target_language_example: Le navire a quitté le port ce matin.
native_language_example: The ship left the port this morning.

additional_notes: A body part. Very common in everyday phrases: « Essuie-toi le nez ! » (Wipe your nose!), « avoir le nez qui coule » (to have a runny nose), and « respirer par le nez » (to breathe through your nose). In expressions like « avoir le nez dans l'écran », it means having your face very close to the screen (being glued to it).
target_language_example: J'ai le nez bouché, je respire mal.
native_language_example: My nose is blocked, I’m breathing badly.

meaning: black; the black one (the item in black).
additional_notes: Often refers to the color black in general or to a specific black item (e.g., a black shirt, dress, or pen) depending on context. With the verb "aller" (as in "Le noir te va bien"), it means black suits you / looks good on you.
target_language_example: Je préfère le noir pour les vêtements.
native_language_example: I prefer black for clothes.

additional_notes: Used to identify what someone/something is called: le nom de la ville (the name of the city), le nom de notre fille (our daughter’s name). Often used with verbs like être (C’est le nom de… ?), savoir (Sais-tu le nom de… ?), dire (Peux-tu dire le nom de… ?), and vouloir (Je veux le nom de…).
target_language_example: Tu connais le nom de ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: Do you know the name of this restaurant?

meaning: “the name of the” (before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the name belonging to someone or something: le nom du film, le nom du père, le nom du compositeur. It’s the contraction of "le nom de" + "le" → "le nom du". For a feminine noun, use "le nom de la"; for plural, "le nom des".
target_language_example: Quel est le nom du restaurant ?
native_language_example: What is the name of the restaurant?

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to talk about how many there are (often in statistics or trends). It takes singular agreement: "Le nombre de touristes a augmenté" (not "ont augmenté").
target_language_example: Le nombre de participants a diminué cette semaine.
native_language_example: The number of participants decreased this week.

additional_notes: Usually means “the new + [masculine singular noun]” (e.g., le nouveau président = the new president). It can also be used on its own as a noun to refer to a new person/thing in a group (“the newcomer”). For feminine, use la nouvelle; for plural, les nouveaux / les nouvelles.
target_language_example: Le nouveau n'a pas encore appris tous les noms.
native_language_example: The newcomer hasn't learned all the names yet.

meaning: ours (the one(s) that belong to us).
additional_notes: A possessive pronoun used to replace a noun already known from context. It agrees with the thing possessed: le nôtre (masc. singular), la nôtre (fem. singular), les nôtres (plural). Often used in comparisons: « le même que le nôtre » (“the same as ours”).
target_language_example: Ce vélo est le nôtre, pas le leur.
native_language_example: This bike is ours, not theirs.

meaning: bread (as a general or specific loaf).
additional_notes: Often refers to a loaf of bread in everyday situations (cutting it, passing it at the table: « Passe-moi le pain. »). In a broader sense, it can mean bread as a staple food in general (« Le pain a permis… »). Common with verbs like « couper le pain » (to cut the bread) and « rompre le pain » (to break bread, sometimes literally, sometimes meaning to share a meal).
target_language_example: Tu peux me passer le pain, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the bread, please?

additional_notes: A common public green space in a town or city. Masculine noun: le parc (singular), les parcs (plural). Often used with location/distance phrases like « être situé… » (to be located) or « se trouver… » (to be located/found).
target_language_example: Le parc est situé au centre-ville.
native_language_example: The park is located downtown.

additional_notes: Refers to past time or past events. Common in set phrases like « C’est du passé » / « C’est le passé » (“That’s in the past / It’s over”). With « vivre dans le passé », it means being stuck in old memories or old ways of thinking.
target_language_example: Il faut laisser le passé derrière soi.
native_language_example: You have to leave the past behind you.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the person in charge at work or in a place (like a shop, restaurant, or company). It can mean your direct boss, or the owner/manager. Feminine: "la patronne".
target_language_example: Le patron n'est pas là aujourd'hui, il revient demain.
native_language_example: The boss isn't here today; he'll be back tomorrow.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “the country” (a nation): quitter le pays = to leave the country. In some contexts (especially with “dans le pays de…”, or in stories like “le pays des géants”), it can mean a land/realm/region. It can also mean “the countryside” in contrast to the city, depending on context.
target_language_example: Je veux visiter le pays l'année prochaine.
native_language_example: I want to visit the country next year.

additional_notes: The meal you have in the morning. Often used with verbs like prendre (to have/eat): « prendre le petit-déjeuner ». Can also refer to the food itself. Note the hyphen and accent: petit-déjeuner.
target_language_example: On prend le petit-déjeuner à 8 heures.
native_language_example: We have breakfast at 8 o'clock.

additional_notes: The usual French word for the morning meal. Often used with verbs like prendre (to have/eat): « prendre le petit déjeuner »; sauter (to skip): « sauter le petit déjeuner ». In hotels/restaurants you might ask if it’s included: « Le petit déjeuner est-il inclus ? ».
target_language_example: On prend le petit déjeuner à 8 h.
native_language_example: We have breakfast at 8 o’clock.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: definite article + adjective + noun. Used to refer to a specific boy (already known, mentioned, or obvious from context). In stories it can also be used more generally for “the little boy” as a character. Feminine equivalent: « la petite fille ».
target_language_example: Le petit garçon cherche sa maman.
native_language_example: The little boy is looking for his mom.

meaning: the people; the population (especially as a political/social group).
additional_notes: Often used in politics and history to mean “ordinary people” or “the nation’s citizens” seen as a collective (e.g., “le gouvernement du peuple…”). It can also refer to a specific nation/ethnic group (“le peuple chinois”, “le peuple américain”). Usually takes singular agreement in French when treated as one group: “Le peuple a choisi…”.
target_language_example: Le peuple demande plus de justice.
native_language_example: The people are demanding more justice.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what you’re going to do (the plan), how something is organized, or a strategy. Very common in questions like « C’est quoi, le plan ? » / « Quel est le plan ? » meaning “What’s the plan?” You can also talk about changes: « le plan a changé » (“the plan changed”). « le plan B » means “Plan B” (a backup plan).
target_language_example: On fait quoi ce soir ? C'est quoi, le plan ?
native_language_example: What are we doing tonight? What's the plan?

additional_notes: used to form the superlative: le/la/les plus + adjective or adverb means "the most" or "-est" depending on the English word (for example, le plus beau = "the most beautiful"). After a verb, it means "most" (for example, plaire le plus = "please the most"). In le plus ... possible, it gives the idea of "as ... as possible." French also often uses this form where English would say "more" when comparing two things.
target_language_example: C'est le sport que j'aime le plus.
native_language_example: It's the sport I like the most.

meaning: the tallest / the biggest; the greatest (most important).
additional_notes: Superlative of « grand » (tall/big/great). Used with masculine singular nouns (e.g., « le garçon le plus grand »). For feminine, it becomes « la plus grande »; for plural, « les plus grands / les plus grandes ». Can also be used in fixed expressions like « avec le plus grand soin » = “with the greatest care.”
target_language_example: Après Taro, Jiro est le garçon le plus grand.
native_language_example: After Taro, Jiro is the tallest boy.

additional_notes: Superlative of proximity: *proche* = close/near, *le plus proche* = the closest one. It agrees with the noun: **le** plus proche (masc.), **la** plus proche (fem.), **les** plus proches (plural). Common for asking where the nearest place/object is (*le supermarché le plus proche*, *le bureau de poste le plus proche*). With people it can mean emotionally closest: *De qui es-tu le plus proche ?* = Who are you closest to?
target_language_example: Où se trouve le supermarché le plus proche ?
native_language_example: Where is the nearest supermarket?

additional_notes: Superlative form of the adjective *rapide* (“fast/quick”). Use it to compare more than two things/people: *C’est le plus rapide* (“It’s the fastest”). It agrees in gender/number with what it describes: *le plus rapide* (masc. sing.), *la plus rapide* (fem. sing.), *les plus rapides* (plural). You can use it after a noun: *le moyen le plus rapide* (“the fastest way”), or on its own when the noun is understood: *Le plus rapide.* (“The fastest one.”).
target_language_example: C’est le plus rapide pour aller à l’aéroport.
native_language_example: It’s the fastest way to get to the airport.

meaning: as soon as possible; as early as possible.
additional_notes: Used to say you want something done without delay. Very common with commands and requests (e.g., Venez…, Rendez…, Téléphonez…) and with verbs like commencer (to start) or réparer (to fix). You can also shorten it to “au plus tôt” (“as soon/early as possible”).
target_language_example: Envoie-moi les documents le plus tôt possible.
native_language_example: Send me the documents as soon as possible.

additional_notes: Used to urge someone to do something with maximum speed (often like “as soon as possible” when talking about coming back or arriving). It commonly follows an imperative (Cours…, Marche…) or a verb of action (revenir, venir, finir).
target_language_example: Envoie-moi les documents le plus vite possible.
native_language_example: Send me the documents as quickly as possible.

meaning: (non standard) intended to mean “the starting point” (standard French: « le point de départ »).
additional_notes: « Le point de partir » is not idiomatic/grammatical in standard French because « partir » is a verb (“to leave”), and French uses the noun « départ » (“departure”) in this fixed expression: « le point de départ ». If you want natural French, use « le point de départ » for the starting point/basis of a trip, plan, project, or argument. The example below includes « le point de partir » only to match your requested term exactly.
target_language_example: Dans ce document, « le point de partir » est défini à la page 2 (formulation non standard).
native_language_example: In this document, “the point of leaving/starting point” is defined on page 2 (non-standard wording).

meaning: fish (the animal or fish as food).
additional_notes: Usually means “the fish” in context, and can also refer to fish in general as a category (often as food). For an unspecified amount as food, French commonly uses the partitive: « du poisson ». With « le poisson », it can sound generic (“fish, as a food/category”) or specific depending on context.
target_language_example: Elle adore le poisson.
native_language_example: She loves fish.

additional_notes: Used for a physical bridge you cross (over a river, road, valley, etc.). The plural is usually "les ponts." It’s also used in some fixed names like "le pont de Golden Gate" (the Golden Gate Bridge).
target_language_example: On traverse le pont à pied.
native_language_example: We’re crossing the bridge on foot.

additional_notes: Usually refers to having control or influence (political, social, or personal). It can also mean the ability/capacity to do something depending on context (e.g., avoir le pouvoir de + infinitive = “to be able to / to have the power to”).
target_language_example: Il veut garder le pouvoir.
native_language_example: He wants to stay in power.

additional_notes: Used for the first person or thing in a sequence, in time, or in rank. Before a noun: le premier jour = the first day. Used on its own, it can mean 'the first one' or simply 'first'. It agrees with gender and number: la première, les premiers, les premières.
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé le premier.
native_language_example: I arrived first.

meaning: the first train (usually the earliest train of the day).
additional_notes: Used when talking about catching the earliest available train, often in the morning (e.g., « prendre/attraper le premier train », « le premier train du matin »). It can mean the first scheduled departure on a route that day, not necessarily the first train ever.
target_language_example: Demain, je prends le premier train pour arriver à l’heure.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, I’m taking the first train to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone is the first person to perform an action. It is followed by an infinitive: « le premier à + verbe » (e.g., « le premier à arriver » = the first to arrive). It agrees with the person/thing described: « le premier à… » (masc. sing.), « la première à… » (fem. sing.), « les premiers/les premières à… » (plural).
target_language_example: Tom fut le premier à arriver.
native_language_example: Tom was the first to arrive.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how much something costs. Common in shopping/negotiation: « Quel est le prix ? » (What’s the price?), « réduire le prix » (lower the price), « le prix reflète la demande » (price depends on demand).
target_language_example: Je trouve que le prix est trop élevé.
native_language_example: I think the price is too high.

additional_notes: Means a difficulty, question, or situation that needs to be examined or solved. Often used with verbs like "repérer" (identify), "résoudre" (solve), and "examiner" (look into). Note: "problème" is masculine, so it takes "le" (or "un problème").
target_language_example: On a trouvé le problème, maintenant il faut le résoudre.
native_language_example: We found the problem; now we have to solve it.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to mean “the next (one)”: le prochain train (the next train), le prochain bus (the next bus), le prochain village (the next village). It agrees with the noun: la prochaine (fem. singular), les prochains / les prochaines (plural). Also, in a different context, "le prochain" can mean "your neighbor / fellow human" (e.g., aimer son prochain), but in everyday travel-style contexts it usually means “the next.”
target_language_example: Le prochain métro arrive dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: The next subway arrives in five minutes.

meaning: the next train (the one that leaves/arrives after the current time).
additional_notes: Used when asking about schedules or making plans at a station. You can specify a destination: "le prochain train pour Paris". In questions, French often drops "est": "À quelle heure est le prochain train ?" = "What time is the next train?"
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, le prochain train pour Lyon part de quel quai ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what platform does the next train to Lyon leave from?

additional_notes: Often means “teacher” (at school, language class, etc.), not only a university professor. For a female teacher, you’ll often hear/see: « la professeure » (formal) or « la prof » (informal).
target_language_example: Le professeur explique la leçon.
native_language_example: The teacher explains the lesson.

meaning: the project; a planned piece of work/initiative.
additional_notes: Used for an organized plan or undertaking (at work, school, politics, tech, etc.). Common with verbs like commencer/terminer/abandonner un projet and phrases like un projet est en cours (ongoing) or en discussion (being discussed).
target_language_example: On lance le projet lundi.
native_language_example: We’re launching the project on Monday.

meaning: the president (head of a country or organization).
additional_notes: Used for the person who leads a country (e.g., le président français) or an organization/meeting (e.g., le président du club). Often followed by "de" to specify which one: "le président de la République", "le président du conseil". "Président" can also be a title used without the person’s first name.
target_language_example: Le président du club a commencé la réunion à 18 h.
native_language_example: The club president started the meeting at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Means a group of people in general (“the public”) or the people watching/listening to a performance or event (“the audience”). Often used with singular verb forms in French (e.g., « Le public est… »), even though it refers to many people.
target_language_example: Le public a applaudi pendant plusieurs minutes.
native_language_example: The audience applauded for several minutes.

meaning: the neighborhood; a district/area of a town or city.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a part of a city where people live or a specific area/section of town. In expressions like « dans tout le quartier », it means “throughout the whole neighborhood” (everyone nearby can see/hear/know).
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé un bon café dans le quartier.
native_language_example: I found a good café in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Most often means a written report/document (e.g., “finir le rapport,” “résumer le rapport”). In questions like “C’est quoi le rapport ?” or “Quel est le rapport avec… ?”, it means “what’s the connection/what does that have to do with…?” Note: French “rapport” is a false friend—English “rapport” usually means a good relationship, which in French is more like “une bonne entente” / “de bons rapports (avec quelqu’un)”.
target_language_example: Quel est le rapport avec ce que tu viens de dire ?
native_language_example: What does that have to do with what you just said?

additional_notes: Used to refer to what remains after something has been taken/used/eaten. Common patterns: "le reste de + noun" ("le reste de votre équipe" = "the rest of your team") and as a pronoun-like noun by itself ("Je prends le reste" = "I’ll take the rest").
target_language_example: Je vais finir le reste plus tard.
native_language_example: I’ll finish the rest later.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to refer to what remains after a part has been taken, used, or considered. It can refer to things (le reste de la boîte, le reste de la maison) or time (le reste de sa vie, le reste de la journée). Note that in speech and writing, "de" may contract with the following article (e.g., "le reste du gâteau" = "le reste de + le gâteau").
target_language_example: On gardera le reste de ce gâteau pour demain.
native_language_example: We’ll save the rest of this cake for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun (le reste du voyage, le reste du chemin) to mean what remains of something. For a feminine noun, use "le reste de la" (le reste de la journée). Before a vowel or silent h, use "le reste de l'" (le reste de l'eau).
target_language_example: Je garde le reste du gâteau pour demain.
native_language_example: I'm keeping the rest of the cake for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Refers to a male monarch (a king). It’s usually used with an article (le roi) or with a modifier: le roi de + place/country ("the king of...") or le roi + name/title ("King Louis"). Feminine: la reine ("the queen").
target_language_example: Le roi de France a vécu au château de Versailles.
native_language_example: The king of France lived at the Palace of Versailles.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens in the end (the outcome of an action, event, effort, test, etc.). Often followed by "de" to show the cause: "le résultat de ..." (the result of ...).
target_language_example: Au final, le résultat n'était pas celui qu'on espérait.
native_language_example: In the end, the result wasn’t what we were hoping for.

additional_notes: Used for sand in general (beach sand, desert sand, sand blown by the wind, etc.). It’s a masculine noun: le sable. You commonly see it with prepositions like sur (on) or dans (in): sur le sable, dans le sable. With an unspecified quantity, French often uses the partitive (du sable), but you’ll still use le sable when referring to sand as a defined substance or in general statements.
target_language_example: Le sable sur la plage est très chaud.
native_language_example: The sand on the beach is very hot.

additional_notes: Common word for a bag (plastic bag, shopping bag, backpack, etc.). Used with a specific bag known from context: Où est le sac ? = “Where is the bag?” Can be modified: un sac en plastique (a plastic bag).
target_language_example: Tu peux porter le sac, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you carry the bag, please?

additional_notes: In a home, *le salon* is the main room where people relax, sit on the sofa, watch TV, and receive guests. Don’t confuse it with *la salle à manger* (dining room). *Salon* can also mean a “salon” (e.g., hair salon or an event), but in everyday home contexts it usually means “living room.”
target_language_example: On se retrouve dans le salon après le dîner.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in the living room after dinner.

additional_notes: Used literally for blood in the body or from a wound. Common in fixed expressions and idioms (e.g., “Ça me fait bouillir le sang” = “It makes my blood boil,” i.e., it makes me very angry). Note: in many everyday contexts French also uses the partitive “du sang” (“there was blood”), but the definite form “le sang” is used for blood as a general substance or concept (“Le sang circule…”).
target_language_example: Le sang circule à travers les veines.
native_language_example: Blood circulates through the veins.

additional_notes: Used for something hidden or kept private (a fact, plan, or explanation). Common with verbs like garder (to keep), connaître (to know), découvrir (to discover), révéler / dévoiler (to reveal). Often followed by de + noun to specify what it’s about: le secret de + [something].
target_language_example: Je te dirai le secret, mais promets de ne rien dire.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you the secret, but promise not to say anything.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or explain what something means: *le sens de cette phrase/ce mot/cette image*. In more concrete contexts, *le sens de* can also mean the direction or orientation of something (e.g., *le sens de la marche* = direction of travel).
target_language_example: Quel est le sens de ce mot ?
native_language_example: What is the meaning of this word?

meaning: the only one to / the only one who can.
additional_notes: Used to say that one person (or thing) is unique in doing something. It’s followed by an infinitive (often with pouvoir, avoir, être, etc.). It agrees in gender/number: le seul à (m. sing.), la seule à (f. sing.), les seuls à (m. pl.), les seules à (f. pl.). You can negate it: ne pas être le seul à… (“not be the only one to…”).
target_language_example: Il est le seul à pouvoir le faire.
native_language_example: He is the only one who can do it.

meaning: his/hers/its/theirs (the one that belongs to him/her/it/them).
additional_notes: "Le sien" is a possessive pronoun (masculine singular) that replaces a noun: "Mon bureau… le sien" = "my office… his/hers." It agrees with the thing owned (masc. sing. = le sien), not with the owner. Other forms: la sienne (fem. sing.), les siens / les siennes (plural). It can refer to different people depending on context (his, hers, theirs).
target_language_example: Je prends mon manteau et il prend le sien.
native_language_example: I’m taking my coat and he’s taking his.

additional_notes: A common noun meaning the absence of sound or speech. Often used with verbs like garder le silence (to keep silent), régner (to reign/prevail: “silence fell”), or in more abstract phrases about dignity/wisdom (in silence).
target_language_example: Après l'annonce, le silence a régné dans la salle.
native_language_example: After the announcement, silence filled the room.

additional_notes: Usually means the surface you walk on. Indoors it’s the floor; outdoors it’s the ground/soil. Common with verbs like regarder (look at), balayer (sweep), and être recouvert de (to be covered with).
target_language_example: J’ai fait tomber mes clés par terre : elles sont sur le sol.
native_language_example: I dropped my keys on the ground: they’re on the floor/ground.

additional_notes: Refers to the sun in the sky. Common with verbs like se lever (to rise) and se coucher (to set): « Le soleil se lève » (the sun rises), « Le soleil se couche » (the sun sets).
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, le soleil brille.
native_language_example: Today, the sun is shining.

additional_notes: A simple present-tense statement about sunny weather. It can be used literally (about the weather) or more figuratively to mean things are going well (“the sun shines for everyone”). For questions, you often invert the verb: “Le soleil brille-t-il dehors ?”
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, le soleil brille et il fait doux.
native_language_example: Today, the sun is shining and it’s mild.

meaning: 'the sun is' (used to describe the sun).
additional_notes: "Le soleil" means "the sun". "est" is the verb "to be" (il/elle/on est). You use "le soleil est" before an adjective (e.g., grand, rouge, important) or before a place phrase with "dans/au-dessus de" to say where the sun is.
target_language_example: Le soleil est très chaud aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: The sun is very hot today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about sunrise as a general fact, a regular event, or something happening now. The verb is reflexive: « se lever » = “to rise / to get up.” You can change the time: « Le soleil se lève à 6 h. » (at 6).
target_language_example: On part tôt, quand le soleil se lève.
native_language_example: We’re leaving early, when the sun rises.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the highest point (peak) of a mountain. Often used with verbs like voir (to see), atteindre (to reach), and être couvert de (to be covered with).
target_language_example: Après trois heures de marche, nous avons atteint le sommet de la montagne.
native_language_example: After three hours of hiking, we reached the top of the mountain.

additional_notes: Refers to sound in general, the sound produced by something ("le son de la radio"), or the audio/volume setting on a device ("Mettre le son", "baisser le son"). Common with adjectives like "fort" (loud) and "faible" (quiet/low).
target_language_example: Le son est trop fort, tu peux le baisser ?
native_language_example: The sound is too loud—can you turn it down?

meaning: the show; the performance (a play, concert, etc.).
additional_notes: Used for an event people watch, especially in the performing arts (concert, theater, comedy show). In fixed phrases like « Que le spectacle commence ! » it means “Let the show begin!” Can also refer more broadly to a “spectacle” (something impressive to watch), but the common beginner meaning is “show/performance.”
target_language_example: Êtes-vous prêts pour le spectacle ?
native_language_example: Are you ready for the show?

meaning: the system (an organized way things work; an organization; a computer/technical system).
additional_notes: Used for a structured set of rules/processes (e.g., school/healthcare/the political system), a technical setup (IT system), or “how things work” in a place (“connaître le système” = know the ropes). In phrases like “Nique le système”, it refers to “the system” as an institution and the tone is vulgar/defiant, but the term “le système” itself is neutral.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas bien le système, tu peux m’expliquer ?
native_language_example: I don’t really understand the system—can you explain it to me?

additional_notes: Most commonly means a painting/artwork (like one hanging on a wall). It can also mean a board used for writing ("le tableau" in a classroom) or a chart/table in documents, depending on context.
target_language_example: J’aime beaucoup le tableau : les couleurs sont magnifiques.
native_language_example: I really like the painting: the colors are beautiful.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the language called Tamazight. In French, languages are often used with the definite article (le / la / l’): e.g., le français, l’anglais. You can use it with verbs like parler (to speak), apprendre (to learn), lire (to read), pratiquer (to practice).
target_language_example: J'apprends le tamazight en ligne.
native_language_example: I'm learning Tamazight online.

additional_notes: French uses the same word for both 'time' and 'weather'. In expressions like avoir le temps and prendre le temps de, it means 'time' or 'enough time'; with words like beau, mauvais, changer, or permettre, it means 'weather'.
target_language_example: Tu as le temps de prendre un café ?
native_language_example: Do you have time to grab a coffee?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say whether someone has enough time to do something. Often in the negative: « ne pas avoir le temps de + infinitive » = “not to have time to…”. Can also be used in questions and the future: « Tu as le temps de… ? » / « Vous aurez le temps de… ».
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas le temps de t'appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to call you tonight.

meaning: "the weather is…" or "time is…" (it depends on context).
additional_notes: Le temps can mean either (1) "weather" (talking about conditions outside: Le temps est horrible / Le temps est à la neige), or (2) "time" in a general or abstract sense (Le temps est précieux; Le temps est écoulé). In English, you usually choose either “The weather is…” or “Time is…”, not “The time is…” unless you mean the clock time.
target_language_example: Aujourd’hui, le temps est très froid.
native_language_example: Today, the weather is very cold.

meaning: "the time that" / "the amount of time that" (how long something takes).
additional_notes: Used before a clause to talk about duration: *le temps que + verb* = “the time it takes for…” / “the amount of time that…”. Common in expressions like **Peu importe le temps que ça prend/prendra** (“No matter how long it takes”).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas le temps que ça va prendre.
native_language_example: I don’t know how long it’s going to take.

additional_notes: Means "tea" as a drink. Used with the definite article (le) when speaking about tea in general or as the item being discussed/served. In "prendre le thé," it often means having tea (and sometimes a small snack) as an afternoon break or social moment.
target_language_example: Je prends souvent le thé après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: I often have tea after lunch.

additional_notes: Possessive pronoun used to replace a noun already understood from context (instead of repeating it). It agrees with the thing possessed (not the person): le tien (masc. sing.), la tienne (fem. sing.), les tiens/les tiennes (plural). Often used after comparisons or questions: «Quel est le tien ?» = «Which one is yours?»
target_language_example: Je ne trouve pas mon stylo : lequel est le tien ?
native_language_example: I can’t find my pen: which one is yours?

additional_notes: Used for the roof of a house/building (also of a car). In sentences it often appears with building-related verbs like réparer (repair), renforcer (reinforce), arracher (tear off), or with damage words like défoncé (caved in/damaged).
target_language_example: Il faut réparer le toit avant l'hiver.
native_language_example: We need to repair the roof before winter.

additional_notes: Refers to a railway train. With le, it usually means a specific train understood from context. Common beginner phrases include prendre le train (take the train), rater le train (miss the train), and attraper le train (catch the train).
target_language_example: Nous attendons le train sur le quai.
native_language_example: We're waiting for the train on the platform.

additional_notes: Usually means “work” in general or “the job/task that needs to be done,” as in finishing or doing something specific. With the definite article (le), it can refer to work as a concept (e.g., work is a duty) or to a particular piece of work already known in context (“finish the work”).
target_language_example: On doit finir le travail avant demain.
native_language_example: We have to finish the work before tomorrow.

additional_notes: A common, neutral term for an earthquake. It’s masculine (le). Often used with verbs like provoquer (cause), secouer (shake), détruire (destroy), arriver (happen/occur), and ressentir (feel).
target_language_example: Après le tremblement de terre, les gens sont sortis dans la rue.
native_language_example: After the earthquake, people went out into the street.

additional_notes: Means a telephone (landline or phone in general). Used with common verbs like décrocher le téléphone (to pick up the receiver/answer), le téléphone sonne (the phone is ringing), and le téléphone ne fonctionne pas (the phone isn’t working).
