target_language_example: Personne ne me répond quand j’appelle.
native_language_example: No one answers me when I call.

additional_notes: Used to start a negative sentence: **Personne ne + verb + nous** = “Nobody/No one + verb + us.” The **ne** is part of French negation with *personne* (and is often dropped in casual speech: *Personne nous croit*). The object pronoun **nous** (“us”) comes before the verb: *Personne ne nous croit* = “Nobody believes us.”
target_language_example: Personne ne nous aide ici.
native_language_example: Nobody helps us here.

additional_notes: Used to say that it’s impossible for anyone to do something. It’s a negative sentence: "personne" means "nobody/no one" (not "person" here), and it pairs with "ne" before the verb: "Personne ne peut + infinitive" (e.g., "Personne ne peut venir."). In informal spoken French, "ne" is often dropped: "Personne peut..."
target_language_example: Personne ne peut répondre à cette question.
native_language_example: No one can answer this question.

additional_notes: Used to say that zero people were able to do something in the past. It’s the negative pronoun personne (“no one”) with ne + the imperfect of pouvoir (pouvait) for ongoing/possible ability in the past. Often followed by an infinitive: personne ne pouvait + verb (e.g., entendre, voir, refuser). In informal speech, ne is often dropped: Personne pouvait…
target_language_example: Personne ne pouvait entrer sans billet.
native_language_example: No one could enter without a ticket.

additional_notes: Common negative pattern: "personne" + "ne" + verb. It means “no one” (not “a person”) when used with "ne". Often followed by an indirect question: "personne ne sait ce que/qui/où/quand/pourquoi/comment..." (= no one knows what/who/where/when/why/how...). You can also add "rien": "personne ne sait rien" (= nobody knows anything).
target_language_example: Personne ne sait pourquoi il est parti si tôt.
native_language_example: No one knows why he left so early.

additional_notes: Used to say the location of someone/something is unknown. Often followed by a subject + verb (e.g., « Personne ne sait où il est. »). Note that « personne » in a negative structure (« personne ne… ») means “nobody,” not “person.”
target_language_example: Personne ne sait où mon téléphone est.
native_language_example: Nobody knows where my phone is.

additional_notes: Common negative pattern: "Personne" (nobody) + "ne" + past tense of "savoir" (to know). It’s often followed by a question word or clause: "personne ne savait où/pourquoi/qui/quoi…" (= no one knew where/why/who/what…). In informal speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Personne savait…"
target_language_example: Personne ne savait quoi répondre.
native_language_example: No one knew what to answer.

meaning: “nobody … you” (no one does something to you).
additional_notes: Used for negation with **personne** (“nobody/no one”) as the subject: **Personne ne + verb**. **Te** is the object pronoun meaning “you” (to you/you as a direct object) before the verb: *Personne ne te voit* = “No one sees you.” Often pairs with verbs like *demander*, *forcer*, *voir*, *trouver*, etc.
target_language_example: Personne ne te connaît ici.
native_language_example: Nobody knows you here.

additional_notes: Standard French negation: **personne** (“no one”) is used with **ne** before the verb: *Personne ne + verbe…* (often *ne* is dropped in casual speech: *Personne veut…*). With **plus**, it means “no one anymore”: *Plus personne ne veut…*
target_language_example: Personne ne veut attendre aussi longtemps.
native_language_example: No one wants to wait that long.

meaning: "no one has (done something to you)" / "nobody has".
additional_notes: Used to say that nobody did something to you (or for you) in the past, using the passé composé. Pattern: « Personne ne + vous + a + past participle… » (e.g., « Personne ne vous a cru » = Nobody believed you). « Vous » comes before the auxiliary « a » because it’s an object pronoun (to you / you). In everyday speech, « ne » is often dropped: « Personne vous a… »
target_language_example: Personne ne vous a prévenus à temps.
native_language_example: No one warned you in time.

additional_notes: Used to say something is pointless or not worth doing. Often appears with "une" (une perte de temps) or as an exclamation: "Quelle perte de temps !" You can also intensify it informally with words like "sacrée".
target_language_example: Faire la queue pendant une heure, c’est une perte de temps.
native_language_example: Waiting in line for an hour is a waste of time.

additional_notes: A common noun for the first meal of the day. Used with verbs like "prendre" (to have/eat) or "faire" (to make/prepare): "prendre le/son petit-déjeuner". Often preceded by "le" when speaking in general ("pour le petit-déjeuner" = for breakfast).
target_language_example: Je prends un café au petit-déjeuner.
native_language_example: I have a coffee for breakfast.

additional_notes: Means your son or daughter’s child (a “grandson” or “granddaughter”). Often used in the plural: « des petits-enfants » (grandchildren). The gender-specific forms are « petit-fils » (grandson) and « petite-fille » (granddaughter).
target_language_example: Chaque petit-enfant reçoit un cadeau à Noël.
native_language_example: Each grandchild receives a present at Christmas.

additional_notes: Means “grandson” (your child’s son). Usually written with a hyphen: petit-fils. Feminine equivalent: petite-fille (“granddaughter”). Possessives are common: mon/ton/son petit-fils, votre petit-fils, etc.
target_language_example: Mon petit-fils a cinq ans.
native_language_example: My grandson is five years old.

additional_notes: Means “boyfriend” (someone you’re dating). The feminine form is *petite amie* (“girlfriend”). It can be used with possessives (*mon/ton/son petit ami*) or with *un/une* (*un petit ami*).
target_language_example: Je te présente mon petit ami.
native_language_example: Let me introduce you to my boyfriend.

meaning: the restroom/toilet (a polite euphemism); also “a small corner/spot.”
additional_notes: Most often used as a polite, indirect way to say you need to use the toilet: « aller au petit coin ». Depending on context, it can also mean a literal “little corner” (e.g., a small nook or area in a room). In the toilet sense, it’s familiar/polite but not formal.
target_language_example: Je dois aller au petit coin.
native_language_example: I need to go to the restroom.

additional_notes: Common, casual way to talk about someone’s boyfriend, especially in teen/young adult contexts. It can also sound a bit “cute” or slightly minimizing depending on tone. Feminine form: « petite copine » (girlfriend).
target_language_example: Je te présente mon petit copain, Lucas.
native_language_example: Let me introduce you to my boyfriend, Lucas.

meaning: little finger; (in “Mon petit doigt me l’a dit”) “a little bird told me”.
additional_notes: Literally means “little finger” (pinky). In the common idiom « Mon petit doigt me l’a dit », it means you won’t say your source (“I heard it somehow / someone told me, but I’m not telling who”). You may also see it used figuratively to mean doing something very easily (“with my little finger”).
target_language_example: Mon petit doigt me dit que tu prépares une surprise.
native_language_example: A little bird tells me you’re preparing a surprise.

additional_notes: The everyday French word for the morning meal. You can use it with verbs like prendre (to have/eat): « Je prends mon petit déjeuner. » It can also be used with préparer (to prepare) or as a question when offering: « Un petit déjeuner ? »
target_language_example: On prend le petit déjeuner à 7 h.
native_language_example: We have breakfast at 7 o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a male sibling who is younger than you. It can also be used figuratively to mean someone you treat like a younger brother ("like a little brother"). In French, "petit" here usually refers to age/younger, not physical size.
target_language_example: Mon petit frère a commencé le lycée cette année.
native_language_example: My little brother started high school this year.

additional_notes: Literally “small/little boy.” Often used affectionately for your son (“mon petit garçon”) even if he’s not very young. With an article it can mean any young boy (“un petit garçon”).
target_language_example: Je vais chercher mon petit garçon à l’école.
native_language_example: I'm going to pick up my little boy from school.

additional_notes: Often used with prepositions like « au petit matin » (= at daybreak/very early in the morning) or « jusqu’au petit matin » (= until early morning, e.g., after partying). It refers to the first hours of the morning, around dawn, before the day is fully underway.
target_language_example: On s'est levés au petit matin pour prendre le premier train.
native_language_example: We got up at daybreak to catch the first train.

meaning: a bread roll (a small piece of bread).
additional_notes: Common in bakeries and cafés. Often used as a general term for a small roll; depending on the type, you may also see more specific items like "petit pain au lait" (a soft milk roll). Note: French "pain" means "bread" (not English "pain").
target_language_example: Je voudrais un petit pain, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a bread roll, please.

additional_notes: Used to describe a slow, progressive change over time. It can go after the verb (Il apprend petit à petit.) or at the start of the sentence for emphasis (Petit à petit, il apprend.). Often implies patience/step-by-step progress.
target_language_example: Je me suis habitué petit à petit à la vie ici.
native_language_example: I gradually got used to life here.

additional_notes: Means your son’s or daughter’s daughter (a female grandchild). Don’t confuse with "petite fille" (without the hyphen), which usually means “little girl.” You can also use it with a name in apposition: "ma petite-fille, Lizzy".
target_language_example: Ma petite-fille vient dormir à la maison ce week-end.
native_language_example: My granddaughter is coming to sleep over at our place this weekend.

additional_notes: Means a (romantic) girlfriend; possessives are common: ma/ta/sa petite amie. Often contrasts with ex-petite amie (“ex-girlfriend”). Not used for a simple female friend (that’s "amie" or "une copine" depending on context).
target_language_example: J’ai une petite amie depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: I’ve had a girlfriend for two years.

additional_notes: Literally “little (female) friend,” but it commonly means “girlfriend,” especially in casual speech. It can sound a bit informal or youthful compared with “ma copine.” Context makes it clear whether it’s romantic or just a friend, but in most everyday situations it’s understood as romantic.
target_language_example: Il sort avec sa petite copine depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: He’s been going out with his girlfriend for two years.

meaning: little girl; young daughter or granddaughter (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally “small girl.” Often means “little girl” in general (e.g., Quelle jolie petite fille !). With a possessive (ma/sa/notre), it can mean either “my/our daughter” (if she’s young) or “my/our granddaughter” (very common: ma petite-fille). If you mean “granddaughter” clearly, you’ll often see it written with a hyphen: petite-fille.
target_language_example: Ma petite fille adore les histoires avant de dormir.
native_language_example: My little girl/my granddaughter loves stories before going to sleep.

meaning: "little mouse"; also an affectionate nickname, and the "Tooth Fairy" in French.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: a small mouse (e.g., in nature). Figurative: used like a pet name for someone small, quiet, or discreet (often addressed directly: « petite souris »). In children’s stories, « la petite souris » is the character who takes lost baby teeth (the French equivalent of the Tooth Fairy).
target_language_example: Quand j’étais enfant, je mettais ma dent sous l’oreiller pour la petite souris.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I put my tooth under the pillow for the Tooth Fairy.

additional_notes: Means your sister who is younger than you. In speech it can also be used as a direct form of address (“Little sis.”). “Petite” agrees with “sœur” (feminine), so it’s always “petite sœur” (not *petit*).
target_language_example: Ma petite sœur arrive demain.
native_language_example: My little sister is arriving tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to refer to “regular” people as a group. Depending on context, it can sound affectionate (e.g., addressing humble folk) or condescending (like “little people”). Note the grammar: even though *gens* is masculine plural, an adjective placed before it often takes the feminine plural form: *de petites gens*.
target_language_example: Il se moque des petites gens et de leurs soucis.
native_language_example: He makes fun of ordinary people and their worries.

additional_notes: Plural of "petit-enfant" (grandchild). Literally "small children," but it means your children’s children. Often used with possessives: "mes/tes/ses/nos/vos/leurs petits-enfants".
target_language_example: Mes petits-enfants viennent nous voir ce week-end.
native_language_example: My grandchildren are coming to see us this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say that only a small number of people do something or are affected by something. It’s followed by a verb: « Peu de gens + verb ». In negative contexts it often implies “hardly anyone.”
target_language_example: Peu de gens comprennent vraiment ce problème.
native_language_example: Few people really understand this problem.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have much time available. Often appears as: « J’ai peu de temps » (I have little time) or « peu de temps après… » (a short time after…). You can intensify it with « très »: « très peu de temps » (very little time).
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai peu de temps aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have much time today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not important, or that the result is the same in any case. Often followed by a clause with **où / quand / comment / qui / ce que** (“no matter where/when/how/who/what”), or by a noun: **peu importe le temps** (“no matter the time/how long”). Can also be used alone as an answer meaning “doesn’t matter / whatever.”
target_language_example: Peu importe ce que tu choisis, je te soutiendrai.
native_language_example: No matter what you choose, I’ll support you.

meaning: to not matter; to be unimportant.
additional_notes: Often used as an impersonal expression meaning “it doesn’t matter.” In everyday French you’ll very commonly see it conjugated as **peu importe**: *Peu importe !* (“It doesn’t matter!”). It can be followed by a noun (*Peu importe le prix*), or by **que** + subjunctive (*Peu importe que tu viennes ou non*).
target_language_example: Peu importer le prix, je le veux quand même.
native_language_example: The price doesn’t matter; I want it anyway.

additional_notes: Most often used as **à peu près** (= “about/approximately”). It can be used with numbers (**Il est 8 heures, à peu près.**) or with general statements (**C’est à peu près la même chose.**).
target_language_example: J’y serai dans dix minutes, à peu près.
native_language_example: I’ll be there in about ten minutes.

additional_notes: Describes something happening slowly over time, step by step. Often placed after the verb (e.g., "ça change peu à peu").
target_language_example: Je me suis habitué peu à peu à la vie ici.
native_language_example: I got used to life here little by little.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as **un peu plus** (“a little more”). Used to add a small amount in comparisons (**un peu plus + adjective/adverb + que** = “a little more … than”) or to ask for a small additional amount on its own (**Un petit peu plus.** = “A tiny bit more.”).
target_language_example: Tu peux parler un peu plus lentement, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little more slowly, please?

meaning: a terrible fright; to be very scared.
additional_notes: Used with "avoir une peur bleue de" (to be terrified of something/someone) or "faire une peur bleue à quelqu’un" (to scare someone a lot). This is an idiomatic expression: it doesn’t translate word-for-word into English.
target_language_example: J’ai une peur bleue des araignées.
native_language_example: I’m terrified of spiders.

additional_notes: Used in the expression **avoir peur de** = “to be afraid of.” It can be followed by a **noun/person** (peur de lui, peur de sa femme) or by an **infinitive** to say you’re afraid to do something (peur de le faire, peur de mourir).
target_language_example: J'ai peur de parler en public.
native_language_example: I'm afraid to speak in public.

additional_notes: Used after the verb phrase "avoir peur de" (to be afraid of): "avoir peur de la mort" = "to be afraid of death." You can also say "la peur de la mort" (the fear of death) as a noun phrase.
target_language_example: Il dit qu'il n'a pas peur de la mort.
native_language_example: He says he's not afraid of death.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being afraid when it’s dark (often said about children, but can describe anyone). With the verb: « avoir peur du noir » = “to be afraid of the dark.” You can also say « vaincre/surmonter sa peur du noir » = “to overcome one’s fear of the dark.”
target_language_example: Quand j’étais petit, j’avais peur du noir.
native_language_example: When I was little, I was afraid of the dark.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a clause to express uncertainty. It’s slightly more formal than "peut-être" alone. You can also say "Peut-être que…" + normal word order (Peut-être que c’est vrai), or omit "que" and invert in more formal style: "Peut-être est-ce vrai."
target_language_example: Peut-être que je viendrai demain.
native_language_example: Maybe I’ll come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or a possibility. It can stand alone as a short answer ("Peut-être." = "Maybe.") or introduce a sentence: "Peut-être qu'on devrait rentrer." You can also see a more formal/literary word order without "que": "Peut-être me trompé-je" (inversion), meaning "Perhaps I’m mistaken."
target_language_example: Peut-être qu’on ira demain.
native_language_example: Maybe we’ll go tomorrow.

additional_notes:
Used to make a cautious suggestion or proposal. 
- peut-être = “maybe/perhaps” 
- devrions-nous = “should we” (conditional of devoir, used for polite/soft advice)
Often followed by an infinitive: « Peut-être devrions-nous + verbe » (e.g., attendre, parler, annuler). Word order can also be: « Nous devrions peut-être… » = “Maybe we should…”.
target_language_example: Peut-être devrions-nous attendre encore cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Maybe we should wait another five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty before a full sentence: "Peut-être que + subject + verb..." In everyday speech, "que" is often dropped: "Peut-être j’ai tort."
target_language_example: Peut-être que je viendrai ce soir.
native_language_example: Maybe I'll come tonight.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a guess or possibility. Often followed by a noun or description: « Peut-être que c'est le destin. » In everyday speech, « que » is sometimes dropped: « Peut-être c'est… » (more casual).
target_language_example: Peut-être que c'est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: Maybe it's a good idea.

additional_notes: "Peut-elle" is the verb "pouvoir" (to be able to, can) in the present tense (elle peut) with inversion (peut-elle) used to form a formal question. In everyday speech, people often use "Est-ce qu’elle peut… ?" or "Elle peut… ?" instead.
target_language_example: Peut-elle venir ce soir ?
native_language_example: Can she come tonight?

additional_notes: Used to form a yes/no question with inversion: verb + subject pronoun (peut + il). Common in more formal French and in writing; in speech you often hear "Est-ce qu'il peut… ?" or "Il peut… ?". "Il" can mean "he" or "it" depending on what it refers to (a person/thing/idea mentioned earlier).
target_language_example: Peut-il venir ce soir ?
native_language_example: Can he come tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask a question with inversion: "peut" (can) + "on" (we/one/people in general). Often corresponds to English "can we…?" (suggesting permission or possibility) or more formal/general "can one…?" / "is it possible to…?".
target_language_example: Peut-on entrer ici sans billet ?
native_language_example: Can we enter here without a ticket?

additional_notes: Formed with peut (the 3rd-person singular of pouvoir, “can”) + faire (“do/make”). The exact English translation depends on what follows: faire quelque chose = “do something,” faire des erreurs = “make mistakes.” In other sentences, the subject may change: je peux faire, tu peux faire, ils peuvent faire, etc.
target_language_example: Il peut faire ça demain.
native_language_example: He can do that tomorrow.

additional_notes: "peut" is the 3rd-person singular of "pouvoir" (can / to be able to). "le" means "it" (a thing/idea previously mentioned). Common with subjects like "il/elle/on" (e.g., "On peut le faire" = "We/one can do it"). Used for ability or possibility; in encouragement it’s like “We can do it.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, on peut le faire ensemble.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we can do it together.

additional_notes: Used when the verb that follows is reflexive or reciprocal: "pouvoir" (can/may) + "se" + infinitive (e.g., "peut se révéler" = can turn out to be / can prove to be; "peut se défaire" = can come undone; "peut se rencontrer" = can meet each other). "Se" changes to "s'" before a vowel or silent h: "peut s'expliquer". In negatives you often see "ne peut se ... pas" (spoken French often drops "ne").
target_language_example: Ça peut se passer très vite.
native_language_example: That can happen very fast.

additional_notes: 3rd-person singular of pouvoir + être. It expresses possibility: something or someone can/may be a certain way. Don't confuse it with the adverb peut-être (with a hyphen), which means 'maybe'.
target_language_example: Ce travail peut être stressant au début.
native_language_example: This job can be stressful at first.

additional_notes: Inverted form of « ils peuvent » used to ask a question in a more formal/written style. Common with a subject noun too: « Les oiseaux peuvent-ils… ? ». In everyday speech, you’ll often hear « Ils peuvent… ? » or « Est-ce qu’ils peuvent… ? ».
target_language_example: Peuvent-ils venir demain matin ?
native_language_example: Can they come tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: "Peuvent" is the 3rd-person plural of "pouvoir" (can/may), used with "être" (to be). It expresses possibility or general ability: "Deux choses peuvent être vraies" = "Two things can be true." With negation: "ne peuvent être" = "cannot be" (often written "ne peuvent pas être" in everyday speech). In more formal style, you may see "ne peuvent être" without "pas" (e.g., "Ils ne peuvent être sauvés").
target_language_example: Ces règles peuvent être difficiles à comprendre.
native_language_example: These rules can be hard to understand.

additional_notes: Question form of tu peux, using inversion. It means 'can you...?' when speaking to one person you address as tu. It can be a real question about ability, or a request like 'could you...?'
target_language_example: Peux-tu m'aider une minute ?
native_language_example: Can you help me for a minute?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone for information. Literally “can you tell me,” with inversion (peux-tu) to form a question. Often followed by an indirect question: "Peux-tu me dire ce que… / qui… / où… / quand… / pourquoi… / comment…" or by a noun: "Peux-tu me dire ton adresse ?" A close equivalent is "Tu peux me dire… ?" (a bit less formal).
target_language_example: Peux-tu me dire où est la gare, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where the train station is, please?

additional_notes: A polite question using inversion (peux-tu) with the verb donner (“to give”) + indirect object me (“to me”). Often followed by a noun: Peux-tu me donner des conseils / la recette / une tranche de pain ? You can also use it more generally: Que peux-tu me donner ? = “What can you give me?”
target_language_example: Peux-tu me donner ton adresse, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you give me your address, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (tu = informal singular "you") to do something for you and others. Often followed by an infinitive (peux-tu nous conduire… = can you drive us…) or by a verb like dire/parler (peux-tu nous dire… = can you tell us…). In questions it’s common to use inversion: "peux-tu".
target_language_example: Peux-tu nous aider avec ces valises ?
native_language_example: Can you help us with these suitcases?

meaning: "can you" (followed by a reflexive verb with "te").
additional_notes: Used to ask someone if they can do something when the verb is reflexive (uses "se" in the infinitive). Here, "peux-tu" = "can you" and "te" = "yourself/you" as the reflexive pronoun (e.g., "te rappeler" = remember, "te renseigner" = find out/get information, "te taire" = be quiet). Word order is typical of a question: verb + "-tu" + pronoun + infinitive.
target_language_example: Peux-tu te dépêcher, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you hurry up, please?

additional_notes: "Peux" is the 1st-person singular of "pouvoir" (I can), used with an infinitive: "je peux utiliser...". It’s common for asking permission politely (often in a question: "Est-ce que je peux utiliser… ?") or stating ability/permission to use something.
target_language_example: Je peux utiliser ton ordinateur un instant ?
native_language_example: Can I use your computer for a moment?

additional_notes: "Peux" is the 1st person singular of "pouvoir" (I can / I’m allowed to). With "venir" it often expresses ability/availability ("I can come") or asks permission in a question ("Je peux venir ?" = "Can I come?/May I come?"). In more formal situations, you may also hear "Puis-je venir ?".
target_language_example: Je peux venir avec toi demain ?
native_language_example: Can I come with you tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used as an adverbial phrase to describe how someone is walking/standing ("marcher/sortir pieds nus"), or as a noun phrase ("ses pieds nus" = "his/her bare feet"). Often used with verbs like "marcher", "sortir", "rester".
target_language_example: Les enfants courent pieds nus dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The kids run barefoot in the garden.

additional_notes: Used when flipping a coin to make a random choice. You’ll often hear it as a question: « Pile ou face ? » (“Heads or tails?”). The verb is usually « tirer à pile ou face » (“to flip a coin / decide by coin toss”).
target_language_example: On décide à pile ou face : si c’est pile, tu commences.
native_language_example: We’ll decide by a coin toss: if it’s heads, you start.

additional_notes: Used literally for an automatic control system (plane, boat, car), and very often figuratively to mean doing something automatically/out of habit. Common phrases: « passer en pilote automatique » = “to go on autopilot / switch to autopilot”, « couper le pilote automatique » = “turn off the autopilot.”
target_language_example: Après une longue journée, je fais le dîner en pilote automatique.
native_language_example: After a long day, I make dinner on autopilot.

additional_notes: Refers to the sport played on a table with small paddles and a light ball. In French you can say either « ping-pong » (very common) or « tennis de table » (more formal/official). Often used with « jouer au ping-pong » (to play ping-pong).
target_language_example: On joue au ping-pong après le dîner ?
native_language_example: Shall we play ping-pong after dinner?

additional_notes: A noun for an outdoor meal where you bring food (often eaten on the grass, in a park, etc.). Used with common verbs like faire (to have/organize), aller à (to go to), and annuler (to cancel): faire un pique-nique, aller au pique-nique/en pique-nique, annuler le pique-nique.
target_language_example: On fait un pique-nique au parc demain ?
native_language_example: Are we having a picnic in the park tomorrow?

meaning: to throw a tantrum; to have a meltdown (to “freak out”).
additional_notes: Used mainly in spoken French to describe someone (child or adult) suddenly getting very angry or upset and reacting dramatically (shouting, crying, refusing, etc.). Often followed by "parce que / quand" to explain why, or used in the negative imperative to tell someone not to do it: "Ne pique pas une crise !"
target_language_example: Il va piquer une crise si on lui dit non.
native_language_example: He’s going to throw a tantrum if they tell him no.

additional_notes: Used for an official document that proves who you are (e.g., passport, national ID card, residence permit; often also accepted: a driver’s license). Common in situations like hotels, banks, airports, or police checks. Often said as: « Une pièce d'identité, s'il vous plaît. »
target_language_example: Vous avez une pièce d'identité sur vous ?
native_language_example: Do you have an ID on you?

additional_notes: Used for a theatrical play (a written work and/or its stage performance). Very common with verbs like voir (to see), jouer (to perform), écrire (to write), and with adjectives like bonne/courte. Not the same as une pièce (a coin/room/piece) on its own—the context of théâtre makes it clear.
target_language_example: On va voir une pièce de théâtre ce soir.
native_language_example: We’re going to see a play tonight.

additional_notes: Used in a meal/menu to refer to the main dish, typically served after the starter (entrée) and before dessert. In a restaurant you might hear it as a question ("Et le plat principal ?") when ordering or when the main course is about to be served.
target_language_example: Comme plat principal, je vais prendre le poulet rôti.
native_language_example: For the main course, I’m going to have the roast chicken.

meaning: platform (a raised area or base; also a service/app “platform”).
additional_notes: Often used for a physical platform (train/metro platform, loading platform, raised structure). It can also mean a technical/digital platform (e.g., an online platform). Spelling is sometimes seen as "plateforme" without the hyphen.
target_language_example: On se retrouve sur la plate-forme 2.
native_language_example: Let’s meet on platform 2.

meaning: “Do you like it?” / “Does it please you?”; also (used alone, very formal) “Pardon?” / “Come again?”
additional_notes: From the verb « plaire » (“to please”). In the inverted question form (« plaît » + « -il »), it asks whether something is pleasing to someone: « Cela te plaît-il ? » = “Do you like it?” Used by itself (« Plaît-il ? »), it’s a very formal way to say you didn’t hear or understand. In everyday speech, people more often say « Ça te plaît ? » or « Pardon ? ».
target_language_example: Cela te plaît-il ?
native_language_example: Do you like it?

additional_notes: Means “a lot of” + noun (usually plural): "plein de choses". It can also be more literal as “full of” (especially with "être" or concrete things): "La pièce est pleine de lumière." In everyday speech, "plein de" is very common and slightly more casual than "beaucoup de".
target_language_example: Il y a plein de gens dans le métro ce matin.
native_language_example: There are lots of people on the subway this morning.

meaning: free will (in the phrase « de son/ton/votre plein gré » = willingly, of one’s own accord).
additional_notes: Almost always used with « de » + a possessive: « de mon/ton/son/notre/votre/leur plein gré ». It means someone is doing something voluntarily, not forced or pressured. Often used in questions to check if someone is there/doing something willingly: « Es-tu ici de ton plein gré ? »
target_language_example: Il a signé le document de son plein gré.
native_language_example: He signed the document of his own free will.

meaning: a lot of; lots of; many.
additional_notes: Very common to talk about a large quantity. Used before a noun: plein de + noun (plein de travail, plein de questions). In speech, it often means “lots of” and can feel a bit informal compared with beaucoup de. It can also be used with a number of times: plein de fois (“many times”).
target_language_example: On a plein de choses à faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: We have lots of things to do today.

additional_notes: Used after a feminine singular noun (or pronoun like elle) to say it is filled with something, either literally (a box full of books) or figuratively (full of life/surprises). For masculine singular: plein de; feminine plural: pleines de; masculine plural: pleins de.
target_language_example: Cette salle est pleine de monde.
native_language_example: This room is full of people.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the lunar phase when the Moon appears completely illuminated. Often used with the article: "la pleine lune" (the full moon). You can say "sous la pleine lune" (under the full moon) or "il y a/ on aura la pleine lune" (there is/there will be a full moon).
target_language_example: On ira se promener au clair de la pleine lune.
native_language_example: We’ll go for a walk in the light of the full moon.

meaning: To rain very heavily (“it’s raining cats and dogs”).
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression meaning it’s pouring. It’s typically used with the impersonal subject “il” and conjugated verb: “Il pleut des cordes.” The dictionary form is “pleuvoir des cordes.” You can use it in other tenses too: “Hier, il pleuvait des cordes.”
target_language_example: Quand il commence à pleuvoir des cordes, je préfère rester à la maison.
native_language_example: When it starts raining cats and dogs, I prefer to stay home.

meaning: to pour down (rain); to rain very heavily.
additional_notes: Used to describe very strong rain (similar to “it’s pouring” / “raining cats and dogs”). Conjugate only the verb: il va pleuvoir à verse (it’s going to pour), il a plu à verse (it poured).
target_language_example: Dépêche-toi : il va pleuvoir à verse !
native_language_example: Hurry up: it’s going to pour down!

additional_notes: Comparative structure: **plus + adjective + que**. Here **belle** is the feminine singular form of *beau* (“beautiful”). With a masculine subject: **plus beau que**; feminine plural: **plus belles que**; masculine plural: **plus beaux que**. Common variations include **plus belle que jamais** (“more beautiful than ever”) and **bien plus belle que** (“much more beautiful than”).
target_language_example: Cette robe est plus belle que l’autre.
native_language_example: This dress is more beautiful than the other one.

meaning: (to) need (something) more; or (with ne…plus) (to) not need (something) anymore.
additional_notes: Used with "avoir besoin de" (“to need”). Without "ne", "plus" usually means “more” (often in comparisons: "plus besoin que…" = “need it more than…”). With "ne…plus", "plus" means “no longer / not anymore”: "Tu n’en as plus besoin" = “You don’t need it anymore.” "en" replaces the thing needed ("de ça / de lui / de ce livre", etc.).
target_language_example: J’en ai plus besoin que toi aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I need it more than you today.

meaning: no need for / no need to … anymore.
additional_notes: Often used to say something is no longer necessary: “(Il n’y a) plus besoin de …” or simply “Plus besoin de …” (common in speech/writing without “ne”). With a verb, use the infinitive: “Plus besoin de discuter.” With a noun: “Plus besoin de médicaments.” Note: “avoir plus besoin de X que de Y” means “to need X more than Y” (here “plus” = “more”).
target_language_example: Plus besoin de courir, le bus arrive.
native_language_example: No need to run anymore; the bus is coming.

additional_notes: With a noun, plus de means more; before a number, it usually means more than. In the negative pattern ne...plus de, it means no more or no longer any. In time expressions like Il est plus de minuit, it means after/past.
target_language_example: Je n'ai plus de lait.
native_language_example: I don't have any milk left.

additional_notes: Without *ne*, it usually means “more time”: *On aura plus de temps.* With *ne ... plus*, it means “no more / not anymore”: *Nous n'avons plus de temps.* In speech, the *ne* is often dropped (*On a plus de temps*), so context matters.
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de plus de temps pour finir.
native_language_example: I need more time to finish.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is an additional amount beyond what was just mentioned. Often appears after a statement like “Et plus encore” (“And even more / And more besides”). It can also stand alone as an emphatic follow-up: “Plus encore.”
target_language_example: Il y a des réductions, et plus encore pendant les soldes.
native_language_example: There are discounts, and even more during the sales.

additional_notes: Used to compare difficulty: plus facile (easier than), often with que (than): « plus facile que… ». It can also be followed by an infinitive: « plus facile à lire » (easier to read), and can take intensifiers like bien/encore: « bien plus facile » (much easier). The superlative is « le/la plus facile » (the easiest).
target_language_example: Avec une carte, c’est plus facile de trouver le musée.
native_language_example: With a map, it’s easier to find the museum.

additional_notes: Used to compare strength or intensity: *Je suis plus fort que toi* = “I’m stronger than you.” In the common expression **C’est plus fort que toi**, it’s often figurative and means “You can’t help it” / “It’s stronger than you (you can’t resist).”
target_language_example: Il est plus fort que moi en natation.
native_language_example: He’s stronger than me at swimming.

additional_notes: Comparative form of "grand/grande" (big/large; tall). Used to compare two things/people: "un bol plus grand" = a bigger bowl; "quelqu’un de plus grand" = someone taller. It can also mean "biggest/greatest" when used like a superlative with context (often with "le/la/les"): "leur plus grand fan" = their biggest fan.
target_language_example: Tu as une taille plus grande ?
native_language_example: Do you have a bigger size?

additional_notes: Comparative phrase: "plus" + adjective + "que" = "more … than". With "grand", it often means "tall" for people and "big/large" for things; it can also mean "older" in contexts like siblings (e.g., "mon frère est plus grand que moi"). Agreement: "grand" can change to match gender/number (e.g., "plus grande que", "plus grands que"), but the base multi-word term is commonly given as "plus grand que".
target_language_example: Il est plus grand que son père.
native_language_example: He is taller than his father.

meaning: bigger / larger / taller (feminine); also “the biggest/greatest” in phrases like “la plus grande …”.
additional_notes: Feminine form of the comparative/superlative of *grand* (“big/large/tall”). Use **plus grande que …** = “bigger/larger/taller than …” (talking about a feminine noun or a woman/girl). With **la plus grande + noun**, it means “the biggest/greatest + noun” (e.g., *ma plus grande peur* = “my biggest fear”).
target_language_example: C’est la plus grande pièce de l’appartement.
native_language_example: It’s the biggest room in the apartment.

additional_notes: Used as a comparative with "que" ("plus important que…" = "more important than…"). With "le" it becomes the superlative: "le plus important" = "the most important". It can also be used after an indefinite like "quelque chose de plus important" ("something more important").
target_language_example: C'est plus important que tu ne le penses.
native_language_example: It's more important than you think.

additional_notes: Used with negation (usually "ne ... plus jamais") to mean that something will not happen again, from now on. Common with verbs like revoir/revenir/faire/croire, and often expresses a strong promise or a permanent change (e.g., "ne ... plus jamais" = "will never again").
target_language_example: Je ne te mentirai plus jamais.
native_language_example: I will never lie to you again.

additional_notes: Literally “more young,” but used like English “younger.” With a family word it often means “the youngest”: « mon plus jeune frère » = “my youngest brother.” In the set phrase « depuis son plus jeune âge », it means “since early childhood / since a very young age.”
target_language_example: C'est ma plus jeune sœur.
native_language_example: She's my youngest sister.

additional_notes: Used to talk about distance or moving beyond a point. Often with verbs like aller/aller plus loin (“go further”), or to compare locations: plus loin que (“farther than”), X maisons plus loin (“X houses further down”). Can also be figurative: aller plus loin (“take it further / go one step further”).
target_language_example: On peut aller plus loin, mais il va faire nuit bientôt.
native_language_example: We can go further, but it’ll get dark soon.

additional_notes: Comparative of duration: *longtemps* = “a long time,” so *plus longtemps* = “for a longer time.” Often used with **ne… plus** to mean “not … any longer” (e.g., *Je ne peux plus attendre* / *Je ne peux pas attendre plus longtemps* = “I can’t wait any longer”). You can also add **que** for comparison: *plus longtemps que je ne pensais* = “longer than I thought.”
target_language_example: Je vais rester plus longtemps, si je peux.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay longer, if I can.

additional_notes: Used to soften or approximate what you’re saying: (1) with adjectives/adverbs to mean 'somewhat' (Il est plus ou moins prêt = he’s kind of ready), (2) with quantities to mean 'approximately' (plus ou moins 10 minutes = about 10 minutes), and (3) alone as an answer meaning 'more or less / sort of' (Oui, plus ou moins).
target_language_example: On est arrivés plus ou moins à l’heure.
native_language_example: We arrived more or less on time.

additional_notes: Used to say that nobody remains or that something no longer happens with anyone. It usually appears in a negative structure with **ne**: **Plus personne ne...** (“No one… anymore”). In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: **Plus personne parle**. It can also be used alone as a short answer: **Plus personne.** (“No one.”).
target_language_example: Plus personne ne vient ici le soir.
native_language_example: No one comes here in the evening anymore.

meaning: no one anymore; nobody any longer.
additional_notes: Used to say that a situation has changed and now nobody does something. It’s a negative structure: "plus personne" = "no one anymore" + "ne" before the verb (in casual speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Plus personne dit la vérité"). Usually followed by a verb; you may also see "plus personne n’..." before a vowel (e.g., "Plus personne n’écoute").
target_language_example: Depuis ce scandale, plus personne ne lui fait confiance.
native_language_example: Since that scandal, no one trusts him anymore.

additional_notes: Used for physical distance ("Assieds-toi plus près de moi") and, with verbs like voir/regarder/inspecter (often in the phrase "de plus près"), to mean looking more closely or examining in more detail.
target_language_example: Viens plus près, je veux te montrer quelque chose.
native_language_example: Come closer, I want to show you something.

additional_notes: Usually means "more than" in comparisons: plus que ceci = "more than this." In the pattern ne... plus que, it means "only" or "all that's left is." In everyday spoken French, ne is often dropped, so phrases like plus que trois can mean "only three left."
target_language_example: C'est plus que suffisant.
native_language_example: That's more than enough.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is stronger or more true now than at any time before. It often comes at the end of the sentence for emphasis, and it can also be used alone as an exclamation: « Plus que jamais ! ».
target_language_example: On a besoin de toi plus que jamais.
native_language_example: We need you more than ever.

additional_notes: Used to compare yourself with someone else. With amounts/quantities it means you have less than the other person: « Il gagne plus que moi » = “He earns more than me.” With verbs, it often means “more than I do”: « Tu l’aimes plus que moi » = “You love him more than I do.” « moi » is a stressed pronoun used after « que » (not « je »).
target_language_example: Elle voyage plus que moi cette année.
native_language_example: She’s traveling more than me this year.

additional_notes: Used to say something goes beyond what was mentioned or expected: “It’s not just that,” “It’s more than that.” With comparisons or self-worth, it can mean “something better/more” (Je veux être plus que ça; Tu mérites plus que ça). It can also be said alone for emphasis, like “More than that!” / “Even more!” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ce que tu as fait est important, mais c’est plus que ça.
native_language_example: What you did is important, but it’s more than that.

additional_notes: Comparative form of the adjective "rapide" (fast). Use "plus rapide que" to compare: "plus rapide que le son" (faster than sound). For the superlative, use "le/la/les plus rapide(s)" (the fastest): "le plus rapide de tous" (the fastest of all). It can describe speed in general, including people, vehicles, computers, or ways of doing something.
target_language_example: On peut y aller en métro : c’est plus rapide que la voiture.
native_language_example: We can go there by subway: it’s faster than the car.

additional_notes: Comparative of "simple" (simple/easy). Used to compare: "C'est plus simple" = "It's simpler/easier." With "le/la/les plus simple", it becomes the superlative: "the simplest" (or "the easiest") depending on context.
target_language_example: On peut prendre le métro : c'est plus simple.
native_language_example: We can take the metro; it’s easier.

additional_notes: Means at a later time. Very common for postponing something: je t'appelle plus tard = I'll call you later. It also follows time expressions: quelques minutes plus tard = a few minutes later.
target_language_example: On en parlera plus tard.
native_language_example: We'll talk about it later.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened (or should happen) at an earlier time than expected or than another time. Often answers “when?” or “how early?” You can use it with past tenses (Je suis rentré(e) plus tôt = I came home earlier) or with devoir/il faut to suggest doing something earlier (Tu dois te lever plus tôt = You have to get up earlier).
target_language_example: On devrait partir plus tôt demain.
native_language_example: We should leave earlier tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed: verb + « plus vite (que…) » = “faster (than…)”. With « le plus vite », it becomes the superlative: “the fastest / the most quickly” (e.g., « nager le plus vite » = “swim the fastest”).
target_language_example: Si on part plus vite, on arrivera à l'heure.
native_language_example: If we leave faster, we'll arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed or how quickly something happens: plus + vite (adverb) + que + the person/thing or clause being compared. You can follow it with a noun/pronoun (plus vite que toi) or a full clause (plus vite que je ne l’imaginais).
target_language_example: On y arrivera plus vite que prévu.
native_language_example: We’ll get there faster than expected.

meaning: “older than me” (used when the person being described is male; the adjective agrees with that person).
additional_notes: Used for age comparisons with the pattern “plus + adjective + que” = “more + adjective + than.” Here, “âgé” refers specifically to age (“old/aged”). If the person being described is female, use “plus âgée que moi.” You can add degree words: “un peu plus âgé que moi” (a little older than me), “beaucoup plus âgé que moi” (much older than me), “deux fois plus âgé que moi” (twice as old as me).
target_language_example: Mon cousin est un peu plus âgé que moi.
native_language_example: My cousin is a little older than me.

additional_notes: Means an indefinite number of years (more than one, usually more than two). Often used with durations: "pendant plusieurs années" (for several years). You can also say "il y a plusieurs années" meaning "several years ago."
target_language_example: J'ai travaillé dans cette entreprise pendant plusieurs années.
native_language_example: I worked at that company for several years.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly (more than once). Also common in the expression « payer en plusieurs fois » = “to pay in installments” (split the payment into several parts).
target_language_example: J’ai déjà vu ce film plusieurs fois.
native_language_example: I’ve already seen this movie several times.

additional_notes: A very strong, dramatic way to refuse something or to say you would never accept it. Often used with the structure “Plutôt mourir que …” (“I’d rather die than …”). It can also appear alone as an emphatic refusal: “Plutôt mourir !”
target_language_example: Plutôt mourir que de mentir à ma famille.
native_language_example: I’d rather die than lie to my family.

meaning: a common point; something in common.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a shared feature between two or more people/things. Often appears in expressions like "avoir un point commun" (to have something in common) or "le seul point commun" (the only thing in common).
target_language_example: On a un point commun : on adore voyager.
native_language_example: We have something in common: we love traveling.

meaning: starting point; beginning (a base to start from).
additional_notes: Used both literally (the place where something starts: a trip, a tunnel, a route) and figuratively (an initial idea, plan, or first step). Common in expressions like « un bon point de départ » (“a good starting point”) and « retour au point de départ » (“back to square one / back to the start”).
target_language_example: Ton résumé est un bon point de départ, mais il faut ajouter plus de détails.
native_language_example: Your summary is a good starting point, but we need to add more details.

additional_notes: Used in a medical context to refer to a single stitch used to close a wound after an injury or surgery. Often used in the plural: « des points de suture » (“stitches”).
target_language_example: Le médecin m’a fait un point de suture au bras.
native_language_example: The doctor gave me one stitch in my arm.

meaning: point of view; viewpoint (opinion or perspective).
additional_notes: Often used with "de" to mean "from ...'s point of view": "de mon/ton/son/notre/votre/leur point de vue". It can also mean a physical viewpoint/lookout spot (a place with a nice view): "un point de vue".
target_language_example: De mon point de vue, c’est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: From my point of view, it’s a good idea.

meaning: weak point; weakness (a vulnerability or area you’re not good at).
additional_notes: Used for a person, group, plan, or system: the thing that is easiest to exploit or the area where someone is least strong (skills, character, temptations, etc.). Often with "avoir un point faible" (to have a weakness) or "découvrir/trouver le point faible" (to find the weak spot).
target_language_example: J'ai un point faible : le chocolat.
native_language_example: I have a weakness: chocolate.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: the punctuation mark at the end of a sentence (also called un point). Figuratively, "mettre un point final à…" means to put a definitive end to something. Used alone ("Point final." / "Point final !") it means “That’s final.” / “End of story.”
target_language_example: On arrête là, point final.
native_language_example: We’re stopping here, end of discussion.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone is especially good at. Often comes after "c'est" or with "être" (e.g., "Les maths sont mon point fort"). The opposite is "point faible" (weakness).
target_language_example: L'organisation, c'est son point fort.
native_language_example: Organization is his/her strong point.

meaning: tiptoes; the tips of your toes (standing/walking quietly).
additional_notes: Usually used in the expression « sur la pointe des pieds » = “on tiptoe / tiptoeing,” often to mean moving quietly so you don’t wake or disturb someone.
target_language_example: Je suis entré sur la pointe des pieds pour ne pas réveiller le bébé.
native_language_example: I came in on tiptoe so I wouldn’t wake the baby.

additional_notes: Used in a medical context for the stitches used to close a wound. Often used with verbs like "avoir besoin de" (to need) and "retirer" (to remove/take out). You may also hear "se faire poser des points de suture" (to get stitches) and "retirer/enlever les points" (to have the stitches removed).
target_language_example: Je me suis coupé le doigt et on m’a mis trois points de suture.
native_language_example: I cut my finger and they gave me three stitches.

additional_notes: Usually used in the plural: « des pois chiches ». Common in cooking (e.g., hummus, couscous, salads).
target_language_example: Je vais faire du houmous avec des pois chiches.
native_language_example: I'm going to make hummus with chickpeas.

additional_notes: Literally “red fish.” Most commonly refers to the pet fish (often kept in a bowl: « un bocal »). It can also name things shaped like goldfish, like « des crackers poisson rouge » (Goldfish crackers). Plural: « des poissons rouges ».
target_language_example: Mon poisson rouge s'appelle Léo et il nage dans son bocal.
native_language_example: My goldfish is called Leo and it swims in its bowl.

additional_notes: Very common everyday noun for the vegetable. It’s feminine: une pomme de terre; plural: des pommes de terre. Often used in cooking contexts (e.g., purée de pommes de terre = mashed potatoes).
target_language_example: Je vais acheter une pomme de terre pour faire une soupe.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy a potato to make a soup.

additional_notes: Common food noun; usually used in the plural (des/les pommes de terre). Literally “apples of the earth,” but it simply means “potatoes.” Often appears in cooking contexts: bouillir (boil), peler (peel), purée de pommes de terre (mashed potatoes).
target_language_example: On mange souvent des pommes de terre avec du poulet.
native_language_example: We often eat potatoes with chicken.

additional_notes: Refers to the business/agency that organizes funerals (transport, ceremony, burial/cremation). Often used with verbs like « aller aux pompes funèbres » (go to the funeral home) or « recommander des pompes funèbres » (recommend a funeral home). Despite « pompes » meaning “pumps” in other contexts, here it has an older meaning linked to ceremony (not a false friend in this expression).
target_language_example: On doit passer aux pompes funèbres pour organiser l’enterrement.
native_language_example: We have to stop by the funeral home to arrange the funeral.

additional_notes: A common noun for the snack, especially at the movies. Often used with an article: du pop-corn (some popcorn), le pop-corn (the popcorn). You may also see the spelling "popcorn" without a hyphen.
target_language_example: On prend du pop-corn ?
native_language_example: Shall we get some popcorn?

additional_notes: A small item you carry to hold money (coins and/or bills) and often cards. Common with possessives: mon/ton/son porte-monnaie. Sometimes used like “wallet” in general French, though “portefeuille” is also common for a wallet (especially for cards).
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon porte-monnaie à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot my wallet at home.

additional_notes: Used as a noun for an object believed to bring good luck (often: un porte-bonheur). It can also be used like an adjective after a noun to mean “lucky”: un nombre/chiffre porte-bonheur, une couleur porte-bonheur, etc. The plural is porte-bonheurs.
target_language_example: J'ai toujours un petit porte-bonheur dans mon sac.
native_language_example: I always have a little good-luck charm in my bag.

additional_notes: A common noun for something you keep money (often coins, sometimes cards/bills) in. In everyday French it can refer to a small coin purse or a wallet; for a larger wallet people also say "portefeuille".
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon porte-monnaie à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot my wallet at home.

additional_notes: From the verb **porter** (“to wear/carry”) + **des lunettes** (“glasses”). You can change **porte** depending on the subject: **je porte** (I wear), **tu portes** (you wear), **il/elle porte** (he/she wears), **nous portons** (we wear), **vous portez** (you wear), **ils/elles portent** (they wear). Often followed by a reason: **pour lire** (“to read”).
target_language_example: Elle porte des lunettes quand elle travaille sur l’ordinateur.
native_language_example: She wears glasses when she works on the computer.

meaning: To bring bad luck; to be a bad omen.
additional_notes: Used when you believe an action, object, or sign will cause bad luck. Common patterns: « Ça peut porter malheur de + infinitive » (It can bring bad luck to…), and « porter malheur à quelqu’un » (to bring bad luck to someone).
target_language_example: Passer sous une échelle peut porter malheur.
native_language_example: Walking under a ladder can bring bad luck.

meaning: to file a complaint (with the police); to press charges.
additional_notes: Used when officially reporting a crime/offense to the police (or authorities). Often appears with verbs like "vouloir" (Je voudrais porter plainte) or "envisager" (Elle envisage de porter plainte). The noun is "une plainte" (a complaint).
target_language_example: Après le vol, il a décidé de porter plainte au commissariat.
native_language_example: After the theft, he decided to file a complaint at the police station.

meaning: to bear fruit; to pay off (produce results).
additional_notes: Used to say that efforts, work, patience, or an investment finally lead to positive results. Often used about a long process: « Avec le temps, ça a commencé à porter ses fruits. »
target_language_example: Après des mois d’entraînement, son travail a enfin commencé à porter ses fruits.
native_language_example: After months of training, his hard work finally started to pay off.

meaning: “do you wear…?” / “are you carrying…?” (formal question form of *tu portes*)
additional_notes: This is the verb *porter* (“to wear/carry”) with subject–verb inversion to form a question: *Portes-tu… ?* = *Tu portes… ?* (more neutral/formal than just using rising intonation). It’s used for clothes (*Portes-tu un jean ?*), accessories/devices (*Portes-tu un appareil auditif ?*), or carrying something. Note that related reflexive forms change the meaning: *Te portes-tu bien ?* (from *se porter*) = “Are you doing well?”, and *Te portes-tu volontaire… ?* (from *se porter volontaire*) = “Do you volunteer…?”.
target_language_example: Portes-tu une veste aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Are you wearing a jacket today?

meaning: "do you wear / are you wearing"; sometimes "are you (doing/feeling)" (with *se porter*).
additional_notes: This is the verb *porter* conjugated with **vous** and used with **inversion** in questions (*Portez-vous… ?* = *Do you wear/are you wearing…?*). It can mean to wear (clothes, glasses, perfume), to carry (a weapon, a bag), or to have (a shoe size: *Quelle taille portez-vous ?*). In the expression *se porter*: *Portez-vous bien* = “Take care / Be well,” and *Comment vous portez-vous ?* = “How are you doing?”
target_language_example: Portez-vous des lunettes ?
native_language_example: Do you wear glasses?

additional_notes: Used with "être" to say someone/something looks exactly like another person/thing: « Tu es le portrait craché de ta mère. » Often followed by « de + quelqu’un/quelque chose ».
target_language_example: C'est le portrait craché de son grand frère.
native_language_example: He’s the spitting image of his big brother.

meaning: to be a problem; to cause a problem.
additional_notes: Used to say that something creates difficulties or is an issue (often about feasibility, rules, timing, etc.). Common patterns: “Ça/Cela pose problème.” (= That’s a problem.) and “Ça ne pose pas de problème.” (= No problem / That’s not an issue.). You can also specify for whom: “Ça me pose problème.” (= That’s a problem for me.).
target_language_example: Pour demain, le changement d’horaire peut poser problème : je ne suis pas disponible.
native_language_example: For tomorrow, the schedule change could be a problem: I’m not available.

additional_notes: An adjective used to describe something that happens after a traumatic event (often used in medical/psychological contexts). Common in the phrase « trouble de stress post-traumatique » (PTSD). In French it’s usually hyphenated: « post-traumatique ».
target_language_example: Il souffre d’un trouble de stress post-traumatique.
native_language_example: He suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

additional_notes: Refers to the building/office where police work (for reporting something, asking for help, etc.). Often used in location questions like « Où se trouve le poste de police ? » or with « le plus proche » (the nearest).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, où est le poste de police le plus proche ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the nearest police station?

additional_notes: Used for a physical place where someone works (a desk/spot in an office) or a computer workstation (especially in IT). Often seen in workplaces: un poste de travail partagé = a shared workstation/desk.
target_language_example: Je vais m’installer à mon poste de travail.
native_language_example: I’m going to sit down at my workstation.

meaning: asked myself the question; wondered (about something).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as the reflexive verb phrase **se poser la question** = “to ask oneself / to wonder.” In the past tense you’ll see **je me suis posé la question** (“I asked myself / I wondered”). Without **se**, **poser une question (à quelqu’un)** means “to ask a question (to someone).”
target_language_example: Je me suis posé la question toute la journée.
native_language_example: I wondered about it all day.

additional_notes: Past form of « poser une question » (to ask a question). Very common with an indirect object: « poser une question à quelqu’un » = to ask someone a question. Even though « poser » looks like English “to pose,” in French this is the standard verb for “ask” in this context.
target_language_example: Elle m’a posé une question pendant le cours.
native_language_example: She asked me a question during class.

meaning: a bribe (money or a gift given illegally to get a favor).
additional_notes: Used for corruption: paying/giving something to influence a decision (e.g., an official, a mayor). Often appears with verbs like donner (to give), recevoir (to receive), demander/chercher (to ask for/look for), refuser (to refuse), nier (to deny).
target_language_example: On lui a proposé un pot-de-vin pour accélérer le dossier.
native_language_example: They offered him a bribe to speed up the case.

meaning: the secret; the truth behind what’s really going on (often something hidden).
additional_notes: Used almost always in the set expression « découvrir le pot aux roses » = “to discover the secret / find out what’s really happening,” often implying you uncover a trick, deception, or hidden plan. It’s an idiom (not about a literal pot of roses).
target_language_example: J’ai fini par découvrir le pot aux roses : ils me préparaient une surprise.
native_language_example: I finally found out the truth: they were preparing a surprise for me.

additional_notes: Informal and often used as a taunt or name-calling, either alone ("Poule mouillée !") or after an exclamation like "Quelle poule mouillée !". With "être" it means “to be a coward” ("C’est une poule mouillée.").
target_language_example: Allez, saute ! Ne fais pas ta poule mouillée !
native_language_example: Come on, jump! Don’t be such a chicken!

additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify what you’re saying, often to signal that a description is not literal but approximate, metaphorical, or a figure of speech. It’s often inserted parenthetically with commas: « Il est, pour ainsi dire, … »; it can also start a sentence to introduce a rephrasing or approximation.
target_language_example: C’est, pour ainsi dire, impossible sans toi.
native_language_example: It’s, so to speak, impossible without you.

meaning: “for all that / nevertheless”; in “pour autant que”: “as long as / provided that”, sometimes “as far as”.
additional_notes: Common in negatives: “pas … pour autant” = “not … for that / that doesn’t mean …” (it doesn’t change the situation). With “pour autant que + subjunctive”: sets a condition (“provided that…”) or a limit of knowledge (“pour autant qu’on sache” = “as far as we know”).
target_language_example: Il est riche, mais il n’est pas heureux pour autant.
native_language_example: He’s rich, but that doesn’t mean he’s happy.

meaning: 'as long as / provided that' (condition), or 'as far as' (as far as I know).
additional_notes: Often introduces a condition and is commonly followed by the subjunctive: « pour autant que tu sois prêt ». Very frequent in the set phrase « pour autant que je sache » = “as far as I know.”
target_language_example: Tu peux venir pour autant que tu m’appelles avant.
native_language_example: You can come as long as you call me beforehand.

additional_notes: Used to limit what you’re saying to your current knowledge (you’re not 100% sure). Often placed at the beginning of a sentence, or used alone as a short reply: « Pour autant que je sache, oui. »
target_language_example: Pour autant que je sache, il n’y a pas de train après 22 h.
native_language_example: As far as I know, there isn’t a train after 10 p.m.

meaning: due to; because of (a stated reason).
additional_notes: Used in fairly formal contexts to give an official-sounding reason for something (often an absence, cancellation, delay, resignation, etc.). It’s commonly followed by a noun phrase: « pour cause de maladie », « pour cause de grève ». Similar to « à cause de », but more administrative/formal.
target_language_example: Le train est annulé pour cause de grève.
native_language_example: The train is canceled due to a strike.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something scheduled, planned, or needed later today/tonight (reservations, departures, availability, arrangements). Often in questions to confirm plans: « C’est toujours bon pour ce soir ? » = “Is it still on for tonight?”
target_language_example: On se retrouve à 20 h pour ce soir ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at 8 p.m. tonight?

additional_notes: Used with numbers to express a proportion out of 100. Often follows the number (e.g., « dix pour cent » = 10%). Common patterns: « X pour cent de + noun » (X percent of…), and « augmenter / diminuer de X pour cent » (to increase/decrease by X percent).
target_language_example: Il y a quinze pour cent de réduction aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: There's fifteen percent off today.

meaning: for how long? (for what length of time?)
additional_notes: Used to ask about the duration of an action or situation. Common with verbs like louer (to rent), rester (to stay), attendre (to wait), and durer (to last). You can also say: « Pour combien de temps ? » as a standalone question.
target_language_example: Vous restez ici pour combien de temps ?
native_language_example: How long are you staying here?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the first point in an explanation, plan, or argument. It can also mean “as a first step” before doing something else: « Pour commencer, il faut… ». Often placed at the beginning of a sentence, followed by a comma.
target_language_example: Pour commencer, on va faire les présentations.
native_language_example: To begin with, we’re going to introduce ourselves.

additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: (1) to insist someone is telling the truth / speaking seriously ("Tell me for real"), often with verbs like dire, promettre, être sérieux; (2) to mean something is final or permanent ("for good"), e.g., partir pour de bon = "to leave for good". You can also use it alone for emphasis: "Pour de bon, cette fois." = "For real, this time."
target_language_example: Tu vas arrêter de fumer pour de bon ?
native_language_example: Are you going to quit smoking for good?

additional_notes: Used to confirm that something is true (often as a question: « C’est pour de vrai ? » = “Is it really true?”). It can also mean you’re doing something seriously/not as a joke (« Je le fais pour de vrai. »). As a sentence starter (« Pour de vrai, ... »), it emphasizes sincerity, like “Seriously,” or “Honestly,”.
target_language_example: Pour de vrai, j’ai oublié ton anniversaire.
native_language_example: Seriously, I forgot your birthday.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a deadline or something intended for the next day. Often follows what is due/needed (e.g., un devoir, un paiement) and can imply “no later than tomorrow.”
target_language_example: J’ai un devoir pour demain.
native_language_example: I have homework due for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the beneficiary/recipient of an action (“do something for them”) or working on someone’s behalf (“work for them”). “Eux” is the stressed pronoun for “them” (masculine or mixed group); for an all-female group, use “pour elles.”
target_language_example: Je vais le faire pour eux.
native_language_example: I’m going to do it for them.

additional_notes: Used at the start (or sometimes mid-sentence) to introduce a brief summary and skip details. Often followed by a comma: « Pour faire court, … ».
target_language_example: Pour faire court, on a raté le train.
native_language_example: Long story short, we missed the train.

meaning: to finish; in order to finish.
additional_notes: “Pour + infinitive” expresses purpose (“in order to…”): “pour finir le rapport” = “to finish the report.” It can also be used after expressions of time/permission (“quelques heures / une semaine pour finir…” = “a few hours / a week to finish…”). In “finir ses jours,” it means “to spend one’s last days” (often about retiring or living somewhere until the end of one’s life).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’une heure de plus pour finir ce travail.
native_language_example: I need one more hour to finish this work.

meaning: “for the love of” (often used to beg/insist: “for heaven’s sake”).
additional_notes: Used to strongly urge someone to do (or stop doing) something; often conveys frustration or impatience. Commonly followed by a person, God, or a valued thing (e.g., « pour l’amour de Dieu »). In careful French spelling, « amour » takes a circumflex: « pour l’amour de ».
target_language_example: Pour l'amour de Dieu, arrête de faire ça !
native_language_example: For God’s sake, stop doing that!

additional_notes: Used to say something is true only at the present time and may change later. Often placed at the start of the sentence (Pour l'instant, …) or after what it modifies (… pour l'instant). Can also be used alone as a short answer meaning “nothing yet/for now.”
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas de décision pour l'instant.
native_language_example: I don't have a decision for now.

additional_notes: "Pour la" = "pour" + "la" and is used before a feminine singular noun. It often expresses purpose/role ("important pour la production" = important for production), what something benefits or relates to ("un grand soir pour la démocratie" = for democracy), or what something is intended for ("signer pour la livraison" = sign for the delivery). Compare: pour le (masc.), pour les (plural).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de ça pour la réunion de demain.
native_language_example: I need that for tomorrow’s meeting.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the most recent (final) time something happened, often when asking when/where you last saw, wore, or did something: « Quand l’as-tu vu pour la dernière fois ? » It can also mean a final goodbye or last chance: « le voir pour la dernière fois » = to see him one last time.
target_language_example: Je l'ai appelé pour la dernière fois hier soir.
native_language_example: I called him for the last time last night.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true in general, but not for everyone/everything. Often set off by commas: « Ils sont, pour la plupart, … ». It can also be a short stand-alone answer meaning “Mostly.”
target_language_example: Pour la plupart, les magasins ferment à 19 h.
native_language_example: For the most part, stores close at 7 p.m.

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening on its first occasion. Often placed after the verb it refers to: « rencontrer quelqu’un pour la première fois », « venir ici pour la première fois ». You can add a time frame: « pour la première fois en huit ans » (“for the first time in eight years”).
target_language_example: Je prends le métro pour la première fois.
native_language_example: I’m taking the subway for the first time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something’s effect on health or something done to maintain/improve health. Often follows a noun (“conséquences pour la santé”) or a verb phrase (“c’est bon pour la santé”).
target_language_example: Manger moins de sucre, c’est mieux pour la santé.
native_language_example: Eating less sugar is better for your health.

additional_notes: Often means “forever / for the rest of one’s life” (e.g., amis pour la vie = friends for life). It can also mean “for (the purpose of) life” in a general sense (e.g., important pour la vie = important for life).
target_language_example: Ils seront partenaires pour la vie.
native_language_example: They will be partners for life.

additional_notes: A common combination of pour + le before a masculine singular noun. Usually means "for the"; with some destinations, English may use "to" instead (for example, partir pour le Canada). Before a vowel sound, it becomes pour l'.
target_language_example: J'ai préparé un café pour le voisin.
native_language_example: I made a coffee for the neighbor.

additional_notes: Used to talk about plans or availability at lunch time, or to invite someone to eat lunch. Often appears with verbs like « être libre », « rester », « se joindre à quelqu’un ». You can also hear « à déjeuner » in some contexts, but « pour le déjeuner » is very common for making lunch plans.
target_language_example: On se retrouve pour le déjeuner vers midi ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet for lunch around noon?

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended/planned for dinner time or for the dinner meal (e.g., setting the table, being late for dinner). In sentences like « Nous sommes neuf personnes pour le dîner », it means the number of people expected for dinner.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'on mange pour le dîner ?
native_language_example: What are we eating for dinner?

additional_notes: Used to say something is true only right now and may change later. Often placed at the beginning (Pour le moment, …) or at the end of the sentence (… pour le moment). Common in polite explanations (e.g., someone is busy/absent) and when you can’t say more yet.
target_language_example: Pour le moment, je travaille, mais je te rappelle ce soir.
native_language_example: For now, I’m working, but I’ll call you back tonight.

meaning: as for the rest; for the remainder (of something).
additional_notes:
Used to refer to whatever is left over after what was just mentioned.

Common uses:
- Topic shift: “Pour le reste, …” = “As for the rest, … / Otherwise, …”
- With “de + noun”: “pour le reste de …” = “for the rest of …” (time, life, etc.)
- Money/quantity: “pour le reste ?” can mean “for the remaining amount?”
target_language_example: J’ai payé une partie, et pour le reste je te fais un virement demain.
native_language_example: I paid part of it, and for the rest I’ll transfer you the money tomorrow.

meaning: for the weekend; for the (coming/this) weekend.
additional_notes: Used to say something is planned for the weekend or that someone is leaving/going somewhere for the duration of the weekend. Often heard in questions about plans: « Tu fais quoi pour le week-end ? » It can refer to the upcoming weekend depending on context.
target_language_example: On va à la campagne pour le week-end.
native_language_example: We’re going to the countryside for the weekend.

additional_notes: Used with a plural noun: pour + les + noun (e.g., « pour les enfants » = “for the children”). For singular, use « pour le » (masc.) or « pour la » (fem.). In fixed expressions, it can also mean “in the eyes of / as far as … are concerned” (e.g., « de la confiture pour les cochons » = “pearls before swine”).
target_language_example: J’ai acheté des billets pour les concerts de ce week-end.
native_language_example: I bought tickets for the concerts this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended for children (songs, gifts, activities) or done for their benefit/protection (worrying about them, being strong for them). Often appears as a short label or heading: "Pour les enfants."
target_language_example: Ce film n'est pas pour les enfants.
native_language_example: This movie isn't for kids.

additional_notes: Usually means “for him” (benefiting him, intended for him, done on his behalf): Je l’ai fait pour lui. It can also introduce someone’s point of view/topic: Pour lui, c’est fini. “Lui” is a stressed pronoun used after prepositions like pour, avec, sans, chez, etc.
target_language_example: J’ai gardé une part de gâteau pour lui.
native_language_example: I saved a piece of cake for him.

meaning: for my part; as for me (in my opinion).
additional_notes: Used to give your personal point of view or preference, often at the start of a sentence to contrast with others (similar to “as for me” / “personally”). It can vary by person: pour ta part (for your part), pour sa part (for his/her part), pour notre part (for our part), etc.
target_language_example: Pour ma part, je pense qu’on devrait partir plus tôt.
native_language_example: As for me, I think we should leave earlier.

additional_notes: Usually means "for me" in a direct sense: something intended for you, affecting you, or suitable for you (e.g. trop sucré pour moi). At the start of a sentence, it can also mean "in my opinion" or "to me" when giving a personal view.
target_language_example: Pour moi, ce film est un peu trop long.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this movie is a bit too long.

meaning: "in order not to" / "so as not to".
additional_notes: Used to express a negative purpose (the reason you do something is to avoid something else). It’s followed by an infinitive: pour ne pas + verb (e.g., pour ne pas tomber). In modern spoken French, the "ne" is sometimes dropped (pour pas tomber), but "pour ne pas" is the standard form.
target_language_example: J’éteins mon téléphone pour ne pas être dérangé.
native_language_example: I turn off my phone so I won’t be disturbed.
