additional_notes: Used to correct yourself or intensify what you just said: you mention a milder description, then add a stronger (often more blunt) one. Common pattern: adjective, pour ne pas dire + stronger adjective (sometimes a bit critical or humorous).
target_language_example: Le film était intéressant, pour ne pas dire fascinant.
native_language_example: The movie was interesting—if not fascinating.

additional_notes: Used to express purpose (the goal of an action). It is normally followed by the subjunctive in French: « pour que je puisse… », « pour qu’il vienne… ».
target_language_example: Je parle doucement pour que le bébé dorme.
native_language_example: I speak quietly so that the baby sleeps.

additional_notes: Used to express a short, approximate duration (often temporary). It can describe trips, absences, stays, etc. Similar ideas: "pendant quelques jours" (during/for a few days).
target_language_example: Je reste ici pour quelques jours, puis je rentre.
native_language_example: I'm staying here for a few days, then I'm going back home.

meaning: 'What for?' / 'What is it for?' (asking the purpose).
additional_notes: Used to ask what something is meant to be used for or what the point/goal is. Common in conversation, often after someone mentions something: « Et pour quoi faire ? » = “And what for?” Not the same as « pourquoi ? » (“why?”); « pour quoi faire ? » focuses on the intended use or purpose (what you’re going to do with it).
target_language_example: Tu veux que j’imprime ce document, pour quoi faire ?
native_language_example: You want me to print this document—what for?

meaning: for nothing; for no reason; for free.
additional_notes: Common meanings depend on context: (1) “in vain / for nothing” = without results or benefit (Je suis venu pour rien.); (2) “for no reason” = without a good reason, often in negatives (On ne fait pas ça pour rien.); (3) “for free” = without paying (Il l’a eu pour rien.). At the start of a sentence, “Pour rien !” can mean “Not at all!/No way!/It’s nothing!” depending on tone and situation.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je l’ai fait pour rien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I did it for free.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done for someone’s birthday (a party, a gift, shopping, a trip). "Son" means "his" or "her" depending on who the birthday belongs to (son anniversaire = his/her birthday). You can replace it with another possessive: "pour mon anniversaire" (for my birthday), "pour ton anniversaire" (for your birthday), "pour leur anniversaire" (for their birthday).
target_language_example: On va au restaurant pour son anniversaire.
native_language_example: We’re going to a restaurant for his/her birthday.

meaning: for his/her age; considering his/her age.
additional_notes: Used to compare someone to what is typical or expected at that age (often meaning “surprisingly” young/old/tall/mature/fit, etc.). It commonly follows an adjective phrase: jeune/grand/petit/mature/en bonne forme pour son âge. You can also change the possessive: pour mon/ton/notre/votre/leur âge.
target_language_example: Il est très autonome pour son âge.
native_language_example: He’s very independent for his age.

additional_notes: Common in spoken French as an emphatic way to say yes or to confirm something. It can be used alone as a reply ("Pour sûr !") or at the start of a sentence ("Pour sûr, mais...") to mean "Sure, but...". "Sûr" means "sure/certain"; with "pour" it works like English "for sure".
target_language_example: Pour sûr, je viendrai demain.
native_language_example: For sure, I’ll come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when something is intended for someone, done on their behalf, or from their point of view. After a preposition like pour, French uses the stressed pronoun toi (not tu). In some contexts, it can mean 'to you' in English, as in Ça a un sens pour toi ? = 'Does that make sense to you?' It also appears in expressions like garder pour toi = 'keep to yourself.'
target_language_example: J'ai une surprise pour toi.
native_language_example: I have a surprise for you.

additional_notes: Used to justify advice or an action as being in the other person’s best interest (often like a warning, instruction, or tough love). Common patterns: « C’est pour ton bien. », « Je fais ça pour ton bien. », and at the start of a sentence: « Pour ton bien, … ». You can change the possessive: « pour mon/son/notre/votre/leur bien ».
target_language_example: Écoute-moi : c’est pour ton bien.
native_language_example: Listen to me: it’s for your own good.

additional_notes: Means “from now on, without end.” Often used with the future or with verbs like rester/vivre/être to express permanence. In some contexts it’s close to “for good” (e.g., rester ici pour toujours = stay here forever).
target_language_example: Je t’aimerai pour toujours.
native_language_example: I will love you forever.

additional_notes: Used to mean something applies to all people in a group, or that there is enough of something to include everyone. Common with “C’est clair pour tout le monde ?” (“Is that clear for everyone?”) and with quantities (“assez de… pour tout le monde”).
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas : il y a assez à manger pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there’s enough food for everyone.

meaning: for a/an (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to express purpose, destination, or intended use: « pour une aventure » (for an adventure), « pour une mission » (for a mission), « réserver pour une occasion spéciale » (save/reserve for a special occasion). It also appears in the pattern « prendre quelqu’un pour une … » meaning “to take someone for a … / to think someone is a …” (often insulting): « Tu me prends pour une idiote ? ».
target_language_example: J’ai acheté ces fleurs pour une amie.
native_language_example: I bought these flowers for a friend.

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening one time (or unusually), often contrasting with what normally happens. It can express pleasant surprise, complaint, or a request: « Fais-le pour une fois » (“Do it for once”).
target_language_example: Pour une fois, il est arrivé à l’heure.
native_language_example: For once, he arrived on time.

additional_notes: Used with the formal/polite possessive "votre" (= your). "Votre" can refer to one person (formal "you") or to multiple people ("you all"). In informal speech you usually use "pour ton/ta/tes" instead. In some fixed expressions like "en avoir pour votre argent", it means getting your money’s worth.
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help.

additional_notes: Used to mean that something is intended for, suitable for, or affects you. In English it can sometimes be translated more naturally as "to you" (for example, important pour vous = "important to you"). In phrases like gardez-le pour vous, it means "to yourself." Note that vous can mean one person formally or more than one person.
target_language_example: J'ai réservé une table pour vous.
native_language_example: I reserved a table for you.

additional_notes: Polite set phrase used when introducing yourself (like a formal “I’m at your service”), or on its own to respond when someone calls you, offers help, or welcomes you. Common in customer-service contexts. Literally “to serve you,” but it’s used idiomatically as a courteous formula.
target_language_example: Bonjour, je m'appelle Claire, pour vous servir.
native_language_example: Hello, my name is Claire, at your service.

additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment usually found after "c'est" or "voilà": "C'est pour ça que tu…" / "Voilà pourquoi tu…" It introduces the reason/explanation for what the person ("tu" = you) does or is experiencing. In careful writing you may also see the more formal "c'est pour cela que tu…".
target_language_example: C’est pour ça que tu es en retard.
native_language_example: That’s why you’re late.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to express purpose or explanation: "pour être + adjective/noun" = "to be + adjective/noun" (purpose), and "réputé/connu pour être..." = "known/reputed for being...". Often followed directly by an adjective: "pour être tranquille" = "so (that I can) be relaxed / to have peace of mind."
target_language_example: Je ferme la porte pour être sûr.
native_language_example: I close the door to be sure.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a frank opinion, confession, or clarification. It can go at the beginning of a sentence (often followed by a comma) or at the end. Common in both spoken and written French; slightly more direct than "franchement" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Pour être honnête, je ne suis pas sûr de comprendre.
native_language_example: To be honest, I'm not sure I understand.

additional_notes: Used to ask “why” about a woman’s action, with subject–verb inversion (a-t-elle = a + elle). Common with the passé composé: « Pourquoi a-t-elle fait ça ? » literally “Why has she done that?” but often translated as “Why did she do that?” in English.
target_language_example: Pourquoi a-t-elle quitté la réunion si tôt ?
native_language_example: Why did she leave the meeting so early?

meaning: "why did he...?/why has he...?" (a formal question).
additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason for something a man did. This is the inverted (more formal) question form: pourquoi + auxiliary verb (a/est) + -t- + il. The tense depends on the auxiliary: "a-t-il" is passé composé (often translated as "did he" or "has he"). In everyday speech, you often hear: "Pourquoi est-ce qu’il a... ?" or "Pourquoi il a... ?".
target_language_example: Pourquoi a-t-il dit ça ?
native_language_example: Why did he say that?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason. It’s the question word "pourquoi" (why) + "as-tu" (have you), which is "tu" inverted with the verb "avoir" to form a formal/neutral question. Often followed by a past participle (passé composé): "Pourquoi as-tu fait ça ?" (note: "fait", not "fais").
target_language_example: Pourquoi as-tu annulé la réunion ?
native_language_example: Why did you cancel the meeting?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind an action done by the person you address with *vous* (one person politely/formally, or multiple people). It’s followed by a past tense with *avoir* (passé composé): *Pourquoi avez-vous + past participle… ?*
target_language_example: Pourquoi avez-vous décidé de partir si tôt ?
native_language_example: Why did you decide to leave so early?

additional_notes: Used to question or challenge the reason for doing something. It’s often a bit skeptical or defensive, like asking for a justification. Built from “pourquoi” (why) + the conditional of “devoir” (devrais, should/ought to) + “je” (I). You usually follow it with an infinitive: « Pourquoi devrais-je partir ? »
target_language_example: Pourquoi devrais-je accepter ça ?
native_language_example: Why should I accept that?

meaning: "why must I" / "why do I have to".
additional_notes: Used to question an obligation. Literally "why" + inverted form of "je dois" (I must). Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., faire, aider, savoir). In everyday speech you also hear: "Pourquoi est-ce que je dois... ?" or "Pourquoi je dois... ?"
target_language_example: Pourquoi dois-je attendre ici ?
native_language_example: Why do I have to wait here?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s state or situation, often followed by an adjective or expression: « Pourquoi es-tu surpris ? » (Why are you surprised?) or « Pourquoi es-tu ici ? » (Why are you here?). « es-tu » is the inverted question form of « tu es » (you are), with a hyphen in writing. You can also ask the same question more casually with « pourquoi tu es… ? ».
target_language_example: Pourquoi es-tu si fatigué aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Why are you so tired today?

meaning: “why are you so…?” (asking why someone is that way).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason/explanation about someone’s mood, behavior, or state, followed by an adjective: « Pourquoi es-tu si nerveuse ? » = “Why are you so nervous?” In speech you may also hear « Pourquoi tu es si… ? » (less formal). Adjective agreement matters: masculine « tendu », feminine « tendue ».
target_language_example: Pourquoi es-tu si pressé aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Why are you so rushed today?

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question before a subject + verb: « Pourquoi est-ce que + sujet + verbe ? ». It’s a common, neutral way to form “why” questions in spoken and written French. In conversation you’ll also hear the shorter « Pourquoi + sujet + verbe ? » (e.g., « Pourquoi tu pars ? »).
target_language_example: Pourquoi est-ce que tu es en retard ?
native_language_example: Why are you late?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s reason. It introduces a question with the subject pronoun "tu" (you, informal singular). After "est-ce que", you keep normal word order: "tu" + verb (e.g., "Pourquoi est-ce que tu cours ?"). In informal speech, you can also say "Pourquoi tu cours ?"; in more formal speech with "vous": "Pourquoi est-ce que vous… ?".
target_language_example: Pourquoi est-ce que tu fais ça ?
native_language_example: Why are you doing that?

additional_notes: Used to propose an idea or gently encourage someone to do something. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb: « Pourquoi ne pas + infinitif ? » You can also use it alone as a short answer meaning “Sure/Why not?”
target_language_example: On a un peu de temps — pourquoi ne pas faire une promenade ?
native_language_example: We have a bit of time—why not go for a walk?

meaning: “why not?” (suggesting or agreeing to an idea).
additional_notes: Used to make a casual suggestion (“How about…?”) or to accept a proposal (“Sure, why not?”). It can also introduce an option: “Pourquoi pas celui-là ?” = “Why not that one?” Often said on its own as a relaxed yes.
target_language_example: On va au cinéma ce soir ? — Pourquoi pas !
native_language_example: Are we going to the movies tonight? — Sure, why not!

additional_notes: A question form using inversion: "pourquoi" (why) + "suis-je" (am I). Used with adjectives, nouns, or other complements: "Pourquoi suis-je fatigué ?" (Why am I tired?), "Pourquoi suis-je ici ?" (Why am I here?). In more casual speech, people often say "Pourquoi je suis... ?" instead of inversion.
target_language_example: Pourquoi suis-je en retard ?
native_language_example: Why am I late?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind something that applies to everyone (or to most people). It’s often followed by a verb: « Pourquoi tout le monde est… ? » (Why is everyone…?) or « Pourquoi tout le monde + verbe… ? » (Why does everyone + verb…?). « Tout le monde » means “everyone/people (in general).”
target_language_example: Pourquoi tout le monde parle de ce film ?
native_language_example: Why is everyone talking about this movie?

additional_notes: Common spoken French pattern for asking a question with tu + verb, instead of more formal forms like pourquoi est-ce que tu... or inversion such as pourquoi pars-tu ? The exact English translation depends on the verb and tense that follow, so it can also mean 'why did you...?' in context.
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu pleures ?
native_language_example: Why are you crying?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question (embedded after another verb like savoir, expliquer, demander, répéter): e.g., "Je sais pourquoi tu es ici." In a direct question, French often uses either "Pourquoi es-tu… ?" (inversion, more formal) or "Pourquoi tu es… ?" (common in speech), or "Pourquoi est-ce que tu es… ?" (neutral).
target_language_example: Je comprends pourquoi tu es fatigué.
native_language_example: I understand why you are tired.

meaning: "Why don’t you…?" or "Why aren’t you…?" (introduces a question with tu + a negation).
additional_notes: Used in spoken French to ask why someone isn’t doing something or to suggest they should do it: « Pourquoi tu ne + verbe + pas ? ». In more formal French you may also hear « Pourquoi ne chantes-tu pas ? » or « Pourquoi est-ce que tu ne chantes pas ? ». In everyday speech, the « ne » is often dropped: « Pourquoi tu chantes pas ? ».
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu ne viens pas avec nous ?
native_language_example: Why don’t you come with us?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone their reason for wanting to do something. It’s a question with subject–verb inversion: "veux" (want) + "-tu" (you). Often followed by an infinitive verb: "Pourquoi veux-tu partir ?"
target_language_example: Pourquoi veux-tu changer de travail ?
native_language_example: Why do you want to change jobs?

additional_notes: Used to question why someone would want to do something or why they would say something. It’s built from "pourquoi" (why) + "voudrais" (would want, conditional of vouloir) + "tu" (you). Often followed by an infinitive: "Pourquoi voudrais-tu partir ?" = "Why would you want to leave?" You may also hear the more common "Pourquoi veux-tu… ?" (Why do you want…?).
target_language_example: Pourquoi voudrais-tu changer de travail maintenant ?
native_language_example: Why would you want to change jobs now?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s reason or motivation. It’s the formal/polite "you" (vous), common with strangers, customers, or in professional contexts. Often followed by an infinitive (apprendre, retourner) or a noun (un chien). In casual speech with friends you’d more often say "Pourquoi tu veux… ?"
target_language_example: Pourquoi voulez-vous venir ici demain ?
native_language_example: Why do you want to come here tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason. This is the formal/plural form with "vous" (“you” to one person politely, or to several people). It uses subject–verb inversion in questions: "êtes-vous" = “are you?”. Often followed by an adjective or past participle (e.g., "Pourquoi êtes-vous fatigué(e) ?" / "Pourquoi êtes-vous venu(e)(s) ?").
target_language_example: Pourquoi êtes-vous en retard ?
native_language_example: Why are you late?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s state or behavior, followed by an adjective (e.g., fatigué(e), occupé(e)). "Êtes-vous" is the inversion form of "vous êtes" (more formal). The adjective agrees with who you’re speaking to: fatiguée (female singular), fatigués (male/mixed plural), fatiguées (female plural).
target_language_example: Pourquoi êtes-vous si pressé aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Why are you in such a hurry today?

meaning: “could I…?” (very polite way to ask permission or make a request).
additional_notes: From the verb *pouvoir* (“to be able to / can”) in the conditional (*je pourrais* = “I could”), with inversion (*-je*) to form a question. It’s formal and respectful; common in polite requests, especially with *vous*. In everyday speech, many people use *Est-ce que je pourrais… ?* or *Je peux… ?* instead.
target_language_example: Pourrais-je ouvrir la fenêtre, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Could I open the window, please?

meaning: “Could I have…?” (very polite way to ask for something).
additional_notes: Used to make polite requests, especially in restaurants, shops, or formal situations. It’s the conditional form of pouvoir (“could”) + inversion (-je) + avoir (“to have”), and is often followed by a noun or phrase: Pourrais-je avoir du café ? / Pourrais-je avoir votre attention ? You can make it even more polite with s’il vous plaît or je vous prie.
target_language_example: Pourrais-je avoir l’addition, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Could I have the bill, please?

additional_notes: Polite question form of "pouvoir" (conditional) + "tu" with inversion: "pourrais-tu… ?" = "could you…?" Often used to make polite requests, similar to "est-ce que tu pourrais… ?". Typically followed by an infinitive: "pourrais-tu + verb".
target_language_example: Pourrais-tu m'aider avec mes devoirs ?
native_language_example: Could you help me with my homework?

meaning: 'could you (please) … for me / to me' (polite request).
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to do something. It’s the conditional of *pouvoir* (“to be able to”), addressed to **tu** (someone you’re on first-name terms with). It’s often followed by an infinitive: *pourrais-tu me + donner / déposer / faire / passer / rappeler / répéter…*.
target_language_example: Pourrais-tu me dire où se trouve la station de métro ?
native_language_example: Could you tell me where the subway station is?

additional_notes: From the conditional of pouvoir ("to be able to / can"). Used with subject-verb inversion to form a question in a more formal/written style. Often refers to "he" (il) or an object/idea (also il = "it"). With other verbs you may see an extra -t- for pronunciation (e.g., "pourrait-il" doesn’t need it, but "pourrait-on" / "a-t-il").
target_language_example: Pourquoi pourrait-il refuser ?
native_language_example: Why could he refuse?

additional_notes: Conditional form of « pouvoir » + infinitive « être ». Used to express possibility or uncertainty (often like English “might be”). It can also mean “could become” depending on context: « il pourrait être grand » = “he could be great / he could become great.”
target_language_example: Ça pourrait être une bonne idée.
native_language_example: That could be a good idea.

additional_notes: Very common polite way to ask someone to do something (more formal than "tu peux...?" / "peux-tu...?"; similar to "could you...?" in English). It’s the conditional form of "pouvoir" with "vous" (used for strangers, customers, or more than one person). Often followed by an infinitive: "pourriez-vous + verb".
target_language_example: Pourriez-vous m’aider, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Could you help me, please?

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to make a request. Follow it with an infinitive (e.g., aider, dire, conseiller, répéter, servir) and optionally details after. Often used with “s’il vous plaît / je vous prie”.
target_language_example: Pourriez-vous me dire où sont les toilettes, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Could you tell me where the bathrooms are, please?

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to ask for information. It’s the conditional of pouvoir (could) + me dire (tell me), often followed by a question word: ce qui/ce que (what), comment (how), quand (when), où (where). You can also use it to ask someone to repeat information: « Pourriez-vous me dire votre nom, à nouveau ? »
target_language_example: Pourriez-vous me dire où se trouve la station de métro ?
native_language_example: Could you tell me where the метро station is?

additional_notes: This is the conditional form of pouvoir (“to be able to”), used to ask politely in questions. Often followed by an infinitive: Pourrions-nous + verb (avoir, nous asseoir, nous rencontrer). More formal/polite than « Pouvons-nous… ? ».
target_language_example: Pourrions-nous parler un instant, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Could we talk for a moment, please?

meaning: to sue (someone); to take legal action against (someone).
additional_notes: Used when you start a lawsuit against someone. Very common pattern: « poursuivre [quelqu’un] en justice » = sue someone. You can negate it (« ne pas poursuivre en justice ») or use it with advice/obligation (« Vous devez le poursuivre en justice. »).
target_language_example: Il menace de me poursuivre en justice si je ne paie pas.
native_language_example: He’s threatening to sue me if I don’t pay.

meaning: 'as long as / provided that' or 'I hope (that)...'
additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive to express either (1) a condition (‘provided that / as long as’) or (2) a strong wish/hope, often with an anxious tone, and it can stand alone as an exclamation. Example of condition: « Tu peux venir, pourvu que tu sois à l’heure. » Example of wish: « Pourvu que tout aille bien ! »
target_language_example: Pourvu que tout aille bien !
native_language_example: I hope everything goes well!

additional_notes: Used to ask a question with vous, so it can address one person formally or more than one person. This inversion form is common in polite requests and more formal written or spoken French.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous m'aider, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you help me, please?

additional_notes: Polite/formal way to ask someone to do something involving you. It’s “pouvoir” (can/to be able to) with inversion for a question (“pouvez-vous…”) + the object pronoun “me” (“me/to me”). It’s usually followed by an infinitive: “Pouvez-vous me + verb… ?”
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me donner un renseignement ?
native_language_example: Can you give me some information?

additional_notes: Very common polite way to ask for information. It’s the inversion form of "vous pouvez" (formal/plural "you can"). Usually followed by an indirect question: "…où", "…ce que", "…pourquoi", "…qui", etc. You can also use "Pouvez-vous me dire s’il y a…?" for “Can you tell me if there is…?”
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me dire à quelle heure le musée ouvre ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what time the museum opens?

additional_notes: From the verb « pouvoir » (can/to be able to) + « donner » (to give). Used to politely ask someone to hand you something or provide information/help (advice, an address, a phone number, etc.). You can place the thing you’re asking for after it: « Pouvez-vous me donner + nom ? »
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me donner un verre d’eau, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Could you give me a glass of water, please?

additional_notes: Question form of « nous pouvons » (inversion: verb + -nous). Often used in polite or slightly formal questions to ask permission or possibility. In everyday speech, you also hear « on peut… ? » or « est-ce qu’on peut… ? ».
target_language_example: Pouvons-nous entrer ?
native_language_example: Can we come in?

meaning: first love (the first person you loved romantically).
additional_notes: Used to talk about your earliest romantic love/relationship. You can say it with possessives (mon/ton/son premier amour). It can also mean the person themselves, not just the experience: « Il/elle était mon premier amour. »
target_language_example: Mon premier amour, je ne l’oublierai jamais.
native_language_example: My first love, I’ll never forget.

additional_notes: Used as an official political title. In French, the title is often written the same way for a woman or a man (e.g., « elle est le premier ministre »). It can be used with an article (« le/la premier ministre ») or directly as a form of address (« Premier ministre ! »).
target_language_example: Le premier ministre a annoncé de nouvelles mesures.
native_language_example: The Prime Minister announced new measures.

additional_notes: Used for the highest/most comfortable class of service when traveling (train, plane, etc.). Often appears with a ticket: « un billet en première classe » or by itself as an answer: « En première classe. » (In first class.)
target_language_example: Je voudrais une place en première classe, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a first-class seat, please.

additional_notes: Means “the first time” something happens. Used with an article: "une première fois" (a first time) or "la première fois" (the first time). Note: "fois" is feminine, so it’s always "première" (not "premier"). Common in the expression "Il y a toujours une première fois" = "There’s always a first time."
target_language_example: C'est ma première fois à Paris.
native_language_example: It's my first time in Paris.

meaning: to catch (someone) off guard; to take by surprise.
additional_notes: Used when something happens unexpectedly and you’re not prepared (emotionally, practically, or with an answer). Very common in the past tense (« a pris / ont pris », etc.) and with an indirect object pronoun: « Ça m’a pris au dépourvu. » You can use it with a person or with « ça » as the subject.
target_language_example: Sa question a vraiment pris Jean au dépourvu, et il ne savait pas quoi répondre.
native_language_example: His/Her question really caught Jean off guard, and he didn’t know what to say.

meaning: to trap; to catch (someone) in a trap.
additional_notes: Used both literally (animals, physical traps) and figuratively (to trap someone with a trick, a question, or in a difficult situation). Often used with a direct object: « prendre quelqu’un au piège ». In the passive, it’s very common: « être pris(e) au piège » = “to be trapped.”
target_language_example: Il a essayé de me prendre au piège avec une question, mais j’ai compris son jeu.
native_language_example: He tried to trap me with a question, but I understood what he was up to.

additional_notes: Used with an object (a person, a comment, a warning, a situation). Object pronouns often come before the verb: « Je ne peux pas te/vous prendre au sérieux » (“I can’t take you seriously”). Can also be used with « le/la/les »: « Nous devons le prendre au sérieux » (“We must take it seriously”).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas te prendre au sérieux.
native_language_example: I can’t take you seriously.

meaning: to take (something) well; to react well (to news/criticism).
additional_notes: Commonly used with a direct object or pronoun: « Je le prends bien » / « Je l’ai pris bien » = “I take it well / I took it well.” The opposite is « mal le prendre » (to take it badly / take it the wrong way). In careful French, « bien le prendre » is often preferred over placing « bien » after the verb, but « prendre bien » is still understandable in speech.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je vais prendre bien la remarque.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to take the comment well.

meaning: to say goodbye; to take one’s leave.
additional_notes: Used when you’re leaving (often in a polite or somewhat formal way). Common with a person you’re leaving: « prendre congé de quelqu’un ». In everyday French you also hear « dire au revoir » for “to say goodbye.”
target_language_example: Je vais prendre congé de vous maintenant.
native_language_example: I’m going to say goodbye / take my leave now.

meaning: to realize; to become aware (of something).
additional_notes: Often used with de + noun/infinitive: prendre conscience de la vérité (become aware of the truth). Typically emphasizes a change in awareness (sometimes sudden): Je viens de prendre conscience… Can be used in the causative: faire prendre conscience à quelqu’un de… (to make someone realize…).
target_language_example: Je viens de prendre conscience de quelque chose.
native_language_example: I just realized something.

meaning: to get in touch (with); to contact.
additional_notes: Usually used with **avec**: *prendre contact avec quelqu’un* = to contact someone / establish contact. Common in polite requests and more formal contexts (email, phone, official situations). Often interchangeable with **contacter**.
target_language_example: Je vais prendre contact avec vous par e-mail demain.
native_language_example: I’ll get in touch with you by email tomorrow.

meaning: to take effect; to come into force (also: to come into circulation).
additional_notes: Used mainly in formal/legal or financial contexts for something that becomes officially valid or starts applying (a law, rule, decision), or for money/notes that begin circulating. Don’t confuse with « prendre des cours » = “to take classes/courses.”
target_language_example: La nouvelle règle va prendre cours le 1er juillet.
native_language_example: The new rule will take effect on July 1st.

meaning: to put on airs; to act superior/affected.
additional_notes: Used to criticize someone’s attitude when they start behaving as if they’re better than others (snobbish, pretentious). Often said with "avec quelqu’un" or after a change in status: "Depuis sa promotion, il/elle prend des airs."
target_language_example: Arrête de prendre des airs, on est entre amis.
native_language_example: Stop putting on airs—we’re among friends.

meaning: to take action; to take steps (measures).
additional_notes: Used in formal or practical contexts (politics, safety, work) to mean doing something concrete to fix a problem or prevent a risk. Often followed by "contre" (against) or "pour" (to/in order to): "prendre des mesures contre...", "prendre des mesures pour...". "Des mesures" here means actions, not measurements.
target_language_example: On doit prendre des mesures pour protéger la population.
native_language_example: We need to take steps to protect the population.

meaning: to take photos; to take pictures.
additional_notes: Very common verb phrase: prendre (to take) + des photos (some photos). Often used with rules/permission: Peut-on prendre des photos ? / C’est interdit de prendre des photos. You can also say: prendre une photo (to take a photo) or prendre des photos de [something/someone] (take photos of…).
target_language_example: On peut prendre des photos ici ?
native_language_example: Can we take pictures here?

meaning: to have a good time; to enjoy yourself.
additional_notes: Means spending time pleasantly (relaxing, having fun). Very common with verbs like vouloir (want to), avoir envie de (feel like), and reminders like souviens-toi / souvenez-vous (remember). It can also appear as an imperative: Prenez du bon temps !
target_language_example: On va à la plage pour prendre du bon temps.
native_language_example: We’re going to the beach to have a good time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about putting on weight over time (in general or because of a cause). Often appears with "se mettre à" / "commencer à" (to start gaining) or "de peur de" (for fear of gaining).
target_language_example: William a commencé à prendre du poids.
native_language_example: William started to gain weight.

meaning: to fall behind; to get delayed (to be running late).
additional_notes: Used when something doesn’t go as planned and ends up delayed—projects, trains, schedules, or even people. Common patterns: "On a pris du retard" (we fell behind), "Le train a pris du retard" (the train was delayed), "Je prends du retard" (I’m getting behind). Note: French "retard" means "delay" here; it is not used the same way as the English insult.
target_language_example: Désolé, je vais prendre du retard à cause des embouteillages.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going to be delayed because of traffic.

meaning: to take care of; to handle; to take responsibility for (also: to cover the costs of).
additional_notes: Used when someone (a person, service, company, etc.) agrees to deal with something or look after someone. Very common in professional/administrative contexts: a doctor/hospital can « prendre en charge » a patient (= care for them), and an insurer/employer can « prendre en charge » expenses (= cover/pay for them). Often followed by a direct object: « prendre en charge un patient / un dossier / les frais ».
target_language_example: L'assurance va prendre en charge les frais médicaux.
native_language_example: The insurance will cover the medical expenses.

meaning: to take into account; to consider.
additional_notes: Used when you need to include a fact or factor in your thinking/decision. Very common with things like des facteurs, son âge, ce fait, ce qui…. Can be used with devoir/falloir (Tu dois… / Il faut…) to express necessity: « Il faut prendre en compte… ».
target_language_example: Avant de décider, il faut prendre en compte le budget.
native_language_example: Before deciding, you have to take the budget into account.

additional_notes: Used with a direct object for the person/thing being photographed: prendre quelqu’un/quelque chose en photo. Common when asking permission: « Je peux vous/te prendre en photo ? ». In the passive/reflexive: « se faire prendre en photo » = “to have one’s photo taken.”
target_language_example: Tu peux nous prendre en photo devant la tour Eiffel ?
native_language_example: Can you take a picture of us in front of the Eiffel Tower?

meaning: to take inspiration from; to follow someone’s example.
additional_notes: Often used with a complement: « prendre exemple sur quelqu’un » or « prendre exemple sur quelque chose » (to use someone/something as a model). It suggests learning from what someone did and trying to do the same (especially in a positive sense).
target_language_example: Tu devrais prendre exemple sur ta sœur : elle travaille régulièrement.
native_language_example: You should follow your sister’s example: she works regularly.

additional_notes: Used when something starts burning (often suddenly). The subject is the thing that burns: « La maison a pris feu. » It’s common in news and emergency contexts. You can also hear it figuratively for emotions or a situation “flaring up.”
target_language_example: La voiture peut prendre feu après un accident.
native_language_example: A car can catch fire after an accident.

meaning: to come to an end; to end.
additional_notes: Used for something that stops or is over (a war, a situation, a period of suffering, a life). Often with an inanimate subject: «La guerre prend fin», «Le supplice peut prendre fin».
target_language_example: J’espère que cette crise va bientôt prendre fin.
native_language_example: I hope this crisis will come to an end soon.

meaning: to take shape; to start becoming clear/real.
additional_notes: Used when something is developing from an idea or early stage into a more defined form (a plan, project, story, design, etc.). Often appears as "commencer à prendre forme" (= to start taking shape). In some contexts it can be literal ("prendre forme physique" = to take physical form), but it’s very often figurative.
target_language_example: Notre projet commence enfin à prendre forme après des semaines de travail.
native_language_example: Our project is finally starting to take shape after weeks of work.

meaning: To catch a cold; to get chilled (and risk getting sick).
additional_notes: Used when someone is exposed to cold weather/air and you worry they’ll get sick (often said as a warning: « Tu vas prendre froid ! »). In the negative (« ne pas prendre froid »), it means to avoid getting chilled/getting a cold. It can also mean simply “to get cold,” but the common idea is catching a cold.
target_language_example: Mets une écharpe, sinon tu vas prendre froid.
native_language_example: Put on a scarf, otherwise you’ll catch a cold.

meaning: to be careful; to watch out.
additional_notes: Often used with **à**: **prendre garde à + noun/infinitive** ("be careful of/to..."). Can be used as a warning, especially in the imperative: **Prenez garde !** (fairly formal/literary; in everyday speech you also hear **Fais attention ! / Attention !**).
target_language_example: Il faut prendre garde à ne pas tomber.
native_language_example: You have to be careful not to fall.

meaning: to get some fresh air; to go out for a bit.
additional_notes: Used when you step outside (often briefly) to breathe fresh air, clear your head, or take a short break. Common with verbs like aller/sortir: « Je sors prendre l’air » (I’m going out to get some air).
target_language_example: On va prendre l'air cinq minutes ?
native_language_example: Shall we go get some fresh air for five minutes?

additional_notes: Used when someone escapes or runs away from a place or situation (often from danger, police, or trouble). Common in news/reporting: «Le suspect a pris la fuite» = “The suspect fled.”
target_language_example: En voyant la police, il a décidé de prendre la fuite.
native_language_example: When he saw the police, he decided to run away.

meaning: to take control; to take over.
additional_notes: Used when someone takes charge of a situation, leads an activity, or takes over from someone else. Common in work or group settings (e.g., a manager taking over a meeting). In tech/support, it can also mean taking control of someone’s computer/session (“remote control”).
target_language_example: Laisse-moi prendre la main, je vais m’en occuper.
native_language_example: Let me take over; I’ll take care of it.

prendre la main dans le sac

target_language_multi_word_term: prendre la main dans le sac
meaning: to catch someone in the act (red-handed).
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression. Most often used with an object: « prendre quelqu’un la main dans le sac » (to catch someone while they’re doing something wrong, like stealing/cheating). A very common related phrasing is the passive: « être pris(e) la main dans le sac » = to be caught red-handed. Note: in practice you’ll more often hear « prendre quelqu’un la main dans le sac » than the bare « prendre la main dans le sac ».
target_language_example: Le vigile a surpris le client et l’a pris la main dans le sac en train de voler dans le magasin.
native_language_example: The security guard caught the customer red-handed stealing in the store.

additional_notes: Literal: to take measurements (e.g., for clothes, a room). Very often used figuratively as **prendre la mesure de + noun** = “to grasp the scale/importance of,” “to size up,” “to fully assess.”
target_language_example: Il faut prendre la mesure de la situation avant de décider.
native_language_example: We need to gauge the situation before deciding.

meaning: To speak up; to take the floor (begin speaking).
additional_notes: Used in meetings, classes, debates, and other formal situations to mean beginning to speak (often after being given permission) or speaking on behalf of someone. Common patterns: « prendre la parole devant + groupe » (to speak in front of), « prendre la parole pour + quelqu’un » (to speak for/defend someone).
target_language_example: Je fus le premier à prendre la parole.
native_language_example: I was the first to take the floor.

meaning: to take the trouble (to do something).
additional_notes: Often used as **prendre la peine de + infinitive** to say you made an effort to do something (sometimes with a hint of “please bother to…” in requests). Common in polite or formal contexts: *Prenez la peine de...* / *Merci de prendre la peine de...*.
target_language_example: Merci de prendre la peine de me répondre.
native_language_example: Thank you for taking the trouble to reply to me.

meaning: to hit the road; to set off (by car).
additional_notes: Used to say you’re leaving and starting a trip, especially driving. Often appears with a time expression: « On va prendre la route à 8 h » (We’ll set off at 8).
target_language_example: On va prendre la route demain matin pour aller à Lyon.
native_language_example: We’re going to hit the road tomorrow morning to go to Lyon.

meaning: to annoy someone; to do someone’s head in (also: to obsess over something).
additional_notes: Very common informal expression. Often used as "Tu me prends la tête" (You’re doing my head in / You’re annoying me) or "Ça me prend la tête" (It’s doing my head in). Can also mean to get fixated on something: "Ne te prends pas la tête" = Don’t overthink it / Don’t stress about it.
target_language_example: Arrête de prendre la tête, on trouvera une solution.
native_language_example: Stop doing my head in, we’ll find a solution.

meaning: to take over; to step in and continue (after someone else).
additional_notes: Used when one person/team replaces another to continue a task, role, or responsibility (at work, in projects, in sports like relay races). Often implies continuity: someone stops, and another person continues from that point.
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, tu peux prendre le relais ?
native_language_example: I’m tired—can you take over?

meaning: to get behind the wheel; to drive (start driving).
additional_notes: Used when someone begins driving or takes over driving from someone else. Often heard with a future/near-future form: « Je prends le volant » (I’ll drive / I’m taking the wheel).
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, tu peux prendre le volant ?
native_language_example: I’m tired—can you drive?

meaning: to take orders (e.g., in a restaurant); to take charge.
additional_notes: Most commonly used for a waiter/waitress who comes to take customers’ orders: « Je viens prendre votre commande. » In a more figurative context, it can mean “to take the helm / take control” of a situation (similar to « prendre les rênes »). « Commande » can mean an order (what a customer requests), not only a “command.”
target_language_example: Le serveur arrive pour prendre les commandes.
native_language_example: The waiter is coming to take orders.

meaning: to take bets; to accept bets.
additional_notes: Used in betting contexts (sports, races, games) for the person or place that accepts people’s bets. Often followed by what the bet is on: « prendre les paris sur + nom » (take bets on …) or « prendre les paris que + proposition » (take bets that …). Note: « paris » here means “bets,” not the city “Paris.”
target_language_example: On va prendre les paris sur le match de ce soir.
native_language_example: We’re going to take bets on tonight’s match.

meaning: to take (something) badly; to react badly; to take offense.
additional_notes: Used when someone reacts negatively to what was said/done, or interprets it in a negative way. Often appears with an object or clause: « prendre mal une remarque / une critique » (take a remark/criticism badly) or with a pronoun: « le prendre mal » (take it badly). Conjugates like any -endre verb: je prends, tu prends, il prend, nous prenons, vous prenez, ils prennent.
target_language_example: Je ne voulais pas te blesser ; ne prends pas mal ce que j'ai dit.
native_language_example: I didn’t mean to hurt you; don’t take what I said badly.

meaning: to take measurements; (less commonly, in fixed expressions) to take action/steps.
additional_notes: In modern French, the most common forms are **prendre des mesures** (“to take measures/steps” or “to take measurements”) and **prendre les mesures** (“to take the measurements,” e.g., for clothing or a room). The singular **prendre mesure** is uncommon on its own and is mainly encountered in set turns of phrase or older/ more literary usage. Also note **prendre la mesure de + nom** = “to grasp/realize the extent of” something.
target_language_example: Avant de commander les rideaux, il faut prendre mesure de la fenêtre.
native_language_example: Before ordering the curtains, you need to take the window’s measurements.

meaning: to take note (of); to write down.
additional_notes: Used when you want to remember information or record it in writing. Very common in formal/polite requests with "Veuillez prendre note de…" (= “Please note…” / “Please write down…”). Often followed by "de" + noun/phrase ("prendre note de mon adresse") or by "en" referring back to something already mentioned ("en prendre note" = “take note of it”).
target_language_example: Veuillez prendre note de mon adresse et de mon numéro de téléphone.
native_language_example: Please take note of my address and my phone number.

additional_notes: Used with « à »: « prendre part à + noun » (prendre part à une réunion, à un dîner, à un jeu, à une course). Slightly more formal than « participer (à) »; means joining an activity or event.
target_language_example: Tu veux prendre part à la discussion ?
native_language_example: Do you want to take part in the discussion?

meaning: to take sides; to take a stand.
additional_notes: Used when you choose one side in a conflict/debate (prendre parti pour quelqu’un/quelque chose), or when you express a clear opinion instead of staying neutral. Not the same as English “to take part” (= participer).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas prendre parti, je n’ai pas tous les détails.
native_language_example: I don’t want to take sides; I don’t have all the details.

additional_notes: Used in polite/formal situations (restaurants, waiting rooms, meetings) to invite someone to sit. Often in the imperative: « Veuillez prendre place. » You’ll also see it with a location: « prendre place à la table », « sur cette chaise ».
target_language_example: Madame, veuillez prendre place, je reviens tout de suite.
native_language_example: Ma’am, please have a seat; I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Often used with **à**: **prendre plaisir à + infinitive** ("to enjoy doing something"). You can also use it with a noun: **prendre plaisir à + nom** ("to take pleasure in something"). Slightly more formal than just **aimer** ("to like/love").
target_language_example: Je vais prendre plaisir à apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I’m going to enjoy learning French.

additional_notes: Used when someone decides to stop working permanently, usually because of age. It conjugates like prendre: je prends / il prend / ils prennent. In the past: il a pris sa retraite. You can also say "partir à la retraite" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Mon père va prendre sa retraite l'année prochaine.
native_language_example: My dad is going to retire next year.

additional_notes: Most often used as **prendre soin de + noun/pronoun**: *prendre soin de sa peau* (take care of your skin), *prendre soin de moi* (take care of me). It can be used for people, things, or health/body parts, and it often implies being careful and attentive.
target_language_example: Je vais prendre soin de toi pendant ton absence.
native_language_example: I’m going to take care of you while you’re away.

additional_notes: Used to say you care for a person/animal/thing, or you pay attention to your own health and well-being. Common pattern: prendre soin de + noun/pronoun (prendre soin de quelqu’un / de quelque chose). Also very common as advice: « Prenez soin de vous. » = “Take care (of yourself).”
target_language_example: Je vais prendre soin de ton chat pendant ton voyage.
native_language_example: I’m going to take care of your cat during your trip.

meaning: to take your time; not to rush.
additional_notes: Used to say you can go slowly and carefully, or that you’re not in a hurry. Often said as a reassurance/permission: « Prenez votre temps. » The possessive changes with the subject: prendre mon/ton/son/notre/votre/leur temps.
target_language_example: Il peut prendre son temps pour répondre.
native_language_example: He can take his time to reply.

additional_notes: Common way to say you are bathing in a tub (not a shower). You can use it for places too: prendre un bain dans la mer / la rivière (to go for a swim/bathe in the sea/river).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un bain ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to take a bath tonight.

meaning: to have a coffee; to grab a coffee.
additional_notes: Very common way to say you’re going to drink coffee, often casually (like “grab a coffee”). Used both for a quick drink alone and for meeting someone for coffee: « Tu veux prendre un café ? » = “Do you want to go for a coffee?” You can replace « un café » with another drink: « prendre un thé », « prendre un verre ».
target_language_example: On se retrouve à 16 h pour prendre un café ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at 4 p.m. for a coffee?

meaning: to go for a drink (have a drink).
additional_notes: Used when inviting someone or suggesting you meet up casually for a drink (alcoholic or non-alcoholic), often in a bar or at someone’s place. Very common with "aller/sortir" (e.g., "Tu veux aller prendre un verre ?") or "monter" meaning to go up to someone’s apartment ("Tu veux monter prendre un verre ?").
target_language_example: On se retrouve après le travail pour prendre un verre ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet up after work for a drink?

additional_notes: Very common everyday phrase. Often used with the near future (je vais prendre une douche / je vais aller prendre une douche) or with a command (va prendre une douche !). Also commonly said as "prendre une douche" vs. "se doucher" (to shower).
target_language_example: Après le sport, je vais prendre une douche.
native_language_example: After exercising, I'm going to take a shower.

meaning: to make a decision; to decide.
additional_notes: A very common, neutral expression. It’s used with the verb prendre (to take) + une décision (a decision), especially when emphasizing the act of choosing (often something important, urgent, or difficult). Often used with devoir / falloir: Je dois prendre une décision. / Il faut prendre une décision.
target_language_example: On doit prendre une décision avant demain.
native_language_example: We have to make a decision before tomorrow.

meaning: “take some / take one (or more) of it/them.”
additional_notes: Imperative of « prendre » + the pronoun « en ». « En » usually replaces something introduced by « de » (e.g., « des bonbons », « du pain ») and is used a lot with quantities: « prends-en deux », « prends-en plus », « prends-en plein ». It can also refer back to a thing/person after « de », for example in « prendre soin de … » → « Prends-en soin » (“Take care of it/them”).
target_language_example: Il y a des brochures sur la table : prends-en une.
native_language_example: There are brochures on the table: take one.

additional_notes: Imperative of « prendre » for « tu » + the direct object pronoun « le » (“it/him”), joined with a hyphen. Often used to tell someone to grab/pick up something quickly: « Prends-le vite ! ». Meaning depends on context (le = “it” or “him”). In « Prends-le par la peau du cul ! », the extra phrase is very vulgar (“by the ass”) and is not beginner-friendly.
target_language_example: Si tu l’aimes, prends-le.
native_language_example: If you like it, take it.

additional_notes: This is the verb–subject inversion form of **tu prends** (“you take”), used to ask a question, often in writing or more formal speech: **Prends-tu du sucre ?** In everyday conversation, people often say **Tu prends… ?** instead. **Prendre** is used broadly: taking medicine/treatment, taking notes, having sugar/food, or eating lunch somewhere.
target_language_example: Prends-tu un café ce matin ?
native_language_example: Are you having a coffee this morning?

additional_notes: Common, friendly way to tell someone to look after themselves (health, safety, well-being). Uses the informal singular command (tu): "prends" + "de" + "toi". You can also say "Prenez soin de vous" (formal/plural) or "Prends soin de toi !" with emphasis as a goodbye.
target_language_example: Prends soin de toi, et à bientôt !
native_language_example: Take care of yourself, and see you soon!

additional_notes: Used when the thing you’re taking is introduced with de (du/de la/des) or is understood from context. En replaces “of it/of them,” especially with quantities: « Prenez-en un/deux/autant que vous voulez » = “Take one/two/as many as you want.” Common in offers (food, items) and instructions (medicine): « Prenez-en un quatre fois par jour » = “Take one four times a day.”
target_language_example: Il y a des biscuits sur la table : prenez-en deux.
native_language_example: There are cookies on the table: take two.

meaning: “Do you take…?” / “Are you taking…?” (formal question form of *prendre*).
additional_notes: This is *prendre* conjugated for **vous** (“you” formal or plural) with **inversion** to form a question. It’s used with many meanings of *prendre*, depending on what follows: **charge** (Combien prenez-vous…? = How much do you charge…?), **have/drink** (Comment prenez-vous votre café ?), **get ideas from** (Où prenez-vous vos idées ?), **take notes/medicine** (Prenez-vous des notes/des médicaments ?). In casual speech, people often say **Vous prenez… ?** instead.
target_language_example: Prenez-vous une carte ou de l’espèce ?
native_language_example: Do you take card or cash?

meaning: Take care of yourself. (formal or plural)
additional_notes: Imperative of "prendre soin de" (“to take care of”). Used as a polite goodbye or a caring instruction. "Vous" is either formal (to one person) or plural (to several people). For informal singular, say "Prends soin de toi."
target_language_example: Merci d’être venu, prenez soin de vous !
native_language_example: Thanks for coming—take care of yourself!

meaning: almost every day; nearly every day.
additional_notes: Used to describe something you do very often (most days), but not literally every single day. It can go at the end of the sentence (Je le fais presque tous les jours.) or at the beginning for emphasis (Presque tous les jours, il va...).
target_language_example: Je prends le métro presque tous les jours.
native_language_example: I take the subway almost every day.

additional_notes: Used to say that most people (in a group or situation) did something, with a few exceptions. It can stand alone as a short answer: « Presque tout le monde. »
target_language_example: Presque tout le monde est d'accord, sauf deux personnes.
native_language_example: Almost everyone agrees, except two people.

additional_notes: Past participle form of "prendre un bain" (to take/have a bath), used with "avoir" in the passé composé: "j'ai pris un bain". It can also be used more broadly for other kinds of baths, like "un bain de boue" (a mud bath).
target_language_example: Après le sport, j'ai pris un bain chaud.
native_language_example: After working out, I took a hot bath.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **prendre** (“to take”) to talk about taking transportation. **pris** is the past participle of *prendre* and is used with **avoir** (e.g., *j’ai pris*, *elle a pris*, *nous avons pris*).
target_language_example: J’ai pris un taxi pour aller à l’aéroport.
native_language_example: I took a taxi to go to the airport.

additional_notes: This is the past participle phrase used with **avoir**: **(quelqu’un) a pris une décision** = “(someone) made a decision.” The full infinitive expression is **prendre une décision** (“to make a decision”). In English you usually say **make** a decision (not *take*), even though French uses **prendre** (“to take”).
target_language_example: Après en avoir discuté, nous avons pris une décision.
native_language_example: After discussing it, we made a decision.

additional_notes: Used mostly on signs, notices, emails, or official instructions to politely tell people what to do: "Prière de" + infinitive (frapper, refermer, respecter, etc.). It’s more formal/impersonal than « s’il vous plaît » and often means “please” or “kindly.”
target_language_example: Prière de ne pas fumer dans tout l’immeuble.
native_language_example: Please do not smoke anywhere in the building.

additional_notes: Used in politics/law for a text that proposes a new law or changes to an existing law. A projet de loi is discussed and voted on (adopté/ rejeté/ approuvé) by institutions like the Assemblée nationale or the Sénat; once adopted and in force, it becomes a loi.
target_language_example: Le gouvernement a présenté un projet de loi sur l’éducation.
native_language_example: The government introduced a bill on education.

additional_notes: A polite, somewhat formal phrase used to wish someone gets well soon, especially in cards, messages, or when someone is ill or recovering. Often used with souhaiter: « Je te/vous souhaite un prompt rétablissement. » (te = informal singular, vous = formal or plural).
target_language_example: Je vous souhaite un prompt rétablissement après votre opération.
native_language_example: Wishing you a speedy recovery after your operation.

additional_notes: Used to warn that a place or piece of land is not public and you’re not allowed to enter or stay without permission. Often seen on signs (sometimes just “Propriété privée.”). You can say “sur une propriété privée” (on private property) or “dans une propriété privée” (inside/on the grounds of private property).
target_language_example: Attention : vous entrez sur une propriété privée.
native_language_example: Warning: you are entering private property.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located at a short distance from something else. It’s followed by a noun or pronoun: près de la gare (near the station). Common with places: près de chez moi = near my home / near where I live.
target_language_example: Il y a un café près de l'école.
native_language_example: There is a café near the school.

additional_notes: Used to indicate physical proximity to a masculine singular noun: près du + noun (du = de + le). With a feminine noun: près de la; plural: près des; vowel/h muet: près de l’. Often interchangeable with "à côté de" (next to), but "près de" can mean generally nearby, not necessarily right beside.
target_language_example: Le café est près du musée.
native_language_example: The café is near the museum.

additional_notes: Inversion of the verb and pronoun: préférer (to prefer) + tu, used to ask someone’s preference. Common in questions like « Tu préfères… ? » (more casual) or « Préfères-tu… ? » (a bit more formal). Often followed by a choice with « ou » (or), or by « Comment/Quelle/Que… ? » to specify what kind of preference.
target_language_example: Préfères-tu le thé ou le café ?
native_language_example: Do you prefer tea or coffee?

additional_notes: Inverted question form of the verb « préférer » with « vous » (you). Used in polite/formal questions: « Préférez-vous A ou B ? » = “Do you prefer A or B?”
target_language_example: Préférez-vous le thé ou le café ?
native_language_example: Do you prefer tea or coffee?

additional_notes: Refers to getting dinner ready (cooking, chopping, organizing, etc.). Commonly used in constructions like « commencer à préparer le dîner » (to start making dinner) and « être en train de préparer le dîner » (to be in the middle of making dinner).
target_language_example: Je suis en train de préparer le dîner, peux-tu mettre la table ?
native_language_example: I’m making dinner right now; can you set the table?

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form addressed to “you” plural or formal (“vous”). It’s used to warn or announce what is about to happen next: *Préparez-vous à + infinitive* (e.g., *mourir, sauter, intervenir*).
target_language_example: Préparez-vous à partir dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Get ready to leave in five minutes.

meaning: to apologize; to offer my apologies.
additional_notes: A polite/formal way to apologize. You can say it alone (Je dois présenter mes excuses.) or add who you’re apologizing to with "à" (présenter mes excuses à quelqu’un). Often used in more serious situations than "je suis désolé(e)".
target_language_example: Je tiens à présenter mes excuses à toute l’équipe pour mon retard.
native_language_example: I would like to apologize to the whole team for being late.

meaning: "do you plan to" / "are you planning to" (asking about someone’s intention).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone intends or expects to do. It comes from the verb "prévoir" (to plan/anticipate). Often followed by an infinitive: « prévois-tu de partir ? » = “are you planning to leave?”
target_language_example: Prévois-tu de venir demain ?
native_language_example: Are you planning to come tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (prêt à + verb) to say someone is ready/prepared or willing to do something: "Je suis prêt à partir" (I'm ready to leave). It can also mean something is ready for the next step: "prêt à imprimer" (ready to print). Agreement: prêt (masc.), prête (fem.), prêts (masc. pl.), prêtes (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas prêt à prendre une décision maintenant.
native_language_example: I'm not ready to make a decision right now.

meaning: ready to leave; ready to go.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is prepared to depart (physically leaving). It agrees with the person: prêt (masc.), prête (fem.), prêts / prêtes (plural). Often used as a question: « Prêt(e) à partir ? » In casual speech you may hear « T’es prêt(e) à partir ? »
target_language_example: Je suis prêt à partir.
native_language_example: I’m ready to leave.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine subject (elle, ma sœur, la personne, etc.). Followed by an infinitive verb: prête à partir, prête à écrire. For masculine: prêt à. For plural: prêts à / prêtes à.
target_language_example: Elle est prête à commencer.
native_language_example: She is ready to start.

meaning: to pay attention; to pay heed.
additional_notes: Commonly used with "à" + a thing/person: "prêter attention à son histoire" (pay attention to his story). With an indirect object pronoun (lui/leur), it means giving someone your attention: "lui prêter attention" = pay attention to him/her; "leur prêter attention" = pay attention to them. Often used in advice or warnings ("Tu devrais...", "Tu dois...").
target_language_example: Tu devrais prêter attention à son histoire.
native_language_example: You should pay attention to his story.

meaning: to take an oath; to swear (an oath).
additional_notes: Used in formal situations (court, official ceremonies) when someone promises to tell the truth or to fulfill a duty. Often appears with "prêter serment" or "prêter serment de + infinitive" (to swear to do something). You may also see "faire prêter serment à quelqu’un" = to administer an oath to someone.
target_language_example: Avant de témoigner, vous devez prêter serment de dire la vérité.
native_language_example: Before testifying, you must swear to tell the truth.

additional_notes: A person or shop that lends you money in exchange for an object you leave as a guarantee (un gage). If you repay the loan, you can get the object back; if not, the pawnbroker may sell it. Also used about the business: « aller chez le prêteur sur gages ».
target_language_example: J’ai mis ma montre chez le prêteur sur gages pour obtenir un peu d’argent.
native_language_example: I pawned my watch at the pawnbroker’s to get a bit of money.

additional_notes: Used with the verb être: être prêt(s)/prête(s)/prêt(e)s à + infinitive. Agree "prêt" with the subject: prêt (m. sing.), prête (f. sing.), prêts (m. plural or mixed), prêtes (f. plural). "prêts à" is the masculine plural (or mixed-group) form.
target_language_example: Nous sommes prêts à partir.
native_language_example: We are ready to leave.

additional_notes: A formal, polite way to ask permission or make an offer, using inversion of je peux. In everyday spoken French, people more often say est-ce que je peux... or just je peux... ?
target_language_example: Puis-je entrer ?
native_language_example: May I come in?

additional_notes: A formal/polite way to ask for something you want to receive (a document, the bill, food, an item) in places like restaurants, hotels, or at a counter. It’s the inverted question form of « je peux avoir… ? ». Often followed by a noun and optionally « s’il vous plaît ».
target_language_example: Puis-je avoir un café, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I have a coffee, please?

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to ask for something, common with strangers or in shops/restaurants. Often followed by a noun: « Puis-je avoir un autographe ? ». Use « une » with feminine nouns (« Puis-je avoir une couverture ? ») and make it plural for more than one (« Puis-je avoir des serviettes ? »).
target_language_example: Puis-je avoir un verre d’eau, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I have a glass of water, please?

additional_notes: A polite, fairly formal way to ask about paying. Uses inversion (puis-je = "can I") and is often followed by how you want to pay: avec la carte (by card), en espèces (in cash), en euros (in euros), par chèque (by check). In everyday speech, people also say: "Est-ce que je peux payer… ?"
target_language_example: Puis-je payer en espèces ?
native_language_example: Can I pay in cash?

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to ask permission or request something. Literally it’s an inverted question: "puis-je" = "can I" + "prendre" = "to take". Used for things like asking to take a day off (prendre un jour de congé), ordering/requesting (prendre votre commande), or asking what amount you might gain/put on (prendre des kilos = gain weight). In casual speech, people often say "Est-ce que je peux prendre…?" or "Je peux prendre…?"
target_language_example: Puis-je prendre un café, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I have a coffee, please?

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to ask for permission or possibility. "Puis-je" is an inverted form of "je peux" (can I) and is common in writing or formal speech. Use it with a noun or object you want to use: "Puis-je utiliser + [object] ?"
target_language_example: Puis-je utiliser votre ordinateur un moment ?
native_language_example: May I use your computer for a moment?

additional_notes: Very polite/inverted question form of "je peux voir…?". Used to ask permission to look at something (a menu, document, ticket, item, etc.). Often followed by a noun or pronoun: "Puis-je voir le menu ?", "Puis-je voir celui-ci ?"
target_language_example: Puis-je voir votre passeport, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I see your passport, please?

additional_notes: Very polite/inverted question form of "je peux" (“can I”). It’s usually followed by a verb: "puis-je vous présenter…" (may I introduce you…), "puis-je vous aider ?" (may I help you?), "puis-je vous donner…" (may I give you…). "vous" is the formal/plural “you” and can be either the direct object (“touch you”) or indirect object (“give you”, “serve you”).
target_language_example: Puis-je vous aider à porter ces sacs ?
native_language_example: May I help you carry these bags?

meaning: "May I ask you…?" / "Can I ask you…?" (polite).
additional_notes: Very polite, formal way to ask permission to ask a question. Uses inversion (puis-je = can I), and vous for a formal/plural "you". Often followed by a question: « Puis-je vous demander où sont les toilettes ? ». Note: « demander » usually means "to ask" or "to request," not "to demand."
target_language_example: Puis-je vous demander votre nom, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I ask your name, please?

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to offer someone something (often a drink or food). Uses inversion for questions: « puis-je » = « can I/may I ». « vous » is the formal/plural “you.” Often followed by « du/de la/des » or « quelque chose à boire/à manger ». You may also hear « Que puis-je vous offrir ? » = “What can I get you?/What may I offer you?”
target_language_example: Puis-je vous offrir un café ?
native_language_example: May I offer you a coffee?

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to ask for a conversation. Used with “vous” (formal ‘you’ or plural ‘you’). Often followed by details like “une seconde / une minute” (for a second/minute), “dehors” (outside), or “seul à seul” (in private, one-on-one).
target_language_example: Puis-je vous parler un instant, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I speak to you for a moment, please?

additional_notes: A noun for a sweater you pull over your head (often just shortened to "un pull" in everyday French). Common with colors and comparisons: "un pull-over bleu", "le plus cher", "le même que". Used when shopping: "Puis-je essayer ce pull-over ?"
target_language_example: Il fait froid : je vais mettre mon pull-over.
native_language_example: It’s cold: I’m going to put on my sweater.

additional_notes: Very vulgar insult/intensifier used to show anger, frustration, or strong emphasis before a noun: "ce putain de + nom" (this fucking + noun), "un putain de + nom" (a fucking + noun), or as an exclamation: "Quel putain de … !" (What a fucking …!). Common in arguments and rude speech; avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: J’en ai marre de ce putain de bruit !
native_language_example: I’m sick of this fucking noise!

meaning: Very strong vulgar swearword: “fucking shit!” / “for fuck’s sake!”
additional_notes: Used to express intense anger, frustration, or contempt. Extremely offensive and not appropriate in polite conversation. Often said as an exclamation on its own or added to an insult (e.g., “Va te faire foutre, putain de merde.”).
target_language_example: Putain de merde, j’ai encore raté le train !
native_language_example: Fucking shit, I missed the train again!

additional_notes: Refers to a man who has children and family responsibilities, often implying a respectable, responsible role. Common with être: « Je suis père de famille. » It can also be used after en (« en père de famille ») meaning “like a responsible family man / in a sensible, prudent way.”
target_language_example: Il agit en père de famille et pense d’abord à ses enfants.
native_language_example: He behaves like a responsible family man and thinks of his children first.

meaning: (very vulgar) to beat someone up; to smash someone’s face in.
additional_notes: Very aggressive, vulgar slang, typically used as a threat. « Gueule » is a crude word for mouth/muzzle/face (used for animals or as an insult for people). The phrase implies serious physical violence. Literally it’s like “to bust the face,” but it’s not a polite/literal expression and should be avoided in civil conversation.
target_language_example: Je vais te péter la gueule.
native_language_example: I’m going to beat you up.

meaning: to lose it; to flip out (suddenly get very angry or panic).
additional_notes: Very informal idiom. Literally evokes “blowing a fuse” (as in an electrical circuit). Used when someone suddenly snaps, gets furious, or can’t handle the stress anymore. Often used in the past tense: « Il/Elle a pété les plombs. » A close synonym is « péter un câble ».
target_language_example: Je vais péter les plombs si ça continue.
native_language_example: I’m going to lose it if this keeps up.

additional_notes: Most often used with the restrictive pattern **ne ... que** (= “only/just”): *Je ne l’ai vu qu'une fois* (“I’ve only seen him once”). It can be used about past events (*je ne l’ai rencontré…*) or future actions (*je ne le demanderai qu'une fois*). Note the elision: **que + une** → **qu'une**.
target_language_example: Je ne l'ai rencontré qu'une fois.
native_language_example: I only met him once.

meaning: contraction of « que à » (often in « n’avoir qu’à » = “just have to / only need to”).
additional_notes: « Qu’à » is used instead of « que à » before a vowel sound. Very common in the pattern « (ne) … avoir qu’à + infinitive » to give a simple suggestion or instruction: « Tu n’as qu’à… » = “You just have to… / All you need to do is…”. It can also appear in fixed expressions like « n’en faire qu’à sa tête » (“to do only what one wants / be stubborn”).
target_language_example: Tu n'as qu'à cliquer ici.
native_language_example: You just have to click here.

meaning: "what did you have?" / "what had you...?" (formal question).
additional_notes: Contraction of « que aviez-vous ». « aviez-vous » is the formal/inverted question form of « vous aviez » (“you had/you used to have”). Used in polite/formal contexts (often written). Can also appear before another verb in the past: « Qu'aviez-vous fait ? » (“What had you done?”).
target_language_example: Qu'aviez-vous commandé ?
native_language_example: What did you order?

meaning: "What about…?" / "How about…?" (asking about the situation/status of someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to ask for an update or clarification about someone/something, often after discussing something else: « Et qu'en est-il de… ? » = “And what about…?”. Typically followed by « de + noun » or « de + stressed pronoun » (de vous / de toi / de lui / d’elle / de nous / d’eux). Fairly formal/neutral in tone; in casual speech, « et … alors ? » or « et … ? » may be used instead.
target_language_example: On a réglé ton problème ; et qu'en est-il de ta sœur ?
native_language_example: We solved your problem; and what about your sister?

meaning: "What’s the matter?" / "What is it?" / "What’s going on?" / sometimes literally "What’s there?"
additional_notes: Very common question whose meaning depends on context. On its own ("qu'est-ce qu'il y a ?"), it usually means "What’s wrong?" or "What’s going on?" You can also add a complement to ask what is present somewhere: "qu'est-ce qu'il y a dehors ?" (what’s outside?), "qu'est-ce qu'il y a là-dessous ?" (what’s underneath?), or "qu'est-ce qu'il y a d'autre/de mieux ?" (what else/better is there?). Literally it’s like "what is it that there is," but in natural English you usually translate it as "What’s the matter?" or "What’s going on?"
target_language_example: Dis-moi, qu'est-ce qu'il y a ? Tu as l’air inquiet.
native_language_example: Tell me, what’s wrong? You look worried.

meaning: 'What is she…?' (used to start a question about what she is doing/saying, etc.).
additional_notes: This is the question starter "qu'est-ce que" + "elle" (she). It’s usually followed by a verb: « Qu'est-ce qu'elle fait ? » = “What is she doing?” You can use it when you don’t do subject–verb inversion (instead of « Que fait-elle ? »).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'elle veut dire ?
native_language_example: What does she mean?

meaning: "What is he doing?" / "What does he do?"
additional_notes: Common way to ask a question with *qu'est-ce que* + subject + verb. In these examples it usually means "What is he doing?" (right now), especially with context like *là-bas/là-haut* or *au juste* ("exactly"). Without context, it can also mean "What does he do?" (as a job), but you'd often add something like *dans la vie ?* to make that clear.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'il fait dehors à cette heure-ci ?
native_language_example: What is he doing outside at this time?

additional_notes: A very common way to ask what is happening (often because something seems wrong or surprising). It’s neutral (not slang). You can add a place or time: « qu'est-ce qu'il se passe en bas ? » (downstairs), « …là ? » (there), « …maintenant ? » (now). In faster or more standard speech, you may also hear « qu'est-ce qui se passe ? » (same meaning).
target_language_example: Maman, qu'est-ce qu'il se passe ?
native_language_example: Mom, what’s happening?

additional_notes: Used to begin a question meaning “what” when the subject is ils (“they”). It’s the common spoken pattern: Qu’est-ce que + subject + verb. The verb tense changes the meaning (present, past, future): Qu’est-ce qu’ils font ? / Qu’est-ce qu’ils ont fait ? / Qu’est-ce qu’ils feront ?
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'ils veulent exactement ?
native_language_example: What do they want exactly?

meaning: "What do we do?" / "What are we supposed to do?"
additional_notes: A very common question to ask what to do next, what the plan is, or how to handle a situation. It can refer to the present moment (Maintenant, qu'est-ce qu'on fait ?), the next step (Qu'est-ce qu'on fait après ?), or what to do with something (Qu'est-ce qu'on fait avec ça ?). "On" here usually means "we" in everyday French (instead of "nous"). Tone can range from neutral planning to worried/urgent depending on context.
target_language_example: Bon, qu'est-ce qu'on fait maintenant ?
native_language_example: So, what do we do now?

meaning: What are we going to do?
additional_notes: Common way to ask what the next step or solution is, often showing worry, confusion, or urgency. Uses “on” (= “we” in everyday French) instead of the more formal “nous”: “Qu’est-ce que nous allons faire ?”. Can be followed by “avec + person/thing” (what are we going to do with her/him/it?) or “de + pronoun” (what are we going to do about them?).
target_language_example: Il pleut et on n’a pas de parapluie… qu'est-ce qu'on va faire ?
native_language_example: It’s raining and we don’t have an umbrella… what are we going to do?
