additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion or information about a singular noun: « Quel est votre + nom (masc. sing.) ? ». It must agree with what follows: « quelle est votre… » (fem. sing.), « quels sont vos… » / « quelles sont vos… » (plural). Also note « votre » (your, singular) vs « vos » (your, plural).
target_language_example: Quel est votre nom ?
native_language_example: What is your name?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s name politely, using the formal “vous.” Often appears with “Excusez-moi,” “Monsieur/Madame,” or “s’il vous plaît.” In an embedded question (no question mark), it keeps the same word order: “Je sais quel est votre nom.”
target_language_example: Bonjour, quel est votre nom, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Hello, what is your name, please?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a concessive clause meaning “no matter what … was.” It’s the imperfect subjunctive of être (“fût” = “was”), mainly found in formal writing. In everyday French you usually see: « quel que soit … » (“whatever … is”) or « quel qu’il était … » depending on context.
target_language_example: Quel que fût son choix, je le respecterais.
native_language_example: Whatever his choice was, I would respect it.

additional_notes: Used to criticize or complain about a group of people: « quelle bande de + nom (pluriel) ! ». Even though it refers to several people, « bande » is feminine singular, so it stays « quelle ». Commonly followed by a pejorative noun; many real-life uses can be vulgar/offensive, so use with care. Note: before a vowel or mute h, « de » often contracts to « d’ » (e.g., « quelle bande d’… »).
target_language_example: Oh, quelle bande de crétins !
native_language_example: Oh, what a bunch of idiots!

additional_notes: Used to express admiration or surprise before a feminine singular noun: « Quelle belle matinée ! ». It agrees with the noun: masculine « Quel beau… ! », feminine plural « Quelles belles… ! », masculine plural « Quels beaux… ! ». Often used with an exclamation mark.
target_language_example: Quelle belle idée !
native_language_example: What a beautiful idea!

additional_notes: A common, polite way to ask for the current time. Often used with an extra detail like "maintenant" (now) or a place/time zone: "Quelle heure est-il à Londres ?"
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, quelle heure est-il ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time is it?

additional_notes: An exclamation used to react to something shocking, disturbing, or unpleasant (bad news, a terrible situation, something disgusting). Often said on its own ("Quelle horreur !") or followed by what you’re reacting to ("Quelle horreur, la guerre !").
target_language_example: Il a encore oublié mon anniversaire — quelle horreur !
native_language_example: He forgot my birthday again—how awful!

additional_notes: Used to ask what language someone speaks/uses, or what language something was written/translated in. Often appears in questions like « Quelle langue parles-tu ? » (What language do you speak?) or « En quelle langue… ? » (In which language…?). Note the related form with de: « De quelle langue… ? » = “from which language…?” (e.g., when translating).
target_language_example: Tu parles en quelle langue au travail ?
native_language_example: What language do you speak at work?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the category, style, or type of something. It agrees with the noun: use "quelle sorte de" with a feminine singular noun (une sorte), and often "quelle sorte d'" before a vowel/h (e.g., "quelle sorte d'activités ?"). For plural nouns, you can also hear/see "quelles sortes de".
target_language_example: Quelle sorte de musique écoutes-tu ?
native_language_example: What kind of music do you listen to?

additional_notes: Used to ask a question about a feminine singular noun: « Quelle est la + noun ? » (e.g., « la définition », « la probabilité », « la taille »). For a masculine singular noun, you usually say « quel est le… ? ». You can also use « quelle est l’… ? » before a vowel sound.
target_language_example: Quelle est la date aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: What is the date today?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to compare two things. It’s typically followed by two items linked with "et" (A et B). You can swap in other question words for different grammar (e.g., "Quelles sont les différences entre…" for plural).
target_language_example: Quelle est la différence entre un bus et un tram ?
native_language_example: What is the difference between a bus and a tram?

meaning: 'what is your…?' (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask a question about someone’s (or something’s) feminine singular thing: *Quelle est ta mission ?* “What is your mission?” **Quelle** agrees with a feminine noun; **ta** is “your” before a feminine singular noun (e.g., *ta valise*, *ta mission*). For a masculine singular noun, you’d usually say **Quel est ton… ?**
target_language_example: Quelle est ta couleur préférée ?
native_language_example: What is your favorite color?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a specific item/information that belongs to the person you’re speaking to, with the formal/polite possessive adjective « votre » (instead of informal « ton/ta »). It often starts a question like « Quelle est votre idée ? » (your idea) or « Quelle est votre destination ? » (your destination). The noun after it should be feminine singular because of « quelle »; for masculine singular you’d use « Quel est votre … ? » and for plural « Quelles sont vos … ? ».
target_language_example: Quelle est votre adresse ?
native_language_example: What is your address?

additional_notes: Used to ask about multiple languages. It’s the feminine plural form of the question word « quel » because « langue » is feminine (« une langue »). Typically followed by a verb like « parler »: « Quelles langues parles-tu ? »
target_language_example: Quelles langues étudies-tu en ce moment ?
native_language_example: Which languages are you studying right now?

additional_notes: Used to ask about several things (plural) when the noun that follows is feminine plural (e.g., les chances, les conditions, les origines, les prévisions, les sources). Often followed by a noun phrase and sometimes by "de" + noun (e.g., "les chances de survie"). For masculine plural, use "quels sont les".
target_language_example: Quelles sont les prochaines étapes ?
native_language_example: What are the next steps?

meaning: "what are your" (asking about plural feminine things).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to list or explain their plural feminine nouns (e.g., conditions, intentions, obligations). It’s formal/polite because it uses "vos" (your, formal or plural). The singular feminine version is "quelle est votre… ?"
target_language_example: Quelles sont vos priorités pour cette année ?
native_language_example: What are your priorities for this year?

additional_notes: An indefinite pronoun for an unspecified person. It is normally treated as singular: quelqu'un est là = 'someone is there.'
target_language_example: Il y a quelqu'un à la porte.
native_language_example: There's someone at the door.

additional_notes: Refers to another person besides the one already mentioned. Very common in questions (e.g., « En avez-vous parlé à quelqu'un d'autre ? » / « Quelqu'un d'autre en veut ? »). In negatives, it often appears as « personne d'autre » (“no one else”): « Je n'en ai parlé à personne d'autre. » Note that the order is fixed: you say « quelqu'un d'autre », not *« d'autre quelqu'un ».
target_language_example: En avez-vous parlé à quelqu'un d'autre ?
native_language_example: Have you talked about it to someone else?

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s character (kind, trustworthy, well-intentioned). It often appears with forms of être ("Tu es quelqu’un de bien.") or penser/croire ("Je pense que tu es…"). "De bien" here means “good/decent” in a moral or personal sense, not “good at something.”
target_language_example: Je pense que tu es quelqu'un de bien.
native_language_example: I think you’re a good person.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified person (you don’t know who, or it doesn’t matter who). Common as a subject: « quelqu'un a appelé » (someone called). In questions like « Quelqu'un à la maison ? », it means “Is anyone home?” Contrast: « quelqu'un » (someone) vs « personne » (nobody/no one when used with negation: « Je ne vois personne. »).
target_language_example: Quelqu'un frappe à la porte.
native_language_example: Someone is knocking at the door.

additional_notes: Used to say that an action is necessary but the person isn’t specified. It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., aller, rester, dire, faire). "Doit" is the present tense of "devoir" (to have to / must).
target_language_example: Quelqu'un doit appeler la police.
native_language_example: Someone has to call the police.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unknown or unspecified place. Common with verbs like aller (go), être (be), partir (leave), voir (see), cacher (hide), déposer (drop off). It can also refer to a vague location in the sense of “in some place/area,” without saying exactly where.
target_language_example: On peut se retrouver quelque part en ville ?
native_language_example: Can we meet up somewhere in town?

additional_notes: Used for an unspecified thing. In positive statements it usually means "something"; in questions and negatives it often corresponds to "anything."
target_language_example: J'ai quelque chose à te dire.
native_language_example: I have something to tell you.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an action, situation, or example of that kind—often with a judgment ("I’d never do something like that") or as a vague add-on at the end ("…or something like that"). "Ça" usually refers to what was just mentioned or what you’re pointing to.
target_language_example: On pourrait aller au cinéma, ou quelque chose comme ça.
native_language_example: We could go to the movies, or something like that.

additional_notes: Used when referring to an additional or different thing from what was just mentioned. Very common in questions (e.g., offering more food or asking if there’s anything else): « Tu veux quelque chose d’autre ? » You can also use it in statements to mean something different happened: « Quelque chose d’autre s’est passé. »
target_language_example: Je cherche quelque chose d'autre, plus simple.
native_language_example: I'm looking for something else, simpler.

additional_notes: Used before an adjective to describe an unspecified thing: quelque chose de grave = 'something serious', quelque chose de différent = 'something different'. In English, you usually just say 'something' + adjective, without 'of'.
target_language_example: Je voudrais quelque chose de chaud à boire.
native_language_example: I would like something hot to drink.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified new thing (an activity, idea, change, item, etc.). Very common in everyday speech. Word order: *quelque chose* (something) + *de nouveau* (new). After *quelque chose*, French often uses *de* + adjective (e.g., *quelque chose d’intéressant* = something interesting).
target_language_example: J’ai envie d’essayer quelque chose de nouveau ce week-end.
native_language_example: I feel like trying something new this weekend.

additional_notes: Used when you want an additional thing or an option that is “more” in some way. Very common patterns: (1) "quelque chose de plus" = something more (another thing, something extra). (2) "quelque chose de plus" + adjective = something more + adjective: "quelque chose de plus petit" (something smaller), "de plus ordinaire" (something more ordinary).
target_language_example: Vous auriez quelque chose de plus simple ?
native_language_example: Would you have something simpler?

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified special thing (a gift, plan, surprise, meal, etc.). Very common in questions and offers: « Tu veux quelque chose de spécial ? » / « J’ai quelque chose de spécial pour toi. ». The structure is « quelque chose » + « de » + adjective (e.g., « quelque chose d’important »).
target_language_example: On prépare quelque chose de spécial pour ton anniversaire.
native_language_example: We’re preparing something special for your birthday.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has something intended for you (a message, a package, news, a gift, etc.): « Avez-vous quelque chose pour moi ? ». In « Fais quelque chose pour moi », it means “do something for me” (a favor/help). « T’as quelque chose pour moi ? » is the informal version of « Tu as… ? ».
target_language_example: Tu as quelque chose pour moi ?
native_language_example: Do you have anything for me?

additional_notes: Used to say you have something intended for the person you’re speaking to (a gift, a message, a favor), or to offer help: « Je peux faire quelque chose pour toi ? » = “Can I do something for you?” Often appears with « avoir » (j’ai quelque chose pour toi) or « faire » (faire quelque chose pour toi). « toi » is informal; in more formal situations use « quelque chose pour vous ».
target_language_example: J’ai quelque chose pour toi : un petit cadeau.
native_language_example: I have something for you: a small gift.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause after *quelque chose* (“something”). The verb in the clause is often in the indicative (*quelque chose que je connais* = something I know), but can be in the subjunctive after ideas like possibility/need (*quelque chose que je puisse faire* = something I can do).
target_language_example: J’ai quelque chose que je veux te dire.
native_language_example: I have something I want to tell you.

additional_notes: Used to offer or ask for a drink in a general way (water, juice, etc.) when you don’t specify what. Very common in polite offers (Puis-je vous offrir… ?) and casual questions (T’as… ?).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre quelque chose à boire, j’ai soif.
native_language_example: I’ll have something to drink; I’m thirsty.

additional_notes: Used when asking or saying you know/heard/read some information related to a topic already mentioned. Common with verbs like entendre (to hear), lire (to read), savoir (to know). Register depends on the rest of the sentence (tu = informal, vous = formal/plural).
target_language_example: Je sais quelque chose à ce sujet, mais je ne peux pas en parler.
native_language_example: I know something about it, but I can’t talk about it.

additional_notes: Used when someone has a comment, explanation, or objection. Often in questions like « Tu as quelque chose à dire ? » / « Vous avez quelque chose à dire ? » meaning “Do you have anything to say?” or “Do you have something to add?” It can also be said on its own (« Quelque chose à dire ? ») as a prompt. In « pour ta défense », it means “in your defense” (a request for an explanation/justification).
target_language_example: Si tu as quelque chose à dire, dis-le maintenant.
native_language_example: If you have something to say, say it now.

meaning: "something to do" (a task/errand; something that needs doing).
additional_notes: Often used with avoir: « J’ai quelque chose à faire » = “I have something to do / I’m busy.” With a place or time: « quelque chose à faire ici/ce soir » = “something to do here/tonight.” In the expression « en avoir quelque chose à faire » (often negative: « j’en ai rien à faire »), it can mean “to care (about it).”
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : j’ai quelque chose à faire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have something to do.

additional_notes: Used to ask if there is any food available, or to offer food. Very common in everyday speech. In questions it often appears as: « Tu as / T’as quelque chose à manger ? » or « Il y a quelque chose à manger ? ».
target_language_example: J'ai faim : tu as quelque chose à manger ?
native_language_example: I'm hungry—do you have something to eat?

meaning: “something to tell me” (as a question: “Do you have something to tell me?”).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has information, news, or a confession to share. Often implies you suspect something is going on. It can be said as a full question (Tu as quelque chose à me dire ?) or as a shortened prompt (Quelque chose à me dire ?).
target_language_example: Avant qu’on parte, tu as quelque chose à me dire ?
native_language_example: Before we leave, do you have something to tell me?

additional_notes: Used for an unknown or unspecified location: Elle est quelque part. It can also mean “around there / somewhere over there” with direction words (quelque part par là). With de, it often means “from somewhere” (I recognize it from somewhere): Je le connais de quelque part. Placed parenthetically (Quelque part, ...), it can be figurative: “in a way / deep down / somehow.”
target_language_example: Je suis sûr que j’ai vu ce film quelque part.
native_language_example: I’m sure I’ve seen this movie somewhere.

additional_notes: Used as an adverb to soften a statement (often more formal than "un peu"). It can modify adjectives or verbs: "quelque peu surpris" (somewhat surprised), "je suis quelque peu inquiet" (I’m a little worried).
target_language_example: Je suis quelque peu fatigué aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I’m a little tired today.

additional_notes: Used to mean an unspecified amount of time. Common patterns: **il y a quelque temps** = “some time ago”; **depuis quelque temps** = “for some time / for a while (now)”; **quelque temps** by itself can mean “for a while” (duration) depending on context.
target_language_example: On ne s’est pas parlé depuis quelque temps.
native_language_example: We haven’t talked for a while.

additional_notes: Feminine plural form of the pronoun phrase meaning “a few (of them).” It refers back to a previously mentioned feminine plural noun (e.g., des œuvres, des frites). Often used with **de** + noun phrase: **quelques-unes de ces…** = “a few of these…”. You can also answer briefly with just **Quelques-unes.** = “A few.”
target_language_example: J’en prends quelques-unes.
native_language_example: I’ll take a few (of them).

additional_notes: Refers to a small number of people or things (plural). Often used with a complement: "quelques-uns de + noun" (Quelques-uns des passagers...) or with "en" to mean "some of them" (Je vais vous en montrer quelques-uns; Il doit en rester quelques-uns). Also used alone as a short answer: "Quelques-uns."
target_language_example: Il me reste quelques-uns de ces biscuits, tu en veux ?
native_language_example: I have a few of these cookies left—do you want some?

additional_notes: Refers to an approximate, small number of years (not exact). Often used to talk about how long something lasts or how long it may take: « encore quelques années » = “a few more years.”
target_language_example: J’ai vécu à Lyon pendant quelques années.
native_language_example: I lived in Lyon for a few years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an approximate, small number of hours (not exact). Common with time expressions: **dans quelques heures** (in a few hours/from now), **il y a quelques heures** (a few hours ago), **en quelques heures** (in/within a few hours), **quelques heures de plus** (a few more hours).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de quelques heures pour terminer ce travail.
native_language_example: I need a few hours to finish this work.

additional_notes: Means an imprecise small number of days (usually more than one). Often used with time expressions like "dans quelques jours" (in a few days), "il y a quelques jours" (a few days ago), "au bout de quelques jours" (after a few days), or "quelques jours plus tard" (a few days later).
target_language_example: Je reviens dans quelques jours.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in a few days.

additional_notes: Means a short amount of time (more than 1 minute, not very long). Common patterns: "pendant quelques minutes" = for a few minutes (duration), "dans quelques minutes" = in a few minutes (from now), "quelques minutes plus tard" = a few minutes later. Often used with "ça fait... que" to say how long something has been true: "Ça fait quelques minutes que..." = It’s been a few minutes since...
target_language_example: Attends quelques minutes, j’arrive.
native_language_example: Wait a few minutes, I’m coming.

meaning: 'a few words' (a small amount of speaking or a short description).
additional_notes: Used literally for knowing only a small amount of a language ("Je ne connais que quelques mots"), and very commonly in set phrases like "échanger quelques mots" (to have a quick chat) and "en quelques mots" (in a few words = briefly). It can also be used idiomatically to suggest a short talk or quick questioning.
target_language_example: On peut se parler quelques mots après la réunion ?
native_language_example: Can we have a quick word after the meeting?

additional_notes: Used when you want to ask a small number of questions, often politely in interviews, at reception, or in customer service. In requests it’s common with verbs like poser (to ask) and avoir (to have): « poser quelques questions », « avoir quelques questions ». With « quelques questions que ce soit », it means “any questions at all” (emphasizing that there are no restrictions).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, j’ai quelques questions sur le formulaire.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a few questions about the form.

additional_notes: Means an imprecise small number of weeks (often 2–4, depending on context). Common in time expressions like "il y a quelques semaines" (a few weeks ago) and with durations like "pendant" (for) or "prendre" (take) to say something will take a few weeks.
target_language_example: Le projet sera terminé dans quelques semaines.
native_language_example: The project will be finished in a few weeks.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified person. Often appears in expressions like « il y a quelqu’un » (there is someone), « quelqu’un d’autre » (someone else), or after a noun/adjective with « de/d’ »: « quelqu’un d’honnête » (someone honest).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de parler à quelqu’un.
native_language_example: I need to talk to someone.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a list or identification of several items. It agrees with the noun that follows: masculine plural quels (quels sont les avantages ?) vs feminine plural quelles (quelles sont les raisons ?). Often followed by a plural noun and sometimes by de (“Quels sont les avantages de… ?”).
target_language_example: Quels sont les documents nécessaires pour l’inscription ?
native_language_example: What are the documents needed for registration?

meaning: “What are your…?” (used before a plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s plural items (goals, plans, symptoms, etc.). Grammar: **quels** (plural masculine) + **sont** (are) + **tes** (your, plural). With a feminine plural noun, use **quelles sont tes…** (e.g., *Quelles sont tes idées ?*). With a singular noun, use **quel/quelle est ton/ta…** (e.g., *Quel est ton objectif ?*).
target_language_example: Quels sont tes hobbies ?
native_language_example: What are your hobbies?

additional_notes: Used to ask which person performed an action. It is often followed by a past participle in the passé composé, where English usually translates it with the simple past: for example, qui a fait = who did / who made.
target_language_example: Qui a pris mon stylo ?
native_language_example: Who took my pen?

additional_notes: Used to question or push back against an idea, assumption, or accusation (often rhetorical). Literally: "who has said that"; in everyday English you usually translate it as "who said that".
target_language_example: Qui a dit que tu n'avais pas le droit d'essayer ?
native_language_example: Who said you didn’t have the right to try?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the person responsible for an action. Often appears as a direct question ("Qui a fait ça ?") or inside a longer sentence after verbs like dire, savoir, découvrir ("Dis-moi qui a fait ça."). "Ça" means “that/this” in a general way.
target_language_example: Je veux savoir qui a fait ça.
native_language_example: I want to know who did that.

additional_notes: Used to ask who the winner is (question), or to describe someone: “(the person) who won.” It uses the past tense (passé composé): gagner → a gagné. Note: French gagner usually means “to win” (a game, a prize), not just “to gain.”
target_language_example: Tu sais qui a gagné le match ?
native_language_example: Do you know who won the game?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or mention the identity of the killer. Built with **qui** (“who”) + **a tué** (past tense of *tuer*, “killed,” using *avoir*). In statements it can introduce a relative clause: *la femme qui a tué…* (“the woman who killed…”).
target_language_example: La police cherche qui a tué le journaliste.
native_language_example: The police are looking for who killed the journalist.

additional_notes: Common, fairly informal way to ask or say who someone is/who the person is. Used both in direct questions (Qui c'est ?) and in indirect questions (Je veux savoir qui c'est.). Often refers to a person you don’t recognize or a caller/visitor. More formal: « qui est-ce ? » (direct question).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas qui c'est, mais il demande à te parler.
native_language_example: I don’t know who it is, but he’s asking to speak to you.

additional_notes: Used after a noun or pronoun to mean “that counts / that matters.” Very common in phrases like: “C’est tout ce qui compte” (“That’s all that matters”) and “Il n’y a que ça qui compte” (“That’s the only thing that matters”). Even though it literally looks like “who counts,” it often refers to things (like “ça”) and means “what matters.”
target_language_example: Ce qui compte, c'est d'être ensemble.
native_language_example: What matters is being together.

additional_notes: Used to ask about an additional person beyond the one(s) already mentioned or implied. Often comes after a person/group (“Vous et qui d'autre ?” = “You and who else?”) or stands alone (“Qui d'autre sait ?” = “Who else knows?”).
target_language_example: Qui d'autre sait que tu possèdes ces photos ?
native_language_example: Who else knows that you have these photos?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s identity, or more broadly to question who someone really is (e.g., their true nature). It’s the standard question form with inversion (subject pronoun after the verb): « Qui es-tu ? ». In casual speech, you’ll also hear « Tu es qui ? » (more informal).
target_language_example: Excuse-moi, qui es-tu ? Je ne te connais pas.
native_language_example: Excuse me, who are you? I don't know you.

additional_notes: Used either to ask about identity (“who is ...?”) or after a noun to mean “who/that is ...” in a relative clause.
target_language_example: Qui est à la porte ?
native_language_example: Who is at the door?

meaning: "who is it (that)…?" (used to form a 'who' question).
additional_notes:
Used in questions with the "est-ce que" pattern: 
- "Qui est-ce que + subject + verb ?" when 'who' is the object: « Qui est-ce que vous cherchez ? » (Who are you looking for?)
- "Qui est-ce qui + verb ?" when 'who' is the subject: « Qui est-ce qui vient ? » (Who is coming?)
Often interchangeable in meaning with simpler "Qui… ?" but a bit more explicit/structured.
target_language_example: Qui est-ce qui t’a donné ça ?
native_language_example: Who gave you that?

meaning: "who" (when asking who is the subject of the verb).
additional_notes: Used to ask who is doing an action (the person is the subject): Qui est-ce qui + verb. Common, neutral spoken French; slightly heavier/more emphatic than just "Qui + verb". Use "qui est-ce que" when "who" is the object (e.g., Qui est-ce que tu vois ? = Who do you see?).
target_language_example: Qui est-ce qui vient ce soir ?
native_language_example: Who is coming tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s identity before a noun: « Qui est ce + noun ? » (e.g., « Qui est ce monsieur ? » = “Who is this man?”). In modern French you may also see the hyphenated form « Qui est-ce ? » when it stands alone (“Who is it?”) or « Qui est-ce que c’est ? ».
target_language_example: Qui est ce professeur dont tu parles ?
native_language_example: Who is that teacher you’re talking about?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s identity. You can add details after it: avec… (“with…”), là-bas (“over there”), qui… (“who/that…”) to specify which man you mean. In polite speech you might say: « Savez-vous qui est cet homme ? » (“Do you know who that man is?”).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, qui est cet homme près de la porte ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, who is that man near the door?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s identity before a masculine singular noun: « Qui est le père ? » (“Who is the father?”). Also used in comparisons/superlatives with « le plus… »: « Qui est le plus fort ? » (“Who is the strongest?”). For feminine nouns you’ll usually see « qui est la… »; for plural « qui sont les… ».
target_language_example: Qui est le responsable de ce projet ?
native_language_example: Who is the person in charge of this project?

additional_notes: Used to ask or point out who is present. Very common in surprises or when you notice someone: « Devine qui est là ! » (“Guess who’s here!”), « Regarde/Regardez qui est là ! » (“Look who’s here!”). By itself as a question (« Qui est là ? ») can also mean “Who’s there?” (e.g., at the door).
target_language_example: Oh, devine qui est là : Marie !
native_language_example: Oh, guess who’s here: Marie!

additional_notes: Used to ask for the identity of a person connected to the listener. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun (ton acteur, ton ami). For feminine nouns, use “qui est ta … ?” (ta amie → actually “ton amie” because the noun starts with a vowel sound). For plural, use “qui sont tes … ?”.
target_language_example: Qui est ton professeur de français ?
native_language_example: Who is your French teacher?

additional_notes: Used in an indirect question (embedded after verbs like savoir, dire, deviner, se demander, se rappeler): «Je ne sais pas qui je suis.» In a direct question, French often uses inversion or est-ce que: «Qui suis-je ?» / «Qui est-ce que je suis ?» (the inversion form is more standard).
target_language_example: Je ne sais plus qui je suis.
native_language_example: I don't know who I am anymore.

additional_notes: Uses the relative pronoun « qui » as the subject of « parler » to describe a person or thing: « un guide qui parle le français » (a guide who speaks French), « un serpent qui parle » (a talking snake). It can also appear in questions like « À qui parle-t-elle ? » (“Who is she talking to?”). With « parler à », it means “to speak to / to resonate with”: « Voilà qui parle à mon âme. »
target_language_example: Je cherche quelqu’un qui parle anglais.
native_language_example: I’m looking for someone who speaks English.

meaning: what’s more; moreover (to add an extra point, often strengthening the argument).
additional_notes: Used to add an additional (often even more important) detail after a first statement, similar to “what’s more” or “on top of that.” It’s typically set off by commas in writing: “..., qui plus est, ...”. The second part can be a full clause or just an adjective/phrase: “..., et qui plus est, trop chère.”
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas le temps et, qui plus est, je n’ai pas l’argent.
native_language_example: I don’t have the time and, what’s more, I don’t have the money.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a concession: the person’s identity doesn’t matter. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., « qui que tu sois », « qui que vous soyez »). Often used at the start of a sentence, sometimes as a standalone opening: « Qui que vous soyez, ... ».
target_language_example: Qui que tu sois, tu peux entrer.
native_language_example: Whoever you are, you can come in.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified person, often in questions and negatives: «Avez-vous vu qui que ce soit ?» = “Did you see anyone?”; «Je n'ai vu qui que ce soit» = “I didn’t see anyone.” It’s common with negation (ne…pas / ne…jamais / etc.) and can also stand alone as a short answer meaning “anyone.”
target_language_example: Je n'ai entendu qui que ce soit pendant la nuit.
native_language_example: I didn’t hear anyone during the night.

additional_notes: Used to mean “any person, no matter who,” especially in questions and negative sentences: « Connaissez-vous qui que ce soit ? » (Do you know anyone?). With negation, it often appears as « ne … qui que ce soit » = “no one / anybody”: « Je ne connais qui que ce soit ici. » It can also be used in formal/neutral style; in everyday speech you may also hear « quelqu’un » in similar contexts.
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu as vu qui que ce soit dans le couloir ?
native_language_example: Did you see anyone in the hallway?

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or speculation, often as a rhetorical question: « Qui sait ce que… ? » (“Who knows what…?”). It can also be used parenthetically to suggest a possibility: « Tu devrais, qui sait ? » (“You should—who knows/maybe.”).
target_language_example: On peut essayer, qui sait ?
native_language_example: We can try—who knows?

additional_notes: "Qui" can mean "who" (for people) or "that/which" (as a relative pronoun). With "sont" ("are"), it’s used for plural subjects: (1) in questions like "Qui sont vos amis ?" (= Who are your friends?) and (2) in relative clauses like "des vêtements qui sont passés de mode" (= clothes that are out of fashion). Note: "À qui sont... ?" means "Whose ... are ...?" (literally "To whom are ...?").
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas qui sont ces gens.
native_language_example: I don't know who these people are.

additional_notes: Used to ask about identity. With a noun, it means “Who are these + noun?”: « Qui sont ces gens ? » (“Who are these people?”). With « à » in front (« À qui sont ces … ? »), it asks about ownership: “Whose … are these?” / “Who do these … belong to?” The verb agrees with « ces » (plural), so it’s « sont ».
target_language_example: Qui sont ces enfants ?
native_language_example: Who are these children?

meaning: "who (to you) has…" / "who … to you?" (used to ask who did something to you).
additional_notes: Used in questions. "qui" = who, "t'" is short for "te" (to you), and "a" is from "avoir" in the passé composé ("has"). It’s followed by a past participle: "Qui t’a dit ça ?" (Who told you that?).
target_language_example: Qui t'a appelé hier soir ?
native_language_example: Who called you last night?

additional_notes: "Qui" means "who/that" (as a subject: "the person/thing that does the action"), and "te" is the unstressed object pronoun "you" (informal singular), placed before the verb. You’ll see "qui te" in relative clauses ("quelqu’un qui te…" = “someone who … you”) and in questions like "Qui te… ?" = “Who … you?”
target_language_example: Je cherche quelqu’un qui te comprend.
native_language_example: I’m looking for someone who understands you.

additional_notes: Used in an indirect question/clause (not a direct question). Common after verbs like savoir (to know), dire (to say), demander (to ask): « Je sais qui tu es. » In indirect questions, French typically keeps normal word order (« qui tu es »), not inversion (« qui es-tu »).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas qui tu es.
native_language_example: I don’t know who you are.

additional_notes: Used to ask who will do something in the near future. It’s usually followed by an infinitive: « qui va + infinitive ? » (e.g., « Qui va gagner ? » = “Who’s going to win?”). It’s the near-future construction with « aller ».
target_language_example: Qui va préparer le dîner ce soir ?
native_language_example: Who is going to make dinner tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask which person wants something. Often followed by a noun ("Qui veut des cookies ?"), an infinitive ("Qui veut le savoir ?" = who wants to know), or a clause with "que" + subjunctive ("Qui veut que vous soyez... ?" = who wants you to be...). Can also be rhetorical (implying “nobody wants that”).
target_language_example: Qui veut venir avec nous au cinéma ?
native_language_example: Who wants to come with us to the movies?

meaning: on the alert; on the lookout (often in « être sur le qui vive »).
additional_notes: Used mostly in the fixed expression « être sur le qui vive » = to be vigilant/ready for something to happen. Historically comes from the old military challenge « Qui vive ? » (“Who goes there?”), so it can sound a bit formal or literary today. Spelling varies (hyphenated « qui-vive » is also common), but this entry keeps the exact form « qui vive ».
target_language_example: Depuis les cambriolages, les voisins sont sur le qui vive.
native_language_example: Since the break-ins, the neighbors are on the alert.

meaning: “Well, look who it is!” (said when you spot someone).
additional_notes: Used as an exclamation when someone arrives or when you notice them, often with surprise or amusement. Commonly appears with interjections like « Mais… ! », « Tiens… », or after « Regarde/Regardez… ».
target_language_example: Oh, qui voilà ! Ça faisait longtemps !
native_language_example: Oh, look who it is! It’s been a long time!

additional_notes: Used to ask who did something to you or for you, often in the past with the passé composé pattern: « Qui vous a + past participle ? » (e.g., « Qui vous a appelé ? » = “Who called you?”). « Vous » is the formal/plural “you.”
target_language_example: Qui vous a donné cette information ?
native_language_example: Who gave you that information?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the identity of the person who gave something to the listener. It uses the polite/plural object pronoun “vous” (“you”), and the past tense “a donné” (passé composé of donner). Often followed by a thing: “Qui vous a donné + [object] ?”
target_language_example: Qui vous a donné ce document ?
native_language_example: Who gave you this document?

meaning: 'who you are' (addressing one person formally or several people).
additional_notes: Used in indirect questions after verbs like dire (to tell), savoir (to know), comprendre (to understand): « Dites-moi qui vous êtes. » It can also appear as a direct question (« Qui vous êtes, vous ? »), but in standard French you more often hear « Qui êtes-vous ? » or (more common in speech) « Vous êtes qui ? ».
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas qui vous êtes, mais je peux vous aider.
native_language_example: I don't know who you are, but I can help you.

additional_notes: Used to ask or report someone’s identity in the past. Often introduces an embedded question after verbs like demander/savoir (e.g., "Il m’a demandé qui était..."), or starts a direct question ("Qui était avec lui ?"). For plural, you’ll usually see "qui étaient" (e.g., "Qui étaient ces gens ?").
target_language_example: Je ne savais pas qui était la personne au téléphone.
native_language_example: I didn’t know who the person on the phone was.

additional_notes: Uses subject–verb inversion (êtes-vous) and the formal "vous". It’s used to ask someone’s identity, often when you don’t know the person: "Pardon, qui êtes-vous ?". Can also appear after "de" in questions like "De qui êtes-vous le/la plus proche ?" (= "Who are you closest to?"). Informal version: "Qui es-tu ?".
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, qui êtes-vous ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, who are you?

meaning: fifteen days; (often) two weeks / a fortnight.
additional_notes: Literally “15 days,” but in everyday French it commonly means “about two weeks.” Common patterns: « pendant quinze jours » (for two weeks), « dans quinze jours » (in two weeks), « depuis quinze jours » (for two weeks, up to now), « tous les quinze jours » (every two weeks).
target_language_example: Je reviens dans quinze jours.
native_language_example: I'll be back in two weeks.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (pendant quinze minutes), time remaining (quinze minutes de reste / plus que quinze minutes), or time until something happens (dans quinze minutes). Can also be used for repeated intervals: toutes les quinze minutes (“every fifteen minutes”).
target_language_example: On part dans quinze minutes, dépêche-toi !
native_language_example: We’re leaving in fifteen minutes, hurry up!

additional_notes: Used to say you’ll do something despite a consequence or risk: “even if I have to… / even if it means…”. Often followed by an infinitive (quitte à + verb), and you can repeat it in advice: “Quitte à le faire, fais-le bien” = “If you’re going to do it anyway, do it well.”
target_language_example: Je veux y aller, quitte à rentrer très tard.
native_language_example: I want to go, even if it means getting home very late.

additional_notes: Used to ask for additional information or other options. Often appears in questions like « Il y a quoi d'autre ? » (What else is there?) or after « Tu sais… » as « Tu sais quoi d'autre ? » (You know what else?). It can also be used on its own as a follow-up: « Quoi d'autre ? » (What else?).
target_language_example: On a déjà parlé du budget — quoi d'autre faut-il vérifier ?
native_language_example: We’ve already talked about the budget—what else do we need to check?

additional_notes: A very common informal greeting used to ask how someone is doing or what’s been happening recently. Often used on its own after “Salut” or directly addressing someone (e.g., « Quoi de neuf, chef ? »). Typical answers can be « Pas grand-chose. » / « Rien de spécial. » / « Ça va. »
target_language_example: Salut ! Quoi de neuf ?
native_language_example: Hi! What’s up?

additional_notes: Used as a rhetorical question to show impatience, frustration, or disbelief, often when another problem/request comes up. Common on its own (“Quoi encore ?”), or after “Et …” (“Et quoi encore ?”).
target_language_example: Quoi encore ? J’ai déjà tout fait !
native_language_example: What now? I’ve already done everything!

additional_notes: Means “what to do” in the sense of knowing the right action. Very common after verbs like "savoir" / "ne pas savoir": "Je ne sais pas quoi faire" (I don’t know what to do). It can also appear in questions: "Tu sais quoi faire ?" (Do you know what to do?).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas quoi faire dans cette situation.
native_language_example: I don’t know what to do in this situation.

additional_notes: Used as a transition to move on from details, uncertainty, or disagreement and return to the main point. Very common at the start of a sentence (followed by a comma), and it can also be used alone to mean “Anyway.” It’s neutral/register-safe (not slang).
target_language_example: Quoi qu'il en soit, on se retrouve demain à 9 h.
native_language_example: Anyway, we’ll meet tomorrow at 9.

additional_notes:
Used to introduce a concessive idea: something is true or will happen regardless of conditions (often with the subjunctive): «Quoi que tu fasses…» = “Whatever you do…”. Common patterns: «quoi que + subject + verb» (whatever/no matter what someone does/says/thinks) and «quoi que + subjunctive + …».
Don’t confuse with «quoique» (one word) = “although/even though.”
target_language_example: Quoi que tu choisisses, je te soutiendrai.
native_language_example: Whatever you choose, I’ll support you.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as part of the fixed expression “quoi que ce soit” (= “whatever / anything at all”). You’ll often see it after a negative: “Je n’ai rien dit, quoi que ce soit.” In modern French, “quoi que ce” by itself is uncommon/incomplete without “soit.”
target_language_example: Je n’ai rien vu, quoi que ce soit.
native_language_example: I didn’t see anything at all.

additional_notes: Used to mean “anything at all,” often in questions or negative statements (with ne…pas / ne…jamais / personne, etc.). It can emphasize “no matter what” or “whatever,” depending on context: Je ne veux pas faire quoi que ce soit = “I don’t want to do anything (at all).”
target_language_example: Si tu as besoin de quoi que ce soit, appelle-moi.
native_language_example: If you need anything, call me.

additional_notes: Used to mean “anything at all,” often in questions and negative contexts: Je n’ai rien dit / Je n’ai dit quoi que ce soit. It can also appear after expressions like « si tu veux… » to mean “anything (you might want to say/do).” Similar idea to « n’importe quoi », but « quoi que ce soit » is more neutral/formal and common with doubt/possibility ("Is there anything…?", "Did I forget anything?").
target_language_example: Est-ce qu’il y a quoi que ce soit que je puisse faire pour aider ?
native_language_example: Is there anything I can do to help?

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to ask “what” + a clause: Qu’est-ce que + subject + verb. It’s very common in spoken and everyday French. For “What is it?”, you often hear: Qu’est-ce que c’est ?
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que tu cherches ?
native_language_example: What are you looking for?

meaning: "what ... you ...?" (used to ask a question, like “What are you…?”).
additional_notes: Very common question starter before a verb: “Qu’est-ce que tu + verb… ?” It introduces a direct question and is followed by the verb (often in the present tense): Qu’est-ce que tu fais ? = What are you doing? More formal alternatives include “Que fais-tu ?” or “Qu’est-ce que vous… ?” (for ‘you’ formal/plural).
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que tu fais ce soir ?
native_language_example: What are you doing tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask “what” when the thing you’re asking about is the subject of the verb (followed directly by a verb: Qu’est-ce qui se passe ?). Compare: “Qu’est-ce que… ?” when “what” is the object (Qu’est-ce que tu fais ? = What are you doing?). Often used to ask what’s wrong/what happened: Qu’est-ce qui ne va pas ? / Qu’est-ce qui cloche ?
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce qui te fait peur ?
native_language_example: What is it that scares you?

additional_notes: Contraction of « que » + « il ». Used after many verbs (e.g., comprendre, répondre, sentir) to introduce a clause: « J’ai compris qu’il voulait… » = “I understood that he wanted…”. Also appears in questions like « Quand est-ce qu’il… ? » where « qu’ » is part of « est-ce que » and doesn’t translate on its own.
target_language_example: Je pense qu’il arrive bientôt.
native_language_example: I think he’s arriving soon.

meaning: “that we / that one” (contraction of « que » + « on »).
additional_notes: « qu’on » is « que » (that) + « on » (we/one/people), with elision before a vowel sound: que + on → qu’on. It’s very common after expressions like « il faut que… » (it’s necessary that…) and « tu as dit que… » (you said that…). In sentences like « Allez, qu’on en finisse ! », it can sound like an exhortation meaning “come on, let’s … / let’s get it over with,” with « on » used like “we.”
target_language_example: Il faut qu’on parte maintenant.
native_language_example: We have to leave now.

additional_notes: Imperative form of *raconter* (“to tell/to recount”) addressed to one person (*tu*). *-moi* is the object pronoun “to me.” Often used to ask for a story or details: *Raconte-moi ce qui s’est passé* (“Tell me what happened”), *Raconte-moi ton premier baiser* (“Tell me about your first kiss”). More formal: *Racontez-moi...* (to *vous*).
target_language_example: Raconte-moi comment ça s’est passé.
native_language_example: Tell me how it went.

meaning: to tell stories; (often) to make things up / tell lies.
additional_notes: Usually means “to tell stories” in a neutral or positive way (e.g., being good at storytelling). In a critical context—especially with phrases like “ne faire que …” (“do nothing but …”) or when someone says “Ça suffit !” (“That’s enough!”)—it often implies the person is inventing excuses or lying. It can also be reflexive: “se raconter des histoires” = “to tell ourselves stories” (to fool ourselves).
target_language_example: Arrête de raconter des histoires : dis-moi la vérité.
native_language_example: Stop making things up: tell me the truth.

meaning: to refresh someone’s memory; to remind (someone).
additional_notes: Used when someone has forgotten or needs a reminder. Often appears as « se rafraîchir la mémoire » (“to refresh one’s own memory”) or with an indirect object pronoun: « Je vais te/lui/leur/vous rafraîchir la mémoire » (“I’m going to remind you/him-her/them/you”). Can sound slightly threatening or sarcastic depending on tone, especially in « Je vais te rafraîchir la mémoire. ».
target_language_example: Tu ne te souviens plus ? Je vais te rafraîchir la mémoire.
native_language_example: You don’t remember anymore? I’m going to refresh your memory (remind you).

meaning: currant (a very small seedless grape, usually dried and used in cooking/baking).
additional_notes: In French, "raisin" usually means "grape." "Raisin de Corinthe" refers to a very small seedless grape commonly dried into currants (often used in baking or cooking). The plural "raisins de Corinthe" is also common when referring to a quantity.
target_language_example: Ils cultivent le raisin de Corinthe dans cette région.
native_language_example: They grow currants in this region.

additional_notes: Common food term. Often used in the plural (« des raisins secs »), but the singular « raisin sec » is correct when referring to one raisin or the ingredient in general. Note the difference between « raisin » (grape) and « raisin sec » (raisin).
target_language_example: Ce gâteau contient du raisin sec.
native_language_example: This cake contains raisins.

meaning: reason for being; purpose (the main justification for something).
additional_notes: Used especially in formal or intellectual contexts to talk about the central purpose or justification of a person, organization, project, or idea. In English it’s also commonly used as a borrowed French phrase (“raison d’être”).
target_language_example: La raison d'être de cette association, c'est d'aider les familles en difficulté.
native_language_example: The purpose of this organization is to help families in difficulty.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of *se rappeler* addressed to **vous** (you plural or formal). Used to tell someone to remember something or keep something in mind: *Rappelez-vous que...* (“Remember that...”). As a question: *Que vous rappelez-vous ?* (“What do you remember?”).
target_language_example: Rappelez-vous de fermer la porte en partant.
native_language_example: Remember to close the door when you leave.

meaning: remember (it), keep in mind (informal singular command).
additional_notes: Imperative form of « se rappeler » addressed to one person you’re on « tu » terms with. It can take a direct object (« Rappelle-toi ceci. », « Rappelle-toi Noël dernier. ») or a clause with « que » (« Rappelle-toi que tu en es capable. »). Often used to emphasize an important instruction: « Et rappelle-toi, pas un mot ! ».
target_language_example: Rappelle-toi de fermer la porte en partant.
native_language_example: Remember to close the door when you leave.

additional_notes: Fairly formal/neutral (often used in medical, legal, or educational contexts). Often appears in the plural (« des rapports sexuels »), but the singular « un rapport sexuel » is also used when referring to one specific act. Common verb phrase: « avoir un rapport sexuel (avec quelqu’un) » = “to have sex (with someone)”.
target_language_example: Elle affirme qu’ils ont eu un rapport sexuel.
native_language_example: She claims they had sexual intercourse.

additional_notes: Most often used in the fixed phrase **par rapport à**: *Par rapport à toi...* (“Compared to you... / Relative to you...”). It can introduce a comparison, or indicate a reference point (“with respect to”). In more formal French, you may also see **avoir rapport à** meaning “to relate to / to have to do with.”
target_language_example: Par rapport à l'an dernier, les prix ont augmenté.
native_language_example: Compared to last year, prices have increased.

additional_notes: A common noun for the animal. It’s masculine: "un raton laveur". In questions, you’ll often see it with articles like "le" (the) or "un" (a).
target_language_example: Il y a un raton laveur dans le jardin.
native_language_example: There’s a raccoon in the yard.

meaning: to make up for lost time.
additional_notes: Used when you’ve fallen behind, wasted time, or been delayed and now need to catch up—by working faster/harder or doing extra. Often follows verbs like devoir/falloir (Tu dois…, Il faut…).
target_language_example: Après nos vacances, on va rattraper le temps perdu au travail.
native_language_example: After our vacation, we’re going to make up for lost time at work.

additional_notes: Used in polite/formal speech ("vous") followed by a past participle: "ravi de vous avoir rencontré / vu / revu / parlé" = “Nice to have met/seen/spoken to you.” Often used at the end of a conversation. Spelling can agree with the speaker: "ravi" (male) / "ravie" (female). The past participle may also agree with who you met/seen: "rencontré" (masc. sg.), "rencontrée" (fem. sg.), "rencontrés" (masc. pl.), "rencontrées" (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Ravi de vous avoir rencontré, à bientôt !
native_language_example: Nice to have met you—see you soon!

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone will not do something: « refuser de + infinitive » (e.g., « refuser de répondre »). You can also use « refuser + noun » without « de »: « refuser une offre » (to refuse an offer).
target_language_example: Elle refuse de partir maintenant.
native_language_example: She refuses to leave now.

meaning: an angry, hostile look; a dirty look.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like jeter/lancer un regard noir (“to shoot someone a dirty look”). It describes a hard stare showing anger, disapproval, or hostility. Literally “black look,” but in English you don’t usually say that.
target_language_example: Le professeur m’a lancé un regard noir quand je suis arrivé en retard.
native_language_example: The teacher shot me a dirty look when I arrived late.

additional_notes: Imperative of regarder ("to look") + moi ("me"). Used to get someone’s attention, to ask them to watch what you’re doing, or to insist that they make eye contact. Often said with emphasis (Regarde-moi !) and can be softened with s’il te plaît. In very informal speech you may hear Regarde-moi bien ("Look at me carefully").
target_language_example: Regarde-moi : je vais te montrer comment faire.
native_language_example: Look at me: I’m going to show you how to do it.

additional_notes: Used to draw someone’s attention to something you did, brought, or to the result of a change: « Regarde ce que j’ai fait » (“Look what I did/made”). Usually followed by a clause with a verb. In casual speech, « Regarde » is often used like English “Look…”.
target_language_example: Regarde ce que tu as écrit !
native_language_example: Look what you wrote!

additional_notes: From the verb "regarder" (to watch/look at) + "la télé" (short for "la télévision"). "Regarde" is the "he/she watches" form (Il/Elle regarde la télé) and also the informal command "Watch..." to one person (Regarde la télé.). With "on", it means "we" or "people" (On regarde la télé = We’re watching TV).
target_language_example: Ce soir, je regarde la télé après le dîner.
native_language_example: Tonight, I’m watching TV after dinner.

additional_notes: Used with the verb regarder (to watch/look at) + la télévision (TV). In your examples, regarde is the he/she/it form (il/elle/on regarde). You can change the subject: je regarde (I watch), tu regardes (you watch), nous regardons (we watch). Often used with time expressions like tous les jours (every day) or en permanence (all the time).
target_language_example: Elle regarde la télévision après le dîner.
native_language_example: She watches TV after dinner.

additional_notes: Very common everyday phrase. "la télé" is short for "la télévision". You can use it after verbs like aimer/préférer/pouvoir: "J’aime regarder la télé", "Je peux regarder la télé ?".
target_language_example: Puis-je regarder la télé ce soir ?
native_language_example: Can I watch TV tonight?

meaning: to watch television / to watch TV.
additional_notes: Uses the verb *regarder* (to watch/look at) + *la télévision* (television/TV). Often used after another verb (e.g., *aimer/détester/pouvoir/aller*) or after *avant de* + infinitive: *Fais tes devoirs avant de regarder la télévision.*
target_language_example: Le soir, j'aime regarder la télévision avec ma famille.
native_language_example: In the evening, I like to watch TV with my family.

additional_notes: Imperative of regarder (“to look”) + moi (“me”). Used to get someone’s attention or to insist they make eye contact. The form regardez is used with vous (formal singular or plural), even if you’re addressing someone by name.
target_language_example: Regardez-moi, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Look at me, please.

meaning: to fall under; to come within the scope of; to be the responsibility/authority of.
additional_notes: Used mainly in formal or written French. Construction: « relever de + nom/groupe nominal » to indicate that something belongs to a domain, category, or authority/responsibility: « Cela relève de la médecine » (it’s a medical matter), « Cette décision relève du juge » (it’s up to the judge). Note that « de » often contracts: de + le → du; de + les → des. It does not mean “to lift from.”
target_language_example: Ce problème doit relever de la direction, pas de moi.
native_language_example: This problem should fall under management’s responsibility, not mine.

meaning: to put (someone) in their place; to put back where it belongs.
additional_notes: Often used about correcting or scolding someone who is being rude, arrogant, or overstepping ("Il fallait le/la remettre à sa place"). It can also be literal (putting an object back in its proper spot). Object pronouns are common: le/la/les remettre à sa place.
target_language_example: Il parlait très mal au serveur, alors je l’ai dû remettre à sa place.
native_language_example: He was talking very rudely to the waiter, so I had to put him in his place.

meaning: to cheer someone up; to boost someone’s morale.
additional_notes: Used when you try to make someone feel better after they’re sad, stressed, or discouraged. It’s often followed by an indirect object: « lui remonter le moral » (cheer him/her up), « te/vous remonter le moral » (cheer you up). In everyday French you also hear « Ça va te remonter le moral » (“That’ll cheer you up”).
target_language_example: On va aller prendre un café pour te remonter le moral.
native_language_example: We’ll go have a coffee to cheer you up.

meaning: to go back in time; to travel back in time.
additional_notes: Used literally for time travel, and also figuratively to mean going back to earlier times (e.g., remembering the past or looking at old photos). Often used with "si" (if) or in storytelling: "Si je pouvais remonter le temps…"
target_language_example: Si je pouvais remonter le temps, je changerais cette décision.
native_language_example: If I could go back in time, I would change that decision.

additional_notes: Used for scheduled appointments (doctor, work, etc.) and also for planned meetings, including a date. Common verbs: avoir un rendez-vous (to have an appointment), prendre rendez-vous (to make/book an appointment), annuler un rendez-vous (to cancel), donner rendez-vous à quelqu’un / se donner rendez-vous (to arrange to meet someone).
target_language_example: J’ai rendez-vous chez le dentiste à 15 h.
native_language_example: I have a dentist appointment at 3 p.m.

additional_notes: Imperative of *rendre* + *moi* (“to me”). Used to demand that something be returned: *Rendez-moi ce livre !* It also appears in fixed expressions like *rendez-moi un service* (“do me a favor”). *Rendez* is used when speaking to more than one person or to one person formally (vous).
target_language_example: Rendez-moi mes clés, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Give me back my keys, please.

additional_notes: Used for a scheduled time and place to meet someone (a personal meeting) or to go somewhere for a service (doctor, dentist, etc.). Common patterns: "J'ai rendez-vous" = "I have an appointment"; "prendre rendez-vous" = "to make/schedule an appointment"; "un rendez-vous" can also mean a date/romantic meeting depending on context. Note: "Où vous rendez-vous ?" (with the verb "se rendre") means "Where are you going?"—that’s a different word from the noun "rendez-vous".
target_language_example: J'ai rendez-vous demain à 9 h chez le médecin.
native_language_example: I have an appointment tomorrow at 9 a.m. at the doctor's.

additional_notes: Used to say you have a scheduled meeting with a person or group. Very common for medical appointments ("prendre rendez-vous avec" = to make/book an appointment with) and for work/official meetings ("avoir rendez-vous avec" = to have an appointment with).
target_language_example: Demain matin, j'ai rendez-vous avec ma conseillère.
native_language_example: Tomorrow morning, I have an appointment with my advisor.

meaning: To realize/become aware (most often as « se rendre compte (de) ») / to report or give an account of (as « rendre compte de »).
additional_notes: Most common: « se rendre compte (de) » = “to realize / become aware (of)”. It typically takes « de » + noun (« se rendre compte de l’erreur ») or « que » + clause (« se rendre compte que… »). You’ll also see « s’en rendre compte », where « en » replaces something previously mentioned (“realize it/that”). Without « se », « rendre compte (de) » means “to report on / give an account of”: « rendre compte du résultat », often in formal/professional contexts.
target_language_example: Vous devez rendre compte du résultat.
native_language_example: You must report on the result.

additional_notes: Used most often with an indirect object introduced by "à": "rendre hommage à quelqu’un". Refers to showing respect/admiration, typically in a formal or public way (speech, ceremony, memorial, artistic work). In English you generally don’t say “render homage”; prefer “pay tribute (to)” or “honor.”
target_language_example: Je voulais leur rendre hommage lors de la cérémonie.
native_language_example: I wanted to pay tribute to them during the ceremony.

meaning: to return the favor; to do the same back (in kind).
additional_notes: Used when you want to repay someone for what they did—often something nice ("return the favor"), but it can also mean retaliation ("pay them back"). Conjugate "rendre" and keep "la pareille" fixed: je te/la lui rends la pareille, on va leur rendre la pareille. The person you’re paying back is typically introduced with an indirect object pronoun (te, vous, lui, leur).
target_language_example: Après tout ce que tu as fait pour moi, je vais te rendre la pareille.
native_language_example: After everything you’ve done for me, I’m going to return the favor.

meaning: to do someone a favor; to help out.
additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object: rendre service à quelqu’un (to do someone a favor). Very common as a polite request: Tu peux me rendre service ? (informal) / Vous pouvez me rendre service ? (formal). Often implies a small, practical help.
target_language_example: Tu pourrais me rendre service et m'envoyer ce document ?
native_language_example: Could you do me a favor and send me this document?

additional_notes: Used with a direct object person (me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur, or a name): rendre visite à quelqu’un / rendre visite à ma tante. It means visiting a person (often at their home). For places, French usually uses "visiter" (visiter Paris). Common pattern: "venir rendre visite" = "to come and visit."
target_language_example: Je vais rendre visite à mes grands-parents ce week-end.
native_language_example: I'm going to visit my grandparents this weekend.

additional_notes: Used for visiting a person (often at their home or in a place where they are). The structure is always **rendre visite à + person** (à Pierre, à ma tante, à eux). For visiting a place, you usually use **visiter** (e.g., visiter Paris).
target_language_example: Je vais rendre visite à mes grands-parents ce week-end.
native_language_example: I’m going to visit my grandparents this weekend.

meaning: "Do me" / "give me" (imperative), often in "Rends-moi un service" = "Do me a favor."
additional_notes: This is the command form (tu) of *rendre* + *moi* (“to me”). In everyday French, it’s very common in the fixed expression **rendre un service (à quelqu’un)** = “to do someone a favor.” It can also mean “give/hand back to me” when talking about returning something: *Rends-moi mon livre.*
target_language_example: Rends-moi mon stylo, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me back my pen, please.

meaning: Go home. / Go back to your place.
additional_notes: Imperative (command) of "rentrer" + "chez toi" (to your home/your place), used when speaking to one person you address as "tu". For a more polite or plural version: "Rentrez chez vous." You can add "maintenant" for emphasis: "Rentre chez toi maintenant."
target_language_example: Il est tard, rentre chez toi.
native_language_example: It’s late, go home.

additional_notes: From the verb rentrer (“to return/get back”). With “à la maison” it means returning home. In context it can be an instruction (Rentre à la maison ! = Go home!) or describe someone’s return (Papa rentre à la maison demain. = Dad is coming home tomorrow).
target_language_example: Rentre à la maison avant la nuit.
native_language_example: Come home before nightfall.

meaning: to go back home (to his place).
additional_notes: "Rentrer" means to return/go back (often home). "Chez lui" means "to/at his place" (for a man). You can change the pronoun: "rentrer chez elle" (her place), "rentrer chez moi" (my place), "rentrer chez nous" (our place), "rentrer chez vous" (your place), "rentrer chez eux/elles" (their place). In the passé composé: "il est rentré chez lui" = he came/got back home.
target_language_example: Il vient juste de rentrer chez lui.
native_language_example: He just got back home.

meaning: to go back home; to return to my place.
additional_notes: Used when you’re away and want/need to return home. « rentrer » = to go back/come back (often to a usual place), and « chez moi » = at my place/home. You can swap the pronoun: rentrer chez toi (your place), rentrer chez lui/elle (his/her place), rentrer chez nous/vous/eux/elles.
target_language_example: Il est tard, je vais rentrer chez moi.
native_language_example: It’s late; I’m going to go back home.

meaning: to go back home (to your place).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "rentrer" (to go back/come back) + "chez" + a stressed pronoun. "chez toi" means “at your place / to your place” when used with a verb of movement. You can swap the pronoun: "rentrer chez moi" (my place), "chez lui/elle" (his/her place), "chez nous/vous/eux/elles". Often used to tell someone to go home: "Il est temps de rentrer chez toi."
target_language_example: Après le cours, je vais rentrer chez toi pour te rendre ton livre.
native_language_example: After the class, I'm going to go back to your place to return your book.

additional_notes: Used when addressing one person formally (vous) or multiple people. With verbs like "aller", "vouloir", "devoir", you often see the infinitive: "Vous devriez rentrer chez vous". "Rentrer" often implies returning home (going back), while "aller chez vous" is simply going to your place.
target_language_example: Après le travail, vous pouvez rentrer chez vous.
native_language_example: After work, you can go home.

meaning: to crash/bump into (someone or something); (figuratively) to go at someone / lay into them.
additional_notes: Common in everyday spoken French. For a physical collision, it often means “to hit/crash into” (e.g., in a car accident). Figuratively, it can mean to confront someone aggressively or tell them off; with an indirect object pronoun it’s frequent: « Je lui suis rentré dedans » (context-dependent).
target_language_example: Il m’a rentré dedans avec son vélo.
native_language_example: He crashed into me with his bike.

additional_notes: Used with many tenses to talk about going back to your home (from work, school, a trip, etc.). Common with "je vais..." (I’m going to...), "tu dois..." (you have to...), and in questions like "Quand vas-tu... ?" (When are you going to...?). Similar idea: "rentrer chez moi/chez toi" = to go back to my/your place.
target_language_example: On peut rentrer à la maison après le dîner.
native_language_example: We can go home after dinner.

meaning: Go home / go back to your place.
additional_notes: Imperative of « rentrer » (to go back/return), used either for (1) one person with « vous » (polite/formal) or (2) several people. « chez vous » means “to your home/at your place.” Often used as an instruction/command.
target_language_example: Il est tard, rentrez chez vous maintenant.
native_language_example: It’s late—go home now.

additional_notes: Past participle of "rentrer" used with "être" in the passé composé: "être rentré(e) à la maison" = to have returned home. It agrees with the subject: rentré (m.), rentrée (f.), rentrés (m. pl.), rentrées (f. pl.). Often used with a time: "Je suis rentré(e) à la maison à 20h."
target_language_example: Je suis rentré à la maison après le travail.
native_language_example: I came back home after work.

additional_notes: Used when you want to reset and begin again as if nothing had been done yet (a project, a relationship, a plan, a game, etc.). Often implies going back to the beginning and rebuilding step by step. Conjugates like repartir (je repars, tu repars, il/elle repart, nous repartons).
target_language_example: Si ça ne marche pas, on va repartir à zéro et on essaiera autrement.
native_language_example: If it doesn’t work, we’ll start over from scratch and try a different way.

additional_notes: An informal singular command (imperative) meaning “rest” or “get some rest,” addressed to one person you call tu. From the verb se reposer (“to rest”); it literally means “rest yourself.” You can add words like bien (well), un peu (a little), ici (here), pendant un moment (for a moment) to specify how/where/for how long.
target_language_example: Tu as l’air fatigué : repose-toi un peu.
native_language_example: You look tired: rest a little.

meaning: “Rest in peace.” (said about someone who has died.)
additional_notes: Used as a respectful expression after someone’s death (like “RIP”). Often appears as a wish with the subjunctive: « Qu’il/elle repose en paix. » You can also address the deceased directly: « Repose en paix. »
target_language_example: Nous ne t'oublierons jamais. Repose en paix.
native_language_example: We will never forget you. Rest in peace.

additional_notes: Used to say who has responsibility, is in charge of something/someone, or is to blame for something. Followed by a noun, pronoun, or infinitive (e.g., responsable de faire...).
target_language_example: Qui est responsable de ce projet ?
native_language_example: Who is responsible for this project?

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something has a similar appearance or seems like something else. Pattern: « X ressemble à Y ». With people, it often means physical resemblance (family likeness). « Ça ressemble à… » can also mean “it seems like…” based on what you see.
target_language_example: Cette maison ressemble à un château.
native_language_example: This house looks like a castle.

additional_notes: From the verb **ressembler à** (“to look like / to resemble”). It’s followed by a person or thing: **Il/Elle ressemble à un/une…**. Use **à un** with masculine nouns and **à une** with feminine nouns (e.g., *Elle ressemble à une actrice*). Note: French uses **à**, even though English says “resemble” (no “to”).
target_language_example: Il ressemble à un professeur avec ces lunettes.
native_language_example: He looks like a teacher with those glasses.

additional_notes: From the verb **ressembler à** (“to look like / to resemble”). You use **ressembler à + noun** to compare appearance or impression. It agrees with the subject: **il ressemble à…**, **elle ressemble à…**, **ça/cela ressemble à…**. Use **à un** for masculine nouns and **à une** for feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Ce dessin ressemble à une photo.
native_language_example: This drawing looks like a photo.

additional_notes: General term for the fast-food industry/style of eating (burgers, fries, etc.). Often used with verbs like manger/consommer (to eat/consume) or with restaurant (un restaurant de restauration rapide).
target_language_example: On évite la restauration rapide pendant la semaine.
native_language_example: We avoid fast food during the week.

additional_notes: From **rester** (to remain) + **-t-** (linking sound) + **il** (he/it). Used in formal/written French to form questions like **Reste-t-il des billets ?** = “Are there any tickets left?” It often means “is there any … left?” or “do we have any … left?” depending on context. With time: **Combien de temps nous reste-t-il ?** = “How much time do we have left?”
target_language_example: Reste-t-il du café, ou faut-il en acheter ?
native_language_example: Is there any coffee left, or do we need to buy some?

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to remain in the same place. It’s the imperative (command) form of *rester* for *tu*: **(tu) reste ici**. For more than one person, you’d say **restez ici**.
target_language_example: Reste ici, s'il te plaît, je reviens tout de suite.
native_language_example: Stay here, please, I'll be right back.

additional_notes: Used when someone is sick, resting, or advised not to get up. Often appears with advice verbs like "devoir" (must) and "(re)commander / conseiller" (recommend/advise): « Tu devrais rester au lit. »
target_language_example: J'ai de la fièvre, donc je vais rester au lit aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I have a fever, so I'm going to stay in bed today.

additional_notes: Means to stay in this place (not leave). Often used with modal verbs like devoir (must), pouvoir (can), and devoir/should expressions like tu devrais (you should).
target_language_example: Je préfère rester ici jusqu'à ce qu'il arrive.
native_language_example: I prefer to stay here until he arrives.

meaning: to stay there; to stay put (not move)
additional_notes: Means remaining in a specific place (“there”), often with the sense of staying put or not moving. Common in questions about duration (e.g., “Combien de temps va-t-il rester là ?”) and in firm instructions (e.g., “Tu vas rester là.”).
target_language_example: Combien de temps va-t-il rester là ?
native_language_example: How long is he going to stay there?

additional_notes: Used to say you will not go out and will remain at your home. Common with near-future plans: « Je vais rester… ». Also used for advice/instructions (e.g., from a doctor): « On te conseille de rester… ».
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, je vais rester à la maison parce qu'il pleut.
native_language_example: Today, I'm going to stay at home because it's raining.

additional_notes: Used literally (stop breathing for a moment, e.g., underwater or from surprise). It can also be used figuratively to mean “to wait anxiously/in suspense” for something to happen. Conjugate the verb: je retiens mon souffle, il/elle retient son souffle, nous retenons notre souffle, etc.
target_language_example: Je vais retenir son souffle quelques secondes.
native_language_example: I’m going to hold my breath for a few seconds.

meaning: back to square one; back to the starting point.
additional_notes: Used when a plan or process fails and you have to start over from the beginning. Often appears after verbs like « être » (être de retour à la case départ) or alone as a comment: « Retour à la case départ. » The image comes from board games: going back to the starting square.
target_language_example: On a perdu le dossier, alors c’est retour à la case départ.
native_language_example: We lost the file, so it’s back to square one.

meaning: to come back to (a topic); to go back on/reconsider (a decision); to return to (a place, esp. Earth).
additional_notes:
Common uses:
1) **Revenir sur + noun** = to return to a subject and talk about it again: *revenir sur une déclaration, un point, un détail*.
2) **Revenir sur + décision/choix/promesse** = to go back on it (change your mind, undo it): *On ne peut pas revenir sur son choix.*
3) With places, especially **revenir sur Terre** = to return to Earth (from space).
target_language_example: Avant de conclure, je voudrais revenir sur un point important.
native_language_example: Before we wrap up, I’d like to come back to an important point.

meaning: to come back/return to; (revenir à soi) to come to (regain consciousness).
additional_notes: Used with a destination: « revenir à la maison » = to go back home. With « soi » (or an indirect object like « lui »): « revenir à lui / à soi » = to regain consciousness or come back to your senses. You may also see « revenir » without « à » when it’s followed by a time: « Il revient à cinq heures » = He’s coming back at five o’clock.
target_language_example: Je vais revenir à la maison après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m going to come back home after work.

meaning: come back right away / be right back.
additional_notes: "Reviens" is the tu (informal singular) command form of "revenir" (to come back). In the examples with "je reviens tout de suite", it means “I’ll be right back” (common when stepping away briefly). For a formal command to one person, use "revenez tout de suite"; for “come back” to someone you’re on first-name terms with, "reviens" is natural.
target_language_example: Je vais aux toilettes, je reviens tout de suite.
native_language_example: I'm going to the bathroom; I'll be right back.

additional_notes: Used for the level at street entrance in a building. In France, floors are often counted as: rez-de-chaussée (RDC), then 1er étage (one floor up), 2e étage, etc. Common on signs and in addresses/elevators.
target_language_example: L’appartement est au rez-de-chaussée, juste à côté de l’entrée.
native_language_example: The apartment is on the ground floor, right next to the entrance.

additional_notes: Used to restrict something to one thing/person: « rien que pour nous » = “just for us / only for us.” It can also mean “merely/by the mere fact of,” especially with an infinitive: « Rien que de voir… » = “Just seeing…”. In the fixed phrase « la vérité, rien que la vérité », it means “the truth and nothing but the truth.”
target_language_example: Je veux rester à la maison, rien que ce soir.
native_language_example: I want to stay home, just tonight.

meaning: just for; only for (for the sole purpose/benefit).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize exclusivity: something is done only for a particular purpose ("rien que pour te voir" = just to see you) or reserved only for someone ("rien que pour elle" = just for her). You can also use "rien que" without "pour" to mean "just/only" ("rien que te parler" = just talking to you).
target_language_example: Je suis venu rien que pour te dire merci.
native_language_example: I came just to say thank you.
