additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is limited to that one thing (“nothing more than that”), or to react with surprise/irony (“Just that?!” / “That’s it?!”). Often follows a statement or answer to stress how small/large/surprising it is.
target_language_example: — Tu as eu 20/20 à l’examen ? — Rien que ça !
native_language_example: — You got a perfect score on the exam? — Just that!

additional_notes: Used with the negative pronoun "rien" to mean "nothing" followed by "de" + noun or adjective/past participle. Common patterns: "ne … rien de + noun" = "not know/have anything about …"; "rien de + adjective/past participle" = "nothing …" (e.g., "rien de nouveau" = "nothing new", "rien de prévu" = "nothing planned"). "De" is used instead of an article after "rien".
target_language_example: Je n’ai rien de nouveau à te dire.
native_language_example: I have nothing new to tell you.

meaning: nothing more; no more than that.
additional_notes: Used to limit or downplay what you just said: “that’s all.” Common after a statement (“Je veux juste être ton ami, rien de plus.”) or alone as a short reply (“Rien de plus, merci.”). With a negative it often means “I won’t say anything else” (“Je ne dirai rien de plus.”).
target_language_example: Je suis venu pour discuter, rien de plus.
native_language_example: I came to talk, nothing more.

meaning: “nothing like that / nothing of the kind”; also “nothing beats…”
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) to say something like that doesn’t exist or won’t happen (often with ne): « Rien de tel ne se produira » = “Nothing like that will happen.” (2) to say something is the best way to get an effect: « Rien de tel pour… » = “Nothing like it / Nothing beats … for …”. On its own (« Rien de tel. ») it can mean “Nothing like that / Not at all.”
target_language_example: Pour se détendre après le travail, rien de tel qu’une promenade.
native_language_example: To relax after work, nothing beats a walk.

additional_notes: Usually used in negatives: «ne ... rien dire» = “not say anything” (often «je peux rien dire» in casual speech, dropping «ne»). Common patterns: «sans rien dire» = “without saying anything”; «ne rien dire» / «ne peux rien dire» = “not to say anything / can’t say anything”; «n’en rien dire» = “not to say anything about it.” In «Ça ne veut rien dire», it means “That doesn’t mean anything.”
target_language_example: Je suis parti sans rien dire.
native_language_example: I left without saying anything.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the negation **ne … rien** with the verb **dire** in the past tense: **(ne) + avoir + rien + dit**. In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: **Elle t’a rien dit ?** = **Elle ne t’a rien dit ?**.
target_language_example: Je suis désolé, je ne t’ai rien dit parce que je ne savais pas.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I didn’t tell you anything because I didn’t know.

meaning: nothing at all; not anything (at all).
additional_notes: Used for strong emphasis with "rien" (nothing), often in negative sentences: "Je ne … rien du tout" = "I don’t … anything at all." You can also use it alone as an emphatic answer: "Rien du tout." = "Nothing at all." In expressions like "plus rien du tout" it means "nothing left at all." In "un/une rien du tout," it means "a tiny insignificant thing" (often said about an object or a very small amount).
target_language_example: Tu as mangé quelque chose ? — Non, rien du tout.
native_language_example: Did you eat anything? — No, nothing at all.

additional_notes: Used as the subject of a negative sentence: "rien" = "nothing" + "ne" before the verb (e.g., "rien ne dure" = "nothing lasts"). Often the negation is completed with another word after the verb ("rien ne … pas"), but with some verbs it’s common to use only "ne" (especially in set phrases like "rien ne va" = "nothing is going well").
target_language_example: Rien ne m'empêchera de venir.
native_language_example: Nothing will stop me from coming.

meaning: 'nothing to do' / 'no business (being here)'; also 'no way!'
additional_notes: Used with a subject + negation: "(Il/Elle) n’a rien à faire ici/là" = “He/She has no business being here/there” (doesn’t belong, shouldn’t be there). Said on its own as an exclamation ("Rien à faire !") it can mean “No way!” / “Forget it!” / “Nothing can be done about it,” depending on context. Often used after a condition: "Si tu… , rien à faire !" = “If you…, no way!”
target_language_example: Tu veux entrer sans billet ? Rien à faire !
native_language_example: You want to come in without a ticket? No way!

meaning: “I don’t give a damn / I don’t care at all.” (very vulgar)
additional_notes: Very informal and aggressive; “foutre” is vulgar. Used alone as an exclamation (“Rien à foutre !”) or with “de + noun/pronoun” to mean you don’t care about something/someone (“Rien à foutre de ça / de lui / de ma vie”). In polite conversation, use “Je m’en fiche” or “Je m’en moque.”
target_language_example: Rien à foutre de ce qu’ils pensent, je fais ce que je veux.
native_language_example: I don’t give a damn what they think; I’ll do what I want.

additional_notes: Used in the expression **(ne) ... avoir rien à voir (avec ...)** to say something is unrelated or not involved: **Ça n’a rien à voir** = “That has nothing to do with it / That’s not the point.” You can add **avec + noun/pronoun**: **Ça n’a rien à voir avec toi** = “It has nothing to do with you.” Often used to deny responsibility or connection: **X n’a rien à voir là-dedans** = “X has nothing to do with it (in this matter).”
target_language_example: Ce problème n’a rien à voir avec toi.
native_language_example: This problem has nothing to do with you.

additional_notes: Refers to rice with the bran removed (as opposed to "riz brun" = brown rice). Often used when choosing a side dish or specifying what kind of rice you want.
target_language_example: Je vais prendre du poulet avec du riz blanc, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll have chicken with white rice, please.

additional_notes: Used for a circular road intersection where you drive around a central island and take an exit (“Prends la deuxième sortie au rond-point”). It’s also sometimes used as a meeting point (“On se retrouve au rond-point”).
target_language_example: Au prochain rond-point, prends la première sortie.
native_language_example: At the next roundabout, take the first exit.

additional_notes: Used when talking about a car’s extra tire/wheel kept for emergencies (like a flat). Often found in the trunk (le coffre). In everyday speech you may also hear "roue de rechange".
target_language_example: On a crevé, mais heureusement on a une roue de secours.
native_language_example: We got a flat, but luckily we have a spare tire.

additional_notes: A noun meaning the cosmetic you put on your lips. Often used with "un/du/le" (un rouge à lèvres, du rouge à lèvres, le rouge à lèvres). You can also talk about marks left by it: "une trace/des traces de rouge à lèvres".
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mon rouge à lèvres dans la salle de bains.
native_language_example: I forgot my lipstick in the bathroom.

additional_notes: A common general term for tape that sticks (often like Scotch tape). Usually used with the partitive: du ruban adhésif (“some tape”). In everyday speech you may also hear simply du scotch (informal/brand-based).
target_language_example: Tu peux me passer du ruban adhésif, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you pass me some tape, please?

meaning: out of stock; sold out (temporarily unavailable).
additional_notes: Used mainly in shopping contexts to say a product isn’t available right now. Most often appears as "être en rupture de stock" (to be out of stock), on signs/websites or in customer service. It implies the item may be restocked later (unlike "ne plus être en vente", no longer sold).
target_language_example: Je voulais ces chaussures, mais elles sont en rupture de stock.
native_language_example: I wanted those shoes, but they’re out of stock.

meaning: rule of the game; rule to follow.
additional_notes: Most often used in the plural: « les règles du jeu » (“the rules of the game”). Can be literal (actual game rules) or figurative for the rules/conditions in a situation (e.g., at work, in politics). In the singular (« règle du jeu »), it often refers to one specific rule/principle.
target_language_example: La règle du jeu est simple : chacun son tour.
native_language_example: The rule of the game is simple: everyone takes turns.

meaning: to reduce to ashes; to burn down completely.
additional_notes: Used for something destroyed by fire (a building, a forest, etc.). Often implies total destruction and is common in news reports or formal writing. Literal: "to reduce into ashes."
target_language_example: L'incendie a tout réduit en cendres.
native_language_example: The fire reduced everything to ashes.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "répondre" with the preposition "à" (répondre à + noun/pronoun). Very common in questions and negative statements: "Je ne peux pas répondre à cette question"; polite request: "Pouvez-vous répondre à cette question ?".
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne sais pas répondre à cette question.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't know how to answer this question.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "répondre" with the preposition "à" (répondre à + noun/pronoun). Common in formal contexts like interviews, court, or school; often appears with verbs like "refuser de" (to refuse to) or "pouvoir" (to be able to).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous répondre à la question, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you answer the question, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a social media service (Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, etc.) or the general concept of a social network. Often used with verbs like "utiliser" (to use), "publier sur" (to post on), "être sur" (to be on), and "s'inscrire à" (to sign up for). Plural: "les réseaux sociaux".
target_language_example: Ce réseau social est très populaire.
native_language_example: This social network is very popular.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *résoudre*: *j’ai résolu*, *tu as résolu*, *il/elle a résolu*. Uses *avoir* as the helping verb. *Résoudre* often translates to “to solve” in everyday contexts (a problem, an issue).
target_language_example: On a enfin résolu le problème.
native_language_example: We finally solved the problem.

additional_notes: Used to say you (or someone) will find a solution to a specific issue. Conjugate "résoudre" to match the subject (je dois résoudre…, nous devons résoudre…). Often used with can/can't, must/have to, need to: "Je peux / je ne peux pas", "Je dois", "Il faut".
target_language_example: On va résoudre ce problème ensemble.
native_language_example: We’re going to solve this problem together.

additional_notes: Used to talk about finding a solution to a difficulty or issue. Often appears with helper verbs like « pouvoir » (As-tu pu…? = Were you able to…?), « finir par » (ended up managing to…), and « parvenir à » (to manage to…). You can specify the type of problem with « le problème de/du… » (e.g., « le problème du logement » = the housing problem).
target_language_example: On doit résoudre le problème avant demain.
native_language_example: We have to solve the problem before tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the verb réussir + à + infinitive to say someone was able to do something (often after effort or difficulty). It’s usually in the past (a réussi à / as réussi à / j’ai réussi à), but can also be present (je réussis à…). Don’t confuse with réussir un examen (“to pass an exam”).
target_language_example: J’ai enfin réussi à finir mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I finally managed to finish my homework.

additional_notes: Imperative of "se réveiller" (to wake up). Used to tell one person to wake up; it uses "toi" because it’s addressed with "tu". For a more formal or plural version, use "réveillez-vous".
target_language_example: Réveille-toi, on est en retard !
native_language_example: Wake up, we’re late!

meaning: the American Dream (the idea of success and a better life in the U.S.).
additional_notes: Usually refers to the cultural idea that anyone can achieve prosperity through hard work and opportunity in the United States. Often used in discussions about society, immigration, and the economy (e.g., “Qu’est-il arrivé au rêve américain ?”). In other contexts, it can simply mean “an American dream” in a literal sense, but the common meaning is the well-known concept.
target_language_example: Il est venu aux États-Unis pour réaliser le rêve américain.
native_language_example: He came to the United States to achieve the American Dream.

meaning: to be about; to concern; to be a matter of.
additional_notes: Usually used impersonally: "il s'agit de ..." (not *je m'agis*). Common for clarifying what something is about: "De quoi s'agit-il ?" (What is it about?/What’s going on?). Takes "de" + noun or "de" + infinitive: "Il s'agit de comprendre" (It’s a matter of understanding).
target_language_example: Il va s'agir de trouver une solution rapidement.
native_language_example: It’s going to be a matter of finding a solution quickly.

meaning: to have fun; to enjoy oneself.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb (amuser = “to amuse,” s’amuser = “to amuse oneself” → “to have fun”). Very common with purpose: « pour s’amuser » (“for fun / just to have fun”). Also used to say people seem to be having fun: « Ils ont l’air de bien s’amuser » (“They seem to be having a good time”).
target_language_example: On va s'amuser ce soir !
native_language_example: We’re going to have fun tonight!

meaning: to work things out; to come to an agreement; to sort itself out.
additional_notes: Used when you think a problem can be resolved or a compromise can be found (often in negotiations: price, schedule, plans). With a subject like « ça / tout », it means things will end up being okay: « Ça va s'arranger » = “It’ll work out.”
target_language_example: Pour l'heure, ne t'inquiète pas : ça va s'arranger.
native_language_example: For now, don’t worry: it’ll work out.

additional_notes: Very common way to say you’re leaving/going away from a place or situation. It’s built from the pronoun se (reflexive) + en (roughly “away/from here”) + aller (“to go”), and it conjugates like a reflexive verb: je m’en vais, tu t’en vas, il/elle s’en va, nous nous en allons, vous vous en allez, ils/elles s’en vont. Frequently used to express necessity or intention: il faut/on doit s’en aller = “we have to leave.”
target_language_example: Il faut s'en aller.
native_language_example: We have to leave.

meaning: to not care (at all); to not give a damn.
additional_notes: Very informal and often considered vulgar because it uses the verb « foutre ». Used to say you don’t care about something: « Je m’en fous » (I don’t care), « Il s’en fout » (He doesn’t care), « On s’en fout » (We don’t care). The « en » refers to “about it/that.” A more polite alternative is « Ça m’est égal » or « Je m’en fiche ».
target_language_example: Arrête de me demander : je vais m'en foutre, et toi tu vas t'en foutre aussi.
native_language_example: Stop asking me: I'm not going to care, and you won’t care either.

meaning: to get by; to get out of a difficult situation; to manage.
additional_notes: Very common pronominal verb used for overcoming trouble or coping with something difficult. Often used with contexts like problems, money, school, addiction, etc. Conjugates like a reflexive verb: je m'en sors, tu t'en sors, il/elle s'en sort, nous nous en sortons, vous vous en sortez, ils/elles s'en sortent. Past: je m'en suis sorti(e).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, on va s'en sortir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we’ll manage / we’ll get through it.

meaning: Pronoun sequence used with the auxiliary être in compound tenses (e.g., passé composé) to express “to have gotten/been … from it/there/of it,” depending on the verb and context.
additional_notes: This is not generally used alone; it appears as part of a larger verb phrase in a compound tense: se + en + être (conjugated) + past participle. “En” refers back to something previously mentioned (“of it,” “from it,” “from there”). Common fixed patterns include: s’en être sorti(e) (to get through it / manage), s’en être allé(e) (to have gone away). In the infinitive (as in the entry term), you’ll see: s’en être + past participle (e.g., s’en être sorti).
target_language_example: Il dit que tout va bien maintenant, après s'en être sorti.
native_language_example: He says everything is fine now, after having gotten through it.

meaning: to get along (with each other); to be on the same wavelength.
additional_notes: Used mostly with people to express compatibility or ease of agreement: "On va (bien) s'entendre" = "We’ll get along (well)." Also common as "s'entendre avec quelqu'un" (to get along with someone). In other contexts, "s'entendre" can mean "to hear oneself" (e.g., a voice carries), but in the examples here it’s about getting along.
target_language_example: Je crois qu'on va bien s'entendre.
native_language_example: I think we’re going to get along well.

additional_notes: Past tense of **se passer** (“to happen/to go”), used with events or experiences (a flight, a trip, an exam, a meeting). It agrees with the subject: **Ça s'est bien passé** (It went well), **Le vol s'est bien passé** (The flight went well), **Tout s'est bien passé** (Everything went well). Often used in questions to check how something went: **Ça s'est bien passé ?**
target_language_example: Votre voyage s'est bien passé ?
native_language_example: Did your trip go well?

additional_notes: From the verb "se passer" (= to happen/to take place). "s'est passé" is the passé composé (past tense): "il/elle s'est passé" = "it happened". It uses "être" as the auxiliary. Often used in questions like "Qu'est-ce qu'il s'est passé ?" (What happened?) and with time/place details (e.g., "ici", "il y a trois ans").
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce qui s'est passé hier soir.
native_language_example: I don’t know what happened last night.

meaning: to take care of; to look after; to handle/deal with (something or someone).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb: s'occuper (de). Conjugates with a reflexive pronoun + de + noun/pronoun: je m'occupe de…, tu t'occupes de…, il/elle s'occupe de…, nous nous occupons de…, vous vous occupez de…, ils/elles s'occupent de…. Meaning varies by context: caring for a person/animal (look after), taking charge of a task/problem (handle it), or dealing with someone’s situation/case; in phrases like « s'occuper de votre cas », it can sound ominous/threatening depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas, je vais m'occuper de tout : je vais s'occuper de ça tout de suite.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to take care of everything: I’m going to deal with that right away.

meaning: to get started (on it); to get down to it.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb used when you finally begin doing a task or make an effort. The pronoun "y" refers to what you’re starting (e.g., work, homework, cleaning). Common patterns: "Faut/Il faut s'y mettre" (We/you have to get started), "Il est temps de s'y mettre" (It’s time to get started), "On va s'y mettre" (We’re going to get started), imperative: "Mets-toi-y !" (Get to it!).
target_language_example: Il est temps de s'y mettre : on commence par la cuisine.
native_language_example: It’s time to get started: we’ll start with the kitchen.

meaning: to go about it; to handle/do something (the way you do it).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the method or approach for doing a task. The "y" refers to what you’re dealing with ("it/that"), often mentioned earlier or understood from context. Very common in questions like "Comment vais-je m’y prendre ?" (= How am I going to go about it?). In "savoir s’y prendre", it means "to know how to do it / to be good at handling it".
target_language_example: Comment vas-tu s'y prendre pour ouvrir ce fichier ?
native_language_example: How are you going to go about opening this file?

meaning: “please” (informal; said to one person you address as tu).
additional_notes: Used to make a request or to soften an order. Literally means “if it pleases you.” You use **s'il te plait** when speaking to one person informally (**tu**). For formal situations or when addressing someone as **vous**, use **s'il vous plait**. Note: in standard French spelling, **plaît** takes a circumflex (s'il te plaît), but the form **s'il te plait** is commonly seen without it.
target_language_example: S'il te plait, ouvre la porte.
native_language_example: Please open the door.

additional_notes: Used to make a request more polite. This is the informal singular form (talking to one person you’d say “tu” to). It can go at the beginning or end of a sentence: “S'il te plaît, …” or “…, s'il te plaît.” For a formal or plural “you,” use “s'il vous plaît.”
target_language_example: Aide-moi, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Help me, please.

additional_notes: Used to make a request more polite. Can appear at the beginning or end of a sentence. The « vous » makes it formal or addressed to more than one person; for informal singular, use « s'il te plait ». It can also be used alone to get attention politely (similar to “Excuse me / please?”). Note: the common spelling is « s'il vous plaît » (with a circumflex on « plaît »), but this entry keeps « s'il vous plait » as requested.
target_language_example: Répondez s'il vous plait.
native_language_example: Please answer.

additional_notes: A polite expression used when making requests, giving polite instructions, or ordering something. It uses vous, so it is formal or addressed to more than one person. The informal singular version is s'il te plaît.
target_language_example: Fermez la porte, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

additional_notes: Used to refer to or address a king, queen, emperor, etc. The possessive changes with the monarch’s gender: « Sa Majesté » for a woman (queen) and « Son Majesté » for a man (king). Often treated as a third-person noun in formal speech: « Sa Majesté attend. »
target_language_example: Sa Majesté recevra les invités à midi.
native_language_example: Her Majesty will receive the guests at noon.

additional_notes: “Sa” is a possessive adjective meaning “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun, not the person). “Sa carrière” refers to someone’s professional life/path (job, artistic/sports career, political career). Common patterns: commencer sa carrière (start one’s career), avancer dans sa carrière (move ahead), fin de sa carrière (end of one’s career), une prestation de sa carrière (a performance in one’s career), sa carrière est en jeu (their career is at stake).
target_language_example: Elle veut changer de domaine, mais sa carrière est en jeu.
native_language_example: She wants to change fields, but her career is at stake.

additional_notes: "Sa" means "his" or "her" depending on who you’re talking about (it agrees with the noun, not the person). "Chambre" usually means a bedroom (a private room for sleeping), but in some contexts it can simply mean a room. Often used with verbs like "ranger sa chambre" (to tidy up one’s room) and "fermer la porte de sa chambre" (to close the door of one’s room).
target_language_example: Elle ne veut pas sortir de sa chambre.
native_language_example: She doesn't want to leave her room.

additional_notes: "Sa" means "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun "chemise," which is feminine, not with the owner). In context it often refers to someone taking off, tearing, ironing, hanging up, or tucking in their shirt. If the owner is a man, you still say "sa chemise" because "chemise" is feminine.
target_language_example: Il a enlevé sa chemise parce qu’il avait trop chaud.
native_language_example: He took off his shirt because he was too hot.

additional_notes: "Sa" means "his/her/their" depending on context (it agrees with the noun "famille," which is feminine singular, not with the owner). Used to talk about someone’s family; in some contexts it can also mean their household/dependents (e.g., supporting a family).
target_language_example: Il voudrait passer plus de temps avec sa famille.
native_language_example: He would like to spend more time with his family.

additional_notes: “Sa” is a possessive adjective meaning “his/her” (it agrees with the noun that follows). Because “femme” is feminine, you say “sa femme” for both “his wife” and “her wife”; the context tells you which. Note: “femme” can mean “woman” or “wife,” but “sa femme” usually means “his/her wife.”
target_language_example: Sa femme arrive dans une heure.
native_language_example: His/Her wife will arrive in an hour.

additional_notes: "Sa" is the feminine form of "his/her" and is used before feminine nouns like "femme" (wife). It can refer to a man’s or a woman’s spouse: French chooses "sa" based on the noun (femme), not on the owner. "Est" is the verb "to be" (il/elle est = he/she is).
target_language_example: Sa femme est médecin.
native_language_example: His wife is a doctor.

additional_notes: "Sa" is a possessive adjective meaning "his" or "her" (it depends on who the owner is). It agrees with the noun possessed: "fille" is feminine singular, so you use "sa". (For plural: "ses filles" = "his/her daughters".)
target_language_example: Sa fille a dix ans.
native_language_example: His/Her daughter is ten years old.

meaning: his/her youth; the time when he/she was young.
additional_notes: Refers to someone’s younger years. Use the possessive adjective to match the person: sa (his/her), ma (my), ta (your), notre (our), leur (their), etc. Often used to talk about memories, dreams, or to ask people to consider someone’s age/immaturity.
target_language_example: Il raconte souvent des histoires de sa jeunesse.
native_language_example: He often tells stories about his youth.

additional_notes: “Sa” is a possessive adjective meaning “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun’s gender, not the owner’s). “Main” is feminine, so it’s always “sa main” (= his hand / her hand). Common expression: “demander sa main” means “to ask for her hand (in marriage).” Note: French “main” means “hand” (false friend with English “main”).
target_language_example: Il a pris sa main et il lui a souri.
native_language_example: He took her hand and smiled at her.

additional_notes: "Sa" is the possessive adjective for a feminine singular noun (here, "maison"). It can mean "his" or "her" depending on who owns it (not the gender of the house). Use "son" instead before a vowel sound: "son ancienne maison".
target_language_example: Il cherche sa maison sur la carte.
native_language_example: He’s looking for his house on the map.

meaning: his/her illness (the illness of someone previously mentioned).
additional_notes: “Sa” means “his” or “her” depending on what is owned (here: “maladie” is feminine), not on the person’s gender. Common with verbs like “se remettre de” (to recover from), “guérir de” (to cure/be cured of), “récupérer de” (to recover from), and with adjectives like “grave” (serious).
target_language_example: Après sa maladie, il a dû reprendre le travail doucement.
native_language_example: After his illness, he had to go back to work gradually.

additional_notes: "Sa" can mean "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun "amie," which is feminine, not with the owner). "Meilleure" is the feminine form of "meilleur" (best). Used for someone’s closest friend who is a woman/girl; for a male best friend you’d say "son meilleur ami."
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma avec sa meilleure amie.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with his/her best friend.

additional_notes: "Sa" is the possessive adjective meaning "his" or "her" (it depends on who died, not on the speaker). It’s used to talk about someone’s death, often in time expressions like "avant sa mort" (before his/her death) or "après sa mort" (after his/her death).
target_language_example: Après sa mort, sa famille a déménagé.
native_language_example: After his/her death, his/her family moved.

additional_notes: Refers to a third person's mother. In French, sa can mean both 'his' and 'her'; context tells you which one. Sa is used here because mère is feminine.
target_language_example: Il téléphone souvent à sa mère.
native_language_example: He often calls his mother.

meaning: his girlfriend (or her girlfriend, depending on context).
additional_notes: "Petite amie" means "girlfriend" (a romantic partner). "Sa" can mean "his" or "her" because it agrees with the noun "amie" (feminine), not with the owner. For a male partner, you say "son petit ami".
target_language_example: Il a invité sa petite amie à dîner.
native_language_example: He invited his girlfriend to dinner.

additional_notes: Literally “his/her place,” using the possessive adjective **sa** (feminine singular). It’s used for a physical place (a seat on a bus, a spot in a line, where something belongs: *Sa place est ici*) and also for someone’s role/position (*prendre sa place* = “take his/her place,” i.e., replace them). The possessive changes with the owner: **ma place** (my), **ta place** (your), **sa place** (his/her), **notre place**, **votre place**, **leur place**.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je crois que c’est sa place.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I think that’s his/her seat.

meaning: his/her proposal; his/her offer; his/her suggestion.
additional_notes: Refers to a plan, idea, or offer made by someone (the person is marked by the possessive adjective: sa = his/her). Often used with verbs like accepter/refuser/décliner (accept/refuse/turn down) and expressions like faire objection à (object to) or mériter réflexion (be worth thinking about). In plural, you’d say ses propositions.
target_language_example: Nous avons discuté de sa proposition avant de donner une réponse.
native_language_example: We discussed his/her proposal before giving an answer.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun to emphasize that something belongs uniquely to someone: "sa propre chambre" = "his/her own room". It agrees with the noun, not the owner: masculine singular = "son propre"; feminine plural = "ses propres"; masculine plural = "ses propres". Often adds emphasis/contrast (e.g., risking "sa propre vie" = "his/her own life").
target_language_example: Chacun a sa propre façon de faire les choses.
native_language_example: Everyone has their own way of doing things.

additional_notes: “Sa” means “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun, not the person). Since “santé” is feminine, you use “sa” even when talking about a man. Common in phrases like “s’inquiéter de sa santé” (to worry about his/her health), “préoccupé(e) par sa santé” (concerned about his/her health), “au prix de sa santé” (at the cost of his/her health), “sa santé a décliné” (his/her health declined), “sa santé est défaillante” (his/her health is failing).
target_language_example: Après l’opération, sa santé s’est améliorée.
native_language_example: After the operation, his/her health improved.

meaning: his/her sister (depending on who owns it).
additional_notes: "Sa" is a possessive adjective that agrees with the noun ("sœur" is feminine), not with the owner. So "sa sœur" can mean "his sister" or "her sister" (and sometimes "their sister" if referring to a singular group like a company/organization). For "your sister" use "ta sœur" (informal singular) or "votre sœur" (formal/plural).
target_language_example: Il vient avec sa sœur.
native_language_example: He’s coming with his sister.

meaning: "his/her head" (also used in expressions about being stubborn).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: someone’s head (sa = his/her/its, depending on who you’re talking about). Often appears in the expression « n’en faire qu’à sa tête », meaning “to do only what one wants” / “to be stubborn, not listen to others.”
target_language_example: Il n’en fait qu’à sa tête et refuse d’écouter les conseils.
native_language_example: He just does what he wants and refuses to listen to advice.

additional_notes: Means “his life” or “her life” depending on who you’re talking about (sa = his/her, vie = life). Often seen in the expression “sa vie durant” = “all his/her life / throughout his/her life.” Possessive changes with the owner: ma vie (my life), ta vie (your life), sa vie (his/her life).
target_language_example: Il a vécu ici toute sa vie.
native_language_example: He lived here his whole life.

additional_notes: "Sa" means "his/her/its" (feminine singular), and "voiture" is feminine, so you use "sa" even when you mean "his" (e.g., "Il est monté dans sa voiture" = "He got into his car"). For emphasis or clarity, you can say "sa voiture à lui" (his car) / "sa voiture à elle" (her car).
target_language_example: Il a garé sa voiture devant la maison.
native_language_example: He parked his car in front of the house.

additional_notes: "Sa" means "his" or "her" depending on who owns the voice (it agrees with the feminine noun "voix," not with the speaker’s gender). Often used to describe the sound or tone of someone’s voice (e.g., "se fit douce" = "became soft/gentle"), or to express annoyance ("me court sur les nerfs" = "gets on my nerves").
target_language_example: J’ai reconnu sa voix tout de suite.
native_language_example: I recognized his/her voice right away.

additional_notes: A common everyday noun for a bag worn on your back. You’ll often see it with colors/adjectives (un sac à dos bleu) and with possessives (mon/ton/son sac à dos).
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon sac à dos à l'école.
native_language_example: I forgot my backpack at school.

additional_notes: A small bag (often carried by women) used to carry personal items. Common with possessives: « mon/ton/son sac à main ». It’s masculine: « un sac à main », « ce sac à main ».
target_language_example: J’ai laissé mon sac à main sur la chaise.
native_language_example: I left my handbag on the chair.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is alive and not injured after danger, an accident, or a difficult situation. Common with verbs like « être », « rentrer », « revenir », « arriver », « repartir », « ramener »: « rentrer sain et sauf », « ramener quelqu’un sain et sauf ». Agreement is possible: « saine et sauve » (feminine), « sains et saufs » (masc. plural), « saines et sauves » (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Je suis soulagé que vous soyez sain et sauf.
native_language_example: I’m relieved that you’re safe and sound.

meaning: "safe and sound"; unharmed (plural masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like rentrer, revenir, arriver, s’en sortir to say people made it back/through something without injury. It agrees with the people: sain et sauf (1 man), saine et sauve (1 woman), sains et saufs (men/mixed group), saines et sauves (women).
target_language_example: Après la tempête, ils sont rentrés sains et saufs.
native_language_example: After the storm, they got home safe and sound.

additional_notes: Inversion of the verb "savoir" + "tu" to form a question, meaning “do you know…?” and often used like “can you…?” for skills/ability. Commonly followed by an infinitive: "Sais-tu nager ?" = “Can you swim?” More formal than "Tu sais… ?".
target_language_example: Sais-tu cuisiner ?
native_language_example: Can you cook?

additional_notes: Question form of tu sais, using inversion with savoir. It means "do you know...?" when speaking to one person informally. This inverted form is common in writing and more formal speech; in everyday spoken French, tu sais...? or est-ce que tu sais...? is often more common.
target_language_example: Sais-tu où il habite ?
native_language_example: Do you know where he lives?

additional_notes: Uses subject–verb inversion ("sais-tu") to form a question; it’s a fairly formal/standard way to ask if someone knows some information. Often followed by a verb clause (e.g., "…ce que ça signifie", "…ce que Tom fait"). A more neutral/common alternative is: "Est-ce que tu sais ce que…" or "Tu sais ce que… ?" in casual speech.
target_language_example: Sais-tu ce que ça veut dire ?
native_language_example: Do you know what that means?

meaning: “Do you know how…?” (asking if someone knows the method/way to do something).
additional_notes: Inversion question form of "Tu sais comment…?" (a bit more formal). Usually followed by an infinitive ("Sais-tu comment ouvrir…?") or a full clause ("Sais-tu comment elle se porte ?" = how she is doing).
target_language_example: Sais-tu comment arriver à la gare d’ici ?
native_language_example: Do you know how to get to the station from here?

meaning: "do you know where" (asking someone for the location of something/someone).
additional_notes: This is an inverted question form: "sais-tu" = "do you know" and "où" = "where". It’s used before a clause giving the thing you’re looking for: "Sais-tu où + subject + verb… ?" You may also see the more common non-inverted form in everyday speech: "Tu sais où… ?"
target_language_example: Sais-tu où se trouve la gare ?
native_language_example: Do you know where the train station is?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows a person’s identity. It’s a question form with inversion (verb + -tu): « sais-tu… ? ». It’s often followed by a clause like « sais-tu qui c’est ? » / « sais-tu qui il est ? ». You can also say the more neutral « Est-ce que tu sais qui… ? ».
target_language_example: Sais-tu qui a appelé tout à l’heure ?
native_language_example: Do you know who called earlier?

additional_notes: very common informal shortening of « ne sais pas » / « je ne sais pas ». In speech and casual writing, French often drops « ne », so « je sais pas » means « I don't know » and « tu sais pas ? » means « you don't know? ». Standard written French usually uses « ne ... pas ».
target_language_example: Je sais pas si elle vient ce soir.
native_language_example: I don't know if she's coming tonight.

meaning: rainy season (the season when it rains a lot).
additional_notes: A common weather/climate phrase, especially for tropical/subtropical regions. Usually used with the definite article: « la saison des pluies ». You can talk about when it happens (« pendant la saison des pluies ») or when it starts/ends (« la saison des pluies commence/se termine en… »).
target_language_example: Pendant la saison des pluies, il pleut presque tous les jours.
native_language_example: During the rainy season, it rains almost every day.

additional_notes: "sait" is the 3rd-person singular present tense of *savoir* (to know), used with "que" to introduce a clause (a complete idea): *Il/Elle/On sait que + [subject + verb]*. For other subjects: *je sais que, tu sais que, nous savons que, vous savez que, ils/elles savent que*.
target_language_example: Elle sait que le train arrive à 18 h.
native_language_example: She knows that the train arrives at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: The lowest legal pay level (usually per hour or per month) that an employer must pay. Often used in discussions about salaries and labor laws: augmenter le salaire minimum (raise the minimum wage), gagner le salaire minimum (earn the minimum wage).
target_language_example: Elle gagne juste le salaire minimum.
native_language_example: She earns only the minimum wage.

additional_notes: The place where you wait before an appointment or service (commonly at a doctor’s office, hospital, or government office). Often used with "dans": "Je suis dans la salle d'attente."
target_language_example: Veuillez patienter dans la salle d'attente.
native_language_example: Please wait in the waiting room.

additional_notes: Literally “bath room.” Refers to a room with a bath/shower (and often a sink); depending on context it may or may not include a toilet. To ask to use it politely: « Je peux utiliser votre salle de bain ? »
target_language_example: La salle de bain est au fond du couloir, à droite.
native_language_example: The bathroom is at the end of the hallway, on the right.

meaning: bathroom; room for bathing (with a bath and/or shower).
additional_notes: Often refers specifically to the room with a bathtub or shower. In some homes the toilet may be separate; for “restroom/toilet” you’ll also hear *les toilettes* or *les WC*. Common patterns: *dans la salle de bains* (in the bathroom), *utiliser la salle de bains* (use the bathroom), *les carreaux de la salle de bains* (bathroom tiles).
target_language_example: La serviette est dans la salle de bains.
native_language_example: The towel is in the bathroom.

meaning: classroom (a room where students have lessons).
additional_notes: Often used with an article: une salle de classe (a classroom), la salle de classe (the classroom). It refers to the physical room, not the school class/group (la classe).
target_language_example: Les élèves sont déjà dans la salle de classe.
native_language_example: The students are already in the classroom.

additional_notes: A room where equipment and operations are monitored and managed (e.g., in a factory, power plant, train station, airport, TV/radio station). Often used with location questions like « Où est la salle de contrôle ? ».
target_language_example: Seul le personnel autorisé peut entrer dans la salle de contrôle.
native_language_example: Only authorized staff can enter the control room.

additional_notes: Used in workplaces, schools, and clubs for a room where people gather to discuss things. Often used with verbs like "entrer" (to go in), "se réunir" (to meet/gather), and with availability phrases like "être occupée" (to be occupied) or "être libre" (to be free).
target_language_example: La salle de réunion est libre à 14 h, on peut s’y retrouver.
native_language_example: The meeting room is free at 2 p.m.; we can meet there.

additional_notes: The room where people eat meals, often with a dining table. Common in phrases like « dans la salle à manger » (in the dining room) and « la table de la salle à manger » (the dining room table).
target_language_example: On dîne dans la salle à manger ce soir.
native_language_example: We’re having dinner in the dining room tonight.

meaning: "Hi" + an affectionate "my …" (used before a term of endearment).
additional_notes: "Salut" is a casual greeting. "Mon" is the masculine form of "my" used before a noun of affection like "amour" (love) or "chou" (sweetie). You’ll also see "ma" (feminine) and "mes" (plural). In nicknames, French sometimes uses "mon" even when speaking to a woman (e.g., "mon amour").
target_language_example: Salut, mon amour, comment ça va ?
native_language_example: Hi, my love, how are you?

meaning: calmness; self-control (especially in a stressful situation).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like garder/mettre ("keep your cool"): « Garde ton sang-froid. » In crime contexts, « de sang-froid » means "cold-bloodedly" (deliberately, without emotion): « Il a été abattu de sang-froid. » Also in « un meurtre de sang-froid » (a cold-blooded murder) and « un tueur de sang-froid » (a cold-blooded killer).
target_language_example: Même sous pression, elle garde son sang-froid.
native_language_example: Even under pressure, she keeps her cool.

additional_notes: Literally “without shelter.” Used as an adjective (Elle est sans-abri = She is homeless) or as a noun with an article (un/une sans-abri; des sans-abri = a homeless person; homeless people). In the plural: des sans-abri.
target_language_example: La ville a ouvert un refuge pour les sans-abri.
native_language_example: The city opened a shelter for homeless people.

meaning: a perfect score; a flawless performance (no mistakes).
additional_notes: Used as a noun ("faire un sans-faute" = to get everything right) or as an adjective meaning "flawless" ("un plan sans-faute"). Common for exams, competitions, presentations, or anything done perfectly.
target_language_example: Elle a fait un sans-faute au test de français.
native_language_example: She got a perfect score on the French test.

additional_notes: Often placed after a verb to mean something happens repeatedly/continuously: « parler sans arrêt », « se plaindre sans arrêt ». Very common in everyday speech to emphasize that something is ongoing or keeps happening.
target_language_example: Il pleut sans arrêt depuis ce matin.
native_language_example: It’s been raining nonstop since this morning.

additional_notes: Used to express strong certainty. It can go at the beginning of a sentence (often followed by a comma) or in the middle after the verb. Common in both spoken and written French. More emphatic than just « sans doute » (which can sometimes mean “probably”).
target_language_example: Elle réussira sans aucun doute son examen.
native_language_example: She will undoubtedly pass her exam.

additional_notes: Used to react to what someone just said. It can be genuine surprise (“Really?”) or irony/sarcasm (“Yeah, no kidding,” “Tell me something I don’t know”). It can also mean “seriously” to insist on being earnest: “Sans blague, ça pourrait marcher.”
target_language_example: Sans blague, tu as vraiment fait ça ?
native_language_example: No kidding—you really did that?

additional_notes: Means something happens repeatedly or continuously. Often placed after the verb ("il parle sans cesse") or at the end of the sentence. Similar to "tout le temps" (all the time) and "continuellement" (continuously).
target_language_example: Il me téléphone sans cesse depuis hier.
native_language_example: He’s been calling me constantly since yesterday.

additional_notes: Very informal slang used to show surprise or to insist you’re telling the truth. Often said as a reaction: « sans dec ?! » = “Seriously?!” or after a statement: « sans dec, c’est vrai. » = “No kidding, it’s true.” Avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: sans dec, t’as déjà fini ?
native_language_example: Seriously, you’ve already finished?

additional_notes: Used after a main verb to show someone did something and didn’t say goodbye (often implying it was abrupt or a bit rude). Structure: "sans" + infinitive (here: dire) + object (au revoir).
target_language_example: Je suis parti sans dire au revoir parce que j'étais pressé.
native_language_example: I left without saying goodbye because I was in a hurry.

additional_notes: Used to express strong likelihood or an assumption based on what you know. It often comes before the part it qualifies ("C’est sans doute une bonne idée"), but it can also be placed after the verb ("il connaît sans doute la vérité").
target_language_example: Il va sans doute pleuvoir ce soir.
native_language_example: It will probably rain tonight.

additional_notes: Used to insist that something should happen right away. Common in instructions, requests, warnings, and formal writing. It can modify a verb (e.g., partir sans délai) or an action (e.g., régler un problème sans délai).
target_language_example: Veuillez nous répondre sans délai.
native_language_example: Please reply to us without delay.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or exists in the absence of water. Often in survival/necessity statements (e.g., living, plants, animals) or practical situations (e.g., a device running without water).
target_language_example: Les plantes ne peuvent pas pousser sans eau.
native_language_example: Plants can’t grow without water.

meaning: safely; without incident; without any problems.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something arrived or happened with no trouble (no accidents, delays, or complications). Often goes with verbs like « arriver », « rentrer », « se passer », or « se dérouler ».
target_language_example: On est rentrés sans encombre après le concert.
native_language_example: We got home safely after the concert.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a statement applies to everyone or everything in a group. Often follows words like "tous" (all) or can be said alone as a firm confirmation.
target_language_example: Toutes les personnes doivent montrer leur badge, sans exception.
native_language_example: Everyone must show their badge, no exceptions.

additional_notes: Used to insist that something must happen or be done, often in promises or instructions. Common with the future tense (Je le ferai sans faute) or in the imperative (Reviens sans faute !).
target_language_example: Je te le rendrai demain sans faute.
native_language_example: I’ll give it back to you tomorrow without fail.

additional_notes: Often used on its own as a short, polite way to refuse an offer: « Merci, sans façon. » / « Non, sans façon. » It can also describe something that’s plain or without fuss/pretension (e.g., a home or a room): « C’est sans façon, mais confortable. »
target_language_example: — Vous voulez un café ? — Sans façon, merci.
native_language_example: — Would you like a coffee? — No thanks.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that seems to continue forever (a war, renovation, repetition, etc.). It can come after a noun ("une rénovation sans fin"), after the verb "être" ("c'est sans fin"), or stand alone as an exclamation to mean "Endless!".
target_language_example: Cette réunion est sans fin !
native_language_example: This meeting is endless!

additional_notes: Used to say something is boring, not worthwhile, or irrelevant. It can stand alone as a short comment (“Sans intérêt.”) or be followed by “pour + person” to specify who isn’t interested (“sans intérêt pour vous”).
target_language_example: Ce film est sans intérêt pour moi.
native_language_example: This movie is of no interest to me.

meaning: broke; with no money at all.
additional_notes: Idiom meaning you’re completely out of money. Used with être: « Je suis/Il est/Nous sommes sans le sou ». « Sou » is an old word for a small coin, so it’s like saying “without a penny.”
target_language_example: Après avoir payé le loyer, je suis sans le sou.
native_language_example: After paying the rent, I’m broke.

meaning: without saying a word; without a word.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone leaves, disappears, or does something in silence (no explanation, no goodbye). Often placed after the verb: « Il est parti sans mot dire ».
target_language_example: Ils ont refusé et sont partis sans mot dire.
native_language_example: They refused and left without saying a word.

additional_notes: Means something can be done easily/without difficulty ("without any problem"). As a short reply, it’s a polite way to say “no problem / sure / you’re welcome.”
target_language_example: Je peux vous aider, sans problème.
native_language_example: I can help you, no problem.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is exceptional because nothing similar has happened before. Often follows the noun it describes (e.g., une crise sans précédent) or is used after être (C’est sans précédent). Common in news and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Nous faisons face à une crise sans précédent.
native_language_example: We are facing an unprecedented crisis.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize continuous effort or action over time, often in a determined or tireless way. Common with verbs like travailler, chercher, observer, essayer.
target_language_example: Elle a travaillé sans relâche pour finir le projet à temps.
native_language_example: She worked relentlessly to finish the project on time.

additional_notes: Used to say you are not included or not present (physically or in helping/participating). Can sound emotional in phrases like « Qu’est-ce que je ferais sans toi ? » (“What would I do without you?”).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas partir sans toi.
native_language_example: I don’t want to leave without you.

meaning: without a/an (before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: sans un + noun (e.g., sans un mot = without a word). For a feminine noun, use « sans une ». Very often French drops the article after « sans » (e.g., « sans argent » = without money), but « sans un/une » is common in set phrases or for emphasis.
target_language_example: Il est parti sans un mot.
native_language_example: He left without a word.

meaning: speechless; unable to speak (often from surprise/shock).
additional_notes: Used with the verb être or rester ("to be/remain") to say you can’t find words—typically because you’re amazed, stunned, shocked, or deeply moved. It can be literal (you can’t speak) or figurative (you’re too surprised to respond).
target_language_example: Quand j'ai vu la surprise, je suis resté sans voix.
native_language_example: When I saw the surprise, I was left speechless.

additional_notes: Refers to the tree people put up and decorate for Christmas. You’ll often see it with verbs like installer/monter (to put up), décorer (to decorate), and with the phrase sous le sapin de Noël (“under the Christmas tree”) for gifts.
target_language_example: On a décoré le sapin de Noël hier soir.
native_language_example: We decorated the Christmas tree last night.

additional_notes: Used to add an important exception, limitation, or twist to what was just said. Often comes at the start of a sentence: « Je voulais venir, sauf que j’étais malade. » It can also be used in a questioning way (« Sauf que quoi ? ») meaning “But what (exactly)?” / “Except what?”.
target_language_example: Je pensais que tout était réglé, sauf que le paiement n’est jamais passé.
native_language_example: I thought everything was settled, except that the payment never went through.

additional_notes: Introduces an exception to what was just said. Often used after a statement to add a condition that would change it: "Je viens, sauf si je suis malade" (I’m coming, unless I’m sick). You can also use it alone as a follow-up question: "Sauf si quoi ?" = "Unless what?".
target_language_example: Je peux t’aider, sauf si tu préfères être seul.
native_language_example: I can help you, unless you’d rather be alone.

meaning: "with all due respect" (polite way to disagree or criticize).
additional_notes: A very formal, old-fashioned set phrase used before (or sometimes alone as) a statement that may contradict, criticize, or correct the listener. It softens what follows and signals respect, especially when addressing someone in a higher position. Often followed by a comma: « Sauf votre respect, … ».
target_language_example: Sauf votre respect, je crois que vous vous trompez.
native_language_example: With all due respect, I think you're mistaken.

meaning: to be obvious; to stand out
additional_notes: Used to say something is immediately noticeable or clearly apparent (often about a detail, a problem, a difference). Common patterns: « Ça va sauter aux yeux » (It’ll be obvious), « ça saute aux yeux » (it’s obvious), « ce détail saute aux yeux » (this detail stands out).
target_language_example: Ça va sauter aux yeux.
native_language_example: It’s going to be obvious.

additional_notes: "Savais-tu" is the informal (tu) past tense of "savoir" (to know): "did you know". It’s used to ask if someone already knew some information, often followed by "que" + a full clause. In more formal speech (vous), use "saviez-vous que".
target_language_example: Savais-tu que le musée est fermé le lundi ?
native_language_example: Did you know that the museum is closed on Mondays?

additional_notes: "savait que" uses "savait", the imperfect third-person singular form of "savoir" (il/elle/on savait), and means that he/she/it/one knew that. It is used for past knowledge, often as background information or an ongoing state in the past.
target_language_example: Tout le monde savait que Tom mentait.
native_language_example: Everyone knew that Tom was lying.

additional_notes: This is the verb *savoir* (“to know how to”) in the *vous* form, with subject–verb inversion to ask a question. It’s often followed by an infinitive to ask about a skill: *Savez-vous nager ?* (“Do you know how to swim?”). More formal than *Vous savez… ?* and much more formal than *Tu sais… ?*.
target_language_example: Savez-vous parler anglais ?
native_language_example: Do you know how to speak English?

meaning: “Do you know how to speak (…)? / Can you speak (…)?”.
additional_notes: Polite/formal question using inversion (savez-vous…). Used to ask if someone speaks a specific language: savez-vous parler le japonais / le russe, etc. In everyday speech you’ll often hear: « Est-ce que vous savez parler… ? » or informal « Tu sais parler… ? ». Note: for some languages French doesn’t use « le » (e.g., « parler français », « parler anglais »).
target_language_example: Savez-vous parler le russe ?
native_language_example: Do you speak Russian?

additional_notes: Formal/polite way to ask a question using inversion: verb + subject ("savez" + "vous"). Often followed by a question word or clause: "Savez-vous ce que…?" (Do you know what…?), "Savez-vous qui…?" (Do you know who…?), "Savez-vous où…?" (Do you know where…?), or "Savez-vous que…?" (Do you know that…?/Are you aware that…?). More neutral/less formal: "Est-ce que vous savez…?" or "Vous savez…?".
target_language_example: Savez-vous où se trouve la gare ?
native_language_example: Do you know where the train station is?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows a specific piece of information. It’s the polite/inverted form of the question (subject-verb inversion): savez-vous…? Often followed by a full clause: « Savez-vous ce que + subject + verb… ? » It can be followed by another verb directly: « Savez-vous ce que signifie ce symbole ? »
target_language_example: Savez-vous ce que vous cherchez exactement ?
native_language_example: Do you know what exactly you’re looking for?

additional_notes: Used to ask politely if someone knows the way to do something or how something works. It’s the inverted (more formal) form of “Vous savez comment… ?”. Often followed by an infinitive (“comment faire…”, “comment ouvrir…”) or a full clause (“comment ceci fonctionne”, “comment je peux y aller”).
target_language_example: Savez-vous comment changer la langue sur ce téléphone ?
native_language_example: Do you know how to change the language on this phone?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a location or destination. It’s an inverted question (verb before subject) and sounds polite/formal; in casual speech you often hear "Vous savez où…?" or "Tu sais où…?". It’s typically followed by a clause like "il est", "elle habite", "on peut le trouver", etc.
target_language_example: Savez-vous où se trouve la gare ?
native_language_example: Do you know where the train station is?

additional_notes: A polite/formal question using inversion (verb + subject): « savez-vous » = “do you know”. It’s usually followed by a clause with « qui » (“who”), e.g., « Savez-vous qui a fait ça ? » In casual speech, people often say « Vous savez qui… ? » or « Tu sais qui… ? »
target_language_example: Savez-vous qui a appelé ce matin ?
native_language_example: Do you know who called this morning?

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of savoir (vous saviez) in a question to introduce information the speaker thinks may be new or surprising. Often used to start a fun fact or check someone’s knowledge. "Vous" can be formal singular or plural; informal would be "Savais-tu que…?".
target_language_example: Saviez-vous que le musée ferme à 18 h ?
native_language_example: Did you know that the museum closes at 6 p.m.?

meaning: to know how to do it; to be good at handling something (or someone).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is skilled, tactful, or has a knack for dealing with a situation (often with people: children, customers, etc.). The “y” refers back to the situation/thing/person you’re dealing with (“with it/at it”). Commonly used in the conjugated form: « Il/Elle sait y faire. »
target_language_example: Elle semble avoir appris à savoir y faire avec les enfants.
native_language_example: She seems to have learned how to handle kids well.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the practical ability to do something well (skills gained from experience), or the technical expertise of a person, company, or craft. Often appears with avoir (“il a le savoir-faire…”) or as a general idea (“une question de savoir-faire”).
target_language_example: Elle a beaucoup de savoir-faire en cuisine.
native_language_example: She has a lot of know-how in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used as a noun to talk about someone’s ability to do something well in a practical, often professional way (experience, technique, tact). Common in contexts like work, crafts, cooking, management, or dealing with people ("le savoir-faire").
target_language_example: Elle a beaucoup de savoir-faire en cuisine.
native_language_example: She has a lot of know-how in the kitchen.

additional_notes: A (fairly formal) noun meaning the rules and habits of polite behavior in society (e.g., being respectful, saying please/thank you, table manners). Often used with verbs like "avoir" (to have) or "manquer de" (to lack): « Il a du savoir-vivre » / « Il manque de savoir-vivre ». Can also refer to etiquette in a specific setting (work, dining, etc.).
target_language_example: Dans ce restaurant, il faut avoir du savoir-vivre.
native_language_example: In this restaurant, you need to have good manners.

meaning: to be grateful; to appreciate (something someone did).
additional_notes: Used mainly in the expression « savoir gré à quelqu’un de + infinitive / noun » (rather formal). It expresses gratitude or appreciation toward someone for something they did: « Je vous sais gré de votre aide » = “I’m grateful to you for your help.” In everyday speech, it’s often replaced by « être reconnaissant(e) » or « merci pour/de… ».
target_language_example: Je tiens à vous savoir gré de votre aide.
native_language_example: I want you to know I’m grateful for your help.

additional_notes: Used as a noun for the genre in books, movies, etc., often after verbs like lire (to read) or regarder (to watch). You can say de la science-fiction for “(some) sci‑fi” in general, or la science-fiction for “sci‑fi” as a genre. It can also be used figuratively to mean something seems unrealistic or far-fetched ("C'est de la science-fiction !").
target_language_example: Ce film de science-fiction est incroyable.
native_language_example: This sci‑fi movie is amazing.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the place where a crime happened, especially in police/news contexts. Often used with a determiner: "sur la scène de crime" (at the crime scene), "une scène de crime" (a crime scene).
target_language_example: La police a bouclé la scène de crime.
native_language_example: The police sealed off the crime scene.

meaning: (informal) to leave; to get out (of here).
additional_notes: Very common spoken/slang French. Used as a reflexive verb: je me barre (I’m leaving), tu te barres, il/elle se barre, on se barre, etc. Often sounds a bit blunt or rude depending on tone/context; in the imperative: Barre-toi ! = Get out!/Go away! You can add a place: se barrer d’ici (get out of here), se barrer de la fête (leave the party).
target_language_example: On va se barrer, il est tard.
native_language_example: We’re going to get out of here; it’s late.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb (uses "se"). It can mean physically fighting ("Ils vont se battre") or fighting/struggling to achieve, defend, or maintain something ("se battre pour ses droits"). Common patterns: "se battre contre" (fight against) and "se battre pour" (fight for). Conjugates with être in compound tenses (e.g., "ils se sont battus").
target_language_example: Elle va se battre pour ses droits.
native_language_example: She’s going to fight for her rights.

additional_notes: From the verb "se cacher" (reflexive). It can mean someone/thing hides itself ("Il se cache") or something is hidden/contained in something else in a more abstract way ("Une possibilité se cache..."). In questions with inversion: "Se cache-t-il...?"
target_language_example: Une surprise se cache dans ce paquet.
native_language_example: A surprise is hidden in this package.

meaning: to break (a bone, a tooth, your neck), to injure yourself.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb used for accidents and injuries. Very common with a body part: se casser le cou (break your neck), se casser une dent (break a tooth). In everyday speech it can also mean “to leave/get out of here” (informal), but in the example given here it’s the literal injury meaning.
target_language_example: Tante Leslie a failli se casser le cou.
native_language_example: Aunt Leslie almost broke her neck.

additional_notes: Used to describe what something includes as its parts or elements. The subject is usually a thing or group (family, year, minute), and what follows “de” is the list or number of components. Very common in factual descriptions and definitions.
target_language_example: Le menu se compose de trois plats.
native_language_example: The menu consists of three courses.

meaning: to go to bed; to lie down; (of the sun) to set.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb (je me couche, tu te couches, il/elle se couche, nous nous couchons, vous vous couchez, ils/elles se couchent). Commonly used with an infinitive construction: « aller se coucher » (to go to bed). Also used for the sun: « Le soleil se couche / va se coucher ».
target_language_example: Thomas est allé se coucher tôt parce qu'il travaille demain.
native_language_example: Thomas went to bed early because he works tomorrow.

meaning: is heading toward; is going in the direction of.
additional_notes: From the verb *se diriger* (a reflexive verb) + *vers* (“toward”). Used for people or things moving toward a place/person/direction. Often translated as “to head for/toward” or “to make one’s way toward.”
target_language_example: On se dirige vers la gare à pied.
native_language_example: We’re heading toward the train station on foot.

meaning: to give oneself; to provide oneself (with); (in set phrases) to give oneself the means / to arrange to meet.
additional_notes:
Reflexive verb used with me/te/se/nous/vous/se. Very common in fixed expressions:
- « se donner les moyens de + infinitif » = to do what’s necessary / to give yourself the means to (do something).
- « se donner rendez-vous » = to arrange to meet / to meet up.
Also frequent: « se donner une chance » (to give yourself a chance), « se donner du mal » (to go to a lot of trouble).
target_language_example: Il était satisfait de se donner tous les moyens de réussir dans la vie.
native_language_example: He was satisfied that he was giving himself every means to succeed in life.

meaning: moves; travels; shifts (from one place to another).
additional_notes: 3rd person singular present of the reflexive verb « se déplacer » (to move/to get around). Used for people, animals, vehicles, or anything that changes position (a target, a glacier, even pain). Often implies moving from one place to another rather than just moving in place.
target_language_example: Le glacier se déplace lentement.
native_language_example: The glacier moves slowly.

meaning: to get late (time is getting late).
additional_notes: Used mostly in the impersonal form: « Il se fait tard » = “It’s getting late.” It’s a common way to suggest it’s time to leave or wrap up. Often followed by « je vais y aller » / « on devrait rentrer » (I’m going to go / we should head home).
target_language_example: Il commence à se faire tard, on devrait rentrer.
native_language_example: It’s starting to get late; we should go home.

meaning: “is done / happens”; in “se faire + infinitive”: “to get (something) done / to have (something) happen to you”.
additional_notes: This is a form of the verb “se faire”. Common patterns: (1) “Ça se fait / Ça ne se fait pas” = it’s (not) done/acceptable socially. (2) “Comment ça se fait que… ?” = how come…? (3) “Il se fait tard” = it’s getting late (a bit formal/old-fashioned). (4) “se faire + infinitive” often expresses a passive idea: “se faire arrêter” = to get arrested, “se faire payer” = to get paid. You can also see it in general statements: “Tout se fait savoir ici” = everything gets known around here.
target_language_example: Ça ne se fait pas de couper la parole aux autres.
native_language_example: It’s not done (it’s not acceptable) to interrupt other people.

meaning: to not give a damn about; to make fun of.
additional_notes: Very informal (can be rude/vulgar depending on tone). Used with an object: se foutre de + [someone/something]. Depending on context it can mean either (1) not caring at all (Je me fous de ça = I don’t care about that) or (2) mocking/teasing someone (Il se fout de moi = He’s making fun of me / He’s messing with me). Commonly used with pronoun changes: je me fous de, tu te fous de, il/elle se fout de, etc. Also often heard as Je m’en fous (I don’t care).
target_language_example: Il va se foutre de toi si tu lui racontes ça.
native_language_example: He’s going to make fun of you if you tell him that.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase: *se laver* (to wash oneself) + *les mains* (the hands). Often used in instructions or general statements about hygiene (e.g., *Il faut / On doit se laver les mains*). When conjugated, the reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: *je me lave les mains, tu te laves les mains, il/elle se lave les mains, nous nous lavons les mains, vous vous lavez les mains, ils/elles se lavent les mains*.
target_language_example: Il faut se laver les mains !
native_language_example: You have to wash your hands!

meaning: to get up; to stand up; (of the sun) to rise
additional_notes: Reflexive verb (se lever): the subject performs the action on themself. Used for getting out of bed (se lever le matin), standing up from a chair/table (se lever de son siège / se lever de table), and for the sun (le soleil se lève = the sun rises). Often followed by a time expression: se lever tôt, se lever à 7 h. Conjugates with être in compound tenses: je me suis levé(e).
target_language_example: Ce sera difficile pour lui de se lever si tôt.
native_language_example: It will be hard for him to get up so early.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb: "se lever" = "to get up" (literally "to raise oneself"). In the infinitive it appears as "se lever"; when conjugated it changes (e.g., "je me lève"). In the passé composé, "se lever" uses être and agrees: "Je me suis levé(e) tôt." Often used to talk about routines or habits (e.g., with "avoir l’habitude de").
target_language_example: Ken a pour habitude de se lever tôt.
native_language_example: Ken is in the habit of getting up early.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb « se lever » (to get up). « se lève » is the present tense for il/elle/on (he/she/one). Often used for habits (e.g., « tous les matins » = every morning). Can also be used figuratively for a place or group (e.g., « Le village se lève tôt » = people in the village start their day early).
target_language_example: Ma grand-mère se lève tôt tous les matins.
native_language_example: My grandmother gets up early every morning.

meaning: “gets married” / “is getting married”; also “goes well with” (pairs well).
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb **se marier**. It most often means someone is getting married (e.g., *Ma cousine se marie demain*). It can also be used more figuratively for food, flavors, colors, etc. to mean they match well: *Le tofu se marie bien avec le saké* (“Tofu goes well with sake”).
target_language_example: Ce vin se marie bien avec le fromage.
native_language_example: This wine goes well with cheese.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb used for the act of getting married (the event/decision): se marier. Often followed by "avec" + person (se marier avec quelqu’un = to marry someone). For wedding plans, you can also use "se marier" + time: se marier en juin (get married in June).
target_language_example: Ils vont se marier l’année prochaine.
native_language_example: They’re going to get married next year.

meaning: to start (doing); to get into a state/position; to set oneself (to)
additional_notes: Reflexive verb (uses se). Common patterns: se mettre à + infinitive = “to start doing” (se mettre à travailler). se mettre au/à la + noun = “to get down to / take up” an activity or regimen (se mettre au travail, se mettre au régime). se mettre en + noun = “to get into a state/position” (se mettre en rang, se mettre en colère). se mettre d’accord = “to agree / come to an agreement.”
target_language_example: Tout le monde a dû se mettre à travailler.
native_language_example: Everyone had to start working.

meaning: to start (doing something); to begin to.
additional_notes: Followed by an infinitive: « se mettre à + infinitive ». It often implies beginning an action (sometimes suddenly or after a pause/hesitation): « se mettre à parler / chercher / neiger ». Used for people and also for things/events (e.g., the weather: « se mettre à neiger »).
target_language_example: Elle se calma avant de se mettre à parler.
native_language_example: She calmed down before starting to speak.

additional_notes: This is the past historic (passé simple) form of "se mettre à + infinitive" (= to start doing something). You’ll mostly see it in novels and formal storytelling; in everyday speech French usually uses the passé composé: "il/elle s’est mis(e) à pleurer". Here, "pleurer" means "to cry".
target_language_example: En entendant la nouvelle, il se mit à pleurer.
native_language_example: On hearing the news, he started to cry.

additional_notes: Often used for events or situations. With subjects like ça, quelque chose, or qu'est-ce qui, it usually means "to happen" or "to occur." It can also describe how something goes or unfolds, depending on context.
target_language_example: Quelque chose vient de se passer.
native_language_example: Something just happened.

meaning: to do without; to go without.
additional_notes: Means managing without something (or someone). Common with negation to express necessity: ne pas pouvoir se passer de = “can’t do without.” It takes de before the thing/person you do without: se passer de voitures, se passer de couvertures, se passer de moi. Can also be used self-deprecatingly about being unnecessary (“They can do without me”).
target_language_example: Les gens modernes ne peuvent se passer de voitures.
native_language_example: Modern people can't do without cars.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb (uses "se"): "je me plains", "tu te plains", "il/elle se plaint", "nous nous plaignons", "vous vous plaignez", "ils/elles se plaignent". Often followed by "de" to say what you’re complaining about ("se plaindre de la chaleur"), or "à" to say who you complain to ("se plaindre au gérant"). Common with expressions like "ne faire que" (do nothing but) and "être en train de" (be in the middle of).
target_language_example: Tom appela le service client pour se plaindre.
native_language_example: Tom called customer service to complain.

meaning: to be doing; to feel (especially regarding health/well-being).
additional_notes: Most often used with an adverb like bien/mal: « Je me porte bien » (I’m doing well / I feel fine), « Il se porte mal » (He’s not doing well). You may also see the more formal/old-fashioned question « Comment vous portez-vous ? » meaning “How are you?” In other contexts, porter has different meanings (e.g., « se porter volontaire » = to volunteer).
target_language_example: Comment allez-vous ? — Je dirais que se porter bien, c’est déjà beaucoup.
native_language_example: How are you? — I’d say that doing well is already a lot.

meaning: to be possible; to be able to happen.
additional_notes: Rare and somewhat literary/old-fashioned as an infinitive; in modern everyday French you usually express the idea with **il se peut que + subj.** or **c’est possible** / **ça se peut**. When it does appear, it conveys possibility/feasibility rather than someone’s ability.
target_language_example: Dans certains cas, cela peut se pouvoir.
native_language_example: In some cases, that can be possible.

meaning: to take oneself (often: to think you are someone / to get caught up / to get tangled).
additional_notes:
Reflexive form of « prendre ». Common patterns:
- « se prendre pour + nom » = to think you are / to take yourself for: « Il se prend pour un médecin. »
- « se prendre à + infinitif » = to start doing something (often suddenly/unexpectedly): « Je me suis pris à rire. »
- Physical sense: « se prendre (dans) … » = to get caught/tangled: « Je me suis pris dans un fil. »
- Very common idiom: « se prendre les pieds dans… » = to trip / get your feet caught in…
target_language_example: Il va se prendre pour un chef, mais il débute.
native_language_example: He’s going to think he’s a boss, but he’s just starting out.

meaning: to happen; to occur (used for events/incidents; sometimes unexpected).
additional_notes: Used with events/things as the subject: « Un accident peut se produire. » In compound tenses it takes être and agrees with the subject: « s’est produit / s’est produite / se sont produits / se sont produites ». Also common in constructions like « imaginer cela se produire » = “imagine that happening.”
target_language_example: Comment cela a-t-il pu se produire ?
native_language_example: How could that happen?

additional_notes: From the verb « se produire » (often used like English “to happen”). Common patterns: « Ça/Cela se produit… » (It happens…), « Quand est-ce que cela se produit ? » (When does it happen?), « Si ça se produit… » (If it happens…). For a planned event, French often uses « avoir lieu » instead of « se produire ».
target_language_example: Si ça se produit encore, préviens-moi tout de suite.
native_language_example: If it happens again, let me know right away.

meaning: to go for a walk; to stroll (to walk around).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb (used with se). Often means walking around in a relaxed way, sometimes just “to walk around” a place rather than walking with a purpose. Conjugates like a regular -er verb: je me promène, tu te promènes, il/elle se promène, nous nous promenons, vous vous promenez, ils/elles se promènent.
target_language_example: Après le dîner, on aime se promener dans le quartier.
native_language_example: After dinner, we like to go for a walk around the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb meaning “to remember/recall.” Common patterns: **se rappeler + noun** (Il a du mal à se rappeler les noms.), **se rappeler de + noun/person** (Je vais me rappeler de toi.), **se rappeler que + clause** (Je me rappelle qu’il est venu.), and **se rappeler ce que/qui/où...** (Je me rappelle ce que tu as dit.). Conjugates like *rappeler* (je me rappelle, tu te rappelles, il/elle se rappelle, nous nous rappelons...). Note: in practice, both **se rappeler + direct object** and **se rappeler de + complement** are used; usage varies by register and region.
target_language_example: Je dois me forcer à se rappeler les noms quand je rencontre quelqu’un.
native_language_example: I have to make myself remember names when I meet someone.

meaning: to go/get to (a place); to surrender.
additional_notes: Often used with a destination: « se rendre à + lieu » (to go to / get to). In the context of conflict or police action, « se rendre » means “to surrender” (to give up, stop resisting): « Il va se rendre » / « Ne vous rendez pas ». In the travel/mobility sense it commonly appears in questions about time or directions: « Combien de temps faut-il pour se rendre à… ? » / « Quel est le chemin pour se rendre à… ? ».
target_language_example: Combien de temps faut-il pour se rendre à Boston ?
native_language_example: How long does it take to get to Boston?
