additional_notes: A time duration or a point in time relative to now. Common patterns: "pendant/durant trois semaines" = for three weeks; "depuis trois semaines" = for the past three weeks (still continuing); "il y a trois semaines" = three weeks ago; "Ça fait trois semaines" = it’s been three weeks.
target_language_example: Je serai en vacances pendant trois semaines.
native_language_example: I’ll be on vacation for three weeks.

additional_notes: Used with the verb « prendre » to mean “to take (something) too seriously.” Very common with the reflexive form « se prendre trop au sérieux » = “to take yourself/oneself too seriously.” It can also refer to taking situations, jokes, rules, etc. too seriously: « prendre tout trop au sérieux ».
target_language_example: Ne te prends pas trop au sérieux !
native_language_example: Don’t take yourself too seriously!

additional_notes: Said when something seems surprisingly good and you suspect there may be a catch or it might not be real. Often used as a stand-alone reaction: « Trop beau pour être vrai. »
target_language_example: Cette offre semble trop beau pour être vrai, je vais vérifier les conditions.
native_language_example: This offer seems too good to be true; I’m going to check the terms.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to say there is more than needed or desirable: "trop de + nom". With uncountable nouns it’s usually "too much" (trop de travail = too much work); with plural countable nouns it’s usually "too many" (trop de pages = too many pages). Often follows a verb like "avoir" or "donner": "On a trop de...", "Il/Elle me donne trop de...".
target_language_example: Il y a trop de bruit ici, je n’arrive pas à travailler.
native_language_example: There’s too much noise here; I can’t manage to work.

meaning: too far; too much (gone too far).
additional_notes: Literally “too far.” Used both for physical distance (“Is it too far to walk?”) and figuratively to mean someone has exceeded acceptable limits (e.g., with words, behavior, or criticism): “Tu es allé trop loin.” Often used with forms of aller (aller trop loin = to go too far).
target_language_example: Désolé, je crois que je suis allé trop loin avec ma blague.
native_language_example: Sorry, I think I went too far with my joke.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens after the right/expected time (often implying it’s missed or no longer possible). Can refer to being late for an event (“arriver trop tard”) or doing something very late at night (“trop tard la nuit”). Often used with "c'est" to reassure: « Ce n'est pas trop tard » = “It’s not too late.”
target_language_example: Dépêche-toi, sinon il sera trop tard !
native_language_example: Hurry up, otherwise it’ll be too late!

additional_notes: Used to say something happens earlier than it should. It often follows the verb ("arriver trop tôt") and can be strengthened with a time amount: "trois heures trop tôt" = "three hours too early". It can also be said on its own as a response or comment: "Trop tôt."
target_language_example: On est partis trop tôt, alors on a attendu dehors.
native_language_example: We left too early, so we waited outside.

meaning: too old to (do something); too old for (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not the right age for an activity or situation. Pattern: « être trop vieux/vieille pour + infinitive » (too old to do) or « être trop vieux/vieille pour + noun/pronoun » (too old for that/for me). Negative/contrast is common: « On n’est jamais trop vieux pour apprendre » (“You’re never too old to learn”). Switch to feminine with a woman: « trop vieille pour ».
target_language_example: Je suis trop vieux pour rester debout toute la journée.
native_language_example: I'm too old to stand all day.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens faster than is appropriate, safe, or desired. Common with verbs like conduire (to drive), parler (to speak), or passer (to pass/go by, for time). It can also be used alone as a short comment or warning: « Trop vite ! ».
target_language_example: Tu marches trop vite pour moi.
native_language_example: You’re walking too fast for me.

additional_notes: Extremely rude/obscene way to insult someone, often used when shouting at them (similar strength to “fucking asshole”). Not appropriate in polite conversation; can easily escalate conflict. Used as a direct form of address (e.g., “Tais-toi, trou du cul !”).
target_language_example: Arrête de faire ça, trou du cul !
native_language_example: Stop doing that, asshole!

additional_notes: Used in science/astronomy to talk about an extremely dense object in space whose gravity is so strong that not even light can escape. In everyday speech it can also mean a 'black hole' in a figurative sense (a missing period of time, lost memory, or something that 'swallows' resources), but the examples here are literal.
target_language_example: Les scientifiques étudient un trou noir situé au centre de notre galaxie.
native_language_example: Scientists are studying a black hole located at the center of our galaxy.

meaning: to find something; to come up with something (a solution/idea).
additional_notes: Used for physically finding an object (e.g., “find something in a bag”) and very often for finding/choosing something suitable (“find you something to do”) or for coming up with an idea or solution (“we’ll find something”). It’s common with an infinitive: “trouver quelque chose à + verb” (to find something to do).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, on va trouver quelque chose.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we’ll figure something out.

additional_notes: A common pattern meaning to find or come up with something, followed by a masculine singular noun: trouver un travail, trouver un moyen. With a reflexive pronoun, as in se trouver un..., it can mean 'find yourself' or 'get yourself' something. The article changes with the noun: un, une, des.
target_language_example: Elle espère trouver un appartement bientôt.
native_language_example: She hopes to find an apartment soon.

additional_notes: Used when talking about solving a problem by identifying an answer or approach. Very common in everyday speech and in formal contexts (work, school). Often followed by “à” for what you’re solving: “trouver une solution à ce problème.”
target_language_example: On va trouver une solution à ce problème ensemble.
native_language_example: We’re going to find a solution to this problem together.

meaning: "do you find…?" / "what do you think…?" (asking for an opinion).
additional_notes: This is the verb "trouver" (to find/think) with subject–verb inversion used in questions: "Tu trouves…" → "Trouves-tu…?" It’s very common for asking how someone feels about something: "Comment trouves-tu Kyoto ?" = "What do you think of Kyoto?" You can also use it with adjectives: "Trouves-tu ce travail trop dur ?" = "Do you find this job too hard?"
target_language_example: Trouves-tu ce film intéressant ?
native_language_example: Do you find this movie interesting?

meaning: "do you find…?" / "what do you think of…?"
additional_notes: This is the verb *trouver* (to find) with **inversion** for questions: *vous trouvez* → *trouvez-vous ?* It’s used both for literally finding something (*Trouvez-vous une place ?* = “Are you finding a seat/spot?”) and very often for giving an opinion: *Comment le/la trouvez-vous ?* = “How do you find him/her/it?” = “What do you think of him/her/it?” (Note the object pronoun can be *le/la/les*.)
target_language_example: Comment trouvez-vous ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: What do you think of this restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to strongly compliment someone or something, or to describe pleasant conditions (especially the weather: « Il fait très beau » = “The weather is really nice”). Agreement: « beau » changes with gender/number (très belle, très beaux, très belles).
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, il fait très beau, alors on va se promener.
native_language_example: Today the weather is really nice, so we're going for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to describe a feminine noun (une ville, une femme) as “very beautiful.” It’s très (very) + belle (beautiful, feminine singular). For a masculine noun/person, use “très beau” (un très beau bâtiment). You can intensify it further with “vraiment”: “vraiment très belle.”
target_language_example: Cette robe est très belle.
native_language_example: This dress is very beautiful.

additional_notes: Most often used to say that someone does, knows, or understands something very well. It can also be said by itself to show agreement, acceptance, or approval, like "all right" or "very good."
target_language_example: Elle parle très bien français.
native_language_example: She speaks French very well.

additional_notes: Used to strongly praise something or someone. It agrees with what it describes: très bon (masc.), très bonne (fem.), très bons / très bonnes (plural). Common with senses: Ça a très bon goût. (tastes really good), Ça sent très bon. (smells really good).
target_language_example: Ce gâteau est très bon, tu veux en goûter ?
native_language_example: This cake is really good—do you want to taste some?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is hard (a task, language, exam, situation). It agrees in gender/number with the noun: très difficile (m./f. singular), très difficiles (plural).
target_language_example: Cet exercice est très difficile, mais je vais essayer.
native_language_example: This exercise is very difficult, but I’m going to try.

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s behavior or attitude. Often said as a complete sentence: « Très gentil. » You can also use it in the polite phrase « C’est/C’était très gentil de votre part » (“That’s/That was very kind of you”). Note agreement: gentil (masc.), gentille (fem.); in plural: gentils / gentilles.
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide, c’est très gentil de votre part.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help, that’s very kind of you.

additional_notes:
Used to express a strong level of happiness. 
- Agreement: heureux (masc. singular), heureuse (fem. singular), heureux (masc. plural), heureuses (fem. plural).
- Common with être: Il/Elle est très heureux/heureuse.
- Can also be used in polite wishes/commands: Soyez très heureux.
target_language_example: Je suis très heureux de te voir.
native_language_example: I’m very happy to see you.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something matters a lot. It can describe a thing (un dossier très important), an idea (c'est très important), or what you’re about to say (quelque chose de très important). Word order: très comes right before the adjective important.
target_language_example: C'est très important de lire les instructions.
native_language_example: It's very important to read the instructions.

additional_notes: Used to strongly express that something is interesting. It agrees in gender and number with the noun: très intéressant (masc. sing.), très intéressante (fem. sing.), très intéressants / très intéressantes (plural). Often used to react to information or describe a topic.
target_language_example: Ton projet a l'air très intéressant !
native_language_example: Your project looks very interesting!

meaning: very pretty; really nice (pleasant to look at or hear).
additional_notes: Used to compliment the appearance (a person, home, outfit, place) or something pleasant like a song/birdsong. Agreement: joli → jolie (feminine), jolis/jolies (plural). You can intensify with repetition: « très très joli ».
target_language_example: Votre robe est très jolie !
native_language_example: Your dress is very pretty!

additional_notes: Used to describe that someone has little free time. It agrees with the person described: très occupé (masc. sing.), très occupée (fem. sing.), très occupés (masc. pl.), très occupées (fem. pl.). Often used politely as a guess about someone’s schedule (e.g., Vous devez être très occupé).
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis très occupé cette semaine.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m very busy this week.

additional_notes: An adverb phrase used to emphasize speed. It often describes how something happens or changes (heals, passes, loses weight, gets worse). You can replace it with "très vite" in many contexts.
target_language_example: On va terminer très rapidement.
native_language_example: We’re going to finish very quickly.

additional_notes: An adverb phrase used to describe how an action is done (how fast). It commonly follows the verb: « marcher/parler/courir très vite ». You can also use it with « aller »: « On va très vite. »
target_language_example: Tu écris très vite !
native_language_example: You write very fast!

additional_notes: "Tu aimes" uses the informal singular "tu" (to one person you know well). It can be a statement ("you like") or a question ("do you like?") depending on intonation or a question mark. Often followed by a noun ("tu aimes la glace") or an infinitive ("tu aimes faire de la randonnée").
target_language_example: Tu aimes ce film ?
native_language_example: Do you like this movie?

additional_notes: Formed from tu + as (from avoir). Used when speaking to one person informally. It can mean possession ('you have') and is also very often used as the auxiliary in the passé composé, as in tu as couru = 'you ran' / 'you have run'.
target_language_example: Tu as un stylo ?
native_language_example: Do you have a pen?

additional_notes: Passé composé of acheter (to buy). Used to talk about a completed purchase in the past. It’s made of tu (you, informal singular) + as (have) + acheté (bought). Often followed by what was bought: « Tu as acheté le billet ? »
target_language_example: Tu as acheté du pain ce matin ?
native_language_example: Did you buy bread this morning?

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "dire" with "tu" (informal singular "you"). Often followed by a quoted word/sentence ("Tu as dit non.") or by "que" + a clause ("Tu as dit que tu pouvais.").
target_language_example: Tu as dit que tu viendrais demain.
native_language_example: You said you would come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report or remind someone of what they previously said, introducing a clause about them. It uses the informal “tu” (you, singular), so it’s for friends, family, kids, etc. In more formal situations, use “vous avez dit que vous…”. Tense in the second part can change: e.g., “tu as dit que tu allais… / que tu avais… / que tu le ferais…”.
target_language_example: Tu as dit que tu viendrais ce soir.
native_language_example: You said you would come tonight.

meaning: "you have already" / "have you already…?" (and often "have you ever…?" in questions).
additional_notes: Made of "tu as" (you have) + "déjà" (already). Very common in spoken questions: "Tu as déjà fini ?" = "Are you done already?" When used with an action in the past (often with a past participle: "tu as déjà + fini/trouvé/visité…"), it can also mean "have you ever…?" depending on context: "Tu as déjà visité Paris ?" = "Have you ever visited Paris?"
target_language_example: Tu as déjà mangé des escargots ?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten snails?

meaning: you must have / you probably had to (past inference or obligation).
additional_notes: Formed with **avoir** in the present + **dû** (past participle of *devoir*) + an infinitive: **tu as dû + infinitif**. It often expresses a logical conclusion about the past (**You must have... / You probably...**) rather than a certain fact. It can also mean past necessity (**you had to...**) depending on context. For feminine/masculine plural objects with *avoir*, *dû* usually stays **dû** (no agreement) because it’s followed by an infinitive.
target_language_example: Avec tout ce travail, tu as dû finir très tard.
native_language_example: With all that work, you must have finished very late.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *entendre* (to hear): **tu as entendu** = “you heard” or, in context, “have you heard?”. Often followed by **ce que + clause** (“what…”) or used alone to confirm someone heard: **Tu as entendu.** = “You heard (it).” Common pattern: **tu as entendu dire (que…)** = “you heard (people) say / you heard about (that…).” Note: *entendre* can sometimes mean “to understand” (e.g., **Tu entends ?**), but **tu as entendu** usually focuses on hearing.
target_language_example: Tu as entendu ce qu’ils ont dit ?
native_language_example: Did you hear what they said?

meaning: 'you had' / 'you got' / 'you have had' (past: you experienced/received).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of avoir (tu as + eu). It’s used to talk about something that happened in the past: having something (tu as eu une voiture), experiencing something (tu as eu un accident / des difficultés), or receiving news (Tu as eu de ses nouvelles ? = Did you hear from them?). Often translated as “you had” or “you got,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu as eu le temps de manger ?
native_language_example: Did you have time to eat?

additional_notes: Addressed to one person (tu). Uses the past tense (passé composé) of faire: tu + as + fait. Often used in questions to ask for the reason or method: Pourquoi tu as fait ça ? (Why did you do that?) / Comment tu as fait ça ? (How did you do that?) / Tu as fait ça pour moi ? (Did you do that for me?).
target_language_example: Je n'arrive pas à croire que tu as fait ça.
native_language_example: I can't believe you did that.

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of **laisser** (“to leave; to let”), used with **tu** (“you” informal singular). It’s often followed by an infinitive: **tu as laissé + verb** = “you let + verb” (e.g., **tu as laissé passer ta chance** = “you let your chance pass / you missed your chance”).
target_language_example: Tu as laissé la porte ouverte.
native_language_example: You left the door open.

additional_notes: "Tu as lu" is the passé composé of "lire" with "tu" (informal singular "you"). It can be a statement ("Tu as lu mon livre." = you read my book) or a question ("Tu as lu les règles ?" = have you read the rules?). It’s also used figuratively in "Tu as lu dans mes pensées" meaning "You read my mind."
target_language_example: Tu as lu ce message ?
native_language_example: Did you read this message?

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of *mettre* with **tu**: *tu as mis* + something. It’s used for putting/placing something (*Tu as mis la clé sur la table*), putting on clothing (*Tu as mis ton manteau ?*), applying something (*Tu as mis de la crème solaire ?*), and sometimes for time: *Tu as mis le temps* = “You took a long time.”
target_language_example: Tu as mis ton pull ?
native_language_example: Did you put on your sweater?

additional_notes: Informal singular ("tu") form of the passé composé of *oublier* (to forget): *tu as oublié* + a thing (*tu as oublié ton manteau*) or + *de* + verb (*tu as oublié de verrouiller la porte*). It can be a neutral statement or a reproach depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Tu as oublié de m’appeler ce matin.
native_language_example: You forgot to call me this morning.

meaning: "did you talk to" / "have you spoken to" (someone).
additional_notes: Used to ask if the person you’re speaking to has talked to someone else. It’s the past tense of "parler à" (to talk to) with "tu" (you, informal singular). The person you spoke to comes after "à": "Tu as parlé à Tania ?". Can also mean "Did you tell (someone)?" depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu as parlé à Marc de la réunion ?
native_language_example: Did you talk to Marc about the meeting?

meaning: “you took” / “did you take?” (past tense of prendre).
additional_notes: Used with many everyday meanings of prendre in the passé composé: taking/grabbing something (Tu as pris tes clés ?), taking photos (Tu as pris ces photos ?), having/eating/drinking something (Tu as pris ton petit déj ?), and in some fixed expressions like prendre son pied (“to have a great time,” informal). Often used in questions like “Tu as pris… ?” = “Did you take/have…?”
target_language_example: Tu as pris mon stylo par erreur ?
native_language_example: Did you take my pen by mistake?

meaning: “you were able to” / “you could” (in the past).
additional_notes: “Tu as pu” is the passé composé of pouvoir (to be able to/can) with tu. It often appears in expressions like “du mieux que tu as pu” or “tout ce que tu as pu,” meaning “as best as you could” / “everything you could.” It’s usually followed by an infinitive (e.g., “Tu as pu venir ?” = “Were you able to come?”).
target_language_example: Tu as pu finir tes devoirs ?
native_language_example: Were you able to finish your homework?

meaning: "you have everything" / "you did everything" (with a past participle).
additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir. By itself, it can mean “you have everything.” Very often it’s followed by a past participle (passé composé), where tout means “everything” as the object: tu as tout trouvé = “you found everything,” tu as tout oublié = “you forgot everything,” etc.
target_language_example: Tu as tout compris.
native_language_example: You understood everything.

additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of *trouver* (“to find”) with **tu** (informal “you” to one person). It’s common in questions: **Tu as trouvé la sortie ?** (“Did you find the exit?”). With **où**, it means “Where did you find it?”: **Tu as trouvé ça où ?**. If addressing someone formally or more than one person, use **vous avez trouvé**.
target_language_example: Tu as trouvé ce que tu cherchais ?
native_language_example: Did you find what you were looking for?

additional_notes: Passé composé of *tuer* (to kill): **tu** (you, informal singular) + **as** (have) + **tué** (killed). Used to state a completed action in the past; in English it’s often translated as simple past ("you killed"). It normally takes a direct object: *Tu as tué mon père.*
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu as tué cet homme ?
native_language_example: Why did you kill that man?

additional_notes: Literally "you have seen" (passé composé of voir), but in everyday English it’s usually "did you see…?" when asking a question about something someone noticed. Uses "tu" (informal "you"), so it’s used with friends, family, kids, etc. You can add an object or clause: "Tu as vu nos dessins ?" (Did you see our drawings?), "Tu as vu à quelle vitesse… ?" (Did you see how fast…?).
target_language_example: Tu as vu le film hier soir ?
native_language_example: Did you see the movie last night?

additional_notes: Past form of "tu es" (you are): "tu" + "as" (have) + past participle "été" (been). Used with adjectives and nouns ("tu as été courageuse", "tu as été mon ami") and in passive constructions ("tu as été embauchée" = you were hired). Agreement can appear in the feminine/passive (e.g., "courageuse", "embauchée").
target_language_example: Tu as été très patient avec moi.
native_language_example: You were very patient with me.

additional_notes: Singular informal/familiar form of avoir with tu. It can be a statement ("you have") or, with intonation, a yes/no question ("do you have?"). It also appears in common expressions like tu as mal ? = "are you in pain?".
target_language_example: Tu as une minute ?
native_language_example: Do you have a minute?

meaning: 'do you have any…?' / 'have you got any…?' (informal 'you' singular).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has some things (plural) in a casual conversation. It’s the question form of "tu as" (= "you have") + "des" (= "some" for plural nouns). With uncountable nouns, French often uses "du / de la" instead of "des" (e.g., "Tu as du temps ?").
target_language_example: Tu as des questions ?
native_language_example: Do you have any questions?

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say someone has some amount of something. **Du** is the partitive article (**de + le**), often meaning “some” (often not translated in English). Common with abstract nouns (Tu as du potentiel ! = “You have potential!”) and with set expressions like **avoir du retard** (“to be late / to be behind schedule”). It can also describe something on you: Tu as du rouge-à-lèvres sur la joue. (“You have lipstick on your cheek.”).
target_language_example: Tu as du café sur ton t-shirt.
native_language_example: You’ve got coffee on your T-shirt.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *avoir* to say someone still has something (time, a chance, a need) or still feels something: *Tu as encore sommeil ?* = “Are you still sleepy?” It can also introduce encouragement: *Tu as encore toute la vie devant toi !* = “You still have your whole life ahead of you!” Note: *encore* can also mean “again” in other contexts, but with *tu as...* it often means “still.”
target_language_example: Tu as encore besoin de moi ?
native_language_example: Do you still need me?

meaning: you feel like (doing); you want to (do).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a desire or urge, often in the moment (what you feel like doing). It can be a question (Tu as envie de… ? = Do you feel like…?) or a statement. Followed by an infinitive: tu as envie de + verb (tu as envie de sortir). With a noun, use "tu as envie de + noun" (tu as envie de pizza) or "tu as envie de quoi ?" (what do you feel like?).
target_language_example: Tu as envie de sortir ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you feel like going out tonight?

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **avoir l’air** (“to seem/appear”). It’s most often followed by an adjective: **Tu as l’air fatigué(e)** (“You look tired”). You can also use **avoir l’air de + infinitive**: **Tu as l’air de comprendre** (“You seem to understand”). Agreement: add **-e** if talking to a woman (**Tu as l’air fatiguée**).
target_language_example: tu as l'air différent.
native_language_example: You look different.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "avoir" (to have) + "peur" (fear): "avoir peur" = to be afraid. Common patterns: "Tu as peur de + noun" (Tu as peur des chiens.) and "Tu as peur que + clause" (Tu as peur qu’il pleuve ?). Often said as a question: "Tu as peur ?"
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu as peur de rentrer seul ?
native_language_example: Why are you scared to go home alone?

additional_notes: Used to agree with someone or confirm that what they said is correct. Literally “you have reason.” You can also use it at the start of a sentence (“Tu as raison, …”) or on its own as a short reply.
target_language_example: Tu as raison, on devrait partir maintenant.
native_language_example: You’re right, we should leave now.

additional_notes: Used with tu, the informal singular 'you'. It introduces a masculine singular noun: tu as un + noun. With a feminine noun, use tu as une. In very informal speech and writing, it is often shortened to t'as un.
target_language_example: Tu as un message pour moi ?
native_language_example: Do you have a message for me?

meaning: "you have a" (talking to one person; before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avoir" (to have) in the present tense: "tu as" = "you have" (informal singular "you"). "Une" is the feminine form of "a/an" and goes before a feminine noun (e.g., "une mère", "une idée"). For a masculine noun, use "tu as un".
target_language_example: Tu as une idée ?
native_language_example: Do you have an idea?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone was supposed to do something in the past (often expressing regret, criticism, or that it was the better choice). It’s the past conditional of devoir (“to have to / must”). It’s followed by an infinitive: tu aurais dû + infinitive (e.g., tu aurais dû partir).
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû me prévenir plus tôt.
native_language_example: You should have warned me earlier.

meaning: 'you could have' (you had the opportunity/ability, but didn’t).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional perfect: "tu" + "aurais" (avoir, conditional) + past participle (here "pu", from "pouvoir"). Often expresses regret, reproach, or a missed possibility: "Tu aurais pu m'appeler" = you could have called me (but you didn’t).
target_language_example: Tu aurais pu me prévenir plus tôt.
native_language_example: You could have warned me earlier.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone will have in the future, often after a condition or in instructions (e.g., “when/if you… you will have…”). It can also express necessity: “tu auras besoin de…” = “you will need…”. In the fixed pattern “tu auras beau + infinitive”, it means “you may try as much as you want / even if you…”, with the idea that it won’t change the outcome.
target_language_example: Si tu travailles bien, tu auras plus de temps libre.
native_language_example: If you work well, you’ll have more free time.

meaning: 'you had' / 'you used to have' (imparfait of avoir).
additional_notes: Used to describe a past state, habit, or ongoing situation (imparfait). Common patterns: *tu avais + noun* (you had), *tu avais + adjective* (you were/ felt: e.g., *tu avais chaud* = you were hot), and in conditional sentences with *si* to express an unreal/imagined situation (*si tu avais...*).
target_language_example: Quand tu avais dix ans, tu avais déjà une grande collection de livres.
native_language_example: When you were ten, you already had a big collection of books.

additional_notes: Literally 'you had reason.' Used to tell someone that their earlier opinion or prediction was correct. It's in the imperfect tense (avais), often referring to something you thought or said before; in the present you'd say 'tu as raison' ('you are right').
target_language_example: Tu avais raison : il pleut aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: You were right: it's raining today.

additional_notes: From the verb *chercher* (“to look for / to search for”) with *tu* (“you”, informal singular). It can be a simple statement (*Tu cherches un appartement.*) or a question (*Tu cherches qui ?*). In some contexts it can be confrontational and mean “are you looking for trouble?” (e.g., *Tu cherches des histoires ?* / *Tu cherches la merde ?*).
target_language_example: Tu cherches quelque chose en particulier ?
native_language_example: Are you looking for anything in particular?

additional_notes: Literally “you understand.” Used with *tu* (informal “you”), often as a question to check understanding: *Tu comprends ?* It can also work like a tag question to seek confirmation, similar to “you understand, right?” or “you know?” (*Tu comprends, n’est-ce pas ?*). Intonation (rising) often signals it’s a question.
target_language_example: Tu comprends ce que je veux dire ?
native_language_example: Do you understand what I mean?

additional_notes: Uses connaître (not savoir): it’s about knowing a person/place/thing, being familiar with something, or recognizing a name. Often used in questions: «Tu connais Tom ?» = “Do you know Tom?” / «Tu connais ce nom ?» = “Do you recognize this name?” Because it uses «tu», it’s informal (to one person you address casually).
target_language_example: Tu connais ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: Do you know this restaurant?

additional_notes: Literally “you believe that.” Used to ask someone what they think, often before another clause: « Tu crois que ça va marcher ? » = “Do you think it’ll work?” Very often it’s rhetorical and challenging/skeptical, like “You really think…?” or “You think I didn’t notice?” In more formal situations you’d use « vous croyez que… » or « tu penses que… ».
target_language_example: Tu crois que je vais te croire, moi ?
native_language_example: You think I’m going to believe you?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or to challenge what they think (often with a skeptical or rhetorical tone). Uses the informal “tu” form; in formal situations use “Vous croyez que c’est… ?”. Commonly followed by an adjective, noun, or pronoun: “...facile ?”, “...grave ?”, “...elle ?”.
target_language_example: Tu crois que c'est aussi simple ?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s that simple?

meaning: “Do you think I…?” / “You think I…?” (often rhetorical).
additional_notes: Used to challenge or question what someone assumes about you. Very common in spoken French, often with a skeptical or annoyed tone (rhetorical questions like “You think I didn’t know?”). Literally “you believe that I…”, but in English it’s usually “you think I…”.
target_language_example: Tu crois que je vais te laisser faire ça ?
native_language_example: You think I’m going to let you do that?

meaning: “Do you think I’m going to…?” (often: “No way I’m going to…”).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you supposedly would do, often as a rhetorical question to show disbelief, refusal, or indignation. Common in spoken French; the tone depends on context and can sound confrontational. You can follow it with an infinitive (e.g., te le dire, y aller) or another verb phrase.
target_language_example: Tu crois que je vais accepter ça ?
native_language_example: Do you think I’m going to accept that?

additional_notes: Used to give advice, recommendations, or a gentle warning. It is the conditional form of devoir with tu, so it often sounds softer and less direct than a command.
target_language_example: Tu devrais te reposer un peu.
native_language_example: You should rest a little.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **devoir** in the conditional (**devrais**) to give gentle advice (“you ought to…”). It’s followed by an infinitive: **aller** + place (**chez le médecin**, **à la maison**) or **aller** + verb (**aller te reposer** = “go rest”).
target_language_example: Tu devrais aller parler au professeur.
native_language_example: You should go talk to the teacher.

meaning: "you should do" (giving advice or a suggestion).
additional_notes: Used to recommend an action to someone. It’s the conditional of devoir ("to have to"), so it sounds softer/politer than "tu dois faire" ("you must do"). Usually followed by an infinitive or by a noun phrase (e.g., "faire attention").
target_language_example: Tu devrais faire une pause et boire un verre d’eau.
native_language_example: You should take a break and drink a glass of water.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or make a suggestion in a softer, less direct way. Literally it’s “you should, maybe”: **tu devrais** (you should, from *devoir*) + **peut-être** (maybe). In speech, it can also trail off: *Tu devrais peut-être…* (“Maybe you should…”) when you don’t want to say the rest directly.
target_language_example: Tu devrais peut-être lui en parler.
native_language_example: Maybe you should talk to him about it.

meaning: “you should (… yourself)” / “you ought to …” (giving advice), used before a reflexive verb.
additional_notes: Used to suggest or advise something to one person you address as tu. Grammatically it’s the verb devoir (“to have to”) in the conditional (devrais), which softens it into advice (“should”) rather than a strong obligation (“must”). The te is the reflexive pronoun that goes with a reflexive infinitive that follows (e.g., te lever, te présenter, te débarrasser de…).
target_language_example: Tu devrais te reposer un peu.
native_language_example: You should rest a bit.

meaning: you should come (it would be a good idea for you to come).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of devoir (tu devrais) to give advice or make a suggestion. It can sound like a friendly invitation or a gentle recommendation. You can add details like time/place: « tu devrais venir ce soir », « tu devrais venir nous voir », « tu devrais venir plus souvent ».
target_language_example: Si tu es libre demain, tu devrais venir avec nous.
native_language_example: If you're free tomorrow, you should come with us.

meaning: “you should be / you ought to be”.
additional_notes: Used to give advice, express an expectation, or say what seems appropriate. It can be followed by an adjective (fier/fière, heureux, prudent), a noun (musulman), a past participle for a passive idea (récompensé = rewarded), or a place expression (à l’hôpital).
target_language_example: Tu devrais être plus patient avec eux.
native_language_example: You should be more patient with them.

additional_notes: "Tu dis" is the informal (tu) way to say "you say/you’re saying" (2nd person singular) with the verb "dire" (to say/tell). It’s often used in questions to react to what someone just said: "Qu’est-ce que tu dis ?" = "What are you saying?" You can add an object after it: "tu dis ça" (you say that), "tu dis la vérité" (you tell the truth).
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que tu dis ? Je n’ai jamais dit ça !
native_language_example: What are you saying? I never said that!

additional_notes: Present-tense form of devoir with tu. It usually expresses obligation and is followed by an infinitive: tu dois partir = 'you have to leave.' In some contexts, it can also express a strong assumption, as in Tu dois avoir raison = 'you must be right.'
target_language_example: Tu dois finir tes devoirs avant le dîner.
native_language_example: You have to finish your homework before dinner.

meaning: "you must have" / "you have to have" (sometimes "you must be" in context).
additional_notes: Formed from devoir (tu dois = you must/you have to) + avoir (to have). It can express (1) obligation/requirement: « Tu dois avoir le permis. » = you need a license, or (2) a logical guess/deduction: « Tu dois avoir très mal. » = you must be in a lot of pain. What follows is often a noun phrase (un plan, beaucoup de questions, le permis), but in context it can imply a state (pain, hunger, etc.).
target_language_example: Tu dois avoir faim après le voyage.
native_language_example: You must be hungry after the trip.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **devoir** (tu dois) + an infinitive to express obligation or necessity. Here it’s followed by **faire** (“to do/make”), often with an object after it (e.g., *faire ton travail*, *faire davantage de sport*). For a softer suggestion, you might also hear *tu devrais…* (“you should…”).
target_language_example: Tu dois faire tes devoirs avant de sortir.
native_language_example: You have to do your homework before going out.

meaning: you have to do it / you must do it.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone they are obligated/required to do something. It can sound firm or like an order depending on tone. "Tu" is informal singular "you"; with someone you address as "vous," say "vous devez le faire." "Le" = "it" (a specific thing already understood). Often followed by conditions like "que ça te plaise ou non" (whether you like it or not) or adverbs like "aussi tôt que possible" (as soon as possible).
target_language_example: Tu dois le faire aujourd'hui, sinon ce sera trop tard.
native_language_example: You have to do it today, otherwise it’ll be too late.

meaning: "you have to / you must" + "yourself" (used before a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone what they need to do when the verb is reflexive (a verb that takes "se"). "dois" is the "tu" form of "devoir" (must/have to). "te" is the reflexive pronoun for "tu" and changes with the subject (je me, tu te, il/elle se, nous nous, vous vous, ils/elles se). Common with daily-routine verbs: te lever (get up), te réveiller (wake up), te préparer (get ready), te contrôler (control yourself), te cacher (hide).
target_language_example: Tu dois te dépêcher, on est en retard.
native_language_example: You have to hurry, we’re late.

additional_notes: "Tu dois" is the present tense of "devoir" (must/have to) + the infinitive "être" (to be). It can express a real obligation ("you have to be...") or a guess/deduction (often in a sympathetic way: "you must be tired"). The adjective that follows usually agrees with "tu" (e.g., with a woman: "tu dois être fatiguée").
target_language_example: Après une si longue journée, tu dois être épuisé.
native_language_example: After such a long day, you must be exhausted.

additional_notes:
"En" replaces something introduced with "de" or a quantity (de ça, de ce livre, des pommes, etc.). So "tu en as" is used when you don’t repeat the noun: 
- quantity: « Tu en as combien ? » = “How many do you have (of them)?”
- amount/time: « Tu en as mis du temps ! » = “That took you a long time!”
- opinion about it: « Qu’est-ce que tu en as pensé ? » = “What did you think of it?”
- enough/too much: « Tu en as assez fait. » = “You’ve done enough.” / « Tu en as tué beaucoup trop ! » = “You killed way too many (of them)!”
Form: tu (you) + en (of it/them) + as (have). In the past tense, you’ll often see « tu en as + past participle ».
target_language_example: Tu en as encore ?
native_language_example: Do you still have some?

additional_notes: "En" replaces something introduced with "de" or an amount/quantity, so "tu en as" often means "you have some (of it/them)" (e.g., "Tu en as un autre" = you have another one). It’s also the base of common expressions: "tu en as de la chance" (you’re lucky), "tu en as l’air" (you look like it), "tu en as marre" (are you fed up?), "tu en as peur" (are you afraid of it?). In questions, you’ll often see it with words like "encore" (still/more), "déjà" (already), "assez" (enough), or "pour longtemps" (for long).
target_language_example: Tu en as encore ?
native_language_example: Do you still have some (left)?

meaning: "you are" (with *en* = "of it / about it / at it").
additional_notes: *Tu en es* is the verb **être** (*tu es*) with the pronoun **en**, which refers back to something already mentioned or understood. Common patterns: **Tu en es sûr / certain ?** = “Are you sure (about it)?”; **Tu en es capable** = “You’re capable of it.”; **Tu en es où ?** = “Where are you at?/How far along are you?” (about a task, project, etc.).
target_language_example: Tu en es fier ?
native_language_example: Are you proud of it?

additional_notes: Present-tense form of être used with tu, the singular informal/familiar 'you'. It usually means 'you are', but before a past participle with certain verbs it also helps form the passé composé, where English often uses 'you have' or a simple past: tu es rentré = 'you came back / you have returned'.
target_language_example: Tu es très gentil.
native_language_example: You are very kind.

meaning: “you are beautiful” (to a woman or girl).
additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s appearance (or sometimes overall charm). Because "belle" agrees with a feminine person, you say "Tu es beau" to a man/boy. Often appears with emphasis like "Que tu es belle !" or "Ce que tu es belle !" meaning “How beautiful you are!” In "Tu es belle en noir", it means “You look beautiful in black.”
target_language_example: Tu es belle aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: You are beautiful today.

meaning: "you are (well/comfortable)" or "you are really/quite" (to emphasize what comes next).
additional_notes: “Bien” after “être” can describe a state (being well/comfortable): « Tu es bien installé ? » = “Are you settled in comfortably?” It can also act as an intensifier meaning “indeed / really / quite,” often before an adjective or noun phrase: « Tu es bien le seul. » = “You really are the only one.” « Tu es bien loin… » = “You’re really far…”.
target_language_example: Tu es bien mieux comme ça.
native_language_example: You’re much better like this.

meaning: "you are still" / sometimes "you are ... again" (and in comparisons: "you are even ...").
additional_notes: Used with *être* to say someone remains in a state: *Tu es encore en retard* = “You’re still late.” With a comparison (*encore plus + adjective*), it means “even more”: *Tu es encore plus belle…* = “You’re even more beautiful…”. Depending on context, *encore* can also mean “again” (e.g., *Tu es encore parti* can mean “You left again”).
target_language_example: Tu es encore fatigué ?
native_language_example: Are you still tired?

additional_notes: Literally “you are here,” used to state someone’s presence in a place. Common in explanations (C’est pour ça que tu es ici / parce que…), in questions about duration (Depuis combien de temps tu es ici ? / Ça fait combien de temps que tu es ici ?), and for emphasis or contrast (Tu es ici et tu y resteras). Note: it’s informal because it uses tu (vs. vous êtes ici for formal/plural).
target_language_example: C'est pour ça que tu es ici.
native_language_example: That’s why you’re here.

meaning: "you are the only one" (speaking to a woman/girl).
additional_notes:
"La seule" is feminine singular (the person you’re talking to is female). For a male, say "tu es le seul". Often followed by:
- "qui" + verb (sometimes in the subjunctive): "Tu es la seule qui puisse…"
- "à" + infinitive: "Tu es la seule à pouvoir…"
target_language_example: Tu es la seule en qui j’ai confiance.
native_language_example: You’re the only one I trust.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is present/has arrived: «Dieu merci, tu es là.» It can also be a check-in question meaning “Are you there?” (in person or on the phone): «Chérie, tu es là ?» With time words it means “you’ve been here/there (since…)”: «Ça fait combien de temps que tu es là ?» Note: «là» can mean “here” or “there” depending on context; English usually uses “here” when speaking to the person.
target_language_example: Enfin, tu es là ! Je t’attendais.
native_language_example: Finally, you’re here! I was waiting for you.

meaning: "you are so..." (very), used before an adjective.
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to intensify it: « Tu es si gentil(le) ! » = “You’re so kind!” Here « si » means “so/that” (degree), not “if” (« si » = “if” in other contexts). Adjective agreement: gentil/gentille, prétentieux/prétentieuse, etc.
target_language_example: Tu es si drôle !
native_language_example: You’re so funny!

meaning: “Are you sure it’s…?” / “You’re sure that it is…?”
additional_notes: Used to confirm or question someone’s certainty about an identification, location, direction, or fact. Typically followed by a person/thing (tu es sûr que c'est elle ?), a place (…ici ?), a direction (…par là ?), or an adjective/noun phrase (…sans danger ?, …la bonne adresse ?). In casual speech it’s often shortened to « T’es sûr que c’est… ? ».
target_language_example: Tu es sûr que c'est la bonne adresse ?
native_language_example: Are you sure it’s the right address?

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or phrase to describe a repeated habit/state (Tu es toujours pressée = You’re always in a hurry) or something that remains true (Tu es toujours Toruk Makto = You’re still Toruk Makto). Can also mean “you’re always there (for me)” in supportive contexts (Tu es toujours là pour moi).
target_language_example: Tu es toujours en retard !
native_language_example: You’re always late!

additional_notes: Used before an adjective: « tu es trop + adjectif ». In standard French, « trop » usually means “too (much)” (often negative: too aggressive, too annoying). In everyday speech, « trop » is also commonly used to mean “so/really” (often positive: « Tu es trop mignon(ne) ! » = “You’re so cute!”). Very often pronounced/written as « t’es trop ».
target_language_example: Tu es trop mignon !
native_language_example: You’re so cute!

meaning: “you are very …” (used to intensify an adjective).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to describe someone strongly: « Tu es très + adjective ». Because it uses « tu », it’s in the familiar/informal address (friends, family, kids). For a formal/polite version, use « vous êtes très ».
target_language_example: Tu es très gentil.
native_language_example: You’re very kind.

additional_notes: A very common pattern: tu + es + un, used to say what someone is, followed by a singular masculine noun. For a feminine noun, use tu es une instead.
target_language_example: Tu es un bon ami.
native_language_example: You are a good friend.

additional_notes: Used to state that someone is (or has become) an adult male. Depending on context, it can also be said in a moral/behavioral sense, meaning the person should act like a grown-up (often contrasted with "agir comme un enfant"). Note: "homme" means "man" (not "home").
target_language_example: Tu es un homme, alors assume tes responsabilités.
native_language_example: You're a man, so take responsibility.

meaning: 'you are a' (addressing one person; before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe someone with a feminine noun: *Tu es une infirmière / une adulte / une espionne.* The noun (and any adjective) typically takes the feminine form. Negative often uses *pas une*: *Tu es une espionne, pas un soldat.* (For masculine nouns: *tu es un*.)
target_language_example: Tu es une bonne amie.
native_language_example: You are a good friend.

additional_notes: Passé composé of **venir** with **être** (so it agrees with the subject: *tu es venu* (m.), *tu es venue* (f.)). Often followed by **+ infinitive** to say what someone came to do: *Tu es venu me dire ça ?* (“Did you come to tell me that?”). You can add a destination (*jusqu’ici*) or a reason with **pour**: *Tu es venu pour la même raison que moi.*
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu es venu si tard ?
native_language_example: Why did you come so late?

additional_notes: Passé composé of venir with être. Used when speaking to one female person (venue agrees with the speaker you’re addressing: venu = male, venue = female). Often followed by an infinitive (tu es venue me voir ? = “did you come to see me?”) or a place/goal (tu es venue à mon secours = “you came to my rescue”).
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu es venue si tard ?
native_language_example: Why did you come so late?

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize an adjective or judgment about someone. Often followed by an adjective (e.g., belle, bon). Tone depends on the adjective and context: it can be a sincere compliment (Tu es vraiment belle.) or an insult/criticism (Tu es vraiment bouchée !).
target_language_example: Tu es vraiment gentil de m'aider.
native_language_example: You’re really kind to help me.

additional_notes: Present-tense form of faire with tu, the informal singular "you." Depending on context, it can also mean "you're doing" or "you're making." Faire is very common in many expressions, so the natural English translation often depends on the words that follow, as in faire confiance (trust), faire partie de (be part of), or faire une erreur (make a mistake).
target_language_example: Tu fais du bon travail.
native_language_example: You're doing good work.

meaning: “What are you doing?” / “What are you up to?”
additional_notes: Very common casual spoken question. It can refer to what someone is doing right now (Tu fais quoi ?), what they’re doing at a specific time (Tu fais quoi ce soir ?), or more generally what they do with their time (Tu fais quoi de tes journées ?). Depending on context it can also mean “What are you doing here/in this?” (Tu fais quoi là-dedans ?).
target_language_example: Salut ! Tu fais quoi ce week-end ?
native_language_example: Hi! What are you doing this weekend?

additional_notes: Common in spoken French to refer back to an action just mentioned or understood from context. Can be a statement (Tu fais ça très bien.), a question (Tu fais ça depuis quand ? / Tu fais ça ?), or part of a warning/condition (Si tu fais ça...). Often corresponds to English "you do that" or "you do it" depending on context.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas comment tu fais ça !
native_language_example: I don’t know how you do that!

meaning: you’d better (do something) / you should really (do something).
additional_notes: Used to give strong advice or a warning about what the other person ought to do. It’s the conditional form of "faire mieux" (“to do better”), followed by "de" + infinitive: "Tu ferais mieux de partir." You can make it negative with "Tu ferais mieux de ne pas + infinitive" (You’d better not…).
target_language_example: Tu ferais mieux de ne pas conduire si tu es fatigué.
native_language_example: You’d better not drive if you’re tired.

meaning: “you play” (games, sports, or a musical instrument).
additional_notes: "Tu" is informal singular “you.” "Jouer" can be used without "de" for playing games/sports (Tu joues au foot ?), and with "de" for playing an instrument (Tu joues de la guitare ? / du piano ?). "Tu joues quoi ?" means “What do you play?” (often about an instrument, depending on context).
target_language_example: Tu joues au tennis ce week-end ?
native_language_example: Are you playing tennis this weekend?

additional_notes: "Tu" = "you" (informal singular). "l'" is a shortened form of "le" or "la" before a vowel and means "him/it" or "her/it" as a direct object: "tu l'aimes" = "you love/like him/her/it." In questions it can be used with intonation ("Tu l'aimes ?") or with tag questions like "hein ?" and "n'est-ce pas ?" ("right? / isn’t it?").
target_language_example: Je pense que tu l'aimes encore.
native_language_example: I think you still love him/her.

additional_notes: Literally "you have it/him/her." l' is the direct object pronoun le or la, shortened before a vowel. Very often, tu l'as is followed by a past participle in the passé composé: Tu l'as mangé ? = "Did you eat it?" Because it uses tu, it is for informal singular "you."
target_language_example: Tu l'as déjà fini ?
native_language_example: Have you finished it already?

meaning: 'You said it!' (strong agreement: 'exactly/you can say that again').
additional_notes: Literally means “you said it.” Common as a short, emphatic reply showing strong agreement with what someone just said. Often reinforced as “Ça, tu l'as dit.” It can also be used literally in context (e.g., “Tu l'as dit toi-même” = “You said it yourself”).
target_language_example: — Il fait super chaud aujourd'hui. — Ouais, tu l'as dit.
native_language_example: — It’s really hot today. — Yeah, you said it.

meaning: "you did it" / "you've done it" (referring to something already mentioned).
additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of faire: tu + l’ (direct object pronoun = “it/that”) + as + fait. l’ stands for a specific thing/action understood from context (e.g., a mistake, a task, a favor). Often appears with emphasis: « Bien sûr que tu l’as fait ! » (“Of course you did!”) or with « exprès »: « Tu l’as fait exprès » (“You did it on purpose”).
target_language_example: Je savais que tu l'as fait, mais je ne comprends pas pourquoi.
native_language_example: I knew you did it, but I don’t understand why.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *voir* (to see): **tu as vu** = “you saw / you have seen.” The **l’** is a direct object pronoun meaning “him,” “her,” or “it,” depending on context. Common in questions like **Tu l’as vu où ?** (“Where did you see him/it?”).
target_language_example: Tu l'as vu hier soir ?
native_language_example: Did you see him/it last night?

additional_notes: "Le" is a direct object pronoun meaning "him" (a man/boy) or "it" (a masculine noun or an idea already mentioned). This phrase is often used in questions with rising intonation (e.g., "Tu le connais ?" = "You know him?") and can be expanded: "tu le connais bien" (you know him well), "tu le connais de réputation" (you know of him by reputation).
target_language_example: Tu le connais depuis longtemps ?
native_language_example: Have you known him for a long time?

additional_notes: "Tu" = you (informal singular). "Le" is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” (a masculine thing or an unspecified action/idea). Used to talk about doing something already known from context: Tu le fais pour toi. (You do it for yourself.) You can add adverbs like "bien" (well) or time expressions like "à chaque fois" (every time).
target_language_example: Je sais que c’est difficile, mais tu le fais très bien.
native_language_example: I know it’s hard, but you’re doing it really well.

additional_notes: Means “you know it/that” (the pronoun "le" refers to something already understood from context). Often used as a quick reminder or emphasis in the middle or at the end of a sentence: "Je ne peux pas, tu le sais" (“I can’t, you know that”). Can also introduce a shared fact, like “as you know”: "Comme tu le sais..." You’ll also hear it with a tag question: "Tu le sais, pas vrai ?" (“You know, right?”).
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, tu le sais.
native_language_example: I’m tired, you know that.

meaning: "you have them" / "you got them" (used with a past participle, e.g. "tu les as trouvés").
additional_notes: Common in the passé composé: **tu** (informal “you”) + **les** (“them”, direct object pronoun) + **as** (present of *avoir*). It usually comes right before the past participle: *Tu les as trouvés ?* (“Did you find them?”). When **les** is placed before *avoir*, the past participle often agrees with **les**: *trouvés* (masc. plural) / *trouvées* (fem. plural), *eus/eues*.
target_language_example: Tu les as achetées où ?
native_language_example: Where did you buy them?

meaning: you told them / you said to them.
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of dire: tu as dit = “you said/told.” Leur is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to them” (to him/them depending on context). Often used in questions to ask what information you gave someone: « Tu leur as dit que… ? » = “Did you tell them that…?”
target_language_example: Tu leur as dit la vérité ?
native_language_example: Did you tell them the truth?

additional_notes: Passé composé of *dire* used with the indirect object pronoun *lui* (= to him/to her). Often followed by *que* + a sentence: *Tu lui as dit que…* (You told him/her that…). You use *tu* when speaking informally to one person.
target_language_example: Tu lui as dit la vérité ?
native_language_example: Did you tell him/her the truth?

additional_notes: From aimer (to love / to like). "Tu m'aimes" can mean romantic love or simply liking someone, depending on context. Adding words can clarify: "Tu m'aimes bien ?" usually means "Do you like me?" (friendlier/less intense), while "Tu m'aimes encore ?" means "Do you still love me?". Often used as a direct question: "Tu m'aimes ?" ("Do you love me?") or with "hein ?" to seek confirmation.
target_language_example: Tu m'aimes ou tu m'aimes bien ?
native_language_example: Do you love me, or do you just like me?

meaning: you have (to me) / you did (to me)
additional_notes: Made of **tu** (informal “you”), **m’** (short for **me**, “me/to me”), and **as** (“have,” 2nd-person singular of **avoir**). It’s commonly used to form the **passé composé** before a past participle: **tu m’as appelé** = “you called me.” It can also appear in questions: **Tu m’as compris ?** = “Did you understand me?” Use **vous m’avez** instead when speaking formally or to more than one person.
target_language_example: Tu m'as appelé ?
native_language_example: Did you call me?

additional_notes:
Past tense (passé composé) of "dire" addressed to "tu". "m'" = "me" (to me). Often followed by:
- "de" + infinitive: "Tu m'as dit de partir." (You told me to leave.)
- "que" + clause: "Tu m'as dit que..." (You told me that...)
target_language_example: Tu m'as dit que tu étais fatigué.
native_language_example: You told me that you were tired.

additional_notes: Past tense of "faire" (passé composé): "tu" + "m'" (to me) + "as fait". Often used in the causative pattern "tu m'as fait + infinitive" (= you made/forced/caused me to do something): "Tu m'as fait venir" (You made me come). Without an infinitive, it can mean "What did you do to me?" depending on context: "Qu'est-ce que tu m'as fait ?"
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu m'as fait attendre si longtemps ?
native_language_example: Why did you make me wait so long?

meaning: "Are you listening to me?" / "Listen to me."
additional_notes: Literally “you (are) listening to me.” Used to check someone’s attention or to insist they pay attention. Often said with emphasis or impatience; can be followed by words like « au moins », « attentivement », « quand je te parle », or tag questions like « oui ? » / « ou quoi ? ». In more polite situations, you might use « Vous m'écoutez ? » or « Écoutez-moi, s'il vous plaît. »
target_language_example: Tu m'écoutes, s'il te plaît ? J'ai quelque chose d'important à te dire.
native_language_example: Are you listening to me, please? I have something important to tell you.

additional_notes: Present tense of *manger* with *tu* (used with friends, family, kids). Depending on context, it can mean a general habit ("you eat") or what’s happening now ("you’re eating"). Often used in questions: *Tu manges quoi ?* (What are you eating?) / *Quand tu manges ?* (When do you eat?). With *bien*, it can mean “well” or “enough/okay” (e.g., asking if someone is eating properly).
target_language_example: Tu manges déjà ?
native_language_example: Are you already eating?

additional_notes: A very common combination of pronouns: tu is informal singular "you," and me means "me" or "to me." It is used when talking to one person you know well, and in French me usually comes before the verb.
target_language_example: Tu me fais rire.
native_language_example: You make me laugh.

additional_notes: From the verb **demander** (“to ask”, “to request”). Often followed by **de + infinitive** to say what someone is asking you to do: *Tu me demandes de partir ?* (“Are you asking me to leave?”). It can also mean “to propose” in fixed phrases like **demander en mariage** (“to ask [someone] to marry you”). **False friend:** *demander* usually means “ask/request,” not “demand.”
target_language_example: Tu me demandes de t’aider maintenant ?
native_language_example: Are you asking me to help you now?

additional_notes: From **dire** (“to say/tell”). **Tu** = “you” (informal singular), **me** = “to me,” **dis** = “tell/say.” Often followed by **que...** (“you tell me that...”), a question (**Qu’est-ce que tu me dis ?** = “What are you telling me?” / “What did you just say?”), or an instruction with **de + infinitive** (**Tu me dis de faire...** = “You tell me to do...” / “You say I should do...”).
target_language_example: Tu me dis la vérité, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Tell me the truth, please.

meaning: "you give me" / "you’re giving me" (often: "you make me feel…").
additional_notes: Literally means “you give to me.” It’s used for giving something (Tu me donnes ton numéro ?), for exchanging (Tu me donnes quoi en échange ?), for estimating/guessing (Quel âge tu me donnes ? = “How old do you think I am?”), and in common patterns where it means “you make me feel” + noun/infinitive (Tu me donnes envie de… / Tu me donnes la chair de poule).
target_language_example: Tu me donnes un coup de main ?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand?

additional_notes: Used with "faire" to mean someone causes you to do/feel/appear something. Very common pattern: "tu me fais + infinitive" (e.g., "tu me fais rire" = you make me laugh). In the example, it’s part of the expression "faire passer quelqu’un pour + noun" = "to make someone look like / to make someone out to be".
target_language_example: Tu me fais attendre depuis une heure.
native_language_example: You’ve been making me wait for an hour.

additional_notes: From the verb "laisser" (to let/allow/leave). Often followed by an infinitive: "Tu me laisses partir ?" = "Do you let me leave?" It can be a request for permission or asking someone to stop blocking you. In the negative: "Tu ne me laisses pas..." = "You won’t let me..."
target_language_example: Tu me laisses passer, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Will you let me through, please?

additional_notes: Literally “you are missing from me.” In French, the person who is missed is the subject: “Tu me manques” (I miss you), “Je te manque” (you miss me). You can add emphasis with words like “vraiment” (really) or “beaucoup” (a lot).
target_language_example: Tu me manques beaucoup depuis ton départ.
native_language_example: I miss you a lot since you left.

meaning: "you’re talking to me" / "you speak to me".
additional_notes: Present tense of "parler" with an indirect object pronoun: "tu" (you) + "me" (to me) + "parles" (speak/talk). Often used in confrontations about tone or respect: "Pourquoi tu me parles comme ça ?" (Why are you talking to me like that?). It can also introduce a topic with "de": "Je veux que tu me parles de…" (I want you to tell me about…). In everyday speech, negation is often shortened: "tu me parles pas" (= "tu ne me parles pas").
target_language_example: Tu me parles de ton travail ce soir ?
native_language_example: Will you tell me about your job tonight?

additional_notes: Literally “you look at me.” Used to point out that someone is staring/looking at you, or that you feel observed or judged. Often appears in questions like “Pourquoi tu me regardes comme ça ?” (“Why are you looking at me like that?”).
target_language_example: Arrête, tu me regardes et ça me met mal à l’aise.
native_language_example: Stop, you’re looking at me and it makes me uncomfortable.

meaning: "you (to) me have" → "you have" (used to form the past tense with "me" as the object).
additional_notes: Contraction of "tu me as". It’s used with verbs that take "avoir" in the passé composé: "tu m’as + past participle" (e.g., "tu m’as aidé(e)", "tu m’as trahi", "tu m’as sauvé"). The "m’" is an object pronoun meaning "me" and comes before the auxiliary verb. Spelling depends on gender/number in some cases (e.g., "tu m’as aidée" to a woman).
target_language_example: Tu m’as oublié ?
native_language_example: Did you forget me?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has never done something. It’s part of the French negation pattern **ne ... jamais** (“never”) with **avoir**: **tu n'as jamais + past participle** (e.g., *tu n'as jamais pris…*). In casual spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: *t'as jamais pris l'avion ?*
target_language_example: Tu n'as jamais pris l'avion ?
native_language_example: Have you never taken a plane?

meaning: you don’t have / you haven’t / you didn’t (with avoir in the negative, 2nd-person singular)
additional_notes: Negative form of « tu as » (you have). It uses « ne … pas » around « avoir », with elision before a vowel: « tu n'as pas ». Common patterns: « tu n'as pas + noun » (you don’t have …) and « tu n'as pas + past participle » (you haven’t/didn’t …). In casual spoken French, « ne » is often dropped: « t'as pas ».
target_language_example: Tu n'as pas dit ça.
native_language_example: You didn’t say that.

meaning: “you don’t have any / you have no …”
additional_notes: Negative form of “tu as” (you have). Used before a noun to say someone doesn’t have something. With negation, “de” replaces “un/une/des” (e.g., “Tu as un frère” → “Tu n’as pas de frère”). Often used in questions: “Tu n’as pas de … ?” = “Don’t you have a … ? / You don’t have any … ?”
target_language_example: Tu n'as pas de temps aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: You don’t have any time today?

meaning: "you just have to" / "all you need to do is".
additional_notes: Used to give a suggestion or instruction: **tu n'as qu'à + infinitive**. It often translates as “just…” in English and can sometimes sound a bit impatient or dismissive depending on tone. Changes with the subject: **vous n'avez qu'à**, **il/elle n'a qu'à**, **on n'a qu'à**, etc.
target_language_example: Tu n'as qu'à m'appeler si tu as un problème.
native_language_example: You just have to call me if you have a problem.

additional_notes:
This is a common combination of:
- **tu** = “you”
- **n’** = **ne** (the first part of French negation; usually paired with **pas**, **jamais**, **plus**, etc.)
- **en** = “of it / about it / some / any”, a pronoun that typically replaces something introduced by **de** (e.g., *parler de ça* → *en parler*; *avoir du café* → *en avoir*).

So **tu n’en…** is the start of a negative sentence meaning “you don’t … of it/about it/any.” The exact English depends on the verb:
- *Tu n’en as jamais parlé.* = “You never talked about it.”
- *Tu n’en es pas sûr.* = “You’re not sure (about it).”
- *Tu n’en veux pas ?* = “You don’t want any?”

Note: In very informal spoken French, **ne** is often dropped (*Tu en as jamais parlé ?*), but the written/standard form keeps **n’**.
target_language_example: Tu n'en es pas sûr.
native_language_example: You’re not sure (about it).

additional_notes: A common negative form of the verb être (to be) in the present tense for "tu" (you, singular/informal). French negation usually uses ne ... pas around the verb; ne becomes n' before a vowel sound, so "tu n'es pas" = "tu ne es pas". Often followed by a noun/adjective (Tu n'es pas prêt) or a past participle in the passé composé with être (Tu n'es pas venue = You didn't come / You haven't come, speaking to a female).
target_language_example: Tu n'es pas prêt aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: You're not ready today.

additional_notes: This is the start of a negative pattern with tu. It usually goes before the verb and is completed by another word such as pas, plus, jamais, rien, or que: tu ne sais pas = you don't know, tu ne viens plus = you don't come anymore, tu ne dis que... = you only say.... In everyday spoken French, ne is often dropped: tu sais pas.
target_language_example: Tu ne comprends pas ?
native_language_example: Don't you understand?

additional_notes: Made of tu (you) + ne…pas (not) + comprends (understand). Often used to state that someone isn’t understanding an idea or situation; it can sound blunt or frustrated depending on tone and context. In questions, it can be surprised or concerned: « Tu ne comprends pas ce qui se passe ? »
target_language_example: Tu ne comprends pas : je n'ai pas dit oui.
native_language_example: You don’t understand: I didn’t say yes.

meaning: "you don’t know" / "you aren’t familiar with" (informal singular).
additional_notes: Used with the verb connaître (to know a person/thing; to be familiar with). Often followed by a noun (Tu ne connais pas ce garçon.) or by a short question like Tu ne connais pas ? (“You don’t know?” / “You’re not familiar?”). For facts/answers, French may also use savoir, but connaître is common with people, places, and things.
target_language_example: Tu ne connais pas ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: You don’t know this restaurant?

meaning: "don’t you think?" / "don’t you believe?" (or "you don’t believe").
additional_notes: Often used as a tag question to ask for agreement: « …, tu ne crois pas ? » = “…, don’t you think?” It can also introduce a clause with « que » (« Tu ne crois pas qu’on devrait en parler ? ») or take « à » for believing in something (« Tu ne crois pas à la Force ? »). Depending on context, it can be a real question or a slightly rhetorical way to challenge someone (“You don’t really believe that, do you?”).
target_language_example: On devrait partir maintenant, tu ne crois pas ?
native_language_example: We should leave now, don’t you think?

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a warning to one person you address as « tu » (informal singular “you”). It’s the negative form of « tu devrais » (“you should”), from « devoir » (to have to / must). Follow it with an infinitive: « Tu ne devrais pas + verbe » (e.g., dire, parler, y aller). For formal singular or plural “you,” use « vous ne devriez pas ».
target_language_example: Tu ne devrais pas conduire si tu es fatigué.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t drive if you’re tired.

additional_notes: Negative form of "devoir" (tu dois = you must / you have to). Used to forbid something or say it’s not allowed: "Tu ne dois pas toucher" = You mustn’t touch. In some contexts it can also express a strong conclusion (deduction): "Tu ne dois pas être ici" can mean "You can’t be here" (that doesn’t make sense / it’s impossible).
target_language_example: Tu ne dois pas traverser la rue ici.
native_language_example: You mustn’t cross the street here.

additional_notes: A common negative pattern: **ne ... pas** around **as** ("have"), with **l'** = "it/him/her" (short for *le* or *la*). It’s typically followed by a past participle: *tu ne l’as pas fait* (you didn’t do it), *tu ne l’as pas vu(e)* (you haven’t seen him/her). With *voir*, you may see **vu** (masculine/it) vs **vue** (feminine) depending on who/what **l'** refers to.
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu ne l'as pas dit ?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you say it?

additional_notes: Used to start a negation with the subject "tu" (you) plus the direct object pronoun "le" (it/him). In full negatives, "ne" is usually paired with "pas": "tu ne le veux pas" = "you don’t want it". When there are multiple object pronouns, they come before the verb: "tu ne le lui as pas dit" = "you didn’t tell it to him/her".
target_language_example: Tu ne le connais pas ?
native_language_example: You don’t know him/it?

meaning: “you don’t … me” / “you didn’t … to me” (start of a negative sentence with “me”).
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment used when speaking to one person (tu). In French negation is typically built with two parts: **ne** + a second negative word like **pas** (not), **jamais** (never), **plus** (no longer), etc. The object pronoun **me** (“me/to me”) usually comes **before** the verb: *Tu ne me dis pas…* (“You don’t tell me…”), *Tu ne me l’as jamais dit* (“You never told me [it]”). In casual speech, **ne** is often dropped: *Tu me suis pas ?*
target_language_example: Tu ne me réponds pas ?
native_language_example: You’re not answering me?

additional_notes: Negative form of "tu peux" (from pouvoir = "to be able to"). Used to say someone is unable to do something or is not allowed to do it. In questions ("Tu ne peux pas… ?"), it can sound like a complaint or a strong request (e.g., "Can’t you wait?").
target_language_example: Tu ne peux pas entrer ici sans badge.
native_language_example: You can't come in here without a badge.

additional_notes: Uses the informal subject pronoun **tu** (“you” to one person you’re on familiar terms with). It’s the negative form of **tu sais** (“you know”). Often followed by a question word: **tu ne sais pas où/pourquoi/comment…** (“you don’t know where/why/how…”).
target_language_example: Tu ne sais pas où j’ai mis mes clés ?
native_language_example: You don’t know where I put my keys?

additional_notes: Direct, second-person phrase using negation (ne…rien). Often used to state that someone lacks information; depending on tone/context it can sound harsh or accusatory (similar to “You don’t know anything!”). You can intensify it with “du tout” (“at all”) or specify a topic with “de…” or “à propos de…”.
target_language_example: Tu ne sais rien de cette histoire.
native_language_example: You don’t know anything about this story.

additional_notes: Future tense of "être" (tu seras = you will be) with negation: "ne ... jamais" = never. Used to say someone will never become or be something in the future, often as a strong judgment or insult (e.g., "Tu ne seras jamais normal" = You’ll never be normal). Common patterns: "tu ne seras jamais + adjective" or "tu ne seras jamais + un/une + noun".
target_language_example: Tu ne seras jamais heureux si tu mens tout le temps.
native_language_example: You’ll never be happy if you lie all the time.

additional_notes: Used to ask for agreement or confirmation (a tag question). Often follows a statement: « C'est dommage, tu ne trouves pas ? » It can also introduce a clause: « Tu ne trouves pas que… ? » or take a direct object: « Tu ne trouves pas ça… ? » Literally it’s “you don’t find,” but it usually means “don’t you think?” in English.
target_language_example: Il fait un peu froid, tu ne trouves pas ?
native_language_example: It’s a bit cold, don’t you think?

meaning: "you're not going to…" / "aren't you going to…?" (near future with aller).
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to talk about a (not) planned or expected action: « Tu ne vas pas venir ? » = “Aren’t you coming?” It can also be used emphatically to protest, warn, or reassure: « Tu ne vas pas mourir ! » (“You’re not going to die!”). In « Tu ne vas pas bien », it means “You’re not well / You’re not right (in the head).”
target_language_example: Tu ne vas pas partir sans dire au revoir ?
native_language_example: You’re not going to leave without saying goodbye?

additional_notes: Literally means “you don’t want (to)…”. In questions, it’s very often used to make a gentle suggestion or invitation: “Tu ne veux pas entrer ?” ≈ “Would you like to come in?” Depending on tone/context, it can also sound surprised or slightly insistent: “You don’t want to…?”
target_language_example: Tu ne veux pas prendre un café ?
native_language_example: Would you like to have a coffee?

meaning: you didn’t want to / you weren’t willing to.
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of vouloir (voulais) with negation ne…pas. It can mean you didn’t want something ("tu ne voulais pas de livres" = you didn’t want any books) or you didn’t want to do something / didn’t want someone to do something ("tu ne voulais pas que je vienne" = you didn’t want me to come). Often used to question or challenge someone about a past preference or refusal.
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu ne voulais pas venir avec nous ?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you want to come with us?

meaning: "you have" / "you did" (to us), used before a past participle in the passé composé.
additional_notes: "Tu" = you (informal singular). "Nous" is the direct object pronoun (us) placed before the verb. "As" is the present tense of "avoir" used to form the passé composé: tu nous as + past participle (tu nous as trouvés / aidés / trompés). If "nous" refers to people and comes before the verb, the past participle often agrees: trouvés (masc./mixed) or trouvées (fem.).
target_language_example: Tu nous as oubliés au restaurant.
native_language_example: You forgot us at the restaurant.

additional_notes: Uses the subject pronoun tu (informal “you”) + negation ne…pas around the verb être (“to be”): tu n’es pas = “you aren’t/you’re not.” Used before an adjective or noun phrase: Tu n’es pas faible (“You’re not weak”). In casual speech, ne is often dropped: Tu es pas…
target_language_example: Tu n’es pas en retard.
native_language_example: You’re not late.

additional_notes: From parler with tu, used for one person you know well or speak to casually. It can mean either "you speak" or "you talk," depending on context. In questions, French often keeps the same word order: Tu parles aussi allemand ? = "Do you also speak German?" With de, it often means "you’re talking about" something: Tu parles du divorce ?
target_language_example: Tu parles trop vite.
native_language_example: You speak too fast.

additional_notes: Used to ask or confirm who/what someone means. Often followed by a person or thing (Tu parles de papa ?), or by a question word (Tu parles de qui ? = Who are you talking about?). In "Comment tu parles de ma sœur ?", it can mean "How are you talking about my sister?" (i.e., watch how you speak about her).
target_language_example: Tu parles de quel film ?
native_language_example: Which movie are you talking about?

additional_notes: "Tu penses" is the informal singular (tu) form of "penser" (to think). It can be a statement ("you think") or, with question intonation/"?", a question ("do you think?"). Common patterns: "penser à" + noun/thing = to think about (Dis-moi à quoi tu penses.); "penser que" + sentence = to think that (Tu penses que c'est vrai ?).
target_language_example: Tu penses qu'on a le temps ?
native_language_example: Do you think we have time?

additional_notes: Literally “you think that.” Used to ask for someone’s opinion or what they believe/expect: Tu penses que + clause. In questions it often means “Do you really think…?” or “Do you expect…?” In more formal French, you may hear “Penses-tu que… ?” instead of “Tu penses que… ?”.
