native_language_example: What are we going to do tomorrow?

meaning: "will have to" / "it’s going to be necessary".
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "il va falloir" (impersonal: "it will be necessary"). In speech, people often drop "il" and just say "va falloir". Common patterns: "va falloir + infinitive" (Va falloir être patient.) and "va falloir que + subject + subjunctive" (Va falloir que tu ranges.). Often implies obligation or necessity, like "we’ll have to".
target_language_example: Va falloir qu’on parte maintenant.
native_language_example: We’ll have to leave now.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase « se passer » (“to happen,” “to take place”). « va se passer » is the near future: « aller » (va) + infinitive (se passer). Often used in questions like « Qu’est-ce qu’il va se passer ? » (“What’s going to happen?”). Not the same as English “to pass.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : rien ne va se passer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: nothing is going to happen.

additional_notes: Part of the near-future pattern aller + infinitive. Here va is the il/elle/on form of aller, and te means singular informal 'you'. In sentences like Il va te chercher or Ça va te plaire, te comes before the infinitive and means 'you' as the object of the next verb.
target_language_example: Ça va te faire rire.
native_language_example: It's going to make you laugh.

additional_notes: Extremely offensive and sexually explicit (literally refers to anal sex). Used to tell someone off aggressively; avoid in polite conversation. You may see it shortened or censored (e.g., “va te faire…” or “va te faire e*****”).
target_language_example: Si tu continues à m’insulter, je m’en vais — mais ne me dis jamais « va te faire enculer ».
native_language_example: If you keep insulting me, I’m leaving — but never tell me “go f**k yourself.”

additional_notes: A very vulgar insult used to tell someone off. Literally uses the verb phrase *se faire foutre* (“to get fucked / to be told off”), but it’s best translated as “go fuck yourself.” *Va* is informal singular (to one person you address as *tu*). Plural/formal versions: *allez vous faire foutre* (to several people or to *vous*). Not appropriate in polite situations.
target_language_example: Si tu n’es pas content, va te faire foutre.
native_language_example: If you’re not happy, go fuck yourself.

additional_notes: A very informal, insulting way to tell someone to go away. Literally “go get yourself seen,” but the real meaning is closer to “piss off” / “get lost.” Often used in the imperative with “tu”; you may also hear “va te faire voir ailleurs” (“get lost somewhere else”). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Oh, va te faire voir !
native_language_example: Oh, get lost!

additional_notes: Formed with the near-future tense: aller (conjugated) + infinitive venir. It can refer to a planned/expected arrival (“who’s going to come”). The subject can change (je vais venir, ils vont venir, etc.).
target_language_example: Je pense qu’il va venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I think he’s going to come tonight.

additional_notes: Near-future form: "aller" (here: "va" = he/she/it goes) + infinitive "être". Used to say something is expected to happen soon or is planned/likely. Changes with the subject: je vais être, tu vas être, il/elle/on va être, nous allons être, vous allez être, ils/elles vont être.
target_language_example: Demain, ça va être difficile.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, it’s going to be difficult.

additional_notes: Refers to repeated movement in two directions or frequent traffic/activity (people, cars, waves, etc.). Often used with adjectives like constant and with "de" to specify what is moving: "le va-et-vient des clients". Usually singular with a hyphenated form.
target_language_example: Le va-et-vient des touristes devant l'hôtel a commencé tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: The comings and goings of tourists in front of the hotel started early this morning.

additional_notes: Imperative (“tu” form) of the verb phrase “s’en aller” (to leave/go away). Often used as an order and can sound rude or angry depending on context and tone. You’ll also commonly see it written “va-t’en” (with an apostrophe).
target_language_example: Va-t-en, je dois étudier.
native_language_example: Go away, I have to study.

meaning: "does it suit him?" / "is he going?" (formal question: "is/does ... he/it ...?").
additional_notes: "Va-t-il" is the inverted question form of "il va" (present tense of aller). It can mean "Is he going? / Where is he going?" or, with "aller" meaning "to suit" (common with clothes, a menu, etc.), "Does it suit him/you?" In writing, French adds a "-t-" between two vowels: "va-t-il", "a-t-il".
target_language_example: À quelle heure va-t-il arriver ?
native_language_example: What time is he going to arrive?

additional_notes: With clothes, colors, or styles plus an indirect object pronoun (me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur), it means something suits someone or looks good on them. With a person as the subject, it means someone is fine or doing well.
target_language_example: Cette chemise te va bien.
native_language_example: That shirt looks good on you.

meaning: Go and get (fetch); go pick up.
additional_notes: Imperative form addressed to one person you’re familiar with (tu). It’s made of va (from aller, “to go”) + chercher (“to look for / to get”). In everyday French, va chercher often means “go get” something or someone (from another room, from outside, etc.), not just “go search.”
target_language_example: Va chercher ton manteau, il fait froid dehors.
native_language_example: Go get your coat; it’s cold outside.

additional_notes: Very vulgar and aggressive. Used to tell someone to go away or express contempt/anger. Avoid in polite conversation; it can easily start a fight. Often addressed directly with “toi,” or followed by a name/insult.
target_language_example: Si ça ne te plaît pas, va te faire foutre.
native_language_example: If you don’t like it, fuck off.

meaning: fits you very well / suits you very well; (also) is doing very well.
additional_notes: From the verb "aller". With clothing/colors, "(ça) va très bien (à + someone)" means it looks good on someone: "Ce manteau vous va très bien" = "That coat suits you very well." With people/things, it means someone/something is doing fine/very well: "Elle va très bien" / "Sa famille va très bien." You can also use it as an answer about how things are going: "Oui, ça va très bien."
target_language_example: Cette couleur te va très bien.
native_language_example: That color suits you very well.

additional_notes: "Vais-je" is the 1st person singular of aller (je vais) used in inversion to form a formal/literary question: "Vais-je + infinitive ?" = "Am I going to + verb?" In everyday speech, people more often say "Est-ce que je vais... ?" or "Je vais... ?".
target_language_example: Vais-je devoir payer maintenant ?
native_language_example: Am I going to have to pay now?

additional_notes: A noun phrase used for a vehicle designed to travel in space. It’s usually masculine: « le vaisseau spatial » (note: sentence 1 should be « Le vaisseau spatial… », not « La… »). Often used in sci‑fi or when comparing something futuristic: « On dirait un vaisseau spatial ! »
target_language_example: Ils ont vu un vaisseau spatial dans le film.
native_language_example: They saw a spaceship in the movie.

meaning: to be worth it / to be worth the effort.
additional_notes: Used to say something is worth doing or worth the trouble. Commonly conjugated with a subject like "ça": "Ça vaut la peine." You can also use "valoir la peine de" + infinitive: "Ça vaut la peine de réessayer." In the negative: "Ça ne vaut pas la peine" = "It’s not worth it."
target_language_example: Ça vaudra la peine de partir plus tôt.
native_language_example: It will be worth leaving earlier.

additional_notes: Used to say something is worth the effort, time, cost, or trouble. Common in questions and negatives: « Est-ce que ça vaut le coup ? » (Is it worth it?), « Ça ne vaut pas le coup. » (It’s not worth it.). In the past: « Ça valait le coup. » (It was worth it.). You can also use it in the infinitive after another verb (e.g., « Ça va valoir le coup. » / « Ça peut valoir le coup. »).
target_language_example: Ça va valoir le coup d'essayer.
native_language_example: It’s going to be worth trying.

meaning: to be better; to be preferable
additional_notes: Commonly used in the impersonal structure: « il vaut mieux + infinitive » = “it’s better to … / you’d better …”. You can also compare two things: « X vaut mieux que Y » = “X is better than Y / preferable to Y”. Note that the verb conjugates (il vaut, ça vaut, etc.), so you won’t always see the infinitive form « valoir ».
target_language_example: Il vaudrait mieux valoir mieux que d'abandonner.
native_language_example: It would be better to be better than to give up.

meaning: "do you go?" / "are you going?" (2nd person singular question).
additional_notes: "Vas-tu" is the inverted question form of "tu vas" (you go/you are going), from the verb "aller" (to go). It’s used to ask about where someone goes, how often, or whether they are going somewhere. It can be followed by a place ("Vas-tu au cinéma ?"), by an adverb ("Vas-tu souvent… ?"), or by "y" to mean "there" ("Y vas-tu ?").
target_language_example: Vas-tu à l’école demain ?
native_language_example: Are you going to school tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to urge or encourage someone to do something, often before another verb: Vas-y, réponds. Depending on tone, it can sound supportive, impatient, or challenging. This is the informal singular form; with vous, use allez-y.
target_language_example: Vas-y, essaie encore.
native_language_example: Go ahead, try again.

additional_notes: Used to talk about plans or availability on Friday evening. In French, "soir" is the evening/night period; depending on context, it often matches English "Friday night" (e.g., going out) or "Friday evening" (e.g., dinner).
target_language_example: On se voit vendredi soir ?
native_language_example: Are we seeing each other Friday night?

meaning: "do you come" / "are you coming"? (formal or plural "you").
additional_notes: Inversion of the verb and subject pronoun to form a question: "venez" (you come/are coming) + "vous". Used for formal "you" (one person) or plural "you". Often appears in questions about where someone comes from ("Venez-vous de… ?" = "Are you from…?") or whether they’re coming ("Venez-vous ou non ?").
target_language_example: Venez-vous avec nous ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are you coming with us tonight?

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) addressed to “vous” (one person formally or several people). Used to ask/tell someone to accompany you; can be followed by a destination: « Venez avec moi à… ».
target_language_example: Venez avec moi au bureau, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Come with me to the office, please.

additional_notes: Means to accompany the speaker. Often used in questions or invitations: « Tu veux (bien) venir avec moi ? » = “Do you want to come with me?” You can switch pronouns depending on who you’re talking to: « venir avec moi » (me), « venir avec nous » (us). In a direct command you’ll often hear « Viens avec moi ! » (informal) or « Venez avec moi ! » (formal/plural).
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu peux venir avec moi au magasin ?
native_language_example: Can you come with me to the store?

additional_notes: Used to invite someone to join your group. "Venir" is "to come" (toward the speaker), and "avec nous" means "with us." Often used in questions or polite invitations: "Peux-tu venir avec nous ?" / "Voudriez-vous venir avec nous… ?"
target_language_example: Si tu veux, tu peux venir avec nous au cinéma.
native_language_example: If you want, you can come with us to the movie theater.

meaning: to come and get / to come pick up (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used when you go somewhere specifically to collect someone/something (e.g., pick up a child, fetch a package, pick someone up by car). It’s often followed by a direct object: « Je viens chercher mon colis. » You can also use pronouns: « Je viens le chercher. » (= I’m coming to get it/him.)
target_language_example: Je viens venir chercher mon colis cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I’m coming to pick up my package this afternoon.

additional_notes: With a person, place, or thing after de, this expression shows origin, source, or cause. It can mean where someone is from, where something comes from, or what is causing something: Ça vient de moi = "it's because of me / it's coming from me." Note: venir de + infinitive is a different common pattern meaning "have just".
target_language_example: Ça doit venir de moi.
native_language_example: It must be coming from me.

meaning: to help; to come to someone’s aid.
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object to express providing assistance, often in a serious, urgent, or practical situation. Common patterns: « venir en aide à quelqu’un » and « venir en aide à + pronoun » (lui/leur/me/te/nous/vous).
target_language_example: Au lieu de lui venir en aide, il est resté planté là en la regardant.
native_language_example: Instead of helping her, he just stood there staring at her.

additional_notes: Used for movement toward the speaker or the place being talked about as 'here'. It's a straightforward combination of venir + ici.
target_language_example: Tu peux venir ici une minute ?
native_language_example: Can you come here for a minute?

meaning: to come see me; to come visit me.
additional_notes: Used to invite or request that someone come to your place (or come to meet you) for a visit. The pronoun changes with the person: venir te voir (come see you), venir le/la voir (come see him/her), venir nous voir (come see us), venir vous voir (come see you/formal or plural), venir les voir (come see them). Often follows another verb: pouvoir venir me voir (can come see me), devoir venir me voir (should come see me), demander de venir me voir (ask to come see me).
target_language_example: Tu veux venir me voir ce week-end ?
native_language_example: Do you want to come see me this weekend?

additional_notes: Used when an idea, memory, or word suddenly occurs to you. Commonly used with an indirect object pronoun: « ça me vient à l'esprit » (it comes to mind), « rien ne me vient à l'esprit » (nothing comes to mind).
target_language_example: Ton nom ne veut pas venir à l'esprit.
native_language_example: Your name won’t come to mind.

additional_notes: Littéralement, un petit ver qui vit dans le sol. Peut aussi s’employer figurativement comme insulte (« Vous êtes un ver de terre. ») ou dans des expressions comme « une vie de ver de terre » pour évoquer une existence misérable et rabaissée.
target_language_example: La poule a mangé un ver de terre.
native_language_example: The hen ate an earthworm.

meaning: towards the right; to the right.
additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement in space (e.g., on a map, in a building, while driving). Common with verbs like tourner (to turn), aller (to go), regarder (to look), se diriger (to head).
target_language_example: Tournez vers la droite au prochain feu.
native_language_example: Turn right at the next traffic light.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement toward something masculine singular (le). Common in phrases like "vers le haut" (upwards) or "vers le Nord" (toward the North). For other genders/numbers: "vers la" (feminine), "vers les" (plural), "vers l’" (before a vowel). It can also be used for approximate time (e.g., "vers le soir" = around evening).
target_language_example: Tourne vers le pont, puis continue tout droit.
native_language_example: Turn toward the bridge, then keep going straight.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction (not a fixed location): looking/moving “up” toward something higher. Often follows verbs like regarder (to look), lever (to raise), monter (to go up), or can be used alone as a direction.
target_language_example: Lève la tête et regarde vers le haut.
native_language_example: Lift your head and look up.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement in the direction of the south. Common with movement verbs like aller, marcher, voler, se diriger. You can also say simply "au sud" for a location (in the south), but "vers le sud" emphasizes heading that way.
target_language_example: Nous allons vers le sud pour les vacances.
native_language_example: We're going south for vacation.

meaning: 'does he want' / 'does he really want it?' (question form).
additional_notes: This is the verb–subject inversion used to form a question in more formal French: "veut" (wants) + "-il" (he) with a hyphen. It’s equivalent to "Est-ce qu’il veut… ?" or the informal spoken order "Il veut… ?". Used with a following infinitive or object: "Où veut-il aller ?" (Where does he want to go?), "Le veut-il ?" (Does he want it?).
target_language_example: Veut-il venir avec nous ce soir ?
native_language_example: Does he want to come with us tonight?

meaning: "wants to talk to you / wants to speak to you."
additional_notes: Built from *vouloir* (to want) + *te* (to you, informal singular) + *parler* (to talk/speak). It’s often used to say someone is asking to see you or has something to tell you: *Le patron veut te parler* (The boss wants to talk to you). With a formal or plural “you,” say *veut vous parler*.
target_language_example: Le professeur veut te parler après le cours.
native_language_example: The teacher wants to talk to you after class.

meaning: 'wants to see you' (wants to meet/speak with you).
additional_notes: Used when someone is asking to meet you or talk to you. Often sounds like a summons when the subject is an authority figure (le directeur, le patron, etc.). You can add details like where/when: « Il/Elle veut te voir en bas / maintenant ». Adding « toi » emphasizes *you* specifically: « Il veut te voir toi, pas moi ».
target_language_example: Le médecin veut te voir tout de suite.
native_language_example: The doctor wants to see you right away.

additional_notes: Combination of vouloir (to want) in the 3rd-person singular present tense: veut + the infinitive être (to be). Used to say what someone wants to become (Il veut être médecin.), or what state/quality they want to have or show (Elle veut être différente / présente.). With a noun, you often use an article: être un/une… (veut être un joueur). With an adjective, no article: veut être célèbre, pauvre, libre, heureux. For other subjects: je veux être, tu veux être, nous voulons être, vous voulez être, ils/elles veulent être.
target_language_example: Il veut être plus patient avec ses enfants.
native_language_example: He wants to be more patient with his children.

additional_notes: Question form of tu veux, using inversion. It is used to ask whether someone wants something or wants to do something. It can sound a bit more formal, direct, or literary than everyday tu veux ... ?
target_language_example: Veux-tu venir avec nous ?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with us?

additional_notes: Question formed with inversion: « veux-tu… ? » = “do you want…?” (addressing one person informally) and « manger » = “to eat.” Often used on its own (« Veux-tu manger ? ») or with what to eat: « Veux-tu manger un morceau / un bout ? » = “Do you want to eat a piece / have a bite?” You can also add timing: « Quand veux-tu manger ? » = “When do you want to eat?”
target_language_example: Quand veux-tu manger ?
native_language_example: When do you want to eat?

meaning: "do you really want to...?" (emphasizes doubt or surprise).
additional_notes: Formed with verb–subject inversion (veux + tu) to ask a question. Commonly followed by an infinitive: "Veux-tu vraiment faire/voir/savoir... ?" You can make it more neutral/less direct with: "Est-ce que tu veux vraiment... ?"
target_language_example: Veux-tu vraiment partir maintenant ?
native_language_example: Do you really want to leave now?

additional_notes: “Veux” is the “I want” form of vouloir. It’s followed by an infinitive: “je veux aller …” = “I want to go …”. Often used with a place (“je veux aller à Paris”) or with expressions like “aller mieux” (“to get better”): “je veux aller mieux” = “I want to feel better / get better.”
target_language_example: Je veux aller au cinéma ce soir.
native_language_example: I want to go to the movies tonight.

additional_notes: Usually appears with the subject: « Je veux que tu saches… ». After « je veux que », French uses the subjunctive: « tu saches » (from « savoir », to know). Used to introduce important information or reassurance.
target_language_example: Je veux que tu saches que je suis là pour toi.
native_language_example: I want you to know that I’m here for you.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of a full sentence like “Je veux que tu viennes.” After “vouloir que” (“to want that”), French typically uses the subjunctive: “tu viennes” (from “venir”). You can swap the subject: “Je veux que vous veniez” (formal/plural), “Je veux qu’il/elle vienne,” etc.
target_language_example: Je veux que tu viennes ce soir.
native_language_example: I want you to come tonight.

additional_notes: Made of the verb *vouloir* (“to want”) conjugated as **veux** (used with **je** or **tu**) + **simplement** (“simply/just”). Often used to soften a request or clarify that you only want one simple thing. With other subjects: **il/elle veut simplement**, **nous voulons simplement**, **vous voulez simplement**, **ils/elles veulent simplement**.
target_language_example: Je veux simplement te parler.
native_language_example: I just want to talk to you.

meaning: viceroy; a ruler who governs in the king’s place.
additional_notes: Used as a title for a high-ranking official appointed by a king/queen to govern a territory (often a colony). You can address someone directly with it like a title: « Oui, vice-roi ? » = “Yes, Viceroy?”
target_language_example: Le vice-roi arrive demain au palais.
native_language_example: The viceroy is arriving at the palace tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when talking about religious/spiritual beliefs about what happens after someone dies. Very often appears with « croire à / en » (to believe in) or in questions like « Y a-t-il une vie après la mort ? ».
target_language_example: Elle ne croit pas à la vie après la mort.
native_language_example: She doesn’t believe in life after death.

additional_notes: Refers to the personal part of someone’s life that isn’t public (relationships, family matters, personal information). Common in phrases like « avoir droit à la vie privée » (to have a right to privacy) and « respecter la vie privée » (to respect someone’s privacy). « Te mêle pas de ma vie privée » is a direct, often annoyed way to say “Don’t meddle in my private life.”
target_language_example: Je tiens beaucoup à ma vie privée.
native_language_example: I care a lot about my privacy.

additional_notes: Refers to a person’s usual routine and normal activities (work/school, errands, habits). Often used after a preposition like "dans la vie quotidienne" (in everyday life) or with a possessive: "ma/ta/votre vie quotidienne".
target_language_example: Dans ma vie quotidienne, je prends le métro et je fais les courses après le travail.
native_language_example: In my everyday life, I take the subway and I do the grocery shopping after work.

meaning: real life; reality (as opposed to fiction, dreams, or online life).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens in the real world (everyday reality), often in contrast with a movie/story, a dream, imagination, or the internet. Often appears with articles: « la vie réelle » (“real life”). You can also say « dans la vie réelle » (“in real life”).
target_language_example: Dans la vie réelle, je suis beaucoup plus timide.
native_language_example: In real life, I’m much more shy.

additional_notes: "Vieil" is the masculine form of "vieux" used before a singular masculine noun that starts with a vowel sound (often a vowel or silent h): vieil homme, vieil ami. Use "vieux" before a consonant (un vieux monsieur) and "vieux" after the noun (un homme vieux).
target_language_example: Ce vieil homme habite ici depuis trente ans.
native_language_example: This old man has lived here for thirty years.

meaning: “spinster / old maid” (an unmarried woman, often said in a judgmental way).
additional_notes: An old-fashioned, often pejorative label for a woman who never married (or is still unmarried at an older age). Commonly used after verbs like "rester" or "finir" (rester/finir vieille fille = to remain/end up a spinster). Be careful: it can sound rude or sexist; in neutral speech you can say "une femme célibataire" (a single woman).
target_language_example: Dans ce village, certaines personnes la traitaient de vieille fille, ce qu’elle détestait.
native_language_example: In that village, some people called her an old maid, which she hated.

meaning: old town; the historic part of a city.
additional_notes: Usually refers to the historic city center (often with older buildings and narrow streets). As an adjective, "vieille" agrees with the noun: "vieille ville" (feminine). Don’t confuse "vieille ville" (the old part of a city) with "une vieille ville" meaning a city that is very old.
target_language_example: On a visité la vieille ville après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: We visited the old town after lunch.

meaning: old school; traditional (in tastes, methods, or values).
additional_notes: Often used in the expression « être de la vieille école » = “to be old-school,” meaning you prefer traditional ways of doing things (sometimes approvingly, sometimes implying you’re a bit behind the times). You can also say « la vieille école » to refer to the old-school style in general.
target_language_example: Mon père est de la vieille école : il préfère appeler plutôt qu’envoyer des messages.
native_language_example: My dad is old-school: he prefers calling rather than sending texts.

meaning: "are you coming?" / "do you come?" (inversion question form of "tu viens").
additional_notes: Used to ask a question with the verb first + subject pronoun after it (inversion), common in more formal written/spoken French. In everyday conversation, you often hear "Tu viens ?" instead. Can refer to coming somewhere ("Viens-tu avec moi ?" = Are you coming with me?) or to the "venir de" construction ("Que viens-tu de faire ?" = What did you just do?).
target_language_example: Viens-tu demain soir ?
native_language_example: Are you coming tomorrow evening?

additional_notes: Used to invite or ask someone to accompany you. It’s the imperative (command/request) form of *venir* addressed to one person you speak to as **tu**. It can sound like a firm command or a polite request depending on tone and words like **s’il te plaît**. Often followed by a destination: **Viens avec moi à la gare** (“Come with me to the station”).
target_language_example: Viens avec moi au café, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Come with me to the café, please.

additional_notes: From the verb *venir* (to come) + *ici* (here). **Viens** is the informal singular command (or present tense for "I come" in context, e.g., *je viens ici* = "I come here"). Often used as an instruction: *Viens ici !* (Come here!), *Viens ici tout de suite* (Come here right away).
target_language_example: Viens ici, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Come here, please.

additional_notes: Imperative form of venir (“to come”) + me voir (“to see me”). Used to invite someone to come to you, either to visit you or to come watch you do something (e.g., jouer = “play/perform”). Often followed by a time (demain, tout de suite) or a condition (si tu es libre).
target_language_example: Viens me voir après le travail.
native_language_example: Come see me after work.

additional_notes: Often used as a friendly invitation to get someone’s attention and show them something. In examples like « Allez, viens voir » or « Peter, viens voir ! », it’s the informal singular imperative (talking to one person you address as tu). It can also be the present tense « je viens voir… » meaning “I’m coming to see…” / “I’m here to see… (someone)”, especially when visiting a person (e.g., a doctor).
target_language_example: Viens voir, j’ai trouvé tes clés !
native_language_example: Come and see, I found your keys!

additional_notes: Used as the near past (passé récent): venir (conjugated) + de + infinitive. « vient » is the 3rd person singular present (il/elle/on vient). Example pattern: « Il/Elle/On vient de + infinitif » = « he/she/one has just + past participle / just + verb ».
target_language_example: Elle vient de terminer son roman.
native_language_example: She has just finished her novel.

additional_notes:
Two common uses:
1) "venir de" + infinitive (here: "vient de" for "il/elle/on") expresses the recent past: something happened very recently. Example pattern: "Il vient de partir" = "He has just left".
2) "venir de" + noun/place indicates origin or source: "Elle vient de Russie" = "She comes from Russia"; "Ça vient de l'ambassade" = "It comes from the embassy".
You can usually tell which meaning is intended by what follows "de" (infinitive vs. noun/place).
target_language_example: Quelque chose vient de se passer.
native_language_example: Something just happened.

additional_notes: Form of the near-future/near-past structure **venir de + infinitive**. With **il/elle/on** in the present: **vient (juste) de + infinitive** = “(he/she/one) just did …”. **Juste** adds emphasis (“just now”). Example: *Il vient de partir* / *Il vient juste de partir* = “He just left.”
target_language_example: Elle vient juste de finir son travail.
native_language_example: She just finished her work.

additional_notes: Used to describe a person, attitude, taste, or ideas that feel behind the times (often a mild criticism, sometimes affectionate). It usually comes after the verb: « Il est vieux jeu » / « Tes idées sont vieux jeu ». Can be intensified with « un peu », « très ».
target_language_example: Je sais que c’est vieux jeu, mais j’aime écrire des lettres à la main.
native_language_example: I know it’s old-fashioned, but I like writing letters by hand.

additional_notes: Used to talk about or order white wine. Often used with articles like "du vin blanc" (some white wine) or "un verre de vin blanc" (a glass of white wine). It contrasts with "vin rouge" (red wine).
target_language_example: On prend une bouteille de vin blanc ?
native_language_example: Shall we get a bottle of white wine?

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "vin" (wine) + "rouge" (red). Often used with partitives when talking about an unspecified amount: "du vin rouge" (some red wine). You can also use it after "un verre de" (a glass of): "un verre de vin rouge".
target_language_example: Au restaurant, je prends un verre de vin rouge.
native_language_example: At the restaurant, I’ll have a glass of red wine.

additional_notes: Used for the number 25: in math (Cinq fois cinq font vingt-cinq), dates (le vingt-cinq décembre = the 25th of December), age/time (vingt-cinq ans = 25 years old), and money to mean a 25-cent coin/bill depending on context (un vingt-cinq cents). Can also be said alone as an answer (e.g., to “How many?”).
target_language_example: J’ai vingt-cinq minutes, puis je dois partir.
native_language_example: I have 25 minutes, then I have to leave.

additional_notes: The number 22. Used for ages (Vingt-deux ans.), dates (le vingt-deux janvier = the 22nd of January), times in the 24-hour clock (à vingt-deux heures = at 22:00 / 10 p.m.), and in counting/reading out numbers (Vingt-deux et vingt-trois !).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à vingt-deux heures devant le cinéma.
native_language_example: Let's meet at 10 p.m. in front of the movie theater.

additional_notes: The number 24. Used for counting and quantities (e.g., hours, years), and can also be said alone as an answer (for example, giving your age or replying to a question). Often written with a hyphen in French: vingt-quatre.
target_language_example: J'ai vingt-quatre ans.
native_language_example: I'm twenty-four years old.

additional_notes: Used for counting (vingt-six ans), giving dates (le vingt-six octobre = October 26th), or answering a question with just the number.
target_language_example: J’ai vingt-six ans.
native_language_example: I’m twenty-six years old.

additional_notes: Used to give a number (age, time, measurements, a count, etc.). In French, compound numbers like this are often written with a hyphen. For time, you can say "à vingt-trois heures" = "at 23:00" (11 p.m.) in the 24-hour clock.
target_language_example: J'ai vingt-trois ans.
native_language_example: I am twenty-three years old.

additional_notes: Used with "avoir" to give someone’s age: "avoir vingt ans" = "to be twenty (years old)." "ans" is used for ages and years (not "années" in this context).
target_language_example: J'ai vingt ans aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I’m twenty years old today.

additional_notes: French uses “et” (and) only with numbers ending in 1 for 21, 31, 41, 51, 61, and 71 (e.g., “vingt et un”). For 81 and 91, it’s “quatre-vingt-un” and “quatre-vingt-onze” (no “et”). You’ll hear it as a short standalone answer when giving a number, and rising intonation (“Vingt et un ?”) can show confirmation/surprise (“Twenty-one?”).
target_language_example: J’ai vingt et un ans.
native_language_example: I am twenty-one years old.

meaning: 'a visit to' (as in "rendre visite à" = "to visit").
additional_notes: Usually used in the expression "rendre visite à + person" to mean "to visit (someone)". In French, you don’t typically say *visiter quelqu’un* for people; *visiter* is more for places (e.g., *visiter Paris*).
target_language_example: Je vais rendre visite à mes grands-parents ce week-end.
native_language_example: I’m going to visit my grandparents this weekend.

additional_notes: "vit" is the 3rd-person singular present of "vivre" (to live). "vit dans" is used with a place (real or figurative): "Il vit dans une maison" (a house), or "Elle vit dans ses souvenirs" (her memories).
target_language_example: Il vit dans un petit appartement à Paris.
native_language_example: He lives in a small apartment in Paris.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the nutrient vitamin A (for example in food, supplements, or health contexts). In French, "vitamine" is feminine: "la vitamine A". You’ll often see it with "contenir" (to contain) or "manquer de" (to lack).
target_language_example: Cette huile est riche en vitamine A.
native_language_example: This oil is rich in vitamin A.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the nutrient found in foods (especially citrus fruits). Common with verbs like contenir (to contain) and être riche en (to be rich in). Often written with a capital letter for the vitamin name: vitamine C.
target_language_example: Les kiwis sont très riches en vitamine C.
native_language_example: Kiwis are very rich in vitamin C.

additional_notes: Often used with être: « Ce sera / Ça va être vite fait » = “It’ll be quick.” Can also be used in the pattern « avoir vite fait de + infinitive » to mean “to quickly/easily end up doing something” (sometimes with the idea that it won’t take much effort). As a short reply (« Vite fait. »), it means “Quickly/No problem, it’ll be quick.” More common in spoken, casual French.
target_language_example: Je te fais un résumé vite fait, et je dois y aller.
native_language_example: I’ll give you a quick summary, and then I have to go.

additional_notes: Form of the verb vivre (to live): ils/elles vivent = “they live.” Used with dans + a place (city, house, neighborhood, etc.) to say where people live. For one person: il/elle vit dans.
target_language_example: Mes voisins vivent dans un petit appartement.
native_language_example: My neighbors live in a small apartment.

meaning: “Do you live…?” / “Are you living…?” (formal or plural “you”).
additional_notes: This is the present tense of **vivre** (“to live”) with **inversion** for a question: **vivez + -vous**. Used when speaking to **one person formally (vous)** or to **multiple people**. It’s typically followed by a place or a time phrase: *Vivez-vous à Paris ?* / *Depuis quand vivez-vous ici ?*
target_language_example: Vivez-vous près d’ici ?
native_language_example: Do you live near here?

meaning: to live with (someone); to live with it (= accept/tolerate it).
additional_notes: Used literally for sharing a home with someone: « vivre avec ma mère », « venir vivre avec moi ». It can also be figurative/incomplete (« vivre avec » / « vivre avec ça ») meaning to accept a situation and deal with it: « Il faut apprendre à vivre avec. »
target_language_example: Je n'aime pas ce bruit, mais je peux vivre avec.
native_language_example: I don't like that noise, but I can live with it.

additional_notes: Used to say you can/can’t manage without something or someone. "Sans" is followed by a noun/pronoun (vivre sans air, vivre sans toi) or sometimes an infinitive (vivre sans se plaindre = to live without complaining). Often used with "ne... pas/plus": "Je ne peux pas vivre sans..."
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas vivre sans toi.
native_language_example: I can’t live without you.

meaning: “There you go, it’s…” / “Right, it’s…” (to confirm or conclude).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to present the result or to wrap things up, often after doing or saying something. Common with past participles or evaluations: « Voilà, c’est fait » (done), « Voilà, c’est dit » (said), « Voilà, c’est bon/mieux » (it’s good/better).
target_language_example: Voilà, c'est terminé.
native_language_example: There you go, it’s finished.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation, method, or instructions. Often followed by a clause (with a verb): « Voilà comment + [subject] + [verb]… ». You can also use it to conclude by saying “that’s how it works/that’s how it happened.”
target_language_example: Voilà comment on fait une crêpe.
native_language_example: Here’s how you make a crêpe.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or point to the information that follows (an explanation, a fact, an opinion, etc.). Often followed by a verb clause: "Voilà ce que je pense..." = "Here’s what I think..."
target_language_example: Voilà ce que je veux dire : on doit partir maintenant.
native_language_example: Here’s what I mean: we have to leave now.

additional_notes: Used to end an explanation or minimize a reason: “simply,” “nothing more.” Often comes after a short statement to mean “that’s the whole story” (sometimes with a matter-of-fact tone). Can also be used alone: “Voilà tout.”
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas envie de sortir ce soir, voilà tout.
native_language_example: I don’t feel like going out tonight, that’s all.

target_language_multi_word_term: avoir (quelque chose / rien) à voir avec
meaning: to have (something / nothing) to do with; to be related to.
additional_notes: Used to link two things and say they are connected (or not). Very common patterns: « avoir quelque chose à voir avec + nom/pronom » (to have something to do with), and « n’avoir rien à voir avec + nom/pronom » / « Rien à voir avec… » (to have nothing to do with / nothing to do with…). Often followed by a person (« avec Linda », « avec vous ») or an idea (« avec la chance »).
target_language_example: Ça n’a rien à voir avec toi.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with you.

meaning: to see/find out what’s going on (what’s happening).
additional_notes: Used when you go check a situation to understand what is happening (often because you heard something, there’s confusion, or you’re curious). Common with aller/va/allons/je vais: « Va/Allons voir ce qui se passe. »
target_language_example: J'entends du bruit dehors : je vais voir ce qui se passe.
native_language_example: I hear noise outside—I’m going to see what’s going on.

meaning: To see clearly; to see things clearly (understand).
additional_notes: Used literally (having good visibility or eyesight) and figuratively (to think clearly, understand a situation, or make things clearer). Often appears with negation: « Je n’y vois pas clair » = “I can’t see clearly / I can’t make sense of it.”
target_language_example: Avec toutes ces informations, j’ai du mal à y voir clair.
native_language_example: With all this information, I’m having trouble seeing things clearly (making sense of it).

meaning: to see/watch a movie (go to the movies).
additional_notes: Means either watching a movie in general or going out to a cinema to watch one—often used with "aller" (aller voir un film) to emphasize going to see it. "Film" can mean a movie (and also a film/movie in a broader sense).
target_language_example: On va voir un film ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we going to see a movie tonight?

meaning: to see a doctor (to consult a doctor).
additional_notes: Common way to say you’re going to consult a doctor (not just ‘see’ visually). Often used with devoir/pouvoir: « Je dois voir un médecin » (I need to see a doctor). You can also say « aller voir un médecin » for emphasis on going to the appointment; with advice: « Tu devrais voir un médecin ».
target_language_example: Si ça ne va pas mieux demain, je vais voir un médecin.
native_language_example: If it’s not better tomorrow, I’m going to see a doctor.

meaning: to see (something) coming; to get by for now / tide things over
additional_notes: 1) With an object ("le/la/ça"), it means to foresee something before it happens: « J'aurais dû le voir venir » = “I should have seen it coming.” 2) Used alone or with « de quoi/pour », it means having enough to manage for the moment (especially money/food/time): « On a de quoi voir venir » = “We’ve got enough to get by for now.”
target_language_example: Avec ce que j'ai économisé, je peux voir venir pendant quelques semaines.
native_language_example: With what I saved, I can get by for a few weeks.

additional_notes: Used to talk about looking at something (often something you’re about to be shown). Common in phrases like "viens/venez voir ça" (come and see this/that), "attends/attendez de voir ça" (wait till you see this/that), and "aller voir ça" (go and have a look). "Ça" usually means "this/that" depending on context.
target_language_example: Viens voir ça, c’est incroyable !
native_language_example: Come check this out, it’s incredible!

meaning: "do you see?" / "can you see?" (also used like "you see...?" or "see?" in conversation).
additional_notes: From the verb *voir* (to see): *tu vois* = "you see". In questions, French often inverts it to *vois-tu ?* (more formal/literary than everyday *tu vois ?*). Can be literal (seeing with your eyes) or figurative (understanding): *Ne vois-tu pas ce qui se passe ?* = "Don’t you see/realize what’s happening?" Often used in rhetorical questions or to prompt agreement.
target_language_example: Vois-tu ce panneau là-bas ?
native_language_example: Can you see that sign over there?

vois-tu un inconvénient à ce que

target_language_multi_word_term: vois-tu un inconvénient à ce que
meaning: "Do you mind if…?" / "Would it bother you if…?"
additional_notes: A polite way to ask permission or check whether something would be a problem. It’s often followed by the subjunctive: « Vois-tu un inconvénient à ce que je + subjunctive… ? » (e.g., « …à ce que nous entrions ? »). You can also use it in a more formal register with « voyez-vous ».
target_language_example: Vois-tu un inconvénient à ce que j’ouvre la fenêtre ?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I open the window?

additional_notes: Common spoken/informal negative form where "ne" is dropped: "je vois pas" = "je ne vois pas" (I don’t see). Used both for literal sight (not seeing something) and figurative meaning (not understanding / not noticing): "Tu vois pas ce qui se passe ?" = "Don’t you see what’s happening?"
target_language_example: Je vois pas pourquoi tu es en colère.
native_language_example: I don’t see (understand) why you’re angry.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a car you rent (from an agency/company) for a short period. Often seen on signs or in contracts (e.g., « Voiture de location exclue » = rental car excluded). You can also say « une voiture de location » or simply « une voiture de location » in conversation when specifying it’s not your own car.
target_language_example: Nous avons pris une voiture de location pour le week-end.
native_language_example: We got a rental car for the weekend.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for a fast, performance-focused car. Use it with articles (une/la/ma voiture de sport) and verbs like conduire (“to drive”) or avoir (“to have”).
target_language_example: Elle rêve d'acheter une voiture de sport.
native_language_example: She dreams of buying a sports car.

additional_notes: A masculine noun. Usually used with the verb jouer: « jouer au volley-ball » (“to play volleyball”). You can also say « un joueur de volley-ball » (“a volleyball player”).
target_language_example: On joue au volley-ball à la plage cet été.
native_language_example: We’re playing volleyball at the beach this summer.

meaning: "are they going?" / "are they going to…?" (question form).
additional_notes: This is the verb "aller" (to go) in the present tense (ils vont = they go/they are going) with inversion for questions: "vont-ils ?" = "are they going?". Very often it’s followed by an infinitive to form the near future: "vont-ils + infinitive" = "are they going to + verb?" (e.g., "Que vont-ils faire ?" = "What are they going to do?").
target_language_example: Vont-ils partir demain ?
native_language_example: Are they going to leave tomorrow?

additional_notes: Refers to a person's personal items (bags, clothes, etc.). Used with "vous" (formal singular or plural), for example in instructions like « Prenez vos affaires » (Take your things) or questions like « Où sont vos affaires ? » (Where are your things?). Note: French « affaires » often means "things"—not necessarily "affairs" in the English sense.
target_language_example: N'oubliez pas vos affaires dans le train.
native_language_example: Don't forget your belongings on the train.

meaning: “your friends” (addressing more than one person, or speaking formally to one person).
additional_notes: “Vos” is the possessive adjective for “your” used with *vous* (formal singular or plural). With *amis* (masculine plural), it can refer to a mixed group of friends (men and women) or all men; for all women, you can say “vos amies.” Often used in questions like “Qui sont vos amis ?” (“Who are your friends?”) or to refer to people waiting/located somewhere (“Vos amis vous attendent.”).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous appeler vos amis ?
native_language_example: Can you call your friends?

additional_notes: "Vos" is the possessive for "your" (used with plural nouns, and also as a polite/formal "your"). "Armes" means weapons (guns, swords, etc.). Often used in commands in a military/police/action context: *Baissez vos armes* (Lower your weapons), *Rendez vos armes* (Surrender your weapons).
target_language_example: Veuillez déposer vos armes au contrôle de sécurité.
native_language_example: Please leave your weapons at the security checkpoint.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective “vos” with the plural noun “enfants.” It can mean “your” when speaking to more than one person (informal plural) or to one person in a polite/formal way (vous). Often used in questions like « Et vos enfants ? » (“And your kids/children?”).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous garder vos enfants avec vous, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Could you keep your children with you, please?

meaning: "your mouths" / "your ugly mugs" (vulgar insult; often = "shut the f*** up!")
additional_notes: "Gueule" is a crude word for a mouth (originally an animal’s mouth) and, in slang, also a person’s face (like "mug"). In the very common command "Fermez vos gueules !", it’s an aggressive way to tell several people to be quiet. It can also be used to mean “your faces” in insults like "Je ne veux plus voir vos gueules" (I don’t want to see your faces again). Extremely rude—avoid in normal conversation.
target_language_example: Fermez vos gueules et écoutez-moi !
native_language_example: Shut the f*** up and listen to me!

meaning: your hands (to multiple people, or politely to one person).
additional_notes: Used with commands/instructions addressing a group (or using polite vous to one person): Donnez-moi vos mains (Give me your hands), Montrez-moi vos mains (Show me your hands). Contrast: tes mains = your hands (informal, one person).
target_language_example: Lavez vos mains avant de manger.
native_language_example: Wash your hands before eating.

additional_notes: Used especially by police, border agents, or security to ask you to show your identification (ID card, passport, residence permit, etc.). Often said as a short command/question: « Vos papiers ! » or « Vos papiers ? ».
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, monsieur, vos papiers, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Excuse me, sir—your ID, please.

meaning: "your parents" (speaking to more than one person, or formally).
additional_notes: Uses the possessive determiner "vos" with the plural noun "parents". "Vos" is used with vous (either plural "you" or formal singular "you"). For one person informally, you’d usually say "tes parents"; for one person formally, "vos parents" is also possible. Common with verbs like "obéir à" (to obey), "manquer à" (to miss someone), and "être proche de" (to be close to).
target_language_example: Vos parents sont très gentils.
native_language_example: Your parents are very nice.

additional_notes: "Vos" is the possessive used with "vous" (either talking to more than one person, or to one person in a polite/formal way). It can be literal (someone’s eyes) or figurative in common expressions like "à vos yeux" = "in your eyes / in your view".
target_language_example: Je peux lire la vérité dans vos yeux.
native_language_example: I can read the truth in your eyes.

additional_notes: A very formal title used when addressing a prince/princess or other high-ranking royal. It’s used as a direct form of address (often with a comma), and it takes the polite pronoun “vous” when speaking to the person.
target_language_example: Votre Altesse, puis-je vous accompagner ?
native_language_example: Your Highness, may I accompany you?

meaning: “Your Excellency” (a very formal title of address).
additional_notes: Used to address certain high-ranking officials/diplomats (e.g., an ambassador). It’s extremely formal. In French it’s commonly followed by a verb in the 3rd person (as in: « Votre Excellence a entendu ? »). Often capitalized: « Votre Excellence ».
target_language_example: Votre Excellence, puis-je vous poser une question ?
native_language_example: Your Excellency, may I ask you a question?

meaning: Your Majesty (formal way to address a king or queen).
additional_notes: A very formal, respectful form of address used when speaking to a monarch. It can be used on its own as a direct address (“Votre Majesté !”) or within a sentence as the subject (“Votre Majesté comprend…”). The noun is capitalized (Majesté), and in speech it’s usually paired with very formal language.
target_language_example: Votre Majesté, puis-je vous poser une question ?
native_language_example: Your Majesty, may I ask you a question?

additional_notes: Used when asking for or requesting someone’s address (postal address, contact address, etc.), often in forms and polite instructions (e.g., veuillez indiquer…). « Votre » is the formal/plural possessive “your.”
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous confirmer votre adresse, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you confirm your address, please?

additional_notes: Uses the polite/plural possessive "votre" with "aide". Common in thank-you phrases (e.g., "Merci de votre aide", "Nous vous remercions de votre aide") and when saying someone needs help ("avoir besoin de votre aide"). In casual one-on-one situations, you may also hear "ton aide" (your help, informal singular).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me donner votre aide, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you help me, please?

additional_notes: Used to address one person politely (vous) or more than one person. Often refers to a bedroom (at home) or a hotel room, depending on context. "Votre" agrees with the noun (chambre is feminine singular).
target_language_example: Votre chambre est au troisième étage.
native_language_example: Your room is on the third floor.

additional_notes: Used to talk politely to one person or several people (votre = ‘your’ formal or plural). Refers to the person’s relatives as a group; can include immediate and/or extended family depending on context.
target_language_example: Comment va votre famille ?
native_language_example: How is your family?

additional_notes: Used to address someone formally ("vous") when talking about their wife. In everyday French, "femme" can also mean “woman,” but with a possessive like "votre" it usually refers to a spouse/partner. For informal "you," use "ta femme".
target_language_example: Comment va votre femme ?
native_language_example: How is your wife?

additional_notes: "Votre" is the formal singular “your” (to one person you address as vous) or the plural “your” (to multiple people). "Fille" means “daughter” (it can also mean “girl” in other contexts). To say “your daughter” informally to one person, use "ta fille".
target_language_example: Est-ce que votre fille habite ici ?
native_language_example: Does your daughter live here?

additional_notes: Used to address someone formally (or to more than one person) when talking about their son. With one person informally, you’d usually say “ton fils”.
target_language_example: Votre fils est à l’école aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Is your son at school today?

additional_notes: “Votre” is the possessive used with “vous”: it can mean either (1) your (to one person, polite/formal) or (2) your (to several people). “Frère” is masculine singular, so it’s “votre frère” even if you’re talking to a woman. In informal speech to one person you’ll often hear “ton frère”.
target_language_example: Votre frère arrive ce soir.
native_language_example: Your brother is arriving tonight.

additional_notes: "Votre" is the formal/plural form of "your" (used with one person you address as "vous," or with multiple people). "Maison" is the physical house; in everyday speech it can also mean "home," especially when talking about leaving/returning to it (e.g., "quitter votre maison").
target_language_example: Je peux venir à votre maison après le travail ?
native_language_example: Can I come to your place after work?

additional_notes: Polite/formal way to address someone and refer to their husband (e.g., with strangers, customers, or in formal situations). Use it when speaking directly to the person (vouvoiement). With friends/family you’d often say "ton mari".
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, votre mari peut venir un instant ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can your husband come for a moment?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective « votre » with « mère ». « Votre » can mean “your” when speaking politely to one person (vous) or when speaking to more than one person. In casual speech to one person you’d usually say « ta mère » (informal “your mom”).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, comment s’appelle votre mère ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is your mother’s name?

additional_notes: Used when speaking politely to one person (vous) or to more than one person. Common in questions and requests for identification: "Quel est votre nom ?" / "C'est quoi votre nom ?". With "déjà", it means the speaker has forgotten and is asking again ("what’s your name again?").
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, quel est votre nom, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is your name, please?

meaning: your point of view; your opinion/perspective.
additional_notes: Polite/formal way to ask for or refer to someone’s opinion (often in discussions, meetings, or debates). You can also say "ton point de vue" (informal singular "you") or "votre point de vue" for one person (formal) or a group. Common verbs: "donner/expliquer/partager son point de vue" (give/explain/share one’s point of view).
target_language_example: J’aimerais connaître votre point de vue sur ce projet.
native_language_example: I’d like to know your point of view on this project.

additional_notes: Means “your father” when talking to one person politely (vous) or to more than one person. It can also be used when addressing someone directly about their father: « Embrassez votre père. »
target_language_example: Je vais appeler votre père pour le prévenir.
native_language_example: I’m going to call your father to let him know.

additional_notes: "Votre" is the formal/polite form of "your" (used with "vous"). "Travail" can mean the work you’re doing (a task, schoolwork, a project) or your job in general; the context makes it clear. Often used in polite questions about progress: « Où en êtes-vous avec votre travail ? »
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous m’envoyer votre travail avant ce soir ?
native_language_example: Can you send me your work before tonight?

additional_notes: Often used with time expressions to mean “in your life” (dans votre vie) or “of your life” (de votre vie), especially in superlatives: le plus beau jour de votre vie (“the best day of your life”). Also appears in fixed expressions like gagner votre vie (“to earn a living”).
target_language_example: C'est la meilleure décision de votre vie.
native_language_example: It’s the best decision of your life.

additional_notes: “Votre” is the possessive adjective used with a singular noun like “voiture.” It can mean “your” when speaking politely to one person (vous = formal singular) or when addressing more than one person (vous = plural). Often used in questions in service situations: “Et votre voiture ?” (“And your car?”).
target_language_example: Où est garée votre voiture ?
native_language_example: Where is your car parked?

additional_notes: Polite way to ask a question with inversion (verb + -tu). It’s the conditional of « vouloir » (to want), often used to soften a request/offer. Common patterns: « Voudrais-tu + infinitive… ? » (Would you like to…?) and « Voudrais-tu + noun… ? » (Would you like a…?). A less formal word order is « Tu voudrais… ? ».
target_language_example: Voudrais-tu venir dîner chez nous ce soir ?
native_language_example: Would you like to come have dinner at our place tonight?

additional_notes: Very polite form of «vouloir» used to make offers, invitations, or requests. It’s the conditional + «vous» (formal/plural “you”), common in restaurants, customer service, and formal situations. Often followed by an infinitive for requests («Voudriez-vous fermer… ?» = “Would you close…?”) or by a noun for offers («Voudriez-vous du café ?» = “Would you like some coffee?”).
target_language_example: Voudriez-vous m'aider, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Would you help me, please?

additional_notes: A polite or formal way to ask what someone wants or to offer something. It uses inversion (verb + subject pronoun), which is common in formal questions. "Vous" can refer to one person formally or to several people.
target_language_example: Voulez-vous venir avec nous ?
native_language_example: Would you like to come with us?

meaning: “Would you like me to … (for you)?” (polite offer).
additional_notes: Used to politely offer to do something for someone. It introduces a verb in the subjunctive: « Voulez-vous que je vous appelle… ? » = “Would you like me to call you…?” « vous » is the formal/plural “you” (to one person politely or to several people). Often used in service situations (hotel, restaurant, customer support) and with helpful offers.
target_language_example: Voulez-vous que je vous aide à porter vos sacs ?
native_language_example: Would you like me to help you carry your bags?

additional_notes: A polite/formal question: "voulez-vous" = "do you want" and "vraiment" adds emphasis ("really"). Often used to challenge or double-check someone’s intention, sometimes sounding skeptical depending on tone. In informal speech, people more often say "tu veux vraiment… ?" or "vous voulez vraiment… ?".
target_language_example: Voulez-vous vraiment partir si tôt ?
native_language_example: Do you really want to leave so early?

meaning: to be willing to; to kindly agree to (do something)
additional_notes: Used to express willingness or polite agreement. Common in requests: « Voulez-vous bien + infinitif ? » ≈ “Would you kindly + verb?” (polite, but can sound firm depending on tone). Also used to accept a request: « Je veux bien. » = “Sure / I’d be happy to.” Here the infinitive may be expressed or implied.
target_language_example: Merci de vouloir bien m'aider demain.
native_language_example: Thank you for being willing to help me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Usually used to talk about the meaning of words, signs, actions, or situations. Although the words literally look like 'to want to say,' the common meaning is 'to mean.' Often appears in questions like Qu'est-ce que ça peut vouloir dire ? ('What could that mean?').
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que ça peut vouloir dire ?
native_language_example: What could that mean?

additional_notes: Used with "vous" to emphasize that the person addressed will do something personally (not someone else): e.g., "Demandez-lui vous-même" = ask him/her yourself. It can be reflexive (about the same person: "à vous-même" = to yourself) or emphatic ("vous-même" = you yourself). For one person informally, use "toi-même"; for "we" use "nous-mêmes"; for "they" use "eux-mêmes/elles-mêmes". Often appears after the verb or after a preposition ("par vous-même", "à vous-même").
target_language_example: Faites-le vous-même, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Do it yourself, please.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize “vous” (“you yourselves”) or after a preposition, especially in phrases like « par vous-mêmes » (“by yourselves”) and « voyez vous-mêmes » (“see for yourselves”). It agrees with the person/number: « moi-même », « toi-même », « lui-même / elle-même », « nous-mêmes », « vous-mêmes », « eux-mêmes / elles-mêmes ».
target_language_example: Faites-le par vous-mêmes.
native_language_example: Do it by yourselves.

additional_notes: Used in yes/no questions with inversion in the passé composé: auxiliary + -t- + il. Here, "vous" is an object pronoun placed before the verb (often meaning "to you" or "you" as the person affected): "Tom vous a-t-il dit… ?" = "Has Tom told you…?" This pattern is quite formal/written; in everyday speech you often hear "Est-ce qu'il vous a… ?" or "Il vous a… ?"
target_language_example: Le médecin vous a-t-il expliqué les résultats ?
native_language_example: Did the doctor explain the results to you?

meaning: "Have you been…?" / "Did someone… to you?" (formal question form).
additional_notes: Used to form a formal yes/no question with inversion in the past tense (passé composé): on (meaning “someone/people”) is the subject, a is the auxiliary “has,” and vous is the object (“you”). The -t- is just a sound link (euphonic) between a and on. Often translates to English with a passive idea (“Have you been told…?”) or “Did someone…?” depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Vous a-t-on demandé votre passeport à l’entrée ?
native_language_example: Did they ask you for your passport at the entrance?

additional_notes: Used with the verb dire in the passé composé: subject + vous + a/ont dit. It refers to what someone told you (either one person you’re addressing formally, or multiple people). Example patterns: « Qu’est-ce qu’il vous a dit ? » (What did he tell you?), « On vous a dit… » (You were told…).
target_language_example: Qui vous a dit ça ?
native_language_example: Who told you that?

meaning: "have I ... you?" (formal/inverted question in the passé composé).
additional_notes: Used in formal or written French to ask a yes/no question with subject–verb inversion: object pronoun + auxiliary + subject (e.g., « Vous ai-je + past participle… ? »). It usually means “Have I [done something] to you/for you?” or “Did I [do something] to you/for you?”
target_language_example: Vous ai-je déjà dit merci ?
native_language_example: Have I already thanked you?

additional_notes: This is a common fragment used after "Je" (or another subject) in the passé composé: "Je vous ai dit de + infinitive". It addresses someone formally or more than one person ("vous"). In casual speech, you’ll often hear "Je t’ai dit de…" for one person you’re on "tu" terms with.
target_language_example: Je vous ai dit de fermer la porte.
native_language_example: I told you to close the door.

additional_notes: "Vous" is the polite/formal singular "you" or the plural "you"; it can refer to one person (formal) or to multiple people. "Vous aider" means "to help you" and is often used after another verb (e.g., "je veux", "je suis venu", "pouvons-nous") or in questions ("Pourquoi dois-je vous aider ?").
target_language_example: Je peux vous aider avec ça ?
native_language_example: Can I help you with that?

additional_notes: "Vous" is the formal "you" (singular) and also the plural "you" (talking to more than one person). "Vous aimez" can be a statement ("You like...") or a question ("Do you like...?")—in speech, the voice usually rises at the end for a yes/no question; in writing you’ll see a question mark. "Aimer" can mean "to like" or, in some contexts, "to love" (stronger), depending on what follows and the situation.
target_language_example: Vous aimez le café ou le thé ?
native_language_example: Do you like coffee or tea?

additional_notes: Usually followed by an infinitive to talk about the near future or a strong prediction: vous allez rater, vous allez faire, vous allez rire. Here, vous can mean either plural "you" or singular formal "you." On its own, vous allez can also literally mean "you are going/you go," but in these examples it is the common futur proche structure.
target_language_example: Vous allez comprendre bientôt.
native_language_example: You’re going to understand soon.

meaning: "you are going to have to" / "you will have to" (formal or plural).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone (politely/formally, or more than one person) that a requirement is coming up. It combines near-future "vous allez" (you’re going to) + "devoir" (to have to / must) + an infinitive verb: "Vous allez devoir attendre / partir / me suivre." Often implies obligation or necessity, sometimes as an instruction.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous allez devoir remplir ce formulaire.
native_language_example: Excuse me, you’re going to have to fill out this form.

meaning: 'you are going to do' (formal or plural).
additional_notes: Uses the near-future construction aller + infinitive: vous allez + faire. Common in questions (Qu’est-ce que vous allez faire ? = “What are you going to do?”) and in firm instructions (Voilà ce que vous allez faire. = “Here’s what you’re going to do.”). "Vous" can mean “you” to one person politely/formally, or “you all.”
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que vous allez faire ce soir ?
native_language_example: What are you going to do tonight?

meaning: “you are going to … me” / “you’re going to … to me” (formal or plural “you”).
additional_notes: Used in the near future construction: **vous allez + infinitive** (“you’re going to do…”). **me** is an object pronoun meaning “me/to me,” placed before the infinitive (e.g., *vous allez me demander…* = “you’re going to ask me…”). **vous** is used for one person formally or for multiple people.
target_language_example: Vous allez me dire la vérité ?
native_language_example: Are you going to tell me the truth?

additional_notes: Used to announce what will happen next or to insist that the listener will realize something soon. Depending on tone and context, it can sound reassuring (“you’ll see, it’s great”), confident (“you’ll see, I’m right”), or threatening (“you’ll see!”). Often said alone as a warning: « Vous allez voir. »
target_language_example: Vous allez voir, ce restaurant est excellent.
native_language_example: You’ll see, this restaurant is excellent.

additional_notes: Reflexive form of "s’asseoir" used with "vous" for polite address (one person) or for multiple people. Often appears after an invitation like "Venez" (Come) or "Pouvez-vous" (Can you).
target_language_example: Vous pouvez vous asseoir ici, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: You can sit here, please.

additional_notes: Future tense of avoir for vous. Used to talk about what someone will possess, experience, need, or have available later (e.g., avoir le temps, avoir besoin de, avoir accès à, avoir le choix). Also used in polite instructions or formal contexts.
target_language_example: Vous aurez la réponse demain.
native_language_example: You will have the answer tomorrow.

meaning: "you should have" / "you ought to have" (formal or plural).
additional_notes: This is the conditional perfect of devoir ("to have to / must"). It’s often used to express criticism, regret, or hindsight about something that didn’t happen: "You should have told me." With "vous," it can address one person formally or several people. It’s followed by an infinitive: "vous auriez dû + infinitive" (e.g., "vous auriez dû me le dire").
target_language_example: Vous auriez dû appeler avant de venir.
native_language_example: You should have called before coming.

meaning: 'you could have' / 'you would have been able to'.
additional_notes: Past conditional of pouvoir (vous + auriez + pu + infinitive). Often used to talk about a missed possibility or to express a reproach/criticism: «Vous auriez pu m’appeler» = “You could have called me (but you didn’t).” Can also express what was possible in a hypothetical past: «Si vous étiez venus plus tôt, vous auriez pu la voir.»
target_language_example: Vous auriez pu me prévenir avant de venir.
native_language_example: You could have warned me before coming.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people being addressed (plural), often to highlight them as a distinct group (e.g., contrasting with "nous autres" = "us"). Common in some varieties of French (notably Canadian/Québécois). It can sound emphatic and sometimes slightly distancing depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Vous autres, vous venez d’où ?
native_language_example: Where are you guys from?

additional_notes: Used with vous, which can mean either one person in a formal way or more than one person. It can show possession/state ('you have'), and it is also very commonly used as an auxiliary in the passé composé: vous avez + past participle = 'you did / you have done' (for example, vous avez menti = 'you lied').
target_language_example: Vous avez une question ?
native_language_example: Do you have a question?

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to say someone did something well ("Vous avez bien expliqué" = "You explained well"). Very commonly used as "Vous avez bien fait de + infinitive" to mean "You did the right thing to..." or "Good thing you...". In questions, it can also check/confirm an action politely: "Vous avez bien reçu mon email ?" = "Did you receive my email?"
target_language_example: Vous avez bien fait de venir plus tôt.
native_language_example: You did the right thing coming earlier.

additional_notes: Polite or plural way to say “you said” (passé composé of dire). Used to refer back to someone’s words: «J’ai réfléchi à ce que vous avez dit.» It can also be used in a question to ask someone to repeat/confirm: «Qu’est-ce que vous avez dit ?»
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous avez dit que le train partait à quelle heure ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time did you say the train was leaving?

additional_notes: Polite/formal question (vous) using the passé composé of voir (“to see”) with déjà (“already/ever”). Used to ask if someone has seen something before, often with surprise: « Vous avez déjà vu… ? » You can swap in objects like « cet homme », « un truc pareil », etc.
target_language_example: Vous avez déjà vu ce film ?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen this movie?

additional_notes: Form of **devoir** in the past (**passé composé**): **vous avez dû + infinitive**. It can mean (1) a past obligation: *Vous avez dû partir* = “You had to leave,” or (2) a deduction about the past (very common): *Vous avez dû confondre* = “You must have been mistaken.” The context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Vous avez dû oublier de fermer la porte.
native_language_example: You must have forgotten to close the door.

additional_notes: Literally the passé composé of entendre (“to hear”). It can be a statement (“You heard…”) or, with rising intonation or a question mark, a question meaning “Did you hear…?” Often used to refer back to something people have just heard (e.g., testimony, an order, what someone said).
target_language_example: Vous avez entendu ce qu’il a dit ?
native_language_example: Did you hear what he said?

additional_notes: Polite/plural "you" (vous) + passé composé of "avoir" (to have): "vous avez eu" literally means "you have had," but in everyday English it’s often "you had" or "you got" depending on context. Common in questions like "Comment vous avez eu… ?" = "How did you get…?" Also appears in the fixed structure "avoir à faire" (to have to do): "Tout ce que vous avez eu à faire…" = "All you had to do…".
target_language_example: Vous avez eu le temps de lire le message ?
native_language_example: Did you have time to read the message?

additional_notes: Passé composé of « faire » with the subject « vous » (formal ‘you’ or plural ‘you’). Often followed by a direct object: « vous avez fait + nom » (you did/made + noun). In « Vous avez fait une bonne affaire », it means ‘you got a good deal’ (literally: ‘you made a good deal’).
target_language_example: Vous avez fait du bon travail.
native_language_example: You did good work.

meaning: you did that / you have done that.
additional_notes: Passé composé of « faire » (vous + avez fait). Used with « vous » for one person you address formally or for multiple people. « ça » means “that/this” depending on context; often used to point out or accuse someone of an action (e.g., « exprès » = on purpose).
target_language_example: Pourquoi vous avez fait ça ?
native_language_example: Why did you do that?

additional_notes: Used with **vous** to address one person formally or multiple people. Often followed by **de + infinitive** for something you forgot to do ("Vous avez oublié de mentionner...") or a direct object for something you left behind ("Vous avez oublié les cuillères"). Can also be used alone as a reminder/question: "Vous avez oublié ?"
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous avez oublié votre sac.
native_language_example: Excuse me, you forgot your bag.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *parler* with *avoir* (used for a completed action in the past). Often followed by **de** to say what you talked about (*vous avez parlé de mon père* = you talked about my father) and by **avec** to say who you talked with (*vous avez parlé avec Tom* = you spoke with Tom). In a relative clause, **dont vous avez parlé** means “that/whom you talked about.”
target_language_example: Vous avez parlé de ce problème hier ?
native_language_example: Did you talk about this problem yesterday?

meaning: “you took” / “you have taken” (passé composé of prendre).
additional_notes: Used with the formal or plural “vous” to talk about something someone took, grabbed, removed, or chose/ordered. In questions, it often means “What did you have?” (e.g., at a restaurant or pharmacy): « Qu’est-ce que vous avez pris ? ». With time: « Vous avez pris votre temps » = “You took your time.”
target_language_example: Pourquoi est-ce que vous avez pris mon stylo ?
native_language_example: Why did you take my pen?

meaning: 'Have you found (it)?' / 'Did you find (it)?' (also: 'Did you figure it out?')
additional_notes: Literally “you have found.” It’s the polite/plural form (vous) of the past tense (passé composé) of trouver. Often used as a question with rising intonation: “Vous avez trouvé le commandant ?” = “Did you find the commander?” It can also stand alone (“Vous avez trouvé ?”) meaning “Have you found it?” or, depending on context (a solution, an answer), “Have you figured it out?”
target_language_example: Alors, vous avez trouvé la bonne adresse ?
native_language_example: So, did you find the right address?

additional_notes: Polite or plural way to ask if someone has seen/noticed something. Literally “you have seen” (passé composé of voir), but in everyday speech it often corresponds to English “did you see…?” or “have you seen…?” Used to draw attention to news, the weather, information, names on a list, etc.
target_language_example: Vous avez vu le nouveau message ?
native_language_example: Did you see the new message?

meaning: “you have been / you were” (past tense, formal or plural “you”).
additional_notes: Passé composé of « être » for « vous » (used for one person formally or for several people). Often followed by an adjective or past participle to describe a past state or situation: « Vous avez été patient. » / « Vous avez été prévenu. »
target_language_example: Vous avez été très patient avec moi.
native_language_example: You have been very patient with me.

additional_notes: Present-tense form of avoir used with vous. It can mean either 'you have' when speaking to several people, or 'you have' in a formal/polite way to one person. It is also common in expressions like vous avez l'air de... ('you seem to...').
target_language_example: Vous avez une minute ?
native_language_example: Do you have a minute?

meaning: "you need" / "do you need" (followed by a noun or an infinitive).
additional_notes: This is the polite/formal way to say someone needs something. It’s built from "avoir besoin de" = "to need." After it, use either a noun ("Vous avez besoin de vacances") or a verb in the infinitive ("Vous avez besoin de dormir"). For a question, use rising intonation ("Vous avez besoin de… ?") or inversion in more formal French ("Avez-vous besoin de… ?").
target_language_example: Vous avez besoin de parler à un médecin ?
native_language_example: Do you need to talk to a doctor?

additional_notes: Used with a plural noun to ask if someone has something (often “any” in questions: Vous avez des suggestions ?) or to state that they have some (Vous avez des raisins.). “Des” is the plural indefinite article (some/any).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous avez des questions ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have any questions?

meaning: "you look" / "you seem" (talking about someone’s appearance or impression).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to comment on how someone appears: "Vous avez l'air + adjectif" (e.g., heureux, fatigué, surpris(e)). Agreement: in writing, the adjective matches the person (surpris / surprise). Common variants: "tu as l'air" (informal singular), "il/elle a l'air", "ils/elles ont l'air".
target_language_example: Vous avez l'air fatigué aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: You look tired today.

meaning: "you have the right to" (you are allowed/entitled to).
