additional_notes: Used to state someone’s rights or legal entitlements, often in formal contexts (police, courts, rules). Followed by an infinitive verb: « Vous avez le droit de + infinitif » (e.g., « ne rien dire », « consulter », « vous défendre »).
target_language_example: Vous avez le droit de poser des questions avant de signer.
native_language_example: You have the right to ask questions before signing.

additional_notes: Used to agree with someone or acknowledge that what they said is correct. “Vous” is the polite or plural “you,” so it’s appropriate in formal situations or when speaking to more than one person. Often followed by “mais…” (“…but…”) to agree while adding a reservation.
target_language_example: Vous avez raison, c’est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: You’re right, it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Formal/polite way to tell someone they’re wrong ("vous" = you). Often used with softeners like "pardon" or "mais" to sound less blunt. You can also say "tu as tort" to one person you’re on "tu" terms with.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, mais vous avez tort sur ce point.
native_language_example: Excuse me, but you’re wrong about that point.

additional_notes: Literally means "you have a," but in questions it commonly means "do you have a ... ?". "vous" is used for plural "you" or polite singular "you," and "un" is used before a masculine singular noun.
target_language_example: Vous avez un moment ?
native_language_example: Do you have a moment?

meaning: "do you have a..." / "you have a..." (to address someone politely).
additional_notes: Polite form with "vous" (you). It can be a question (often with rising intonation or in "Est-ce que vous avez une... ?") or a statement ("Vous avez une..." = "You have a..."). "Une" is the feminine form of "a/an"; use "vous avez un" for masculine nouns. Often used to ask for an item or a document: "Vous avez une carte d'identité ?"
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous avez une minute ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have a minute?

meaning: "you had" / "you were" (imperfect past, formal or plural).
additional_notes: "Vous" can mean "you" (formal singular) or "you" (plural). "Aviez" is the imperfect tense of "avoir" (to have), used for ongoing states, descriptions, or habitual situations in the past. It often translates as "you had" (Vous aviez raison. = You were right.) or, in common expressions, "you were" (Vous aviez l'air fatigué. = You looked tired.)
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, vous aviez déjà terminé.
native_language_example: When I arrived, you had already finished.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of avoir (vous aviez) with raison to say someone was correct about something in the past. Addressed to one person you’re being polite with (vous) or to multiple people. Often followed by sur + topic: « Vous aviez raison sur le règlement. »
target_language_example: Pardon, vous aviez raison depuis le début.
native_language_example: Sorry, you were right from the start.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: it starts the past infinitive, with the object pronoun vous placed before avoir, as in vous avoir vu = "to have seen you." It is used for an action completed earlier, often after expressions like content de, regretter, penser, or se souvenir. vous means "you" (formal singular or plural).
target_language_example: Je suis content de vous avoir vu.
native_language_example: I'm glad to have seen you.

additional_notes: Uses the verb *comprendre* in the present tense with *vous* (talking to one person formally, or to several people). Often used to check understanding or add emphasis, like “you see?” / “you understand, right?”.
target_language_example: Vous comprenez ce que je veux dire ?
native_language_example: Do you understand what I mean?

additional_notes: From connaître (“to know / be familiar with”). Used with vous (formal singular “you” or plural “you”). Often followed by a person, place, or thing you’re familiar with: « Vous connaissez cet endroit ? » = “Do you know this place?” Also used reflexively as « vous vous connaissez » (“you know each other”). For information/facts, French often uses « vous savez » instead.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous connaissez le chemin pour aller à la gare ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you know the way to the train station?

meaning: “do you think that…?” / “you think that…?” (often challenging or sarcastic).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone believes or assumes. Very common in questions like « Vous croyez que… ? », often implying doubt, disbelief, or criticism (similar to “Do you really think…?”). In neutral situations you can also say « Vous pensez que… ? ».
target_language_example: Vous croyez que je vais accepter ça ?
native_language_example: Do you really think I’m going to accept that?

meaning: “do you think/believe that it’s…?” (used to ask someone’s opinion or guess).
additional_notes: Formal/polite: uses "vous". Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or adjective to propose a possibility or challenge someone’s assumption (e.g., "possible", "ce garçon", "pour l'argent", "un jeu"). In casual speech you may also hear it used similarly to "vous pensez que c’est…".
target_language_example: Vous croyez que c'est possible ?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s possible?

additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity. "Vous" can mean either plural "you" or formal singular "you". It is usually followed by an infinitive verb: "vous devez partir" = "you must leave."
target_language_example: Vous devez attendre ici.
native_language_example: you must wait here.

meaning: “you must have / you must be” (you’re supposed to have; strong assumption).
additional_notes: Used to address someone formally (vous). With a noun, it often means “you must have …” (Vous devez avoir beaucoup de questions.). With certain adjectives like faim/soif/peur, French uses avoir (“to have”), so it translates as “you must be …” (Vous devez avoir faim = “You must be hungry”). Often expresses a logical guess (“I assume you…”), not just an obligation.
target_language_example: Après ce long voyage, vous devez avoir envie de vous reposer.
native_language_example: After that long trip, you must feel like resting.

additional_notes: Uses the verb devoir (vous devez) + infinitive faire to express obligation or necessity. Used with vous for speaking politely to one person or to multiple people. Often followed by another infinitive or phrase: vous devez faire comme…, vous devez faire de votre mieux, etc.
target_language_example: Pour réussir, vous devez faire attention aux détails.
native_language_example: To succeed, you must pay attention to details.

additional_notes: Uses the verb *devoir* ("to have to / must") + *partir* ("to leave"). *Vous* is the formal or plural "you". Often used to give a firm instruction or express urgency, especially with additions like *tout de suite* (right away) or *et vite* (and quickly).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous devez partir immédiatement.
native_language_example: Excuse me, you must leave immediately.

meaning: you must stay / you have to remain.
additional_notes: Uses the formal/plural subject "vous" + "devoir" (devez = "must/have to") + the infinitive "rester" (to stay). Often followed by a place (rester là-bas), an adjective (rester tranquille = stay calm/quiet), or a state like "rester éveillé" (stay awake). With adjectives, agreement can change: "éveillé" (one person) vs "éveillés" (several people).
target_language_example: Vous devez rester ici jusqu'à 18 h.
native_language_example: You must stay here until 6 p.m.

meaning: "you must / you have to" + "yourself" (used before a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive infinitive: « vous devez vous + verb » (e.g., vous reposer, vous détendre, vous laver, vous entraîner). « Vous devez » = a strong obligation/necessity; « vous » here is the reflexive pronoun that matches the subject « vous ».
target_language_example: Vous devez vous arrêter ici.
native_language_example: You have to stop here.

additional_notes: Uses the verb devoir + infinitive (être). It can mean obligation (“you have to be…”) or a logical guess/deduction (“you must be…”). With vous, this can address one person formally or multiple people; the adjective that follows often agrees accordingly (fatigué/fatiguée/fatigués/fatiguées).
target_language_example: Vous devez être très occupé aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: You must be very busy today.

additional_notes: Used to make a likely assumption about someone, often as a polite comment: «Vous devez être très fiers de votre fille.» = “You must be very proud of your daughter.” It addresses one person formally (vous) or several people. The adjective that follows usually agrees in gender/number (e.g., fier/fière/fiers/fières; occupé/occupée/occupés/occupées).
target_language_example: Vous devez être très fatigué après le voyage.
native_language_example: You must be very tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Used to give advice, recommendations, or mild criticism. "Vous" can mean plural "you" or formal singular "you." It is usually followed by an infinitive verb: "vous devriez attendre" = "you should wait."
target_language_example: Vous devriez essayer ce restaurant.
native_language_example: You should try this restaurant.

additional_notes: Polite/formal way to give advice or a recommendation. Built from: vous (you, formal/plural) + devriez (conditional of devoir, “should/ought to”) + aller (to go). Often followed by an infinitive (aller lui parler = “go talk to him”) or a place (aller chez un dentiste = “go to a dentist”; aller chez vous = “go home”).
target_language_example: Vous devriez aller consulter un médecin.
native_language_example: You should go see a doctor.

meaning: "you should" (giving advice) + a reflexive verb ("yourself" / "to ... yourself").
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression, but a common pattern: the conditional of devoir ("vous devriez" = "you should") followed by the reflexive pronoun "vous" before a reflexive verb (e.g., vous excuser, vous mettre en route, vous faire examiner, vous mettre au régime). The second "vous" refers back to the subject and is required by the reflexive verb.
target_language_example: Vous devriez vous reposer un peu.
native_language_example: You should rest a little.

additional_notes: Used to give advice, express expectation, or make a recommendation to one person politely (vous) or to multiple people. Followed by a place/state/adjective (au lit, content, silencieux) or by an adjective + de + infinitive (capable de faire...). It’s the conditional of devoir (vous devriez), which often sounds a bit softer/more polite than the simple present vous devez ('you must').
target_language_example: Vous devriez être plus prudent quand vous traversez la rue.
native_language_example: You should be more careful when you cross the street.

additional_notes: Used with vous meaning either 'you' (formal singular) or 'you' (plural). Often appears after another verb, as in je peux vous dire or je veux vous dire, with the object pronoun vous placed before dire.
target_language_example: Je vais vous dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I'm going to tell you the truth.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker wants to say something to the person they’re addressing (vous = “you” formal singular or plural). It often introduces an important, personal, or attention-getting remark. Common with different verbs to show nuance: je veux/je dois/je devrais/je voudrais/je peux/je vais vous dire quelque chose.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je dois vous dire quelque chose d’important.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have to tell you something important.

meaning: to tell you something (let me tell you something).
additional_notes: Common setup phrase used before giving an important point, warning, or opinion. The object pronoun "vous" means "you" (formal singular or plural). Often appears with verbs like "je vais / je devrais / je voulais" and with "Laissez-moi..." to mean "Let me tell you something."
target_language_example: Laissez-moi vous dire une chose : ce n'est pas une bonne idée.
native_language_example: Let me tell you something: it's not a good idea.

additional_notes: Form of the verb *dire* used with **vous** (for one person formally, or several people). Used to report what someone claims (**Vous dites avoir…** = “You say you have…”), to question or challenge what someone just said (**Pourquoi vous dites ça ?**), or to clarify meaning (**Vous dites ‘assez’, qu’entendez-vous par là ?**). On its own (**Vous dites ?**) it’s a polite way to ask someone to repeat: “Sorry?” / “Pardon?” / “Come again?”
target_language_example: Vous dites que vous êtes prêt, mais vous avez tout vérifié ?
native_language_example: You say you’re ready, but have you checked everything?

meaning: “you have some/any (of it/them)” or “you’ve had/done some (of it)” (with *en* = “some/of it/of them”).
additional_notes: *En* replaces something introduced with *de* (or an implied “of it/them”). It’s very common with quantities (*combien ?*, *beaucoup*, *assez*) and after verbs where English might use “about it/it” or “some”: *Vous en avez parlé ?* (“Did you talk about it?”), *Vous en avez pris combien ?* (“How many did you take?”), *Vous en avez assez dit* (“You’ve said enough.”). The exact meaning depends on the verb and context; *en* points back to the thing/topic/quantity.
target_language_example: Vous en avez encore ?
native_language_example: Do you have any more (of it/them)?

additional_notes: "En" is a pronoun that replaces something introduced with "de" (some of it/them, from it/them, about it/them). So "vous en avez" means "you have some" or "you’ve got it" depending on context. It’s often followed by another word/phrase, e.g. "vous en avez marre ?" (= are you fed up with it?) or "vous en avez encore à apprendre" (= you still have more to learn about it).
target_language_example: Vous en avez assez ?
native_language_example: Have you had enough (of it)?

additional_notes: Most often appears in the full phrase "je vous en prie". It’s used (1) to politely insist or beg someone to do something: "Écoutez-moi, je vous en prie" = "Listen to me, please"; and (2) as a formal/polite reply to "merci" meaning "you’re welcome" / "not at all". Uses "vous" (formal or plural).
target_language_example: Entrez, je vous en prie.
native_language_example: Come in, please.

meaning: “you are … (about it / from it)” (with **en** = “of it / about it / from it”).
additional_notes: **En** replaces something introduced with **de** (or “about it / from it”). So **vous en êtes + adjective** means “you are + adjective about it”: **Vous en êtes sûre ?** = “Are you sure (about it)?”; **vous en êtes amoureuse** = “you’re in love (with him/her).” With a reflexive verb you can also get **vous vous en êtes sorti(s)** (“you got out of it / managed”).
target_language_example: Alors, vous en êtes content(e) ?
native_language_example: So, are you happy about it?

meaning: “What are you doing?” / “What do you do?” (polite/formal).
additional_notes: Uses the formal/polite “vous.” Often means “What are you doing (right now)?” from context, but it can also mean “What do you do (for work/in general)?”; add “ce soir / maintenant / exactement” to specify time or emphasis. In everyday speech it’s common; a more formal word order is “Que faites-vous ?”.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous faites quoi ce soir ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what are you doing tonight?

additional_notes: From the verb "falloir" ("il faut" = "it is necessary"). "Il vous faut..." means "you need..."; "vous faut-il... ?" is the inverted question form, common in formal/written French. Often used after question words like "combien" (how many/much): "Combien de X vous faut-il ?" = "How many X do you need?"
target_language_example: Vous faut-il une autre minute ?
native_language_example: Do you need another minute?

additional_notes: Used to give strong advice or a warning. It’s the conditional of « faire »: « vous feriez mieux de + infinitive » (e.g., vous feriez mieux de partir). Often implies “it would be wiser/safer if you did this,” sometimes with a slight threat or consequence in context.
target_language_example: Vous feriez mieux de partir maintenant, il va pleuvoir.
native_language_example: You’d better leave now; it’s going to rain.

meaning: to join us (to come with us / take part with us).
additional_notes: Polite/formal way to invite someone (vous) to come along or participate in an activity. Uses the reflexive verb se joindre à + person/group (je me joins à…, tu te joins à…, vous vous joignez à…). Often followed by an event: « pour dîner », « pour la réunion », etc.
target_language_example: Est-ce que vous voulez vous joindre à nous pour un café ?
native_language_example: Do you want to join us for a coffee?

additional_notes: "Vous" is formal singular or plural "you." "l'" is the shortened form of "le" or "la" ("him/it" or "her/it") used before a vowel sound. Very often, "vous l'avez" is the start of the passé composé (past tense): "vous l'avez + past participle" → "you (did) ..." (e.g., "vous l'avez su" = "you found out/you knew"). Sometimes it can also mean "you have it" depending on context.
target_language_example: Vous l'avez oublié ?
native_language_example: Did you forget it?

meaning: "Have you seen it/him?" or "You saw it/him." (formal or plural "you").
additional_notes: "Vous" is used for one person formally or for multiple people. "l'" is short for "le" or "la" and means "him" or "it" (a person/thing mentioned earlier). In questions, it often means "Have you seen him/it?" (passé composé), and context tells you whether it’s "him" or "it."
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous l'avez vu ce matin ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, did you see him/it this morning?

additional_notes: `vous` means either plural `you` or formal singular `you`, and `le` is a direct object pronoun meaning `it` or `him`. In French, `le` comes before the verb: `vous le savez` = `you know it`. `Le` can also refer to an idea or situation, and in some expressions it may be left untranslated in natural English, as in `comme vous le souhaitez` = `as you wish`.
target_language_example: Vous le voyez maintenant ?
native_language_example: Do you see it now?

meaning: “Do you know him?” / “You know him.” (formal or plural “you”).
additional_notes: Used to ask or state that someone is acquainted with a person (connaître = to know/be familiar with). **Le** is an object pronoun meaning “him” (or sometimes “it” for a masculine noun) and comes before the verb: *Vous le connaissez ?* In the negative you’ll often hear *Vous le connaissez pas* (informal spoken); in careful French: *Vous ne le connaissez pas.* If you mean “know (a fact)” you usually use *savoir*, not *connaître*.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous le connaissez personnellement ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you know him personally?

additional_notes: Used when the thing being told is replaced by the direct-object pronoun **le** (= “it/that”). With an infinitive like **dire**, the pronouns come before it: **je dois vous le dire** (“I have to tell you”). In a question: **Combien de fois dois-je vous le dire ?** (“How many times do I have to tell you?”).
target_language_example: Je dois vous le dire : je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I have to tell you: I can't come tonight.

additional_notes: Polite/formal way to refer to something the listener already knows. The pronoun “le” stands for an idea or fact (“it”), not a specific object: e.g., “Vous le savez déjà” = “You already know (that).” Often used to introduce a reminder: “Comme/Ainsi que vous le savez…” = “As you know…”.
target_language_example: Comme vous le savez, le magasin ferme à 18 h.
native_language_example: As you know, the store closes at 6 p.m.

meaning: you have them / you’ve got them.
additional_notes: “Vous” is formal “you” or plural “you.” “Les” is the direct object pronoun (“them”) and it comes before the verb: vous + les + avez. With the past tense (passé composé), “avez” is the helping verb (avoir): « vous les avez vus » = “you saw them.” If the direct object is before the verb, the past participle can agree in gender/number (e.g., « vous les avez volées » if “them” refers to feminine plural things).
target_language_example: Vous les avez déjà achetés ?
native_language_example: Have you already bought them?

meaning: “you have” / “you’ve” (formal or plural) + “me” (used before the auxiliary verb to form the passé composé).
additional_notes: Used in the **passé composé** (and other compound tenses): **vous** (you: formal singular or plural) + **m’** (me; shortened form of *me* before a vowel) + **avez** (have) + a **past participle** (aidé, donné, appris, fait, etc.). The object pronoun **me** comes *before* the auxiliary: *Vous m’avez aidé* = “You helped me / You’ve helped me.” In English this is often translated as the simple past (“you helped me”).
target_language_example: Vous m'avez aidé.
native_language_example: You helped me. / You’ve helped me.

additional_notes: A pronoun pattern with vous as the subject ('you' formal singular or plural) and me as the object ('me' or 'to me'). In French, object pronouns usually come before the verb: vous me comprenez = 'you understand me', vous me dites = 'you tell me'.
target_language_example: Vous me connaissez ?
native_language_example: Do you know me?

additional_notes: Formed from "vous" (you, formal or plural) + "me" (to me) + "faites" (you do/make). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive or an expression: "Vous me faites rire" (You make me laugh), "Vous me faites peur" (You scare me). In "Vous me faites chier", it introduces a very vulgar insult meaning “You’re pissing me off / You’re really annoying me.”
target_language_example: Vous me faites rire !
native_language_example: You make me laugh!

meaning: to show you; (also) to be/show yourself (e.g., polite).
additional_notes:
Most often, it’s the verb *montrer* with the indirect object pronoun *vous* (“to you”): *Je vais vous montrer X* = “I’m going to show you X.”

It can also be from the reflexive verb *se montrer* (“to show oneself / to prove to be”), followed by an adjective: *Veuillez vous montrer poli/polie(s)* = “Please be polite.” In this case, *vous* is reflexive (“yourselves”), not “to you.”
target_language_example: Je vais vous montrer comment ça marche.
native_language_example: I’m going to show you how it works.

additional_notes: Uses the formal/polite object pronoun "vous" (for one person you don’t know well, or for several people). Common with polite requests: "Je peux... ?", "Puis-je... ?", "Je voudrais..." and with past intentions: "Je voulais...", "J’ai voulu...".
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je peux vous montrer quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I show you something?

additional_notes: "Vous" is the formal singular or plural "you." "N'avez pas" is the negative form of "avoir" (to have) in the present tense, and it’s also used as the auxiliary in the passé composé to mean "you have not / you haven't" + past participle (e.g., "vous n'avez pas compris" = "you didn't understand/you haven't understood"). In casual speech, "ne" is often dropped: "vous avez pas…"
target_language_example: Vous n'avez pas votre passeport ?
native_language_example: You don't have your passport?

meaning: "you don't have any" / "you don't have a".
additional_notes: Negative form of "vous avez" (you have). In French, "de" replaces the usual article (un/une/des/du/de la) after "ne...pas": « Vous n'avez pas de voiture ? » = “You don’t have a car?” Used to ask politely/formally (vous) whether someone has something.
target_language_example: Vous n'avez pas de billet ?
native_language_example: You don't have a ticket?

additional_notes: Uses French negation: "ne" + verb (être) + "pas". It’s used with "vous" for one person you address formally (e.g., a stranger, a customer) or for multiple people. Often appears in questions like "Vous n'êtes pas… ?" to check or confirm something ("Aren’t you…?").
target_language_example: Vous n'êtes pas prêt(e) ?
native_language_example: Aren’t you ready?

additional_notes: Used with formal singular or plural "you" (vous) to begin a negative sentence or question. "Ne" is usually completed by another negative word such as "pas," "jamais," "plus," or "rien". In everyday spoken French, the "ne" is often dropped.
target_language_example: Vous ne pouvez pas entrer ici.
native_language_example: You can't come in here.

additional_notes: Uses "vous" for one person in a polite/formal way or for more than one person. Often used to say someone hasn’t understood an explanation ("Je crois/pense que vous ne comprenez pas" = “I think you don’t understand”) or as a correction/insistence ("Non, vous ne comprenez pas" = “No, you don’t understand”). Can also be a question: "Vous ne comprenez pas ?"
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous ne comprenez pas cette phrase ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you not understand this sentence?

meaning: "you must not" / "you are not allowed to" (formal/plural).
additional_notes: Used with the verb infinitive to express a prohibition or a strong instruction: « Vous ne devez pas + infinitive ». « Vous » can be polite singular (to one person formally) or plural (to several people). Stronger/more rule-like than « vous ne devriez pas » (“you shouldn’t”).
target_language_example: Vous ne devez pas utiliser votre téléphone ici.
native_language_example: You must not use your phone here.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of **devoir** (“must / have to”) to give advice or a recommendation (softer than an order). **Vous** is used for one person formally or for several people. It’s usually followed by an infinitive: *vous ne devriez pas + verbe* (e.g., *vous ne devriez pas partir*).
target_language_example: Vous ne devriez pas conduire si vous êtes fatigué(e).
native_language_example: You shouldn’t drive if you’re tired.

additional_notes: "Vous" = formal/plural "you". "ne...pas" makes the verb negative. "l'" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" or "him/her" (replacing something already mentioned). "avez" is "have" (used to form the past tense: "vous avez dit" = "you said"). The exact English tense depends on context: "Vous ne l'avez pas dit" can be "You didn't say it" or "You haven't said it." The ending can agree in gender/number when the object is "l'": "revue" (her), "suivie" (her).
target_language_example: Vous ne l'avez pas reçu ?
native_language_example: You haven't received it?

meaning: 'you don’t … it / him' (with the verb that follows).
additional_notes: Used to start a negative sentence with an object pronoun. In standard French, negation is often "ne … pas" around the verb: "Vous ne le voyez pas" = "You don’t see it/him." The pronoun "le" (it/him) comes before the verb.
target_language_example: Vous ne le comprenez pas ?
native_language_example: You don’t understand it?

meaning: 'you don’t … me' / 'you aren’t … to me' (start of a negative sentence with “me”).
additional_notes: Used when addressing someone formally or a group (“vous”) and making a negation with “ne … pas/jamais/plus/rien”. “Me” is the object pronoun (“me/to me”) and comes before the verb: « Vous ne me voyez pas » = “You don’t see me.” In speech, “ne” is often dropped: « Vous me voyez pas ? »
target_language_example: Vous ne me comprenez pas.
native_language_example: You don’t understand me.

additional_notes: Uses the verb « pouvoir » (to be able to / can) with « ne…pas » to make a negative. « Vous » is used for one person in a formal/polite situation or for multiple people. Often expresses a prohibition (“you’re not allowed to…”) or an impossibility (“you’re unable to…”).
target_language_example: Désolé, vous ne pouvez pas entrer ici.
native_language_example: Sorry, you can’t come in here.

meaning: "you don't know" / "you don't know (how/what/where/who...)" (formal or plural).
additional_notes: "Vous" is used for one person in a formal/polite situation or for more than one person. This phrase is often followed by a question word or clause: "vous ne savez pas où..." (you don’t know where...), "ce que..." (what...), "qui..." (who...). In questions, it can be said with rising intonation ("Vous ne savez pas où il est ?") or with "Est-ce que" ("Est-ce que vous ne savez pas... ?").
target_language_example: Vous ne savez pas comment ça marche ?
native_language_example: You don’t know how it works?

additional_notes: Made of: vous (you, formal/plural) + ne…pas (not) + vouloir (to want). Often used in questions as a polite invitation or suggestion (similar to “would you like to…?”), even though it’s grammatically negative: « Vous ne voulez pas venir ? » = “Would you like to come?” In statements, it can express refusal or lack of desire: « Vous ne voulez pas de visite » = “You don’t want visitors.”
target_language_example: Vous ne voulez pas un café ?
native_language_example: Would you like a coffee?

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb avoir to form the passé composé (past tense): vous + nous + avez + past participle (e.g., « Vous nous avez aidés » = “You helped us / You have helped us”). The object pronoun « nous » comes before the verb « avez ». If « nous » is a direct object, the past participle may agree (aidés/aidées, abandonnés/abandonnées). Some verbs take « nous » as an indirect object (e.g., « Vous nous avez menti » = “You lied to us”; « Vous nous avez manqué » = “We missed you” literally “You were missed by us”).
target_language_example: Vous nous avez appelés hier soir.
native_language_example: You called us last night.

additional_notes: This is an inversion used to ask a question with the subject elles (“they”, feminine plural) in the passé composé: ont-elles = “have they”. The pronoun vous comes before the auxiliary and means “you” (to you / you-plural / you-formal). What follows is usually a past participle (frappé, payé, recruté, etc.). The past participle may agree with vous (frappé/frappée/frappés/frappées) when vous is the direct object placed before the verb.
target_language_example: Pourquoi vous ont-elles appelé(e) ?
native_language_example: Why did they call you?

meaning: “did they … to you?” / “have they … to you?” (formal question).
additional_notes: Used to form an inversion question with “ils” (they) in the passé composé: object pronoun “vous” (to you / you) + auxiliary “ont” + “-ils”. It often asks about what other people did to you: « Vous ont-ils payé(e) ? » (“Did they pay you?”). With a feminine direct object, the past participle can agree: « Ils vous ont frappée ».
target_language_example: Vous ont-ils appelé hier ?
native_language_example: Did they call you yesterday?

additional_notes: Usually means talking to someone addressed as vous, which can be one person formally or several people. After verbs like pouvoir, vouloir, or devoir, the pronoun comes before the infinitive: je peux vous parler. In some plural/reflexive contexts, it can also mean 'talk to each other.'
target_language_example: Je voudrais vous parler après la réunion.
native_language_example: I'd like to talk to you after the meeting.

additional_notes: "Vous" is the polite singular or plural "you". "Vous parlez… ?" is used both for talking in general and for languages: "Vous parlez français/anglais ?" (= Do you speak French/English?). To say what someone is talking about, use "parler de" + noun/pronoun: "Vous parlez de moi ?" (= Are you talking about me?). You can also say "parler en" + language to emphasize the language being used: "Vous parlez en anglais ?" (= Are you speaking in English?).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous parlez français ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you speak French?

additional_notes: "Vous" is the polite (or plural) "you". This phrase is used to ask for someone's opinion or guess, often followed by a full clause ("vous pensez que + [sentence]"). It can be a question ("Vous pensez que... ?") or a statement ("Si vous pensez que..."). In careful French, "Pensez-vous que... ?" is another common way to form the question.
target_language_example: Vous pensez que c'est une bonne idée ?
native_language_example: Do you think it's a good idea?

additional_notes: Used with "vous" (formal "you" or plural "you"). Often introduces an opinion or a question: "Vous pensez que c'est… ?" (Do you think it’s…?). Followed by an adjective, a noun, or a longer clause (e.g., "vous pensez que c'est possible", "vous pensez que c'est une bonne idée").
target_language_example: Vous pensez que c'est une bonne idée ?
native_language_example: Do you think it's a good idea?

additional_notes: Used with the verb plaire. French structures this as something pleasing someone: Cela vous plaît ? literally means “Does that please you?” but usually translates as “Do you like that?” Here vous is the formal singular or plural “you.”
target_language_example: Prenez ce qui vous plaît.
native_language_example: Take whatever you like.

meaning: to ask you a few questions.
additional_notes: Polite/formal way to say you want to ask someone several questions. Used with "pouvoir" (Puis-je…?) to ask permission, or with "devoir" (Je vais devoir…) when it’s necessary (e.g., in an interview, at the doctor’s, with police/administration). "Poser une question" literally means "to put/pose a question" but is the normal French verb for "to ask a question."
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je voudrais vous poser quelques questions avant de commencer.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I’d like to ask you a few questions before we start.

additional_notes: Polite/formal phrasing (using "vous"). Commonly used with verbs like "vouloir" (Je veux…), "voudrais" (Je voudrais… = more polite), or "laisser" (Laissez-moi… = Let me…). Literally "to put a question to you," but it simply means "to ask you a question."
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je peux vous poser une question ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask you a question?

additional_notes: Form of "pouvoir" in the conditional tense (vous = formal/plural "you"). Used to suggest something politely ("You could try"), or to express possibility ("You might be right"). Often followed by an infinitive: "vous pourriez + verb" (e.g., "vous pourriez essayer").
target_language_example: Vous pourriez m'aider, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Could you help me, please?

additional_notes: Present tense of pouvoir with vous. It is used for plural 'you' or polite singular 'you', and can express ability, permission, or possibility depending on context.
target_language_example: Vous pouvez entrer maintenant.
native_language_example: You can come in now.

meaning: “you can do / you may do” (formal or plural).
additional_notes: Used with "vous" to talk politely to one person (vous-form) or to several people. It can express ability (“you can do”) or permission (“you may do”). "Faire" often means “to do” or “to make,” depending on context (e.g., "faire ça" = do that; "faire de moi…" = make me into…).
target_language_example: Vous pouvez faire une pause si vous voulez.
native_language_example: You can take a break if you want.

meaning: "you can do it" / "you can do it (for me)".
additional_notes: Uses the polite/plural subject « vous ». « Pouvez » (from pouvoir) expresses ability or permission depending on context. « le » is a pronoun meaning “it,” referring to something already mentioned (an action/task). Can be used as a question (« Vous pouvez le faire ? » = “Can you do it?”) or as encouragement/assurance (« Vous pouvez le faire. » = “You can do it.”).
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas, vous pouvez le faire.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you can do it.

meaning: "can you" / "you can" + "me" (used to start a request or statement).
additional_notes: Common lead-in before an infinitive verb: « Vous pouvez me + VERBE… ? » = “Can you + VERB… for me?” It’s polite/formal because of « vous ». For a more standard question form, you can also say « Pouvez-vous me… ? » (same meaning). Often followed by verbs like aider (help), dire (tell), montrer (show), rendre service (do a favor), tenir (hold).
target_language_example: Vous pouvez me dire où est la station de métro ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where the метро station is?

meaning: You can leave. / You may leave.
additional_notes: Uses «vous» (formal or plural “you”) + «pouvoir» to give permission or say that leaving is possible. Often used politely (e.g., by a host, teacher, or staff). Can add a time word: «maintenant» (now), «demain» (tomorrow). In questions, it can become «Vous pouvez partir ?» (“Can I/Can we leave?” depending on context).
target_language_example: Merci, vous pouvez partir maintenant.
native_language_example: Thank you, you can leave now.

additional_notes: Uses the polite/plural subject “vous.” Often said to allow someone to remain somewhere (“You may stay / You’re welcome to stay”). Can also mean it’s possible for you to stay, depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Si vous voulez, vous pouvez rester un peu plus longtemps.
native_language_example: If you want, you can stay a little longer.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase *se rappeler (de)* (“to remember”). This is the inverted question form used in more formal French. It’s often followed by a question word: *Vous rappelez-vous qui/quoi/quand/comment…?* or by a noun: *Vous rappelez-vous votre numéro…?* You can also say it less formally as *Vous vous rappelez… ?* or *Tu te rappelles… ?*
target_language_example: Vous rappelez-vous où vous avez mis vos clés ?
native_language_example: Do you remember where you put your keys?

additional_notes: Uses the verb « rencontrer » (“to meet/encounter”) with « vous » as the direct object. « Vous » is used for one person in a formal/polite context, or for more than one person (“you all”). Common in polite introductions: « Content de vous rencontrer » / « C’est un plaisir de vous rencontrer » / « Ça m’a fait plaisir de vous rencontrer ». In the past, you’ll often see « vous rencontrer » after another verb: « Je voulais venir vous rencontrer » (“I wanted to come meet you”).
target_language_example: Je suis ravi de vous rencontrer enfin en personne.
native_language_example: I’m delighted to finally meet you in person.

meaning: to see you again (formal or plural “you”).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like vouloir, pouvoir, devoir, espérer, souhaiter: « Je veux vous revoir » = “I want to see you again.” Often implies a future meeting or reunion, and keeps a polite/formal tone because of « vous ».
target_language_example: J'espère vous revoir bientôt.
native_language_example: I hope to see you again soon.

additional_notes: Formal or plural form of savoir. It can state that someone knows something, ask a question depending on intonation, or be used as a conversation opener like "you know, ...".
target_language_example: Vous savez où il habite ?
native_language_example: Do you know where he lives?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question before stating what you mean (often rhetorical or to build suspense). It’s the polite/plural form (“vous”); with one person informally you’ll often hear “tu sais ce que…”. Common pattern: “Vous savez ce que + subject + verb ?” (e.g., “Vous savez ce que je veux ?”).
target_language_example: Vous savez ce que je préfère ? Un café bien chaud.
native_language_example: You know what I prefer? A nice hot coffee.

meaning: "you know what…" (introducing what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Used to get someone’s attention and introduce a point, often with a following clause or question: « Vous savez ce qui est drôle ? » / « Vous savez ce qui s’est passé ? ». In everyday speech it can sound conversational and can be said a bit like a filler before an announcement.
target_language_example: Vous savez ce qui est drôle ? Je n’ai pas du tout reconnu Paul.
native_language_example: You know what’s funny? I didn’t recognize Paul at all.

meaning: 'you know how…' / 'you know what it’s like.'
additional_notes: Used to ask or check whether someone knows the way to do something ("Vous savez comment faire ?" = "Do you know how to do it?"). It’s also used to appeal to shared understanding, especially in expressions like "Vous savez comment c'est" or "Vous savez comment ils sont" ("You know how it is / how they are"). Sometimes it’s left unfinished ("Vous savez comment.") to imply "you know the rest / you know what I mean."
target_language_example: On est un peu en retard, vous savez comment c'est.
native_language_example: We’re a little late—you know how it is.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows the location of a person/place/thing or where to go. It’s often followed by an infinitive (vous savez où aller ?) or by a full clause (vous savez où elle est ?). It can also be used on its own as an elliptical question or hint (“Vous savez où ?” / “Vous savez où.” = “you know where”).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous savez où se trouve la gare ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you know where the train station is?

meaning: “you know that …” (stating/reminding someone of a fact).
additional_notes: Used with **vous** (formal or plural “you”) to introduce information you assume the listener already knows, or to emphasize a point: *Vous savez que je ne bois pas.* It can sound like a reminder, a warning, or an appeal to shared knowledge depending on tone.
target_language_example: Vous savez que ce n’est pas possible aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: You know that it’s not possible today.

meaning: “You know what?” (used to introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French, often as a rhetorical lead-in to announce a decision, reveal news, or add emphasis (not always a real question). Can be followed by a statement.
target_language_example: Vous savez quoi ? Je vais accepter le poste.
native_language_example: You know what? I’m going to accept the job.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *sembler* to give an impression or appearance. Common patterns: **vous semblez + adjective** (*Vous semblez fatigué(e).*), **vous semblez + infinitive** (*Vous semblez tout savoir.*), or **vous semblez + noun phrase** (*Vous semblez une bonne personne.*). *Vous* is either formal (one person) or plural (you all). Adjectives agree with the person being addressed: *déprimé* (to a man) / *déprimée* (to a woman).
target_language_example: Vous semblez très occupé aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: You seem very busy today.

additional_notes: From the verb *se sentir* (“to feel”). This is the inverted question form used in more formal French, often followed by an adjective: *Vous sentez-vous seul(e) ?* (“Do you feel lonely?”). In everyday speech, people often say *Est-ce que vous vous sentez… ?* or *Vous vous sentez… ?*
target_language_example: Vous sentez-vous prêt à commencer ?
native_language_example: Do you feel ready to start?

additional_notes: Future tense of être (“to be”). Used with vous = either formal singular “you” (to one person politely) or plural “you” (to several people). Often followed by an adjective or noun: Vous serez bien ici. / Vous serez payé.
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas, vous serez prêt à temps.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you’ll be ready on time.

additional_notes: Inversion question form of se souvenir de (“to remember”). It’s followed by de + noun (Vous souvenez-vous de son nom ?) or de ce que + clause (…de ce que vous avez fait…). In everyday speech, people often say: « Vous vous souvenez de … ? »
target_language_example: Vous souvenez-vous de l’adresse de l’hôtel ?
native_language_example: Do you remember the hotel’s address?

meaning: “you work” / “you are working” (to one person formally, or to multiple people).
additional_notes: Present tense of *travailler* with **vous**. It can mean a general fact (“you work here”) or something happening right now (“you’re working now?”), depending on context. Used for polite/formal address to one person (e.g., a customer speaking to an employee) or when speaking to more than one person. Common with place/time details: **vous travaillez ici**, **vous travaillez ce soir**, **vous travaillez à cette heure-ci**.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous travaillez ici ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you work here? / Are you working here?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something happened moments ago: « vous venez de + infinitif ». Example: « vous venez de dire », « vous venez de voir », « vous venez de gagner ». In speech, it can also sound like a strong reaction (“you just…!”).
target_language_example: Vous venez de rater le train ?
native_language_example: Did you just miss the train?

additional_notes: The object pronoun vous comes before voir. vous can mean one person formally or several people, so this can also mean 'to see you all.' Depending on context, it may imply visiting or meeting with someone.
target_language_example: Je voudrais vous voir demain.
native_language_example: I'd like to see you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Present-tense form of vouloir with vous. It can mean plural "you want" or polite singular "you want." In questions, it often translates naturally as "do you want...?" and in offers or invitations it can sound like "would you like...?"
target_language_example: Vous voulez venir avec nous ?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with us?

meaning: 'you mean…' / 'do you mean…?' (to clarify what someone is saying).
additional_notes: Literally "you want to say," but it’s used like English "you mean" to ask for clarification or confirm understanding. Uses the polite/formal subject "vous" (to a stranger, in customer service, to more than one person). Common patterns: "Vous voulez dire que…" (You mean that…), "Qu’est-ce que vous voulez dire ?" (What do you mean?), and "Vous voulez dire ?" (You mean?/Pardon?).
target_language_example: Vous voulez dire que le train est annulé ?
native_language_example: You mean the train is cancelled?

meaning: “Do you want me to…?” / “Would you like me to…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask (politely) what the other person wants you to do. It’s the start of a question, followed by a verb in the subjunctive: « Vous voulez que je + verbe… ? » (e.g., « que je continue », « que je les appelle », « que je revienne »).
target_language_example: Vous voulez que je vous aide avec ça ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you with that?

meaning: “Do you want me to… (for you / to you)?”
additional_notes: Used to offer or ask permission to do something for someone. It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive: « Vous voulez que je vous accompagne ? » (= Do you want me to come with you?). « vous » is the formal/plural “you,” and « je vous… » means “I … you” (e.g., tell you, show you).
target_language_example: Vous voulez que je vous aide avec ça ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you with that?

meaning: “you want to know” (addressing one or more people politely).
additional_notes: Used to ask what information someone wants (“Vous voulez savoir quoi ?”), or to introduce an explanation (“Je vais vous dire ce que vous voulez savoir”). Common in questions like “Vous voulez savoir la vérité ?” or “Vous voulez savoir ce que j’en pense ?”. It uses the polite/plural “vous”.
target_language_example: Vous voulez savoir comment ça marche ?
native_language_example: Do you want to know how it works?

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of vouloir used with vous (formal “you” or plural “you”). Often used in questions to ask what someone wanted or meant: « Qu’est-ce que vous vouliez ? » = “What did you want?” It can also introduce another verb or clause: « vous vouliez venir » (you wanted to come), « vous vouliez que je… » (you wanted me to…).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous vouliez quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, did you want something?

meaning: “you … (from it/with it/away)” — a pronoun pattern used in verbs like s’en aller, s’en sortir, s’en charger, s’en faire, s’en sentir capable.
additional_notes:
This is not a standalone expression: it’s the pronoun combo **vous** (object/reflexive “yourself/yourselves”) + **en** (“from it / some of it / about it”). It appears before the verb in common set phrases:
- **vous vous en allez** = you’re leaving / going away
- **vous vous en sortez** = you manage / get by / get out of it
- **vous vous en chargez** = you take care of it
- **vous vous en faites (trop)** = you worry (too much) about it
- **vous vous en sentez capable** = you feel capable (of it).
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas : vous vous en sortirez.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’ll manage.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **se rappeler** (“to remember”). It’s often used as a question to check if someone remembers a person/thing/event. You may see **vous vous rappelez + noun** (no *de*), or **vous vous rappelez de + noun** (common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Vous vous rappelez de ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: Do you remember that restaurant?

meaning: 'you feel' (asking about your physical or emotional state).
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb "se sentir" in the present tense for "vous". Often used with an adjective ("mieux", "coupable", "capable") or with "comment" ("comment vous vous sentez" = "how you feel"). It can refer to health (feeling better) or emotions (feeling guilty).
target_language_example: Comment vous vous sentez aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: How do you feel today?

meaning: "do you remember" / "you remember" (formal or plural), followed by "de".
additional_notes: From the verb "se souvenir de" = "to remember" (it takes "de" before the thing you remember). "Vous" can be formal "you" (one person) or plural "you" (several people). Often used as a question: "Vous vous souvenez de… ?"
target_language_example: Vous vous souvenez de cette adresse ?
native_language_example: Do you remember this address?

additional_notes: Used to start the passé composé with reflexive verbs for "vous" (plural "you" or formal "you"). Structure: "vous" + reflexive pronoun "vous" + "êtes" (être) + past participle: "Vous vous êtes levés" (You got up). With reflexive verbs, the past participle often agrees with "vous" (e.g., "Vous vous êtes rencontrés" for a mixed/masculine group; "rencontrées" for an all-female group).
target_language_example: Vous vous êtes trompés d'adresse ?
native_language_example: Did you get the address wrong?

additional_notes: Literally means “you see” (from voir). Often used to point something out or check understanding, like “You see (this)?” / “You know?” In speech it can also work as a short filler to explain something: « Vous voyez, c’est compliqué. »
target_language_example: Vous voyez ce panneau ? Il faut tourner à droite.
native_language_example: Do you see that sign? You have to turn right.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of être with vous (“you” formal singular or plural). Used for ongoing states, background descriptions, or habitual situations in the past (often with time phrases like hier, la semaine dernière, quand…).
target_language_example: Vous étiez très fatigué hier soir.
native_language_example: You were very tired last night.

additional_notes: Present-tense form of être with vous. Vous can mean plural "you" or formal singular "you," so this can refer to more than one person or to one person politely.
target_language_example: Vous êtes en retard.
native_language_example: You are late.

meaning: "did you … ?" (formal or plural), used in a past-tense question with a reflexive verb.
additional_notes: This is the question form (inversion) of "vous vous êtes …" in the passé composé with a reflexive verb. It’s used with "vous" (polite singular or plural). In your examples: "Vous vous êtes amusé(e)(s)" → "Vous êtes-vous amusé(e)(s) ?" The past participle often agrees in gender/number: amusé / amusée / amusés / amusées.
target_language_example: Vous êtes-vous levés tôt ce matin ?
native_language_example: Did you get up early this morning?

meaning: “you really are / indeed you are” (emphasis or confirmation); also “you’re fine/okay.”
additional_notes: With **bien**, *être* can strongly confirm or emphasize what follows: *Vous êtes bien son frère !* (“You really are his brother!”), *Vous êtes bien loin…* (“You are really far…”), *Vous êtes bien la fille de votre père* (“You certainly are your father’s daughter”). Said on its own (*Vous êtes bien.*), it often means “You’re fine/okay/comfortable.”
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas : vous êtes bien ici.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’re fine here.

additional_notes: Used with a plural noun to say what a group of people are (nationality, job, identity, etc.). It’s the plural form: vous (you all / formal you) + êtes (are) + des (some). Note: before plural adjectives, use "vous êtes" without "des" (e.g., "Vous êtes gentils."), but with a noun you typically keep "des" ("Vous êtes des profs.").
target_language_example: Vous êtes des touristes ?
native_language_example: Are you (all) tourists?

additional_notes: Literally “you are there.” Used to state or check someone’s presence (“Vous êtes là depuis longtemps ?”), to ask about someone’s purpose (“Vous êtes là pour ça ?”), or as an exclamation meaning “You’re here!/You made it!” (“Vous êtes là !”). In writing, “là” can refer to being physically present or being there in a situation/at an event.
target_language_example: Ah, vous êtes là ! Je vous cherchais.
native_language_example: Oh, you’re here! I was looking for you.

additional_notes: Used to address a group with the polite/plural “vous.” “Tous” emphasizes that it includes everyone in the group. Word order can vary; you may also see “vous êtes tous + adjective/past participle” (Vous êtes tous prêts / Vous êtes tous venus) or “vous êtes tous les deux/trois…” (you are both/all three…).
target_language_example: Vous êtes tous prêts à partir ?
native_language_example: Are you all ready to leave?

additional_notes: Use before an adjective: « Vous êtes trop + adjectif ». Literally it means “you are too …” (too kind, too tall, etc.). In everyday spoken French, « trop » is very often used as an intensifier meaning “so/really/very” (especially in compliments): « Vous êtes trop aimable ! » = “You’re so kind!” Context tells you whether it’s a complaint (“too much”) or praise (“so/really”).
target_language_example: Vous êtes trop gentil, merci !
native_language_example: You’re so kind, thank you!

additional_notes: Used to describe someone with an adjective. "Vous" is for one person you address formally (a stranger, a customer, someone older) or for more than one person; the adjective may change to match gender/number (e.g., gentil/gentille/gentils/gentilles). Often followed by an adjective like "gentil(le)", "talentueux/talentueuse", etc.
target_language_example: Vous êtes très aimable.
native_language_example: You are very kind.

additional_notes: Used with the subject pronoun «vous» + verb «être» to say what someone is (identity/role). «Vous» can be formal singular (polite “you”) or plural (“you all”). «Un» is masculine singular; for feminine use «vous êtes une…», and for plural use «vous êtes des…».
target_language_example: Vous êtes un excellent professeur.
native_language_example: You are an excellent teacher.

additional_notes: Uses the formal/plural subject “vous” + “êtes” (to be). Can address one person formally (polite “you”) or multiple people (“you all”). Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase to describe someone: “Vous êtes un homme courageux / d’honneur / de parole.”
target_language_example: Vous êtes un homme très gentil.
native_language_example: You are a very kind man.

meaning: “you are a …” (polite/plural), before a feminine noun.
additional_notes: Used with **vous** (formal “you” or “you all”) + **êtes** (“are”) + **une** (“a/an” feminine) to identify or describe someone: *Vous êtes une étrangère.* (“You are a foreign woman.”). The word after **une** is typically a **feminine noun** (or a noun phrase). For masculine nouns, use **vous êtes un …**.
target_language_example: Vous êtes une étudiante ?
native_language_example: Are you a student? (female)

meaning: "you came" / "you have come" (formal singular or plural).
additional_notes: Passé composé of *venir* uses **être**: *vous êtes venu(e)(s)*. The past participle agrees with the person(s) you’re speaking to: **venu** (to a man / mixed group), **venue** (to a woman), **venus** (to men/mixed group), **venues** (to women). Often used to say someone came to a place or came for a purpose: *vous êtes venu au bon endroit* (“you came to the right place”).
target_language_example: Pourquoi est-ce que vous êtes venu ici ?
native_language_example: Why did you come here?

meaning: "you really are" (used to emphasize what someone is).
additional_notes: Used with "vous" (formal/plural "you") to strongly emphasize a description, often before an adjective or noun: « Vous êtes vraiment gentils. » / « Vous êtes vraiment une sorcière ? ». It can also sound surprised, impressed, or sarcastic depending on tone.
target_language_example: Vous êtes vraiment très patient.
native_language_example: You really are very patient.

additional_notes: Used to say a trip is for work/professional reasons. Very common with the pattern "être en voyage d'affaires" (= to be away on a business trip): "Il est en voyage d'affaires" (He’s on a business trip).
target_language_example: Je pars demain en voyage d'affaires à Lyon.
native_language_example: I’m leaving tomorrow on a business trip to Lyon.

additional_notes: Refers to moving to the past or the future (often in sci‑fi). Usually used with the verb "faire" (faire un voyage dans le temps) or in general statements like "Le voyage dans le temps est possible/impossible."
target_language_example: Dans ce film, ils font un voyage dans le temps pour sauver la ville.
native_language_example: In this movie, they time travel to save the city.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the trip taken by newlyweds after a wedding. Often appears with the article: « le voyage de noces » (the honeymoon) or « un voyage de noces » (a honeymoon), and can be followed by a destination: « un voyage de noces à + place ».
target_language_example: On part en voyage de noces en Italie.
native_language_example: We're going on our honeymoon to Italy.

meaning: "do you see?" / "you see" (used to check understanding or add emphasis).
additional_notes: Literally from voir (“to see”) in the vous form: “(do) you see?” Often used as a parenthetical like “you see,” to explain or insist on a point (Les gens, voyez-vous, …). It can also be a straightforward question meaning “Do you see …?” (Voyez-vous la maison blanche ?), including in questions like “Do you see any problem with that?” (Voyez-vous un inconvénient à cela ?).
target_language_example: Je préfère partir tôt, voyez-vous, parce que je dois travailler demain.
native_language_example: I'd rather leave early, you see, because I have to work tomorrow.

voyez-vous un inconvénient à ce que

target_language_multi_word_term: voyez-vous un inconvénient à ce que
meaning: “Would you mind if…?” / “Do you have any objection to…?”
additional_notes: A polite, fairly formal way to ask permission. It’s typically followed by "ce que" + a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., "je fume", "je dorme", "je prenne"). Often used to soften a request or check that something won’t bother the other person.
target_language_example: Voyez-vous un inconvénient à ce que j’ouvre la fenêtre ?
native_language_example: Would you mind if I opened the window?

additional_notes: Used to pause and check something, often before examining, deciding, or testing. Literally “let’s see,” with both verbs from *voir* (“to see”); very common in spoken French, including when you’re about to look at what you have or see what someone can do.
target_language_example: Voyons voir si ça marche.
native_language_example: Let’s see if it works.

meaning: real life (as opposed to fiction/online/a game).
additional_notes: Often used with "dans la vraie vie" (“in real life/IRL”) or "comme dans la vraie vie" (“like in real life”) to contrast everyday reality with movies, books, video games, or online situations. You can also add it as an уточнение: "Dans la vraie vie, je veux dire" = “In real life, I mean.”
target_language_example: On se parle souvent en ligne, mais dans la vraie vie on se voit rarement.
native_language_example: We talk online a lot, but in real life we rarely see each other.

meaning: "really have to go" / "really need to go there".
additional_notes: Built from "vraiment" (really) + "y aller" (to go there). In conversation, "Je dois/Il me faut vraiment y aller" is often used as a polite way to insist you need to leave or go somewhere, or to emphasize you strongly want/need to go.
target_language_example: Désolé, il se fait tard : je dois vraiment y aller.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s getting late: I really have to go.

additional_notes: Very common in French (borrowed from English). You’ll also see the spelling "weekend". Often used with "bon" (Bon week-end !) and with prepositions like "ce week-end" (this weekend) or "le week-end" (on weekends). "À ce week-end" means "See you this weekend."
target_language_example: On se voit ce week-end ?
native_language_example: Are we seeing each other this weekend?

meaning: 'was there?' / 'were there?' / 'have there been?' (past tense, in a question).
additional_notes: Inverted question form of "il y a eu" (past of "il y a"). Used to ask about the existence/number of people or things in the past: "Combien de X y a-t-il eu ?" = "How many X were there?"
target_language_example: Y a-t-il eu des blessés ?
native_language_example: Were there any injured people?

additional_notes: Formal question form of « il y a » (“there is/there are”). Use it to ask whether some plural things/people exist or are available. « des » is the plural “some/any”; in negatives it usually becomes « de » (e.g., « Il n’y a pas de sacs. »).
target_language_example: Y a-t-il des restaurants ouverts près d’ici ?
native_language_example: Are there any restaurants open near here?

additional_notes: Question form of « il y a » (“there is/are”) using inversion (« a-t-il »). Often followed by « que… » to mean “Is there something that…?”. In questions, « quelque chose » is common when you expect there might be something; « quoi que ce soit » is more like “anything at all.”
target_language_example: Y a-t-il quelque chose à boire ?
native_language_example: Is there something to drink? / Is there anything to drink?

additional_notes: Interrogative form of "il y a" (there is/there are). Used in polite, fairly formal questions to ask if something exists or is available: "Y a-t-il un hôtel… ?" = "Is there a hotel…?" Can also be used in more abstract questions: "Y a-t-il un rapport ?" = "Is there a connection/relationship?" Often followed by a noun; use "y a-t-il une" for feminine nouns, and for plurals "y a-t-il des".
target_language_example: Y a-t-il un supermarché près d’ici ?
native_language_example: Is there a supermarket near here?

additional_notes: Interrogative form of « il y a » (“there is/are”), used mainly in formal or careful speech/writing. « une » is the feminine singular article, so it’s followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., une banque, une clé, une forme). In conversation, people often use « Est-ce qu’il y a une… ? » or « Il y a une… ? ».
target_language_example: Y a-t-il une pharmacie près d’ici ?
native_language_example: Is there a pharmacy near here?

meaning: “there isn’t any / there’s no …” (informal for “il n’y a pas de …”).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: drops “il” and usually “ne” from “il n’y a pas de…”. Used before a noun: “Y a pas de problème.” In careful/formal French, say “Il n’y a pas de …”.
target_language_example: T’inquiète, y a pas de problème.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, there’s no problem.

meaning: There’s nobody / no one is here.
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French as a shortened form of « (Il) n’y a personne ». In casual speech, people often drop « il » and/or the negative « ne »: « Y a personne ici » = « Il n’y a personne ici ».
target_language_example: Y a personne au bureau aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: There’s nobody at the office today.

meaning: “There’s only that / that’s the only thing (that matters/works).”
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French; it’s a contraction of « il n’y a que ça ». Used to insist that one thing is the only true/important/valid option: « Y a que ça qui compte » (“That’s all that matters”), « Y a que ça pour… » (“Only that will…”). Often said on its own (« Y a que ça ! ») to mean “That’s the only way / nothing else compares.”
target_language_example: Pour réussir ici, y a que ça : travailler tous les jours.
native_language_example: To succeed here, there’s only one thing: work every day.

additional_notes: Spoken (and often written informally) version of « il y a quelques… » meaning “there are a few/some…”. Commonly followed by a plural noun: « y a quelques minutes », « y a quelques personnes ». In more formal writing, use « il y a quelques… ».
target_language_example: Y a quelques problèmes, mais ça va.
native_language_example: There are a few problems, but it’s okay.

meaning: Colloquial for « il y a quoi ? »: “what’s in it?” / “what is there?” / “what’s wrong?” (depending on context).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French. « y a » is a reduced form of « il y a » (“there is/are”). Used to ask what something contains (« Y a quoi dans ce sac ? ») or, by itself (« Y a quoi ? »), what the problem is / what’s happening (similar to “What is it?” or “What’s up?”).
target_language_example: Y a quoi à manger ce soir ?
native_language_example: What’s there to eat tonight?

additional_notes: y replaces a place or destination already mentioned, so y aller usually means "to go there." In some common expressions like il faut y aller or allez-y, it can mean "we have to go / get going" or "go ahead."
target_language_example: On va y aller demain matin.
native_language_example: We're going there tomorrow morning.

meaning: to go there now; to leave/go now (right away).
additional_notes: “Y aller” literally means “to go there/to it” (y = there/to it). In everyday speech it can also mean simply “to go/leave” depending on context (head out, go to the place being discussed). “Maintenant” adds immediacy/urgency: “now / right now.” Common in questions (Est-ce que tu veux y aller maintenant ?) and with obligation (Il faut/Tu dois y aller maintenant).
target_language_example: Il faut y aller maintenant.
native_language_example: We have to go now.

meaning: to go there alone; to go by yourself.
additional_notes: "Y" means "there" (to that place, previously mentioned or understood). "Aller" is "to go" and "seul" means "alone". Often used in advice or warnings (especially about safety): "Tu ne devrais pas y aller seul" = "You shouldn’t go there alone." You can also change "seul" to agree with the person: "seule" (feminine), "seuls/seules" (plural).
target_language_example: Je préfère ne pas y aller seul le soir.
native_language_example: I prefer not to go there alone in the evening.

additional_notes: Means being able to do something successfully (often after effort): «Tu peux y arriver» = “You can do it / You can make it.” The pronoun «y» refers back to a goal/task already mentioned (roughly “at it/there”), so it often translates as “do it” rather than “arrive there.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tu vas y arriver.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you’re going to manage it / you’re going to make it.

additional_notes: This is the inverted (more formal/written) question form of the future expression **il y aura** (“there will be”). Used to ask whether something will exist/occur in the future. In everyday speech you often hear **Est-ce qu’il y aura… ?** or **Il y aura… ?** instead.
target_language_example: Y aura-t-il assez de temps pour finir ?
native_language_example: Will there be enough time to finish?

additional_notes: Question form (inversion) of **il y avait** (“there was/there were”). Used to ask if something existed/was present, or how many there were: **Y avait-il un problème ?** (“Was there a problem?”). With **combien**, it means “how many were there?”: **Combien y avait-il de… ?**
target_language_example: Y avait-il des places libres dans le train ?
native_language_example: Were there any free seats on the train?

additional_notes: Used in existential expressions, usually with impersonal il: il y a = 'there is/there are'. With other verbs, it gives meanings like 'there can be', 'there must be', or 'there will be' (for example, il peut y avoir, il doit y avoir, il va y avoir). It does not mean 'to have' in the normal possession sense. In informal speech, il is sometimes dropped: va y avoir....
target_language_example: Il va y avoir un problème si on part trop tard.
native_language_example: There will be a problem if we leave too late.

additional_notes: Used to add something/someone to a group that was just mentioned. Common pattern: « ..., y compris + noun/pronoun » (= including ...). As a standalone after a statement, « Vous y compris » / « Y compris toi » means “you included / you too (as part of it)”.
target_language_example: Tout le monde est invité, y compris les enfants.
native_language_example: Everyone is invited, including the children.

meaning: to believe it / to believe in it.
additional_notes: Used with the pronoun “y” to refer back to what was just mentioned (a fact, a story, an idea, a possibility). Common in reactions like “Je refuse d’y croire !” (“I refuse to believe it!”) or in talking about hope/faith: “Je veux encore y croire” (“I still want to believe in it”).
target_language_example: J’ai du mal à y croire, mais c’est vrai.
native_language_example: I have a hard time believing it, but it’s true.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French. It’s a shortened, informal form of "Il y en a qui..." used to introduce a general remark or complaint about a type of people/behavior. Often followed by a verb: "Y en a des qui pensent que..." (= Some people think that...).
target_language_example: Y en a des qui se plaignent tout le temps.
native_language_example: Some people complain all the time.

meaning: to take a quick look at it/there (normally completed by a noun like « coup d’œil » or « œil »).
additional_notes: « y » replaces a place or thing previously mentioned (≈ “there/at it”). In real usage, « y jeter un… » is typically incomplete by itself and is most often finished as « y jeter un coup d’œil » or « y jeter un œil » meaning “to have a quick look.”
target_language_example: Je vais y jeter un coup d’œil et je te dis.
native_language_example: I’m going to take a quick look and I’ll tell you.

meaning: 'to take a look at it' / 'to have a quick look'.
additional_notes: Common, casual way to say you’ll look at something briefly. "jeter un œil" literally means "to throw an eye," but it’s used like English "take a look." The pronoun "y" usually means "at it/there" and refers to something already mentioned (a document, a screen, a place, etc.). You can replace "y" with a specific object: "jeter un œil au menu" (take a look at the menu).
target_language_example: Tu peux y jeter un œil ce soir ?
native_language_example: Can you take a look at it tonight?

meaning: to spend time on it; (informal) to die / get killed.
additional_notes: With a duration, it usually means “to spend time on it”: « On ne va pas y passer trois heures » = “We’re not going to spend three hours on it.” Without a duration, « y passer » is often an idiom meaning “to die / to be killed” (or “to almost die” with « j’ai cru y passer »).
target_language_example: Fais attention en traversant : tu vas y passer !
native_language_example: Be careful crossing: you’re going to get yourself killed!

additional_notes: Used with the pronoun "y" to refer to something already mentioned or understood ("it"/"that"). Often follows another verb (e.g., "prendre du temps pour y penser", "essayer de ne pas y penser", "j'aurais dû y penser").
target_language_example: Je vais y penser ce soir.
native_language_example: I’ll think about it tonight.

meaning: to die (in an accident / because of something).
additional_notes: Literally “to stay there,” but very often used idiomatically to mean “to end up dead” (e.g., in a crash, an attack, a dangerous situation): « Elle aurait pu y rester » = “She could have died.” Often appears with « faillir », « manquer de », « croire » or « j’ai cru que j’allais… ». In « T’aurais dû y rester », it’s a harsh remark meaning “You should’ve died.” In some contexts it can also be literal (“you must stay there”), but the “die” meaning is common in warnings about danger.
target_language_example: Sans la ceinture, on aurait pu y rester.
native_language_example: Without the seat belt, we could have died.

meaning: to go back there; to return to it.
additional_notes: "Y" replaces a place (there) or something previously mentioned. "Retourner" means "to go back/return". Common with verbs like vouloir, pouvoir, devoir: "Je veux/pourrais/devrais y retourner."
target_language_example: On peut y retourner demain si tu veux.
native_language_example: We can go back there tomorrow if you want.

meaning: to think about it; to consider it.
additional_notes: “Y” is a pronoun that replaces something introduced with “à” (or “sur”, etc.), meaning “about it/that.” Common in phrases like “Il faut y réfléchir” (We need to think about it) and “Laisse-moi y réfléchir” (Let me think about it).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de temps pour y réfléchir.
native_language_example: I need time to think about it.

additional_notes: Used with the verb aller: "y" replaces a place (there) or something previously mentioned. Very common in "On y va !" = "Let’s go!" and questions like "Qui y va ?" = "Who’s going?". Note the fixed expression "Il y va de ..." meaning "... is at stake" (e.g., "Il y va de ta vie" = "Your life is at stake").
target_language_example: Allez, on y va !
native_language_example: Come on, let’s go!

meaning: “are you there?” / “did you get there?” (with y = “there”).
additional_notes: Used in questions with inversion (êtes-vous = “are you”) when the pronoun y (“there”) replaces a place (or sometimes a situation/goal mentioned earlier). In compound tenses with verbs that use être (like arriver, parvenir), y goes before the auxiliary: « À quelle heure y êtes-vous arrivé(e)(s) ? » = “What time did you get there?” The ending changes for gender/number in the past participle: arrivé / arrivée / arrivés / arrivées.
target_language_example: Pourquoi y êtes-vous allé si tôt ?
native_language_example: Why did you go there so early?

additional_notes: y replaces a place or location already mentioned or understood from context. It is commonly used to say that someone is present at a place, will arrive there, or feels as if they are there.
target_language_example: J'aimerais y être ce soir.
native_language_example: I'd like to be there tonight.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s eye color. Often appears with verbs like « avoir » (Il/Elle a des yeux bleus) or with possessives (ses/tes/vos yeux bleus). In French, you typically use the plural « yeux » even though English might say “blue eyes” or “blue-eyed.”
target_language_example: Elle a les yeux bleus et les cheveux blonds.
native_language_example: She has blue eyes and blonde hair.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like aider/commencer/avoir du mal + à apprendre (to help/start/have trouble learning). It can also describe something as being learnable or needing to be learned: "Il y a quelque chose à apprendre" (there’s something to learn) or "C’est difficile à apprendre" (it’s hard to learn).
target_language_example: J’ai encore beaucoup à apprendre.
native_language_example: I still have a lot to learn.

meaning: to something else; about something else.
additional_notes: Used after verbs with "à". Common patterns: "penser/réfléchir à autre chose" = think about something else (often when distracted), and "passer à autre chose" = move on to something else (change topic/activity). In commands: "Passe/Passez à autre chose" and "Pense/Pensez à autre chose".
target_language_example: On a fini ce dossier, passons à autre chose.
native_language_example: We’re done with this file—let’s move on to something else.

additional_notes: Used mostly in slogans, protests, or strong statements: « À bas + noun/name ! » = “Down with + noun/name!” You often see it with something being rejected (a regime, a law, a leader). On its own (« À bas ! ») it can mean “Down!” but it’s most natural with what you’re opposing right after it.
target_language_example: À bas la dictature !
native_language_example: Down with the dictatorship!

meaning: made from; based on (as the main ingredient).
additional_notes: Used to describe what something is primarily made from or centered around, especially ingredients (food, cosmetics, medicine): « un produit à base de… ». Often corresponds to “plant-based” in « à base de plantes ».
target_language_example: Je cherche une crème à base de aloe vera.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a cream made with aloe vera.

additional_notes: A common farewell meaning you expect to see the person again in the near future. Used in person, on the phone, in messages/emails, etc. You can add a name after it (e.g., « À bientôt, Ian. ») or soften/qualify it (e.g., « À bientôt, sans doute. » = “See you soon, probably.”).
target_language_example: Bon, je dois y aller — à bientôt !
native_language_example: Well, I have to go — see you soon!

meaning: flat out; at full capacity; all out.
additional_notes: Colloquial. Used to say someone or something is working at maximum effort or intensity: « Je suis à bloc » (I’m slammed / going full speed). Can also describe setting a level to the maximum (music, heating, etc.): « Mets le son à bloc » (Turn the sound all the way up).
target_language_example: En ce moment, je suis à bloc au travail.
native_language_example: Right now, I’m working flat out.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like donner, servir, or demander to mean “(something) to drink”: « Donne-moi à boire » = “Give me something to drink.” In « se laisser aller à boire », it means “to let oneself go and start drinking (often alcohol)”, i.e. drinking when you shouldn’t or drinking too much.
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu as quelque chose à boire ?
native_language_example: Do you have something to drink?

additional_notes: Used for being on a vehicle (plane, train, boat, bus, etc.) or sometimes figuratively as “on the team/involved” (“Je suis heureux de vous avoir à bord.”). Common with verbs like “être/se trouver à bord” (to be on board), “monter à bord” (to board), and “prendre à bord” (to take on board/pick up).
target_language_example: Il n’y a personne à bord du bus.
native_language_example: There’s nobody on board the bus.

meaning: at the end of your strength/patience; exhausted; at the end of your rope.
additional_notes: Used after the verb être ("il est à bout", "je suis à bout") to mean someone is completely worn out (physically or mentally). Common with "à bout de" + noun: "à bout de force" (out of strength), "à bout de patience" (out of patience).
