You can also use it with things like "ma patience est à bout" to mean your patience has run out.
target_language_example: Après cette semaine, je suis à bout de forces.
native_language_example: After this week, I'm completely exhausted.

meaning: at the end of; out of (energy/patience/breath).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to say someone has no more of something (often a resource like strength, patience, or breath): « à bout de forces », « à bout de patience », « à bout de souffle ». Often implies being exhausted or worn out.
target_language_example: Je suis à bout de forces, je dois me reposer.
native_language_example: I’m out of energy; I need to rest.

meaning: out of breath; breathless (sometimes: worn out / running out of steam).
additional_notes: Used for people after physical effort (running, climbing stairs, etc.). It can also describe things (like a car, a project, a system) that are failing or have no energy/power left. Often used with être: «Je suis à bout de souffle».
target_language_example: Après avoir monté les escaliers, je suis à bout de souffle.
native_language_example: After climbing the stairs, I'm out of breath.

additional_notes: Used to give a cause/reason, usually with a noun/pronoun (e.g., à cause de la pluie, à cause de toi). Often implies a negative cause/blame (“because of you”), but it can also be neutral depending on context. Also used with a clause via “à cause du fait que …” (“because of the fact that …”).
target_language_example: Le train est en retard à cause de la neige.
native_language_example: The train is late because of the snow.

meaning: "because of the rain" / "due to the rain."
additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something (often a negative result like a cancellation). The pattern is: « à cause de + noun » (e.g., à cause du trafic, à cause de mon travail). It’s generally neutral, but can sound like blaming the cause; for a more positive/neutral “thanks to,” use « grâce à ».
target_language_example: Le match a été reporté à cause de la pluie.
native_language_example: The match was postponed because of the rain.

meaning: "because of the storm" / "due to the storm."
additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something (often a problem or negative outcome). You can place it after the main clause (Ils sont en retard à cause de la tempête.) or at the beginning (À cause de la tempête, ils sont en retard.). More generally, it's the pattern "à cause de + noun" (à cause du trafic, à cause de la pluie).
target_language_example: À cause de la tempête, le train a été retardé.
native_language_example: Because of the storm, the train was delayed.

meaning: because of me; due to me (my fault).
additional_notes: Used to say you are the reason for something (often something negative). In questions like « C’est à cause de moi ? », it means “Is it because of me?/Is it my fault?”. Can also be used neutrally, but it commonly carries blame or guilt.
target_language_example: Je suis désolé : c’est à cause de moi.
native_language_example: I’m sorry: it’s because of me./It’s my fault.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is the reason something happened. It often implies blame (“it’s your fault”), especially in negative sentences, but it can also be neutral depending on tone and context. You can negate it with “pas” or “ce n’est pas” to reassure someone: “Ce n’est pas à cause de toi.”
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas venir ce soir à cause de toi.
native_language_example: I can’t come tonight because of you.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason or cause for something. It is followed by a plural noun phrase: à cause des travaux (because of the roadworks), à cause des coûts (because of the costs). Often used for a negative cause, but it can be neutral depending on context.
target_language_example: Le match est annulé à cause des intempéries.
native_language_example: The game is canceled because of bad weather.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something, often with a negative idea (problem, blame, etc.). It’s the form of « à cause de » + « le » → « du ». For feminine singular, use « à cause de la »; for plural, « à cause des »; before a vowel/h mute: « à cause de l’ ».
target_language_example: Le train est en retard à cause du trafic.
native_language_example: The train is late because of the traffic.

meaning: to this day; as of today; to date (so far).
additional_notes: Used to say something is still true up to now, often in more formal contexts. Common with durations or ongoing situations: « Il travaille ici à ce jour » (“He still works here to this day”). Also used with superlatives/comparisons: « le meilleur … à ce jour » (“the best … to date/so far”).
target_language_example: À ce jour, je n'ai reçu aucune réponse.
native_language_example: As of today, I haven't received any reply.

meaning: at that time; at that moment (then).
additional_notes: Refers to a specific moment in the past or future that’s already known from context (often translated as “then” when the timing has just been mentioned). It can go at the end of the sentence or at the beginning for emphasis: « À ce moment-là, … ».
target_language_example: Je n’étais pas disponible à ce moment-là, mais je le suis maintenant.
native_language_example: I wasn’t available at that time, but I am now.

meaning: about that; regarding that; on that topic.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific subject already mentioned or understood from context. Common after verbs like parler (to talk), savoir (to know), and être anxieux/anxieuse (to be anxious) to mean “about it/that.”
target_language_example: Je n’ai rien à dire à ce propos.
native_language_example: I have nothing to say about that.

meaning: "at this point" / "at this stage" (in a situation or process).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the current moment in an ongoing situation, discussion, plan, or process—often to say what is (or isn’t) possible now. Common in both spoken and written French, and often followed by a statement of limits or conclusions (e.g., "je ne peux rien dire", "ça ne sert à rien").
target_language_example: À ce stade, on doit attendre la réponse.
native_language_example: At this point, we have to wait for the answer.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a topic that has already been mentioned or is understood from context. Common after verbs like parler (to talk), dire (to say), savoir (to know), penser (to think): « Qu’est-ce que tu sais à ce sujet ? »
target_language_example: Je n'ai rien à ajouter à ce sujet.
native_language_example: I have nothing to add on that subject.

meaning: at this place/spot; here (at that location).
additional_notes: Used to point to a specific location (often a particular spot on a street, map, river, etc.). It can refer to the place you’re currently indicating rather than a general area. Similar in meaning to "ici" but more specific/explicit: "at this exact spot."
target_language_example: Attention : à cet endroit, la route est très glissante.
native_language_example: Careful: at this spot, the road is very slippery.

meaning: at this time (of day); at this hour.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the current time, often with surprise or disapproval (especially if it’s late or unusual): « Encore dehors à cette heure ! » = “Still out at this hour!” Can also be polite in apologies: « Excusez-moi de vous déranger à cette heure. » = “Sorry to bother you at this hour.”
target_language_example: Tu m’appelles à cette heure ?
native_language_example: You’re calling me at this hour?

meaning: at this time (of day); at this hour.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the current time (often meaning “right now, at this point in the day”). Very common in questions or comments expressing surprise/complaint: « À cette heure-ci ? » = “At this hour? (Now?)”. It can be used at the start of a sentence as a time phrase: « À cette heure-ci, … ».
target_language_example: À cette heure-ci, les magasins sont déjà fermés.
native_language_example: At this time of day, the stores are already closed.

additional_notes: Used after nouns like "réponse" (answer) or verbs like "répondre" (to answer) to indicate which question the answer/responding is directed to: "répondre à cette question" / "la réponse à cette question". "À" can often mean "to" or "for" in this context.
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas de réponse à cette question.
native_language_example: I don’t have an answer to this question.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a particular period in the past (or a previously mentioned time period). Often placed at the beginning of a sentence for context: « À cette époque, ... ».
target_language_example: À cette époque, je vivais encore chez mes parents.
native_language_example: Back then, I was still living with my parents.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on every occasion. Very common with the present tense (Je stresse à chaque fois.) and with a clause: « à chaque fois que + subject + verb » (“whenever/every time that…”). Can also be used alone to confirm repetition: « À chaque fois. » (“Every time.”).
target_language_example: À chaque fois que j’y vais, il pleut.
native_language_example: Every time I go there, it rains.

additional_notes: Used after a noun (often a person or people) to say they are someone’s dependents, usually in the sense of financial responsibility: « avoir des enfants/une famille à charge ». Common in administrative or legal contexts (forms, benefits, taxes).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas changer de travail facilement : j’ai trois enfants à charge.
native_language_example: I can’t change jobs easily: I have three dependent children.

additional_notes: Used in contrast with « à froid » (“once things have cooled down / with hindsight”). It can be literal (e.g., doing something while a part is still hot) or figurative (giving an immediate reaction, decision, or opinion right after an event). Often appears with verbs like « réagir », « commenter », « décider », « analyser ».
target_language_example: Je préfère ne pas réagir à chaud et y réfléchir d’abord.
native_language_example: I’d rather not react in the heat of the moment and think about it first.

additional_notes: Used mainly after verbs like monter (to ride), être monté(e) (to have ridden), or aller (to go) to indicate that you are on a horse (not in a vehicle). You can also use it in expressions like à cheval sur… (“straddling/overlapping; astride”), but the most common beginner meaning is “on horseback.”
target_language_example: J'adore me promener à cheval le week-end.
native_language_example: I love going for rides on horseback on the weekend.

additional_notes: Two common uses: (1) physical: something is positioned across two areas (e.g., a border), as if it were “straddling” them. (2) figurative (often with a person + a value/rule): being very insistent on respecting something (e.g., punctuality, principles): « Il est à cheval sur la ponctualité. » = he’s really strict about being on time. Usually followed by a noun: « à cheval sur + la frontière / les principes / la ponctualité ».
target_language_example: Le village est à cheval sur deux communes.
native_language_example: The village straddles two towns/municipalities.

additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar insult/criticism meaning something is extremely bad (a situation, a performance, a person/thing, etc.). Often used with "être" (e.g., "C’est/Il est à chier"). Avoid in polite company; use "nul", "très mauvais", or "horrible" for a less crude alternative.
target_language_example: Ce film est à chier, je veux partir.
native_language_example: This movie is really shitty; I want to leave.

additional_notes: Introduces a requirement that must be met for something to happen. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (often in the past: « à condition de rester », « à condition de ne pas… »). With a full clause, you’ll usually see « à condition que » + subjunctive.
target_language_example: Je viens à condition de partir avant 22 h.
native_language_example: I’ll come provided that we leave before 10 p.m.

meaning: against the current; against the trend.
additional_notes: Used literally for moving against the flow of water (e.g., swimming upstream) and figuratively for going against what most people do or think. Often with verbs like nager, aller, remonter, se tenir.
target_language_example: Il a choisi de vivre à contre-courant, loin des modes.
native_language_example: He chose to live against the trend, far from fashion/fads.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something even though they don’t really want to. Often follows the verb: accepter à contrecœur, faire quelque chose à contrecœur. Close in meaning to « à regret » (with regret) or « malgré lui/elle » (against his/her will).
target_language_example: J’y suis allé à contrecœur, parce que je n’avais pas le choix.
native_language_example: I went reluctantly because I had no choice.

meaning: with (repeated) blows of; by means of (often repeatedly/forcefully).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the instrument or means used to obtain a result, often with an idea of repetition, effort, or force. Very frequently used in the plural: « à coups de + nom » (e.g., « à coups de marteau »). It can also be figurative: « à coup de publicité » (through lots of advertising), « à coup de millions » (by pouring money into it). Invariable phrase; the choice between singular (« à coup de ») and plural (« à coups de ») depends on whether you’re conceptualizing a single blow/means vs repeated blows/means.
target_language_example: Il a cassé la porte à coup de pied.
native_language_example: He broke the door down with a kick.

meaning: breathtaking; stunning (so impressive it “takes your breath away”).
additional_notes: Used after the verb (often with "être") to describe something very impressive or beautiful: "C’est à couper le souffle" / "Elle est à couper le souffle". Can also describe an experience or challenge: "un défi à couper le souffle". The literal idea is “to cut the breath,” but the natural English equivalent is “to take your breath away.”
target_language_example: La vue depuis le sommet est à couper le souffle.
native_language_example: The view from the top is breathtaking.

meaning: using repeated blows/hits with; by repeatedly (doing something) with.
additional_notes: Used to describe an action done by repeated strikes, often in a violent or forceful way: « à coups de barre de fer » (with repeated blows of an iron bar), « à coups de pied » (by kicking repeatedly). It can also be used more broadly for repeated acts with something (even in a joking way), like throwing food or giving taps with a ruler.
target_language_example: Il a cassé la vitre à coups de marteau.
native_language_example: He broke the window by repeatedly hitting it with a hammer.

additional_notes: Most often used as « être à court de + noun » to mean you don’t have enough of something or you’ve run out: « à court de temps » (short on time), « à court d’argent/de fonds » (out of money), « à court de nourriture » (out of food). With « à court de mots », it means “at a loss for words.” You can also say « Je suis à court » when the missing thing is understood from context (e.g., out of money/ideas).
target_language_example: On est à court d’idées, tu peux m’aider ?
native_language_example: We’re out of ideas—can you help me?

additional_notes: Used after words like "plein/pleine" or "bondé(e)" to emphasize that something is extremely full/crowded—so full it could "burst". Common with places (a restaurant, a room, the streets) and containers (a bag, a suitcase).
target_language_example: Le bus était plein à craquer ce matin.
native_language_example: The bus was packed this morning.

additional_notes: Used after an adjective or noun to intensify: « Il fait une chaleur à crever ! » = “It’s insanely hot!” Literally “to burst/die,” but in everyday speech it often just means “really, extremely.” In « chercher à crever » / « tenir à crever », it means “to be looking to get yourself killed / to insist on dying,” and it’s aggressive and vulgar in tone.
target_language_example: J'ai faim à crever.
native_language_example: I’m starving (literally “hungry to die”).

meaning: on credit; with delayed payment (pay later).
additional_notes: Used when you receive something now and pay later—either by having a tab/account with the seller or by borrowing money (a loan). Common with verbs like acheter (à crédit), vendre (à crédit), payer (à crédit). Often contrasts with payer comptant (pay in cash / pay upfront).
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas assez d’argent aujourd’hui : est-ce que je peux acheter à crédit ?
native_language_example: I don’t have enough money today: can I buy on credit?

additional_notes: Most often used as « à côté de + noun/pronoun » = “next to/beside”: « Je suis assis à côté de Marie. » It can also be used alone to mean “nearby/next door” depending on context: « Il habite à côté. » As an exclamation (« À côté ! »), it means “Wrong!” / “Not even close!” Finally, « à côté de… » can mean “compared to…”: « À côté de toi, je suis débutant. »
target_language_example: Assieds-toi à côté de moi.
native_language_example: Sit next to me.

additional_notes: Used to say something is right next to another place/person/thing. It can describe location (unlike "à côté" alone, which can also mean "wrong"). Often followed by a noun or stressed pronoun: "à côté de la banque", "à côté de lui".
target_language_example: Je suis assis à côté de toi.
native_language_example: I’m sitting next to you.

meaning: completely off the mark; totally wrong (missing the point).
additional_notes: An idiomatic, fairly informal expression used to say someone’s idea, guess, or understanding is way off. Often intensified with "complètement" (completely). You can use it about a person ("Tu es à côté de la plaque") or about what they said/thought ("Ton hypothèse est à côté de la plaque").
target_language_example: Non, tu es à côté de la plaque : ce n’est pas lui le responsable.
native_language_example: No, you’re completely off the mark: he isn’t the one responsible.

additional_notes: Literally “at the side of him.” Used for physical position (sitting/standing next to a man). It can also be used figuratively to mean “compared to him” (e.g., someone seems small à côté de lui).
target_language_example: Je suis resté à côté de lui pendant le concert.
native_language_example: I stayed next to him during the concert.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is right by your side (physical position). Often follows verbs like être/aller/se mettre/s’asseoir/dormir (e.g., « être à côté de moi » = to be next to me).
target_language_example: Tu peux t’asseoir à côté de moi.
native_language_example: You can sit next to me.

additional_notes:
Often used with common verbs:
- « tenir à cœur (à quelqu’un) » = to matter a lot to someone / to be close to someone’s heart. (Ex: « Cela me tient à cœur. »)
- « prendre (quelque chose) à cœur » = to take something seriously / to take something to heart. (Ex: « Il prend son boulot à cœur. »)
- « prendre (les choses) trop à cœur » = to take things too personally / too much to heart.
target_language_example: Je prends ce projet vraiment à cœur.
native_language_example: I take this project really seriously / to heart.

meaning: “Yeah right!” / “Tell that to someone else!” (I don’t believe you).
additional_notes: Often used as the exclamation « à d'autres ! » to show disbelief or to reject an excuse or a claim. Literally “to others,” implying “tell that to other people, not me.” Typically informal and often followed by an exclamation point.
target_language_example: Tu dis que tu n’as pas triché ? à d'autres !
native_language_example: You say you didn’t cheat? Yeah right!

additional_notes: Used as a goodbye when you expect to see the person the next day. You can add a time of day: « à demain matin » (tomorrow morning), « à demain soir » (tomorrow evening).
target_language_example: Bon, je rentre. À demain !
native_language_example: Okay, I'm heading home. See you tomorrow!

additional_notes: Used on transport announcements/signs to indicate where a bus/train/flight is going. It’s followed by a place name: « un train à destination de Paris ». In questions, it often appears with « être »: « Ce train est-il à destination de… ? ».
target_language_example: Le prochain vol est à destination de Montréal.
native_language_example: The next flight is bound for Montreal.

additional_notes: Used to say something nearly happened or someone nearly did something. Very often followed by "de" + infinitive: "à deux doigts de partir" (this close to leaving). It can also be left implied in speech ("J’étais à deux doigts…") when the action is obvious from context.
target_language_example: J’étais à deux doigts de lui dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I was this close to telling him the truth.

meaning: very nearby; just a short walk away.
additional_notes: Used to say something is very close (often “just around the corner”), usually followed by de/du/de la/des + place: « à deux pas du métro ». Can also be used alone (« J’habite à deux pas. »). It’s a fixed expression: it doesn’t mean literally “two steps.”
target_language_example: La boulangerie est à deux pas d’ici.
native_language_example: The bakery is just a short walk from here.

additional_notes: Used after another verb to express something that is to be said. Very common in the pattern "avoir + [something] + à dire" = "to have + [something] + to say" (often implying obligation or that you have something to say): "C'est tout ce que tu as à dire ?" / "J'ai un truc à dire." Also appears in set phrases like "avoir son mot à dire" = "to have a say" (to have the right to give your opinion).
target_language_example: J'ai quelque chose à dire, mais je ne sais pas comment le dire.
native_language_example: I have something to say, but I don't know how to say it.

additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone is ready to be used or can be provided if needed. Often appears with « être à disposition » (e.g., « Je suis à disposition » = “I’m available.”) or « mettre ... à disposition » (to make something available). « À votre disposition » is more formal/polite; « à ta disposition » is used with someone you address as « tu ».
target_language_example: Si vous avez des questions, je suis à disposition.
native_language_example: If you have any questions, I’m available.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done without being physically present ("remotely": commander à distance, obtenir un diplôme à distance) or to tell someone to keep away from something/someone ("stay/keep your distance": rester/tenir/se tenir à distance de). Often followed by "de" + noun/person.
target_language_example: Je travaille à distance deux jours par semaine.
native_language_example: I work remotely two days a week.

additional_notes: Used for directions and location. With movement/turning, it often means “to the right” (Tourne(z) à droite). With position, it can mean “on the right” (à droite de… = to the right of…). In the fixed expression « à droite et à gauche », it means “here and there / left and right,” not literally about direction.
target_language_example: Le café est juste à droite de la boulangerie.
native_language_example: The café is right to the right of the bakery.

additional_notes: Usually comes after a noun: quelque chose à faire = "something to do," des choses à faire = "things to do." It can also imply something that still needs to be done or that someone has to do, as in ce qu'il avait à faire = "what he had to do."
target_language_example: J'ai encore quelques courses à faire.
native_language_example: I still have a few errands to do.

additional_notes: Used as “à” + infinitive (“faire”) + “ça” (“that/this”) after many verbs and expressions. Common patterns: “arriver à faire ça” (manage to do that), “passer du temps à faire ça” (spend time doing that), “forcer quelqu’un à faire ça” (force someone to do that), “avoir intérêt à faire ça (bien)” (had better do that (well)). “Ça” can mean “that” or “this” depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu n’es pas obligé(e) à faire ça.
native_language_example: You don’t have to do that.

meaning: right at the surface of; level with.
additional_notes: Used mostly in fixed expressions. With a noun it means something is right at the surface/edge: « à fleur de peau » (very sensitive, emotions close to the surface), « à fleur d’eau » (at water level). It often suggests something is barely covered or almost showing.
target_language_example: Avec le stress, j’ai les nerfs à fleur de peau.
native_language_example: With the stress, my nerves are on edge (my emotions are close to the surface).

meaning: all out; fully / all the way (to the max).
additional_notes: Often used to encourage someone to give maximum effort: « Donne-toi à fond » (“Give it everything / Go all out”). It can also mean turning/lowering something completely (e.g., volume, a window blind): « baisser / descendre à fond » (“turn down / lower all the way”). Common in spoken French and a bit informal.
target_language_example: Vas-y à fond, tu vas y arriver !
native_language_example: Go for it all out, you’re going to make it!

meaning: from/through repeated effort; as a result of doing something a lot.
additional_notes: Often used as **à force de + infinitive** (“by/through doing … repeatedly/so much”), to explain a cause and its consequence: *À force de pleurer, ses yeux étaient rouges.* It can also appear alone with a noun to mean “by dint of/through repeated exposure”: *Je sais le rôle à force de l'entendre.*
target_language_example: À force de travailler tous les jours, elle a fini par réussir.
native_language_example: By working every day, she eventually managed to succeed.

meaning: by/through (doing something) repeatedly or with great effort; from (doing something) too much.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive or noun to show that something happens as a result of repeated actions or persistence ("à force de travailler")—or because of overdoing it ("à force de rester ici"). Often translates as “by dint of,” “through,” or “from.”
target_language_example: À force de répéter, tu vas y arriver.
native_language_example: By repeating it (enough times), you’ll manage it.

meaning: cold; when cold (not heated / after cooling).
additional_notes: Used to describe something done or experienced while it is cold or without warming it up first. Common in cooking (manger/goûter un plat à froid = eat/taste it cold) and mechanics (un moteur à froid = a cold engine). It can also be used more figuratively to mean “with a cool head / without emotion” (analyser à froid).
target_language_example: Je préfère goûter le café à froid.
native_language_example: I prefer to taste the coffee cold.

additional_notes: Used for location and directions: à gauche = on/to the left (often with verbs like être, se trouver, tourner). In the expression « à droite et à gauche », it means “here and there / left and right,” i.e., in various places or in an unsystematic way.
target_language_example: La banque est juste à gauche de la poste.
native_language_example: The bank is just to the left of the post office.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like être/rester (to be/stay), se mettre/mettre (to get/put someone), tomber (to fall) to describe a position on the knees. Common as an order: « À genoux ! » = “On your knees!” Opposes « debout » (standing) in phrases like « mourir debout que vivre à genoux » (“better to die standing than live on your knees,” i.e., in submission).
target_language_example: Il s’est mis à genoux pour demander pardon.
native_language_example: He got down on his knees to apologize.

meaning: in big strides; quickly; rapidly (often said of something approaching or progressing fast).
additional_notes: Less common in the singular; more frequently encountered as « à grands pas », especially with verbs like « approcher » or « avancer ». In the singular, it still conveys the idea of moving forward quickly, step by step.
target_language_example: L’hiver approche à grand pas.
native_language_example: Winter is fast approaching.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like « approcher » or « arriver » to say an event/date is coming soon, as if it were taking “big steps” toward you: « Noël approche à grands pas. » It’s a common, neutral expression.
target_language_example: Les vacances arrivent à grands pas.
native_language_example: The holidays are coming up fast.

meaning: out loud; aloud (in a loud voice).
additional_notes: Used with speaking/reading verbs (e.g., parler, lire) to mean the words are said audibly for others (or yourself) to hear. It can also be used alone as an instruction (“Out loud.”).
target_language_example: Peux-tu le dire à haute voix, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you say it out loud, please?

meaning: up to the height/level of; to the amount of.
additional_notes: Used (1) literally for physical height or level: « L’eau monte à hauteur des genoux » (“up to knee level”). (2) figuratively for a quantity, often money or a percentage: « subvention à hauteur de 500 € », « indemnisé à hauteur de 10 % » (= “up to / in the amount of”). Common in formal or administrative contexts.
target_language_example: La ville financera le projet à hauteur de 200 000 euros.
native_language_example: The city will fund the project to the amount of 200,000 euros.

additional_notes: Used with "à" to give a specific time on the clock for an event (meeting, departure, waking up, etc.). You can swap in other times: à sept heures, à huit heures et demie (8:30), à huit heures du matin (8 a.m.), à huit heures du soir (8 p.m.).
target_language_example: Le train part à huit heures.
native_language_example: The train leaves at eight o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to express that something will last indefinitely. Common with verbs like rester (to stay), se souvenir (to remember), survivre (to live on), and in emphatic exclamations: « À jamais ! » It often sounds emotional or dramatic, like “forever” in English.
target_language_example: Je t’aimerai à jamais.
native_language_example: I will love you forever.

meaning: on an empty stomach; having had nothing to eat (or sometimes: not having drunk alcohol).
additional_notes: Most often means you haven’t eaten (e.g., before a blood test, surgery, or taking medicine): « être à jeun » / « venir à jeun ». In casual speech it can also mean being sober/not drunk, depending on context. Often used with « être » or « rester ».
target_language_example: Je dois être à jeun avant la prise de sang.
native_language_example: I have to be on an empty stomach before the blood test.

additional_notes: Used with **être** to say something is updated/current: *Mon appareil est à jour.* Very common in tech with **mettre à jour** = “to update”: *Mets ton système/logiciel à jour.* The noun **une mise à jour** means “an update” (e.g., *des mises à jour*).
target_language_example: Je dois mettre l'application à jour avant de l'utiliser.
native_language_example: I need to update the app before using it.

additional_notes: Used to say that a feeling, reaction, criticism, or pride is justified (for a valid reason). Often comes after a statement for emphasis: « …, et à juste titre. » or « …, à juste titre. »
target_language_example: Elle est inquiète, et à juste titre : il n’a pas répondu depuis deux jours.
native_language_example: She’s worried, and with good reason: he hasn’t replied in two days.

meaning: safe; sheltered (out of danger or bad weather).
additional_notes: Often used with **être** (to be safe/sheltered) or **mettre** (to put someone safe): *On va te mettre à l'abri.* You can also specify what you’re protected from with **à l’abri de**: *à l’abri de la pluie* (sheltered from the rain), *à l’abri du danger* (safe from danger).
target_language_example: Entre vite, tu seras à l'abri de la pluie.
native_language_example: Come in quickly, you’ll be sheltered from the rain.

additional_notes: Used as an urgent cry when you need assistance or are in trouble. Often said alone ("à l'aide !") or alongside "au secours !". You can add context after it: "à l'aide, s’il vous plaît !" / "à l'aide, je suis tombé(e) !" Note: in running text it’s often written in lowercase; at the start of a sentence it may be capitalized ("À l'aide !").
target_language_example: à l'aide ! Je suis perdu(e).
native_language_example: Help! I'm lost.

additional_notes: Used to talk about feeling relaxed physically or socially, or feeling confident with a situation/person. Common in polite phrases like « Mettez-vous à l'aise » (“Make yourself comfortable”). Often followed by « avec » + person/thing: « être à l’aise avec quelqu’un » = “to feel comfortable with someone.” Can also be used as a question: « T’es à l’aise ? » / « Vous êtes à l’aise ? » = “Are you comfortable?”
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas encore à l'aise en français, mais je progresse.
native_language_example: I’m not comfortable in French yet, but I’m improving.

additional_notes: Used to describe something in an old, traditional style (furniture, decor, clothing, cooking), or to say you’ll do something the “old-school” way (often implying without modern tools/technology). Can be said alone as a suggestion/decision: « À l’ancienne. »
target_language_example: Pas de GPS : on y va à l'ancienne, avec une carte.
native_language_example: No GPS: we'll do it the old-school way, with a map.

additional_notes: Used in radio/TV contexts to indicate that someone/something is live or currently being broadcast. Common as a quick check right before speaking: « On est à l'antenne ? » = “Are we on air?” It can refer to right now (« Tu es à l'antenne. ») or to very soon (« On est à l'antenne dans une minute. »).
target_language_example: Attention, on est à l'antenne dans trente secondes.
native_language_example: Careful, we’re on air in thirty seconds.

meaning: in the back; at the rear.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a position behind something (the back of a room, a line, a building, etc.). Very common for vehicles: à l'arrière = in the back seat/in the back. Often contrasts with à l'avant (“in the front”).
target_language_example: Les enfants sont assis à l'arrière de la voiture.
native_language_example: The kids are sitting in the back of the car.

meaning: at the airport; to the airport.
additional_notes: Uses « à » with a place. It can mean being located there (« Je suis à l'aéroport. » = I’m at the airport) or going there with a verb of movement like « aller » (« aller à l'aéroport » = to go to the airport). « l’ » is « le » shortened before a vowel: « le aéroport » → « l’aéroport ».
target_language_example: On se retrouve à l'aéroport à 8h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the airport at 8.

meaning: backwards; the wrong way around; upside down.
additional_notes: Used for things written or done in reverse (compter à l'envers = count down), or physically oriented the wrong way (tenir quelque chose à l'envers = hold it upside down / the wrong way). Also in the expression « le monde à l'envers » meaning “everything is upside down / things are completely backwards.”
target_language_example: Tu as mis ton pull à l'envers.
native_language_example: You put your sweater on inside out.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is outside a place, or to contrast the outside with the inside (à l'intérieur): croustillant à l'extérieur, moelleux à l'intérieur. Often answers “Where?” (Où ?): Je suis / je serai à l'extérieur.
target_language_example: On peut manger à l'extérieur s'il fait beau.
native_language_example: We can eat outside if the weather is nice.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something arrives at the scheduled time (not late). Common with être: « être à l'heure » (to be on time). You can emphasize it with words like « pile » or « juste »: « pile/juste à l'heure » = exactly on time.
target_language_example: Le train est arrivé à l'heure.
native_language_example: The train arrived on time.

meaning: to the hospital; at/in the hospital.
additional_notes: Used with motion verbs (aller, conduire, emmener) to mean “to the hospital.” With a state (être), it means someone is “in/at the hospital” (usually as a patient or because they’re hospitalized).
target_language_example: Après l'accident, elle est restée à l'hôpital pendant deux jours.
native_language_example: After the accident, she stayed in the hospital for two days.

meaning: at the hotel; to the hotel.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of location (être, rester) to mean “at the hotel,” and with verbs of movement (aller, retourner) to mean “to the hotel.” Often refers to the hotel you’re staying at or meeting at.
target_language_example: On se voit à l'hôtel à 18 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at the hotel at 6 p.m.?

meaning: just now; a moment ago; right away (immediately).
additional_notes: Often used to talk about something that happened very recently ("just now / a moment ago"). With verbs like partir, venir, commencer, etc., it can also mean "right away / immediately" (stronger than "maintenant"). You can also say "à l'instant même" for extra emphasis, or "juste à l'instant" = "just just now".
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas : je dois partir à l'instant.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t: I have to leave right away.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone/something is within an enclosed place (inside a building, room, box, etc.). Often used to answer questions like « Et à l'intérieur ? » (“And inside?”) or « Qu’y a-t-il à l'intérieur ? » (“What’s inside?”). Can also be used more abstractly to mean “inside (it)” / “on the inside,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Il fait froid dehors, je reste à l'intérieur.
native_language_example: It’s cold outside, I’m staying indoors.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is located within an enclosed space, object, or defined area. Often more formal or precise than "dans", and common in instructions, signs, and descriptive writing. Typically followed by a noun phrase (e.g., "à l'intérieur de la maison") or a pronoun (e.g., "à l'intérieur de ça").
target_language_example: Il fait chaud à l'intérieur de la voiture.
native_language_example: It’s warm inside the car.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically at school or is attending school. With verbs of movement it can mean “to school” (Je vais à l’école = I’m going to school). With a person (envoyer quelqu’un à l’école), it means “to send someone to school.”
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, les enfants sont à l'école.
native_language_example: Today, the kids are at school.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is listening attentively or ready to receive information. Common in radio/TV: « Restez à l'écoute » = “Stay tuned.” With « être à l'écoute de + [source/person] » it means “to be listening to” or “to be attentive to” (e.g., a station, a person).
target_language_example: Restez à l'écoute, on revient après la pub.
native_language_example: Stay tuned, we’ll be back after the ads.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (aller, emmener, suivre une route) to mean going to the church building (destination). It can also mean being/meeting at church (location), depending on context.
target_language_example: Je travaille le dimanche, mais ma famille va à l'église.
native_language_example: I work on Sundays, but my family goes to church.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a past period being talked about (often implying “in those days,” compared to now). It can be placed at the end of the sentence or used alone to correct a time reference: « Pas à l'époque. » = “Not back then / Not at the time.”
target_language_example: À l'époque, on n'avait pas de smartphones.
native_language_example: Back then, we didn’t have smartphones.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located on a higher floor in a building. Often answers “Où ?” (Where?) and can be used alone as a short reply: « À l'étage. »
target_language_example: Les toilettes sont à l'étage.
native_language_example: The toilets are upstairs.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like être/vivre/travailler/partir to say someone is (living/working/going) abroad. It can also describe where something was bought: acheté à l'étranger = bought abroad. Often implies “outside one’s home country” without specifying which country.
target_language_example: Elle travaille à l'étranger depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: She has been working abroad for two years.

meaning: (to) keep an eye on (someone/something); (have something) in your eye.
additional_notes: In expressions like « Je t’ai à l’œil » / « Je l’ai à l’œil », it means “I’m watching you/it” (often with a warning or suspicious tone). In questions like « Qu’est-ce que tu as à l’œil ? » / « T’as quoi à l’œil ? », it can literally mean something is in/with your eye (e.g., irritation, a speck).
target_language_example: Je t’ai à l'œil, alors ne fais pas de bêtises.
native_language_example: I’m keeping an eye on you, so don’t do anything stupid.

additional_notes: Usually just the preposition à + the feminine singular article la. Its exact meaning depends on the verb and context: often "to the," "at the," or sometimes "about the." Unlike à + le, it does not contract further (à + le = au, but à + la stays à la). In other contexts, à la can also mean "in the style of."
target_language_example: Nous allons à la gare maintenant.
native_language_example: We're going to the station now.

meaning: at the bank; to the bank.
additional_notes: “À” can indicate location (“at”) or destination (“to”), depending on the verb/context: Je suis à la banque (I’m at the bank) vs. se rendre/aller à la banque (to go to the bank). It can also be used as a short answer to say where you’re going: « À la banque. »
target_language_example: Je dois aller à la banque cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I have to go to the bank this afternoon.

meaning: at the bar (the witness stand / the ship’s helm / the ballet barre).
additional_notes: Used in several common contexts: (1) In court, "à la barre" means at the witness stand (the place where someone is called to testify): "à la barre des témoins". (2) On a ship (or by extension in sci‑fi/aviation), it can mean at the helm/in control (the person steering or piloting): "à la barre !" can be an order meaning “to the controls!” (3) In dance, "la barre" is the handrail used for warm-ups, so "danse à la barre" refers to barre work.
target_language_example: Le témoin est appelé à la barre.
native_language_example: The witness is called to the stand.

meaning: at the base / back at base; at the root (fundamental).
additional_notes: Used literally for a physical base (often a military base or headquarters): «à la base» = “at base,” and «à la base de …» = “at the base of …”. It can also be figurative to mean “at the root of / underlying,” referring to the fundamental cause or foundation of something.
target_language_example: Je reste à la base pendant que vous partez en mission.
native_language_example: I’m staying back at base while you go on the mission.

meaning: (to sleep) outdoors, under the open sky; under the stars.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like dormir or passer la nuit to mean sleeping outside without a roof (no tent/room), literally “under the beautiful star.” Often suggests camping out, sleeping rough, or an improvised night outside.
target_language_example: On n'avait pas de tente, alors on a dormi à la belle étoile.
native_language_example: We didn’t have a tent, so we slept under the stars.

meaning: at the library; to the library.
additional_notes: Uses the preposition "à" with the definite article "la" to mean being at a place or going to a place. With verbs of movement like "aller" or "se rendre", it often means "to the library"; with verbs describing location or activity like "étudier" or "travailler", it often means "at the library".
target_language_example: Je vais à la bibliothèque après le cours.
native_language_example: I'm going to the library after class.

meaning: in the countryside; in a rural area.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like vivre, habiter, aller, passer des vacances to say someone is in (or going to) the countryside. Opposite idea: à la ville (in the city).
target_language_example: On va passer le week-end à la campagne.
native_language_example: We're going to spend the weekend in the countryside.

meaning: in the cellar / in the basement; (going) down to the basement.
additional_notes: Used to say something is located in the cellar/basement (e.g., wine storage), or as a short answer to indicate where something/someone is. It can also be used jokingly/figuratively to mean putting someone “out of the way” or hidden/neglected (e.g., « On va quand même pas mettre maman à la cave ! »).
target_language_example: Les valises sont à la cave.
native_language_example: The suitcases are in the basement.

additional_notes: Very informal and insulting. Used after a noun to mean “stupid/dumb” (un truc à la con, un boulot à la con), or after “raison” to mean a silly/pointless reason (une raison à la con). Avoid in polite situations; safer alternatives: « bête », « idiot », « stupide », « nul ».
target_language_example: On a perdu du temps à cause d'une règle à la con.
native_language_example: We wasted time because of a stupid rule.

meaning: on/using a rope; (in « sauter à la corde ») jump rope.
additional_notes: Used with verbs to show an action done with a rope: « monter à la corde » = to climb up a rope; « s’accrocher à la corde » = to hold on to the rope; « sauter à la corde » is the set phrase for playing jump rope.
target_language_example: Les enfants font un concours pour voir qui peut sauter à la corde le plus longtemps.
native_language_example: The kids are having a contest to see who can jump rope the longest.

meaning: at the last minute; at the very last moment.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens very late, just before a deadline or just before it’s too late. Often implies it was rushed, unexpected, or done without much time to prepare. Can describe plans made late or changes/discoveries made right before something happens ("À la dernière minute, ...").
target_language_example: On a réservé l’hôtel à la dernière minute.
native_language_example: We booked the hotel at the last minute.

additional_notes: "Fac" is short for "la faculté" and is common in everyday speech. Used with verbs like "aller" (to go), "être" (to be), "étudier" (to study) to talk about being at or going to university (often implying a university campus or studies).
target_language_example: Je suis à la fac aujourd'hui, mais je rentre tôt.
native_language_example: I'm at university today, but I'm coming home early.

meaning: at the end; in the end; finally.
additional_notes: Often refers to the end of something specific: à la fin du film/de la semaine/de la phrase (“at the end of the movie/week/sentence”). Without “de + noun,” it can also mean “in the end/finally” (the final outcome): Pierre perdra à la fin (“Pierre will lose in the end”). You can also use it to mean “right at the very end” with juste/tout: juste à la fin, tout à la fin.
target_language_example: On se verra à la fin du cours.
native_language_example: We’ll see each other at the end of the class.

meaning: at the end of the month.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the last days of a month. It can mean the end of the current month (from context), or you can specify which month: « à la fin du mois de novembre » (at the end of November). Often used with deadlines or planned events.
target_language_example: Je te paierai à la fin du mois.
native_language_example: I’ll pay you at the end of the month.

additional_notes: Used to say two qualities or ideas are true simultaneously: «à la fois A et B» = “both A and B.” It can also mean “one at a time” in instructions like «Un/Une … à la fois» (only one at a time).
target_language_example: Je suis à la fois fatigué et content de te voir.
native_language_example: I’m both tired and happy to see you.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like être, aller, rester, venir, passer du temps to say someone is/was/goes/stays/comes at a party (fête = party/celebration). Often contrasts with "en fête" (= in a festive mood/celebrating).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la fête ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we meeting up at the party tonight?

additional_notes: "à" can mean either "at" (location) or "to" (destination), depending on the verb and context. Common with travel verbs like "aller / se rendre à la gare" (to go to the station), "arriver à la gare" (to arrive at the station), and with requests like "me déposer / me conduire à la gare" (drop me off / drive me to the station).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la gare à 8 heures.
native_language_example: We'll meet at the train station at 8 o'clock.

additional_notes: Used to locate an event in the context of a war or military conflict (e.g., being injured, dying, taking risks). With verbs of going (aller), it can mean “to go to war.” In games, jouer à la guerre means “to play war” (play at war/war games).
target_language_example: Mon grand-père a été prisonnier à la guerre.
native_language_example: My grandfather was a prisoner in the war.

meaning: up to it; up to the task; good enough; able to meet expectations.
additional_notes: Often used with être: « être à la hauteur (de ...) » = to be capable of meeting a standard, responsibility, or challenge (« être à la hauteur de la situation / du travail »). Very common in the negative (« je ne suis pas à la hauteur » = I'm not up to it). Can describe people or things (skills, performance, results).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, tu es à la hauteur.
native_language_example: Don't worry, you're up to it.

additional_notes: Means something is done quickly, often too quickly and without much care (which can lead to mistakes). Common with verbs like écrire, partir, prendre (un repas), reposer (le téléphone), etc.
target_language_example: J'ai préparé ma valise à la hâte avant de partir.
native_language_example: I packed my suitcase in a hurry before leaving.

additional_notes: Means doing or following something with complete precision, without changing anything. Common with verbs like « suivre » (suivre les règles/consignes/conseils à la lettre). Depending on context it can mean “literally/word for word” or “to the letter” (exactly).
target_language_example: Il a appliqué les instructions à la lettre.
native_language_example: He followed the instructions exactly.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the facts, context, or information you are taking into account before making a decision or conclusion. Often followed by a noun phrase (à la lumière de ces résultats) or a clause with "ce que" (à la lumière de ce que tu as dit). Common in formal or written French.
target_language_example: À la lumière de ces informations, on va changer de plan.
native_language_example: In light of this information, we're going to change plans.

additional_notes: Most often used with "prendre" ("prendre [qqch] à la légère") to mean treating something as unimportant, without enough care or seriousness. Often said as a warning or reproach: "Ne prends pas ça à la légère."
target_language_example: On ne peut pas prendre la sécurité à la légère.
native_language_example: You can't take safety lightly.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe holding something (un bâton à la main = “a stick in his hand”). Also used with verbs like faire/laver/écrire to mean doing something manually, not with a machine (tout fait à la main). With avoir, it means you have something on you / readily available (Je les ai à la main = “I’ve got them right here”).
target_language_example: J’ai mon téléphone à la main, mais je peux le ranger.
native_language_example: I have my phone in my hand, but I can put it away.

additional_notes: Literally means 'at the house', but in everyday French it usually means 'at home'. After movement verbs like aller or rentrer, it often means 'home' ('go home', 'come home').
target_language_example: Ce soir, je reste à la maison.
native_language_example: I'm staying home tonight.

meaning: 'at home for' (a purpose, a deadline time, or an event).
additional_notes: Used with (1) an infinitive to express purpose: « à la maison pour me reposer » (“at home to rest”); (2) a time/deadline: « à la maison pour minuit » (“home by midnight”); or (3) an occasion: « à la maison pour Noël » (“home for Christmas”). With verbs like « rentrer », it often means “go/come back home for…”.
target_language_example: Je suis à la maison pour travailler au calme.
native_language_example: I'm at home to work in peace.

meaning: to the sea; at/by the seaside.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of going or staying (aller/rester/passer des vacances) to mean spending time at the seaside. In some contexts it can be literal (“into the sea”), especially with verbs like jeter (“throw”).
target_language_example: Dimanche, on va à la mer si le temps est beau.
native_language_example: On Sunday, we’re going to the seaside if the weather is nice.

meaning: at the mercy of; dependent on (and vulnerable to).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something has no control and is exposed to another person, situation, or force (often with a negative idea). Usually followed by a noun or pronoun: « à la merci de quelqu’un / de la météo / des circonstances ».
target_language_example: Sans argent, ils sont à la merci de leur propriétaire.
native_language_example: Without money, they’re at the mercy of their landlord.

meaning: made to order; prepared on the spot (fresh).
additional_notes: Common in restaurant/cooking contexts to say a dish is prepared right when you order it, not in advance. It can look like it means “at the last minute” or “to the minute,” but here it means freshly cooked/prepared immediately.
target_language_example: Le poisson est préparé à la minute.
native_language_example: The fish is made to order (prepared on the spot).

additional_notes: Used after a noun (or with “être”) to say something is trendy or currently popular: “une chanteuse à la mode” (a fashionable/trendy singer), “Les jeans sont à la mode” (Jeans are in style). Can also mean “in the fashion/style of …” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ces chaussures sont vraiment à la mode cette année.
native_language_example: These shoes are really in style this year.

meaning: "to death" / "from life to death"; also "at the death of" (à la mort de…).
additional_notes: Used with verbs to indicate being close to dying or the idea of death: « échapper à la mort » (escape death), « penser à la mort au combat » (think about death in battle), « de la vie à la mort » (from life to death). With « à la mort de + [person] », it means “at/after the death of …” (i.e., when someone died).
target_language_example: Il a frôlé la catastrophe et a échappé à la mort.
native_language_example: He narrowly avoided disaster and escaped death.

additional_notes: Used to say that you cross or travel through water by swimming (e.g., traverser un lac/une rivière/la Manche à la nage). Often follows verbs like "traverser" (to cross).
target_language_example: On peut rejoindre l’île à la nage si la mer est calme.
native_language_example: You can reach the island by swimming if the sea is calm.

meaning: on page (number); up to date/in the know.
additional_notes: Most commonly used with books: « à la page 10 » = “to page 10 / on page 10.” In « mettre quelqu’un à la page », it means “to bring someone up to date” (give them the latest information).
target_language_example: On est à la page 25 ; vous pouvez lire le premier paragraphe.
native_language_example: We’re on page 25; you can read the first paragraph.

additional_notes: Used after a verb to emphasize that something is done extremely well (e.g., "parler à la perfection"). Often used with verbs like aller/être (for clothes: "ça te va à la perfection" = it suits you perfectly), réussir, maîtriser, connaître, etc. Means "in a perfect way," not "in perfection" as a place.
target_language_example: Tu as préparé ce plat à la perfection.
native_language_example: You cooked this dish to perfection.

additional_notes: Used to talk about replacing one thing with another: Je viens lundi à la place. = “I’ll come Monday instead.” You can also specify what it replaces with de: à la place de Paul = “in Paul’s place / instead of Paul.” It can be literal (“in the spot where something else should be”) or figurative (une pierre à la place du cœur = “a heart of stone”).
target_language_example: On peut prendre le bus à la place du métro.
native_language_example: We can take the bus instead of the subway.

additional_notes: Used to talk about replacing/substituting one person or thing with another: « X est allé à la place de Y » = X went in Y’s place. Often followed by a noun or stressed pronoun (moi, toi, lui/elle, nous, vous, eux/elles): « à la place de lui ». Don’t confuse with « à ta place » (without de), which can mean “if I were you.”
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un thé à la place de mon café.
native_language_example: I’m going to have a tea instead of my coffee.

meaning: to the beach; at the beach.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (aller, se rendre) to mean “to the beach,” and with activities/being somewhere to mean “at the beach.” The preposition “à” commonly indicates a destination or location.
target_language_example: On va à la plage cet après-midi.
native_language_example: We're going to the beach this afternoon.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like dire (to tell), avouer (to confess), rapporter (to report), remettre (to hand over) to indicate the police are the recipient. "Police" is feminine singular in French, so you say "la police" (not *le police*).
target_language_example: On a signalé le vol à la police.
native_language_example: They reported the theft to the police.

meaning: at the door; (be) at the door/entrance.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like être/se tenir (to be/stand) to say someone is at the door, and with frapper to mean knocking at the door. Often refers to the entrance of a room/house.
target_language_example: Il y a quelqu’un à la porte.
native_language_example: There’s someone at the door.

meaning: within reach of; accessible to; achievable by.
additional_notes: Used to say something is easy enough or available for a person/group. Often followed by a noun or pronoun like « tous », « tout le monde », « n’importe qui » (e.g., « à la portée de tous » = accessible to everyone). Can be literal (physically within reach) or figurative (within someone’s abilities/budget).
target_language_example: Avec un peu d’entraînement, ce niveau est à la portée de la plupart des débutants.
native_language_example: With a bit of practice, this level is within reach of most beginners.

meaning: first thing (in the morning); very early.
additional_notes: Used to mean as early as possible, typically at the start of the day (often with demain / demain matin). It can sound a bit formal or businesslike (deadlines, appointments).
target_language_example: Je vous appelle à la première heure demain matin.
native_language_example: I’ll call you first thing tomorrow morning.

meaning: at the next (one): election, station, time, etc.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the next occurrence of something, often followed by a noun: à la prochaine station (next station), à la prochaine élection (next election), à la prochaine intersection (next intersection), à la prochaine occasion (next opportunity). It agrees with a feminine noun (la); with a masculine noun you’d use: au prochain (e.g., au prochain arrêt = at the next stop).
target_language_example: À la prochaine station, descendez du train.
native_language_example: At the next station, get off the train.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like aller/partir (“to go/leave”) to talk about the activity of fishing: aller à la pêche = “to go fishing.” It’s also used in expressions like être à la pêche (“to be out fishing”).
target_language_example: On va à la pêche demain matin ?
native_language_example: Are we going fishing tomorrow morning?

meaning: 'to the question' (used with verbs like répondre / answer).
additional_notes: Often used after verbs that take the preposition "à", especially "répondre à" (to answer) and in phrases like "la réponse à la question" (the answer to the question). In French you say "répondre à une question" (literally, respond to a question), not *répondre une question*.
target_language_example: Je vais répondre à la question maintenant.
native_language_example: I’m going to answer the question now.

meaning: on the radio; on/through the radio (broadcast).
additional_notes: Used to say something is heard, said, or broadcast via radio. Common with verbs like entendre (to hear), écouter (to listen to), passer (to be played/air), parler (to talk about). With people or programs it often means “on air” (e.g., Je vous ai entendu à la radio = I heard you on the radio). Not the same as "dans la radio".
target_language_example: J'ai appris la nouvelle à la radio en allant au travail.
native_language_example: I heard the news on the radio on my way to work.

additional_notes: Expression meaning being or going in search of something. Common after être (Je suis à la recherche de…) and with verbs of movement/action (partir, aller, retourner…) to mean going in search of something. Typically followed by a noun phrase or pronoun. Note contractions: de + le → du, de + les → des; but de + un/une does not contract (de un → d’un; de une → d’une).
target_language_example: Je suis à la recherche de un appartement près du métro.
native_language_example: I'm looking for an apartment near the metro.

additional_notes: Used with être to mean “to be retired” (Mon père est à la retraite) and with partir/prendre to mean “to retire” (Je suis parti à la retraite / Il a pris sa retraite). It can also be used alone as a short label or answer (e.g., on a form or in conversation: À la retraite.).
target_language_example: Depuis 2020, ma tante est à la retraite.
native_language_example: Since 2020, my aunt has been retired.

meaning: homeless; out on the street (kicked out/with nowhere to live).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone has ended up with no place to live: «se retrouver à la rue» (to end up homeless) or «jeter/mettre quelqu’un à la rue» (to throw/kick someone out). In other contexts, «à la rue» can also be literal (“to the street”), but when talking about people it usually implies being left without housing. Colloquial register.
target_language_example: S’il perd son travail, il risque de se retrouver à la rue.
native_language_example: If he loses his job, he might end up on the street.

meaning: at the meeting; to the meeting.
additional_notes: Means being present at a meeting ("at") or going/heading there ("to"), depending on the verb: être/absent à la réunion (to be at/absent from the meeting), aller/se rendre/assister à la réunion (to go to/attend the meeting).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la réunion à 14 h.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the meeting at 2 p.m.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition « à » + « la » (often contracted to « au » with masculine nouns). With « être/rester », it usually means being at the event (location/time): « rester à la soirée » = to stay at the party. With verbs like « inviter », « aller », « participer », it often means going/being invited/participating in the event: « inviter quelqu’un à la soirée » = to invite someone to the party.
target_language_example: Je vais aller à la soirée avec des amis.
native_language_example: I’m going to the party with some friends.

meaning: at the station; to the station.
additional_notes: Means being located at a station (at the station) or going there (to the station), depending on the verb and context. Often used for meeting points (se rencontrer à la station) or drop-offs (me déposer à la station). Can be followed by a type or name: à la station de métro / à la station Ueno.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la station à 18 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at the station at 6 p.m.?

meaning: to temptation (in phrases like “resist/give in to temptation”).
additional_notes: Used after verbs that take the preposition à, especially: résister à la tentation (to resist temptation) and céder à la tentation (to give in to temptation). Also appears in the biblical phrase: « Ne nous conduis pas à la tentation » (“Lead us not into temptation”).
target_language_example: J’ai réussi à résister à la tentation d’acheter quelque chose.
native_language_example: I managed to resist the temptation to buy something.

meaning: 1) (toast) “Cheers!” 2) “to yours” (referring to a feminine noun: your life/opinion/etc.).
additional_notes:
Two common uses:
- As a toast, short for “À ta santé !” (literally “to your health”). You can also hear “À la vôtre !” (more formal/plural).
- In comparisons, “à la tienne” means “to yours” where “la” replaces a previously mentioned feminine noun: “ma vie… à la tienne” = “my life… compared to yours.” For a masculine noun you’d say “au tien”/“au tien(ne)” depending on the noun.
target_language_example: À la tienne ! On se revoit bientôt.
native_language_example: Cheers! See you soon.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is falling behind in progress, level, or results: *être à la traîne* (in school, technology, sports, etc.). It can also refer to the back/rear of a group or line (e.g., “Don’t leave anyone behind” / “Watch the back”). Often contrasts with *en avance* (ahead).
target_language_example: En informatique, notre entreprise est un peu à la traîne.
native_language_example: In IT, our company is a bit behind.

meaning: hard at work; working hard (especially in « être dur à la tâche »).
additional_notes: Often used in set expressions: « être dur(e) à la tâche » = to be hardworking / a hard worker. With verbs like « se tuer à la tâche », it means working yourself too hard (overworking). Refers to effort and persistence rather than a specific “task.”
target_language_example: Il est dur à la tâche, mais il faut aussi qu’il se repose.
native_language_example: He’s a hard worker, but he also needs to rest.

additional_notes: Used to say something is broadcast or seen on television. Very common in speech; “télé” is short for “télévision.” Often with verbs like voir (to see), regarder (to watch), passer (to be shown/broadcast).
target_language_example: On a regardé le match à la télé hier soir.
native_language_example: We watched the game on TV last night.

additional_notes: Used to say something is broadcast or watched via television. Common with verbs like parler (to speak), voir/regarder (to see/watch), passer (to be shown/appear), and with nouns like une émission (a show) or un match (a game).
target_language_example: On regarde les infos à la télévision tous les soirs.
native_language_example: We watch the news on TV every evening.

meaning: to/on the head; at the head (of), in charge.
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to the body part: *blessé à la tête* (injured in the head), *un coup à la tête* (a blow to the head), *des pieds à la tête* (from head to toe), *monter à la tête* (go to your head, e.g., alcohol). With **être à la tête (de)** it means being the leader/in charge of something (*à la tête de l’entreprise*).
target_language_example: Elle est à la tête de l’équipe depuis 2023.
native_language_example: She has been in charge of the team since 2023.

meaning: on the front page; in the headlines (top story).
additional_notes: Used mainly in news/media contexts. With **être à la une** = “to be in the headlines / front-page news.” With **mettre à la une** = “to feature as the top story.” (La « une » is the front page of a newspaper, or the main headline/story.)
target_language_example: Ce scandale est à la une des journaux aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: This scandal is in the headlines today.

additional_notes: Used in set expressions like « revenir à la vie » / « ramener quelqu’un à la vie » (“to come back to life” / “to bring someone back to life”). Also appears after adjectives like « nécessaire/indispensable à la vie » (“necessary/essential for life”), often with a qualifier: « à la vie moderne » (“for modern life”).
target_language_example: Après l’accident, il est revenu à la vie.
native_language_example: After the accident, he came back to life.

meaning: at the sight of; when (someone) sees.
additional_notes: Used to describe a reaction triggered by seeing something. Often follows a verb expressing an emotion or change (rire, pleurer, être effrayé, se mettre à...). Can be used at the start of a sentence: « À la vue de..., ... ».
target_language_example: À la vue des nuages noirs, ils ont décidé de rentrer.
native_language_example: At the sight of the dark clouds, they decided to go back home.

meaning: (1) “to yours” (referring to something feminine, like an opinion) (2) “cheers!” (a toast).
additional_notes: Literally “to yours.” In ordinary sentences it uses the possessive pronoun *la vôtre* (“yours,” feminine singular): *mon opinion… contraire à la vôtre* = “my opinion… opposite to yours.” Very commonly used on its own as a toast when drinking: *À la vôtre !* = “Cheers!” (also said as *À la tienne !* to one person informally, or *À votre santé !*).
target_language_example: On trinque ? À la vôtre !
native_language_example: Shall we toast? Cheers!

meaning: "to do it" (after a verb that takes "à").
additional_notes: Used when a verb is followed by "à" + infinitive, and "le" stands for “it” (a thing/action already mentioned). Common patterns include: "forcer quelqu’un à le faire" (force someone to do it), "hésiter à le faire" (hesitate to do it), and "avoir à le faire" (have to do it).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas le faire, mais je vais devoir à le faire.
native_language_example: I don’t want to do it, but I’m going to have to do it.

additional_notes: Most commonly used in two ways: (1) after an adjective, it means “to read / readable” (e.g., facile à lire = easy to read). (2) after a noun/quantity, it means “(something) to read” or “left to read” (e.g., trois pages à lire = three pages to read). Not to confuse with the verb phrase “arriver/parvenir à lire” = “manage to read.”
target_language_example: J'ai un article à lire ce soir.
native_language_example: I have an article to read tonight.

meaning: in the long term; over the long run.
additional_notes: Used to talk about long-range time horizons and lasting effects (plans, projects, investments, outcomes). Often contrasts with "à court terme" (in the short term). Can modify a verb ("ça marchera à long terme") or a noun ("un projet à long terme").
target_language_example: À long terme, j’aimerais acheter une maison.
native_language_example: In the long term, I’d like to buy a house.

additional_notes: Common in ads and on signs (like “Appartement à louer”). It uses “à + infinitive” to describe something that is available for an action (compare: “à vendre” = for sale).
target_language_example: Appartement à louer, disponible dès avril.
native_language_example: Apartment for rent, available starting in April.

meaning: “to the” / “at the” (contraction of « à + le » before a vowel sound).
additional_notes: « à l’ » is used before a masculine singular noun that starts with a vowel or silent h: « à l’intérieur », « à l’horizon », « à l’ère ». It can express location (at), direction (to), or more abstract links like giving priority: « donner la priorité à l’engagement ». (Feminine « à la » does not contract.)
target_language_example: On se retrouve à l’entrée du musée.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the entrance of the museum.

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take an indirect object introduced by « à » (e.g., parler à, expliquer à, promettre à, demander à). It marks the person you’re speaking to or doing something for: « à ma femme » = “to my wife.”
target_language_example: Je vais téléphoner à ma femme ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to call my wife tonight.

meaning: "to my mother" / "for my mother"; with "être à": "(belonging) to my mother."
additional_notes: Most often used after a verb like parler à (talk to), demander à (ask), donner à (give). With the structure "être à + person", it means something belongs to that person: « Il est à ma mère » = « It belongs to my mother ».
target_language_example: J’ai donné les clés à ma mère.
native_language_example: I gave the keys to my mother.

meaning: in my place; if you were me.
additional_notes: Used either literally (returning to your seat/spot) or figuratively (put yourself in my situation, do something instead of me). Often appears with verbs like « se mettre à ma place » (put yourself in my shoes) and in questions like « Qu’est-ce que tu ferais à ma place ? » (What would you do if you were me?). You can change the possessive: « à ta place » (in your place), « à sa place » (in his/her place), « à notre/votre/leur place ».
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que tu ferais à ma place ?
native_language_example: What would you do if you were me?

additional_notes: Used after verbs like répondre (to answer), usually in répondre à + [question]. In French you answer *to* a question (répondre à une question), not “answer a question” directly.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous répondre à ma question, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you answer my question, please?

additional_notes: Uses the preposition « à » with an indirect object (often after verbs like « parler à » = to talk to). It can also mark a relationship or link to someone, as in « fiancé à ma sœur » (engaged to my sister). « Ma sœur » means “my sister” (feminine singular).
target_language_example: J’ai envoyé un message à ma sœur.
native_language_example: I sent a message to my sister.

additional_notes: Used mainly in legal/news contexts to describe a crime committed while the person has a weapon (often a gun or knife). Common collocations: « vol à main armée » (armed robbery), « agression à main armée » (armed assault). Placed after the noun it modifies: « un vol à main armée ».
target_language_example: Ils ont été arrêtés pour cambriolage à main armée.
native_language_example: They were arrested for armed burglary.

additional_notes: Used for doing something without tools or weapons (literally “with naked hands”). Common with verbs like attraper (catch), tuer (kill), se battre / combat (fight). Can also describe a type of fighting: un combat à mains nues = a bare-knuckle/hand-to-hand fight.
target_language_example: Il a attrapé le serpent à mains nues.
native_language_example: He caught the snake with his bare hands.

additional_notes: Often refers to food in a general way: apporter à manger = “bring something to eat.” Very common in the expression donner à manger à [quelqu’un/animal] = “to feed [someone/animal]” (literally “to give to eat”).
target_language_example: Tu as quelque chose à manger ?
native_language_example: Do you have something to eat?

meaning: to tell me; to say to me.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive after a noun/pronoun (often with **avoir + quelque chose/rien/autre chose + à + infinitive**) to express what someone has to tell you. Common in questions: **Qu’as-tu à me dire ?** = “What do you have to tell me?”; **Tu as autre chose à me dire ?** = “Do you have anything else to tell me?” The pronoun **me** changes with the person (e.g., **à te dire**, **à lui dire**).
target_language_example: Tu as autre chose à me dire ?
native_language_example: Do you have anything else to tell me?

additional_notes: Means something is going extremely well or fits/works perfectly. Common with verbs like aller (Ça va à merveille.), se sentir (Je me sens à merveille.), s’entendre (Nous nous entendons à merveille.), and aller avec (This goes perfectly with that). Can be used alone as a short positive answer (À merveille, merci.).
target_language_example: Tout s’est passé à merveille.
native_language_example: Everything went wonderfully.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being in the middle point of a route, journey, or process. Common with verbs like être (to be) and se rencontrer (to meet): se rencontrer à mi-chemin = “to meet halfway” (often meaning each person travels part of the way, or figuratively to compromise).
target_language_example: On peut se retrouver à mi-chemin, devant la gare.
native_language_example: We can meet halfway, in front of the station.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens at 12:00 in the daytime. In everyday speech, especially in France, "à midi" can also mean "at lunchtime" (the midday meal), depending on context.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à midi devant le café.
native_language_example: Let's meet at noon in front of the café.

additional_notes: Literally means "to me." It's used after verbs and expressions like penser à moi = "think about me" or venir à moi = "come to me." With être, it often means possession: c'est à moi = "it's mine." After a noun, it can mean "of mine": un ami à moi = "a friend of mine."
target_language_example: Ce sac est à moi.
native_language_example: This bag is mine.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition that must be met for something to be true. It’s typically followed by an infinitive (à moins de + verb: « À moins de partir maintenant… ») or by « que » + subjunctive (à moins que + subjunctive: « À moins qu’il ne pleuve… »).
target_language_example: On ira se promener, à moins de la pluie.
native_language_example: We’ll go for a walk, unless it rains.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an exception or condition that would prevent something. It’s followed by the subjunctive (e.g., « à moins que tu aies… »). You often see « ne » after it (« à moins que tu ne… »); this is a stylistic/optional “ne explétif” and does not make the sentence negative.
target_language_example: On peut se voir demain, à moins que tu ne sois trop fatigué(e).
native_language_example: We can see each other tomorrow, unless you’re too tired.

additional_notes: Used to say something is only partly the case (often with an adjective: à moitié pourrie, à moitié aveugle) or done only half-heartedly/incompletely (s'entraîner à moitié). You can also use it with a noun to mean “half of” something: à moitié prix (“half price”).
target_language_example: Je suis à moitié prêt : donne-moi cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I'm halfway ready—give me five minutes.

additional_notes: Used in ads and shopping to say something is discounted by half: «Tout est à moitié prix.» You can also use it for reduced fares/prices for certain groups: «Les écoliers sont à moitié prix.» Often follows the noun («des chaussures à moitié prix») or is used with «être» («c’est / c’est à moitié prix»).
target_language_example: J’ai acheté ce manteau à moitié prix.
native_language_example: I bought this coat for half price.

additional_notes: A very common, compositional combination of the preposition à + mon ('my' before a masculine singular noun). The exact English translation depends on context: direction ('to my apartment'), location or setting ('at my place'), speaking to someone ('to my lawyer'), and fixed expressions like à mon tour ('my turn') or à mon rythme ('at my pace').
target_language_example: Je vais à mon bureau maintenant.
native_language_example: I'm going to my office now.
